title: America's Nuclear Revival Is Running Into a Fuel Supply Wall | OilPrice.com
description:
The Trump administration has been bullish about restoring the country’s nuclear energy sector to its former glory, but growing the country’s nuclear energy capacity raises a new problem – where to source the nuclear fuel to power it.
The geopolitical risks inherent to current nuclear fuel supply chains represent a key and growing concern.
The world’s nuclear energy fuel supply chains are extremely geopolitically fraught.
The country is indeed getting closer to establishing nuclear fuel independence – but it still has a long way to go.
At present, a whopping 93 percent of the United States’ raw uranium for nuclear fuel is coming from foreign markets.
text:
The United States boasts the largest nuclear power production capacity in the world, but decades of insufficient funding and policy support is now posing an existential threat to the ageing sector. In the past decade, the United States has added just one new nuclear power plant to its fleet, while many more plants are drawing close to being decommissioned, at a time when clean, round-the-clock energy production has never been more needed. The Trump administration has been bullish about restoring the country’s nuclear energy sector to its former glory, but growing the country’s nuclear energy capacity raises a new problem – where to source the nuclear fuel to power it.

Countries around the world are racing to build up nuclear power capacity as the artificial intelligence boom places unprecedented strain on global power supplies, the war in Iran sustains volatility in oil and gas markets, and decarbonization deadlines draw nearer. As a result, competition over scarce enriched uranium supplies has ramped up at a rapid pace. As a result, U.S. nuclear energy now “faces fuel supply chain vulnerabilities, with tight uranium supplies, geopolitical risks, and rising costs,” threatening both existing reactors and advanced reactor development, according to a January report from Stanford Energy.

The geopolitical risks inherent to current nuclear fuel supply chains represent a key and growing concern. The world’s nuclear energy fuel supply chains are extremely geopolitically fraught. At present, just five plants in the entire world operate large-scale uranium conversion, and nearly half of global enrichment capacity is controlled by Russia. And if Russia decides to cut the United States off, or vice versa, the alternative could be even worse.

“The West needs more converted uranium than it can process, and cutting off Russian supply could leave its reactors dependent on a single Chinese facility,” an article from the National Interest warned earlier this week.

ADVERTISEMENT

In recent years, leadership in the United States has made considerable inroads toward building up domestic uranium production and conversion capabilities, as it has benefited from being one of the rare forms of energy supported by both the Trump and Biden administrations. Just last month, the National Enrichment Facility, located in Eunice, New Mexico, announced that its planned expansion is ahead of schedule and on budget. Currently, the singular plant converts enough uranium to cover about one-third of U.S. enriched uranium demand, with plans to raise enrichment output by more than 50 percent to reach 7 million separative work units (SWUs) as reactor demand grows.

The country is indeed getting closer to establishing nuclear fuel independence – but it still has a long way to go. And in today’s geopolitical climate, no one knows just how much time we have before a supply chain snag could cause the next global energy crisis. At present, a whopping 93 percent of the United States’ raw uranium for nuclear fuel is coming from foreign markets. If those supply chains dry up, it won’t matter how much uranium the country is capable of enriching.

And the issue is not limited to the United States alone, but to Western nuclear power markets in general. “To keep the lights on in the West every year, the nuclear reactor fleet requires approximately 44,000 metric tons of uranium feedstock. Western supply lines [including the United States, Canada, and France] are estimated to have processing capability of just 34,000 metric tons when fully operational,” the National Interest details. “Traditionally, reactors have relied on Russian or Chinese fuel producers to make up the shortfall, but as global trade corridors constrict and relationships become contentious, over-reliance on Russian or Chinese nuclear fuel could represent a serious national security risk.”

By Haley Zaremba for Oilprice.com

title: Opposition to AI data centers in the midterms foreshadows tougher regulations ahead - PBS

text:
HARRISBURG, Pa. (AP) — After a campaign season filled with outrage against artificial intelligence data centers, the midterm elections ushered in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.

A tougher regulatory environment for AI giants and data center developers is expected to follow, even if President Donald Trump — perhaps the industry's biggest champion — stalls any federal crackdown.

Data center regulation itself was not on most midterm ballots, and it wasn't among the top issues for most voters. But hard-line stances against the server warehouses were woven into the platforms of many candidates, including the Democrats who upended longtime Republican control of the governorships in Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Nevada and Iowa, many of which are data center hot spots.

Skepticism of data centers, and their impact on electricity prices, often blended with the fight for affordability — a key campaign talking point for Democrats.

In Texas, Clayton Tucker, the first Democrat elected state agriculture commissioner since 1986, said his pledge to fight data center development was critical to his victory. Everywhere he went, he said, ranchers worried that data centers posed an existential threat to their dwindling water supplies.

"You know, there's an old saying around here that 'whiskey's for drinking and water's for fighting,'" Tucker told The Associated Press. "And that's exactly what happened."

Data centers were a persistent bogeyman in attack ads

According to data from AdImpact, campaigns large and small spent more than $380 million on television ads mentioning data centers. Democrats outspent Republicans on the topic by a more than 3-to-1 ratio.

Sweeping wins by Democrats could have far-reaching implications for data centers. Besides taking control of Congress, Democrats flipped at least five governors' offices and took full control of state governments in five more states: Wisconsin, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Nevada and Michigan.

Data Center Watch, a project of AI security consultancy 10a Labs, said it tracked winning candidates for Congress and governorships and found the vast majority had expressed support for stronger regulation or even a moratorium.

Among governors, 32 of the 34 victorious candidates in races where AP called a winner support stronger regulation or restrictions. Twelve of the 34 support bans or moratoriums, it said.

During the campaign, Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley, a Democrat, changed his position under pressure from his Republican opponent to take a harder line against data centers. Initially opposed to any moratorium, Crowley later said he supported one as well as abolishing the state's sales tax exemption for data center operators and developers.

In an interview Thursday with AP, Crowley said he's having discussions now about what he'll propose once he takes office.

In the mix are things like requiring developers to disclose more about their water and energy consumption, ensuring a community supports a project before it can go forward and insulating ratepayers and taxpayers from the energy costs of the projects, Crowley said.

The industry sees a need to build trust

AI giant OpenAI published a framework Thursday enumerating new commitments to the communities where it develops data centers. The company said it was asking federal, state and local policymakers to write "clear rules for how the industry builds."

"Lawmakers should establish rules to advance responsible investment, protect residents, and ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared," the post said.

An industry association, the Data Center Coalition, echoed the sentiment that developers need to keep trying to build trust with public officials and communities. A coalition official, Dan Diorio, said the industry is aware many midterm winners have vowed to impose a moratorium.

"We should expect them to want to deliver on those promises, but there are going to be real world consequences of that," Diorio said in an interview.

Those consequences, Diorio said, could include host communities missing out on tax revenue or payments from tech companies. Data centers are also driving a broader economic expansion that encourages investment in domestic manufacturing, he said.

Wall Street sees red lights ahead after the election

The election of data center skeptics adds challenges to stock markets riding high on the AI boom.

On Thursday, the Nasdaq, which is full of AI-related and other tech stocks, sank 11% below its all-time high amid worries that data center construction may slow because it's getting costlier to borrow money.

AI data center construction is driving much of the U.S. economy's growth, and any slowdown could have a broader chilling effect.

In an analyst report, Morgan Stanley said decisive results for Democrats carry "greater expectations for data center restrictions" that, under new state regulations, could "split the country into areas that are open to new data centers and those without."

It singled out Texas' election of Democrat Gina Hinojosa for governor as the "most important election result" for data center development. Hinojosa has said she'd block a permit for a data center if it wasn't a good deal for Texans or residents hadn't gotten a say in the matter. She defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who had touted Texas as "the epicenter of AI development" before trying to clamp down on it late in the campaign.

Morgan Stanley also said Ohio's election of Democrat Dr. Amy Acton as governor "creates significant risk of data center project delays in the state." Acton has pledged to block a data center project unless it meets certain standards.

Local elections didn't go well for data centers, either

Voters in local referendums cast ballots overwhelmingly in favor of restricting data centers, according to an analysis by polling and data science firm Redbud Consulting.

Redbud tracked 47 referendums in 44 municipalities in 12 states, including 21 in Ohio alone, eight in Maine, seven in Illinois and four in Kansas. Restrictions were approved in 44 of the 45 elections where counting was complete, Redbud reported.

Most voters don't want a data center built near them

About three-quarters of U.S. voters oppose the construction of a new data center in their community, according to The AP Voter Poll.

In red and blue states alike, majorities of voters were opposed to adding a data center where they live.

Support was higher in some traditionally red states, including Wyoming, West Virginia, Louisiana and Mississippi. In Texas, voters in the Senate race were similarly likely to say they oppose a new data center being built in their community.

Despite voters' deep opposition to data centers near them, The AP Voter Poll suggests it was not a particularly motivating issue in this election.

About one-quarter of U.S. voters said AI data centers were "crucial" to their vote for Congress, which is well below the shares that said government corruption or the cost of living were highly important to their vote.

The stakes were especially high in Texas

Texas is poised to overtake northern Virginia as the largest global data center market by 2030, according to a report by commercial real estate giant JLL.

In the campaign, Hinojosa aggressively attacked Abbott as having rolled out the welcome mat for data centers.

Stephen Sanders, a Republican who co-founded a data center protest group in Lubbock, said Texans were especially attuned to the issue because of talk that data centers pose a threat to their electricity and water in the drought-stricken state.

"I would say data centers were on the ballot," Sanders said.

Associated Press reporters Scott Bauer in Madison, Wisconsin, Kaitlyn Huamani in Los Angeles and Linley Sanders in Washington contributed to this report.

name: Congress
title: Clear the grid backlog and lower Vermont's power bills - VTDigger
description:
There’s a new bipartisan bill in Congress that will significantly reduce emissions, speed up clean energy and lower energy costs for us here in Vermont.
Much of the energy capacity stuck in interconnection queues comes from clean energy projects.
Several solar developers in Vermont have told me they’ve found it difficult to get clean energy projects connected to the grid.
Reforming the process will help America build and connect clean energy much faster while preserving bedrock environmental laws.
More abundant, affordable electricity will help lower energy costs for households and businesses.
text:
This commentary is by Alex Messinger, co-leader of the Vermont chapter of Citizens’ Climate Lobby.

There’s a new bipartisan bill in Congress that will significantly reduce emissions, speed up clean energy and lower energy costs for us here in Vermont.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is a comprehensive package of permitting reforms that was recently introduced in the Senate. Climate champions Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., and Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., were at the forefront of bipartisan negotiations, ensuring the final product advances climate goals and supports clean energy while maintaining important environmental safeguards.

The Senate is set to take up the bill in November, and I am urging Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Peter Welch, D-Vt., to support it with a “yes” vote. I encourage my fellow Vermonters to do the same.

This bill matters to Vermont residents like me because it will lead to significant emissions reductions, which are necessary to address climate change. The bill contains strong transmission provisions that can help unlock the enormous amount of clean energy waiting to connect to the grid.

And there’s lots of clean energy waiting to come online. Much of the energy capacity stuck in interconnection queues comes from clean energy projects. Several solar developers in Vermont have told me they’ve found it difficult to get clean energy projects connected to the grid. Reforming the process will help America build and connect clean energy much faster while preserving bedrock environmental laws.

More abundant, affordable electricity will help lower energy costs for households and businesses. According to analysis by the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions, transmission and interconnection reforms like those before Congress would reduce Americans’ residential electricity bills by $19 billion through 2040.

We need these changes in Vermont. Since 2019, average monthly residential bills in the state have risen from $97.25 to $135 in 2026, a 39% increase. One reason for this increase is the need to bolster the electricity grid against stronger storms caused by climate change.

It may be helpful to compare this bill with the cost of doing nothing. Climate impacts are accelerating, and we can’t wait for the next Congress to put forth a better bill. Since the bill requires 60 votes in the Senate to advance, now is our best chance. Passing this bill will speed the clean energy transition, while reducing costs for all of us.

I’m proud that Sanders and Welch have been longstanding advocates for weatherization and energy retrofits, which have helped thousands of Vermonters reduce energy bills while addressing climate change.

But Congress must go further. It needs to act now by passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

title: BAAJA Blast Part 4: Plugging In – Distributed Energy Resources and Virtual Power Plants ...

text:
This is the fourth and final post in our four-part “BAAJA Blast” series covering the proposed Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, released on September 30, 2026. Check out our earlier posts on the bill’s provisions on transmission, offshore wind, and data centers and large loads.

A note on timing. We close out this series in a very different political climate than the one in which we began it. This week’s midterm elections, which handed Democrats control of both congressional chambers starting in January 2027, have called this legislation’s future into question. Will BAAJA disappear into the ether during the lame-duck session? We can’t say for sure. Some House Democrats, including the member in line to chair the House Natural Resources Committee, argue that Democrats could write a better bill next Congress; the bill’s sponsors and major industry groups, on the other hand, are pushing to finish the job this year, and the November 9 Senate cloture vote should be the first real test of whether they can. Come what may, we close out our BAAJA Blast series today with our observations on the bill’s treatment of DERs and VPPs.

On September 30, 2026, Senate negotiators released the text of the proposed Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (“BAAJA”). For distributed energy resources (“DERs”) and virtual power plants (“VPPs”), the bill comes at a critical moment. Aggregators (which we call “VPP providers” here) increasingly bundle behind-the-meter resources—which continue to proliferate year-over-year—into VPPs that sell services back to the grid. Yet six years after the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) issued Order No. 2222, several grid operators have yet to fully comply, and VPPs have begun striking deals directly with buyers.

As we have written before, AI-driven load growth is creating immense pressure to activate the demand side of the grid, and deploying VPPs is among the fastest ways to unlock new capacity. If enacted, BAAJA would replace the tariff-by-tariff process under Order No. 2222 with a statutory deadline: Section 2108 would require grid operators to admit qualifying aggregations into their wholesale markets within 18 months, limit utility interference, bar double payment, and fund a voluntary program to streamline local permitting for rooftop solar, batteries, and EV chargers. In our view, Section 2108 would likely get aggregations through the market door faster than Order No. 2222 has; whether it makes operating VPPs in the wholesale markets a durable business, however, would depend on questions the bill leaves to grid operators and states.

Our data center post previewed Section 2108’s basic market-access rule. In this post, we take a closer look at the provision as a whole, even as we note that the bill itself still faces significant hurdles. A Senate cloture vote on the motion to proceed is expected as early as November 9; passage would require 60 votes, and any Senate bill would have to be reconciled with the House’s permitting legislation before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027. A promised manager’s amendment could change the text. And again, with this week’s midterm elections turning control over Congress to the Democrats come January 2027, the fate of the bill is even less certain.

What Counts as a DER Under BAAJA

DERs are small generation, storage, or load-management assets on the distribution system, such as rooftop solar, batteries, EV chargers, and smart thermostats. A VPP is a group of DERs that a VPP provider controls through software to act like a single power plant.

Industry observers will be familiar with both these concepts; BAAJA, however, uses neither term. Section 2108, titled “Dispatchable energy systems market access,” instead defines a “qualifying behind-the-meter distributed energy system facility” (a “qualifying BTM DES facility”). The facility must be an energy storage system, fuel cell, generator, or “other resource” that can be brought online within 15 minutes and whose output the grid operator can dispatch on signal. It must sit behind a retail customer’s meter, have a rated capacity of at least 5 kilowatts, and have metering and telemetry sufficient to dispatch and settle it. That equipment need not be owned or installed by the utility and may include device-level equipment such as inverters. A “qualifying BTM DES aggregation” is two or more such facilities with a combined capacity of at least 100 kilowatts.

Points to Watch: The dispatchability test is a question many VPP businesses already grapple with in assembling their aggregations. Standalone rooftop solar would not appear to qualify unless paired with storage. Less clear is whether controllable load, such as a network of smart thermostats, counts as an “other resource” whose “output” can be dispatched. In our view, the better reading is that flexible load able to respond within 15 minutes would qualify, but the text does not say so expressly, and the question could surface in the first round of compliance filings. Separately, the definition includes generators with no emissions condition, so on-site gas units could qualify. This language is worth watching in the promised manager’s amendment.

Wholesale Market Access (New FPA Section 229)

Section 2108 would add a new Section 229 to the Federal Power Act, the foundational statute establishing federal jurisdiction over interstate transmission and wholesale power sales. Beginning 18 months after enactment, it would not be “just and reasonable” (the legal standard FERC uses to evaluate the legality of jurisdictional rates) for any Regional Transmission Organization (“RTO”) or Independent System Operator (“ISO”) to maintain rules that prevent a qualifying aggregation from participating in its energy, capacity, or ancillary services markets.

The bill would also declare three specific practices unjust and unreasonable: imposing metering, telemetry, or equipment requirements beyond the statutory definitions; requiring participation in the energy market as a precondition to participation in the capacity market; and requiring a facility to participate jointly with a co-located resource in order to join an aggregation. Each RTO and ISO would have to file compliant market rules within 180 days of enactment, and FERC would have 180 days to approve them or impose changes. FERC would also have to act on complaints alleging noncompliance within 180 days.

Section 2108 is best understood as a legislative fix for Order No. 2222, under which three barriers have persisted: costly metering requirements, unclear rules for resources earning revenue in both state programs and wholesale markets, and distribution utilities’ control over interconnection. Section 2108 would address each directly, though it reaches only behind-the-meter resources, and its fixed deadline would leave far less room for grid operator stakeholder-process delay.

Point to Watch: Compliance filings would be due at 180 days, but the market-access standard would not take effect until 18 months, and it does not depend on a new FERC rulemaking, making it less exposed to the missed-deadline risk that hangs over other provisions. But access is not the same as value. The economics of market participation would turn on details the bill leaves to grid operators, especially how much capacity credit aggregations receive. If accreditation methods discount aggregated resources heavily, aggregations could win market entry and still find margins too thin to justify participating. We expect capacity accreditation to become the main battleground once the access question is settled.

Dual Participation, Not Double Payment

Many DERs already earn money from state programs, such as net metering or a utility demand response program. Section 2108 would let them keep doing so: participation in a state program would not disqualify a facility from wholesale markets, and nothing would require a facility to enter wholesale markets at all. What the bill would bar is “double compensation,” meaning payment from both a wholesale market and a state program for the same service in the same time interval.

Within 180 days, each RTO and ISO would have to file settlement rules that exclude, service by service, any quantity already compensated under a state program. The bill’s own example illustrates the approach: a battery that earns retail credit for energy, but not for capacity or ancillary services, could still earn wholesale capacity and ancillary services revenue, just not wholesale energy revenue. Distribution utilities would have to supply the interval metering and program-participation data needed to make this work, subject to state customer-privacy protections.

VPP providers would carry much of the compliance burden. Each would have to certify which state programs paid each facility and that no double compensation was retained, and those certifications would be treated as statements to FERC for enforcement purposes. FERC would have to order disgorgement of any double compensation and, if it was knowingly retained, could impose penalties of up to three times the amount per day and suspend or terminate participation. Participants would also file public annual reports, due each March 30.

Point to Watch: The enforcement framework cuts both ways for VPP providers. A complainant would bear the burden of proving double compensation occurred or is imminent and could not be avoided through reasonable billing adjustments, and complaints would be limited to five years. But VPP providers should expect to invest in settlement tracking and data systems well before market access takes effect. On balance, we think the framework is workable, but compliance costs and treble-penalty exposure could weigh more heavily on smaller providers.

Distribution Utility Obligations (New FPA Section 230)

Section 2108 would also add a new Section 230 targeting distribution-level obstacles that have kept DERs out of wholesale markets. Within an RTO or ISO footprint, distribution utilities would have to interconnect wholesale-eligible behind-the-meter resources in a timely way, allow them to export, accept the same metering and telemetry data the wholesale market uses, and not use their control of the distribution system or retail sales to block or unreasonably condition market participation. Actions reasonably necessary for safety and reliability would remain permitted. FERC would enforce these obligations and would have to act on complaints within 180 days.

The provision includes significant limits. The interconnection obligation would yield to state law, and FERC would gain no authority over distribution-level interconnection rates or terms. State regulators would decide how wholesale metering data adjusts retail bills. For public power utilities and certain cooperatives, the requirements would be voluntary unless state law requires them. And qualifying a facility would not, by itself, bring it or its retail or distribution service under FERC jurisdiction. In practice, the utility obligations would operate more as a federal default than a guarantee.

Points to Watch:

State regulators would be in the driver’s seat. Because the utility obligations yield to state law, state commissions, such as the New York Public Service Commission for NYISO-area resources, would largely determine how much of the distribution-side benefit reaches aggregations. We expect the provision to work best in states already pushing VPP policy, where the federal default would reinforce existing direction, and least in states whose utilities have resisted aggregation. Developers should track state proceedings as closely as FERC compliance filings.

Data access. VPPs depend on utility distribution data to verify performance and get paid in full. The bill’s data-sharing requirement would help, but it is among the provisions most likely to be honored in form and slow-walked in practice, and its effectiveness would depend on grid operator formats and schedules, state privacy rules, and how quickly FERC acts on complaints.

Beyond Market Access: Local Permitting and Storage

Most rooftop solar, building batteries, and campus microgrids need only local permits, so the bill’s federal environmental review reforms would largely bypass them. Section 2108(e) instead would have the Department of Energy (“DOE”) stand up, within 180 days, a program supporting voluntary, streamlined local permitting and inspection for solar, batteries of at least 2 kilowatt-hours, EV chargers of at least 2 kilowatts, and hydrogen refueling, including an expanded online platform, technical assistance, and possible certification and prizes for participating jurisdictions. The bill would authorize $20 million per year for fiscal years 2026 through 2031.

Other provisions would ease siting for storage. Adding energy storage at or near an existing transmission or distribution facility would be categorically excluded from review under the National Environmental Policy Act (“NEPA”) and Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, as would reconductoring, which we discussed in our transmission post. The Departments of the Interior and Agriculture would also have to adopt categorical exclusions for batteries on previously disturbed land and for small solar installations on federal property.

Point to Watch: The DOE program would be voluntary for local governments, and its funding would be authorized, not appropriated. At $20 million a year, it is modest relative to the number of permitting jurisdictions nationwide. We see it as a useful nudge toward standardized, faster local permitting rather than a fix, and its impact would depend on whether Congress funds it and how many jurisdictions sign on.

Looking Ahead

For VPP providers and device makers, Section 2108 would offer guaranteed RTO and ISO market access, fewer utility equipment requirements, and a firm deadline, along with real compliance obligations. Building owners could gain a new revenue stream from dispatchable equipment. Utilities would take on new interconnection and data-sharing duties, tempered by state authority. Customers outside RTO and ISO regions, including much of the Southeast and West, would see less direct benefit. An open question is whether the provision ultimately favors storage paired with clean generation or opens a new path for behind-the-meter gas.

So, would it work? We think that, if enacted, Section 2108 would deliver on market access: the deadline would be firm, the standard would be self-executing, and the prohibited practices target the barriers that have stalled Order No. 2222.

It is less likely, on its own, to make VPPs a mainstream grid resource. That outcome would depend on capacity accreditation, on how states use their room to displace the utility obligations, and on whether the dispatchability test is read to include flexible load. Aggregators, device makers, and building owners should expect compliance filings, accreditation proceedings, and state dockets to be where the practical value of Section 2108 is decided, and should plan their engagement accordingly.

This concludes our BAAJA Blast series; thank you for following along. We will continue to track the bill’s progress and its implications for developers, investors, and other market participants.

text:
OLYMPIA – Washington’s sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) industry has unlocked a new tax credit that will attract investment and meet growing demand for locally produced jet fuel, Governor Bob Ferguson announced today.

Governor Ferguson speaking at Cascadia Sustainable Aviation Accelerator in January 2026

The new tax credit gives Washington the strongest set of sustainable aviation fuel incentives in the country. Washington’s tax credit offers $1 per gallon for jet fuels that generate at least 50% lower greenhouse gas emissions compared to conventional jet fuel and up to $2 for fuels with even lower emissions. Washington’s industry recently reached the milestone needed to unlock this credit — the ability to produce at least 20 million gallons of sustainable aviation fuel annually in Washington. The Department of Ecology confirmed this week that this threshold had been met.

“Aerospace has long been a cornerstone of Washington’s economy, supporting generations of good-paying jobs and driving innovation across our state,” said Governor Ferguson. “It’s also in our DNA to make big bets on bold ideas, which is what we’re doing with sustainable aviation fuels. Between our long history of aviation innovation, our intentional investments into the sector and our climate-forward policies, we’re making sure Washington is the best state in the country to produce sustainable aviation fuels.”

“Washington is leading the way by investing in clean technologies and lowering emissions,” said Casey Sixkiller, Ecology’s director. “This tax credit will support our state’s aerospace industry and put us in the pilot’s seat for the future of aviation. It’s good for the climate and for business.”

Washington has made major investments in the SAF industry over the last two years. State funding is helping to build SkyNRG’s new production facility in Walla Walla and establish Washington State University as a global leader in sustainable aviation fuel research. The state also funded the formation of the Cascadia Sustainable Aviation Accelerator, which carries out research and streamlines access to infrastructure, energy, partners, and financial capital.

"Sustainable aviation fuel works today,” said Jake Gentry, Executive Director of the Cascadia Sustainable Aviation Accelerator. “The challenge has been making it affordable at commercial scale, and this credit goes a long way toward closing that cost gap. Washington state built the aviation industry, and this type of investment positions us to lead in the next chapter of sustainable aviation. We thank the Governor, Ecology and the Legislature for their leadership.”

Thanks to state investment and incentives, several new sustainable aviation fuel startups have recently built factories in the state or are considering doing so. In June, Governor Ferguson joined sustainable aviation fuel startup Twelve to celebrate the opening of the company’s one-of-a-kind facility in Moses Lake that combines carbon dioxide with water and clean electricity to make fuel.

Alaska Airlines Managing Director of Sustainability, Ryan Spies:

"As a longtime industry leader in advancing sustainable aviation fuel, Alaska Airlines knows SAF is the best technology available today to meaningfully reduce aviation’s carbon emissions. Washington’s position as a global aerospace leader, combined with strong partnerships across industry, academia and government, makes the state uniquely positioned to lead in SAF, and policies like the SAF tax credit can help accelerate production and adoption while supporting clean energy jobs and economic growth. We appreciate the leadership of Governor Ferguson and state lawmakers in advancing this important work and remain committed to working together to ensure these policies achieve our shared objectives."

Boeing Vice President of Sustainability, Allison Melia:

"Sustainable aviation fuel is one of the most powerful levers to reduce aviation emissions - cutting lifecycle carbon by up to 80% versus conventional jet fuel - and the alternative jet fuels tax credit is a critical step to scale SAF here in Washington. text:
It is often said that elections have consequences. And that couldn’t be truer when it comes to the defining challenge of our time—the climate crisis.

The blue tsunami in the midterm elections swept Democrats to power in both houses of congress, key governorships, and state houses. Although inflation and the cost of fuel were at the top of voters’ minds, bipartisan concern over data centers—driven by fears of soaring electricity rates, heavy water consumption, and increased reliance on fossil-fuel energy—helped power victories for democratic candidates, underscoring the role that energy and climate played in the election.

After being urged to stay quiet about climate while campaigning, I hope that Democrats will recognize the unprecedented opportunity this provides for re-engaging on climate action, making it a central feature of their legislative agenda as they take power early next year. After all, actions speak louder than words.

Democrats have a clear mandate from the voters, if they can connect the dots for the public. Voters made it clear that affordability and government corruption were the defining issues for them. But as popular political figures like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani recognize, the climate crisis is an affordability issue.

The affordability crisis is being driven by higher energy prices, which propagate through the entire economy, raising the costs of most goods and services. Those higher prices, as I’ve discussed elsewhere, were a consequence of the corrupt policies of the Trump administration and enabled by the rubber stamp of a Republican congress—policies which I presaged would follow from a second Trump presidency as it sought to implement Project 2025.

Foremost among those policies were Trump’s tariffs. He sought to boost the fossil fuel industry by penalizing renewable energy, such as solar panels from China, while using trade threats to force foreign nations to buy American energy. Meanwhile, sweeping tariffs on foreign steel and aluminum inflated the cost of energy infrastructure. Ultimately, these supply chain strains—combined with retaliatory foreign tariffs—further drove up energy prices.

Then there’s Trump’s assault on domestic renewable energy. The administration has systematically targeted the renewable energy sector by halting major offshore wind projects, clawing back billions in federal clean energy funding, and eliminating key tax credits in an aggressive effort to favor the fossil fuel industry. By taking the least expensive sources of energy out of the mix available to consumers, Trump has further driven up energy costs.

And we haven’t even mentioned the impact of extreme weather events, made more frequent and more damaging by human-caused warming, that destroy infrastructure, kill crops, and disrupt supply chains and distribution systems, further driving up prices. A recent UN report found that Trump’s dismantling of US climate policy, including his withdrawal from the Paris agreement, noticeably bumped up planetary warming by an additional 0.1 degrees Celsius. That might sound like a small amount, but as I told the AP, it would shave about $1.2 trillion from the global economy.

Last but certainly not least is Trump’s misguided war of choice against Iran that, despite an ever-shifting list of supposed reasons, was ultimately about maintaining access to Middle Eastern fossil fuels. The war drove up energy prices for all of us but increased profits for American fossil fuel companies—something he misguidedly chose to boast of in the waning days of the election.

Our fragile fossil fuel-based economy leaves us exposed to volatility and conflict, making an urgent, accelerated transition to renewable energy essential for both economic stability and planetary survival. The ongoing conflict involving Iran under the Trump administration exemplifies the deep vulnerabilities and geopolitical dangers of global reliance on fossil fuels. Cutting funding for the senseless ongoing war on Iran would be a critical first step for the new congress.

But what can they do legislatively? Trump after all, wields veto power for ostensibly two more years.

Quite a lot, actually. Jake Bittle of Grist, for example, argues that newly empowered Democrats now have leverage to counter the Trump administration’s attempts to roll back federal climate regulations and can use budget oversight to compel federal agencies to release clean energy funding.

This will require true leadership. And if the senior institutionalists, like presumptive Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries, aren’t up to the challenge, they should move aside and let others step forward.

I think they might find some willing colleagues in the freshman class. Consider, for example, William Lawrence, part of a new generation of younger, and more environmentally conscious progressives. Lawrence was co-founder of the climate activist group known as the Sunrise Movement. He prevailed in a razor’s-edge House of Representatives race in central Michigan, ousting incumbent Republican Tom Barrett in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District. Lawrence made opposition to data centers a focal point of his campaign. He has called for a national moratorium on data centers.

There are many reasons that people oppose data centers. There are concerns over massive electricity and water consumption that drive up local utility bills, the chronic noise and air pollution from operations and backup generators, minimal creation of permanent local jobs, and broader skepticism toward the artificial intelligence boom. And of course, there is concern about the increasing carbon footprint and climate impact that comes with them. Opposition to the rapid growth of data centers is one of the few issues in modern American political history that unites citizens across the political spectrum. According to USA Today, “Data centers were on the ballot across the nation. They got crushed.”

A November 2026 national survey by USC Annenberg revealed that 77 percent of Americans believe the government is doing too little to regulate data centers. That’s miracle level bipartisan appeal. The only other things in America that garner that level of public support are Tom Hanks and a moratorium on robocalls.

A data center regulation bill could be the gateway to a broader climate and energy legislative agenda in the new congress. Democrats, however, would need to deal with the problematic Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) bill currently under consideration, a bill that is highly problematic from a climate and environmental standpoint because it guts foundational environmental laws to fast-track and “lock in” major fossil fuel infrastructure and gas-powered AI data centers.

Hakeem Jeffries has already signaled a bit more willingness to fight the BAAJA bill since the midterms results came rolling in.

Democrats could instead “pirate” BAAJA’s most popular ratepayer protection mechanisms while aggressively stripping out or replacing the environmental rollbacks, as they prepare the prospective new data center bill.

They could use fast-track parliamentary rules immediately after the new Congress convenes on January 3 to get the prospective new data center bill placed on Donald Trump’s desk by the second week of January. Dare him to veto it. And dare Republicans to sustain the veto if he does.

We’ve already lost two critical years under Trump and GOP congressional control, and when it comes to delay, the climate crisis is most unforgiving.

There is no time to waste. So how about it, Dems?

title: Russia's Nuclear Offerings to Africa Are Attractive. That's Why the US Needs to Step Up ASAP

While floating nuclear reactors are a different technology, the underlying procurement risks still apply.
text:
Russia announced nuclear energy initiatives with at least six African countries at last week’s summit in Moscow. Its state-owned Rosatom is reportedly in advanced talks with Egypt, Togo, Namibia, and Tanzania about floating nuclear power plants, seeking to become the world’s first commercial exporter of this technology. During the summit, Russia also signed a cooperation agreement with Ghana aiming to eventually construct a 2,000 megawatt (MW) nuclear plant.

Nuclear power is attractive because African countries need more clean, firm power to meet industrialization ambitions and create jobs. We score eight African countries as ready (or nearly so) for nuclear power. Another 14 could be ready by 2050.

Package Deals Beat Complex a la Carte Projects

Russia offers nuclear packages of technology alongside state-backed financing and operating support. Russia has also trained many of the continent’s nuclear engineers. Meanwhile, Western governments have long been ambivalent about supporting nuclear tech abroad, while its private companies — many of which are still startups — are themselves struggling with financing and regulatory hurdles.

The conclusion for African leaders is thus understandable: the Russian option is far easier (and closer to delivery) than the multiple uncertainties of choosing a Western design. The flurry of summit deals shows how far Russia is ahead — and why the United States needs to get its act together ASAP.

Russia’s Nuclear Relationships Could Shape African Energy for Decades

Unlike most power infrastructure, nuclear plants operate for 80-100 years and can tie countries to foreign suppliers for decades through fuel contracts, maintenance, technical support, and spent fuel management. These relationships can create commercial, strategic, and security dependencies that create vulnerabilities — and are difficult to undo. Rosatom has signed cooperation and construction agreements with at least 20 African countries. Egypt is building Russian reactors at El Dabaa, and will soon be the second nuclear-powered country on the continent.

In comparison, the United States has had limited nuclear engagement in the continent. Though the Trump administration has directed officials to pursue at least 20 new 123 Agreements (which permits US nuclear exports) by the end of his term, Morocco is the only African country with an active 123. South Africa’s 123 Agreement expired in December 2022.

Floating Plants Have a Poor Track Record in Africa

Ship-based nuclear reactors might be especially tempting because they can be pre-built and delivered quickly to coastal grids. For the Russians, they’re also attractive because they can sail away if the country doesn’t pay — or does something Moscow does not like. The prospect of sudden removal of a sizable portion of a country’s power system provides Russia with tremendous geopolitical leverage.

Africa’s experience with floating power plants has also been mixed. Several countries have contracted Karpowership, a Turkish company operating floating fossil fuel power plants, to address emergency shortages, only to face high electricity costs and long-term payment obligations. While floating nuclear reactors are a different technology, the underlying procurement risks still apply. Without competitive bidding, regulatory oversight, time-bound contracts, contract disclosure, and careful assessment of long-term obligations, emergency power solutions can create expensive dependencies.

Announcements Are Not Power Plants

The new agreements demonstrate interest, not necessarily construction commitments. Russia’s proposed 2,000 MW plant in Ghana equals more than one third of Ghana’s current installed capacity. Integrating a project of this scale would require substantial grid upgrades and long-term energy planning. (A general rule of thumb is that no one power plant should be more than 10% of national capacity to prevent dependence on a single facility.) And it’s far from clear who would pay for that much power over many decades, creating massive debt risks for a country that has just resolved its last debt crisis (in part created by massive energy sector debts).

Russia has signed similar oversized agreements with other African economies. Some countries are also signing agreements well before establishing the necessary institutions or regulatory requirements of the International Atomic Energy Agency. So the summit announcements should be seen not as the end of the game, but as a warning sign to the West.

The US and Development Financiers Need to Step Up

The World Bank lifted its nuclear ban only in June 2025 and is still finding its feet. (The Asian and Inter-American Development Banks followed suit, but the African Development Bank has not yet). The World Bank, as a first step, could help African countries build the necessary foundations for nuclear deployment, including setting up relevant commissions, providing technical assistance, and especially helping design open competitive procurement. Concessional financing for nuclear construction will be needed soon, too.

The United States can play its part by supporting the World Bank nuclear trust fund. A $2 million down payment was recently announced by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, but more will be needed. Other agencies can actively support workforce training, regulatory capacity, and feasibility studies. Most importantly, competing with Russia’s state-backed construction packages will require long-term, affordable financing.

The Development Finance Corporation lifted its own nuclear ban back in 2020, but no projects are yet close to financing. That’s why US reactor companies (both conventional and next generation) should expand their presence in Africa. Earlier this year, US-based Holtec signed a preliminary agreement with Rwanda to support the deployment of its modular technology. But this kind of contract is no match for what Russia offers.

There’s No Time to Waste in the Nuclear Race

Russia is moving quickly to establish nuclear relationships that could shape African energy systems for generations. African countries should have the capacity to evaluate these offers on their own terms, rather than choose between Russian financing and no nuclear option at all. The US and development financiers have an opportunity to provide that alternative, but only if they move beyond light-touch cooperation agreements toward credible technical support and financing. Otherwise, by the time competing offers emerge, many of Africa’s future nuclear markets may already be locked in by Moscow.

text:
To speed up operations, cut costs and incorporate clean energy into local food systems, the state has awarded roughly $450,000 to Franklin County farms.

The funding comes from the latest round of the Massachusetts Department of Agricultural Resources’ (MDAR) Climate Smart Agriculture Program. The streamlined grant application aims to help Massachusetts farmers secure the right equipment and start the right projects to get the best use out of their land, promote food safety, improve composting, incorporate clean energy and curb energy costs.

“Our farmers are keeping Massachusetts traditions alive, and we’re helping them adapt to a changing world,” Gov. Maura Healey said in a statement. “These grants will ensure Massachusetts farming families can invest in clean and efficient equipment so they can do what they do best — growing great produce, managing livestock, and keeping our communities fed and healthy.”

From surprise frosts to droughts, MDAR Commissioner Ashley Randle said farmers across the state are “on the front lines of unpredictable and extreme weather.”

“The Climate Smart Agriculture Program is about giving them the tools to adapt to those pressures,” the South Deerfield native said in a statement. “By investing in operational and infrastructure upgrades, we are helping Massachusetts farms adapt to an ever-changing environment, protect their livelihoods and continue to thrive as the backbone of our local food system that benefits us all.”

Of the 68 total farms and agricultural businesses that received a slice of the more than $2 million in grants, 11 are located in Franklin County.

Ashfield

Two Ashfield farms received grants through the Climate Smart Agriculture Grant program, those being Bear Hill Sugar Farm and Cranston’s Tree Farm.

Seth Cranston, co-owner of Cranston’s Tree Farm, said the farm received two grants: $19,034 for a reverse osmosis machine, and $22,163 for a maple vacuum and tank monitor.

“It allows us to more efficiently process sap and spend less time in the sugarhouse to get the final product, and using less energy in the process,” Cranston said of the reverse osmosis machine. “Before we had a [reverse osmosis machine], we’d go through upwards of 20 cords of wood per year; now it’s down to eight or somewhere in that range. It’s just utilizing better, more efficient ways to process the sap.”

Cooper Deane of Bear Hill Sugar Farm shared that the farm received $28,063, also for the purpose of purchasing a reverse osmosis machine.

“Our new reverse osmosis will help increase productivity by allowing us to run sap through quicker, which allows us the ability to continue collecting rather than waiting for our old machine to lower the level of our tank,” Deane said. “In return, it allows us to start boiling our concentrated sap sooner. Upgrading allows us to go from processing 1,000 gallons an hour to 1,800 gallons an hour [while] reducing energy cost.”

In the case of the maple vacuum on Cranston’s Tree Farm, Cranston said the money went toward a vacuum and a tank level monitoring system. He said the addition of the sensors makes the operation more efficient when it comes to wood management, and the farm operators can view the level of the tank on their phones instead of manually checking.

Deane said these grants are important for Franklin County and the surrounding counties, as programs like it support the future of farming. Cranston added that with the price of new equipment being as high as it is, grant programs such as the Climate Smart Agriculture Program make it possible for farms to operate with updated equipment, without needing to spend an arm and a leg.

“I’m glad that the opportunity is out there, that MDAR is able to get together and provide these grants in Massachusetts to farmers statewide,” Cranston said, “to allow us to stay in business, to further our ability to make more efficient decisions and ultimately keeping farms viable in the state.”

Deerfield

Three Deerfield farms earned grants, including Clarkdale Fruit Farms, which received $23,760 to install 25.97 kilowatts of solar panels on the roof of the barn beside the cold storage room.

“The sun is always shining. It just makes a lot more sense than fossil fuels,” said Ben Clark, the fourth-generation owner of Clarkdale Fruit Farms. Plus, as the source of energy for the farm, “It’s going to pay for itself,” he said.

Clark said he is thankful for the state’s support. He described the grant as an acknowledgment from State House officials that investing in farms not only means supporting the scenic views, but the farmers who are fighting food insecurity. From Rachel’s Table to Stone Soup Café and the Food Bank of Western Massachusetts, Clarkdale Fruit Farms contributes to local organizations that are dedicated to feeding locals who need it most.

“We’re trying to do our part,” he said.

Across town, the state provided $50,000 for Atlas Farm to buy and install a new walk-in cooler to help the farm control the temperature of its products and reduce spoilage and the risk of contamination, according to the state’s announcement. The farm also earned $39,200 for a no-till drill to improve soil health on the farm’s fields.

The Yazwinski Farm Partnership also received $50,000 for a similar no-till drill.

Leyden

With $50,000 from the state program, Bree-Z-Knoll Farm plans to buy a manure spreader. According to the state’s announcement, the new equipment should improve the management of manure and nutrients, and protect the farm’s soil and water while boosting efficiency.

Orange

The Farm School Inc., a nonprofit educational agriculture organization, used a $6,960 reimbursement grant to purchase a compost screener to sift out larger items from unfinished compost meant for garden beds.

“It will allow us to make our own potting soil for the greenhouse,” said Patrick Connors, the organization’s facilities and operations director. He estimated that producing its own potting soil, made up mostly of compost, will likely save The Farm School $1,500 to $2,000 per year.

Connors said any material destined for compost ages for a year before it is used. The larger components that are sifted out by the screener will be set aside to continue aging. Rocks, however, will be discarded, he said.

“This just helps us make an even better product,” Connors said of the screener.

He said applying for the state grant was a collaborative effort by people at The Farm School, which has an Athol mailing address, despite its location in Orange.

Sunderland

With its $30,654, Kitchen Garden Farm’s team plans to install solar panels.

Like Kitchen Garden Farm, Reed Farm received $30,702 to install solar panels on the roof of one of its buildings. According to the state’s announcement, the solar panels are expected to generate 17.94 kilowatts of energy at a time. The solar panels will power the farm’s refrigeration units that store poultry products, offsetting that expense, said Kat Chang, who owns the farm with her husband Peter Laznicka.

“We’ve wanted it for a while, and now it’s happening,” Chang said, “so it’s very exciting.”

The state also awarded Reed Farm another $25,480 for a manure spreader. With manure from the chickens and ducks that the couple raises being the “starting ingredient” for compost, Chang expects the new tool will ensure the compost remains “nutrition-dense.” She added that she and Laznicka “try to close that loop” of waste on the farm by composting and repurposing other leftovers from the farmers’ daily operations.

“It’s keeping that material local,” Chang said. “Otherwise, we’d be paying to truck it and it would just be more trash, instead of something that’s actually really usable.”

Chang stressed that investments in local farms branch out to benefit the entire community.

“We’re really fortunate that Massachusetts has such a dedicated agricultural department. Our small farms are what protect our land — it’s an ecological effort, it’s feeding our communities. The stronger our local food infrastructure is, the more secure food can be for the state, and that really comes down to local farms,” Chang said. “We’re so grateful to not just the state for having this kind of programming available to local farms, but also we’re lucky that in western Mass., people really understand and value local farms and local foods. … That support makes all the difference.”

Warwick

Like many other recipients, Chase Hill Farm plans to install a 25.97-kilowatt solar energy system with its $50,000 grant.

Whately

Sobieski’s River Valley Farm received $20,110 for a mulch spreader, an investment that should strengthen soil health and build climate resilience, according to the state’s announcement.

text:
This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.

The Environmental Protection Agency late last week announced it would end a 20-plus-year effort to develop methods to monitor air pollution from factory farms, effectively shuttering the agency’s stop-and-start attempts to regulate the potentially pollutant-spewing facilities under the Clean Air Act.

The announcement came just days before the midterm elections and was characterized by the agency as a long-awaited reprieve for farmers, a historically important constituency for Trump and the Republican party.

When tens of thousands of animals are packed into one place, pollution from their waste is blown from ventilation fans or emanates from giant lagoons of liquid effluent. Livestock facilities emit fine particulate matter, ammonia, nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide and volatile organic compounds, all contributing to a toxic mix. Research has shown that emissions from these operations are a major cause of air pollution, causing nearly 12,700 deaths in the United States a year.

Strictly speaking, concentrated animal feeding operations, or CAFOs, are required to get permits under the Clean Air Act and report emissions of these pollutants under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability and Act and the Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act. But through a deal crafted in tandem with the EPA and the livestock industry, they’ve been given amnesty from doing so for more than 20 years.

The arrangement goes back to the early 2000s when the agency attempted to prosecute CAFOs for exceeding limits on some of these pollutants. The industry pushed back, arguing there was no adequate way of measuring them. So the agency worked with industry groups to develop what was dubbed the Air Consent Agreement, through which the EPA granted thousands of CAFOs safe harbor from legal action in exchange for their participation in a study that was funded by the industry.

The goal of the study, the agency said, was to develop tools and models that CAFOs could use to “determine whether they emit pollutants at levels that require them to apply for permits under the CAA or submit notifications under CERCLA or EPCRA” and “produce a scientifically sound basis for measuring and estimating air emissions” from these facilities.

But since the adoption of the agreement in 2005, the agency has failed to produce any air “emissions estimating methodologies,” even prompting a 2017 report from the agency’s Office of Inspector General that faulted it for slow-walking the process.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration and Congress have also gutted reporting requirements for factory farms to report air pollutants under CERCLA, also known as the Superfund Act, and EPCRA.

“As EPA has been saying it’s proceeding with this plan, it’s been dismantling all of its own tools to regulate emissions,” said Tarah Heinzen, the legal director for the advocacy group Food & Water Watch, which has tracked the proceedings from the beginning and filed dozens of lawsuits attempting to push regulators to control pollution from CAFOs. “Now it has announced it has no intention, basically, of ever holding factory farms accountable under the Clean Air Act, either.”

In its Oct. 30 announcement, the agency noted that in the two decades since the study, known as the National Air Emissions Monitoring Study, was conducted, many farms have modernized their barns and manure systems.

“Good science requires good data, and these data are too old and too limited to support methods that farms could rely on,” said Abigale Tardif, the acting assistant administrator for the agency’s Office of Air and Radiation, in a statement. “We would rather tell farmers that plainly than issue numbers we cannot stand behind.”

Rob Brenneman, president of the National Pork Producers Council, which has long pushed for the decision, said in a statement: “This move confirms what farmers have long known: Every farm is different, and there is no one-size-fits-all model to apply to them.”

Heinzen noted that the agency’s decision simply means that this administration has no intention of regulating air emissions from CAFOs, but for now, the Clean Air Act still requires permits for facilities that exceed emissions thresholds. The amnesty granted to these facilities will no longer be in effect now that the agreement has concluded.

“There’s no EPA-issued methodology to estimate emissions,” she said. “That doesn’t mean that there aren’t good studies out there of emissions from different types of animal feeding operations that can be used.”

Heinzen pointed to California, which has models for livestock emissions that it uses to enforce its own air regulations. “We just don’t have one set of national emissions factors from EPA,” Heinzen said. “That does not absolve these factory farms from their obligation to comply with federal law.”

Still, under this administration, it’s clear air emissions from factory farms won’t be measured and monitored any time soon. “No one’s going to estimate anything,” Heinzen noted. “As EPA said in its press release, we’re certainly not about to try to enforce the law.”

The Air Compliance Agreement did not extend to methane. The U.S. livestock industry is the single-biggest source of methane in the country, but Congress effectively blocks livestock facilities from reporting methane emissions in annual spending bills.

text:
Under the new plan, industrial companies can offset their emissions by funding commercial vehicle upgrades or other mitigation efforts in other industrial facilities.

The EPA praised the county's new scheme, while one critic said it fails to require businesses to curb their own emissions in the first place — essentially it's a license to pollute.

Maricopa County's air quality is one of the worst in the country and exceeds federal limits per the Clean Air Act.

Maricopa County is a rapidly growing industrial hub and the region ranks among the worst in the country for air pollution.

But the county has no plans to stop developing. To accommodate more growth without adding to the air quality problem, the county has expanded the menu of options for developers coming online to offset their emissions. Permit seekers can now look to commercial vehicles, public transit and car manufacturers to counterbalance their own air pollution.

On Nov. 5, the Environmental Protection Agency approved the plan.

The new policy enlists industry to be part of the solution and still grow, said Kate Brophy McGee, chair of the Maricopa County Board of Supervisors and District 3 representative.

“It is an incentive for them so that they can continue to employ people, so that they can continue to operate and to do it in a manner which in effect cleans up our air,” she said.

Tackling vehicle emissions

Before large industrial facilities like power plants and manufacturers can operate, they need to seek preconstruction permits from authorities. These permits usually carry environmental regulations, such as limits on the amount of pollutants applicants can emit in accordance with the Clean Air Act.

To meet these caps, businesses can restrict their own footprint or sponsor other permit holders to tamp down on their pollution.

Maricopa County’s Air Quality Department allows companies to trade what are called emissions reduction credits, which are a company’s total allowable emissions. Those who come under the regulatory limit can sell some of their credits to those that overshoot, allowing the extra pollution from one player to be canceled out by another with emissive room to spare.

Traditionally, the county has allowed permit applicants to trade with already permitted stationary sources, funding initiatives such as installing air scrubbers in factory smokestacks or improving industrial furnaces so they have a smaller environmental burden. But these permits can be challenging to find or economically infeasible to obtain.

Now, the new air quality plan allows companies to buy credits from “mobile sources” — manufacturers and commercial owners of vehicle fleets. Initiatives that could qualify include funding efficiency upgrades to garbage trucks, replacing aging fleets of cars or the electrification of municipal buses.

Representatives of the EPA lauded the county’s plan.

“It's really a win-win,” said Michael Martucci, the EPA administrator for Region 9 that encompasses the Southwestern states, Hawaii and Pacific territories. “It allows business and industry to grow in a place where they would otherwise be restricted.”

Martucci added that industry has already expressed interest.

Is it a license to pollute?

The plan has drawn skepticism about how much it could do for the Valley’s air quality. Echoing criticisms of existing carbon-trading schemes, one expert said this program could similarly give prospective developers a license to pollute, a way of punting their carbon-curbing responsibility to other polluters.

“Providing more flexibility to trade emission credits in or near non-attainment areas is not in the best interest of air quality or public health,” said Diane Brown, executive director of the nonprofit Arizona Public Interest Research Group. “While additional funds to mitigate air quality issues can be helpful, it is far better to reduce emissions at the source versus creating a system that leads to trading.”

So, instead of polluters reining in their own emissions, they now have more flexibility to pay to make it someone else’s problem.

Residents living near the original permit holder won’t get to enjoy the air quality benefits if mitigation is outsourced to another company located elsewhere, Brown said.

She said Maricopa County needs to beef up its permitting requirements rather than letting companies get around proper caps on emissions. For starters, the county could set stricter limits on emissions for everyone.

Maricopa County is already out of compliance with the Clean Air Act. Part of the reason is topographic — Phoenix sits in a valley, where haze can accumulate as if in a sump. Local government officials have also claimed that contaminants waft in from other states and across international borders, and are out of their hands to control.

In March, the EPA chose not to upgrade the severity of the Phoenix-Mesa area’s nonattainment status from “moderate” to “serious,” where it should be according to federal standards. A “serious” label would have forced local officials to do more to cut down on pollution.

In 2026, the American Lung Association rated Maricopa County a grade of F for its ozone and particle pollution, whose levels are far higher than any other county in Arizona.

The credit trading expansion won’t exacerbate pollution levels, the EPA estimates, and potentially whittle them down in the long run. “It's meant to make sure you're still making incremental progress,” said Lisa Beckham, a supervisory environmental engineer at the EPA who worked with Maricopa County on modifying the credit plan.

Still, any concern that tighter air quality regulations might hobble economic growth means little if local communities don’t have clean air and an environment to live in, Brown said.

“Air quality and public health should not be sacrificed for the purpose of growing the economy,” she added.
