text:
SAN JUAN – New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul pledged more support for Puerto Rico on Friday as it remains mired in multiple crises, asserting during a trip to the island that the sweeping Democratic win in the U.S. midterm elections will be a boon for the U.S. territory.

“There’s a potential in that we can finally start to deliver for working-class people across this country,” Mamdani said. “What we heard today was the fact that so often what’s described as a natural crisis here in Puerto Rico is in fact a political crisis, one that is the result of political choices.”

Hochul said the election results represent “a whole new day” for Puerto Rico and warned that the federal government will be held responsible.

“What we’ve seen over the last two years is really an abandonment of that commitment," she said. "And we hope to have all those wounds heal, making sure that we continue bringing resources for resiliency, energy projects, building up the grid, as well as healthcare being restored, nutrition programs.”

Mamdani and Hochul are part of a group of New York government officials who are in Puerto Rico for a four-day, annual conference. They met with local nonprofits on Friday as officials announced a $280,000 partnership to help the island confront emergencies.

Puerto Rico struggles to emerge from crises

The partnership between Hispanic Federation and the Federal Home Loan Bank of New York comes as Puerto Rico struggles with chronic power outages and intermittent water shortages while it tries to rebuild from Hurricane Maria and other disasters.

The nonprofit Hispanic Federation said the money would equip 10 community-run resiliency hubs across the island with increased water storage capacity; some also would receive rain-collection systems, kitchen infrastructure and solar power with battery storage.

“We have to start working with the leadership to make sure that the Puerto Rico agenda is not forgotten,” Frankie Miranda, president and CEO of Hispanic Federation, told The Associated Press.

“In Puerto Rico, there are still some huge challenges," he said. “All the public policies have been so harmful to Puerto Rico.”

The announcement comes months after the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump canceled solar projects in Puerto Rico that were supposed to help thousands of low-income families. One project, worth $400 million, would have seen the installation of solar and battery storage systems in low-income homes and those with medical needs.

The U.S. Department of Energy has said the money initially slated for solar projects would instead be used to help maintain Puerto Rico’s crumbling power grid, which was razed by Hurricane Maria in September 2017. The grid, however, was already weakened given a lack of maintenance and investment.

The decisions prompted outrage on the island as federal support for solar projects fades.

Puerto Ricans sue US government

Last week, six Puerto Rico residents sued the U.S. Energy Department and its secretary, Chris Wright, following the scrapping of a $1 billion federally funded program to provide solar power and battery storage to those who most needed it.

“The cost of such systems remains out of reach for the majority of Puerto Ricans,” the lawsuit stated.

Among those suing is 63-year-old Arecibo resident Ileana Ríos, who is diabetic and needs to refrigerate her insulin. Meanwhile, her son has asthma and needs to use a nebulizer, which requires electricity.

The lawsuit noted that Ríos “regularly loses power when the weather is stable and always loses power during storms, sometimes for several weeks at a time.”

The other residents who sued also have serious health conditions and need equipment or medications that rely on electricity.

The lawsuit requests that a judge order the U.S. Energy Department to reinstate the grant program, among other things. The agency did not return a message seeking comment.

The funding loss has been a blow to nonprofits and others who faced months of uncertainty and confusion as they awaited the Trump administration’s decision on whether and how it would continue the program.

“We had a lot of uncertainty. ... At some points it just felt like we were talking to no one," said Sybelle Rodriguez del Valle, director of operations at the energy resilience nonprofit Barrio Eléctrico, which was part of the U.S. Energy Department program.

Barrio Eléctrico provides electric service to more than 500 families and was poised to provide resilient energy for 1,200 families with funds from the federal program. It had only completed about one-third of its projects before the program ended, losing an estimated $16 million to $20 million in funding.

Associated Press reporter Gabriela Aoun Angueira contributed to this report.

text:
Keller city leaders have approved a settlement regarding a proposed Westlake data center that includes nearly $1.9 million in payments and new protections for nearby residents, such as noise restrictions and environmental safeguards.

The agreement does not prevent the planned 1.1-million-square-foot project along Highway 377 in neighboring Westlake from moving forward.

The Keller City Council unanimously approved settlement terms with Circle T Owner LP and the town of Westlake. Keller's city manager finalized the agreement on the city's behalf Thursday, the city said.

The Westlake Town Council must still review and approve the settlement at an upcoming meeting.

"Keller's first responsibility has been, and will always be, to protect our residents," Keller Mayor Ross McMullin said in a news release. "Throughout this process, we have fiercely advocated for our residents - especially those living closest to the proposed data center site.

"For that reason, I'm pleased to announce that we have secured the ability to enforce meaningful protections for our residents that span even beyond our own City borders related to Westlake's data center. We will always stand up for Keller and our residents."

The full settlement terms have been made available on the city's website.

The agreement comes after homeowners in Keller's Marshall Ridge neighborhood said they were blindsided by plans for the massive data center just a few hundred feet from their properties.

Concerns about noise, environmental impacts, and the approval process led to lawsuits and a temporary court order blocking Westlake from advancing the project's development agreement. The order was later dissolved.

Residents have also agreed to settle their lawsuit.

"Per legal counsel, we have agreed to terminate our lawsuit regarding the proposed Circle T Data Center in Westlake," the Lakes at Marshall Ridge HOA Board said in an email Thursday night.

"We appreciate the City of Keller and City Council for showing up when we asked. Not only did they listen to the concerns of our community, they took action on our behalf," said Rodney Eiland, Marshall Ridge HOA board member, in the release. "Knowing our city leaders were willing to roll up their sleeves and jump in and fight means a great deal."

"Residents living near the proposed data center site have had understandable concerns about how it could impact our neighborhoods," said Mark Mathews, Lakes of Marshall Ridge HOA member. "We're grateful to Mayor McMullin and the City Council for taking those concerns seriously and working to secure meaningful protections for our community."

The dispute also strained relations between Keller and Westlake, with Westlake voting against renewing its police services contract with Keller. The existing contract runs through October 2028.

What does the settlement include?

Under the agreement, Keller would gain contractual rights to enforce certain noise, screening, and operational requirements at the site, despite its location outside Keller city limits.

According to the city, the settlement includes:

Noise restrictions: Daytime and nighttime noise limits at residential property lines, an independent baseline noise study, and quarterly monitoring for three years after operations begin.

Landscaping: A 10-foot landscaping berm to help screen the facility from nearby neighborhoods. Trees that die or sustain significant damage affecting their screening function must be replaced.

Community funding: A $1.5 million contribution for noise monitoring, environmental mitigation, and other municipal programs and services benefiting Keller residents.

Fire protection: A $300,000 contribution toward Keller Fire Rescue training, equipment, decontamination and other emergency response costs associated with the project.

Generator restrictions: Diesel-powered backup generators must incorporate EPA Tier 4 emissions controls, with generator testing limited to daytime hours.

Grading and drainage: Circle T must provide the project's grading plan, including the proposed berm and associated drainage improvements.

Legal expenses: A $76,000 payment toward Keller's attorney fees and expert consultant costs.

"The city also remains invested in continued statewide discussions and both Gov. Greg Abbott and Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa's directives regarding the demands data centers place on Texas's electric grid and water resources, including the importance of ensuring those facilities bear the costs associated with their operations," Keller city officials said in the news release.

Data centers become a political issue in Texas

The rapid expansion of AI data centers became a political challenge for Republicans ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, amid growing opposition to electricity costs, water consumption, and the impact on nearby communities.

According to Cleanview Research, 75% of data centers under construction in the U.S. and 80% of planned projects are in predominantly Republican states.

Texas leads the nation in data centers under construction. Earlier this year, Abbott directed state agencies to pause the issuance of environmental permits and new grid connections for data center projects.

The issue also became part of the Texas governor's race, in which Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Abbott on Tuesday.

President Donald Trump has supported data center development, citing its importance to economic growth and national security. But public opposition has grown, with some Republican leaders, including Abbott, taking steps to restrict new projects.

CBS News Texas will provide updates as more information becomes available.

To the Members of the United States Congress:

On behalf of the undersigned organizations, we urge Congress to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, historic comprehensive permitting reform legislation, and send it to the President’s desk as soon as possible. At a time when affordability remains a top concern for American families, there is no greater opportunity to lower costs and improve everyday life than by ensuring needed projects, investments, and other activities can move forward in a timely, predictable, and transparent manner.

Communities across the country are waiting to invest in improvements that will make everyday life better and more affordable. From critical infrastructure and communications networks to natural resource management, water, and all kinds of energy projects, these investments will lower costs, strengthen the economy, create jobs, and improve quality of life in communities across the country. Yet far too often, these improvements are delayed for years by a broken permitting process that has become overly complex, unpredictable, and inefficient.

Permitting reform is ultimately about delivering results. When needed investments are delayed, families and businesses face higher costs, longer wait times, and fewer opportunities. Communities wait longer for congestion relief, the broadband connections needed to support work, education, health care, and entrepreneurship, improved access to clean water, and the energy infrastructure needed to meet growing demand. A more efficient permitting process can help deliver these benefits sooner by reducing unnecessary delays and improving certainty while maintaining strong environmental protections and opportunities for community engagement.

Congress has a historic opportunity to modernize a system that too often delays progress and drives up costs. Americans are ready to see projects built, communities strengthened, and investments translated into real-world benefits. We cannot afford to wait any longer to enact comprehensive permitting reform, which is why we the undersigned organizations urge Congress to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 as quickly as possible.

This Cookies Privacy Notice explains how cookies and other tracking technologies are used on our websites (including mobile optimized versions of our websites) and the various social networking platforms that we use.

"Cookies" are small text files placed on your hard drive that assist us in providing a more customized website experience. Cookies are used to collect information about how visitors use our websites. If you visit a mobile optimized version of the website, we may receive data from or about the mobile phone or devices that you use to access the website, including type of device and mobile carrier. We may also capture certain "clickstream data" pertaining to your website usage. Clickstream data includes, for example, information about your computer or device, Web browser and operating system and their settings, the referring page that linked you to the website, the pages, content or ads you see or click on during your visit and when and for how long you do so, items you download, the next website you visit when you leave our website, and any search terms you have entered on the website or a referral site.

In addition, we may deploy various tracking technologies on our websites to collect additional information about your website visits. For example:

(a) HTML5 (the language some Web sites are coded in) may be used to store information on your computer or device about your website usage activities. This information can be retrieved by us to determine how our website is being used by our visitors, how it can be improved, and to customize it for our users.

(b) A pixel tag (also known as a "clear GIF" or "web beacon") is a tiny image – typically just one-pixel – that can be placed on a web page or in our electronic communications to you in order to help us measure the effectiveness of our content by, for example, counting the number of individuals who visit us online or verifying whether you've opened one of our e-mails or seen one of our websites.

These tracking technologies may be deployed by us and/or by our service providers or partners on our behalf.

Information collected on our websites through tracking technologies includes personal data, such as the IP address of the user and the device ID.

text:
The Washington-based American Biogas Council (ABC) has released new research, which states that the potential to capture energy from food waste is substantial.

Food waste produces biogas when the microorganisms in it break down the organic material, ABC says. Biogas systems capture all the biogas to keep it from going into the air and use it to generate renewable electricity and heat, or it can be processed into renewable natural gas (RNG).

ABC’s research team reports 404 operating facilities across 48 states produce biogas from food waste. About 200 of these facilities operate at farms and wastewater treatment plants and combine food waste with manure or wastewater to capture biogas. According to ABC, another 204 facilities make use of food waste alone, capturing approximately 36 billion cubic feet of biogas annually and representing nearly $3 billion in capital investment.

ABC says its expanded research uncovered projects not previously included in its inventory, showing an increase of 73 percent over last year’s count.

“America is literally throwing away enough renewable energy to power millions of homes,” says ABC Executive Director Patrick Serfass. “The technology to make energy from food waste is already operating, but the potential to turn more of what we routinely discard into a valuable domestic energy resource is enormous.”

Food waste is already producing energy

The facilities identified by ABC handle food waste from food manufacturers, grocery stores, restaurants and other sources. ABC says some capture energy from food and beverage manufacturing, and others process consumer and retail food waste, including food that spoils, is rejected or remains unsold.

Of the 204 food-waste-only facilities, 161 process preconsumer food waste, primarily wastewater from food processing and beverage manufacturing, according to ABC’s research. Another 43 facilities handle retail and consumer food waste, capturing approximately 8.2 billion cubic feet of biogas annually.

ABC says most facilities use biogas to generate electricity and heat. The research states 164 food-waste-only facilities produce power, heat or both, and another 38 upgrade biogas into RNG.

Bigger projects and more investment

ABC says food waste biogas projects are getting larger and attracting more investment. The 42 facilities that have come online since 2020 account for 32 percent of the sector's annual biogas production and 45 percent of its total investment, according to the research. On average, ABC says, these newer projects capture nearly twice as much biogas as earlier projects and cost about three times as much to build.

The momentum continued in 2025, when seven new food waste projects came online, all of which produce RNG. Together, ABC says they added more than twice the biogas capture capacity of any other year since 2020.

ABC estimates that if all 70 million tons of discarded food generated in the United States in 2024 were processed through anaerobic digestion, it could produce approximately 181 billion cubic feet of additional biogas annually—roughly five times the amount currently captured by the country's dedicated food waste biogas facilities.

That additional biogas represents approximately 113 million British thermal units of energy, enough to meet the annual energy needs of approximately 1.5 million U.S. households, ABC says.

(Canary Media, Canary Media)
text:
This analysis and news roundup come from the Canary Media Weekly newsletter. Sign up to get it every Friday.

Americans aren’t happy about the data center boom, and they made their displeasure pretty clear this Election Day. Voters not only selected a slate of Democratic candidates who campaigned against data centers; they also approved more than 30 ballot measures aimed at reining in the power-hungry facilities.

You could argue that the ​“data center elections” really started a year ago, when Virginians selected Democrat Abigail Spanberger as their next governor. Virginia has more than earned its status as the data center capital of the world, with the latest estimates counting more than 700 facilities around the state, and Spanberger ran on a promise to keep their intense power demand in check.

In the months that followed, it became clear that data center developers were circling in on Great Lakes states and their abundant water resources — and that fighting the facilities was a winning campaign strategy. Take Michigan’s Democratic U.S. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who made data center regulation a prominent piece of his candidacy, and William Lawrence, a Democrat who won his U.S. House race after showing up at a local council meeting to fight a proposed data center.

Meanwhile in Ohio, Sherrod Brown, a three-term Democratic senator who was ousted in 2024, will return to the chamber. Brown’s campaign painted his Republican opponent as ​“the face of data centers,” even though it cost Brown the support of some union labor allies who’ve backed him for decades but see data centers as creators of construction jobs.

Data centers’ threat is even more palpable in Georgia and Texas, which have more projects in the pipeline than any other state except Virginia. Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) was easily reelected after criticizing data centers as part of his campaign and investigating their impact on power bills in the Senate. Georgia’s Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms has meanwhile pledged a ​“pause” on new data center construction once she takes office in January. And Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa scored historic wins in Texas for U.S. Senate and governor, respectively, after promising to pursue a slate of data center regulations.

Anti–data center sentiment this election cycle was so strong that even some Republicans promised restrictions — Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers called for a one-year moratorium in the state, for example. But some still sided with data centers, like Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina, who benefited from an industry-funded ad campaign before losing a seat she had been expected to retain.

And when the data center debate showed up in ballot measures across dozens of counties and municipalities, voters gave a resounding response: Rein them in.

More big energy stories

How energy prices showed up on the ballot

Data centers weren’t the only energy issue motivating voters this week. With gasoline prices at their highest level of any Election Day in U.S. history, and falling temperatures getting Americans thinking about heating bills, it’s no wonder that voters were looking for a change.

While President Donald Trump has been promising to curb energy costs since his 2024 campaign, his decisions have driven prices in the opposite direction. Experts say that perhaps his most drastic mistake was starting a war with Iran, spiking oil prices that have yet to return to anything resembling the pre-conflict normal. That impact has been especially obvious in Maine, where half the residents rely on heating oil — and where voters ousted longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins on Tuesday.

Utility bills were literally on the ballot in nine states this week, as voters selected new members to regulatory boards that oversee utility rate hikes and other energy-related decisions. While most of the states preserved the status quo and elected Republicans, Georgia voters gave Democrats the majority on their Public Service Commission for the first time in 30 years.

What do Democrats’ wins mean for permitting?

As the U.S. Senate prepares for its drastically new makeup come January, it’s also got a major vote to tackle in the next few days. The chamber is planning to vote Nov. 9 on long-awaited energy permitting reform legislation — that is, if newly emboldened Democrats don’t try to reshape the bill.

While the package was crafted by two Democrats and two Republicans, some Congress members on the left have demanded edits to minimize its benefits for fossil fuels and prioritize clean energy development. They’ve renewed that call in the blue wave’s wake, with Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), who is likely to chair the House Natural Resources Committee in a Democrat-led Congress, saying that voters showed ​“they don’t want this dirty, fossil-fuel-expanding bill.” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D) also called for revisions to the bill to protect tribal sovereignty and blunt impacts to the National Environmental Policy Act.

Bill co-sponsor Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) contended that the election results revealed the opposite: Americans are focused on ​“affordability,” he wrote on X, and achieving that requires building more clean energy projects by passing the permitting bill.

CANARY CATCH-UP

More election results: Democrats are poised to take full control of six more state governments, giving them leverage to enact more ambitious clean-energy policies. Voters also approved a handful of clean energy–boosting ballot measures, and rejected some that would prop up fossil fuels and weaken environmental regulations. (Canary Media, Canary Media)

Thankful for solar: Two cranberry bogs in Massachusetts are marking their second harvest of fruit grown in the shadow of solar panels — and just may be the only cranberry bogs in the world paired with solar. (Canary Media)

A real Revolution: Danish developer Ørsted says its Revolution Wind farm off the Connecticut and Rhode Island coasts is fully operating, a major win as the Trump administration tries yet another tactic to shut down the project. (Canary Media)

Data center solutions? Two new reports make the case for how batteries and virtual power plants can address some of data centers’ biggest challenges to the grid and customers’ utility bills. (Canary Media, Canary Media)

text:
Even before the midterm election results, Roth Capital’s Philip Shen, managing director and senior research analyst, had been hearing that the solar tax credit was still on the minds of many in Washington D.C.

“Our checks suggest that Republicans are open to extending the ITC and 45X. A contact that has insight into the GOP shared that, ‘we are moving into a positive political environment for solar,’” said Shen late this September

If solar was in a positive political environment in late September, then this November’s election creates the environment for tax credit reinstatements

The President has signed an extension before. In December 2020 he signed a two-year solar tax credit extension in 2020 as part of a COVID relief and government spending package.

Since the signing of the One Big Beautiful Bill (OBBB), at least seven federal pieces of legislation have been filed seeking to reinstate some or all of the Inflation Reduction Act’s (IRA) solar-related tax credits. None of these bills has had a committee hearing, and all of them expire when the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027, so anything that can be acted on would need to be refiled next year.

S. 2681, Lowering Electric Bills Act

H.R. 5862, American Energy Independence and Affordability Act

H.R. 6900, American Affordability Act of 2025

S. 3722, Lowering Home Energy Costs Act

H.R. 7977, Energy Bills Relief Act

S. 4175

H.R. 8477, American Energy Dominance Act

Each of the bills comes at the law in a slightly different manner, but most seek to simply reinstate the pre-existing language of the IRA. For instance, S. 2681, filed four weeks after the OBBB was signed, strikes the paragraphs that ended the residential credit after 2025 and cut off wind and solar projects placed in service after 2027, and puts the IRA’s emissions-based phaseout back in place. It leaves the rest of the OBBB alone.

H.R. 5862, and H.R. 6900 similarly restore the IRA. Filing S. 3722 revokes the OBBB as well, but only specifically focused on the residential tax credit.

H.R. 7977 goes further than most, getting rid of FEOC, and reinstating grant money, adds in a transmission tax credit, and goes after the administration’s executive orders regarding wind and solar.

It’s as if the OBBBA never existed.

H.R. 8477 – submitted by a Republican – also reinstates the tax credits, but doesn’t re-up electric vehicle tax credits or manufacturing credits.

Sen. Wyden’s S. 4175 reinstates the clean electricity credits, with some nuance. The credits would run until the later of 2032 or six years after any “price or demand increase year,” defined as a year in which the national average retail electricity price rises more than 2% or electricity sales rise. The residential credits would come back for two years after any such year.

text:
Takeaways

The EPA proposes to significantly revise New Source Performance Standards and Emission Guidelines for the Crude Oil and Natural Gas Source Category, referred to as OOOOb and OOOOc.

The latest proposed rule includes a more substantial overhaul of the 2024 Rule’s compliance requirements.

Until a final rule takes effect, the 2024 Rule’s requirements, as modified by the Delay Rule, remain in place.

On October 29, 2026, the EPA published in the Federal Register a 128-page proposed rule to amend New Source Performance Standards and Emission Guidelines for the Crude Oil and Natural Gas Source Category, referred to as OOOOb and OOOOc. (Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OAR-2025-0163). If finalized, it would substantially modify many of the EPA’s 2024 Rule’s monitoring, operating and reporting requirements. The EPA estimates that the proposed rule could generate approximately $45 billion in economic savings over 2027-2060 through reduced compliance costs and increased oil and gas production.

The EPA will hold a public hearing on the proposed rule on November 16, 2026, and is accepting public comments until December 16, 2026.

History of Oil and Gas Regulations in OOOOb and OOOOc

The EPA has regulated volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions from the oil and natural gas sector since 1985. In 2016, it began regulating methane emissions as well, known as OOOOa.

In 2024, the EPA issued a rule intended to reduce emissions of methane and VOCs from oil and gas operations. The 2024 Rule includes standards to reduce emissions, including New Source Performance Standards to reduce methane and smog-forming volatile organic compounds, prohibitions on releasing associated gas from oil wells through a control device or flare, and the Super Emitter Program, which allows third parties to monitor oil and gas sites for emissions.

Since promulgating the 2024 Rule, the EPA has taken steps to reduce compliance burdens. In December 2025, the EPA issued a final rule extending compliance deadlines of the 2024 Rule (known as the Delay Rule). Several environmental groups petitioned the DC Circuit for review of the Delay Rule on the grounds that it is arbitrary and capricious and violates the Clean Air Act’s rulemaking requirements. The court heard oral argument on October 14, 2026.

In April 2026, the EPA issued a final rule revising the temporary flaring provisions, and in May 2026, it issued guidance allowing flaring at new oil wells in limited circumstances. The latest proposed rule includes a more substantial overhaul of the 2024 Rule’s compliance requirements.

Components of the EPA’s Proposed Rule

The proposed rule, if finalized, would rescind the Super Emitter Program, create subcategories of well sites, and revise BSER for gas emissions. It would also reduce other operating and reporting requirements.

Rescinding the Super Emitter Program

The Super Emitter Program allows certified third-party entities to monitor oil and gas sites for large emission events and notify the EPA if they occur. Upon receiving a notification of an emission event, the EPA must notify the owner and require the owner to investigate. The program was intended to serve as a backstop for other regulations requiring emissions monitoring and control.

If finalized, the proposed rule would remove provisions related to the Super Emitter Program not only from OOOOb and OOOOc, but also from the earlier OOOO and OOOOa subparts. The EPA made this proposal based on findings that other emission limitation, monitoring and mitigation requirements are sufficient in controlling large emissions, that reports from third-party entities were ineffective, and that the EPA does not have the legal authority to allow third-party monitoring and reporting.

Creating new subcategories for certain well sites

The proposed rule, if finalized, would create subcategories for certain well sites. The EPA proposed two options for categorization and is soliciting comments to select one: marginal and non-marginal sites, and conventional and non-conventional sites. Under the proposed rule, a marginal well site is a site producing less than or equal to 15 barrels of oil equivalents per day. According to the EPA, 78 percent of existing oil and gas wells in the U.S. are marginal wells. Conventional wells refer to the structure of the well—shallow and drilled vertically—but like marginal wells, conventional wells typically produce less than deeper, non-conventional wells.

Because compliance costs are large for marginal and conventional wells, the EPA proposes to relax regulations on either marginal wells or conventional wells to make compliance less expensive. This includes modified compliance requirements for fugitive component emissions, pumps, associated gas and storage vessels.

Revising best system of emission reduction (BSER) for gas emissions to allow flaring

The EPA is proposing to allow operators to route gas associated with an oil well to a control vent or flare that achieves 95 percent reduction in emissions or greater. This would revise the EPA’s 2024 Rule, which requires operators to recover associated gas to a flow line or collection line, or use it as an onsite fuel source. This proposed change responds to industry concerns that requiring sites to rely on a flow line or collection line to recover gas would raise costs and burden isolated well sites without easy access to a collection line. It also addresses concerns that the 2024 Rule forces oil and gas producers, especially smaller operations, to rely on third-party gathering systems to collect and accept associated gas.

Redefining “no identifiable emissions” (NIE) to add leniency for accidental leaks

The 2024 Rule requires covers and closed vent systems (CVSs) to be designed and operated to comply with NIE, meaning no emissions imaged with an OGI camera. Industry petitioners, however, raised concerns that covers and CVSs are subject to wear and tear, which can cause unintended leaks.

The proposed rule would amend the definition of NIE to mean no emissions or defects, or that if emissions or defects occur, the facility repairs them within the applicable timeframe. The EPA proposes a 24-hour timeframe, or, if repair within 24 hours is not possible, a first attempt at repair within five days. If three emission events occur within one year, the facility must complete an investigative analysis to determine the cause of the defect.

Relaxing other operating and reporting requirements of the 2024 Rule

The proposed rule, if finalized, would reduce compliance requirements for a variety of processes. It would reduce reporting requirements for non-venting liquids unloading well sites and allow the routing of vented gas to temporary control devices. It proposes to amend requirements for zero-emissions process controllers in existing facilities. It seeks to revise the 2024 Rule requiring zero emissions from pumps, instead allowing existing pumps to comply by reducing emissions by 95 percent. It also proposes amendments to parts of the rule governing storage vessels, equipment leaks and control devices, including added flexibility for flame monitoring data deviations and control device alerts.

What is not included?

The EPA has regulated greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, in the form of methane, from the oil and gas sector since 2016, when the EPA recognized GHG as contributing to climate change. This proposed rule does not modify this finding. However, the EPA is undertaking separate and ongoing rulemaking to consider how it will regulate GHGs in the oil and natural gas industry going forward.

As EPA did not propose removing GHG requirements, state plans would still be required under the Clean Air Act. Additionally, the EPA did not change the compliance date for states to submit state plans under OOOOc by January 22, 2027. Therefore, the EPA would need to take another action to provide states additional time to take the new rule into account.

Until a final rule takes effect, the 2024 Rule’s requirements, as modified by the Delay Rule, remain in place, so operators should continue planning for current compliance obligations. Any final rule is likely to face judicial review, with potential challenges focusing on EPA’s explanation for departing from its 2024 findings and the technical and economic support for the revised standards. The final administrative record, including EPA’s responses to comments on emissions, costs, feasibility, and alternative approaches, will be important to the rule’s durability. Operators should consider submitting facility-specific information supporting workable standards and compliance options. Members of the public can submit comments on the proposal until December 16.

description:

text:
KEY POINTS

Constellation received a conditional DOE loan commitment of up to $5 billion for potential uprates at eight US nuclear plants.

The facilities are in Illinois, Maryland and Pennsylvania, yet, the company’s release does not estimate the added capacity from these potential projects.

Due diligence and financing conditions remain, and the commitment is not a final decision to proceed with any individual uprate project.

Commitment Targets Existing Nuclear Plants

Constellation announced Oct. 27 that the U.S. Department of Energy made a conditional loan commitment of up to $5 billion to support potential uprates at select facilities. Uprates increase electricity production at existing nuclear plants.

The company said the commitment could help accelerate additional capacity, but its release does not estimate how much power these potential DOE-backed projects would add.

An image of the Limerick Nuclear Power Station located near Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Constellation

announced Oct. 27 that the U.S. Department of Energy made a conditional loan commitment of up to $5 billion to support potential uprates at select facilities, including the Limerick location. Image: Shutterstock

Which Eight Facilities are Under Consideration

The listed US nuclear power plants are Braidwood, Byron, Clinton, Dresden, LaSalle and Quad Cities in Illinois; Calvert Cliffs in Maryland; and Limerick in Pennsylvania.

Constellation said the commitment remains subject to due diligence, definitive financing documents and applicable conditions. It does not itself represent a final decision to proceed with any individual uprate or project at every facility under consideration, according to the company.

The company separately said long-term Google and Amazon agreements have incentivized more than $7 billion in investments to add about 1,080 megawatts of nuclear capacity. That figure applies to those separate customer-backed investments, not an announced capacity estimate for the potential DOE-financed uprates.

Power Infrastructure: 68% of Civil Construction Gains through September

Constellation said on its website that rapid advances in generative AI are a "a once-in-a-generation catalyst for American growth" and are driving projections of unprecedented electricity-demand growth. The company added that powering AI with safe, secure and reliable U.S. electricity adds to rising demand from electrification and the resurgence of American manufacturing.

ConstructConnect News reported Oct. 27 that power infrastructure accounted for 68% of civil-construction gains through September. ConstructConnect Chief Economist Michael Guckes said that the power infrastructure "current total of $30.7 billion is well above last year’s comparable period spending of $11.7 billion."

Guckes pointed out that, "Among the largest projects lifting the subcategory are an earlier $13 billion Commonwealth liquefied natural gas export terminal, and two September projects including a $4.0 billion North Dakota power plant and a $1.6 billion Texas substation."

Stay Connected

Stay connected with ConstructConnect News for construction industry news and construction market analysis to stay ahead of what’s building next.

About ConstructConnect

At ConstructConnect, our software solutions provide the information construction professionals need to start every project on a solid foundation. For more than 100 years, our insights and market intelligence have empowered commercial firms, manufacturers, trade contractors, and architects to make data-driven decisions and maximize productivity.

ConstructConnect is a business unit of Roper Technologies (Nasdaq: ROP), part of the Nasdaq 100, S&P 500, and Fortune 1000.

text:
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) would reform outdated permitting laws for transmission lines, power plants, and natural gas infrastructure, and make sure data centers pay their fair share of grid costs.

We conducted an analysis of manufacturing domestic employment requirements and input-output tables to evaluate the impact of the BAAJA on employment in the industrial sector, covering both the investment in renewable energy and transmission infrastructure the bill would accelerate and its effects on energy prices. We estimate that these reforms could add up to 105,600 industrial jobs in manufacturing, mining, and construction through 2040 compared with current law, in three ways:

Building additional wind plants, solar farms, battery facilities, and transmission lines would support up to 38,900 jobs in manufacturing, mining and other industrial sectors and 35,800 construction jobs through 2040.

Maintaining these additional facilities would support an additional 12,300 jobs in on-site operations and maintenance and manufacturing replacement equipment after the buildout.

Cheaper electricity and natural gas would support 9,200–18,600 lasting manufacturing jobs by reducing manufacturing costs, improving the international competitiveness of American manufacturing, and reshoring manufacturing jobs.

Building new generation facilities and transmission infrastructure will employ tens of thousands of Americans in industrial sectors.

BAAJA will remove barriers to building hundreds of gigawatts of renewable generation capacity in wind, solar and battery storage, and thousands of miles of additional transmission lines. Building these new facilities will require American labor to construct these facilities and build the turbines, photovoltaic panels, inverters, and wires that will be needed to power the next era of domestic energy production.

In a scenario where BAAJA enables 247GW of additional wind, solar and battery capacity, we estimate that the additional buildout of these facilities will employ up to an additional 37,500 workers in manufacturing and mining and 33,500 construction workers.[1] The construction of additional transmission infrastructure will employ up to 1,400 workers in manufacturing and mining and 2,300 construction workers. Fabricated metal, electrical equipment, and aluminum products are among the manufacturing sectors that will benefit most from the buildout.

A larger energy system will require more jobs to maintain it.

Even after the buildout, we estimate that an additional 12,300 industrial workers will be required to keep those facilities running. 8,800 workers will be needed for on-site operations and maintenance, and another 3,500 manufacturing workers will be needed to build replacement parts for these additional facilities.

Cheaper energy supports manufacturing jobs, especially in energy-intensive, trade-exposed sectors.

BAAJA can reduce the cost of the electricity and natural gas used by American manufacturing by building out the grid and pipelines required to connect utilities and businesses to cheaper, more reliable sources of energy and preventing data centers from offloading their costs onto other users. We estimate that BAAJA effects on energy prices will ultimately add 9,200–18,600 manufacturing jobs by improving the competitiveness of American manufacturing, with half of these jobs coming from domestic reshoring. Energy-intensive sectors such as foundries, steel and aluminum processing, pulp and paper manufacturing, and petrochemical manufacturing are especially likely to benefit. States in the South like Texas, Louisiana, Oklahoma, Arkansas, and Mississippi are also likely to be large beneficiaries of the BAAJA’s natural gas reforms.

title: Why Tesla is ending Cybertruck production for Cybercab - USA Today
description:
Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production in mid-2027 to increase production of its Cybercab.
The decline in Cybertruck sales coincides with a broader 30% drop in overall electric vehicle sales.
"Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk wrote.
The comments come as Tesla's Cybertruck sales have fallen 28% so far in 2026, according to new data released by Cox Automotive.
Why is Tesla shutting down Cybertruck production?
text:
Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production in mid-2027 to increase production of its Cybercab.

Cybertruck sales have fallen 28% in 2026, according to data from Cox Automotive.

The decline in Cybertruck sales coincides with a broader 30% drop in overall electric vehicle sales.

Tesla is winding down production of its unconventional Cybertruck electric pickup truck to focus on the Cybercab, the company's CEO Elon Musk said in a Nov. 6 X post.

"Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk wrote.

The comments come as Tesla's Cybertruck sales have fallen 28% so far in 2026, according to new data released by Cox Automotive.

Tesla is planning to expand its Robotaxi service to a "dozen or so states" by the end of the year, CEO Elon Musk told investors as his company was reporting first-quarter earnings on April 22.

Tesla said on its website that Cybercab will be a "purpose-built fully autonomous vehicle, will offer rides in your area in the future."

Musk has also said the robotaxi will be a big part in his company's "overall shift to an autonomous future."

Why is Tesla shutting down Cybertruck production?

Tesla sold 11,586 Cybertrucks in first three months of 2026, compared to 16,097 in the first three months of last year.

The vehicle was first introduced for the 2024 model year.

The Cybertruck sales decline came as overall electric car sales fell in the last few years, following President Donald Trump and Congress eliminating a popular EV $7,500 tax credit.

Carmakers sold 725,888 electric cars in the first nine months of 2026, according to data released Oct. 12 by Cox Automotive, which was down 30% from the over 1 million EVs they sold through the same period last year.

What to know about Tesla's Cybercab?

Tesla revealed in documents submitted to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency in May that the Cybercab will have a fully electric motor. It will weigh 3,113 pounds and have a 48 kWh lithium-ion battery with a charge depleting range of about 418 miles.

Tesla said the Cybercab will be all-wheel drive and have 219 horsepower. The vehicle will have regenerative braking that is commonplace on most fully electric cars.

How will riding in Tesla Cybercab compare to the experience of being an Uber or Lyft passenger?

Tesla said rides in Cybercab robotaxi will be ordered using a cell phone app that is similar to the ones riders use now to search for Uber and Lyft rides.

The company says drivers will have create an account, and the app is currently only available on Apple iOS devices.

Tesla says drivers will wait for their Cybercab rides at a designated pickup location, and they will notified when the car arrives via the app. But there's one catch: In a Tesla Cybercab, there will no human driver behind the wheel to greet when you open the door.

Tesla says passengers will simply tap a "Start Ride" button when they enter the Cybercab cars to get their trip going. The company said riders will be able to personalize their Robotaxi experience with different features such as climate settings and seat position. They will also be able to stream much the Robotaxi app, and certain driver profile settings will carry over for Tesla vehicle owners.

It's an experience Zoox and Waymo riders have already grown accustomed to in select U.S. markets, providing some ready-made competition as Tesla enters the autonomous rideshare game.

What has Musk said about the future of the Cybertruck?

Musk told investors on Tesla's Jan. 28 earnings call that its unconventional Cybertruck electric pickup truck may be heading for an autonomous, commercial future.

In response to a question about whether he would be willing to design "a more conventional looking pickup" given the sluggish Cybertruck sales, Musk said on the January earnings call, "We will transition the Cybertruck line to just a fully autonomous vehicle."

"There’s obviously a market there for cargo delivery, like say like localized cargo delivery with a city, with a few hundred miles something like that," Musk said. "There’s a lot of cargo that needs to move locally within a city, an autonomous Cybertruck could be very useful for that."

Industry analysts have noted the impact of Musk's work with Trump in 2025 and staunch conservative political stances on the sales performance of the company's cars.

The Cybertruck in particular launched during the height of the 2024 presidential campaign, when Musk vocally supported Trump, and the cars became a symbol for some of shoppers' alignment with Musk and Trump's politics.

According to a November 2025 Yale University study, Tesla sold 1 million-1.26 million fewer vehicles between October 2022 and April 2025 than it otherwise would have without what the study's authors dubbed the "Musk partisan effect." The study found Musk's public political stances also helped to increase the sales of other automakers' electric and hybrid vehicles by 17-22% as drivers who were opposed to the CEO's politics fled to other EV manufacturers.

According to a poll released on Jan. 12 by EVs for All America, an advocacy group that works with car manufacturers to push U.S. and state lawmakers to adopt EV-friendly policies, 44% of people who said they are seriously considering buying an EV had a mostly unfavorable opinion of Musk.

name: Congress
title: Advice for California's Next Governor: Transportation - Legal Planet
description:
In this post, I’ll discuss our clean transportation strategies.
So what should Governor-Elect Becerra prioritize in this sector that impacts quality of life, job access, affordability, economic development, air quality, and climate change?
The Trump Administration and Congress have attacked California’s clean vehicle regulations.
Through support for litigation, partnership with the new Congress, and ambitious leadership at the California Air Resources Board, the Governor can help overcome this roadblock.
As the incoming Becerra Administration takes shape, transportation policy presents a key opportunity to address environmental and cost of living concerns together.
text:
Recommendations from CLEE’s policy roadmap for the incoming administration

Tuesday’s elections delivered a nationwide sweep of results with positive potential for climate and environmental policy.

The new Congress will have power to slow or reverse some of the Trump Administration’s attacks on federal clean air and clean water policy and the opportunity to reinstate some clean energy tax credits. State legislatures and governorships in places like Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Texas can tackle the data center question with an eye toward protection of communities and the environment. Even nationally low-profile bodies like the Georgia Public Service Commission will have the power to shift energy regulation more in favor of consumers and climate.

While these topics did not dominate the national conversation, the cost of gas and diesel–which sits at the core of the climate effort–did. And while the results here in California are perhaps not as surprising as the rest of the country, the environmental policy stakes of the leadership transition remain high.

As my CLEE colleague Louise Bedsworth discussed last week, CLEE and a group of expert partners developed a suite of environmental policy recommendations for the incoming governor, on topics ranging from electricity affordability to water sustainability. With Xavier Becerra now confirmed in that role, we will highlight groups of these recommendations in a series of posts over the coming weeks. In this post, I’ll discuss our clean transportation strategies.

Transportation was not a top issue during the gubernatorial race (though it’s difficult to say what was a top issue in this race) aside from the rising cost of gas and diesel resulting from the Iran War. Steve Hilton promised $3 gas and to dismantle the DMV (?), Becerra promised to stabilize prices and also indicated openness to relaxing vehicle electrification standards, they disagreed about the gas tax and replacements, and that was about it.

However, transportation was on the California ballot on Tuesday. Bay area residents approved Regional Measure RTM, which will provide nearly $1 billion per year to funding BART, Caltrain, SF Muni, and AC Transit service via a sales tax increase. San Francisco voters also approved Proposition H, a parcel tax that will raise an additional $160 million per year for SF Muni service. Meanwhile, Fresno voters appear to have rejected Measure S, which would have raised about $250 million per year for local transit services.

Despite a lack of candidate attention, transportation is perhaps the top climate issue for voters when viewed holistically: how we get around determines how we live. Access to a car or to quality transit is a key determinant of economic opportunity and quality of life. Overlong commutes dominate the weeks of far too many Californians who lack the latter but are priced out of urban centers. High fuel and insurance costs can displace other life necessities. And cars and trucks are the leading contributors to our climate and air quality crises.

So what should Governor-Elect Becerra prioritize in this sector that impacts quality of life, job access, affordability, economic development, air quality, and climate change? CLEE and our partners offered key strategies such as:

Facilitate leadership and coordination across transportation agencies. California spreads state authority for transportation matters across nearly a dozen agencies, ranging from Caltrans (highway construction and transportation planning) to the California Air Resources Board (vehicle emissions regulation and incentive funding) to the Governor’s Office of Business and Economic Development (clean vehicle market development and charging strategies). The Governor appoints leadership at all of these agencies and can direct them to take coordinated action prioritizing mobility, affordability, and emissions reduction.

Renew California leadership on vehicle electrification and explore legal innovations. The Trump Administration and Congress have attacked California’s clean vehicle regulations. Through support for litigation, partnership with the new Congress, and ambitious leadership at the California Air Resources Board, the Governor can help overcome this roadblock. Policies that focus on the cost and resilience benefits of grid-integrated vehicle batteries, address air quality within the often low-income districts that suffer from the air pollution from truck and logistics traffic, and consumer protection for drivers including EV buyers should be at the top of the list.

Preserve and expand public transit funding. Tuesday’s measures in the Bay Area provide a needed lifeline, but California’s public transit systems are suffering from low ridership and funding cuts across the board. Ensuring these systems–major rail networks like BART and LA Metro as well as rural bus services–maintain service is vital for both our sustainability goals and economic opportunity for those who do not have automobile access. The Governor can both support this baseline funding and work with the Legislature to expand service to serve communities and reduce emissions across the state.

These are just a few among many subject-matter recommendations we’ll be sharing in the coming weeks. As the incoming Becerra Administration takes shape, transportation policy presents a key opportunity to address environmental and cost of living concerns together. Doing so can continue California’s long record of leadership on this issue while shaping a new era of clean, equitable mobility.

name: Clean Energy
title: Why Countries Need National Plans to Manage the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels (TAFF)
description:
This article makes the case for why countries need explicit planning for the transition away from fossil fuels, what these plans could address, and what considerations should shape countries’ plans.
These could include climate planning tools such as updated NDCs or just transition plans to core economic and sectoral plans such as long-term development strategies, national energy plans, or other national planning instruments.
Planning the transition away from fossil fuels can expand the scope for national planning and ask the questions that clean energy plans often leave unanswered.
Malaysia’s National Energy Transition Roadmap, published in 2023, is designed around the trilemma of energy security, affordability and environmental sustainability.
Whether pursued through roadmaps, NDCs, long-term strategies or other national planning tools, national TAFF planning can also inform wider debates on development, finance and economic resilience.
text:
In the span of just a few years, governments have watched a war in Ukraine upend Europe's gas supply and a war between the United States and Iran threaten the Strait of Hormuz, which carries a fifth of the world's oil. The pattern is hard to miss: Fossil-fuel dependence has become a recurring source of economic pain and strategic vulnerability.

While clean energy deployment has accelerated, few governments have developed explicit plans for managing fossil fuel consumption and, where relevant, shifts in fossil fuel demand and production. This matters because fossil fuel demand does not automatically fall when clean energy grows. Rapid growth in the absolute amount, or even the share, of clean energy may not lead directly to a decline in fossils, but rather serve at least partly to meet rising energy demand (from cooling, industrialization or data centers). Without such planning, governments risk treating fossil fuel decline as a by-product of clean energy growth rather than as a structural, economy-wide transformation that must be deliberately managed.

National planning for transitioning away from fossil fuels (TAFF) can therefore set out how national fossil fuel use will evolve; how existing energy transition strategies can be integrated into a coherent whole; and how governments will manage the fiscal, infrastructure, investment and social dimensions of the transition. Given the necessary scale of the transformation over the coming decades and the uncertainties around how it will unfold, governments need plans that provide a long-term direction while enabling them to anticipate emerging risks and adapt to changing circumstances. While planning alone will not deliver the transition, it is a vital stepping stone to integrating such plans into more economic and sectoral planning, policies and investment choices.

This article makes the case for why countries need explicit planning for the transition away from fossil fuels, what these plans could address, and what considerations should shape countries’ plans. It also explores how COP31 and other international forums could help advance this agenda.

What Is National TAFF Planning and Why Is It Important?

National TAFF planning sets out how fossil fuel consumption and, where relevant, production, will evolve, how clean alternatives will scale, and how the macro-fiscal, social, infrastructure, and investment consequences of that shift will be managed.

Planning for the transition can be done through standalone plans or roadmaps, or embedded in a variety of policy instruments. These could include climate planning tools such as updated NDCs or just transition plans to core economic and sectoral plans such as long-term development strategies, national energy plans, or other national planning instruments. Regardless of the approach, TAFF planning needs to address the difficult choices and trade-offs that countries face in managing the transition alongside their broader economic and development implications.

TAFF plans can serve three practical functions. First, they can improve policy coherence by linking separate climate, energy, fiscal, industrial and just transition strategies in a common framework. Second, they can support domestic coordination by giving ministries and other stakeholders a shared reference point for making decisions that may otherwise be made in silos. And third, they can provide clear signals to investors and trading partners, helping reduce policy uncertainty and showing that a country is not only expanding clean energy, but also deliberately managing its fossil fuel dependence.

Why Are Existing Climate and Energy Plans Not Enough?

Most existing climate and energy plans miss the mark, focusing more on building the “clean” energy system than on governing the decline of fossil fuel systems. For example, WRI analysis finds that while many NDCs seek to expand clean energy, few explicitly focus on policies for the shifts away from fossil fuel use and production.

Some NDCs and other national plans include commitments to increase the share of non-fossil energy use, providing a helpful sense of direction for reducing fossil fuel dependence. But clean energy plans mainly focus on renewables, grids, storage, efficiency and electrification without necessarily addressing how existing fossil fuel systems will be managed.

Planning the transition away from fossil fuels can expand the scope for national planning and ask the questions that clean energy plans often leave unanswered. These include specific sectoral issues involving fossil-based power plants or oil demand for transport, as well as critical issues with the political economy and broader economic and social implications such as public revenues, subsidies, employment, regional economic impacts and decommissioning liabilities. A solar or wind energy target by itself does not tell a country how workers will transition or how changing fossil revenues will be managed.

Focusing on expanding clean energy can often draw more political support because it promises new investment, industries and jobs — all essential objectives. But planning for TAFF can be politically valuable by making the challenges and opportunities visible early and then addressing them squarely. Managing the transition also requires governments to confront risks that may emerge unevenly or abruptly as the energy system evolves. Volatile global markets, shifting demand and infrastructure tipping points can create sudden economic and social pressures, requiring ministries to develop stronger capabilities for anticipating, stress-testing and managing transition risks. Planning for TAFF can help make these vulnerabilities visible early, identify economic diversification opportunities, sequence reforms, develop support measures, and build broader coalitions around a managed transition rather than through fragmented policies and short-term crisis response.

Existing Plans Provide a Starting Point

National TAFF planning does not need to be built from scratch. Many countries already have parts of the architecture in place through NDCs, long-term strategies, plans to decarbonize power systems, subsidy reforms and just transition frameworks. IISD notes that at least 46 countries already have power-sector decarbonization plans. A growing number also have demand-side or decommissioning frameworks. The challenge is less about creating an entirely new planning tool than about integrating existing policies into a coherent framework that explicitly addresses the transition away from fossil fuels.

Countries are approaching this challenge in different ways, from explicit national TAFF roadmaps to broader energy transition strategies that provide important building blocks:

France, the Netherlands and Germany were the first three countries to develop a more explicit national TAFF roadmap in 2026. France’s TAFF roadmap, released at the Santa Marta conference, brings existing national climate and energy commitments under a fossil-fuel specific roadmap and sets end-of-consumption targets for coal by 2030, oil by 2045 and fossil gas by 2050 for energy purposes. The Dutch roadmap brings together existing and planned measures across different fossil fuels while stopping short of setting a single phase-out date. Germany’s roadmap also builds largely on its existing climate and sectoral policies and sets out how these contribute to transitioning away from fossil fuels by 2045.

Colombia’s Just Energy Transition Roadmap in 2025 defines decarbonization trajectories and covers hydrocarbons, mining, electricity, new energy and demand management. It was built through a broad social-dialogue process involving communities, business and sectoral actors.

The United Kingdom’s carbon budget and clean power plans provide examples of economy-wide delivery and power-sector transformation, while its North Sea strategy engages more directly with the future of domestic oil and gas production.

Malaysia’s National Energy Transition Roadmap, published in 2023, is designed around the trilemma of energy security, affordability and environmental sustainability.

Ghana’s long-term energy transition framework and investment plan outlines a pathway to net-zero by 2060, across oil and gas, transport, cooking, industry and power.

At the regional level, Pacific Island countries have also begun developing a similar approach. Six Pacific governments adopted the Tassiriki Call for a Fossil Fuel Free Pacific in April 2026, setting out a common vision for 100% renewable energy and a just transition away from fossil fuels. Pacific ministers are now taking this forward through work on a regional TAFF roadmap. Other countries are beginning to explore similar approaches, with support from the NDC Partnership and Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance (BOGA).

None of these examples is a perfect template. But together, they show that countries are already developing many of the core ingredients of a fossil fuel transition plan. National TAFF planning can help advance these pieces, identify what is missing, and ensure that the transition away from fossil fuels is treated not as an assumed by-product of clean energy deployment, but as an explicit and governed process.

What Questions Should TAFF Plans Answer?

There is no single template for national TAFF planning. Countries differ widely in their energy systems, economic structures, levels of development and exposure to fossil fuels. As a result, its design will necessarily vary and should reflect principles of equity and national circumstances while maintaining ownership, credibility and coherence. Emerging guidance, including recent guidance by IISD, suggest that credible TAFF planning needs to answer five core questions:

How will fossil fuel use and, where relevant, production evolve? Credible TAFF planning can set goals and a clear direction of travel while recognizing that countries will move at different speeds depending on national circumstances. In many developing countries, the pathways must also account for rising energy demand, access and affordability — where the transition must be designed as a development strategy as much as a decarbonization one, including through expanding clean, decentralized energy access. Goals may take the form of fuel-specific benchmarks, sectoral milestones or qualitative transition objectives, but their purpose is to provide a reference point against which policy, finance, governance, infrastructure and just transition measures can be designed and assessed.

How will the transition be financed and linked to economic diversification? TAFF plans can identify the investment needed to implement the transition, including for industrial conversion, decommissioning and site rehabilitation, worker support and regional diversification. It can also help prioritize investments, determine the respective roles of public, private, domestic and international finance, identify the enabling policies and institutions, support project pipeline development and specify appropriate financing instruments. For fossil fuel-dependent economies, this financing framework needs to be linked to a broader economic diversification strategy: identifying new sectors, export opportunities and domestic industries that can absorb capital and labor losses as fossil fuel revenues and jobs shifts. For many developing countries, high costs of capital can constrain investment in clean alternatives, making concessional finance, guarantees and other risk-sharing instruments particularly important. Fossil fuel-exporting economies face an additional challenge: financing economic diversification as export earnings, revenues and associated economic activity change.

How will macroeconomic and fiscal risks be managed? For exporting countries, this means explicitly addressing how revenues tied to extraction and exports will be replaced as fossil fuel income changes. Fossil fuel importers may also see changes in tax revenues and continued exposure to external price shocks. Geopolitical conflicts can fuel “fossilflation,” or fossil fuel-driven inflation that raises living costs and risks interest rate hikes, potentially constraining investment in clean energy. Central banks therefore have an important role in assessing these risks and their implications for monetary policy and financial stability. TAFF planning can help governments identify where these vulnerabilities lie, assess how they may evolve over time, and put in place the macroeconomic and fiscal measures needed to manage the transition without majorly destabilizing public finances or the broader economy.

How will workers, households, communities and regions be supported? TAFF plans should identify which workers, industries and regions face the impact of the transition. They should set out how these groups will be supported to ensure that economic restructuring does not deepen existing inequalities but instead minimizes costs, supports equitable sharing of opportunities and promotes decent work. This includes provisions for reskilling, retraining, early retirement, social protection, community investment and regional economic diversification, as well as reforms to fossil fuel subsidies that protect affordability and provide better- targeted support to vulnerable households. Participatory processes are also key. Meaningful engagements with workers and communities to build trust and ensure they have a role in shaping decisions for better outcomes, particularly in regions most exposed to transition impacts, are both important for procedural justice and political durability.

Who will be responsible for implementation and accountability? Making any plan operational requires cross-ministerial coordination, bringing finance, energy, industry, labor and regional subnational stakeholders under a shared framework, as well as clear institutional ownership, review cycles and robust monitoring systems. Such monitoring systems can track indicators related to changing fiscal and macroeconomic exposure to fossil fuels, shifts in economic and labor structures, adequacy of social safety nets for affected communities, availability of workforce transition programs, investment in cleaner economic sectors as well as small and medium enterprises (SMEs), and more. In large and regionally diverse economies, national TAFF planning should also be informed by subnational actors.

What Should Shape the Design of TAFF Planning?

Having the right content in a TAFF plan is one thing; whether it can be implemented depends on the political, financial and institutional realities countries actually face, as well as the wider global environment in which the transition unfolds. Countries will be managing these shifts amid volatile fossil fuel markets, geopolitical tensions, trade disruptions and rapidly changing energy value chains. TAFF planning therefore needs to be both grounded in domestic realities and robust enough to adapt as external conditions change.

Finance is often the most immediate constraint. For many developing economies, high debt burdens and the cost of capital limit their ability to invest in clean alternatives and economic diversification. Credible TAFF planning will therefore depend on these countries increasing their fiscal space and reducing the cost of capital, whether through debt restructuring or relief, recognition of a well-managed transition strategy in their credit rating, receiving concessional finance and international support, access to other forms of lower-cost capital and availability of risk-sharing arrangements such as guarantees.

Political economy is equally important. Subsidy reform, plant closures and industrial restructuring create visible losses, often before benefits arrive. Governments that have not prepared the ground politically will struggle to sustain them. Credible planning therefore needs to sequence reforms carefully, communicate clearly, bring incumbent industries and trade unions on board, and provide targeted protections for vulnerable workers and households.

Equity between countries should also shape TAFF planning from the outset. TAFF will not unfold at the same pace or in the same way across countries. For many developing and fossil fuel-dependent economies, the feasibility of transitioning will depend on energy access, fiscal space (including debt sustainability, access to international public and private finance, and domestic resources), and the ability to diversify before revenues fall. TAFF planning should therefore identify who is affected, who participates, how costs and benefits are shared, and how national circumstances shape the pace and sequencing of the fossil fuel transition.

Finally, implementation depends on state capacity and coordination. The transition is inherently complex and involves a large set of actors: line ministries, subnational governments, central banks, private investors, energy companies, workers and communities. Durable and decentralized governance structures, political buy-in, and stakeholder and community engagement are necessary for an effective governance of the transition.

What’s Next for National TAFF Planning?

Political momentum behind TAFF is building. At COP30 in Belem, more than 80 governments supported a global roadmap on transitioning away from fossil fuels. While the final negotiated decision did not include one due to a lack of consensus, the Brazilian COP30 Presidency committed to developing its own global TAFF roadmap, which they published just ahead of COP31. In April 2026, Colombia and the Netherlands hosted the first Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels, which brought together 57 countries to discuss practical ways to manage the transition.

Under the Turkiye-Australia COP partnership, COP31 is explicitly being framed as an “Implementation COP,” with climate finance and the energy transition among its priority areas. That creates a natural opening for further progress on taking practical steps to transition away from fossil fuels.

Given the lack of consensus at COP30, COP31 may be better suited for advancing national TAFF planning through voluntary participation and coalition building rather than relying solely on a negotiated outcome. For example, a coalition of countries could arrive at COP31 with completed TAFF plans in hand, whether standalone roadmaps or embedded in existing plans and policy instruments, or with a commitment to produce them by COP32 in Ethiopia. Such a coalition should not be limited to a group of countries that are able to move fastest. Its credibility will depend on whether it includes, or at least creates space for, fossil fuel-dependent developing countries whose transitions require more finance, fiscal space, coalition-building and time.

These outcomes would not create new obligations. But they would help turn the political language of “transitioning away from fossil fuels” into something more concrete: country-owned strategies that show how governments intend to deliberately manage the fossil side of the transition in ways that are orderly, just, equitable and economically credible. COP32 in Ethiopia next year would then provide a useful checkpoint for assessing whether that planning effort is spreading beyond first movers.

Nor should this agenda of national TAFF planning remain confined to the COP process. The next TAFF conference, co-hosted by Tuvalu and Ireland in the spring of 2027, could provide another opportunity for countries to present TAFF plans and announce commitments to develop them. More broadly, the fiscal and macroeconomic stakes of the transition are also increasingly relevant in other forums such as G20 discussions, BRICS and regional forums. Whether pursued through roadmaps, NDCs, long-term strategies or other national planning tools, national TAFF planning can also inform wider debates on development, finance and economic resilience.
