text:
Transmission projects could become much easier to build.

Originally published in the Washington Post by Zachary Liscow, a professor at Yale Law School and former chief economist at the Office of Management and Budget, and Joseph Shapiro, a professor at the Energy Institute at Haas.

As the Senate takes up a landmark permitting bill next week, lawmakers will be asking themselves a simple question: What happens if we make it easier to build interstate power lines? They don’t have to wonder about the answer. Congress ran a version of that experiment nearly 80 years ago.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is the most comprehensive permitting overhaul Congress has ever seriously considered. Nineteen former economic and national security officials, including former treasury secretaries Janet L. Yellen and Steven Mnuchin, sent a letter to congressional leaders calling the bill “the most significant bipartisan legislative effort that Congress has undertaken in decades” to address America’s permitting challenges.

“Our inability to build threatens our national security and economic growth,” they wrote. It takes more than four years for a new power plant to move from requesting grid connection to producing power, more than double the wait time in the early 2000s. Families pay for these delays when cheap power can’t reach them.

The bill’s opponents have raised environmental concerns, and senators are weighing those against the legislation’s potential upsides — one of which is the effect of removing barriers to transmission-line construction. So far, most estimates of that payoff have come from models making forward-looking guesses.

But better evidence comes from an earlier time Congress tried this.

In 1947, Congress gave natural gas pipeline companies the power of federal eminent domain, preventing a single state from blocking the construction of a pipeline running through it. Oil pipeline companies were not granted the same power.

Both industries were riding the same postwar boom. But, according to calculations in our new paper with Heidi Williams, annual additions to gas pipeline mileage rose to nearly six times the pre-1947 baseline, while oil pipeline construction stayed steady. Congress gave long-distance gas infrastructure a federal override, and construction boomed.

Today, electric transmission works the way oil pipelines did then. An interstate gas pipeline has its route approved by one federal regulator often with the authority to largely override a holdout state. An interstate power line, however, typically needs approval from every state it crosses. That gives each state a veto over projects in which the benefits often flow mostly to its neighbors.

New England has experienced the consequences. In 2016, Massachusetts attempted to import Canadian hydropower. New Hampshire, which would have hosted the power lines without getting the same influx of cheap energy, rejected it. A second route through Maine was blocked in a referendum and didn’t deliver power until January. Meanwhile, Massachusetts households paid some of the highest electricity prices in the country.

Texas is an example of what construction looks like when other states can’t interfere. Its grid sits almost entirely inside its own borders. In 2005, Texas set out to connect its windiest regions to its biggest cities, ultimately stringing more than 3,500 miles of transmission. Between 2009 and 2014, the share of wind power going to waste fell from 17 percent to 0.5 percent. The new wind power also cut the premium that fossil fuel plants could charge at peak hours, reducing their excess profits by $237 million a year, according to one study. Texas now generates more wind and solar power than any other state, nearly twice California’s total in 2024.

Some environmental advocates will read the 1947 history as a warning: Give Washington a veto over states, and you get more fossil fuel infrastructure. But they have it backward. Since 1947, interstate gas pipelines have been able to use federal eminent domain to bypass holdout states. Because transmission lines don’t have the same override, today’s siting rules tilt toward gas and away from renewable energy.

A gas plant can be built near the city it serves, with its fuel arriving by pipeline. But the best wind and solar resources are often hundreds of miles from population centers, and their power has to travel by transmission line. According to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, roughly 85 percent of the generation and storage capacity seeking to connect to the grid is from solar, wind and batteries. How much of those clean-energy resources get tapped depends heavily on whether transmission lines can be built.

For nearly 80 years, gas pipelines have been able to get past holdout states. Beginning Nov. 9, senators will decide whether power lines can, too.

text:
This past October was the warmest on record, about 1.76 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than temperatures before the widespread burning of fossil fuels began driving climate change. As we head into what is expected to be another historically warm winter, mitigating the worst impacts of the climate crisis has never been more urgent.

The Senate’s proposed permitting bill, the so-called Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), purports to accelerate clean energy deployment with the scale and speed needed to fight the climate crisis. But the stakes are too high not to fully examine whether the bill’s handouts to the oil and gas industry (among other industries) will cancel progress made elsewhere.

The bill threatens to create a set of laws under which oil and gas development essentially becomes untouchable.

Provisions in Sec. 1401 that seek to guarantee “project certainty” are highly problematic because they will make federal oil-and-gas leases virtually impossible to overturn, even if they’re issued in violation of law. While proponents of the bill emphasize that it covers “permits,” it’s important to note that the language is much broader, covering federal “authorizations,” “permits,” “records of decision,” and “any other approval or order” necessary for a project. Courts would likely view an oil and gas lease to be a federal authorization necessary for a fossil-fuel company to obtain the right to extract oil and gas on federal lands or waters. Thus, the certainty provisions can be read to cover federal oil and gas leases just as they would other federal approvals.

Two examples of what this could mean in practice are the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge in Alaska and Chaco Canyon National Historic Park in New Mexico. Both places hold enormous cultural and historic significance to Tribal stakeholders with ancestral ties to those lands. Because of the permitting bill’s “project certainty” provisions, oil and gas leasing decisions made in either the Arctic Refuge or Chaco Canyon would be incredibly hard, if not impossible, for a future administration to undo. Even if it were possible, you can’t re-create a cultural landscape once it’s been industrialized.

Moreover, the Trump administration is proposing to vastly expand offshore oil and gas leasing to areas, such as the California and Florida coasts, where public opinion overwhelmingly opposes it. By making federal approvals so difficult to reverse, the bill’s “project certainty” provisions would leave states and local communities with very little ability to stop this destructive fossil fuel development.

There’s a difference between providing certainty for lawful decisions and making federal actions effectively irreversible. Congress can promote predictability without eliminating agencies’ ability to correct mistakes, respond to new information, protect cultural resources, and comply with court rulings. This bill goes far beyond certainty and risks creating permanence, even for deeply flawed decisions.

Sec. 1402 of the bill would create a disturbing new system where the oil industry can claim it is the “victim” and get paid for it.

To understand this provision, it’s useful to reflect on the concept of “disparate impacts” from the world of environmental justice. The phrase conveys the reality that many communities are overly burdened by industrial pollution; most often, lower-income communities of color shoulder a disproportionate burden compared with whiter and more affluent neighborhoods. One of the most prominent clusters of disproportionately impacted communities is along the Gulf Coast, where oil refineries and petrochemical facilities process raw products shipped in by oil tankers from offshore oil-drilling platforms. Because of the massive volume of toxic pollutants released into the air, such as benzene, formaldehyde, and chloroprene, nearby residents face a localized cancer risk that is up to 50 times higher than the national average.

Under this bill, the fossil fuel industry would be able to sue a future administration for so-called “disparate treatment” if it is not awarded a similar number of federal permits for fossil fuel development projects as it received under the Trump administration. A company could argue in court that it was treated differently from other energy projects and seek compensation from taxpayers for the project’s expected value. As a result, taxpayers could be on the hook for paying companies not to develop based on future losses calculated solely by that company.

The bill tilts the playing field even further toward approving oil and gas projects by establishing a five-year “lookback” period as the baseline for determining whether oil and gas companies have been treated “unfairly.”

The difference between the Trump administration’s approach and past administrations is significant. For example, in 2024, the Biden administration finalized a federal offshore drilling program with just three lease sales. In 2025, the Trump administration proposed 34(!) offshore lease sales, including in coastal areas that have never been offered for leasing.

By using this period as the benchmark, the bill effectively enshrines the Trump administration’s unusually aggressive leasing approach as the “appropriate level of oil and gas development” standard against which future decisions will be judged. This so-called “disparate impact” provision would allow oil companies to seek taxpayer-funded compensation by claiming they were harmed whenever a future administration approves fewer permits or leases than those being given to other industries, such as wind or other renewable industries.

There is way, way more.

The bill proposes major changes to the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), enacted in 1970 after the Santa Barbara oil spill to prevent similar disasters from happening ever again. The bill would severely limit communities’ ability to have their concerns heard and considered during the decision-making process as required under NEPA. Under BAAJA, many fossil fuel projects are exempted entirely from the NEPA statute. If BAAJA passes, there will be minimal review, no opportunity for public input, and even courts will have little ability to stop projects that fail to comply with the law.

Similarly, changes to the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) will make it far more likely that oil-and-gas companies will simply ignore the process of consulting with tribes to learn how their plans might adversely affect cultural resources – a process currently required by law. BAAJA’s proposed changes to NEPA, the NHPA, the Endangered Species Act, and the Clean Water Act would reduce public input, Tribal consultation, wildlife and clean water protections, and state and Tribal authority over harmful projects. These are just a few of the many anti-environmental provisions in this bill.

Every member of Congress is aware that rising carbon-dioxide emissions lead to a hotter planet. When a bill includes this many handouts to the oil and gas industry, it begs the question of whether provisions that shield fossil fuel projects from meaningful review and challenge will outweigh any clean energy benefits the bill contemplates.

From our point of view, the answer is a resounding No.

Meta, the parent company of popular social media platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and messaging services like WhatsApp, is championing a 250-megawatt (MW) solar power project in Arkansas. The tech giant has agreed to purchase the cleaner electricity the farm generates.

​The solar farm is being developed by EDP Renewables North America (EDPR NA), an American subsidiary of a Portuguese-Spanish Renewable Energy Company.

​On Wednesday (November 4), the company broke ground on Cypress Knee Solar in Chicot County, towards the southeastern end of the state. The project is expected to be completed in the next two years, said officials.

​Capacity boosts to 545 MW

Earlier in May, Meta and EDPR NA announced the deal. Under the agreement, the tech company signed a pact to support the clean energy the latter produces. Cypress Knee is the third such project among them, with Meta’s commitment to buy 545 MW from EDPR NA.

​To offset its carbon emissions, Facebook and Instagram’s parent company pledges long-term power purchases of cleaner energy. This contributes to the company’s larger goal of matching 100 percent of its annual electricity use with renewable energy generation.

​Beyond providing reliable energy to support America’s power grid, the Kansas project is expected to boost jobs and strengthen the state’s economy.

More from Energy

See All

​”As energy demand continues to rise, projects like Cypress Knee Solar help strengthen grid reliability while creating jobs, generating meaningful local revenue, and delivering long-term benefits to the communities that host them,” said EDPR NA CEO Sandhya Ganapathy.

​The company estimates that the new solar farm project, once completed, is likely to bring $25 million in revenue over its lifetime.

Meta’s previous solar power purchases

​Last month, the Silicon Valley company also bought long-term power purchase agreements for a 203 MW solar project in Indiana from the Spanish renewable energy company Zelestra.

​The project is being built on reclaimed land from former coal mining operations in southwest Indiana and is expected to go live by 2027.

​The moves are in line with the company’s efforts to embrace the shift to cleaner energy.

​More and more data centers are being built across the country to provide services such as instant search results and streaming videos to hundreds of followers on social media platforms, and they are massive consumers of electricity. With the recent addition of artificial intelligence (AI) services, tech companies are building even larger data centers to train and run AI models in the future.

​To counter their energy consumption needs from fossil fuels, the tech giants are investing in sustainable energy generation.

​Two years ago, Meta secured 300 MW of clean solar energy for its Texan data center from a Boston-based renewable energy supplier, Longroad Energy.

​The project, called 1000 Mile, with support from the technology company for the entire output, will provide solar-powered energy for Yoakum County in Texas. It has an output capacity of 300 MWac or 400 MWdc and lies within the footprint of the Southwest Power Pool (SPP).

​All energy generated during the 1000 Mile project will be delivered to SPP’s grid, which will then be supplied to Meta’s data center operations, according to a previous report.

text:
The following blog is part of a series examining specific provisions in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). Clean Air Task Force is taking a close look at the bill to identify opportunities to strengthen its provisions, address potential gaps, and improve its effectiveness in meeting the country’s energy needs reliably and affordably.

As electricity demand grows and discussions around permitting and energy infrastructure continue, improving the process for connecting new generation to the grid will be increasingly important to meeting the country’s energy needs. CATF’s new report on interconnection queue reform does a deep dive into key principles necessary for getting new energy resources online more quickly and efficiently, and evaluates how several existing planning processes measure up to these ideals. The analysis offers a practical framework for policymakers, regulators, and grid operators to reduce unnecessary delays, improve planning, and make more efficient use of existing grid infrastructure.

Provisions in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) point toward a better interconnection framework. In particular, the bill’s consolidated planning provisions align with CATF’s view that linking interconnection planning with transmission planning processes will improve system outcomes. However, providing additional resources and clearer direction to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) is needed to improve the odds of implementing BAAJA successfully, particularly given the challenges facing independent agency action in a post-Slaughter, post-Loper Bright, and post-Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) world.

We therefore recommend that Congress build on existing BAAJA text to provide FERC with more detailed direction to implement policies most likely to improve interconnection outcomes. Below, we outline suggested improvements with explanations for each. These recommendations are intended to provide extra detail and clarity for FERC, transmission planners, and courts, increasing the odds that this critical reform will succeed in unlocking stalled interconnection queues.

***

The draft BAAJA bill text as of November 5, 2026, includes a short provision requiring a “Consolidated Planning Process” (CPP), as a new section 318 in the Federal Power Act. The bill text provides that within 18 months of its enactment, FERC must issue a rule requiring each transmission planning region to “file a consolidated interconnection and regional transmission planning process that –

Jointly evaluates electric transmission facilities and the generating capacity reasonably anticipated to be needed to meet future forecasted demand and forecasted generation over the next 20 years;

Routinely identifies and publishes resource and fuel-neutral planned interconnection locations for generating capacity and an upfront, fixed, zonal, per-megawatt cost for each planned interconnection location; and

Establishes a streamlined generator cluster study process with a single decision point, meaningful and nonrefundable financial security, and withdrawal penalties sufficient to deter speculative projects.”

Transmission planning regions would be required to submit their consolidated planning process to FERC within two years of the bill passing and would be required to update the plan at least every two years.

This provision may be intended to model the Southwest Power Pool’s (SPP’s) own Consolidated Planning Process, which we rated highly when we evaluated it in our report against key interconnection reform principles. When applying those same principles to BAAJA’s provision, we find the provision needs additional specificity to receive the same high marks. CPP is a detailed program that combines holistic, scenario-based long-term transmission and interconnection planning. The combined program assesses how numerous factors will influence transmission and interconnection needs, evaluates the costs and benefits of potential solutions, and sets procedures for project selection and cost allocation. SPP’s program essentially combines, streamlines, and improves the transmission and interconnection planning requirements under FERC Orders 1920 and 2023. BAAJA’s CPP, in contrast, currently lacks the same level of detail. As a result, the program’s impact will depend on FERC’s discretionary implementation (and, to the extent FERC’s action under the provision is ever challenged, the discretion of a reviewing court).

Our research shows that transmission and interconnection planning should ideally be consolidated and co-developed. The BAAJA CPP provision is in an entirely separate section from, and makes no reference to, BAAJA’s regional and interregional transmission sections. It also does not reference existing 20-year transmission and interconnection planning requirements under FERC Orders 1920 and 2023 – nor the SPP CPP itself. Rather, it mandates that FERC issue a new rule meeting BAAJA’s specific requirements – creating the possibility of an additional, specialized process added to all the others, instead of streamlining multiple existing planning processes into one combined process.

Additionally, unlike the more comprehensive language found in BAAJA’s other transmission provisions, the BAAJA CPP establishes three broad requirements but leaves all necessary details on how to meet these requirements to FERC.

For example, BAAJA’s CPP provision does not explicitly require transmission providers to use Order 1920 long-term transmission planning in their consolidated plans. It also contains a number of essential yet undefined terms such as “evaluates,” “reasonably anticipated,” “forecasted,” and “planned interconnection location,” and does not require the study of interconnection needs per se. Subparagraph (2) (see above) does not actually require the planned interconnection locations to be informed by the results of the evaluation in subparagraph (1), nor does it provide any basis for selecting the locations or allocating their costs. And while planning regions must “routinely” identify planned interconnection locations, that timeline is unbounded. Because most transmission owners profit by building more, not less, they have strong economic incentives to minimize the efficiency of transmission and interconnection processes. Consequently, BAAJA CPP’s lack of detail and clear requirements enables incumbent transmission owners to legally comply with its requirements through a bare minimum of effort that largely preserves the status quo.

These examples illustrate a broader issue with BAAJA’s approach given institutional constraints: insufficient detail may hinder implementation of an otherwise well-intended provision. Particularly in the context of the energy system, certainty that survives administrations is critical, as building out the grid takes years and involves long-term planning. To provide that certainty, laws must use clear, specific language that mandates good planning practices; otherwise, consumers and industry will not be able to rely on it. Recent Supreme Court decisions underscore this point.

After Loper Bright,1 courts (rather than agencies with subject matter expertise) interpret ambiguous language in statutes. As a result, Congress must—even moreso now than before Loper Bright—use unambiguous, precise language in statutes or risk ceding the law’s core meaning to the judiciary. And the Supreme Court’s decision in Slaughter2 called into question the independence of agencies like FERC, which has maintained some core policy consistency across administrations. Indeed, even before Slaughter, FERC has seen wide swings in policy-based rulemaking between administrations that have had significant impacts on the energy system, such as the expansion of Minimum Offer Price Rules that artificially elevated the capacity market prices of state supported clean energy generation in 2018 and 2019 that were rescinded in 2021. To avoid policy swings in areas that require long-term certainty and durability, Congress must provide agencies with concise, unambiguous instructions that limit discretionary interpretation.

Congress can strengthen the current Consolidated Planning Process section with just a few edits. Below is a sample redline, followed by explanations of the edits.

‘‘(a) CONSOLIDATED GENERATION AND TRANSMISSION PLANNING.—Not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (referred to in this section as the ‘Commission’) shall issue a rule requiring each transmission planning region (as defined in section 225(a)) to file a:

(1) consolidate interconnection and Order 1920 regional transmission planning into one process that—

‘‘(A) no less than every 3 years, as part of the Order 1920 planning process, jointly evaluates electric transmission facilities and interconnection needs necessary to efficiently and rapidly connect the generating capacity reasonably anticipated to be needed to meet future forecasted demand and forecasted generation over the next 20 years; and

‘‘(B) routinely uses this joint evaluation to identifyies and, assess, and select locations on the grid for interconnection facilities that maximize the efficient connection of multiple generating resources, and annually publishes these locations as resource and fuel-neutral “planned interconnection locations” for generating capacity, and an upfront, fixed, zonal, per-megawatt cost for each planned interconnection location, before the interconnection application window opens; and

‘‘(2) an amended interconnection application process with establishes a streamlined generator cluster study process with a single decision point, meaningful and nonrefundable financial security, and withdrawal penalties sufficient to deter speculative projects.

Explanation of suggested redline edits:

First, given that the purpose of consolidated planning is to efficiently combine long-term transmission planning and interconnection planning, Congress should clarify that planners must use the existing Order 1920 long-term planning to evaluate transmission and generation, such that it is all one “consolidated” process—as SPP does. This clarifies that transmission providers should not create a separate transmission planning process, as the current draft suggests.

Second, Congress should set firm planning intervals, rather than using the more open-ended term, “routinely.” A 3-year requirement mirrors the SPP CPP cycle, which does a consolidated transmission and interconnection planning evaluation (using 1920) every 3 years.

Third, in new subparagraphs (A) and (B) above, it is critical to require use of the combined planning process to identify and select the planned interconnection locations, which the current draft does not connect. Such a disconnect opens the door for transmission providers to minimize the number of interconnection points or place them in a way that favors some resources or customers over others, independent of holistic system needs.

Fourth, because the current version does not define “planned interconnection location,” it is not clear what that term means and leaves it up to FERC or planners to decide. We therefore propose defining “planned interconnection locations” in paragraph (B) as “locations on the grid that most efficiently connect multiple generating resources.”

Fifth, we also propose clarifying that planned interconnection locations should be updated and published annually. This mirrors SPP’s CPP, which updates its planned interconnection locations as part of its annual CPP-10 (10-year planning horizon) process. It is important to require planning regions to identify and update these locations at set intervals, since interconnection application periods are often annual.

Sixth, Congress should explicitly require upfront costs to be set and published before the interconnection application opens—which is a central feature of SPP’s process. Ensuring applicants know whether they can meet the requirements of interconnection is a core need to speed connection and lessen queue withdrawals.

Finally, new subparagraph (2) recognizes that the interconnection application process itself will be separate from consolidated interconnection and transmission planning. Putting the number (2) here (and a (1) above) means FERC is still directed to issue one rule, but transmission planning regions are directed to do two things: (1) submit one consolidated Order 1920-based transmission and interconnection planning process; and (2) submit an amended interconnection application process.

* * * *

Our suggested edits follow from decades of litigation experience demonstrating that every word matters when it comes to building durable policies that all stakeholders can rely on and safely invest in—a goal we all share. As our report details, consolidated planning by organizations like SPP and CAISO can dramatically improve interconnection planning and implementation. Making this a national requirement would be a massive win for everyone—but only if we get it right.

CATF looks forward to working with Congress, FERC, and other stakeholders to advance these recommendations and develop an interconnection framework that gets new energy resources online more efficiently, makes better use of existing grid infrastructure, and helps meet the country’s growing energy needs.

title: National Review: Congress Seeks a Shot Clock on the Permitting Fast Lane
description:
Congress is on the verge of fixing one of the strangest defects in federal permitting: an environmental review designed to be fast that has no time limitation.
The bill was introduced only six weeks after new research from the Pacific Legal Foundation (PLF) identified essentially the same flaw in federal geothermal permitting.
Congress missed on solving this problem the last time it reformed the federal permitting system.
CXs are supposed to reduce the time and burden of federal review for projects unlikely to have significant environmental effects.
Congress deserves credit for identifying an erroneous feature of federal permitting and proposing a fix.
text:
Congress is on the verge of fixing one of the strangest defects in federal permitting: an environmental review designed to be fast that has no time limitation.

Introduced on September 30, the Senate’s new Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) would, among many other permitting changes, impose a one-year deadline on federal permitting decisions for certain energy and infrastructure projects that do not require an environmental assessment or environmental impact statement.

The bill was introduced only six weeks after new research from the Pacific Legal Foundation (PLF) identified essentially the same flaw in federal geothermal permitting. The study found that the supposed “fast lane” under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) — categorical exclusions (CXs) — sometimes took longer than Congress ordinarily allows the more intensive environmental assessment process to take.

Congress missed on solving this problem the last time it reformed the federal permitting system. In 2023, the Fiscal Responsibility Act imposed a one-year deadline on environmental assessments and a two-year deadline on environmental impact statements. But it left CXs, which are assumed to be much faster than the other two processes, without any deadline at all.

CXs are supposed to reduce the time and burden of federal review for projects unlikely to have significant environmental effects. In fact, the Trump administration recently issued a CX-first policy intended to relieve “excessive permitting burdens” and “help decrease project delays.” Yet today, a project placed in the CX fast lane can theoretically remain there longer than a project subjected to a far more intensive review.

And that happens.

PLF examined 133 geothermal exploration projects, including 88 approved through CXs. Eighteen percent of those CXs took more than 200 days to approve, 8 percent took more than a year, and 6 percent took more than a year and 100 days.

At first glance, one might assume that projects facing the longest delays were unusually large or environmentally consequential. But the available data suggest otherwise.

The PLF study found virtually no relationship between delay and project size. Among CXs, neither the amount of land disturbed nor the number of wells drilled meaningfully predicted how long review would take. Moreover, CXs are available precisely because an agency has determined that the activity is unlikely to have significant environmental effects.

Consider Nevada’s Hinds Temperature Survey. The project proposed taking basic subsurface temperature measurements at 35 locations. A vehicle would drive a 1.5-inch-wide steel rod roughly 50 feet into the ground to measure underground heat. The rod would then be removed, allowing the hole to collapse naturally or be filled. It required no new roads and would disturb less than one square meter of ground in total — about the size of a bath towel. Yet federal approval took one year and 182 days.

That is not careful environmental review scaling with project scope and intensity. At the very least, we should question whether long reviews simply reflect greater environmental risk.

CX delays likely make energy more expensive for Americans than it otherwise would be. Every project in the PLF study was geothermal exploration — the early work needed to locate and test geothermal resources that can provide clean, around-the-clock electricity. But permitting barriers make that exploration slower and more expensive. A Department of Energy analysis found that faster permitting alone could more than double geothermal capacity by 2050. Beyond geothermal, studies have found that permitting delays constrain a wide variety of energy infrastructure, contributing to higher costs and greater price volatility for consumers.

Enter the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, the bipartisan permitting bill now reviving hopes for faster infrastructure development and cheaper energy.

For projects involving federal permits or authorizations but no environmental assessment or impact statement, the BAAJA would require agencies to make their permitting decisions within one year. Projects that avoid the National Environmental Policy Act’s more intensive forms of review would finally get a time limit of their own.

A one-year deadline is not perfect. Small projects searching for reliable, clean energy that are unlikely to affect the environment should ideally obtain government approval in a matter of months, if that. But one year is still a dramatic improvement over the open-ended timetable that exists today.

Congress deserves credit for identifying an erroneous feature of federal permitting and proposing a fix. Now it must follow through: preserve this important provision of the bill and pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

text:
A rare-earth facility to be built at the former Kodak Park is in line for $54.2 million in combined state and local government assistance.

Much of the package aiding Massachusetts-based Phoenix Tailings consists of tax credits and exemptions, rather than direct funding, according to the company. The total does not include investment to upgrade power infrastructure by RED-Rochester, which oversees park utilities. The railroad spur serving the 1600 Lexington Ave. facility also will require investment.

The forthcoming facility, announced last month, would cull the highly sought-after metals from mine waste and other industrial sources at an Eastman Business Park industrial warehouse complex in Greece.

Phoenix's capital outlay is estimated at $375 million, according to Gov. Kathy Hochul. But the company estimates its total costs, including needed chemicals and other operational expenses, at $600 million.

The combined public commitment, announced by Phoenix on Thursday, "underscores New York’s commitment to the project and bipartisan support for expanding U.S. production of critical materials," a company statement read.

Those rare earth metals are key in the production of electric vehicles, electronics, and defense equipment, but China currently controls most of the supply.

Local operations are scheduled to ramp up in 2027, with full production planned for 2028. The Eastman Business Park facility is projected to support 90 jobs at launch, and more than 200 when fully operational.

The award breaks down in general terms as follows:

Up to $3 million in performance-based tax credits through Empire State Development’s Excelsior Jobs Program

$15.9 million in New York State investment tax credits.

$35.3 million in tax savings on eligible equipment and construction materials, including local tax breaks, along with anticipated funding for power infrastructure improvements serving the project.

The company anticipates additional support for equipment purchases and workforce training through county programs.

Phoenix's Greece facility is part of the company's larger $1.2 billion "Freedom Project" described as "an integrated separation-and-metallization platform designed to close a critical gap in U.S. midstream rare earth processing capacity.

The Trump administration has additionally committed more than $550 million combined to support the company.

“Building America’s rare earth supply chain is a national security imperative and bipartisan government priority,” Phoenix Chief Strategy Officer Pat Kumashiro said in a prepared statement. “We are excited to see federal, state, and local stakeholders collaborate to support domestic production of the critical materials America needs.”

The company statement described Freedom Separation as "designed to process more than 18,000 tons of rare earth feedstock annually, producing more than 4,400 tons of separated rare earth oxides at full capacity for downstream production."

The project, the company said, "is designed to strengthen access to domestic processing for America and her allies while reducing reliance on foreign supply chains and advancing environmentally responsible production."

text:
As Americans prepare Thanksgiving meals, stock their refrigerators and eventually clear their plates, much of the food that goes uneaten will end up discarded. But food that can’t be eaten doesn’t have to go to waste entirely. Across the country, biogas capture facilities are recycling discarded food into renewable energy ─ and new research from the American Biogas Council finds that the opportunity to do more is enormous.

Food waste naturally produces biogas when the microorganisms in it break down the organic material. Biogas systems capture all the biogas to keep it from going into the air and use it to generate renewable electricity and heat, or be processed into renewable natural gas (RNG).

ABC’s research team reports 404 operating facilities across 48 states that produce biogas from food waste. About 200 of these facilities operate at farms and wastewater treatment plants and combine food waste with manure or wastewater to capture biogas. Another 204 facilities make use of food waste alone, capturing approximately 36 billion cubic feet of biogas annually, and representing nearly $3 billion in capital investment.

ABC’s expanded research this year uncovered projects not previously included in its inventory. The increase of 73% over last year’s count reflects a more complete picture of the industry.

“America is literally throwing away enough renewable energy to power millions of homes,” said Patrick Serfass, executive director of the American Biogas Council. “The technology to make energy from food waste is already operating, but the potential to turn more of what we routinely discard into a valuable domestic energy resource is enormous.”

Food waste is already producing energy across America

The facilities identified by ABC handle food waste from food manufacturers, grocery stores, restaurants and other sources. Some capture energy from food and beverage manufacturing. Others process retail food waste, including food that spoils, is rejected or remains unsold.

Of the 204 food-waste-only facilities, 161 process pre-consumer food waste, primarily wastewater from food processing and beverage manufacturing. Another 43 facilities handle retail food waste, capturing approximately 8.2 billion cubic feet of biogas annually.

Most facilities use their biogas to generate electricity and heat. In fact, 164 food-waste-only facilities produce power, heat or both. Another 38 upgrade biogas into RNG.

A growing industry, with bigger projects and more investment

Food-waste biogas projects are getting larger and attracting more investment. The 42 facilities that have come online since 2020 account for 32% of the sector’s annual biogas production and 45% of its total investment. On average, these newer projects capture nearly twice as much biogas as earlier projects and cost about three times as much to build.

text:
TEXAS — Tesla is considering a potential $10 billion deal that could bring nearly 10,000 jobs and thousands of dollars in revenue to Fort Bend County. It involves the construction of what officials call the largest single solar cell manufacturing site in the country.

In January, Tesla CEO Elon Musk shared plans for solar manufacturing.

“The SpaceX and Tesla teams both separately are working to build to 100 gigawatts a year of solar power in the U.S., and of manufactured solar power,” Musk said.

Months later, the Fort Bend County Commissioners Court approved a tax abatement agreement for Tesla’s Project Crystal Sun.

The electric vehicle and clean energy company proposed building a $10 billion solar cell manufacturing plant on more than 3,000 acres of land near Richmond. Officials say the potential 30-year agreement would create more than 9,700 permanent jobs paying at least $55 an hour.

The Lamar Consolidated Independent School District approved tax incentives for Tesla in September. Supporters say the plant would provide job opportunities for local students and residents. However, there’s no guarantee Tesla will build the plant at the proposed location at FM 1994 and FM 762 near Needville in Fort Bend County. The company says the county is competing with another location outside of Texas.

Spectrum News looked at documents to see how the agreement would work if Fort Bend lands the deal. They show the county agrees to waive property taxes for machinery and equipment and eliminate inventory-related taxes for 10 years. We also learned the Lamar CISD approved tax incentives through the fairly new Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation Act (JETI), which requires Tesla to pay full debt service taxes on voter-approved bonds and pay half of the taxes used to fund day-to-day operations.

Neighbors like Daniel Saffron say not everything is written in fine print.

“It’s gonna leave local taxpayers to hold the financial bag on day one,” Saffron said. “There’s no promises to protect the environment that it’s being built on. There are no promises to rebuild any of the infrastructure around it. They say they have this water recycling system, but there’s no specifics behind it.”

Carlos Guzman, the county’s economic opportunity and development agency director, says that the infrastructure, workforce and proximity to Houston are what sparked Tesla’s interest in Fort Bend.

“If it were to locate here in Fort Bend County, we fully expect to have other companies start looking to set up shop as close as possible,” Guzman said, adding that once Gov. Greg Abbott signs off, Tesla will make its decision. “We’re very excited. I hope we get selected because I know it would change the trajectory of this county.”

In the meantime, opponents of the tax incentive program hope industrial expansion won’t strip away the soul of Fort Bend County.

“Anytime there’s a new bill, there’s paperwork, there’s loopholes that people find,” said Saffron, referring to JETI.

If Fort Bend is selected, construction could start this year.

title: Business leaders urge COP31 Presidency to commit to global action on clean electrification ...
description:
The signatories ask the Presidency to place two priorities at the centre of the COP31 outcome: Accelerate clean electrification by backing the target of 35% electrification by 2035 and developing country strategies to deliver it.
The letter pushes back against a growing discourse suggesting the Paris goal of limiting global warming to well below 2°C is out of reach.
"Keeping global warming well below 2°C is still vital and still possible," said Adair Turner, Co-Chair of the Energy Transitions Commission.
"Clean electrification has momentum, like a boulder rolling downhill.
What the ETC's new analysis shows Clean electrification can deliver the biggest cut to projected warming, to around 2.3°C.
text:
Global warming will reach 2.6°C by 2100 if no new policy support is offered and technologies are adopted only when they become cost-competitive, say signatories of a letter published today.

Clean electrification, with electricity meeting over 50% of final energy demand by mid-century, and phasing down coal use for electricity generation could cut projected warming to around 2.3°C, with low or no cost.

But projected temperatures will not reach below 2°C without action to decarbonise heavy industry, aviation and shipping, deeply cut methane emissions and end deforestation.

Combined, these five priority action areas could reduce warming to around 1.8°C – but this is not cost-free and requires policy support.

Exponential growth in carbon removals is required to bring potential warming down to 1.5°C.

LONDON, Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Over 30 members of the Energy Transitions Commission (ETC) today urge COP31 President Murat Kurum and President of Negotiations Chris Bowen to put clean electrification and the hard-to-electrify sectors at the centre of the climate summit's outcome, as new ETC analysis shows current policies leave the world on course for 2.6°C of warming.

Their letter, published today alongside the ETC briefing Still vital, still possible: How governments and businesses can work together to limit global warming, comes days before negotiators gather in Türkiye. Signatories include ETC Commissioners from Arup, Envision, Grantham Research Institute (LSE), Octopus Energy, Rothschild, Schneider Electric, Tata Steel, and Vattenfall alongside other leaders from clean power and utilities, heavy industry, transport, and finance.

The signatories ask the Presidency to place two priorities at the centre of the COP31 outcome:

Accelerate clean electrification by backing the target of 35% electrification by 2035 and developing country strategies to deliver it.

Act on the hard-to-electrify sectors by committing globally to faster decarbonisation of steel, cement, aluminium, chemicals, aviation and shipping, including through carbon prices.

The letter pushes back against a growing discourse suggesting the Paris goal of limiting global warming to well below 2°C is out of reach. It argues this narrative risks weakening climate policy and corporate commitments just as clean technologies reach scale. Conversely, strong commitments on clean electrification and the hard-to-electrify sectors could relaunch the 'ambition loop' of policy, private investment and falling technology costs that followed the Paris Agreement and already curbed future warming projections from upper bounds of 4°C to 2.6°C.

"Keeping global warming well below 2°C is still vital and still possible," said Adair Turner, Co-Chair of the Energy Transitions Commission. "Costs of solar, wind, batteries and electric vehicles have fallen faster than forecast 10 years back, reducing the danger of catastrophic global warming above 3°C. But with unchanged policies, we're still on track to about 2.6°C by 2100. To keep well below 2°C, we must turbocharge clean electrification which in many applications will deliver both lower emissions and lower costs. But we must also meet more difficult challenges – reducing the utilisation of existing coal plants; decarbonising heavy industry, shipping and aviation; and radically reducing methane emissions from fossil fuel production and agriculture. In many cases, this will entail accepting some increased costs, but these costs are far less than the cost of unchecked climate change."

"Clean electrification has momentum, like a boulder rolling downhill. We need to clear its path with faster grids and permitting for it to accelerate. Heavy industry, methane, deforestation and removals are like boulders stuck at the foot of the hill, needing carbon prices and finance to push them uphill. Move both and we take almost a degree off future warming with a huge impact: fewer wildfires, floods and failed harvests, and a lower risk of irreversible tipping points," said Jules Kortenhorst, Co-Chair of the Energy Transitions Commission.

What the ETC's new analysis shows

Clean electrification can deliver the biggest cut to projected warming, to around 2.3°C. That involves building the new energy system and phasing out the old: electricity's share of final energy rises from 20% to over 50% by 2050, and coal falls to under 5% of power. Past forecasts underestimated falling solar and battery costs, so faster electrification could cut bills and emissions. Only early coal retirement carries a clear cost.

Decarbonising heavy industry, aviation and shipping can remove about 0.2°C, but faces a green premium. However, green steel costs around 45% more than conventional steel, but only adds around 1.2% to the price of a car. Carbon prices of around $100 per tonne, close to EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) prices today and in the coming years, would drive decarbonisation of steel and cement; aviation and shipping need $200–300 per tonne.

A cut of around 45% in annual fossil, agricultural and waste methane emissions by 2050 removes about 0.2°C. Ending deforestation by 2035 removes a further 0.07°C.

Returning warming to 1.5°C by 2100 is more costly, requiring over 500 Gt of CO₂ removals this century, costing over $500 billion a year, or about 0.4% of today's global GDP. Today, purchased removals total less than 20 Mt per year.

Download the briefing.

The ETC is a global coalition of leaders from energy producers, energy-intensive industries, technology providers, finance and environmental NGOs, committed to achieving net-zero emissions by mid-century, in line with the Paris climate objective of limiting global warming to well below 2°C and ideally to 1.5°C. The ETC is hosted by Systemiq Ltd.

name: Congress
title: Real Clear Energy: Permitting Reform Could Be a Victory for the Environment
description:
This might be reasonable if foregoing natural resources altogether were an option.
Indeed, living itself requires the disturbance of land and use of natural resources in some form.
That is why four senators just unveiled a major permitting bill aimed at accelerating energy and resource development by streamlining environmental reviews.
A blocked resource project can be celebrated as an environmental victory at home even as foreign landscapes continue supplying the same resource.
So long as we continue to need natural resources, wouldn’t it be more just for Americans to develop our own abundant resources?
text:
America has the seventh-largest known unmined copper reserves in the world. Those reserves alone could meet current U.S. demand for more than two decades, supplying the copper needed for electricity, buildings, and other critical infrastructure. Yet we still import 57% of the copper we use—much of it from Chile.

American environmentalism often asks us to leave valuable resources untouched for the sake of protecting the landscapes housing them. This might be reasonable if foregoing natural resources altogether were an option. But it is not. Modern society depends on natural resources. Indeed, living itself requires the disturbance of land and use of natural resources in some form.

That is why four senators just unveiled a major permitting bill aimed at accelerating energy and resource development by streamlining environmental reviews. Many environmental groups pushed back. Some warn the bill would weaken the environmental authority “used to stop projects like the Pebble [copper] Mine in Alaska.”

The environmentalists’ concern is straightforward. Development comes with environmental costs. But so does refusing to develop the resources we continue to consume. Therein lies a lesson that American environmentalism has yet to learn: moral victories for some are not moral victories for all. A blocked resource project can be celebrated as an environmental victory at home even as foreign landscapes continue supplying the same resource.

Enormous mines operate in the Atacama Desert, the driest non-polar place on Earth. In Antofagasta, mining accounts for nearly half of all water consumed, further depleting the region’s scarce groundwater. Copper production also requires moving immense amounts of rock, storing mine waste, and permanently altering portions of the landscape.

Chile’s environment has been altered to extract the copper making American life possible. To read this article, turn on the lights, or drive a car, we depend on copper extracted in Chile.

But that dynamic is not inevitable. America has abundant copper of its own. In some cases, we elect to leave viable deposits underground — often for environmental reasons. Chile, by contrast, has been more willing to extract its copper. And Americans benefit.

Consider Pebble Mine, the very proposed copper project that environmental groups cite both as an example of what current permitting laws can stop and as a reason Congress should reject permitting reform.

Pebble sits atop an enormous copper, gold, and molybdenum deposit in Alaska. Copper is critical for nearly everything electric, gold for many electronic devices, and molybdenum for construction. But in 2023, a federal agency used a rarely invoked provision of the Clean Water Act to effectively restrict development of the deposit.

That decision may have protected a portion of American nature, but it left our demand for copper unchanged. So long as we continue to need natural resources, wouldn’t it be more just for Americans to develop our own abundant resources?

Doing so would not entail rubber-stamping every project. As New Mexico Senator Martin Heinrich, one of the bill’s authors, put it, the goal is “to have the same standards, but to get to ‘yes’ — or if it’s a bad project, get to ‘no’ — a whole lot faster.”

Currently, federal permitting burdens can delay domestic resource production for decades—or prevent it altogether—as found by a recent suite of research from Pacific Legal Foundation.

PLF’s review of major mining projects found that some of the very burdens Congress is now looking to fix can trap mineral deposits underground for decades. One copper-nickel project, for example, has been stalled by regulations for more than 20 years. Across the country, opening a new mine takes an average of 29 years.

Separate PLF research found major mineral deposits locked away on federal lands (often for environmental reasons), including nickel equal to roughly 56 years of current U.S. production and copper equal to more than five years.

But what if developing those resources could reduce pressure on islands in Indonesia and deserts in Chile while helping power America’s economy and meet environmentalists’ climate goals?

Both nickel and copper are crucial for everything electric and environmentalists’ decarbonization goals, and a significant copper supply shortage driven by increasing electrification is projected by 2035. The problem is not that copper does not exist — it is that too little is being developed.

Yet a coalition of environmental groups has mobilized to stop the permitting bill. In a leaked strategy call, organizers discussed spurring opposition to the bill while hiding their strategy from the senators involved. One organizer said the goal is “to stop this bill, not to make it better.”

Before decrying permitting reform’s potential environmental effects, objectors should consider the consequences of continuing to rely on foreign countries to produce the materials American environmental policy makes exceedingly difficult to produce at home.

text:
WASHINGTON – Nov. 6, 2026 | Verra has approved the first carbon credits under its carbon capture and storage (CCS) methodology for a project in northern Texas. Credits can now be issued to the Barnett Zero Project (Verra Project 6016) in the city of Bridgeport. The project captures CO2 separated from raw natural gas at a processing plant, then compresses the CO2 and stores it permanently in an injection well nearby.

The credits were generated under Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) methodology VM0049 Carbon Capture and Storage v1.0, which establishes criteria and procedures for quantifying greenhouse gas emission reductions and carbon dioxide removals from projects that capture CO2 and store it permanently.

The project was developed by BKV Corporation (NYSE:BKV) and verified by the independent validation/verification body (VVB), GHD Limited. It uses module VMD0062 CO2 Capture from Natural Gas Processing together with VM0049 to account for the emissions impact of diverting CO2 separated from natural gas streams and storing it permanently. The module addresses a specific and largely unavoidable emissions source from an energy source that will continue to be relied on as part of the net-zero transition.

“The approval of the first credits under Verra’s CCS methodology is an important milestone for BKV and for the broader carbon management industry,” said Chris Kalnin, Chief Executive Officer of BKV. “Meeting Verra’s rigorous standards demonstrates that permanently sequestering CO2 from natural gas processing can be credibly measured, independently certified and recognized through a robust market framework. This achievement reflects BKV’s commitment to advancing practical emissions solutions across our operations and delivering lower-carbon energy to our customers through our closed-loop business model.”

ICVCM Approval

VM0049 and modules VMD0056 to VMD0059 were recently approved by the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM) as meeting the Core Carbon Principles (CCPs). VMD0062 is currently being reviewed by the ICVCM.

text:
Ottawa, ON — The Federal Budget, Masters of our Destiny, and its implementation of the National Electricity Strategy, is a landmark commitment that recognizes electricity as the foundation of Canada’s economic growth. It’s a welcome green wallet but some environmental experts are concerned.

Through investments exceeding $50 billion, the federal government has taken a significant step toward its goal of doubling Canada’s electricity system by 2050 while accelerating electrification and strengthening Canada’s position as an energy superpower.

“Being masters of our destiny is about having the confidence to build on our strengths and shape our own future,” said François-Philippe Champagne, the federal Minister of Finance and National Revenue. “Canada has the resources, talent and ambition to succeed. Budget 2026 builds on those strengths by unlocking investment, building more at home, strengthening our energy and natural resource advantage, and helping Canadian businesses grow and compete on the world stage. That’s how we will create good jobs, make life more affordable, and build a stronger, more resilient and more united Canada for generations to come.”

François-Philippe Champagne, the federal Minister of Finance and National Revenue presents the federal budget in the House of Commons on November 5, 2026. Credit: Government of Canada.

The federal budget aims to super charge the economy and support sovereignty in the following ways:

Lower deficits

Direct program spending growth lowered from 8% to 2%

Kickstarting Investment Supercycle

$400B capital investments over 6 years

$22B of new affordability measures

Supercharging the clean economy

The budget is paired with Powering Canada Strong: From Strategy to Action, the federal action plan to double Canada’s electricity system by 2050, backed by $52 billion in new funding. The plan includes nearly $4 billion to expand electricity infrastructure and renewable energy, including new funding for the Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways Program. It also draws on Clean Power Nation research showing up to $100 billion in Canadian manufacturing opportunities for wind, solar and battery technologies.

The budget delivers on that vision by supporting infrastructure needed to power a growing economy, including:

Positioning electricity investment as an affordability measure, with electrification helping to reduce Canadians’ overall “energy wallet”

More than $50 billion in support of the National Electricity Strategy and the goal of doubling Canada’s electricity system by 2050, which includes:

Extension of the Clean Electricity and Clean Technology Investment Tax Credit to 2040, providing long-term certainty for investors and utilities

Expanding the Clean Electricity Investment Tax Credit to include critical intra-provincial transmission

Funding of nearly $4 billion over 10 years, starting in 2027-28, to support electricity infrastructure expansion, renewable energy and priority electricity sector projects across Canada, including new funding for the Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways Program

Advancing projects such as the Taltson Hydro, Mayo Hydro Facility and Atlin Hydro

Announcing the implementation of the EIFEL exception for utilities, including expanding the Utility exception to including holding companies

Green Wallet, Grey Areas: Comments from the industry

Electricity Canada emphasizes that growing and modernizing Canada’s electricity system is a nation-building endeavour and welcomes the significant commitments to Canada’s electricity future.

“By investing more than $50 billion through the National Electricity Strategy and providing long-term certainty through measures such as extending the Clean Electricity Investment Tax Credit to 2040, the federal government has demonstrated the bold leadership required to meet a challenge that will define Canada’s economic future. It recognizes that Canada must finance the build, modernize regulatory processes, adapt to a rapidly evolving grid shaped by electrification, artificial intelligence, data centres, and industrial growth, and ensure the electricity system can support the country’s broader economic ambitions,” said Josée Guibord, President and CEO of Electricity Canada.

“We commend the government for thinking at the scale this moment demands. The focus now must be delivery. Canada must move with urgency to turn financing into projects, approvals into construction, and ambition into infrastructure. Success will ultimately be measured not by what was announced today, but by the generation, transmission, and distribution assets we build together over the coming decades.”

The Canadian Renewable Energy Association (CanREA) welcomes Budget 2026 and federal advocacy to build more affordable electricity for Canadians.

“This is a strong budget for affordable, reliable electricity, and we’re proud to see key Clean Power Nation recommendations adopted,” said Vittoria Bellissimo, CanREA’s President and CEO. “Affordability is Canadians’ top priority, and wind, solar and energy storage deliver affordable, clean power quickly. The federal government has shown vision by extending tax credits to 2040, giving investors the certainty to build more projects, create jobs and strengthen Canada’s renewable energy industry.”

The Canada Energy Regulator projects that electricity demand could grow by 26% to 85% by 2050. About 24 GW of wind, solar and energy storage is already being procured across Canada, and with stable, competitive policies, the sector could attract up to $200 billion in investment by the mid-2030s and support 250,000 to 350,000 job-years.

“Transmission connects the lowest-cost new power to the people and businesses who need it,” said Bellissimo. “Extending the Clean Electricity Investment Tax Credit to high-voltage transmission within provinces is a smart, practical move. It lowers the cost of building those lines, and that helps keep power bills down for families and businesses.”

Marine Renewables Canada (MRC), the national association representing offshore wind, tidal, wave, and river current energy, also applauds the budget and says the proposed extension of the Clean Technology and Clean Electricity investment tax credits (ITCs) through 2040 marks a significant milestone in MRC’s sustained advocacy for the long-term investment certainty needed to advance Canada’s marine renewable energy sector.

“Budget 2026 recognizes that building Canada’s electricity system is fundamental to our energy security and economic competitiveness,” said Elisa Obermann, Chief Executive Officer of MRC. “MRC has advocated for extending clean energy investment tax credits through 2040 because developers and investors need certainty that reflects the time required to bring projects into operation. Together with investments in transmission, renewable energy, and community capacity, this proposal would help create the conditions to advance Canada’s marine renewable energy sector.”

The David Suzuki Foundation also welcomes the clean electricity investments.

“For over five years we’ve advocated alongside dozens of allied groups and tens of thousands of people throughout Canada for this level of clean electricity investment. It’s a hard-fought, generational win, and now all people living in Canada can reap the benefits,” said Stephen Thomas, Clean Energy Manager at the David Suzuki Foundation.

“Investments in affordable, reliable, clean electricity will save households money on their energy bills and secure our economy for the long term. It will create over a million good jobs, it can use Canadian steel and aluminum, and it supports the leadership of Indigenous communities to build renewable projects on their territories. If we want more affordability and a resilient economy, we need to get serious about building clean electricity throughout Canada and reducing reliance on volatile fossil fuels for our energy needs and economic strength.”

However, the Foundation warns that continued backing for polluting fossil fuel projects, keeping gas on the grid and environmental rollbacks puts this progress at risk. Lisa Gue, national policy manager at David Suzuki Foundation, said: “Gaps remain when it comes to scaling up funding to meet Canada’s nature commitments and tackling plastic pollution. With the government investing in expanding forestry and mining, we need strong legal guardrails to protect nature and uphold Indigenous rights, yet in Bill C-39 the government is proposing to unravel these very protections.”

Similarly, Climate Action Network Canada and its member organizations has concerns about the impacts to Canadian communities and the ongoing support for oil and gas.

“The result of years of advocacy for consequential investments in renewables and electricity transmission can be found on the cover of the 2026 budget. An electrified economy based on renewables can help lower Canadians’ energy bills, boost our independence and ensure our resilience to external shocks — whether extreme weather or volatile fuel prices. The next step is ensuring that projects get built right, with communities, Indigenous Peoples and civil society taking part of the process from the beginning,” said Caroline Brouillette, Executive Director of Climate Action Network Canada.

“Investments and regulations should go hand in hand. The cover of this year’s budget tells only half of the story. Building a net-zero economy requires action to diversify away from costly infrastructure that risks holding us back. The Carney government continues to prioritize costly fossil fuel projects that risk leaving Canada behind, like subsidizing the Pacific Link Pipeline and creating new incentives that continue to benefit the expansion of oil and gas.”

The International Institute for Sustainable Development (IISD) also states its concerns, citing that the positive signals of the budget are offset by the decision to direct more tax dollars to oil and gas, further fuelling climate change. The budget increases fossil fuel production subsidies by offering tax breaks for constructing new liquefied natural gas (LNG) facilities while at the same time extending an existing investment tax credit for carbon capture and storage. These subsidies lock-in new and expanded fossil fuel production and, in the case of LNG, violate the Canadian government’s own policy to avoid new inefficient fossil fuel subsidies. This diverts scarce resources away from low-carbon innovation in a world where rapidly expanding renewable energy is driving down global demand for oil and gas.

“Committing to build a low-carbon economy while at the same time subsidizing a growing fossil fuel industry is like trying to drive forward while the gearshift is in reverse,” says Nichole Dusyk, Senior Policy Advisor and Lead, Canada Energy team at IISD. “By funding and relying on carbon capture and storage and LNG as ‘climate solutions,’ the federal government is sapping resources from real, globally competitive climate solutions.”

State of the current economy

Despite a challenging global environment, the Canadian economy has shown resilience:

Canada’s economy grew by 3.3% in the second quarter, the fastest pace in the G7.

The IMF expects Canada to be the second-fastest growing economy in the G7 in 2027.

Canada is expected to maintain one of the lowest deficit-to-GDP ratios in the G7, signaling fiscal strength and the capacity to invest in the future.

More Canadians are benefitting from labour market strength. Over the past year, Canada’s economy has added 214,000 jobs in private employment, while the unemployment rate has fallen to 6.5%, near its lowest level in two years.

Since the end of 2024, Canada has also created nearly twice as many jobs per capita as the United States.

text:
Lehigh has received $1.6 million to participate in the “Commonwealth of Pennsylvania EGS Pilot Demonstration,” a U.S. Department of Energy-funded project led by the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (DEP).

The total project budget is about $14 million. The “EGS” stands for enhanced geothermal system.

“This project shows what’s possible when faculty work across disciplinary and college boundaries,” said Robert Flowers, Herbert J. and Ann L. Siegel Dean of the College of Arts and Sciences.

“Earth scientists from the College of Arts and Sciences and engineers from the P.C. Rossin College of Engineering and Applied Science are bringing complementary expertise to a problem neither could solve alone.

“Research like this matters because discoveries don't stay in the lab. It’s designed to bring new possibilities to Pennsylvania communities, and it reflects Lehigh’s commitment to scholarship that serves the people and places around us.”

The goal is to generate one megawatt of electricity from a low-enthalpy, underperforming Marcellus Shale gas well in Indiana County, Pennsylvania.

The project will draw heat from an underperforming natural gas well by circulating water at depth, and then bring that heated water to the surface.

That heated water energy will produce electricity for the local grid and supply direct-use heat to nearby homes and businesses.

“Pennsylvania’s conventional hydrocarbon industry, followed by the shale oil and gas revolution left behind a vast network of wells and related infrastructure ,” said Frank Pazzaglia, professor of Earth and environmental sciences in Lehigh’s College of Arts and Sciences and the principal investigator. “This project asks whether we can give that infrastructure a second life as a clean, renewable energy source.”

The pilot will use a deep existing unconventional gas well in Indiana County, PA where the geology is favorable for tapping geothermal resources.

The well is operated by CNX Green Ventures, an Appalachian oil and gas producer.

“Repurposing abandoned hydrocarbon wells for low-enthalpy geothermal mining represents an economic and environmental opportunity, transforming the methane-leaking liability into a predictable source of clean, local energy,” said Carlos Romero, professor of mechanical engineering and mechanics in the Rossin College and director of Lehigh’s Energy Research Center.

Project leaders say the approach could also create opportunities for displaced oil, gas, and coal workers, whose subsurface experience transfers directly to the geothermal industry.

By extending the useful life of existing wells, the project aims to stimulate geothermal energy development, particularly in the eastern US where geothermal resources are more restricted than in the western US, and demonstrate that the approach is portable.

“The project is a chance to train the next generation of scientists and engineers while helping to show that geothermal energy can work in places many people wouldn’t expect,” Pazzaglia said.

Lehigh’s funding will support five researchers and students from two units.

The Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences (EES) will include three principal investigators, a postdoctoral researcher and a graduate student, while the Energy Research Center will include two principal investigators and a graduate student.

Project personnel from Lehigh include Frank Pazzaglia; Steve Peters, associate professor of EES; Anne Meltzer, professor of EES; Carlos Romero and Muhannad Suleiman, professor of civil and environmental engineering.

DEP is the project lead, working in coordination with the Pennsylvania Geological Survey. Partners include Gradient Geothermal Inc., Teverra Inc., Idaho National Laboratory, CNX Green Ventures, and Seequent, in addition to Lehigh University.

President Donald Trump has thrown the federal government's weight behind massive data center build-outs needed to power the country's artificial intelligence (AI) boom. But a historic Democratic sweep in Texas has put one of the nation's biggest AI infrastructure hubs under new political leadership, raising questions about the future of billions of dollars in planned investments.

The victories marked a historic midterm night for Texas Democrats, who captured the governor's mansion for the first time in more than three decades and won a U.S. Senate seat for the first time since 1988.

Texas is poised to overtake Virginia as the nation's largest data center market and is projected to account for roughly a quarter of new U.S. data center power capacity through 2030. With at least 248 projects planned across the state, investment bank Jefferies estimates that 13.3 gigawatts of announced developments could be at risk under a moratorium backed by Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa.

ONE STATE IS GROUND ZERO AS TRUMP'S MULTIBILLION-DOLLAR TECH AMBITIONS FACE A MIDTERM TEST

Texas was hardly alone in facing growing opposition to data center development. In Ohio, voters weighed 21 data center-related ballot questions across 18 communities in the midterm elections, more than any other state, highlighting the mounting resistance to America's rapidly expanding AI infrastructure.

The results this week are now forcing some developers to reconsider where to invest billions of dollars in future projects as political power shifts.

"It makes us and our investors pause and think if we should be investing somewhere else," Brittany Kaiser, CEO of Alpha Compute, told Fox News Digital following the Republican bloodbath in Tuesday's election.

Kaiser warned that political shifts in traditionally Republican states could push billions of dollars in planned investments elsewhere, including overseas, as companies weigh growing opposition to data center development — especially within the Democratic Party.

"There's new decision making that needs to come into play and a lot more to think about than there was before the election," she said.

But relocating projects already underway is far more complicated, particularly when developers have secured land, negotiated power agreements and committed substantial capital.

"It's not very easy to pivot after you've already made contractual and financial commitments to these types of builds," Kaiser said.

For projects still in the pipeline, however, companies have more flexibility. Kaiser said Alpha Compute has already invested in data centers in Canada, Europe and Mexico, where regulatory approvals are more straightforward.

The backlash highlights growing tensions between Washington's push to accelerate AI development and voters' concerns about electricity costs and the impact of data centers on their communities.

Kaiser urged incoming lawmakers to strike a balance between addressing community concerns and preserving what she called "the biggest economic opportunity of our generation."

text:
[BENGALURU] Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around the middle of 2027, chief executive officer Elon Musk said on Friday (Nov 6), as the futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy pickup trucks struggles to win mass market appeal.

Musk said in an X post the production wind-down would enable the automaker to accommodate increased output of its newly-launched Cybercab model, which the billionaire has made central to Tesla’s robotaxi ambitions.

While it was not immediately clear whether Cybertruck production would be moved to another facility or phased out entirely, the automaker’s Austin plant is the only known Tesla facility equipped to manufacture the model’s specialised components.

Tesla did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment sent outside regular business hours.

“Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time,” Musk said in response to a user on X, calling the model the “best vehicle Tesla has ever made” and the wind-down the “end of an era”.

“Polarising” technology

Musk had, during Cybertruck’s launch in 2023, touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors and Ford. But the vehicle has struggled to meet those expectations.

Often described as polarising, Cybertruck’s unorthodox sharp-edged stainless steel design has limited its prospects outside the US.

Regulatory approval became difficult to come by in parts of Europe, depriving Tesla of major markets that could have helped turn the pickup into a higher-volume product.

The model has also faced multiple recalls and quality-control issues, while Tesla has repeatedly revised prices.

Tesla does not officially disclose individual sales figures for the Cybertruck. Instead, the automaker groups it into an “Other Models” category, which accounted for just 8,295 deliveries in the third quarter, down from 12,364 deliveries in the second quarter.

“Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab,” Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X.

Musk’s new bet

The Cybercab, which has butterfly doors and no steering wheel, pedals or mirrors, is one of Musk’s key bets in his push to turn Tesla into an artificial intelligence and robotics company.

He has said he sees it as Tesla’s main autonomous model within a larger driverless network and that it will eventually be the company’s highest-volume vehicle, supplying a global network of robotaxis.

After years of delays to Musk’s self-driving targets, Tesla began offering paid rides in a small fleet of Cybercabs in Austin in September.

However, the automaker still has to answer the US auto safety agency’s questions on whether it properly self-certified Cybercab to demonstrate compliance with federal motor vehicle safety standards. REUTERS

title: Bringing the coast to the classroom: What FUEL's Coastal Center conference means for Nicholls
description:
When leaders, innovators and energy stakeholders gathered at the Coastal Center, it wasn’t just a routine conference.
