Hosting a FUEL-centered event at the Coastal Center bridges high-level statewide policy with the physical reality of our coastline.
What This Means for Nicholls Students For students studying energy management, business and environmental science at Nicholls, these developments translate directly into career momentum.
The conference at the Coastal Center may have passed, but its impact is just beginning to ripple across campus.
text:
When leaders, innovators and energy stakeholders gathered at the Coastal Center, it wasn’t just a routine conference. The event marked a milestone for Future Use of Energy in Louisiana, a statewide engine driving the future of energy transition, traditional manufacturing and carbon management.

While the conference has already concluded, its echoes are reshaping what it means to study energy, management and environmental resilience right here in Thibodaux.

What is FUEL and Why is it Vital to the Coast?

FUEL is a collaborative coalition anchored by major research institutions, industry partners and economic developers. Backed by historic support, including a landmark National Science Foundation Regional Innovation Engines award, FUEL is designed to transition Louisiana from powering the nation through legacy oil and gas to leading the world in next-generation energy technologies, carbon capture and grid modernization.

For Thibodaux, sitting squarely in the bayou region, this mission is personal. Our local geography makes us both a frontline witness to coastal changes and the beating heart of the state’s energy infrastructure.

Hosting a FUEL-centered event at the Coastal Center bridges high-level statewide policy with the physical reality of our coastline. It acknowledges that the solutions to coastal protection, energy security and economic longevity must be engineered, managed and sustained right here in south Louisiana.

Igniting a Venture Studio Model: Innovation in Action

The timing of the Coastal Center conference closely mirrors FUEL’s rollout of its brand-new FUEL Venture Studio and its appointment of inaugural Innovator-in-Residence Daryl Roy.

Rather than just offering traditional grants to pre-existing companies, this venture studio model actively builds new startups from the ground up. By pairing cutting-edge academic research, like that coming out of university labs, with seasoned operators, private investors and corporate partners, FUEL is actively creating companies focused on carbon management and modernized infrastructure.

Bringing conversations around this model to Thibodaux signals a shift from textbook theory to market-driven execution. It answers why the conference happened, to root high-tech entrepreneurship directly in the communities most impacted by shifts in the energy sector.

What This Means for Nicholls Students

For students studying energy management, business and environmental science at Nicholls, these developments translate directly into career momentum. Hosting high-level regional conferences right in their backyard at the Coastal Center gives students a front-row seat to network directly with the policymakers, startup founders and corporate leaders steering Louisiana’s economic future.

As FUEL builds a venture studio to commercialize new technologies, students are positioned at the doorstep of an emerging job market focused on keeping high-paying careers, intellectual property and startup creation within the state.

Because modern energy management has expanded beyond traditional extraction to complex landscapes, carbon management economics and sustainable infrastructure, witnessing statewide initiatives like FUEL unfold on campus ensures that student coursework aligns in real time with the skill sets regional employers are hunting for.

The conference at the Coastal Center may have passed, but its impact is just beginning to ripple across campus. For Nicholls students, it’s a clear reminder: the future of energy isn’t being written in a distant boardroom–it’s being engineered right down the bayou.

text:
Governor Newsom prioritized cleaning up neighborhoods impacted by decades of Exide pollution, investing more than $500 million in one of the largest residential lead cleanups in U.S. history.

California has completed cleanup at:

🏡 6,495 residential parcels

🛣️ 7,818 parkways

✏️ 12 schools

🧑‍🧑‍🧒 68 childcare centers

🛝 5 parks

“Clean air, soil and water should be basic rights. That’s why California is committed to cleaning up the decades of pollution left behind by Exide, affecting far too many families and communities,” said Secretary for Environmental Protection, Yana Garcia. “The investments made by this administration mean that in Southeast Los Angeles, nearly 6,500 families have cleaner properties, and impacted communities have safer childcare centers, schools and parks where they can safely live, work and play.”

“DTSC is delivering real and measurable progress for families living near the former Exide facility,” said DTSC Director Katherine Butler. “Every home we clean brings communities closer to the safe, healthy future they deserve after decades of industrial pollution. California remains steadfast in completing this cleanup thoroughly, safely, and with full transparency.”

How we got here

The former Exide facility in Vernon, located five miles southeast of downtown Los Angeles, operated for decades, recycling lead-acid batteries. In 2002, DTSC required Exide to investigate and clean up releases from its operations. In 2014, testing revealed elevated lead levels in nearby residential soil. In 2015, DTSC ordered Exide to withdraw a pending permit to operate, effectively closing the facility. Cleanup has continued ever since.

When a federal bankruptcy court later allowed Exide to abandon the site, Governor Newsom condemned the decision, declaring that California would continue fighting to hold Exide and its creditors accountable for poisoning the residential parcels, playgrounds and backyards surrounding the facility.

Since then, California has made sustained investments to accelerate cleanup and protect surrounding communities, including major state funding in 2021 for demolition, site cleanup and residential remediation, additional funding in 2023 for parkway cleanup, and continued funding to clean more contaminated residential parcels. The Newsom administration also took decisive steps to request the addition of the former Exide facility to the federal Superfund National Priorities List that, if successful, would bring additional federal resources to one of the largest contamination cleanups in U.S. history.

Today’s progress reflects years of work by the state and community partners to clean contaminated soil, protect families, and address what Governor Newsom has called Exide’s “toxic legacy” and a “decades-long injustice.”

How the cleanup works

California conducts comprehensive soil sampling to guide cleanup decisions. Initial sampling identifies properties eligible for cleanup, while spot-check verification and retrospective sampling confirm that completed work meets the state’s high standards.

To date, DTSC has performed sampling of 10,028 parcels to determine cleanup priority. 9,016 parcels have been identified as eligible for further remediation (about 80% of those contacted have granted DTSC access), based on soil lead concentration greater than 80 parts per million and/or a single sample greater than 1,000 ppm. DTSC conducted verification and retrospective sampling on 623 properties.

text:
ISTANBUL (AP) — The Turkish energy minister has laid out plans for his country to wean itself away from coal and other fossil fuels as it prepares to host the COP31 climate change summit.

World leaders are due to arrive next week in the Mediterranean city of Antalya, and Turkey’s hosting of the annual environmental conference has thrown a spotlight on its own coal, oil and gas usage.

Turkey is Europe’s largest coal power generator, according to energy think tank Ember. The Turkish Energy Ministry says coal remained its largest source of power last year, accounting for 33% of generation. The share of solar and wind in electricity generation stood at nearly 23%.

Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar revealed the National Energy Plan 2040 to reporters in a presentation made public Friday, in which he said Turkey would aim to transition from coal to cleaner energy sources — a process known as electrification. This would help it fulfil its pledge to reach net zero emissions by 2053.

“When we reach 2040 we are going to reduce our emissions by 40%. This big change in electrification will make this happen,” he said, adding that the use of solar and wind energy sources would more than quadruple over the next 13 years.

“Our aim is to reach 36% electrification by the year 2040,” he told a news conference in Istanbul. Using transport as an example, Bayraktar said the number of electric cars on Turkey’s roads would increase from around 500,000 to 20 million in the next 13 years.

The aim of the plan is to produce a “paradigm shift” in how energy is used in Turkey. “We have a huge project list ahead of us,” the minister added.

Huge level of investment needed

Such a shift, however, would require a huge level of investment — $500 billion in the next 13 years, some $210 billion of which would come from Turkish public sector companies with much of the rest from foreign investment.

“If the world is serious about carbon neutrality and if we would like to fund (fighting) climate change and global warming, we need to find the money,” Bayraktar said. “Everyone needs to take some responsibility and provide money for that.”

He also emphasized the importance of a transition from coal to clean energy that would not negatively impact communities reliant on mines and power stations for employment.

“We are looking for a just transition from coal to relatively cleaner sources of energy… but we need coal for security of supply,” he said.

“Equally important is that (coal mining) is providing at least 30,000 to 40,000 people with employment and labor opportunities. How are we going to make these miners into AI experts or high-tech experts? It’s not going to be easy. We need a just transition period.”

Despite aiming to break away from coal, Turkey will remain tied to other fossil fuels, particularly natural gas, for the foreseeable future.

Turkey recently started drilling gas reserves in the Black Sea and Bayraktar said production would double to 7.5 billion cubic meters annually in the coming years.

Growing nuclear power

Another key area would be nuclear power. The Akkuyu nuclear power plant on the Mediterranean coast is nearing operation and there are plans for another nuclear station by the Black Sea.

These would contribute towards the “very ambitious target” of Turkey becoming energy independent by 2040, Bayraktar said.

Turning to the “turbulent times” facing energy markets, Bayraktar described how sanctions around the wars in Ukraine and Iran were impeding efforts to fight global warming.

“We are trying to become carbon neutral in less than three decades’ time and with all these difficulties it’s very difficult to achieve this,” he said.

According to the Climate Action Tracker, which measures countries’ progress against goals of the 2015 Paris Agreement, Turkey’s climate targets and policies are “critically insufficient.”

The agreement set a target of limiting global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) compared with the early 1800s.

Looking ahead to COP31, Bayraktar said his key message would be for countries to adopt “responsive and realistic policies” to achieve carbon neutrality.

text:
Legislation to lower energy bills and speed up permitting for clean energy projects will likely be one of the top 10 priorities when Democrats regain control of the U.S. Congress in early January, Rep. Sean Casten (D-IL) told a triumphant media briefing Nov. 4, just hours after Donald Trump’s crushing and historic defeat in midterm elections.

I’m awake, barely,” said Casten (D-IL), a former clean energy entrepreneur first elected to Congress in 2019. “I think we’re all still processing the victory from last night.”

“The American people made their voices heard at the polls by resoundingly rejecting the destructive, corrupt actions of the Trump administration, including the war in Iran, the attacks on clean energy that have driven up costs for everyday people, and while they’re doing this, they’re boosting the profits of fossil fuel polluters,” said Gretchen Goldman, president of the Union of Concerned Scientists.

“Polling has showed that voters across the country are concerned about affordability,” Goldman added. “There’ve been news stories about regular people going without medicine and even food to fill their gas tanks. And yet the Trump administration has moved full speed ahead with repealing popular vehicle emission standards, among the strongest policies we’ve had to curb fossil fuel pollution and save drivers money at the pump.”

While Democrats in the House of Representatives are still working through their initial priorities for early 2027, energy affordability will be high on the list, with more than 160 legislators already signed on to support an Energy Bills Relief Act, Casten said. The bill will focus on “changing the incentives so that energy producers can make money by working to the benefit of energy consumers and lowering costs, which is not the way our regulatory structure works right now.”

At the same time, the veteran legislator didn’t minimize the challenge of trying to get anything done in Washington when Trump has already pledged to become “Mr. Veto” if Democrats won the midterms.

“We don’t have veto-proof majorities in the House or Senate, in spite of all the wins we had last night,” he told reporters. So “it’s important for us to put forward an agenda to try to get it passed, to not shy away from our values, but I think the strongest tools we’re going to have will be in appropriations and in oversight,” using Congressional authority to shift spending and “shine a light on some of the horrific things this administration has done.”

The Union of Concerned Scientists has tracked 625 attacks on science by the Trump administration over the last two years, and “each brazen attack served as a catalyst to mobilize scientists and science supporters across the country,” Goldman added. “But now we have more science champions in Congress, making it possible to limit the administration’s worst excesses and to hold them accountable for harms they’ve caused at home and on the global stage.”

As this story went to virtual press, Democrats had seized 54 of the seats in the 100-member U.S. Senate with races in Mississippi and Alaska still too close to call, and latest projections showed an overwhelming 259-176 Democratic Party margin in the House of Representatives. The early days since the polls closed have seen furious speculation about what’s next—for intensive Congressional investigations of Trump’s family and political cronies and attempts to roll back many of his most egregious policies, nowhere more urgently than on climate change and energy.

An ‘Important Diplomatic Function’ at COP31

But the change in tone stemming from the midterms might become evident as soon as next week, long before the new Congress is sworn in Jan. 3, when this year’s United Nations climate summit, COP31, convenes in Antalya, Türkiye.

“In the immediate term, we have a really important diplomatic function,” Casten said. “There are going to be about 20 of us going to the COP. We will not of course be in the majority [in Congress] at that point, but we will be received with the understanding of what just happened. We will be the entirety of the United States federal delegation in Türkiye, which makes our role very important.”

Those delegates will have to step carefully, he conceded, because “the rest of the world knows that the United States is the country that failed to ratify Kyoto. We’re the country that dropped out of [the Paris climate agreement], not once, but twice. But I think also there’s real value in us being able to convey to the world that America has spoken, and that so many of the challenges we face are the same,” from climate refugees on the move to the way climate change distorts and destabilizes financial systems.

Something else the U.S. has in common with other countries, Casten added, is the large share of the economy that rises or falls with the price of oil.

“Speaker [Mike] Johnson (R-LA) represents a district that wants people to consume as much natural gas as possible, pay as much as possible for that natural gas, and to force the export of LNG to the rest of the world,” he said. The likely incoming Speaker of the House, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY), “has a very different set of values from his constituents. But I think we can approach this moment with an empathy to realize that the climate demands action, the economy demands action, the rest of the world is already making that transition… but we need to do that with an appropriate amount of empathy and an appropriate amount of urgency.”

Goldman described the latest science on climate change as “sobering”, with decades of “insufficient policy-maker action and fossil fuel industry duplicity” now making it inevitable that humanity will overshoot a 1.5°C limit on average global warming.

“People in the U.S. and around the world are experiencing the deadly and costly effects of those rising temperatures,” she said, and “public polling routinely shows that voters across the country support common sense, science-backed policies to keep their families and communities safe”—including 75% of registered voters in the U.S. who say they want to see carbon dioxide regulated.

The Momentum is Local

While change in Washington, DC will be slower and less decisive while Trump is still in office, much of the momentum will come from state and local governments—just as it has over the last two years, only more so. Democrats are now the governors of 30 of the 50 states, and former Washington State governor Jay Inslee said 22 states now have Democratic “trifectas”, where one party holds the state house, senate, and governor’s office. At the same time, the veteran legislator didn’t minimize the challenge of trying to get anything done in Washington when Trump has already pledged to become “Mr. Veto” if Democrats won the midterms.

“We don’t have veto-proof majorities in the House or Senate, in spite of all the wins we had last night,” he told reporters. text:
Musk touted the Cybertruck as a futuristic rival to the conventional pickup, and Tesla built it at Gigafactory Texas. Now it is the thing being moved out of the way. According to Musk, winding down Cybertruck output around the middle of 2027 frees up the line for the Cybercab.

That is a notable reordering of priorities. The Cybertruck was Tesla's electric pickup, the vehicle Musk billed as the future of the segment. Handing its production space to the Cybercab says plainly which product Tesla now considers worth the factory footprint.

The Cybercab is the vehicle Tesla is ramping up production of at Gigafactory Texas. Ending Cybertruck production to make room for it is a bet that whatever the Cybercab represents, not a niche electric pickup, is where the volume and the margins live.

It is also a reordering of the product lineup. A vehicle that launches as a flagship and gets its production line reassigned inside a few years is no longer the priority it once was. Rather than keep both products running in parallel, the company is choosing the one it has yet to prove at scale over the one already on the road.

Whether the Cybercab justifies that confidence is the open question. A mid-2027 handoff gives the company a hard deadline to have the Cybercab ready to fill the space the Cybertruck leaves behind. For now, the message is clear enough: the Cybertruck era at Gigafactory Texas has an expiration date.

text:
Modeling from C2ES and Greenline Insights finds Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would save consumers billions, strengthen and diversify the nation’s energy mix

Modeling outlines cost of delayed reform, which could forgo $55 billion in savings and 800 MMt of power sector emissions reductions

WASHINGTON – The Center for Climate and Energy Solutions (C2ES) and Greenline Insights today released new national modeling showing how the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) can deliver substantial economic, reliability, and climate benefits by modernizing the nation’s electricity infrastructure and making it easier to build in America. The analysis finds that proposed reforms would boost deployment of clean energy, strengthen grid reliability, lower electricity costs, and reduce carbon pollution. The analysis, which also highlights the significant cost of delaying reforms, comes as electricity demand continues to rise, driven by growing data center development, electrification, and domestic manufacturing expansion.

READ THE MEMO HERE.

Expanding on an earlier regional analysis, the new study evaluates impacts across the contiguous United States, examining how key provisions of BAAJA could reshape the electric power system by 2035. More than 2,000 GW of proposed generation and storage projects remain stuck in queues today, while fewer than 900 miles of high-capacity transmission were added in 2024.

Compared to a “business as usual” scenario, by 2035 the modeled reforms would enable 170 GW of additional wind, solar, and battery storage capacity, including 83 GW of solar, 67 GW of wind, and 20 GW of battery storage, and expand interregional transmission capacity by 61 GW.

And in 2035 alone, reform would:

Reduce annual electricity system costs by $11.7 billion.

Lower residential electricity bills by approximately $2.5 billion annually.

Eliminate power shortfalls and avoid roughly $900 million in annual reliability-related costs.

Reduce annual power sector carbon dioxide emissions by 173 million metric tons, a 13 percent reduction relative to business as usual. That’s the equivalent to the emissions of more than 40 million gas-powered cars driven for one year.

The modeling suggests the climate benefits would start before 2035 and continue well beyond that year. Assuming new projects come online gradually over time, cumulative power-sector emissions reductions could reach approximately 1.7 gigatons by 2040.

The new analysis also outlines how delays in reforms could leave significant cost savings – and emissions reductions – on the table. Because new interconnection processes and transmission projects take years to deliver, a delay until 2030 would mean achieving only about 40 percent of the modeled benefits by 2035, while reducing reliability, limiting the expansion of clean technology, and increasing reliance on new, inefficient natural gas “peaking” units. Through 2040, this delay would forgo roughly $55 billion in electricity system savings and 800 million metric tons of emissions reductions.

Reforms would strengthen and diversify nation’s energy mix

The analysis finds that reform would strengthen and diversify the nation’s energy mix. Wind and solar would provide roughly 40 percent of U.S. electricity generation in 2035 under the reform scenario, compared with approximately one-third under business as usual. At the same time, natural gas generation falls from 44 percent of total generation to 36 percent. Reforms would also benefit both electricity-exporting and electricity-importing regions. Expanded transmission increases electricity trade between regions by approximately 70 percent, allowing regions with abundant wind and solar resources to meet growing demand elsewhere while reducing overall system costs. In addition to these reforms, the legislation makes significant improvements to unlock next generation energy technologies like geothermal, updating permitting and leasing rules to boost development,

“As electricity demand surges across the country, America faces a choice. We can continue with a broken status quo, or we can make it easier and faster to build the cleaner, modern electric grid our economy needs,” said C2ES President Nat Keohane. “This analysis shows that durable, bipartisan reforms can help deploy more clean energy, lower costs for consumers, improve reliability, and significantly reduce emissions. The benefits are substantial, but the clock is ticking and we cannot afford further delay.”

The modeled emissions reductions are driven by BAAJA’s interconnection provisions, which address lengthy studies, uncertain upgrade costs, and project withdrawals that prevent or delay proposed resources from reaching commercial operation.

“Grid constraints don’t just delay clean energy projects. They fundamentally change which resources get built,” said Ashna Aggarwal, Director of Analysis at Greenline Insights. “Our modeling finds that without interconnection reform, the emissions benefits of this legislation essentially disappear. With electricity demand rising and thousands of gigawatts of proposed generation and storage waiting to connect to the grid, maintaining the status quo risks locking in more natural gas infrastructure for decades to come.”

Notably, the benefits hold under alternate assumptions about natural gas pipeline expansion and electricity demand, including under scenarios with lower natural gas prices, lower data center demand, and with additional pipeline capacity in regions where permitting barriers have constrained development. The findings released today are also echoed in recent modeling analyses released by experts including Rhodium Group and Resources for the Future.

The findings reinforce the urgent need for durable, bipartisan permitting and grid reforms that can accelerate investment while maintaining certainty for developers, communities, and consumers. Through its permitting reform campaign, C2ES has worked with businesses, policymakers, and stakeholders to advance solutions that improve interconnection processes, expand transmission infrastructure, streamline permitting, and strengthen America’s ability to build the energy infrastructure needed for future economic growth and a stable climate.

text:
Tesla CEO Elon Musk on Friday said the electric vehicle maker will “be winding down” production of the Cybertruck at its Texas gigafactory around the middle of next year.

Musk, who hailed the Cybertruck as the future of the pickup truck segment, said in a post on X early Friday morning that the end of production at the massive facility would make room for production of its Cybercab robotaxi.

The Cybertruck is exclusively produced at the company’s plant in Texas alongside the Tesla Model Y and two-seat Cybercab, which Musk has touted as a crucial product for the automaker moving forward.

Musk did not say whether the company would produce the Cybertruck at a different facility, but he later responded to a user on X who called the update an “end of an era” and said the Cybertruck was the “best vehicle Tesla has ever made.”

“True, but the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time,” Musk said.

Tesla began Cybertruck deliveries in late 2023. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC.

The Cybertruck and its polarizing design gained a niche following, but it did not achieve mass-market sales, despite Musk’s pre-launch prediction that annual sales would eventually total 250,000.

“Trucks have been the same for a very long time,” Musk said when the truck was unveiled in 2019. “Like 100 years. Trucks have been basically the same. We want to try something different.”

While Tesla does not break out its sales by model or region, Cox Automotive estimated sales of the Cybertruck last year at 20,237 units in the U.S., down 48% from 38,965 in 2024.

One big buyer of the Cybertruck last year was Elon Musk’s aerospace and tech conglomerate, SpaceX , which spent $131 million buying up the angular steel trucks at Tesla’s suggested retail price, according to a SpaceX financial filing.

The distinct look of the vehicle made some owners a target of rude gestures and more serious road rage, one owner told CNBC last May, after Musk became the biggest funder of Donald Trump’s presidential campaign and led the Department of Government Efficiency, an effort to slash the federal workforce and regulations.

Wired wrote in an October 2025 feature story, “There is likely no object that feels more emblematic of US president Donald Trump’s return to the White House than the Tesla Cybertruck.” The magazine interviewed owners who described being spit on and sworn at due to their choice of vehicle.

The Cybertruck’s specifications also fell short of those Tesla advertised early on, and in some cases fell short of those offered by leading fuel-burning pickups. There have also been many quality and production problems associated with the vehicles.

The 2024 Tesla Cybertruck was the subject of 11 voluntary recalls, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration website. Issues ranged from a “trapped” acceleration pedal risk that could cause unintended acceleration, to software defects and an inverter fault that could result in sudden loss of drive power.

text:
Polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are known as "forever chemicals" because of the impact they make on the environment and human bodies. Much of modern manufacturing relies on these substances for safe packaging, fire protection and waterproof coatings.

Despite the billions of dollars in economic burden PFAS place on human health and the environment, the PFAS materials themselves are relatively affordable and abundant. So when WashU chemical engineers wanted to come up with an alternative that meets manufacturing needs, they turned to a different material that is also affordable and abundant: lignin, or plant waste material. In new research published in Matter, researchers from Washington University in St. Louis outline the chemical processes used to turn lignin and fatty acids into a viable PFAS replacement called SLIP, or superhydrophobic lignin-integrated particles.

"We actually use this waste material to turn it into a valuable product," said Joshua Yuan, the Lucy & Stanley Lopata Professor and chair of energy, environmental and chemical engineering at WashU McKelvey Engineering. Yuan, who serves as director of the NSF Carbon Utilization Redesign for Biomanufacturing (CURB) Energy Research Center at WashU, has long taken inspiration from the natural world to find solutions to replace petrochemical-based materials.

In SLIP, the researchers found a viable waterproof coating to replace PFAS and lose the toxic side effects. "It's not going to stay in the environment forever and it can be degraded," Yuan added.

To make SLIP, Yuan and his team, including first authors Puneet Dhatt and Weiwei Li, took inspiration from plant vascular tissue called xylem. Within xylem is a waterproof molecule called suberin, which transports water throughout the plant. The team incorporated suberin's structure into lignin particles by linking lignin to fatty acids and further added a polylactic acid (PLA) binder. The resulting material demonstrated a highly superhydrophobic performance and included features of mechanical robustness and ultraviolet stability.

That's not everything PFAS does, but it's a substantial start, the researchers said, especially considering the sheer number of waterproof coatings used in modern manufacturing.

Tests show water literally bouncing off the new SLIP material. "The water will just run off," Dhatt said, adding that the material was tested with wood-degrading fungus that showed the coating can break down into harmless organic matter within the expected time period.

Lignin and fatty acid "evolved to degrade in the environment for a long time," Dhatt noted, saying that the replacement material could help avoid the societal cost of forever chemicals.

The WashU team collaborated with researchers at Texas A&M University to estimate the cost savings of replacing PFAS. Looking at the global impacts to human health and the environment from forever chemicals, the Texas researchers estimated that total societal damage avoided by replacing forever chemicals with SLIP in waterproofing could reach $1.1 billion annually.

For now, the scientists will continue to add attributes to this new coating. SLIP could be used in packaging and for construction material coatings, but the next step will be to make it oil- and fireproof to vastly expand its applications. The team also is working to scale up the process and integrate it with biorefinery and paper and pulping industries.

"This study represents the perfect example, where we learn from nature and design a sustainable material critical to our society, with a life cycle similar to nature polymers, where everything can degrade without causing harms," Yuan said.

title: Most Europeans want action to tackle climate crisis but not at any cost, poll shows - The Guardian
description:
Europeans believe human-made climate change is real, a survey has shown, with most feeling action must be taken soon – as long as they do not have to sacrifice too much to achieve it.
Days before the Cop31 climate conference in Turkey, the polling showed vast majorities (79-89%) in Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK thought countries would combat the crisis more effectively by working internationally.
Majorities of between 65% and 83% in each country surveyed said they were worried about the climate crisis, including 23%-42% who were “very worried”.
In April, 74% of respondents in France said they were worried about the climate crisis but that figure was up to 83% by mid-August and still at that level last month.
The number of French people who were “very worried” about climate change also rose, from 28% in April to a record high of 42% in August, a level it held last month.
text:
Europeans believe human-made climate change is real, a survey has shown, with most feeling action must be taken soon – as long as they do not have to sacrifice too much to achieve it.

The YouGov poll of six European countries showed between 69% (Germany) and 80% (France) of respondents believed the climate was changing, with few (1%-4%) denying it and 14-20% believing it was changing, but not as a result of human activity.

Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent and scientists say human-driven climate breakdown through the burning of fossil fuels is increasing the frequency and intensity of heatwaves, droughts, wildfires and destructive storms.

Days before the Cop31 climate conference in Turkey, the polling showed vast majorities (79-89%) in Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK thought countries would combat the crisis more effectively by working internationally.

Those in the EU were more likely to say that climate action decisions should be made at EU rather than national level, a feeling shared by 50-54% of respondents in France, Italy and Germany as well as 61% in Denmark and 64% in Spain.

Majorities of between 65% and 83% in each country surveyed said they were worried about the climate crisis, including 23%-42% who were “very worried”. YouGov noted an uptick in concern during this summer’s heatwaves.

In April, 74% of respondents in France said they were worried about the climate crisis but that figure was up to 83% by mid-August and still at that level last month.

The number of French people who were “very worried” about climate change also rose, from 28% in April to a record high of 42% in August, a level it held last month. Concern in other countries spiked in August but has since dipped.

In Germany, for example, the number very concerned rose from 27% in April to 40% in August but has now fallen back to 31%. Concern remained relatively stable in Denmark, at 66%-69% “worried” and 20%-23% “very worried”.

Across the six countries surveyed, respondents mostly (45%-63%) thought it was not too late to avert the worst impacts of the climate crisis but that it would require a drastic change in approach. Only 11%-24% believed it was already too late.

Between 9% and 20% said they thought current measures would be enough to prevent the most serious impacts. But in terms of what climate actions had support, those not directly affecting people’s lives were the most popular.

Measures such as planting more trees, subsidising energy efficiency, banning single-use plastics and taxing big emitters were all favoured, while increasing fuel duty, limiting meat and dairy, taxing air fares and banning new petrol and diesel cars were opposed.

A similar pattern emerged when respondents were asked what steps they would be prepared to take: cheap and easy actions such as creating green space at home and eating only seasonal fruit and vegetables were popular, but not shopping exclusively secondhand or paying more for flights.

text:
Billions of dollars for solar energy projects nationwide remain in limbo more than a month after two federal judges ruled in separate cases that the Environmental Protection Agency illegally canceled the "Solar for All" program.

Massachusetts won $156 million under the competitive Biden-era initiative intended to expand access to solar energy in low-income communities. The EPA shuttered the program in August 2025 and rescinded all grants. Despite the recent court rulings, the fate of that money remains uncertain.

The EPA has until mid-November to appeal the court rulings. A spokesperson for the agency said in an email that “EPA is reviewing the decision and considering options for appeal.”

“This is a program that has the potential to lower people's energy bills, get inexpensive clean electricity on the grid, and help the communities that the Solar For All program was designed to help,” said James Crowley, a senior attorney at the Conservation Law Foundation, which is representing plaintiffs in one of the court cases.

“We hope that EPA is considering all that — along with Congress's intent — and they might choose not to appeal,” Crowley said.

Congress funded the $7 billion Solar For All program through the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act. Two years later, Massachusetts won $156 million. The Healey administration said the program could reduce energy costs by 20% for 31,000 low-income and disadvantaged homes, support 2,800 clean energy jobs and dramatically decrease greenhouse gas emissions.

Soon after President Trump’s second term began, his administration froze the Solar for All funds. In July 2025, Congress passed the "One Big Beautiful Bill," a massive tax and spending law that terminated the program. The bill stipulated that grants already obligated under Solar for All were not affected, but EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin argued that the bill repealed EPA’s authority to administer the program and rescinded the funds.

The EPA then officially canceled the program, calling it a “boondoggle.”

In a statement, Zeldin said the EPA would be "an exceptional steward of taxpayer dollars," not "a frivolous spender in the name of ‘climate equity.’ ”

A variety of groups that won Solar for All grants sued the EPA, including nonprofits, solar companies and states.

Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell, a plaintiff in one of the lawsuits, said in a statement that “the Trump Administration’s attempt to illegally gut this program will eliminate good-paying jobs, neglect the dangers of climate change, and raise costs for low-income residents.”

In September, a federal judge in Rhode Island ruled the Trump EPA exceeded its authority when it shut down the program. A few days later, a federal judge in the Washington D.C. ruled in a separate case that the EPA’s termination of the initiative was illegal, arbitrary and capricious.

The EPA has 60 days to appeal the ruling. For now, the Massachusetts Solar for All program remains “on pause,” according to a state spokesperson, as “Massachusetts continues to monitor the status” of the funding.

It’s unclear if the Democrats' gains in Congress in the midterm elections will affect the EPA's decision on whether to appeal, or the status of the canceled grants.

Phil Thompson, a professor of urban planning and politics at MIT, said it was possible the incoming Congress could pass legislation to release the funds. With both legislation and the court rulings, he said, "chances are pretty good that the money could be released."

Even so, he said the delays represent a missed opportunity to address both climate change and rising energy costs.

"People's utility bills have been going up and up," he said. "Had we built more alternative sources of energy — whether it's solar or geothermal or other — it would have stabilized those prices."

Gretchen Goldman, president and CEO of the Union of Concerned Scientists, said the incoming congressional Democrats will offer climate advocates an opportunity “to make sure that the funds that Congress has obligated get out the door and are used."

“We've seen that be a challenge in the last two years,” she said.

Rep. Katherine Clark, a Massachusetts Democrat, told WBUR after the election that one of her party's priorities will be to “restore the cuts” made under the One Big Beautiful Bill.

Clark, who is positioned to become House majority leader when the Democrats take control of Congress in January, did not address Solar for All directly, but said bringing down basic living costs would be a priority.

"We're going to do quick things, small things, and also start to work on big transformative policies," she said, "but all focused on making sure that we are fighting for those families who feel like they are drowning in this cost of living crisis.”

name: Texas Environment
title: Democratic Sweep in Texas Could Usher in Environmental Reforms - Mother Jones
authors: Arcelia Martin, Dylan Baddour, Tim Murphy, Isabela Dias, Laura C. Morel, Dan Friedman, Pema Levy, Ari Berman, Sonel Cutler, Mariana Duran
description:
When the Democratic administration takes office in January, data centers will sit at the center of its political crosshairs.
“That’s really exciting.” Hinojosa’s election has panicked the data center industry over its future in one of the largest markets in the United States.
Voters clearly want the data center industry to be held accountable, said the Lone Star Chapter of the Sierra Club’s legislative director, Cyrus Reed.
Hinojosa’s election signals a significant shift in Texas’ data center policies, global analysis firm Wood Mackenzie said Wednesday.
As governor, Hinojosa will appoint commissioners to lead state regulators like the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, the Public Utility Commission and the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department.
text:
This story was originally published by Inside Climate News and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

Democrats’ historic sweep of Texas on Tuesday raises new possibilities of environmental reform after more than 30 years of Republican rule in the home of the nation’s oil and gas industry.

That includes opportunities to cement safeguards for data center development, lower energy costs and, over time, appoint new commissioners to the state’s regulatory agencies and boost environmentally protective standards.

“We have a generational shift in leadership here,” said Adrian Shelley, state director of Public Citizen, a consumer advocacy group. “I think there’s going to be a real appetite for reform.”

Both the US Senate and governor races were called before midnight Central Time, quickly crushing the longheld skepticism of the potential of a Democrat-led Texas. Democrats also took the House in the state Legislature.

The blue wave in Texas resulted, in part, from an upswell of public outrage over the state’s booming buildout of data centers for artificial intelligence that are gobbling massive amounts of electricity and failing to disclose their water use, experts said Wednesday. When the Democratic administration takes office in January, data centers will sit at the center of its political crosshairs. “The new state leadership has a clear mandate to rein in the data center industry,” Shelley said. “I think the days of Texas being unequivocally open for business are over.”

Gina Hinojosa, a Democratic state representative who was largely unknown earlier this year, unseated three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who was backed by some of the richest and most powerful forces across the country.

Hinojosa will be the first Hispanic politician to lead the state, where Latinos make up the largest population, and will preside over the second-largest state economy in the country, after California.

The victory of James Talarico against Attorney General Ken Paxton ends decades of Republican rule in the US Senate, with the last Democratic senator elected in 1988. It was also the most expensive Senate race in history, with the richest man on earth, Elon Musk, contributing more than $160 million to secure Paxton’s victory.

Democrat Jon Rosenthal defeated a former Tarrant County GOP chair with a storied record of extremism, Bo French, for one of three seats at the state’s oil and gas regulator, the Railroad Commission.

“Pretty much everyone who won the statewide level is a champ on the environment,” said Luke Metzger, executive director of Environment Texas. “That’s really exciting.”

Hinojosa’s election has panicked the data center industry over its future in one of the largest markets in the United States. While Abbott switched from issuing an enthusiastic invitation for data centers to invest and develop in Texas to a list of stringent directives, Hinojosa has campaigned on calling an immediate moratorium on new data centers.

Voters clearly want the data center industry to be held accountable, said the Lone Star Chapter of the Sierra Club’s legislative director, Cyrus Reed. “For a long time, they’ve had not only a seat at the table, they’ve actually been creating the table with some of the laws that have been passed,” Reed said.

Hinojosa’s election signals a significant shift in Texas’ data center policies, global analysis firm Wood Mackenzie said Wednesday.

Even so, the state will remain a leading market for data center investments, given its renewable resources, natural gas infrastructure and regulatory autonomy from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, Wood Mackenzie added.

Jess Heck, the director of Texas government affairs for the Data Center Coalition, the industry’s largest trade group, said its members will continue to engage with residents and local leaders to understand community priorities and ensure the growth of digital infrastructure delivers clear benefits for Texans.

“Enhancing affordability, creating jobs, and keeping the state’s economy strong are top priorities for Texans,” Heck said in a statement to Inside Climate News. “Data centers can continue to play a crucial role in advancing those priorities by bringing investment to local communities and generating critical tax revenue to support local governments and school districts across the state.”

The Dallas-Fort Worth region has the largest concentration of data centers in the state. The most rapid expansion of the industry is in Ellis County, some 30 minutes south of downtown Dallas.

On Election Day, Lacey Hamel, 39, and Jazmin Villegas, 44, stood outside the Red Oak Municipal Center waving at voters driving in and out of the building’s lot. The two wore bright yellow shirts that said, “No More Data Centers.” They’re members of Save Our Red Oak, a group tracking and trying to slow down the expansion of data centers across seven campuses in the city.

As in other rural Texas counties with swaths of land, data centers emerged as a critical issue for the election in Red Oak.

Members of the Red Oak group had asked Abbott to call a special legislative session over the industry’s rapid growth. “That ship has sailed,” Hamel said.

Among their data center protest group, set in a staunchly Republican county where nearly two-thirds of residents voted for President Donald Trump in 2024, several people crossed party lines over frustrations on data centers, Hamel said. It informed how she voted, too. “This is one of those issues where it’s affecting our air, it’s affecting our land, it’s affecting our water, it’s affecting our kids,” Hamel said.

A survey published a week before Election Day by the University of Houston’s Hobby School of Public Affairs found that nearly 80 percent of Texas voters would support a policy limiting the number of data centers that can be built in the state.

Those who intended to vote for Hinojosa were significantly more likely than Abbott voters to be extremely or very concerned about data centers’ impact on electricity prices, water supply, power outages, noise and air pollution, the survey found.

Hinojosa can chart a new course and safeguard natural resources, Colin Leyden, Texas state director of the Environmental Defense Fund, said in a statement. “Voters made clear that they expect their governor to put the health, safety, and well-being of Texas families first,” Leyden said.

As governor, Hinojosa will appoint commissioners to lead state regulators like the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, the Public Utility Commission and the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department.

Every current commissioner was appointed by Abbott. New appointees might take a more aggressive approach to enforcing air quality standards, limiting industrial water pollution or expanding land conservation, said Environment Texas’ Metzger.

Hinojosa’s record suggests an interest in environmental enforcement. In 2021, Hinojosa and 15 Democratic colleagues proposed a “Texas Climate Plan,” a package of 41 bills aimed at reducing carbon emissions and increasing regulation of the state’s fossil fuel industry.

She celebrated proposed legislation, part of their climate plan, that sought a 25 percent tax on gas flared in production fields.

While the oil and gas industry widely opposed the proposed legislation, Democrats and environmentalists saw it as an opportunity to incentivize infrastructure for energy producers to capture and transport the gas, rather than pollute the air. The bill, authored by Lt. Governor-Elect Vikki Goodwin, never made it to a vote on the House floor.

Reed, with the state Sierra Club chapter, said Texas has never taken methane pollution very seriously. There aren’t state rules on it, nor is there a statewide implementation plan as Trump seeks to roll back the Biden administration’s methane rule.

But with the combination of a new commissioner at the Railroad Commission, the potential for new commissioners at the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality and emboldened Democrats in the Legislature, there’s potential to take action on pollution, Reed said.

“Hopefully there’s more attention to the impacts on communities,” Reed said. “Instead of always seeing additional regulation as a bad thing, maybe it’s seen as a way to protect communities from pollution.”

text:
Democratic legislators have wrested the majority of both the House and Senate from the Republicans’ grasp following a historic midterm election this week. The clean energy industry is clamoring for a sea change in federal support for renewables after the Trump administration razed incentives and funding since taking office in 2025.

While each candidate’s stance on clean energy isn’t apparent — nor is the effect this midterm election will have on domestic renewable energy markets — Democrats and left-leaning legislators have historically supported renewables more than their counterparts across the political aisle.

Wood Mackenzie is predicting that permitting reform will be a high priority for this new class of federal legislators, because of the rising costs of fuel and electricity from oil supply pressures brought on by the United States’ war with Iran and data center proliferation. However, the firm is also predicting that President Donald Trump could exercise his executive power to hamper proposed federal renewable energy subsidies.

“While we see the likelihood for permitting reform, how policy is legislated and implemented remains a risk to the U.S. economy,” said David Brown, director, global integrated research for Wood Mackenzie. “Entrenched partisanship could fuel policy stagnation and regulatory confusion.”

Representatives from the renewable energy industry and environmental organizations provided statements following the midterm results. Heres’ what they had to say.

Energy affordability was a key issue in this election, reflecting the real pressures facing American households and businesses. The solar and storage industry looks forward to working with newly elected federal and state leaders to bring more affordable, reliable power online and deliver the energy savings Americans are demanding.

– Tim Pawlenty, CEO of the Solar Energy Industries Association

Families and businesses need affordable, reliable power, and strengthening America’s solar manufacturing base in a bipartisan manner will help deliver lower electricity bills. Over the past several years, American manufacturers have invested billions of dollars in new factories, expanded domestic production and created good-paying jobs in communities all across the country. With electricity demand rising, solar remains one of the fastest and most affordable ways to bring new power onto the grid, and the next Congress has an opportunity to ensure that power is American-made.

That starts with reinstating the domestic content incentives, so factories Congress helped bring online have a strong domestic market for American-made solar. It also means robust enforcement of our trade laws to ensure a level playing field for American solar manufacturers and continued investment in next-generation technologies so we can compete with, and leapfrog, China. We look forward to working with the new Congress to advance these shared priorities, keep electricity affordable for American families and strengthen our energy security and industrial workforce.

– Yogin Kothari, chief Strategy officer of the SEMA Coalition

Today, the clean power industry directly employs more than 400,000 Americans, and the U.S. has nearly 388 GW of clean power online, enough to power more than 83 million homes — but we’ll need a lot more than that to meet skyrocketing demand. Modernizing our outdated permitting process is key to unlocking over $800 billion in new infrastructure and 350-plus GW of new clean energy, keeping prices in check and the lights on at home for families and businesses across the country.

This Congress’ work isn’t done.

– Jason Grumet, CEO of the American Clean Power Association

Since their inception, competitive power markets have delivered billions in consumer savings while spurring innovation. They are the best way to make sure power generation investments are disciplined and efficient, with companies, not ratepayers, bearing the risk. EPSA looks forward to working with lawmakers on both sides of the aisle on policies that keep the grid reliable, protect customers and bring down costs in the long run.

– Todd Snitchler, president and CEO of the Electric Power Supply Association

The message from voters is clear: Americans want greater economic security, relief from rising costs and an energy system that works for them. This election put a bright spotlight on how this country’s outdated energy system and dependence on fossil fuels leave families and businesses exposed to unaffordable price shocks … Some of the biggest opportunities for progress may come at the state and city level. New governors, state legislatures and mayors have the power to move quickly on solutions that address the needs of their constituents: strengthening local economies, creating jobs and lowering bills. From ensuring data centers provide real benefits to communities to expanding clean energy, modernizing the grid, enabling affordable and accessible housing, and improving public transit, state and local leaders can walk-the-talk that climate action delivers real benefits for people.

– David Widawsky, director of World Resources Institute United States

Regardless of election outcomes, access to affordable, reliable energy and energy infrastructure remains essential to nearly every aspect of our daily lives, from powering our homes and businesses to keeping the cost of everyday goods and services within reach. As these leaders prepare to take office, we encourage them to make energy access, affordability, and reliability a priority.

We are ready to work with policymakers on both sides of the aisle to advance policies that support the development of critical energy infrastructure to create jobs, strengthen our nation’s energy security and ensure families and businesses have access to the energy they need.

– David Holt, president of the Consumer Energy Alliance

We just witnessed the collective power voters showed to beat back the Trump regime and fight for their country. Trump and his GOP cronies tried to drive our economy into the ground, but the American people stood up and made it clear that they reject Trump’s disastrous agenda.

We are committed to working with the incoming Congress to hold the administration accountable for the harm they have done to working people and pass legislation to build a clean economy that works for us all — not just billionaires. Creating opportunity for workers and communities while addressing environmental challenges is not just good policy, it’s also good politics.

title: Tesla US Sales Q1 2026: Down 8.4%, Share 54.2% - Tech Insider
description:
Add Now Tesla US Sales Q1 2026: The Numbers at a Glance Start with the headline figures.
With 54.2% of all U.S. EV sales, Tesla sold more electric vehicles in the quarter than every other brand combined.
Tesla U.S. sales, Q1 2026: 117,300 vehicles (down 8.4% year over year) Total U.S. EV sales, Q1 2026: 216,399 (down 27% from 296,589) Tesla’s U.S. EV market share: 54.2%, up from 43.2% Non-Tesla EV sales: down 41% Model Y: 78,591 sales.
How Tesla Lost Sales but Gained Market Share Market share is a ratio.
Tesla remained the leading U.S. EV seller in Q1 2026, with a 54.2% share of the market.
text:
Tesla sold an estimated 117,300 vehicles in the United States in the first quarter of 2026, down 8.4% from a year earlier, according to Cox Automotive estimates reported by InsideEVs. That is the lowest quarterly U.S. figure the company has posted since late 2021. Yet the same data shows Tesla’s share of the U.S. EV market jumping from 43.2% to 54.2%.

Both numbers are true at once, and the gap between them is the real story. The U.S. EV market shrank far faster than Tesla did. Our earlier look at Tesla’s uneven European rebound showed how much the brand’s fortunes vary by region, and the American picture adds another layer. This analysis walks through the Q1 2026 data, the math behind the share jump, and what it signals for buyers, rivals and the broader EV hardware market.

·

Google · Preferred Sources

Don't miss new tech stories on Google

Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions.

Add Now

Tesla US Sales Q1 2026: The Numbers at a Glance

Start with the headline figures. Cox Automotive’s estimates, as relayed by InsideEVs, put Tesla’s U.S. sales at 117,300 vehicles for the quarter. The year-over-year decline was 8.4%. InsideEVs describes the total as Tesla’s weakest U.S. quarter since late 2021.

The wider market looked far worse. Cox Automotive counted 216,399 EVs sold in the U.S. in Q1 2026, a 27% drop from the 296,589 sold in Q1 2025. Strip out Tesla and the damage becomes clearer. InsideEVs’ analysis of the Cox data found that non-Tesla EV sales fell 41%.

Tesla stayed the leading U.S. EV seller throughout. That was true a year ago too, but the lead is now much wider. With 54.2% of all U.S. EV sales, Tesla sold more electric vehicles in the quarter than every other brand combined.

Here is how the key facts stack up. Each figure below comes from the Cox Automotive data as reported by InsideEVs.

Tesla U.S. sales, Q1 2026: 117,300 vehicles (down 8.4% year over year)

Total U.S. EV sales, Q1 2026: 216,399 (down 27% from 296,589)

Tesla’s U.S. EV market share: 54.2%, up from 43.2%

Non-Tesla EV sales: down 41%

Model Y: 78,591 sales. Model 3: 31,672 sales

What the 117,300 Figure Actually Measures

One caution before going further. The 117,300 number is a Cox Automotive estimate, not a figure Tesla itself disclosed. Estimates like this can be revised as better data arrives.

That matters for how you read the 8.4% decline. It is a best estimate, and the direction is clear even if the final decimal moves. Every number in this piece carries the same caveat. When InsideEVs and Cox report a figure, we name them. When we do our own arithmetic, we label it as ours.

The estimate also covers Tesla’s full U.S. lineup. The Model Y and Model 3 account for the bulk of it, and the fact sheet we are working from lists more than 101,000 combined U.S. sales for the two cars. The remaining volume comes from the rest of the range, which the source material does not itemize.

How Tesla Lost Sales but Gained Market Share

Market share is a ratio. When the denominator shrinks faster than the numerator, the ratio rises even as the numerator falls. That is exactly what happened here.

Our own arithmetic, based on the reported figures, shows the mechanism. Tesla’s 117,300 sales divided by the market’s 216,399 gives 54.2%, matching the reported share. Working backward from the 8.4% decline, Tesla’s Q1 2025 U.S. total comes out near 128,000. Divide that by the 296,589 market total from a year earlier and you land at roughly 43.2%, again matching the reported figure.

So Tesla lost about 10,800 sales year over year, while the market as a whole lost about 80,000. Tesla’s loss represents a little over 13% of the total market decline. The other 87% or so came from everyone else. This is the core of the “tanked but gained share” framing that InsideEVs highlights.

Share gains of this kind are real in a statistical sense, but they carry a different meaning than share gains in a growing market. Winning a bigger slice of a shrinking pie does not add revenue. It does, however, signal that Tesla’s buyers proved more resilient than the buyers of competing brands.

The Non-Tesla EV Collapse: Down 41%

The sharpest number in the data set is not Tesla’s. It is the 41% fall in non-Tesla EV sales, which InsideEVs derived from Cox Automotive’s figures. Subtracting Tesla’s 117,300 from the 216,399 market total leaves roughly 99,100 non-Tesla EVs sold in Q1 2026, by our math. A year earlier the same group sold about 168,500.

That is a loss of roughly 69,000 vehicles across every brand other than Tesla selling EVs in America. The reported sources do not break the decline down by brand, and we will not guess at it. What the aggregate shows is that the pressure fell overwhelmingly on Tesla’s competitors.

Individual brands tell similar stories at smaller scale. Our report on Subaru’s WRX outselling all three Subaru EVs in October, 1,707 to 843 shows a legacy automaker whose gas-powered performance car still beats its whole electric range. It is one data point, but it fits the broader picture of weak demand outside Tesla.

The source material does not explain why non-Tesla sales fell so much, and neither will we. Any explanation tying the drop to a specific cause remains unconfirmed unless an on-record source documents it. The numbers describe what happened, not why.

Model Y and Model 3: Two Opposite Stories

Tesla’s headline decline hides a split inside its own lineup. The two volume cars moved in opposite directions, according to the reported Cox Automotive data.

Model Y: the volume engine

The Model Y sold 78,591 vehicles in the U.S. in Q1 2026. Reported Cox data shows that is an increase of approximately 23% year over year. By our arithmetic, that implies a Q1 2025 figure near 63,900. The Model Y alone accounted for about two-thirds of Tesla’s estimated U.S. total for the quarter.

A growing Model Y sitting inside a falling Tesla total tells you the weakness came from somewhere else in the lineup. The Model Y’s growth is also the main reason Tesla’s overall decline stayed in single digits.

Model 3: the weak spot

The Model 3 went the other way. It sold 31,672 vehicles in Q1 2026, down 39.7% from 52,520 a year earlier. That is a loss of about 20,850 units, which is nearly double Tesla’s entire net decline of roughly 10,800. In other words, the Model 3’s slide more than explains the company’s overall drop, and gains elsewhere partly offset it.

Combined, the Model Y and Model 3 produced more than 101,000 U.S. sales in the quarter, per the fact sheet. Their two reported totals actually add to roughly 110,000, comfortably above that floor. The remainder of Tesla’s estimated volume came from its other models, which the sources do not detail.

Data Table: Q1 2026 vs Q1 2025 in the US EV Market

The table below lays out the market-level numbers side by side. Figures marked with an asterisk are our own calculations from the reported data, not figures published by Cox Automotive or InsideEVs.

The table makes the asymmetry plain. Tesla’s share climbed 11 percentage points while its own volume fell by roughly one in twelve vehicles. Non-Tesla brands lost about four in ten of their sales.

Data Table: Tesla Model Breakdown for Q1 2026

The concentration is the takeaway. Two cars deliver roughly 94% of Tesla’s U.S. volume by our math. That gives the company scale, and it also means a swing in either model moves the whole quarter.

Historical Context: The Lowest Since Late 2021

InsideEVs reports that 117,300 is Tesla’s lowest quarterly U.S. sales figure since late 2021. The source material does not list the intervening quarters, so we will not reconstruct them. What the statement does tell us is that Tesla has gone more than four years without a quarter this soft in its home market.

Dropping back to late-2021 levels in 2026 is a clear step backward for the market leader. It also arrives while the EV market itself retreats, which separates this slump from one driven purely by Tesla-specific problems.

Regional data adds texture. Our October coverage of Tesla’s Northern Europe registrations, with Sweden up 248% and Norway at 1,548 cars shows the company can post dramatic gains in some markets while sliding in others. The U.S. result for Q1 fits a pattern of uneven global performance rather than a single worldwide trend.

Competitive Comparison: Tesla vs the Rest of the Field

Treat the U.S. EV market as two groups. Tesla is the first. Everyone else is the second. In Q1 2026, the first group sold about 117,300 vehicles and the second sold roughly 99,100 by our calculation. A year earlier the groups sat at about 128,000 and 168,500.

That flip, from a market where rivals collectively outsold Tesla by about 40,000 units to one where Tesla outsells them by about 18,000, is the most important competitive change in the data. A single brand now holds more than half of all U.S. EV sales. For rivals, that raises the bar for every product launch and every pricing decision.

Legacy automakers are not standing still. Our coverage of BMW’s third-quarter results, where EVs reached 20% of deliveries shows one rival gaining traction in a different quarter and a different region. The comparison is imperfect, since it spans different periods, but it reinforces a point. EV demand has not vanished. It has concentrated around a few products.

For readers following the hardware side of the story, our hardware coverage hub tracks the batteries, chips and devices behind the vehicles.

Market Impact: What a 54.2% Share Means

A 54.2% share gives Tesla pricing power in some ways and exposure in others. The company sets the reference price that every competitor measures against. When one brand is more than half the market, buyers shopping for an EV often start with a Tesla and then look for reasons to choose something else.

The exposure comes from dependence on the overall market. If total EV demand keeps falling, Tesla’s volume is likely to fall with it, even at constant or rising share. Share cannot protect a company from a shrinking category. Tesla’s 8.4% decline, set against the market’s 27% drop, shows it cushioned the blow without escaping it.

Brand sentiment is a separate variable. Our report that Democrats are cooling on Tesla, with the Mercedes EQB scoring 604 covers one slice of the opinion data. The Cox figures show sales held up better than some sentiment surveys might suggest, though the sources do not connect the two, and we will not claim a link.

Suppliers, charging operators and used-car markets all sit downstream of these numbers. A market 27% smaller means fewer new EVs entering the pipeline. The reported sources do not quantify those downstream effects, so they remain areas to watch rather than conclusions.

What Buyers Should Take From the Data

If you are shopping for an EV, the data points to a few practical conclusions. Tesla’s lead means broad availability of its two core models. The collapse in non-Tesla sales may mean more inventory and more negotiating room at other brands, though the sources do not report discounting and we cannot confirm it.

Incentives matter as much as sticker prices. Our guide to state EV rebates, including $3,500 in California and $2,500 in Minnesota is worth checking before you commit, since state programs can shift the math between brands.

Two cautions apply. First, a market-share headline says nothing about whether a particular car suits your commute, budget or charging access. Second, estimates from Cox Automotive can be revised, so treat today’s figures as the current best read rather than a final count.

What Remains Unconfirmed

Several claims circulating around this story lack on-record support, and we are holding the line on them. The first is causation. Neither InsideEVs nor the Cox data attributes Tesla’s sales or share results to any specific cause, so any explanation, whether about pricing, policy, competition or brand perception, is unconfirmed.

The second is anything attributed to Elon Musk. Available results indicate that Musk shared or quoted a post related to the story. No direct, independently verified statement from him about the headline appears in the source material. We are not putting words in his mouth.

Third, no figures here describe Tesla’s global deliveries, its profit margins or its stock performance. The fact sheet covers U.S. Q1 sales and market share only. Readers looking for the full-year picture should wait for later Cox Automotive quarterly estimates and Tesla’s own disclosures.

Predictions: Where the US EV Market Goes Next

The following are our analytical judgments based on the reported data, not forecasts from Cox Automotive, InsideEVs or any named analyst.

Tesla’s share stays above 50% in the next Cox report. A gap of more than 11 points over a year earlier is hard to close in one quarter, and the non-Tesla group would need a sharp rebound to pull it back.

The Model 3 becomes the figure to watch. A 39.7% decline cannot continue indefinitely, so the next reading will show whether the car stabilizes or keeps shrinking.

Rivals respond with product and price, not messaging. A 41% sales drop gives non-Tesla brands a strong reason to cut prices or accelerate new launches.

Total EV sales remain below the Q1 2025 level for the next quarter. A 27% hole takes more than one quarter to fill, even in an optimistic case.

Tesla’s U.S. total depends on the Model Y. With roughly two-thirds of volume in one car, a miss there would erase any gains elsewhere.

The Bottom Line on Tesla’s Q1 2026 US Results

Tesla’s U.S. sales fell 8.4% to an estimated 117,300 vehicles, its lowest quarter since late 2021, while its market share rose from 43.2% to 54.2%. Both facts come from Cox Automotive’s estimates as reported by InsideEVs, and both hold together because the overall EV market dropped 27% to 216,399 vehicles.

The Model Y grew about 23% to 78,591 sales while the Model 3 fell 39.7% to 31,672. Non-Tesla brands absorbed most of the market’s pain, with their sales down 41%. The numbers show a company that shrank less than its category, not one that grew.

The explanation for all of this remains unconfirmed, and we will update the analysis if a named, on-record source documents one.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many vehicles did Tesla sell in the US in Q1 2026?

Cox Automotive estimates, as reported by InsideEVs, put Tesla’s U.S. sales at 117,300 vehicles in Q1 2026. That is down 8.4% from the same quarter a year earlier.

How can Tesla’s sales fall but its market share rise?

The total U.S. EV market fell 27%, from 296,589 to 216,399 vehicles, which is a much steeper drop than Tesla’s 8.4%. Because Tesla shrank less than the market, its share rose from 43.2% to 54.2%.

Is 117,300 Tesla’s worst US quarter ever?

No. According to the report, it is the lowest quarterly U.S. sales figure since late 2021, which means earlier quarters were lower.

How did the Model Y and Model 3 perform?

The Model Y sold 78,591 vehicles, up approximately 23% year over year. The Model 3 sold 31,672, down 39.7% from 52,520. Together they exceeded 101,000 U.S. sales.

How much did non-Tesla EV sales fall?

InsideEVs’ analysis of Cox Automotive data found that non-Tesla EV sales dropped 41% in Q1 2026, far more than Tesla’s own decline.

Why did Tesla’s US sales fall?

The sources do not document a cause. Any explanation tying Tesla’s results to a specific factor is unconfirmed unless a named, on-record source backs it.

Did Elon Musk comment on the sales figures?

Available results say Musk shared or quoted a related post, but no direct, independently verified statement from him about this headline appears in the source material.

Is Tesla still the top-selling EV brand in the US?

Yes. Tesla remained the leading U.S. EV seller in Q1 2026, with a 54.2% share of the market.

title: Energy isn't just about climate change
description:
If you’re a Democrat, the term “energy policy” may as well have been “environmental policy.” Should we expand natural gas?
Should Congress pass a permitting bill to make it easier to build infrastructure?
Cheap, clean, and consistent: It’s hard to get all three Traditionally, energy policy has been a delicate balance between three objectives: affordability, reliability, and sustainability, the so-called “energy trilemma.” Different sources of energy can fare better on any one or two objectives, but they often struggle to excel across all three.
For centuries, energy access has been enabled by the relative affordability of coal energy, at great cost to the physical environment (our air quality).
For the past two decades, that emphasis has shifted in the Democratic Party, where the dominant paradigm has become sustainability — narrowly understood in terms of restricting fossil fuels to mitigate climate change.
text:
If you’re a Democrat, the term “energy policy” may as well have been “environmental policy.”

Should we expand natural gas? Let’s figure out how much this will increase or decrease emissions.

Should we shutter a nuclear plant? Consider the risks of radioactive waste.

Should Congress pass a permitting bill to make it easier to build infrastructure? Time to consider the impact on endangered species.

With the midterms in the rearview, ascendant Democrats face their first major policy opportunity of the new era: the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). BAAJA may be the most ambitious regulatory overhaul of our lifetimes, and the debate on the Democratic side about whether to support it has at times seemed mostly focused on its implications for the climate.

BAAJA, which not only has bipartisan congressional support but also the president’s backing, would overhaul federal permitting procedures, set the stage for faster interstate transmission build-out, and curb the ability of judges to block infrastructure projects indefinitely (a concern that extends beyond energy into the realms of industrial policy and public transit). We think that it would be a net positive for the climate. But evaluating this bill solely on its climate impact is like evaluating a car solely on its fuel efficiency, without considering safety, reliability, or cost.

Cheap, clean, and consistent: It’s hard to get all three

Traditionally, energy policy has been a delicate balance between three objectives: affordability, reliability, and sustainability, the so-called “energy trilemma.” Different sources of energy can fare better on any one or two objectives, but they often struggle to excel across all three.

For centuries, energy access has been enabled by the relative affordability of coal energy, at great cost to the physical environment (our air quality). Nuclear power is uniquely clean and reliable, but efforts to affordably construct new capacity have been a historic challenge. Wind and solar fare well on sustainability and on local estimates of affordability, but making that power more reliable when scaled comes with steeper system costs.

For the past two decades, that emphasis has shifted in the Democratic Party, where the dominant paradigm has become sustainability — narrowly understood in terms of restricting fossil fuels to mitigate climate change. Consequential policy decisions have been shaped without sufficient consideration of affordability and reliability goals.
