title: You Can't Make America Healthy by Letting Polluters Off the Hook - TIME
description:
They’ve been handed yet another free pass to keep emitting harmful air pollution without the protections that safeguard our health.
Each one is an attack on climate protections and our children’s health at the very moment these protections are most needed.
This growing reliance on methane gas for electricity will drive demand for methane production, and this could mean more oil and gas activity and methane leaks.
Recent polling finds broad support for strong methane protections in five major oil and gas-producing states.
Worsened air pollution from longer, more intense wildfire seasons also means more asthma, immune dysfunction, learning and behavioral problems, and poor birth outcomes.
text:
One might think, from President Donald Trump’s recent announcement of his administration’s plan to gut federal methane protections, that he was doing everyday Americans a huge favor. He claimed that this action was a win for consumers, but the real winners are polluters. They’ve been handed yet another free pass to keep emitting harmful air pollution without the protections that safeguard our health.

The gutting of oil and gas protections should be shocking, but it was to be expected following closely on the heels of his administration’s actions a few weeks ago to repeal limits on climate pollution from fossil fuel power plants. Each one is an attack on climate protections and our children’s health at the very moment these protections are most needed.

As mothers who care deeply about the well-being of our children and the only planet they can call home, we are frightened. Trump’s plans come as data center expansion is rapidly increasing power demand across the country, and the many utility companies and developers are responding with plans for additional fossil fuel generation, including old jet engines and heavily polluting methane gas-fueled turbines.

This growing reliance on methane gas for electricity will drive demand for methane production, and this could mean more oil and gas activity and methane leaks. And when methane leaks from oil and gas operations, toxic air pollutants such as benzene are released along with it, which has been linked to various forms of cancer. Already, nearly 18 million people in the United States, including more than 1 million young children, live near oil and gas wells that will now pollute more freely because of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)’s actions. No parent wants pollution in their child’s lungs.

We aren’t the only ones concerned. Recent polling finds broad support for strong methane protections in five major oil and gas-producing states. Across California, Colorado, New Mexico, Pennsylvania, and Texas, 72% support their state adopting stringent rules to reduce methane emissions from the oil and gas industry, including regular inspections of low-producing wells.

Methane is also a potent climate pollutant that accelerates global warming far faster than carbon dioxide over a 20-year timeframe, making it a key driver of the health harms of climate change that come with escalating weather extremes. Extreme heat raises the risk of heat-related illnesses, which are especially dangerous for children’s developing bodies. Worsened air pollution from longer, more intense wildfire seasons also means more asthma, immune dysfunction, learning and behavioral problems, and poor birth outcomes.

The Trump-Zeldin Environmental Protection Agency may want to ignore the moment of climate urgency we’re living in, but we cannot. Like caregivers around the country and around the world, we’re trying to figure out how to raise our children in uncharted climate terrain. We cannot see how the administration’s attempts to eviscerate federal climate protections—including rolling back methane and power plant pollution safeguards—are in any way aligned with its public messaging on making American families healthy again and saving money for U.S. families and consumers.

title: Low Energy Fridays: What do the midterm results mean for energy policy? - R Street Institute
description:
The results of Tuesday’s midterm elections have sent a seismic jolt throughout the American political system.
The impact of the election will be felt in areas ranging from judicial nominations to border security to healthcare.
But if you’re like me, your reaction to all of this was “What does this mean for energy policy?” Despite the starkness of the results, the short-term impact of the election on energy may be minimal.
Donald Trump remains the president, and most of the action on energy and environmental issues has come via executive rather than legislative action.
To the extent the election results are perceived as partly due to the Democrats’ anti-data center turn, this could also embolden elected officials to enact similar bans and restrictions elsewhere.
text:
The results of Tuesday’s midterm elections have sent a seismic jolt throughout the American political system. Democrats retook both houses of Congress with sizable majorities and won a number of governorships and control of state houses in key states like Texas. The impact of the election will be felt in areas ranging from judicial nominations to border security to healthcare. But if you’re like me, your reaction to all of this was “What does this mean for energy policy?”

Despite the starkness of the results, the short-term impact of the election on energy may be minimal. Donald Trump remains the president, and most of the action on energy and environmental issues has come via executive rather than legislative action. Trump’s second-term energy actions have been consequential: His attempts to reform federal nuclear regulation to encourage faster development of next-generation nuclear reactors have met with success. His attempts to roll back a variety of environmental regulations, such as the Environmental Protection Agency’s rescission of its Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding, are currently subject to court challenge but will not go away. And he is unlikely to back off of his antipathy to wind power either.

When it comes to Congress, 2027 will bring a shift from Republicans holding both chambers without a filibuster-proof majority to Democrats holding both chambers without a filibuster-proof (or veto-proof) majority. The loss of Republican control means Trump will be unable to lock in many of his executive actions on energy through legislation, leaving them vulnerable to the whims of a future administration. But because the president had not devoted much energy to enacting such legislation to begin with, the real-world change will be slight.

One big open question is what the shift in Congressional control will mean for permitting reform. With support from both Democrats and Republicans—indeed, some of the bill’s biggest proponents, such as Rhode Island Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, are Democrats—the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) remains the major vehicle for permitting reform. The change in majority control does not spell doom for the bill; however, BAAJA has sparked opposition from some environmental groups that don’t like its broad approach toward building out natural gas and clean energy infrastructure. In a world where Democrats have the majority, some will feel the temptation to alter the deal to better reflect their own priorities, which could delay or even blow up the compromise. We don’t think delay is prudent, no matter who controls Congress. It takes a long time to build big things, and laying a solid permitting foundation now will pay dividends in the future.

It’s also worth considering the impact of some state-level races. Texas, where Republicans have governed for a generation, was politically upended on Tuesday with a Democratic sweep of all statewide offices plus the statehouse, although the state senate remains in Republican hands. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa promised during her campaign to impose a data center moratorium in the state—a significant statement, as Texas was fast becoming a data-center mecca. A quarter of data-center capacity is supposed to be built in Texas, meaning the election results could drastically impact the buildout of artificial intelligence (AI) as well as the electric generation needed to power it. To the extent the election results are perceived as partly due to the Democrats’ anti-data center turn, this could also embolden elected officials to enact similar bans and restrictions elsewhere.

It’s important to remember that a flipped seat still has similar constituencies it had six years ago; for example, there’s still plenty of oil and gas production and export in Texas, and farmers in Kansas still care about fuel prices and leasing their land for wind turbines. The change in party affiliation doesn’t change the physics or economics of the American economy. While Tuesday’s election (and the reasons why the pendulum swung as hard as it did) will be analyzed in the weeks and months to come, we still need more electricity and more energy to continue to flourish as a nation.

title: Shapiro Administration Helps Cut Red Tape for Three Key Energy Projects
description:
Harrisburg, PA – Three key Pennsylvania energy projects supported by the Shapiro Administration have been selected for PJM’s first Expedited Interconnection Track (EIT), a new process designed to help major energy projects connect to the electric grid more quickly.
“I’m an all-of-the-above energy Governor, and that means advancing every source of energy that can help power our homes and businesses.
My Administration is working to cut red tape and move projects forward, and these three Pennsylvania projects are an important step to accomplishing that.
Under Governor Shapiro’s leadership, his Administration has taken steps to get more energy generation and storage projects online faster.
Through hisLightning Plan(opens in a new tab) and thePA Permit Fast Track Program(opens in a new tab), the Shapiro Administration is cutting permitting delays and helping new energy projects move forward.
text:
Harrisburg, PA – Three key Pennsylvania energy projects supported by the Shapiro Administration have been selected for PJM’s first Expedited Interconnection Track (EIT), a new process designed to help major energy projects connect to the electric grid more quickly. Three of the four projects selected across the PJM region are located in Pennsylvania, representing 68 percent of the total proposed capacity, and are expected to add a combined 1.7 gigawatts (GW) of energy generation and storage capacity by mid-2029 — enough to power nearly 900,000 homes. Two of the three projects are battery storage facilities that will contribute 1.36 GW of clean energy storage capacity, helping strengthen grid reliability, increase the supply of energy, and put downward pressure on electricity costs.

Governor Josh Shapiro has spent years pushing PJM to move faster to connect new energy projects to the grid, strengthen reliability, and protect consumers from rising electricity costs. In January 2026, he joined the 12 other PJM governors and the federal government in issuing a historic Statement of Principles calling for greater affordability, reliability, and meaningful market reform. The EIT advances the broader effort to get more energy online faster and meet growing demand.

“We need to get more reliable energy onto the grid faster to meet growing demand and help protect Pennsylvanians from rising electricity costs,” said Governor Shapiro. “I’m an all-of-the-above energy Governor, and that means advancing every source of energy that can help power our homes and businesses. My Administration is working to cut red tape and move projects forward, and these three Pennsylvania projects are an important step to accomplishing that. PJM must continue to move faster to bring new energy resources online, strengthen transparency and accountability, and ensure decisions are made in the best interest of the 67 million people who rely on this grid.”

The selection of these projects follows the Shapiro Administration’s work to identify projects that can add power to the grid quickly and help them advance through the state permitting process. The Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) and Department of Community and Economic Development (DCED) supported the Commonwealth projects through PJM’s expedited review process, while DEP is also helping the projects move through permitting efficiently. DEP has hosted initial consultation meetings with each project.

Under Governor Shapiro’s leadership, his Administration has taken steps to get more energy generation and storage projects online faster. In April, DEP published aRequest for Information(opens in a new tab) seeking energy generation and battery storage projects that could enter service quickly and help prevent higher energy costs for Pennsylvanians, resulting in the projects being announced today.

“DEP is committed to working closely with these projects to ensure they have the permits they need to be ready to provide electricity to the grid by 2029,” said DEP Secretary Jessica Shirley. “DEP continues to advance the Governor’s all-of-the-above energy approach, supporting cleaner energy sources and innovative technologies, including battery storage, that can help reduce pollution and strengthen grid reliability. These projects will help ensure that when electricity demand is highest, reliable power is available for homes, critical health facilities, and public safety buildings across the Commonwealth.”

“The success of Pennsylvania’s economic development strategy is closely tied to its leadership in energy production,” said DCED Secretary Rick Siger. “Increasing the energy supply in the Commonwealth reinforces our leadership as the largest power producing state in PJM — helping us continue to win major economic development projects. By accelerating these three EIT projects, the Commonwealth is taking meaningful action to enhance grid reliability and ensure our energy infrastructure meets the needs of Pennsylvania businesses.”

Pennsylvania Projects Selected for PJM’s Expedited Review Process

PJM created the EIT to help large, ready-to-build projects connect to the grid faster than under its typical review process. The program is designed to support up to 10 eligible projects per year in 2026 and 2027. To qualify, projects must have at least 250 megawatts (MW) of electric capacity, be able to begin operating within three years, and receive support from a state siting authority or governor. Through the EIT, PJM will review projects in approximately 12 months, cutting the typical timeline by more than half.

As of October 28, 2026, PJM approved four projects for the 2026 EIT window. Three of those projects are in Pennsylvania and received support from Governor Shapiro and DCED. The projects include two new battery storage facilities and an expansion of an existing natural gas power plant:

French Creek Storage (Crawford County): Developed by Engie North America, this project will create an 860 MW battery storage facility that can store electricity and release it when demand is high, improving grid reliability and energy availability.

Sammis Project (Beaver County): Developed by Little Blue Solar, this project would add a 500 MW battery storage facility that can store electricity and release it when demand is high, improving grid reliability and energy availability

Hunterstown Expansion (Adams County): Developed by Hunterstown Generation, this project would conduct an update at an existing natural gas power plant, adding 367 MW of generating capacity.

Together, the projects are expected to add 1.7 GW of generation and storage capacity to the PJM region by mid-2029. The need to bring new energy resources online is increasingly urgent. In its July 2026 capacity auction, PJM fell short of its reliability requirement by more than 6.8 GW, despite nearly every available megawatt of electricity clearing the auction. The shortfall underscores the need to accelerate new energy generation and storage as electricity demand grows and projects continue to face delays in PJM’s interconnection queue.

Governor Shapiro’s Work to Increase Energy Supply and Protect Ratepayers

Governor Shapiro has spent years pushing PJM to modernize its rules, speed up its interconnection process, and protect consumers from unnecessary electricity cost increases. Throughout 2024, he urged PJM to cut red tape, move new energy projects through its interconnection queue faster, reform its capacity market, and improve reliability during extreme weather. When PJM failed to act, Governor Shapiro sued(opens in a new tab), challenging an auction structure he warned would saddle consumers with billions of dollars in unnecessary costs. That legal action led to a January 2025 settlement(opens in a new tab), later approved by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), that significantly lowered PJM’s capacity price cap.

The settlement and its subsequent extension have helped protect consumers from billions of dollars in unnecessary energy costs. The July 2026 auction results(opens in a new tab) brought total projected savings to $45 billion across the 13-state PJM region, including more than $2 billion in savings for Pennsylvania homes and businesses in the 2028-29 delivery year alone — an average of approximately $207 per household. Across the PJM region, the settlement is projected to save consumers an average of $800 per household over four years. In April 2026, FERC approved an extension of the price cap for two additional auctions, through 2030.

Protecting Pennsylvanians as Energy Demand Grows

Governor Shapiro is also working to ensure that growing electricity demand — including demand from data centers — does not drive up costs or threaten reliable service for families and businesses. In August, he signedExecutive Order 2026-05(opens in a new tab), establishing the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development (GRID) Requirements for data center developers seeking Commonwealth support. The requirements establish that developers must pay the full cost of the new generation, transmission, distribution, and other infrastructure needed to power their projects.

In October, the Governor also filed a petition(opens in a new tab) to intervene in a Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission proceeding involving PPL Electric Utilities, supporting efforts to ensure large data centers pay their fair share of electricity costs and that existing customers are protected from potential reliability risks. The Governor’s petition advances his Executive Order’s direction to prevent data centers from shifting costs to other electricity customers.

The Governor is also working to make it faster and easier to build new energy projects in Pennsylvania. Through hisLightning Plan(opens in a new tab) and thePA Permit Fast Track Program(opens in a new tab), the Shapiro Administration is cutting permitting delays and helping new energy projects move forward. These efforts build on Pennsylvania’s position as the nation’s second-largest energy producer and exporter and support the Administration’s goal of bringing more power online while keeping costs down.

text:
LG Energy Solution has signed a US$4.3 billion agreement to supply Tesla with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic battery cells made at its plant in Lansing, Michigan. Production is expected to start in 2027, according to CNBC. The cells are earmarked for Tesla’s Megapack 3 energy storage systems built in Houston, and the cited reporting says the output is not currently for Tesla’s electric vehicles.

The LG Energy Solution Tesla battery deal is not brand-new. The U.S. government named Tesla as the buyer in March 2026, identifying the customer behind a large battery order that LG had disclosed in July without naming the buyer. What has changed since then is the world around it. Megapack 3 production in Texas has moved forward, rival makers have started turning out LFP cells on American soil, and tariff policy keeps tilting the economics. This analysis lays out what is confirmed, what is not, and what the deal signals for the U.S. storage supply chain as of November 6, 2026.

The timing matters for Tesla’s broader story. The company’s car lines are shifting, with reported plans to wind down Cybertruck production in 2027, while its energy business keeps absorbing capital and attention. A multibillion-dollar cell contract for stationary storage fits that pattern. It also lands in the hardware beat because the real story sits in factories, chemistry and supply lines rather than in a stock ticker.

What the LG Energy Solution Tesla Battery Deal Covers

Strip away the headlines and the confirmed core is short. LG Energy Solution and Tesla signed a supply agreement worth US$4.3 billion. The product is LFP prismatic battery cells, the flat, rectangular format common in stationary storage. The cells will be built at LG Energy Solution’s facility in Lansing, Michigan, with production expected to begin in 2027. The end use is Tesla’s Megapack 3 systems, which Tesla produces in Houston.

Those five facts appear consistently across the coverage, from CNBC to Seoul Economic Daily to the Energy Storage news desk. The U.S. Department of the Interior supplied the official language, and LG Energy Solution’s spokesperson, Phil Lienert, confirmed the production plan in a statement. Bloomberg’s headline put the commitment plainly: LG says it will supply Tesla with $4.3 billion of batteries.

Two details deserve emphasis because they shape how to read the number. First, this is a supply agreement, not a plant construction project. The cited reporting says the existing Lansing facility will be used, so headlines that describe a brand-new factory overstate the case. Second, the cells are for energy storage. Anyone hoping the deal signals a new battery source for Tesla’s Model 3 or Model Y will not find that in the confirmed record.

Timeline: From an Unnamed Buyer to Tesla

The path to the named deal ran through a regulatory trail. IANS reported that the U.S. government confirmed Tesla as the buyer of what it called LG Energy Solution’s July battery deal. Until then, the order had circulated as a mystery customer with a headline figure and little else. Seoul Economic Daily and Energy Storage both carried the March confirmation, and both reported the same two facts: the customer was Tesla, and the value was $4.3 billion.

That sequence explains why the story keeps drawing search interest. Readers who saw the July disclosure still ask who the buyer was. Readers who saw the March confirmation now ask what happens next, and the honest answer is that the next visible milestone is the 2027 production start in Lansing. Until LG Energy Solution or Tesla publishes more detail, the timeline stays thin between the announcement and first output.

Why LFP Prismatic Cells Fit Grid Storage

LFP chemistry earned its place in stationary storage by trading energy density for durability and cost. A grid battery sits in a yard or a warehouse, so weight and volume matter less than they do in a car. What matters is cycle life, thermal stability and price per kilowatt-hour. LFP scores well on all three, which is why it has become a default choice for large storage projects worldwide.

The prismatic format adds a manufacturing logic. Large rectangular cells stack neatly into racks and containers, cut the number of connections per module, and simplify the mechanical design of a unit as big as a Megapack. Pouch and cylindrical cells can do the job, but prismatic cells have become the common pick for utility-scale boxes. The LG Energy Solution Tesla battery deal specifies exactly this format, and the choice tells us the Megapack 3 design leans on large LFP prismatic cells for at least part of its supply.

There is a supply-chain angle as well. LFP production has long been concentrated in China, which gave Chinese suppliers a cost and scale lead in storage cells. Building LFP lines in Michigan is a direct attempt to shift some of that capacity onto U.S. soil. Whether the cost gap closes depends on factors the confirmed record does not cover, including line yields, material sourcing and the level of tariff protection.

Lansing: Existing Plant, New Production Lines

Lansing is the physical center of the agreement. LG Energy Solution said it will establish dedicated production lines at its Lansing facility to deliver on the contract. WLNS in Lansing reported that the $4.3B Tesla-LG battery production is set for 2027 in the city, and local coverage has treated the deal as a significant win for the Lansing area.

What “dedicated lines” means

The phrase signals that the Tesla order will not share capacity with other customers. In practice, a dedicated line is configured for one cell design, one customer’s specifications and one qualification process. That approach speeds quality control and gives the buyer more certainty on volume. It also ties the line’s fate to the contract. If demand for the product softens, the line has fewer easy alternatives.

What is not confirmed about Lansing

Neither company has published a gigawatt-hour figure, an annual cell count, a headcount or a capital budget for the new lines. The sources available for this analysis do not say how long retooling will take, how many lines will run, or how fast output will ramp after 2027. Anyone quoting those numbers as fact is guessing.

Megapack 3 and the Houston Connection

The other end of the supply line is Houston. The Department of the Interior said American-made cells will power Tesla’s Megapack 3 systems produced there. ESS News framed the confirmation as Tesla emerging as the mystery buyer in a deal for domestic Megapack 3 production.

Reports from later in the year add context. Electrek reported on November 3 that Tesla’s Houston-area Megapack factory began Megapack 3 production in August 2026, that the site carries a planned capacity of roughly 50 GWh a year, and that it received foreign-trade-zone status that allows duty deferral on eligible imported parts. Treat those figures as reported rather than official, because they do not appear in the company statements tied to the LG deal. The point stands either way: Tesla already builds Megapack 3 in Texas, so the Lansing cells arrive in 2027 to feed a factory that is running and ramping.

The timing gap is worth reading closely. If Megapack 3 production began in 2026 and the Lansing cells do not arrive until 2027, Tesla must be sourcing cells from elsewhere in the meantime. The record does not say from whom or in what quantity. Tesla’s first-quarter 2026 investor update also pointed to LFP cell ramp-up at its own Nevada site, which suggests the company is building several supply routes at once. Owners of Tesla’s smaller home battery products face a different question about reliability and service, a topic covered in our report on a Powerwall 3 owner reporting a replacement after one year.

Storage, Not Cars: What the Deal Means for Tesla Vehicles

A common misreading treats every Tesla battery contract as a car story. This one is not. The cited reporting is explicit that production at Lansing is not currently for Tesla electric vehicles. That matters for investors and buyers alike, since it means the deal does not directly address vehicle costs, range or supply for any Tesla model.

Tesla’s car business has its own pressures. Our earlier coverage of Tesla’s first-quarter U.S. sales decline alongside a 54.2% share shows a company holding share in a shrinking slice of the market. Energy storage offers a different growth curve, one driven by utilities, developers and data center operators rather than by consumer vehicle demand. A $4.3 billion cell contract is a bet that the storage curve keeps bending upward.

The deal also says something about how Tesla thinks about vertical integration. The company builds cells in-house at some sites and buys them at others. Rather than relying on one path, it is stacking supply from a Korean partner with American production, its own LFP ramp and, according to reports, imported material under trade-zone rules. That mix looks like risk management for a product line where a cell shortage would idle an assembly plant.

What Is Confirmed and What Is Not

Coverage of this deal has mixed solid facts with inference, so a clean split helps. The table below separates what the announcement and the cited reports establish from what remains open.

The contract length is the one that tempts writers most. Some outlets have described a multiyear window with an option to extend supply. The sources used here do not verify those terms, so this analysis leaves them out of the confirmed column. If LG Energy Solution files more detail with regulators or discusses it on an earnings call, the table will need an update.

What Officials and the Company Said

The official language is short, and it reveals the framing both sides want. The U.S. Department of the Interior said: “American-made cells will power Tesla’s Megapack 3 energy storage systems produced in Houston, creating a robust domestic battery supply chain.” The emphasis falls on domestic content and supply chain security, not on price or performance. That fits a policy environment where federal agencies promote U.S. manufacturing, and Seoul Economic Daily’s account of the confirmation carried the same message to a Korean audience.

LG Energy Solution spokesperson Phil Lienert focused on execution: “We will establish dedicated production lines at our Lansing facility to deliver on this agreement.” The sentence commits the company to build capacity rather than draw down existing inventory. It does not set a date beyond the 2027 start, and it does not name a capacity.

Both statements are notable for what they leave out. Neither mentions price per kilowatt-hour, Tesla’s share of Lansing output, or any penalty for missed deliveries. Those are the terms that determine whether the contract is a good deal, and they remain private.

The Competitive Picture: Other U.S. LFP Storage Cell Sources

LG Energy Solution is not the only company moving LFP production onto American soil. Reports from early November describe Samsung SDI beginning mass production of prismatic LFP cells in October 2026 at its StarPlus Energy site in Kokomo, Indiana. Coverage from pv magazine USA and others tied the plant to roughly $6.3 billion in investment and said Samsung SDI booked more than 60 GWh of U.S. storage orders. Tesla itself reports that LFP cells in Nevada, cathode materials in Texas and lithium refining in Texas have entered ramp-up.

The table shows a market that is crowded sooner than many expected. Two Korean groups are racing to supply American storage buyers, and Tesla is building its own capacity at the same time. For LG Energy Solution, the Tesla contract is an anchor customer that secures utilization before the Lansing lines even start. For Samsung SDI, the early production start and large order book show that the competition has a head start on actual cell output.

Tariffs and Policy Behind the Push

Policy explains why a Korean battery maker would reconfigure a Michigan plant for a rival chemistry. Electrek reported that Chinese non-EV lithium-ion batteries entering the United States still face a 25% Section 301 tariff, even where a facility holds foreign-trade-zone status. That tariff narrows the price advantage of imported cells and makes domestic output more competitive than it would be on pure cost.

Federal messaging reinforces the same direction. The Interior Department’s language about a domestic battery supply chain reads as policy endorsement, and Washington’s decision to confirm a private commercial buyer is itself worth noticing. In our view, it suggests officials wanted a public marker of progress for the project.

Local politics add a second layer. Data center and grid-infrastructure projects now face voter scrutiny, a trend we tracked in our report on five state levers that shape AI data center builds. Storage is the companion technology for those loads. Every large data center that struggles to secure grid capacity becomes a potential buyer of on-site batteries, which links a Michigan cell line to the debate over how America powers its AI buildout.

Market Impact for Suppliers, Investors and Buyers

The market impact splits into three groups. For LG Energy Solution, a $4.3 billion contract with a named U.S. buyer diversifies revenue away from a weaker electric vehicle cycle and toward storage. It also gives the company a story to tell about American manufacturing. For Tesla, the deal secures a domestic cell source for a product line where supply continuity matters. For utilities and developers who buy Megapacks, it promises future units built with American-made cells, a selling point for projects with domestic-content goals.

Upstream, the ripple reaches materials suppliers. KED Global reported on November 4 that L&F plans a new 60,000-ton LFP cathode plant as ESS orders swell. That headline shows how storage demand pulls on the whole chain, from cathode to cell to cabinet. The LG Energy Solution Tesla battery deal is one visible order inside that wave.

Investors should keep the scale in view. A US$4.3 billion contract stretched over several years is large for a single customer, but its annual effect on a company of LG Energy Solution’s size depends on a delivery schedule nobody has published. Market sentiment around Tesla also remains volatile. Our look at the $456 billion market cap loss across Tesla and SpaceX after the midterms shows how quickly political news can swamp operational progress, so storage wins may not move the share price in a clean line.

Historical Context: Korean Battery Makers Pivot to Storage

Korean cell makers built their reputations on cells for electric vehicles, and LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI both put capital into U.S. production. Storage has since become a second customer base for those American sites. The Tesla contract and the Kokomo start show that shift in practice.

The shift to LFP is the more telling change. LFP production has long sat mostly with Chinese producers. The Lansing plan and the Kokomo start both show Korean groups moving into that chemistry for storage. Our read is that storage buyers value cost and durability, and that U.S. policy now rewards domestic production, which makes the move sensible.

Tesla’s own plans matter too. The company reports LFP cell ramp-up in Nevada, and the LG contract does not replace that effort. It adds a second pillar that could let Tesla scale Megapack output faster than a single supply route would allow.

Risks to Watch Before 2027

Execution risk in Lansing

Converting or adding lines at a plant looks simpler than building a new one, but yield problems, equipment delays and qualification cycles can push a start date. A 2027 target leaves little slack for a first-of-its-kind product at that site. Any slip would ripple into Tesla’s Houston plans.

Policy and demand risk

Tariff rules and federal incentives can change quickly. A contract signed under one policy regime may face a different one by the time cells ship. Demand risk also exists on the Tesla side, since Megapack orders depend on utility and developer budgets. Tesla’s Texas operations are also in motion, as our report on reported added 12-hour shifts at Giga Texas shows.

Five Predictions for the LG Energy Solution Tesla Battery Deal

The following forecasts are this publication’s analysis, not reported facts. Each rests on the confirmed record above and on patterns in the cited coverage.

LG Energy Solution will add detail before 2027. Investors and local officials will push for capacity, hiring and timing figures. Expect an earnings-call or regulatory disclosure that puts numbers on the Lansing lines.

More U.S. LFP storage supply deals will follow. With Samsung SDI already producing in Indiana and demand for storage cells rising, other buyers will seek domestic contracts, and other makers will seek anchor customers.

Tesla will keep a mixed supply model. The company has several cell routes in motion, and the evidence points to a continued blend of in-house, partner and imported sourcing rather than a single winner.

Tariff treatment will shape pricing more than chemistry. If the 25% tariff on Chinese non-EV lithium-ion batteries holds, domestic LFP cells will stay competitive. If it changes, the Lansing economics will tighten.

Data center demand will become a bigger storage driver. As AI facilities hunt for power, storage will move from a utility add-on to a standard part of large-load planning, which supports long-term demand for Megapack-class products.

The Takeaway for Readers

The confirmed facts are tidy: US$4.3 billion, LFP prismatic cells, Lansing, 2027, Megapack 3, Houston. The unconfirmed list is longer than the confirmed one, and that gap is where careful readers should focus. Volume, schedule, contract length and economics all remain private.

For anyone tracking U.S. battery manufacturing, the useful signal is directional. Storage has become the growth lane for domestic cell production, LFP has crossed from a Chinese specialty into a Western manufacturing priority, and Tesla is willing to anchor a Korean supplier’s American lines. Watch for the first Lansing output in 2027, for Samsung SDI’s order fulfillment, and for any change in tariff treatment. Those three markers will tell us whether this deal marks the start of a durable supply chain or a one-off contract.

FAQ

What is the LG Energy Solution Tesla battery deal?

It is a US$4.3 billion supply agreement under which LG Energy Solution will provide Tesla with LFP prismatic battery cells for energy storage. The cells will be made at LG’s facility in Lansing, Michigan.

When does production start?

Production is expected to begin in 2027, according to the cited reporting. No firm delivery schedule beyond that start has been published.

Will the batteries go into Tesla cars?

No, not currently. The cited reporting says the production is not for Tesla electric vehicles. The cells are intended for Megapack 3 energy storage systems built in Houston.

Is LG Energy Solution building a new factory for this?

Reporting says the existing Lansing facility will be used, with dedicated production lines set up for the Tesla order. A new plant has not been confirmed.

How many batteries or gigawatt-hours does the contract cover?

That is not confirmed. Neither company has published a capacity, cell quantity or annual volume figure, so any number you see quoted is an estimate.

Who confirmed that Tesla is the buyer?

The U.S. government confirmed Tesla as the customer in March 2026, as reported by CNBC, Energy Storage, IANS and Seoul Economic Daily. The Department of the Interior supplied the official statement.

What is Megapack 3?

Megapack 3 is Tesla’s stationary energy storage product, produced in Houston according to the Interior Department. It is the destination for the Lansing-made cells.

Why does LFP matter for U.S. battery manufacturing?

LFP is a cost-effective, durable chemistry that suits grid storage, and its production has long been concentrated in China. Building LFP lines in Michigan and Indiana moves some of that capacity into the United States.

text:
Now that the dust is settled, Matzzie told me that most of the races they intervened in wound up flipping red to blue: “I think we’re on track to win 12 or 13 of the 18 we invested in. We had seven or eight marquee races and we’re winning the majority of those. We were hopeful we’d get one in a tough district. We didn’t expect to get this many.”

Their favorite trophy is Indiana’s 5th congressional district in the northern Indianapolis region, where Rep. Victoria Spartz lost a historically comfortable GOP seat to J.D. Ford, a Democratic state senator. Matzzie told me the Super PAC invested $2 million in the race to beat Spartz, which he claimed is more than both campaigns spent combined. (My search of FEC records shows that may be true, if you don’t count other outside assistance.)

After Spartz was declared the loser, the Super PAC sent an email blast to the media with a short statement: “Tell Victoria Spartz. We want her to know it was us.”

The Super PAC also claims at least partial responsibility for helping oust Rep. Lauren Boebert of Colorado, who lost by just a few thousand votes. I’m told they invested $1.5 million in the race, including on a digital ad centered around an incident where Boebert was escorted out of a live stage performance of “Beetlejuice.” The ad claimed Boebert couldn’t be trusted around children. It prompted Boebert to do a whole segment bashing the Super PAC while guest hosting former Rep. Matt Gaetz’s One America News show.

“Oh, I love it when they complain about us. I love it when they whine about us. We want them to spread the word to other members of Congress about what we’re doing,” Matzzie told me. “We want to send a message that we will do what is necessary to defeat you in your next election, including getting down in the mud if needed, and we have limits on what we say and won’t say, but it has to be truthful.”

Since it is already time for 2028 discussions, I asked Matzzie if the Super PAC had any ambitions to be involved in the presidential primaries next. Absolutely, he said. First that involvement will look like education. That could look like having pro-renewables voices urging GOP candidates to be more receptive to the sector, whether they be representatives of the business community or landowners with solar on their properties.

“The accountability part of this comes later as people firm up their point of view on what they’re running on and we don’t know what that is yet. We totally invite all of the candidates to be supportive of the clean energy industry if they’re running for president. That is our ideal outcome,” Matzzie said.

But if candidates don’t get the message will they go on the attack against primary candidates? “I have no hesitation about doing it.”

Emily Pontecorvo and Jael Holzman took on the biggest question that now faces Congress: What will come of the bipartisan permitting deal?

Matthew Zeitlin took stock of Wall Street’s winners and losers, as nuclear stocks suffer and solar stocks take off.

It’s a Zeitlin double-header: Here’s his second piece from yesterday on the double-edged sword of high gas prices for Democrats.

And Katie Brigham looked at what climate-tech investors who trained themselves not to call it “climate tech” are thinking now.

2. Oil prices plunge below $100 a barrel

Vice President JD Vance is openly blaming the Trump administration’s war with Iran for Republicans’ midterm shellacking, and Democrats are formulating a new approach after campaigning against the conflict and its associated energy shock. Iran, meanwhile, is signaling its openness to peace talks, even as Tehran turns to guerrilla tactics to regain control over the Strait of Hormuz. All that looks to oil traders like more crude hitting the market. On Wednesday, the price of West Texas Intermediate crude, the U.S. benchmark, fell more than 8% to $88 per barrel. Brent crude, the global price measure, plunged nearly 9% to just under $95 per barrel. Murban crude, the stuff that leaves a Persian Gulf port in the United Arab Emirates, dropped 1% to just under $101 per barrel.

3. Data centers’ electricity demand is mostly an American problem

Data centers? Tellement américain. Rhodium Group

Big meals, big trucks, big computers — it’s the American way. Only one of those is a problem for electricity prices — a problem that’s also uniquely American. New projections from the Rhodium Group suggest that the U.S. is the only major market where data centers are the primary driver behind surging electricity demand, constituting between 62% and 77% of gross demand growth. In China, Europe, India, and the Middle East, residential and commercial buildings are by far the biggest new sources of demand for electricity to power air conditioning, heating, and appliances. Meanwhile, according to data from the consultancy Cleanview, upward of 41% of planned data centers in the U.S. are in states where newly elected governors are considering moratoria on new projects

.

China, burnishing its electro-state status. Rhodium Group

The Rhodium forecast also shows big global challenges for the fight to slow global warming. Electricity serves just 21% of the world’s end-use energy; by 2035, countries pledged to raise that figure to 35%. But the global average for electrification is on track to hit just 28% in the next nine years, threatening to maintain planet-heating pollution levels even as renewables surge and power emissions fall. Low-carbon sources of electricity are on track to generate upward of 80% of the power in China and the world’s richest economies, with variable renewables such as wind and solar producing the bulk of the output. Clean firm sources such as nuclear power and geothermal maintain a steady share of total output as variable sources eat into fossil fuels’ market. As a result, emissions shift to the parts of the world where fossil fuels will remain dominant. China and rich countries will account for 37% of emissions in 2050, down from 54% in 2024. India’s emissions will rise 26% by the middle of the century, and the entire African continent’s output by 37%. Worldwide industrial emissions are on track to stay static as the benefits of low-carbon steel are offset by the spike in production from coal-fired blast furnaces.

4. Exclusive: U.S. creates a benchmark for testing what AI can do in a nuclear power plant

Whenever OpenAI or Anthropic releases a new model, the healthcare industry, say, can measure its capabilities by seeing how quickly it can pass a medical board test. Last year, the AI startup Atomic Canyon — which formed to help nuclear plant operators sift through mountains of documents using large language models — inked a deal with the Idaho National Laboratory to create a test that can check the software’s ability to work with a nuclear plant. Fourteen months later, the partnership has yielded results. On Thursday, I can report exclusively for this newsletter, Atomic Canyon is set to launch what it calls NuclearBench, the first open-source benchmark designed specifically to evaluate how LLMs perform on questions related to nuclear energy. “Think about it like an open-book exam for AI models,” Trey Lauderdale, Atomic Canyon’s founder and chief executive, told me. The company worked with INL to design a 280-question exam, which can then be administered to AI models, whose answers are judged by accuracy and context.

“As you’d expect, the more advanced models perform better. You’ve got OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic all vying at the top,” Lauderdale said. “Nothing we wouldn’t expect, but it’s nice to have actual metrics and information that validate general hypotheses you might have. You could instinctively say, This model is doing better. But it’s really important as an industry that you start benchmarking what these models can do.” Atomic Canyon’s test is not yet at the level of a medical board exam, he said. But the company plans to continuously update its exam to account for the growing sophistication of LLMs. Eventually, Lauderdale hopes to roll out more targeted tests focusing on safety and risk, reactor engineering, emergency preparedness, radiation, and other factors. “It’s the equivalent of the tests to become a general physician or those to become a cardiologist, dermatologist, or gastroenterologist,” he said.

5. Exclusive: U.S. startup eyeing 1.2 gigawatts of nuclear uprates gets a big endorsement

Last month, I told you when tech giants announced a series of deals to help fund “uprates” at existing nuclear plants, renovations that potentially squeeze hundreds of megawatts of new generation out of reactors that are already running. The deals with Google and Amazon looked to generate more than a gigawatt of new power through uprates across PJM Interconnection, the most stressed grid system in the U.S. Now a startup specifically designed to affordably uprate reactors is considering projects to generate as much as 1.2 gigawatts of new power out of existing plants — and it just received a major endorsement from a utility industry heavyweight. I can exclusively report that, on Thursday, the developer Alva Energy plans to announce that Jeff Lyash, the former chief executive of the Tennessee Valley Authority and Ontario Power Generation, would join its board of directors. Lyash has plenty of nuclear experience. OPG, owned by Canada’s most populous province, operates the second-largest nuclear fleet in North America after the U.S.-based Constellation Energy. It’s also building the continent’s first small modular reactor, the first of GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy’s 300-megawatt units. The federally owned TVA, from which Lyash retired last year following Trump’s return to the White House, operates three nuclear plants and is building what’s expected to be America’s first SMR, the second GE-Hitachi BWRX-300 after OPG’s project at its Darlington plant. Lyash will be the fifth member of Alva’s board. After former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, he’s the second to come from outside the company; the other three board members are Alva’s co-founders.

“What’s been pretty amazing is that we’re starting to attract top-tier industry talent,” James Krellenstein, Alva’s chief executive and co-founder, told me. “Jeff joining the board has been pretty transformational because he brings a massive amount of experience in modifying existing plants.” At OPG in particular, Krellenstein said, Lyash oversaw refurbishments of the utility’s CANDU reactors. He also sits on the boards of the utility Dominion Energy, the Canadian construction giant Aecon, the industrial conglomerate Curtiss-Wright, and the European reactor startup Newcleo, which Krellenstein said lends Alva greater insight into other sectors’ large-scale project management. “What the economy of the United States is looking for is sources of clean, 24/7 power. Nuclear power uprates are a way in the short term to get that demand fulfilled in the United States while simultaneously rebuilding the execution capability necessary to create new plants. That’s the exact scaling strategy that Alva is working on.”

THE KICKER

It’s no Norway, where electric vehicles make up nearly 99% of new car sales. But EVs’ share of Germany’s new car market soared to a record 37% last month, according to data from the country’s national motor vehicle authority, the Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt. That, according to Electrek, equates to 94,086 new battery-electric vehicles, up nearly 80% from the 53,425 sold a year earlier.

“This was not an election that was a referendum about climate or energy or anything even close to that,” Lara Pierpoint, managing director at the philanthropic climate tech firm Trellis Climate, told me. The consensus was that voters were far more concerned with affordability, Trump’s deep unpopularity, and, to some extent, the data center backlash. Sure, all of these issues touch on climate, but it was by no means anyone’s central message.

But that doesn’t mean Tuesday wasn’t still a win for the energy transition.

“This new Congress, controlled by Democrats, will focus mostly on energy affordability and access,” Gabriel Kra, managing director at Prelude Ventures, told me. That, he said, will likely encompass a push for more solar, wind, and batteries in energy planning — but “all in the name of affordability and reliability, not focused on climate.”

Susan Su, a climate investor and analyst, expects this El Niño cycle to bring climate back into the conversation, but “maybe more in the form of adaptation, extreme weather, and just resilience,” she told me.

“I don’t think we’re going to rush back to talk about climate this or that. I think we will rush back to acknowledging that this is the macro of all macros,” Andrew Beebe of Obvious Ventures told me, meaning climate remains one of the biggest forces shaping the global economy, whether or not investors and policymakers choose to call it that. “Maybe it’ll just get more attention in whatever name, I don’t really care.”

Still, investors aren’t expecting an immediate flood of federal climate action in the lame-duck session, although, of course, passing the permitting bill would ease the way for economy-wide electrification. And Kra told me it’s still too soon to know whether some of the Trump administration’s canceled or frozen grants for technologies like clean cement, steel, hydrogen, and carbon capture could be revived under a Democratic Congress. Restarting that funding would certainly offer a beacon of hope for clean industries that have yet to move down the cost curve and into the realm of true affordability.

Investors’ most realistic near-term hope is that Tuesday’s results mark the beginning of a more stable era for the clean energy ecosystem. “The Trump administration has just introduced so much chaos, and markets hate chaos. They love certainty,” Su told me. She pointed out that as the results rolled in, the 10-year Treasury yield dipped. Su read that as a sign that investors were rushing to lock in today’s higher rates, betting that a more stable political environment would lower borrowing costs down the road. That would both make first-of-a-kind projects cheaper to finance and push investors to chase riskier, higher-return bets in the venture market.

“Even just the perception of more certainty via a potential check on Trump — a legislative check on Trump — could bring cost of capital down, which is going to have a positive halo effect across our whole sector,” Su told me.

Kra expressed a similar hope: that the next two years will lay the groundwork for a more durable U.S. energy and industrial policy framework. “By durable, I mean guidelines and rules and laws that can survive a changed administration and a change of control of Congress,” he told me. “That will unlock affordable reshoring of American manufacturing. That will unlock an industrial and commercial response that will really catalyze growth in the economy, in clean electricity and energy, and in the innovation economy.”

I also heard some optimism that Republicans, battered by Tuesday’s results, might start to find their voice on clean energy as they begin to break free from Trump’s yoke. “My big hope would be that we finally enter a phase where Republicans can not be threatened to say what I think most of them already know, which is that the climate issues are real and need addressing,” Beebe told me. “It’s truly possible that a lot of people will wake up and realize that the spell is broken from Trump, and they will be able to, in the plain light of day, evaluate things at face value again.”

That could help depoliticize and expedite the rollout of technologies like electric vehicles and heat pumps, which have become partisan products in recent years. Meanwhile, Rajesh Swaminathan of Khosla Ventures told me via email that he sees lots of potential for bipartisan momentum behind superhot rock geothermal, fusion, critical minerals, and cost-competitive clean cement and steel.

Now, Su told me, it’s time for climate technologies that have talked a big game on affordability to prove it, giving investors and Republican skeptics no reason to dismiss them. “For years, founders have been talking about, ‘Oh, we’re not just cleaner, but we’re actually cheaper and better.’ Okay, so now it’s time to put your money where your mouth is,” she told me.

She’s also optimistic that this younger generation of newly elected lawmakers will be more open to the full spectrum of climate solutions, from adaptation and carbon removal to more speculative and unconventional ideas like solar geoengineering. “It’s not going to be Al Gore anymore,” she told me. “I think younger people have a very different view on, let’s do what we need to do to make ourselves have a livable future versus sticking to older mental models.”

But perhaps the most liberating takeaway from Tuesday night for Su and her fellow investors? “We don’t have to pretend that we’re friends with Donald Trump anymore.”

title: 4 things Democrats could do for the environment with a simple Senate majority | CNN
description:
The Democrats’ upcoming simple majority in the Senate will enable them to take multiple actions on climate, public lands, endangered species and other environmental issues.

text:
The Democrats’ upcoming simple majority in the Senate will enable them to take multiple actions on climate, public lands, endangered species and other environmental issues. But the lack of a veto-proof majority means that Democrats’ power will still be somewhat limited, given the need for President Donald Trump’s signature on legislation.

Here are some of the concrete actions that a Democrat-led Senate could take to advance their environmental priorities.

Investigate the war on wind

Like the House, the Senate has the authority to launch investigations of the Trump administration’s actions, including the power to issue subpoenas to compel documents and testimony. The White House’s energy policies and extensive regulatory rollbacks of clean air, climate and species protection regulations are likely to be targets for committees overseeing those areas, such as the Environment and Public Works Committee.

Other potential investigatory targets include the funding of Trump’s Washington, DC, construction projects, specifically whether any of the money for them came out of the National Park Service’s maintenance budget.

Watch for Senate committees to call for testimony from Energy Secretary Chris Wright and EPA administrator Lee Zeldin in particular, since their agencies have executed much of the administration’s fossil fuel-centered energy policy and deregulatory agenda.

The administration’s war on wind power is also likely to come under scrutiny and may ensnare Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.

Another possible investigatory target? The DOGE cuts to environmental agencies.

Although investigations can partly be political theater, they can have real consequences if they uncover wrongdoing on the part of officials or agencies. Even bureaucratic snafus, like not following the proper procedures when making major changes to regulations, can yield meaningful results, potentially leading to the overturning of regulatory rollbacks and even legal trouble for agency officials.

The all-powerful budget process

Senate Democrats could seek to prevent the administration’s environmental actions through the appropriations process by attaching language to bills that would prohibit any money from being spent to keep coal-fired power plants open, something that the Energy Department has used emergency orders to do on multiple occasions. Democrats could also prohibit spending money to build data centers on public lands or only allow their construction after soliciting extensive local public input, Michael Gerrard, an environmental law professor at Columbia University Law School, said.

“Appropriations riders are one thing with real teeth that they could insist on,” Gerrard said of Senate Democrats. “However, the larger appropriations bills that such language would be attached to require a 60-vote threshold to pass, which means there would need to be some cooperation from the other side of the aisle.”

But that isn’t necessarily a deal breaker, because some of the things Democrats will want to do — such as breaking the logjam of approvals for wind and other renewable energy projects around the country — do have bipartisan support.

Democrats will lack a veto-proof majority in the Senate, however, which means that if Trump vetoes such bills, they will serve more as a signal to voters about Democratic priorities rather than becoming laws.

Block confirmation on anti-environment officials

The ascendant Democratic majority in the Senate will have the ability to block Trump’s nominees for environment-related positions, including for independent regulatory agencies like the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission that play a large role in setting US energy policy.

A Democrat-led Senate could also choose not to act on or oppose nominees for some independent agencies, Gerrard said, rendering those entities without a quorum and thus unable to function. This could suit Democrats’ interests in some cases, while irritating the White House, he said. It could also serve as a deterrent against the president when it comes to firing members of independent agencies.

The Senate confirms higher-profile nominees as well, including nominees for the Supreme Court, should a vacancy occur, along with cabinet secretaries. The confirmation process is likely to be far more confrontational under Democrats than it was during the administration’s first two years in office with unified Republican control of Congress.

Roll back Trump’s rollbacks

Democratic senators can also work to pass bills that would accomplish their key environmental goals, regardless of whether the president signs it. This could include bills aimed at fully staffing environmental agencies like the US Geological Service, EPA, NPS and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration after DOGE cuts reduced their headcounts.

If Democrats want to restore certain clean energy subsidies that Republicans ended, they could try to do so through a process known as reconciliation, which has a simple majority threshold but strict requirements for what can go into the legislation. But that would still need the president’s signature.

Ultimately, a simple Democratic majority in the Senate can accomplish some of the Democrats’ environmental agenda and undo some of the actions that the president and Republican Congress took during the first two years of Trump’s second term in office. But it would take a larger majority, or capturing the White House, to make more sweeping and lasting policy changes.

text:
Conventional lithium-ion batteries are nearing their practical energy limit of about 300 Wh kg-1, while liquid electrolytes raise leakage and fire risks. Lithium (Li) metal anodes offer a high theoretical capacity of 3,860 mAh g-1 and low potential, and lithium-rich manganese-based oxide (LRMO) cathodes can exceed 250 mAh g-1, making Li-LRMO solid-state batteries attractive. In situ polymerized quasi-solid-state gel electrolytes (QSEs) are promising, but they usually require thermal initiation above 60 °C with azobisisobutyronitrile (AIBN) as initiator.

This can cause instant polymerization, heat and gas buildup, uneven solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) and cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI) layers, and electrode degradation. Based on these challenges, further research is needed to develop mild, uniform and electrode-compatible in situ polymerization for energy-dense solid-state batteries.

In a study published (DOI: 10.1016/j.esci.2026.100626) online on 20 July 2026 in eScience, researchers at Nankai University and the Haihe Laboratory of Sustainable Chemical Transformations in Tianjin, China, developed a room-temperature free-radical polymerization route for QSEs. The team used high-ESPmax (maximum molecular surface electrostatic potential) activators to activate acrylate monomers and enable uniform gelation inside batteries. Their Li-LRMO pouch cell with a high-areal-capacity cathode delivered 656.6 Wh kg-1, demonstrating a practical path toward energy-dense solid-state lithium batteries and a general design rule for activators and monomers.

The team selected pentaerythritol tetraacrylate (PETEA) as an acrylate monomer, AIBN as the initiator and tris(pentafluorophenyl)borane (TPFPB) as a high-ESPmax activator. TPFPB coordinates with the carbonyl (C=O) group, redistributing electron density away from the carbon-carbon double (C=C) bond and increasing its condensed local softness. Boron-11 nuclear magnetic resonance (11B NMR) showed a shift from -0.07 to 0.66 ppm, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations showed the initiation barrier dropped from 0.46 eV to 0.11 eV. This enabled room-temperature polymerization in both bottles and coin cells. The RT-QSE formed uniform, lithium fluoride (LiF)-rich SEI and CEI layers, supported stable Li plating/stripping for more than 1,200 h at 0.5 mA cm-2 and 1.0 mAh cm-2.

Atomic force microscopy (AFM) showed a higher Derjaguin-Muller-Toporov (DMT) modulus for the RT-QSE-derived SEI than for the high-temperature QSE (HT-QSE). The RT-QSE also maintained a more stable LRMO lattice without voids or vacancies, while the HT-QSE showed disordered surfaces and uneven interphases. A 4 mAh cm-2 LRMO cathode retained 95.1% capacity after 100 cycles. Ultrasonic scanning showed better electrolyte infiltration. The 9.53 Ah pouch cell, with a cathode exceeding 10 mAh cm-2, delivered 656.6 Wh kg-1 and 94.4% initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE).

The authors indicated the advance addresses a long-standing trade-off in free-radical in situ polymerized electrolytes: high temperature speeds gelation but damages interfaces, while room temperature is mild but often cannot start initiation effectively. They said "the high-ESPmax activator strategy turns sluggish acrylate monomers into reactive coordination compounds, allowing uniform gelation inside thick electrodes." According to them, the design is not limited to one monomer or activator, offering a practical route to scale up quasi-solid-state Li-LRMO pouch cells. They added that the approach could make solid-state battery manufacturing more uniform and compatible.

The RT-QSE platform could accelerate practical solid-state lithium batteries for electric vehicles, low-altitude aircraft and grid storage, where safety and energy density are critical. Because it builds on acrylate chemistry and can be tuned through activator ESPmax, the approach may fit scalable pouch-cell manufacturing. The authors said low-temperature performance of thick LRMO cathodes still needs improvement through cathode modification and plasticizer engineering. If these issues are addressed, the strategy could help move solid-state batteries from laboratory coin cells and Ah-level pouch cells to practical applicable batteries with more uniform interfaces and longer cycle life. It also offers a general design rule for selecting activators and monomers.

On Election Day, Michigan voters delivered a resounding win for lower energy bills and cleaner power.

text:
To: Interested parties

From: Evergreen Action Senior Regional Director Courtney Brady

Date: Thursday, November 5, 2026

Re: Michigan voters elected leaders to take on energy affordability. Here’s where they should start in 2027.

On Election Day, Michigan voters delivered a resounding win for lower energy bills and cleaner power. Jocelyn Benson will be Michigan’s next governor, Eli Savit will be its next attorney general, and Democratic majorities will lead both the House and the Senate. Come January, Michigan will have a government positioned to work together on an ambitious energy agenda. But this election was about more than political victories. Voters expect results, starting with lower energy bills.

For Michigan families, rising energy costs are no longer an abstract policy debate. They’re a monthly reality, and voters increasingly want to know who’s responsible and what can be done about it. They see an energy system that all too often puts corporate interests ahead of household budgets, with utilities rewarded for spending more on infrastructure, large corporations driving up demand on the grid, and politicians who protect the status quo. However, voters also saw a better way forward—one that puts consumers first, holds utilities accountable, and makes greater use of affordable clean energy. And the candidates who named the problem plainly and offered a credible plan to lower costs earned a mandate to deliver it.

That mandate demands urgent action. Michigan’s 2023 energy rewrite built the foundation, with a 100 percent clean energy standard, stronger efficiency targets, and a faster path for new wind and solar. If the last democratic trifecta was about setting targets, this one has to be about cutting costs, and the work needs to start now.

Here’s the agenda Governor-elect Benson and the incoming legislature should pursue in 2027.

Executive Action: What the Governor Can Do From Day One

The governor-elect does not need to wait for a vote to start lowering costs. Appointments, agency direction, and the administration’s influence with regulators are among the strongest tools in state government. Here are three tactics the governor’s office should pursue to lower household energy bills:

Protect Michigan families from rising data center energy costs: Data centers and other large users are looking to Michigan for sites, incentives, and grid capacity, and the governor should direct state regulators to set firm terms for serving them. Those new large users should bear the cost of generation, transmission, and distribution—not Michigan households or small businesses.

Hold utilities accountable and lower household energy bills: Utilities earn an allowed profit on the infrastructure they build, which rewards spending more rather than wisely, and families are left holding the bill. Through appointments, a strong legislative agenda, and public direction, the governor can build a commission that stops treating rate hikes as routine: one that challenges capital spending plans, holds profit margins down, and rejects unjustified rate increase requests. The attorney general’s office can also reinforce this work by stepping in on behalf of customers in rate cases.

Expand transportation choices and maximize taxpayer value: Lowering the cost of living also means giving people more affordable ways to get where they need to go. This starts with appointing a Michigan Department of Transportation director committed to accessibility, safety, and real alternatives to driving. That leader can equip the department to rank projects by what they deliver, including connections to jobs, links between rural Michigan and downtowns, and support for local economies.

Legislative Action: What Lawmakers Should Pass First

The strongest protections are the ones codified into law by the legislature and a governor’s signature. Aligned majorities can pass safeguards that outlast any one administration to serve Michiganders for generations to come. Here’s what the legislature should focus on when the 2027 session convenes:

Establish strong protections against rising data center energy costs: The legislature should guarantee in state law that the growth of data centers and similar large users does not push up electricity costs for existing customers. Michigan can still welcome responsible development on fair terms, with transparency about energy and water use, and a dedicated revenue stream from the mega corporations driving new demand can fund clean energy and efficiency programs that lower costs across the system.

Advance energy affordability and utility accountability: Lawmakers should strengthen the standards for how utilities request rate increases and give regulators and the public better tools to challenge unnecessary costs. That way, cost control is built into how utilities operate rather than coming second to corporate earnings. Paired with expanded affordable clean energy options for households and employers, customers would have even more ways to cut what they pay.

Modernize transportation funding and investment: : Transportation spending should flow to the projects delivering the most benefit, expand access for people of every age and ability, and give residents more affordable ways to reach work, school, health care, and one another. Getting there means reexamining the funding formulas and project selection rules that currently steer money toward a highway-first system.

The Work Starts Now

Michigan has a rare chance to show the country what a government can do when it puts energy affordability and people-focused reforms at the top of the list. A governor, attorney general, and two chambers of the legislature, all elected on a promise to cut costs, can deliver lower bills, cleaner power, and good jobs at the same time—proving that the three go hand in hand.

Michigan voters chose a cleaner, more affordable future. The work of building it begins now.

text:
FRANKFURT – President Donald Trump's plan to allow imports of Russian diesel appeared to falter this week after state and federal officials warned that handling any shipments could bring legal consequences and two tankers initially bound for the United States changed course.

Trump announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 9 to make more than 300,000 metric tons of Russia's diesel available immediately to U.S. and global markets, with larger shipments to follow. The U.S. banned Russian energy imports after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and the deal angered some lawmakers and foreign allies.

The arrangement has yet to produce a confirmed U.S. delivery. Analysts have said the imports were unlikely to do much to lower U.S. diesel prices, which have reached record highs during the U.S. war with Iran.

Two sanctioned tankers that departed from the Baltic Sea port of Primorsk last month originally declared their destinations as the U.S. East Coast. As of Thursday, both had changed course, one toward Brazil and the other into the Mediterranean, according to marine data company Kpler and vessel traffic site MarineTraffic.com.

A third vessel was still in the North Atlantic headed toward the U.S. but changed its destination from New York to “for orders,” which leaves the unloading point open. Neither the White House nor the Kremlin have disclosed whether the agreement was put in writing or revealed the price, payment terms or participating companies.

Although the Treasury Department temporarily authorized Russian diesel transactions that would ordinarily be subject to U.S. sanctions, New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill advised port and terminal operators in her state to turn away ships carrying the fuel, warning in a letter dated Monday that “any effort to profit from the illegal trade in Russian fuel will be met with harsh penalties.”

Sherrill argued that the Trump administration lacked authority to override the import ban enacted by Congress more than four years ago and said New Jersey would use its legal and regulatory powers to prevent state facilities and companies from handling Russian fuel.

A bipartisan group of senators has urged Trump to negate the deal, saying the U.S. “should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline.” Lawmakers also have warned major banks, port authorities and fuel distributors that facilitating the imports could expose companies to civil or criminal liability and future congressional investigations.

The administration maintains its authorization was lawful, and no court has ruled on the dispute.

In response to a request for comment Thursday, the Treasury Department issued a statement saying the sanctions exemption its Office of Foreign Assets Control issued for the sale, delivery, unloading and importing of Russian diesel until April 7 was consistent with previous actions and "in compliance with all applicable laws.”

A Trump administration official who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity said en route Russian diesel shipments would reduce price pressures for Americans. The official said increasing shipments was in keeping with Putin and Trump’s agreement but did not specify whether any Russian fuel would reach the U.S. directly.

Expensive diesel can have wide-ranging economic effects, including on consumer prices, since the trucking industry and many farmers use the fuel to produce and transport goods.

Trump has tried blaming Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for this year's diesel spikes. He has pressed Ukraine to halt drone attacks that damaged Russian refineries and curbed production of the fuel.

The Financial Times first reported the diverted courses of the two sanctioned vessels, the Russian tanker Talisman and the Sierra Leone-flagged Leruo.

Kpler analyst Matt Smith said it was not clear if Russian diesel shipments had U.S. buyers yet and that the third tanker in the North Atlantic also might change course.

“Because of regulatory, sanctions concerns, we may not see this cargo discharge on the U.S. Atlantic coast,” Smith said. “It’s clear there’s hesitancy here in bringing these barrels onshore just because of the implications of doing so.”

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said details were not available about commercial shipments but that “all the diesel will find its buyers.”

Putin’s special envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, dismissed the Financial Times report.

“Fake. Tankers destined for the US continue on course,” Dmitriev posted on X.

___

Wiseman reported from Washington.
