text:
ISTANBUL – The Turkish energy minister has laid out plans for his country to wean itself away from coal and other fossil fuels as it prepares to host the COP31 climate change summit.

World leaders are due to arrive next week in the Mediterranean city of Antalya, and Turkey’s hosting of the annual environmental conference has thrown a spotlight on its own coal, oil and gas usage.

Turkey is Europe’s largest coal power generator, according to energy think tank Ember. The Turkish Energy Ministry says coal remained its largest source of power last year, accounting for 33% of generation. The share of solar and wind in electricity generation stood at nearly 23%.

Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar revealed the National Energy Plan 2040 to reporters in a presentation made public Friday, in which he said Turkey would aim to transition from coal to cleaner energy sources — a process known as electrification. This would help it fulfil its pledge to reach net zero emissions by 2053.

“When we reach 2040 we are going to reduce our emissions by 40%. This big change in electrification will make this happen,” he said, adding that the use of solar and wind energy sources would more than quadruple over the next 13 years.

“Our aim is to reach 36% electrification by the year 2040,” he told a news conference in Istanbul. Using transport as an example, Bayraktar said the number of electric cars on Turkey’s roads would increase from around 500,000 to 20 million in the next 13 years.

The aim of the plan is to produce a “paradigm shift” in how energy is used in Turkey. “We have a huge project list ahead of us,” the minister added.

Huge level of investment needed

Such a shift, however, would require a huge level of investment — $500 billion in the next 13 years, some $210 billion of which would come from Turkish public sector companies with much of the rest from foreign investment.

“If the world is serious about carbon neutrality and if we would like to fund (fighting) climate change and global warming, we need to find the money,” Bayraktar said. “Everyone needs to take some responsibility and provide money for that.”

He also emphasized the importance of a transition from coal to clean energy that would not negatively impact communities reliant on mines and power stations for employment.

“We are looking for a just transition from coal to relatively cleaner sources of energy… but we need coal for security of supply,” he said.

“Equally important is that (coal mining) is providing at least 30,000 to 40,000 people with employment and labor opportunities. How are we going to make these miners into AI experts or high-tech experts? It’s not going to be easy. We need a just transition period.”

Despite aiming to break away from coal, Turkey will remain tied to other fossil fuels, particularly natural gas, for the foreseeable future.

Turkey recently started drilling gas reserves in the Black Sea and Bayraktar said production would double to 7.5 billion cubic meters annually in the coming years.

Growing nuclear power

Another key area would be nuclear power. The Akkuyu nuclear power plant on the Mediterranean coast is nearing operation and there are plans for another nuclear station by the Black Sea.

These would contribute towards the “very ambitious target” of Turkey becoming energy independent by 2040, Bayraktar said.

Turning to the “turbulent times” facing energy markets, Bayraktar described how sanctions around the wars in Ukraine and Iran were impeding efforts to fight global warming.

“We are trying to become carbon neutral in less than three decades’ time and with all these difficulties it’s very difficult to achieve this,” he said.

According to the Climate Action Tracker, which measures countries’ progress against goals of the 2015 Paris Agreement, Turkey’s climate targets and policies are “critically insufficient.”

The agreement set a target of limiting global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) compared with the early 1800s.

Looking ahead to COP31, Bayraktar said his key message would be for countries to adopt “responsive and realistic policies” to achieve carbon neutrality.

title: The wins and weak spots in America's solar supply chain | Canary Media
description:
Now that solar has become America’s go-to choice for new power plants, the pressure is on to assemble a fully domestic supply chain for the technology.
The expansion represents a major change of fortune for domestic solar manufacturing, which had nearly disappeared, but has blossomed in recent years thanks to federal incentives and stiffer tariffs against foreign products.
Still, the panel is just the final step in the solar supply chain.
Domestic factories can make up to 19.5 GW annually, after several factory openings this year.

text:
Now that solar has become America’s go-to choice for new power plants, the pressure is on to assemble a fully domestic supply chain for the technology. Data from the latest Clean Investment Monitor shows that this onshoring process is well underway.

Factories in the U.S. can produce more than enough finished solar panels — also known as modules — to supply the nation’s annual installations, which last year hit 47.9 gigawatts (measured in direct current capacity). Module production could grow by about 83% if all the projects that have been announced or are going through construction and commissioning come to fruition. The expansion represents a major change of fortune for domestic solar manufacturing, which had nearly disappeared, but has blossomed in recent years thanks to federal incentives and stiffer tariffs against foreign products.

Still, the panel is just the final step in the solar supply chain. To truly onshore this critical industry, the U.S. also needs to make the components that go into the module: photovoltaic cells, which are etched onto silicon wafers, which are made from processed polysilicon.

So far, cells have shown the most success among those precursors. Domestic factories can make up to 19.5 GW annually, after several factory openings this year. If projects currently wrapping up construction all come online, the country will be able to make enough solar cells to match 2025 deployments.

Crucially, it’s not guaranteed that solar developers will maintain 2025 levels of installations in the years to come, once lucrative federal tax credits run out. The Rhodium Group modeled a range of scenarios for the post-2030 era, and found that the U.S. could install an annual average of anywhere between 8 and 52 GW of direct current solar capacity. That’s an enormous range: If the solar market tanks, the manufacturing sector could be self-sufficient, but if installations rebound, the country will need more polysilicon and wafer production to keep pace.

Ultimately, building out these factories is just the first step toward full self-sufficiency. Next, solar manufacturers need to prove that they can operate sustainably in the U.S. over the long haul.

title: How the EU can rescue its battery industry | Centre for European Reform
description:
Many EU battery manufacturing projects have failed, however, despite EU support for the sector.
As the European economy recovered from the Covid-19 pandemic, European battery manufacturers enthusiastically announced large new factories, particularly in 2022.
South Korea already has a strong position in EU battery manufacturing, indeed (Chart 3).
While Europe must maintain a presence in battery manufacturing using existing technologies, it should also invest in emerging battery technologies.
Failing to do so will inevitably result in the European battery industry following the solar industry into manufacturing oblivion.
text:
The EU risks becoming totally dependent on China for batteries. It can avoid this outcome through supporting its existing battery manufacturers, collaborating with trusted middle powers and investing in next-generation storage technologies.

Batteries are an essential part of our energy system today – powering homes, industries and transportation. Many EU battery manufacturing projects have failed, however, despite EU support for the sector. China now accounts for more than 80 per cent of the world’s output of battery cells. It is the dominant manufacturer of most mature battery technologies. Europe needs to act urgently if it wants to retain a foothold in the global battery market

The EU must balance several policy goals at the same time: retaining access to affordable batteries to accelerate the energy transition; reducing dependency on Chinese battery cells; and developing a domestic battery sector that can compete and therefore support Europe’s economic growth.

Batteries: A critical technology

Improvements in performance and rapid cost reductions have made batteries – once thought to be of only marginal use at best – a key technology for balancing the variable output of solar and wind power. In 2025, Europe installed 36 gigawatt-hour (GWh) of stationary batteries, an increase of 48 per cent compared to a year earlier. To put that into perspective, if all the batteries installed in the EU in this period were fully charged and discharged at once, they could supply all of Lithuania’s total daily electricity needs. This is in addition to approximately 200 GWh worth of batteries installed in newly registered cars and trucks.

As electrification has become important for the wider economy, battery manufacturing has acquired a more strategically significant role. China recognised this as early as the late 1990s, both in relation to electricity storage and as a key component of electric vehicles. More than two decades of focused industrial policy have enabled China to scale up production and become a leading manufacturer across a range of battery technologies.

As electrification has become important for the wider economy, battery manufacturing has acquired a more strategically significant role.

Tweet thisBluesky this

The EU has also recognised the strategic importance of batteries. The EU and its member-states have supported battery manufacturing through R&D funding (Horizon Europe’s Batt4EU partnership); relaxed state aid rules for two battery projects worth over €6 billion; provided Innovation Fund grants for cell factories; and made EIB loans to battery manufacturers. In December 2025, the Commission announced the Battery Booster, a €1.8 billion package that included €1.5 billion in interest-free loans for battery cell producers.

Made in EU: Ambition meets reality

While EU initiatives have brought together hundreds of industry actors and mobilised billions in capital, the sector has suffered from intense price competition from China, leading to many stalled or cancelled projects. As the European economy recovered from the Covid-19 pandemic, European battery manufacturers enthusiastically announced large new factories, particularly in 2022. Volkswagen alone planned to develop 240 GWh of battery factories in Europe, enough to supply battery packs for over 3 million cars.

Yet the sector soon hit a wall. Several European battery companies failed, with the collapse of Northvolt being the most prominent example. The Swedish company – and Europe’s best-funded battery start-up – had raised around €14 billion since 2016 before filing for bankruptcy in March 2025.

The sector faced a combination of high interest rates, global overcapacity and difficulties in scaling up production. Some European battery manufacturers struggled to move from pilot projects to commercially viable production. Others saw key customers pull back their orders, undermining the business case for expanding domestic manufacturing capacity. The slower-than-expected transition to electric vehicles (EVs) in Europe – compounded by pressures from the car sector to prolong the production of vehicles with internal combustion engines – added further uncertainty about future battery demand for EV manufacturing in Europe.

At the same time, China expanded battery production far beyond current demand, creating global overcapacity. For Chinese companies, the problem of over-production was managed through a series of government-led capacity restraints and selective support for battery manufacturers. For European producers, however, there was no such protection. As demand for their batteries declined, the utilisation rate of their factories and their profitability fell.

As a result, the European battery dream was shattered. Chart 1 shows the announcements and the relative flatlining of battery manufacturing capacity in Europe. Since 2024, 559 GWh worth of projects have been cancelled across Europe. Some projects have survived the onslaught, although most of them involved non-European producers with more experience of managing these types of factories, such as the Korean firm LG Energy Solution’s Wrocław plant in Poland, which is Europe’s largest battery factory. Europe’s battery sector now risks following the same trajectory as its solar panel manufacturers, which went from having 40 per cent of the global solar module manufacturing capacity in 2008 to being almost wiped out by cheaper Chinese competitors, possessing about one per cent of global production capacity in 2025. Europe is in danger of ceding another strategic sector to China – and one which is much more important to other sectors of the economy than the photovoltaic panel industry.

Can Europe recover?

Chinese manufacturing capacity – and the speed with which it continues to expand – make it unlikely that Europe, despite its ambitions to be a clean technology leader, will be able to build enough capacity to become a net exporter of the most produced battery types in the short-term. Chinese companies such as CATL and BYD each have more manufacturing capacity than the whole of the EU combined – with CATL alone holding roughly three times the capacity of the entire EU. Both companies produce good-quality batteries in such large amounts that they will likely dominate third markets, crowding out future battery exports from Europe. For the foreseeable future, Europe’s opportunity to export the most common battery types is exceedingly small.

Europe should not try to challenge the dominance of China in current types of battery technology. Rather, it should prioritise preserving a viable domestic manufacturing base that can meet some of its strategic needs. Domestic production matters for European security, not least because drones, military vehicles and grid storage depend on batteries. Once lost, the skills, suppliers and production know-how needed for next-generation battery technologies are hard to rebuild.

Domestic production matters for European security, not least because drones, military vehicles and grid storage depend on batteries.

Tweet thisBluesky this

Europe’s battery strategy should be based on three pillars: building a minimum level of strategic production reserve, deepening partnerships with other battery-producing middle powers, and pivoting to next-generation batteries.

Pillar 1: Build a minimum necessary strategic production reserve

Europe should maintain sufficient domestic battery manufacturing capacity to avoid becoming entirely reliant on China. Managing supply chain vulnerabilities through battery stockpiling would be expensive and difficult given the wide variety of battery types, standards and rapid technological change. Instead, the EU should build a strategic production reserve that would allow Europe to retain some of its production capacity for times of geopolitical turbulence.

The Net Zero Industry Act (NZIA) – an EU law passed in 2024 to support the bloc’s clean tech sector – set the objective of at least 550 GWh of battery production in Europe, which was initially expected to cover approximately 90 per cent of EU demand. Later estimates by the European Parliamentary Research Service (EPRS) and the Karlsruher Institut für Technologie (KIT) put EU demand for batteries in 2030 at 1000 GWh, which would mean the NZIA target would cover only 55 per cent of EU’s domestic needs.

The scale of potential demand is substantial. If the EU wants to produce all the batteries for its own car fleet domestically – 11.5 million cars are produced in Europe per annum, (let us assume they will all be EVs) – automotive demand alone would amount to approximately 690 GWh a year. The 550 GWh production capacity would not fully cover that demand, let alone stationary storage and e-trucks, which would increase the demand for battery capacity. To reach the NZIA 550 GWh benchmark, the EU would need an additional 265 GWh (see Chart 2).

Of the current 285 GWh battery manufacturing capacity in the EU, a significant portion is foreign-owned. Ideally, the share of European-owned factories would increase to retain ownership over production assets. While foreign-owned production plants can support jobs, tax revenue and knowledge transfer, incidents like the Nexperia case show how fragile supply chains become when the owners of key facilities are established in hostile or potentially hostile countries. After the Dutch government took control of the Chinese-owned chipmaker in 2025, Beijing blocked chip exports from Nexperia’s Chinese plants, and European carmakers faced severe shortages.

The good news for the EU is that it does not have to start from scratch to hit the NZIA target. Current unfinished battery projects have enough potential to fill the remaining gap (see Table 1).Many of these projects are stalled or struggling, however. Completing them will require additional financial support.

In the short term, policy-makers should make every effort to prevent pre-construction or dormant projects from being shelved entirely, as happened this year with plants planned by Norway’s Morrow Batteries and the innovative French battery manufacturer Tiamat. Without targeted policy support for battery manufacturers, most of these projects will probably remain unrealised.

There are two important levers that together unlock local battery manufacturing: procurement policies and production subsidies.

Firstly, the EU can create local demand for European batteries by including local content requirements in public procurement policies. The EU is considering such requirements as part of the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) currently under negotiation. The local content requirements should furthermore include EU partner countries such as the UK, Turkey and other countries with which the EU has Free Trade Agreements. Shutting out key partners of our public procurement policies will unnecessarily damage diplomatic relations with these countries.

The EU can create local demand for European batteries by including local content requirements in public procurement policies.

Tweet thisBluesky this

The second part of the approach to stimulate production in the EU is through production subsidies. Historically, the EU has not allowed this type of industrial support in its state aid framework. However, as more countries are using production subsidies (including India, the US, Canada, Australia, Korea and Japan), the EU risks falling behind if they do not support localised manufacturing. Ideally, production subsidies are temporary, which allow businesses to scale up in Europe until they have attained sufficient knowledge and economies of scale to be able to survive without subsidies.

Together, these two measures will shut out unfair competition while at the same time incentivising production within the EU without alienating its key trading partners. Not unimportantly, the subsidies will make European batteries more affordable, maintaining momentum in the energy transition.

Nevertheless, the EU seems to be heading in the wrong direction. The Automotive Package proposal, put forward by France and Germany, would not provide adequate support for the battery industry. Member-states should require stronger local content requirements for battery cells in the final text of the IAA.

Also, production subsidies are not yet allowed. The current EU Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework (CISAF) does not include production-based incentives. The European Commission should start allowing this, or the EU will risk being outcompeted not only by China, but also by partner countries that offer such incentives.

Pillar 2: Leverage middle power partnerships

The EU should not completely close its doors to foreign batteries and battery manufacturers. Economic alliances between the EU and middle powers can help to diversify battery imports. South Korea, Japan and India, in particular, could prove useful partners. South Korea already has a strong position in EU battery manufacturing, indeed (Chart 3). The expected EU demand for batteries – even if the EU would hit its NZIA benchmarks for local production – is such that part of it will have to be met by foreign suppliers. The ‘Made in EU’ requirements for batteries are only relevant for public procurement and subsidy programmes. Foreign firms should be allowed in the rest of the battery market.

Ideally, foreign companies would invest directly in the EU, creating jobs and supply chains. Direct imports should also be possible, however, provided that this still resulted in purchases from a more diverse range of trade partners than at present, thus reducing any third country’s leverage over the EU.

Pillar 3: New opportunities for a strategic edge

While Europe must maintain a presence in battery manufacturing using existing technologies, it should also invest in emerging battery technologies, in which it has a better chance of developing a competitive edge.

One promising area is long-duration storage. Most battery storage systems currently supply energy for several days rather than several hours, but these new systems could store energy for much longer periods. This would, in turn, help speed up the energy transition, as long-duration storage could reduce the need to back up intermittent power sources such as wind and solar with nuclear or gas-fired power plants. Long-duration batteries could also become an export product for European companies. Europe already has potential in this area, with firms like Ore Energy (the Netherlands), Kraftblock (Germany) and Polar Night (Finland) all developing new battery technologies. Markets for such batteries are still relatively underdeveloped, which means there is scope for Europe to gain a competitive advantage.

While Europe must maintain a presence in battery manufacturing using existing technologies, it should also invest in emerging battery technologies.

Tweet thisBluesky this

Another promising area is the development of batteries with a much higher energy density for niche applications. The energy density of a battery measures how much power it generates per unit of volume. Products for sectors such as defence often require high energy density batteries due to their power requirements (for example, ground vehicles or radars). Defence manufacturers also need secure supply chains, less likely to be disrupted in times of conflict or tension by supply chain problems outside the EU. Another area where the new generation of batteries could produce dramatic change is in aviation: lighter, more energy-dense batteries are key to sustaining longer flights powered by electricity in both the civilian and military domains.

EU member-states are investing heavily in their defence bases, and have a strong position in the aviation sector thanks to companies such as Airbus (full disclosure: a CER corporate member) and its suppliers. Where realistically possible, EU member-states should maximise the use of EU-made batteries in defence goods. Building capacity for secure and energy-dense batteries would strengthen both defence supply chains and economic security. Companies such as Saft (France), Theion (Germany) and Basquevolt (Spain) operate in the next-generation battery space.

Conclusion

The EU is right to identify batteries as a strategic technology, given how important they are to transport, defence and the energy system. But without a strategy, European manufacturers will fail to scale up production of next-generation battery technologies, just as they are struggling with current generation of batteries. The EU should map the emerging ecosystems for the new technologies, and provide adequate public support both for next-generation battery research and current projects through grants, loans, subsidies and clear ‘Made with EU’ procurement rules.

The trajectory of the European battery industry shows that new technologies are hard to scale due to intense international competition. China and the US are already moving forward, providing various forms of state support for promising companies and projects of their own. If the EU wants to maintain its autonomy in crucial areas like energy and defence, it can no longer rely on open markets and fair competition to produce its desired outcomes – they no longer exist. It will have to intervene more actively to achieve the outcomes it seeks. Failing to do so will inevitably result in the European battery industry following the solar industry into manufacturing oblivion.

text:
ISTANBUL (AP) — The Turkish energy minister has laid out plans for his country to wean itself away from coal and other fossil fuels as it prepares to host the COP31 climate change summit.

World leaders are due to arrive next week in the Mediterranean city of Antalya, and Turkey’s hosting of the annual environmental conference has thrown a spotlight on its own coal, oil and gas usage.

Turkey is Europe’s largest coal power generator, according to energy think tank Ember. The Turkish Energy Ministry says coal remained its largest source of power last year, accounting for 33% of generation. The share of solar and wind in electricity generation stood at nearly 23%.

Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar revealed the National Energy Plan 2040 to reporters in a presentation made public Friday, in which he said Turkey would aim to transition from coal to cleaner energy sources — a process known as electrification. This would help it fulfil its pledge to reach net zero emissions by 2053.

“When we reach 2040 we are going to reduce our emissions by 40%. This big change in electrification will make this happen,” he said, adding that the use of solar and wind energy sources would more than quadruple over the next 13 years.

“Our aim is to reach 36% electrification by the year 2040,” he told a news conference in Istanbul. Using transport as an example, Bayraktar said the number of electric cars on Turkey’s roads would increase from around 500,000 to 20 million in the next 13 years.

The aim of the plan is to produce a “paradigm shift” in how energy is used in Turkey. “We have a huge project list ahead of us,” the minister added.

Huge level of investment needed

Such a shift, however, would require a huge level of investment — $500 billion in the next 13 years, some $210 billion of which would come from Turkish public sector companies with much of the rest from foreign investment.

“If the world is serious about carbon neutrality and if we would like to fund (fighting) climate change and global warming, we need to find the money,” Bayraktar said. “Everyone needs to take some responsibility and provide money for that.”

He also emphasized the importance of a transition from coal to clean energy that would not negatively impact communities reliant on mines and power stations for employment.

“We are looking for a just transition from coal to relatively cleaner sources of energy… but we need coal for security of supply,” he said.

“Equally important is that (coal mining) is providing at least 30,000 to 40,000 people with employment and labor opportunities. How are we going to make these miners into AI experts or high-tech experts? It’s not going to be easy. We need a just transition period.”

Despite aiming to break away from coal, Turkey will remain tied to other fossil fuels, particularly natural gas, for the foreseeable future.

Turkey recently started drilling gas reserves in the Black Sea and Bayraktar said production would double to 7.5 billion cubic meters annually in the coming years.

Growing nuclear power

Another key area would be nuclear power. The Akkuyu nuclear power plant on the Mediterranean coast is nearing operation and there are plans for another nuclear station by the Black Sea.

These would contribute towards the “very ambitious target” of Turkey becoming energy independent by 2040, Bayraktar said.

Turning to the “turbulent times” facing energy markets, Bayraktar described how sanctions around the wars in Ukraine and Iran were impeding efforts to fight global warming.

“We are trying to become carbon neutral in less than three decades’ time and with all these difficulties it’s very difficult to achieve this,” he said.

According to the Climate Action Tracker, which measures countries’ progress against goals of the 2015 Paris Agreement, Turkey’s climate targets and policies are “critically insufficient.”

The agreement set a target of limiting global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) compared with the early 1800s.

Looking ahead to COP31, Bayraktar said his key message would be for countries to adopt “responsive and realistic policies” to achieve carbon neutrality.

title: Why Mini Splits Aren't As Popular In The US As The Rest Of The World - SlashGear
description:
Why aren't mini splits more popular in the US?
Willis Carrier is credited for making the first modern AC unit in 1902, which gave rise to mass adoption of central air systems.
This is precisely why mini splits took off in countries outside the US: They didn't have the ductwork of American houses.
Mini splits cooled European and Japanese homes without the need to install massive systems.
While most US households rely on central air and AC systems, mini splits are gradually becoming more popular stateside.
text:
How do you stay cool during the summer? If you live in the US, you probably use an energy-efficient window air conditioner or a different type of A/C like a central cooling unit. If you live anywhere else, you likely rely on a mini split — a ductless heating and cooling system that uses heat absorption to cool houses. Why aren't mini splits more popular in the US? Blame the government.

While the first mini split system was invented in the late 1950s, the technology didn't travel over to the US until the late 1960s via Comfort-Aire's Twin Pac, which was sold by Sears. However, the U.S. Congress cut that particular system's life short. Kind of, anyway; in 1987, Congress passed the National Appliance Energy Conservation Act, which set up energy efficiency ratings for electrical devices. The Twin Pac couldn't meet those standards, so retailers had to pull it from store shelves. But do you know what met the energy efficiency standards? Cooling systems that came preinstalled in many US homes.

Countless US households use air conditioning because it is a national treasure. Willis Carrier is credited for making the first modern AC unit in 1902, which gave rise to mass adoption of central air systems. By the 1950s and 60s, houses with air ducts were commonplace across the US, which uses central AC units or other cooling systems. Even if a house's original central AC units didn't meet new energy standards, it just made more sense to buy a new one that did. This is precisely why mini splits took off in countries outside the US: They didn't have the ductwork of American houses. Mini splits cooled European and Japanese homes without the need to install massive systems.

While most US households rely on central air and AC systems, mini splits are gradually becoming more popular stateside. You can buy plenty of systems built by quality mini split manufacturers, but that raises the question of why the stars are suddenly aligning for the products. It comes down to a mix of market and technological factors.

As with many home improvement projects, the upfront cost of installing a new cooling system is a major hurdle, but local and federal governments have taken an interest in subsidizing heat pumps. 2022's Inflation Reduction Act offered tax credits for homeowners who tried to make their houses more energy efficient with certain heat pumps. Yes, in the decades since the National Appliance Energy Conservation Act, mini splits have become far more energy efficient, and since mini splits are technically heat pumps, the act covered them — at least until the highly controversial "One Big Beautiful Bill" gutted the tax credit. Yet despite this setback, many state governments run local rebate programs that help offset the cost of installing and running heat pumps.

Mini split technological advances don't end with just energy efficiency. Well over a decade ago, Mitsubishi revolutionized the mini split industry with the Hyper-Heating Inverter, which not only acts as a heating system but can function in sub-zero temperatures. Mitsubishi basically developed a system that can both heat and cool a house, which is a boon in the US where temperatures can fluctuate rapidly. But efficiency also factors into this capability, as electric heat pumps cost less to heat your house during the winter than even natural oil. What US resident wouldn't love saving money during the most expensive time of the year?

text:
Introduction

Congress has discussed high-blend fuel (HB fuel) and has provided support for HB fueling infrastructure.1 In short, a biofuel is a fuel (e.g., ethanol, biodiesel, biogas) produced from a biomass feedstock (e.g., crops, tree residue, animal waste, food waste) that can be used for transportation (e.g., cars, aviation). Typically, for most applications, biofuel has been blended at a low level with its petroleum counterpart for use in vehicles as a transportation fuel. For this report, low-blend fuel (LB fuel) includes ethanol blended at a rate of 10% or lower (e.g., E10) and biodiesel blended at a rate of 5% or lower (e.g., B5).2 The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) reports that the "most common blend of ethanol is E10 (10% ethanol, 90% gasoline)."3 And, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) reports that "almost all gasoline are E10 blends."4 In general, an HB fuel is a biofuel-petroleum fuel mixture with biofuel blended at a higher rate, such as ethanol blended at a rate greater than 10% (e.g., E15, a fuel blend of gasoline blended with 10.5-15% ethanol).

One type of HB fuel that has received attention from Congress is E15, gasoline blended with 10.5-15% ethanol.5 In January 2026, the House established the E-15 Rural Domestic Energy Council (Council) to investigate the sale of E15, among other actions.6 In May 2026, the House passed H.R. 1346, the Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act of 2025, which would, in part, allow for the year-round sale of E15.7 In a supplemental funding request sent to Congress in June 2026, the Trump Administration requested "an urgent and needed fix that codifies the permanent, year-round sale of E-15."8 In September 2026, the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry reported out of committee S. 5526, the Agricultural Act of 2026, which would also allow for the year-round sale of E15.9

Congress has considered the year-round sale of E15 previously. Congress included a provision for the permanent year-round sale of E15 in a short-term FY2025 spending bill introduced in the House in December 2024 (H.R. 10445; 118th Congress), but it was removed from the FY2025 continuing resolution package that became law (P.L. 118-158).

Congress has taken action to both revoke and issue federal funding for HB fueling infrastructure (e.g., blender pumps).10 For example, the Agricultural Act of 2014 (2014 farm bill; P.L. 113-79) precludes the use of Rural Energy for America Program (REAP) funding for any mechanism for dispensing energy at the retail level (e.g., ethanol-gasoline blender pumps).11 Conversely, the law commonly known as the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (P.L. 117-169) provided $500 million to the Higher Blends Infrastructure Incentive Program (HBIIP) for "installing, retrofitting, or otherwise upgrading fuel dispensers or pumps," among other investments.

HBIIP is an initiative led by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to "increase significantly the sales and use of higher blends of ethanol and biodiesel."12 In 2025, the Trump Administration froze funding for HBIIP and then announced it would release obligated funding under the program.13 In 2026, the Trump Administration announced that "[f]unds for the program have now been exhausted, and USDA will not be making further obligations absent future appropriation."14

This report provides an overview of HBIIP and HB fuel usage and infrastructure costs and contains questions Congress may consider in its oversight of HBIIP.

Biofuels

Biofuels are liquid fuels and blending components produced from biomass feedstocks, used primarily for transportation.15 The two leading biofuels produced and used for transportation in the United States are ethanol and biomass-based diesel.16 LB fuel is approved for use in light-duty vehicles by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and vehicle manufacturers.17 HB fuels include higher blends of "ethanol (i.e., greater than 10 percent ethanol) and biodiesel (greater than 5 percent biodiesel)."18 The approval to use HB fuels in light-duty vehicles can vary by fuel type, vehicle model year, and vehicle manufacturer.19

In general, infrastructure required for HB fuel is the same type of infrastructure required for LB fuel (e.g., fuel dispenser, underground storage tank), but the HB fueling infrastructure is constructed specifically to endure the composition of HB fuel.20 In short, not all vehicles on the road are certified by their vehicle manufacturer to use HB fuel, and not all fueling stations have the required infrastructure to sell HB fuel.

Both corn-starch ethanol and biomass-based diesel are established biofuels that can be blended into conventional fuel (i.e., petroleum fuel). For several years, production, consumption, and logistics for these fuels have been traditionally centered on low percentage levels (i.e., 10% ethanol and 5% biodiesel). In current LB fuel markets, industry knows how to produce the biofuel, the infrastructure exists to get the LB fuel to market, and consumers know that their vehicle manufacturer has approved the use of the LB fuel. Corn-starch ethanol and biomass-based diesel may be blended into conventional fuel at a higher rate. Using these biofuels at higher-blend rates could require different infrastructure and may raise some questions by lawmakers, consumers, and others.21

The predicament, mainly for biofuel supporters, is adapting the existing infrastructure—potentially nationwide—to use HB fuel.22 This might require, at a minimum, legislative and regulatory changes (depending on the HB fuel), funding (e.g., private funding, federal appropriations), administrative support (e.g., program staff to issue federal funding, technical expertise to install the infrastructure), and a willingness by industry and consumers to do so (e.g., a station owner who will upgrade their equipment, a consumer who will purchase an HB fuel). It remains unclear whether federal involvement and investment would encourage fueling station owners and others to upgrade their infrastructure to handle HB fuel and motivate consumers to purchase HB fuel.

HB fuel brings opportunities and challenges. Increased production of biomass feedstocks and biofuels could stimulate certain rural economies and segments of the agricultural sector. Conversely, if consumers were to purchase additional amounts of HB fuels, the increased demand could cause competition for feedstocks, interrupt feedstock pricing, and raise environmental concerns, among other issues.

Some HB fuels face circumstances unique to the biofuel blend type. For example, for ethanol, consumers may consider the energy content and engine performance of the HB fuel (e.g., E15). Ethanol has a lower energy content than gasoline yet a higher octane rating than gasoline.23 Consumers choosing to use HB fuel may consider fuel economy and performance, among other factors.

HB Fuel Consumption and Infrastructure

It is not clear how much HB fuel is consumed in the United States annually.24 Due to variations in fuel mixtures (e.g., E15, E20, E85, B20), infrastructure capacity, vehicle manufacturer requirements, and state regulations—and for other reasons—it is difficult to ascertain nationwide consumption trends for HB fuel using publicly available data.25

Some states and stakeholders monitor HB fuel consumption, but their observations are generally focused on specific HB fuel(s) and/or a particular region. For example, the Iowa state government prepares an annual report of fuel gallons sold or dispensed in Iowa.26 The report contains a table that provides Iowa gasoline, diesel, and biofuel sales for 2025, as reported by retailers, including 870.7 million gallons of E10, 410.1 million gallons of E15, 0.9 million gallons of E20, and 24.0 million gallons of E85.27 The annual report also states that "ethanol blends of E15 or higher constituted 27 percent of all gasoline sold or dispensed in 2025."28

It is also not clear how many fueling stations sell HB fuel. This is partly due to the variety of HB fuels that can be sold. Some data are available for certain HB fuels, but comprehensive data are not available. For example, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) reports that more than 3,000 fueling stations sell E15, and more than 4,200 fueling stations sell E85.29 DOE also provides the number of public and private biodiesel fueling station locations by state that offer HB fuel of B20 or higher.30 For example, DOE reports Illinois has 490 such public biodiesel fueling stations.31 The fueling stations that sell HB fuel are a small fraction of the total number of fueling stations located in the United States. For example, the Oak Ridge National Laboratory reports there were 142,000 conventional refueling stations in 2020.32

The cost of equipping a fueling station to sell HB fuel varies.33 Infrastructure costs are facility-specific depending on what HB fuel will be sold and what equipment the station may need to upgrade to sell HB fuel. DOE reports there are approximately 60 pieces of equipment at a fueling station that handle fuel and vapor, some of which are below ground.34 Station owners interested in selling an HB fuel might inspect their fueling station equipment to determine what equipment may be compatible and what equipment would need to be upgraded, and may also take into consideration the design life of the existing equipment and consumer demand, among other things, before making a decision to upgrade or not upgrade their equipment to sell an HB fuel.

Using ethanol as an example, USDA reports that "[w]hile virtually all stations have equipment necessary for storing and dispensing E10, it is difficult to discern how many have fueling equipment compatible with ethanol blends above E10."35 USDA reports the costs, as calculated by researchers with the U.S. DRIVE Partnership, under various conversion scenarios for a station to sell different ethanol-gasoline fuel blends.36 As of 2019, the individual equipment station upgrade costs for E11-E25 fuel ranged from approximately $21,000 for a light conversion scenario to $379,000 for an extensive conversion scenario.37

EPA has taken actions pertaining to HB fueling infrastructure. In 2021, EPA released a proposed rule to, in part, make "changes to E15 fuel dispenser labeling requirements" and "to modify underground storage tank (UST) regulations to accommodate the safe storage of E15 and higher gasoline-ethanol blends at retail stations' existing tank systems."38 EPA reports that "the chemical and physical properties of biobased fuels, such as ethanol and biodiesel, can be more degrading to certain UST system materials than petroleum alone."39 EPA also acknowledges the growth in biofuels over time and the fuel waivers EPA issued allowing for the sale of E15 in the summer, and EPA thus proposed "a requirement that UST systems installed, or UST equipment and components replaced, must be constructed with equipment and components compatible with ethanol blends up to 100 percent."40 EPA has not yet issued the final rule.41

The Higher Blends Infrastructure Incentive Program

Program Overview

HBIIP, a USDA initiative created in 2020, aims to "increase significantly the sales and use of higher blends of ethanol and biodiesel" and "is intended to encourage a more comprehensive approach to marketing higher blends by sharing the costs related to building out biofuel-related infrastructure."42 HBIIP awards cost-share grants that assist transportation fueling and biodiesel distribution facilities with upgrading or installing new infrastructure to be compatible with high-blend ethanol and biodiesel (e.g., E15 fuel dispensers, B20 fuel dispensers, ethanol storage tanks, and biodiesel storage tanks).43 USDA reports that consideration will also be given to biodiesel terminal operations and home heating oil distribution centers.44

HBIIP has been mentioned in the Unified Agenda of Federal Regulatory and Deregulatory Actions (unified agenda).45 According to the Fall 2023 unified agenda, HBIIP is "intended to encourage a more comprehensive approach to market higher blends by sharing the costs related to building out biofuel-related infrastructure."46 The Fall 2023 unified agenda also states that the USDA Rural Business-Cooperative Service (RBCS) implements the program and that the "underlying statutes authorizing RBCS to create these regulations are 5 U.S.C. 301 and 7 U.S.C. 1989."47 According to a 2026 unified agenda entry for HBIIP, RCBS intends on "proposing a rule to codify the policies and procedures for the program in the Code of Federal Regulations" and "intends to conduct public engagement to hear from stakeholders and potential applicants about what they would like to see in the regulation."48

Funding

HBIIP funding comes from the USDA Commodity Credit Corporation (CCC).49 The program received $500 million in supplemental funding from the law commonly known as the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA; P.L. 117-169).50 The funding is statutorily authorized in 7 U.S.C. §8103(i).51 Congress has not authorized or directly appropriated additional funding for the program since the IRA. USDA last issued a Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) for HBIIP in June 2023, establishing five consecutive quarterly application windows that accepted submissions starting July 1, 2023, through September 30, 2024, with the option for a sixth application window if funding was not exhausted.52 As of October 2026, USDA reports that "[f]unds for the program have now been exhausted, and the Department will not be making further obligations absent future appropriation."53

Award Administration

USDA has released some award data for HBIIP (see Table 1). CRS estimates of HBIIP awards provided in Table 1 are not comprehensive, were derived from publicly available information, and may not reflect all HBIIP awards granted by USDA. The publicly released HBIIP award data announced in 2026 are less granular than the award data announced in prior years. In January 2025, USDA reported that "[t]o date, USDA has invested … more than $287 million in 345 projects through HBIIP that increase the availability of domestic biofuels across the country" and "[s]ince the start of the Biden-Harris Administration, USDA has invested … more than $323 million in 399 awards through HBIIP."54 CRS estimates in Table 1 for HBIIP awards that USDA announced in 2020 through 2025 derived from publicly available information differ from what USDA reported on January 10, 2025.

The HBIIP awards announced in January 2025 give financial support for infrastructure (e.g., fuel pumps, dispensers, and storage tanks) that supports ethanol and biodiesel fuel mixtures, mostly in the forms of E15, E85, and B20.55 The program also supports B100.56 For example, there is a project focused on the infrastructure for a home heating oil distribution facility company (i.e., modify a storage tank to store B100 and blend B20) and a fleet facility company (i.e., install two B100 fuel dispensers and one B100 storage tank).57

Selected Actions Under the Second Trump Administration (2025 Through June 2026)58

In the first three months of the second Trump Administration, the White House froze funding for HBIIP, implemented USDA staffing changes, and reported that it had released obligated funding under HBIIP for projects. On January 20, 2025, President Trump issued Executive Order 14154, which paused the disbursement of funds appropriated through the IRA and required a review of the processes for issuing grants for programs funded by the IRA, among other things.59 Also on January 20, 2025, President Trump ordered a hiring freeze for the executive branch and requested the creation of a federal hiring plan, among other things.60 On March 31, 2025, the Trump Administration announced it would release approximately $537 million in obligated funding for HBIIP for 543 projects, including "new projects approved within the first 100 days of the Trump Administration".61

The second Trump Administration continues to take actions where the outcome to HBIIP is unclear. For example, it is not clear if the staffing changes at USDA will impact USDA's implementation of HBIIP.62 On June 17, 2026, USDA announced the reorganization of the Rural Development (RD) mission area, including for the RBCS, which administers HBIIP. USDA reported, "Select functions and positions with the Rural Business-Cooperative Service will relocate from the [National Capital Region] to Dallas-Fort Worth, Texas, which will serve as the primary national hub for the agency's RBCS and RUS [Rural Utilities Service] loan and grant functions."63 On July 24, 2025, USDA Secretary Rollins announced the reorganization of USDA.64 Finally, on July 29, 2026, Secretary Rollins announced a USDA "100 Hires in 100 Days" initiative that will "recruit veterans, transitioning service members, and military spouses."65

Issues for Congress

The Supreme Court has established that Congress has the power to conduct oversight of federal programs.66 As such, Congress may or may not choose to assess past, current, and potentially future HBIIP administration by USDA. And Congress may or may not choose to consider HB fuel consumption rates, infrastructure costs, potential environmental impacts, and other issues related to HBIIP. Congress could choose to take no action. Alternatively, Congress could decide to explore the above-mentioned areas, and may consider the following questions and data requests, which are presented in no order of priority.67

Program Funding and Outlays

Request USDA provide a comprehensive funding and spending history for HBIIP for each fiscal year since FY2020, to include funding from the CCC, the IRA, and any other sources as well as unobligated funding, rescinded funding, and carryover funding.

Request USDA provide the HBIIP funding amount, funding source, and funding announcement date USDA anticipates for future fiscal years, if any.68

Program Implementation

Request USDA summarize any new priorities and program implementation changes the Trump Administration has made regarding HBIIP, including the Administration's anticipated timeline for implementing any program changes, and specify how and when the Administration will communicate any changes to Congress and the public.

Request USDA explain how or if it will consider program continuity in its administration of the program. For example, how will the Trump Administration carry out HBIIP if awards are issued and there is a sudden funding lapse or program personnel change so that awardees can continue their business operations and fulfill any commitments that may be dependent on the HBIIP award they received?

What criteria will USDA use to measure the success of the program?

How will USDA report HBIIP performance to Congress and how often?

How much financial support will USDA provide for the program and for how long? Where will the financial support come from (e.g., the CCC)?

Program Awards

Request USDA provide a list of HBIIP awards for each fiscal year granted under the second Trump Administration. For each award, list the award recipient, amount awarded, project location, project status, and project summary.69

Request USDA provide the current operational status of the infrastructure that was installed using HBIIP funds for each fiscal year since FY2020.

Request USDA provide the value and volume of HB fuel annual sales for locations that installed infrastructure using HBIIP funds for each fiscal year since FY2020.

Program Communication

Request USDA provide past written and oral HBIIP communications for each fiscal year since FY2020, to include announcements such as a notice of funding opportunity, award recipients, and other communications (e.g., Federal Register notices, press releases, stakeholder announcements, social media).

Request USDA explain how and when it will provide communications about HBIIP, in written and oral form, to both Congress and the public (e.g., program alerts, listservs, webinars, a performance dashboard).

Staffing

Request USDA provide the current HBIIP staffing chart and any significant changes from the past two years.

Request USDA explain to what extent, if any, the USDA Rural Development relocation and reorganization will impact HBIIP.

General Considerations

A US energy giant will deliver a total of 10 mobile turbines capable of generating up to 300 megawatts (MW) of electricity to a US customer amid growing demand for reliable power across the country.

New York’s New Fortress Energy (NFE) announced the deal on Thursday, October 29. As part of it, will lease the turbines to the undisclosed investment-grade firm for an initial period of five years.

According to the company, the equipment will be delivered in stages, starting in the fourth quarter of 2026. The final deliveries are expected in the first quarter of 2027. The deal is set to bring in more revenue from NFE’s existing equipment.

Wes Edens, NFE’s CEO, stressed the significance of the agreement. “We evaluated several opportunities for these turbines, and we believe that partnering with an investment-grade counterparty in the United States best aligned with NFE’s priorities,” he added.

Mobile energy capacity

Mobile turbines are a useful alternative to traditional power plants. The reason for this is that they can be transferred to locations where additional power is required and supply extra electricity during periods of high demand.

Under the agreement, the 10 turbines have a combined generation capacity of up to 300 MW. Still, NFE has not disclosed their models, fuel requirements, or where they will operate. The firm also did not identify the US customer or specify how the electricity would be used.

More from Energy

See All

NFE stressed that the deal follows an evaluation of several potential opportunities for the equipment. It selected the US customer as the agreement aligned with its financial and operational priorities.

“It provides the company significant, high-quality cash flows, puts our assets to work more quickly than alternative uses, and serves the growing demand for power in the USA,” Edens explained in a press statement. However, he did not disclose the financial value of the partnership or the expected lease payments.

LNG facility restart

At the same time, NFE also shared an update on its FLNG 1 liquefier. The floating facility is located offshore of Altamira, Mexico. It uses gas from the Sur de Texas-Tuxpan pipeline to produce LNG for customers.

The FLNG 1 was shut down following a mechanical problem with its gas turbine. The issue disrupted operations and reduced LNG exports from the site. It consists of three converted jack-up rigs.

The company said it remains on track to return to service in the fourth quarter of 2026. However, it did not provide an exact restart date or further details about the mechanical issue affecting the unit.

The site, which can produce more than 1.4 million tons of LNG per year, kicked off production in July 2024. Its first shipment followed in August, when the Energos Princess LNG carrier transported the fuel to NFE’s La Paz terminal.

NFE later secured USD 700 million in financing for its LNG operations in Mexico. As per online reports, part of the funding will also cover construction of FLNG 2, which will use the same modular technology as FLNG 1.

“Our FLNG complex is advancing at a rapid pace as we have now produced LNG at our first unit, and fully financed our second,” Edens concluded. “These are large infrastructure projects that add considerable financial and operational value to our Company and we are thrilled with the progress to date.”

text:
North Carolina's drought continues to worsen, with parts of Wake County now in extreme drought.

The areas shown in red below are in extreme drought, according to the latest drought status report released on Thursday, Nov. 5.

According to WRAL meteorologist Grant Skinner, the drought has worsened since the last Oct. 29 update, with 8% of the state now in extreme drought (as opposed to 2% last week) and 39% of the state now in extreme drought (as opposed to 32% last week).

Additionally, severe drought conditions in North Carolina have expanded farther east.

The last measurable rain in our area was Oct. 17, when we got three-fourths of an inch, according to Skinner.

Lake levels continue to fall, as well. As of Nov. 5, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers reported Falls Lake had fallen to 245.3 feet, its lowest point during this drought and more than 6 feet below its conservation pool for water storage. Falls Lake is the primary source of water in the Raleigh area.

Durham's reservoirs are also low, with Lake Michie at only 42% of its storage capacity.

Water concerns and lake levels are not the only concern in the drought. With 8% of the state in extreme drought, fire danger is top of mind, especially for people who plan to use fire pits this fall.

Trees may also drop their leaves earlier than usual.

Durham has been in Stage 2 water restrictions for months and is approaching the trigger for Stage 3. Wake County is not currently under any restrictions.

Rain and storms are in the forecast for Friday, the day after the drought report was released, but it likely won't do much to improve the drought.

WRAL meteorologists said over 12 inches of rain is needed to start climbing out of the drought and only one-fourth of an inch to 1 inch of rain is expected this week.

text:
BY RANDALL RYTI

Los Alamos

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), introduced by New Mexico’s U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich and three senators from both parties, offers an opportunity to make progress on these challenges. The bill would streamline energy project approvals, expand transmission capacity and modernize the electric grid, making it easier to connect new energy sources and deliver electricity where it is needed.

Communities that have lived with pollution from fossil fuel power plants deserve a path toward cleaner energy and healthier air. Expanding clean energy and transmission infrastructure can help make that transition possible while creating jobs, improving grid reliability and putting downward pressure on electricity costs.

BAAJA is a bipartisan compromise, and not every provision is without concern. Some permitting changes could also facilitate fossil fuel development. Tribal Nations have raised important concerns about provisions affecting historic preservation reviews, Tribal sovereignty and the protection of cultural resources. These concerns deserve serious attention, and meaningful Tribal consultation must remain an essential part of the permitting process.

We should be able to modernize energy permitting while protecting our natural and cultural resources and ensuring communities have a meaningful voice in decisions that affect them.

No legislation of this scope will satisfy every stakeholder. But maintaining the status quo also has consequences, including delays in building cleaner energy infrastructure, continued pollution and higher costs. On balance, BAAJA offers meaningful progress toward a cleaner, more reliable and affordable energy future. I support its passage and encourage Congress to move this bipartisan legislation forward.

title: Trump's Executive Actions and the Future of Urban Mobility | E+E Leader
description:
Recent executive actions by President Donald Trump signal a dramatic shift in U.S. transportation policy, particularly in urban mobility.
With the suspension of federal EV funding, elimination of mandates, and potential legal challenges, the road ahead remains uncertain for urban transit and clean energy initiatives.
Suspension of EV Infrastructure Programs One of the most immediate impacts of Trump’s executive actions is the suspension of the $5 billion National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) program.
His administration has also placed a hold on several transportation-related federal funding programs, creating uncertainty for urban transit systems.
The Road Ahead The implications of Trump’s executive actions for urban mobility are profound.
text:
Recent executive actions by President Donald Trump signal a dramatic shift in U.S. transportation policy, particularly in urban mobility. These measures could reshape how cities plan for sustainable transportation, EV adoption, and infrastructure development. With the suspension of federal EV funding, elimination of mandates, and potential legal challenges, the road ahead remains uncertain for urban transit and clean energy initiatives.

Suspension of EV Infrastructure Programs

One of the most immediate impacts of Trump’s executive actions is the suspension of the $5 billion National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) program. States have been instructed to halt spending on allocated federal funds while awaiting new guidance from the administration. This decision is expected to delay the rollout of EV charging stations, which are critical for the expansion of electric mobility in urban areas. The move may also discourage private investment in charging infrastructure, as businesses hesitate to commit capital amid policy uncertainty.

Rollback of EV Mandates and Incentives

The administration’s new policy, dubbed “Unleashing American Energy,” seeks to remove what it refers to as the “electric vehicle mandate,” instead promoting consumer choice. This includes efforts to roll back incentives that have accelerated EV adoption over the past decade. The potential elimination of federal EV tax credits could slow the growth of electric vehicle ownership, disproportionately affecting urban areas where electric cars are becoming more common due to environmental and economic incentives.

Impact on Federal Transportation Funding

Trump’s policies extend beyond EV infrastructure. His administration has also placed a hold on several transportation-related federal funding programs, creating uncertainty for urban transit systems. Large-scale projects like high-speed rail initiatives, public transit expansions, and smart city developments could face delays or funding cuts. Without clear guidance from the federal government, state and local agencies must navigate financial uncertainty while attempting to maintain progress toward modern, sustainable urban mobility solutions.

Legal and Economic Consequences

Several of these executive actions are expected to face legal challenges, particularly regarding the suspension of previously allocated funds and the rollback of established regulations. Environmental groups and state governments have already signaled their intent to contest these moves in court, arguing that they undermine prior commitments to clean transportation and energy efficiency. Furthermore, critics warn that halting EV infrastructure investments could have economic consequences, as it could slow job growth in the clean energy and transportation sectors.

City Responses and Alternative Strategies

Despite federal roadblocks, some cities are taking independent action to advance their mobility goals. Several urban centers have announced plans to self-fund EV infrastructure projects, leveraging public-private partnerships to maintain progress. Cities such as Los Angeles, New York, and Seattle are expanding local incentives for electric vehicles and developing municipal charging networks. Additionally, some states are considering legislation to compensate for lost federal funding, ensuring continued investment in clean transportation initiatives.

Other cities are accelerating commitments to alternative transit options, including expanding bike lanes, investing in bus electrification, and integrating smart transportation technologies. Local governments aim to maintain sustainability goals by diversifying their mobility strategies and reducing reliance on federal support.

The Road Ahead

The implications of Trump’s executive actions for urban mobility are profound. Cities that have been at the forefront of electric vehicle adoption and sustainable transit may now face significant hurdles in achieving their long-term goals. The uncertainty surrounding federal funding and incentives adds complexity to urban planning efforts, forcing local governments and businesses to reconsider their strategies.

As the political and legal battles unfold, the future of urban mobility in the U.S. will depend on how states, cities, and private enterprises adapt to these shifting federal policies. Whether through alternative funding mechanisms or local initiatives, the transition to a cleaner, more efficient transportation system remains a priority for many urban centers despite new federal roadblocks.

Three-wheeler exports grew 30 per cent and commercial vehicle exports surged 72.5 per cent.
Agarwal said the underlying demand fundamentals remain supportive and that the industry expects momentum to sustain going forward.

text:
The domestic automotive industry will sustain its growth momentum in the second half of this fiscal year though sales will moderate on a high base, said Shenu Agarwal, president at industry body Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (SIAM).

Automobile sales across categories surged 20 per cent on year in the six months ended September 30. Full-year growth will be fuelled by improved affordability following GST 2.0 reforms, strong financing support, resilient rural and urban markets, and festive demand, Agarwal told ET in his first interview since assuming charge in September.

“New launches, infrastructure spending, healthy freight movement and fleet replacement are also driving demand,” said Agarwal, also the managing director of truck and bus maker Ashok Leyland.

Advt

Alternate fuels and electric vehicles (EVs) helped drive a 31 per cent surge in passenger vehicle sales in the July-September period. Agarwal said the EV ecosystem is maturing, with multiple offerings, improving charging network and supportive policy.

“Alternative fuel technologies are also gaining wider acceptance,” he said. “We expect demand for cleaner and more efficient vehicles to keep rising in the mid-term. These technologies will play an important role in India’s sustainable mobility transition.” Recently notified CAFÉ III norms will attract more investments in new and sustainable technologies, he said.

Agarwal pointed to continued risks of inflationary pressures, higher interest rates and rising input costs on demand. The industry however remains “cautiously optimistic, we expect growth to stay positive,” he said.

Exports were largely strong last quarter despite geopolitical uncertainties, said Agarwal. Two-wheeler exports grew 28 per cent to 1.65 million units in Q2, the highest ever for a second quarter. Three-wheeler exports grew 30 per cent and commercial vehicle exports surged 72.5 per cent.

Agarwal said passenger vehicle exports fell 5.2 per cent to 229,000 units in the September quarter amid a high base and logistics constraints sparked by the West Asia crisis. “In the mid-term, we will keep watching geopolitical developments closely,” he said. “The broad-based growth in most segments shows the strength/ resilience of Indian automotive products in overseas markets.”

Advt

The entry-level car segment, meanwhile, is also staging a strong comeback after the cuts in goods and services tax (GST) from September 2025 led companies to drop prices, indicating a revival in consumption among first-time buyers.

Agarwal said the underlying demand fundamentals remain supportive and that the industry expects momentum to sustain going forward.

In H1 FY27, sales of entry-level passenger cars of up to 3.6 metres in length surged 86 per cent. Among mass-market two-wheelers, entry-level scooters of up to 125 cc engines rose 17.5 per cent, mopeds (75-100 cc) climbed 22 per cent, and 110cc motorcycles grew 5.1 per cent.

Overall, with vehicle penetration in the country still low, the headroom for expansion is significant, according to Agarwal.

text:
Massachusetts Maritime Academy was awarded a $260,000 grant from the Mass Clean Energy Center (MassCEC) to further develop its Offshore Wind Training Program and strengthen workforce development for the clean energy industry.

The funding will support the equipment, certifications and instructional capacity required to deliver helicopter underwater escape training, a critical offshore safety credential. Training will be provided on the academy’s campus in partnership with RelyOn USA, a leading provider of safety and emergency response training for the offshore wind, maritime and energy industries.

The grant is part of $4.2 million in state funding recently announced by Governor Maura T. Healey and MassCEC. The investment will support 20 projects statewide that strengthen the offshore wind and maritime workforce and advance research on fisheries, wildlife, and the marine environment.

“The clean energy industry is creating new opportunities for skilled mariners and technicians,” said Rear Admiral Francis X. McDonald, USMS, president of the Massachusetts Maritime Academy. “This grant helps ensure that our students are prepared to meet that demand with industry-recognized safety training. We’re grateful for MassCEC’s continued investment in workforce development.”

text:
HARRISBURG, Pa. – After a campaign season filled with outrage against data centers, the midterm elections ushered in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.

A tougher regulatory environment for artificial intelligence giants and data center developers is expected to follow, even if President Donald Trump — perhaps the industry’s biggest champion — stalls any federal crackdown.

Data center regulation itself was not on most midterm ballots, and it wasn't among the top issues for most voters. But hardline stances against the server warehouses were woven into the platforms of many candidates, including the Democrats who upended longtime Republican control of the governorships in Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Nevada and Iowa, many of which are data center hotspots.

Skepticism of data centers, and their impact on electricity prices, often blended with the fight for affordability — a key campaign talking point for Democrats.

In Texas, Clayton Tucker, the first Democrat elected state agriculture commissioner since 1986, said his pledge to fight data center development was critical to his victory. Everywhere he went, he said, ranchers worried that data centers posed an existential threat to their dwindling water supplies.

“You know, there’s an old saying around here that ‘whiskey’s for drinking and water’s for fighting,’” Tucker told The Associated Press. “And that’s exactly what happened.”

Data centers were a persistent bogeyman in attack ads

According to data from AdImpact, campaigns large and small spent more than $380 million on television ads mentioning data centers. Democrats outspent Republicans on the topic by more than three to one.

Sweeping wins by Democrats could have far-reaching implications for data centers. Besides taking control of Congress, Democrats flipped at least five governors’ offices and took full control of state governments in five more states: Wisconsin, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Nevada and Michigan.

Data Center Watch, a project of AI security consultancy 10a Labs, said it tracked winning candidates for Congress and governorships and found the vast majority had expressed support for stronger regulation or even a moratorium.

Among governors, 32 of the 34 victorious candidates in races where AP called a winner support stronger regulation or restrictions. Twelve of the 34 support bans or moratoriums, it said.

During the campaign, Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley, a Democrat, changed his position under pressure from his Republican opponent to take a harder line against data centers. Initially opposed to any moratorium, Crowley later said he supported one as well as abolishing the state’s sales tax exemption for data center operators and developers.

In an interview Thursday with AP, Crowley said he’s having discussions now about what he'll propose once he takes office.

In the mix are things like requiring developers to disclose more about their water and energy consumption, ensuring a community supports a project before it can go forward and insulating ratepayers and taxpayers from the energy costs of the projects, Crowley said.

The industry sees a need to build trust

AI giant OpenAI published a framework Thursday enumerating new commitments to the communities where it develops data centers. The company said it was asking federal, state and local policymakers to write “clear rules for how the industry builds.”

“Lawmakers should establish rules to advance responsible investment, protect residents, and ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared,” the post said.

An industry association, the Data Center Coalition, echoed the sentiment that developers need to keep trying to build trust with public officials and communities. A coalition official, Dan Diorio, said the industry is aware many midterm winners have vowed to impose a moratorium.

“We should expect them to want to deliver on those promises, but there are going to be real world consequences of that,” Diorio said in an interview.

Those consequences, Diorio said, could include host communities missing out on tax revenue or payments from tech companies. Data centers are also driving a broader economic expansion that encourages investment in domestic manufacturing, he said.

Wall Street sees red lights ahead after the election

The election of data center skeptics adds challenges to stock markets riding high on the AI boom.

On Thursday, the Nasdaq, which is full of AI-related and other tech stocks, sank 11% below its all-time high amid worries that data center construction may slow because it’s getting costlier to borrow money.

AI data center construction is driving much of the U.S. economy’s growth, and any slowdown could have a broader chill.

In an analyst report, Morgan Stanley said decisive results for Democrats carry "greater expectations for data center restrictions" that, under new state regulations, could “split the country into areas that are open to new data centers and those without.”

It singled out Texas' election of Democrat Gina Hinojosa for governor as the “most important election result" for data center development. Hinojosa has said she’d block a permit for a data center if it wasn’t a good deal for Texans or residents hadn’t gotten a say in the matter. She defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who had touted Texas as "the epicenter of AI development” before trying to clamp down on it late in the campaign.

Morgan Stanley also said Ohio's election of Democrat Dr. Amy Acton as governor “creates significant risk of data center project delays in the state.” Acton has pledged to block a data center project unless it meets certain standards.

Local elections didn’t go well for data centers, either

Voters in local referendums cast ballots overwhelmingly in favor of restricting data centers, according to an analysis by polling and data science firm Redbud Consulting.

Redbud tracked 47 referendums in 44 municipalities in 12 states, including 21 in Ohio alone, eight in Maine, seven in Illinois and four in Kansas. Restrictions were approved in 44 of the 45 elections where counting was complete, Redbud reported.

Most voters don't want a data center built near them

About three-quarters of U.S. voters oppose the construction of a new data center in their community, according to The AP Voter Poll.

In red and blue states alike, majorities of voters were opposed to adding a data center where they live.

Support was higher in some traditionally red states, including Wyoming, West Virginia, Louisiana and Mississippi. In Texas, voters in the Senate race were similarly likely to say they oppose a new data center being built in their community.

Despite voters’ deep opposition to data centers near them, The AP Voter Poll suggests it was not a particularly motivating issue in this election.

About one-quarter of U.S. voters said AI data centers were “crucial” to their vote for Congress, which is well below the shares that said government corruption or the cost of living were highly important to their vote.

The stakes were especially high in Texas

Texas is poised to overtake northern Virginia as the largest global data center market by 2030, according to a report by commercial real estate giant JLL.

In the campaign, Hinojosa aggressively attacked Abbott as having rolled out the welcome mat for data centers.

Stephen Sanders, a Republican who co-founded a data center protest group in Lubbock, said Texans were especially attuned to the issue because of talk that data centers pose a threat to their electricity and water in the drought-stricken state.

“I would say data centers were on the ballot,” Sanders said.

___

Associated Press reporters Scott Bauer in Madison, Wisconsin, Kaitlyn Huamani in Los Angeles and Linley Sanders in Washington contributed to this report.

More than 50 manufacturers of DC fast chargers use technology from both companies. “Our customers build their charging systems on SIMATIC automation, and that will not change,” said Siemens Digital Industries Product Manager Automation Systems René Kuroczka. “For integration in the field, we have found a partner in EcoG with whom we combine an established charging infrastructure ecosystem with industrial automation.”
