The Basics of Climate Mobility Modeling

Before diving into existing models and how policymakers can use them for their objectives, a brief overview of the field is useful. While there are still few climate mobility models, there are emerging trends in the questions they seek to answer and the tools they bring to bear.

Why You Can’t “Count” Climate Migrants

Climate change is almost never the sole or primary driver of migration. Individual and household migration decisions are also the product of other overlapping pressures: economic opportunity, social networks, conflict, governance, and household circumstances. Because climate is entangled with these other drivers, producing a single count of climate-driven migrants requires making modeling choices about how to isolate climate’s contribution—and different choices produce different numbers.

Models of climate mobility must deal with this complexity of drivers and cannot be conflated with estimates of risk exposure. Astronomical, widely cited figures, such as “1 billion by 2050,” typically come from overlaying population maps with hazard maps or assuming all people in highly climate-exposed areas will move. However, displacement risk is more complicated and is a function of not just exposure, but vulnerability and capacity as well. Some modelers have added proxies of vulnerability and capacity, such as education and poverty, to varying degrees of success. Yet calculations of climate exposure and displacement risk are still different types of estimates than climate mobility estimates of future movement—the latter is the focus of this paper.

Box 1. The Human Mobility Spectrum

Human mobility is an umbrella term for the diverse ways people move. It is meant to capture a holistic range of movement: voluntary, involuntary, or somewhere in between. And the movement may be short or long term, cover short or long distances, and occur within or across borders. It may involve a single individual, a household, or an entire community. The reasons behind it are similarly varied.

This paper focuses primarily on migration, which typically refers to longer-term movement away from one’s place of origin, usually across an administrative boundary. Conventionally, migration is distinguished from displacement by the degree of choice involved, but in the climate context that line gets blurry. Movement in response to a slow-onset stressor such as declining yields or salinizing soil is rarely either freely chosen or straightforwardly forced.

In addition, each model assessed here varies in its approach to defining and measuring migration. While many models like the Global Centre for Climate Mobility’s (GCCM) Caribbean Shifts Model (2025) deliberately exclude temporary or nonpermanent migration from their future projections, in other cases, such as for the Small-Island Developing States, where nonpermanent or seafaring labor migration is essential to a country’s economy or forms part of historic traditions, such movements necessarily form an important part of mobility projections.i

Notes

i “Great Caribbean Shifts: The Greater Caribbean Climate Mobility Report,” Global Centre for Climate Mobility, September 2025, https://d2seg4j92fgtle.cloudfront.net/GCCMI+Report+-+28.08.pdf; and Robert Oakes, Andrea Milan, and Jillian Campbell, “Kiribati: Climate Change and Migration—Relationships Between Household Vulnerability, Human Mobility and Climate Change,” United Nations University Institute for Environment and Human Security (UNU-EHS), Report no. 20, November 2016, https://www.unescap.org/resources/kiribati-climate-change-and-migration-relationships-between-household-vulnerability-human.

Climate mobility models are inherently complex and uncertain and need to be understood more as hypotheses than facts. Each model is the product of stacked assumptions, including emissions pathways, economic development, and policy choices, over a long time horizon. Uncertainty compounds at each step, so the headline number is always a simplification, not a fact. Thus, models may have one well-known number (for example, 216 million, cited in the World Bank’s Groundswell report), but they should always be understood in the context of a range, stated time frame, and scenario—in other words, 216 million by 2050, in a pessimistic scenario—instead of a single point estimate that implies more precision than the underlying methodology can support.

Stripped of context, as often happens in media coverage, a projection can become a scare statistic rather than a meaningful policy input. Inflated, decontextualized numbers can feed securitized “climate refugee wave” narratives, be weaponized in anti-migration politics, and—when a predicted crisis does not materialize on schedule—erode credibility for the field and for legitimate adaptation and mobility policy arguments.

None of this is an argument for dismissing climate mobility models outright but is instead an argument for better understanding where they come from. The variation in headline numbers reflects real differences in how researchers model human behavior, translate climate hazards into economic or social pressure, and define what counts as a climate-related move in the first place (or in some cases, common misunderstandings from policymakers about what the modelers actually find). Below is an overview of the four most common modeling approaches behind these estimates, so that any number encountered later in this paper—or elsewhere in the literature—can be read with a clearer sense of what it does and does not represent.

Understanding Current Approaches

Researchers rely on several distinct modeling approaches to project or explain climate-related mobility. Each embeds different assumptions about human behavior and requires different data, which is a large part of why the same climate scenario can produce different mobility estimates depending on which approach is used. Table 1 lays out in detail the four most common approaches, explains how they work, and analyzes their pros and cons.

Traditional modeling approaches commonly fall into four categories:

Gravity models: There is rarely a singular reason as to why people move and why they choose, among myriad possible destinations, one place as their new home. Modeling all the reasons, especially at the individual level, is often impossible. However, in observations where there are thousands or perhaps millions of people choosing whether to move, certain aggregate patterns regularly materialize. Often, the population size of a destination and its geographic distance are the most important and useful factors for modeling a process like migration. Thus, size and distance are the starting point of the gravity approach, and through the incorporation of climate stressors (like drought, sea-level rise, and crop failure) as factors that adjust the attractiveness between places, gravity models represent a signature approach in the current climate mobility modeling field. But while they are especially useful in anticipating destination pressures for infrastructure and housing planning, they are largely silent on who is moving or why.

Computable general equilibrium (CGE) models: Climate shocks rarely affect migration directly; instead, they can alter agricultural productivity, wages, prices, and the availability of work, which in turn can change people’s incentives and ability to move. CGE models are designed to capture these economy-wide interactions by representing how households, firms, and markets respond to a shock and how changes in one part of the economy ripple through others. In climate mobility research, this makes it possible to translate specific climate-related effects (such as drought, heat, or flooding) into economic effects (such as low productivity, poor industry health, or unemployment) that may affect migration. Because these models can represent interactions across sectors and regions, they are particularly useful for testing “what-if” scenarios (for example, how adaptation investments or labor market policies might alter the effects of a climate shock). This model’s reliance on detailed economic and demographic data, however, can limit its application in regions most vulnerable to climate change, where the data needed to calibrate the model are scarce.

Agent-based models (ABMs): Many models describe migration by looking for patterns across populations, geographies, or markets. ABMs, however, start from the constituent units of a system (individuals, households, or communities) and ask how their decisions and interactions might produce or reproduce those larger-scale patterns. It is therefore easier to understand an ABM as a framework, rather than a technology—one that describes a system from the perspective of its constituent units (agents). These units can differ in their circumstances, information, preferences, and responses to climate hazards. In climate mobility research, this makes it possible to examine not only how many people move, but also who moves, who stays, or who becomes trapped, making ABMs particularly useful for targeted, equity-focused policy design. Their bottom-up approach, however, means that findings are often closely tied to the assumptions, behavioral rules, and context of the particular population and place being modeled, making results difficult to generalize beyond the modeled setting.

Econometric models: Migration responds to many overlapping economic, social, and environmental factors, making climate change’s contribution to migration hard to isolate. Econometric models address this by utilizing the observed variation in climate conditions and migration to estimate the relationship between them. For climate mobility researchers, this provides an empirical basis from which the relationship between migration and hazards such as extreme heat, changing rainfall, and drought can be modeled. Because these models are grounded in historical relationships, they offer the strongest evidence base—as they are based on demonstrated (not just projected) impact—but their findings may be less informative where future climate conditions or socioeconomic circumstances differ substantially from those observed in the data. Moreover, because the focus of these models is on the observed relationship between climate change and migration, they often fail to account for populations that are unable to move.

Box 2. The Role of Scenario Planning in Climate Mobility Modeling

Quantitative modeling and scenario planning serve different purposes but are best treated as complementary, not incompatible.

Modeling—using gravity, computable general equilibrium, agent-based, or econometric approaches—produces quantitative estimates grounded in data and statistical or simulated relationships. Even if these estimates are ranges, the models are rigorous, comparable across studies, and testable through sensitivity analysis and thus give more robust, testable, and specific estimates. But modeling has weaknesses, including false precision, heavy data requirements, overly complex findings, and difficulty capturing deep uncertainty or genuinely novel futures.

Scenario planning builds multiple internally consistent narratives about how the future could unfold, based on different potential situations and policy responses—not just physical climate variables—as an axis of difference. The process embraces deep uncertainty rather than hiding it, focuses on how different assumptions and policy choices lead to different results, and thus is well suited to stress-testing plans and helping stakeholders understand their roles. However, scenario planning is not quantitative, so it is less suited for budgeting or evidencing specific, detailed policy choices (where modeling may provide more granular, albeit imperfect, evidence). Also, its quality depends heavily on who is in the room defining the scenarios, and its findings are harder to communicate to audiences who expect a single number.

Key Findings at a Glance

With this grounding in modeling approaches and complexity, the next step is to take stock of the climate mobility modeling landscape itself. Academic meta-analyses already exist, but the field is also young and moving quickly, with 62 percent of models published after 2020. Therefore, this paper distills the six most salient findings to orient readers new to the field. The full list of models assessed is included in the appendix.

Key Finding 1: There is No “Best” Global Headline Number

There are currently seven different global climate migration projections, with four providing internal and cross-border migration estimates (see figure 1).

These global projections tell different stories partly because of their methodologies and how they present findings. First, gravity models typically produce estimates of internal or international migration in a specific scenario, but some models like Groundswell aggregate the total number of people who will have moved by 2050, while other models like the Bilateral Gravity and World Economy report numbers moving within a given period, not a running sum, and so appear smaller. Second, CGE models, such as the Dynamic General Equilibrium Model, treat mobility as one output of a broader economic reallocation. This makes their estimates more conditional and often narrower in scope, typically capturing south-to-north movement among working-age populations. Finally, econometric models like First Street Global estimate the historical sensitivity of migration to climate variables, then apply that relationship to future climate projections. This is often why exposure-based models, especially those reporting cumulative headline figures, can appear to dwarf estimates from other approaches.

Key Finding 2: Models Cover Bangladesh and the United States More Than Anywhere Else in the World

Of the thirty-seven models assessed, six focus on Bangladesh and five on the United States (in other words, 29 percent of all models reviewed cover just these two countries) (see figure 2). Six models operate at the global level; six take regional approaches, with two covering the South American and African continents; and four provide coverage of nine subregions, including the Caribbean, Central America, Central Asia, East Asia and the Pacific, Eastern Europe, the Mediterranean, North Africa, and sub-Saharan Africa. Other regions, notably Western Europe and Australia, have less or no similar modeling.

Key Finding 3: Most Models Cover Internal Migration, with Nearly Half Only Focusing on It

Internal migration data are more widely available in most countries, as international movement can be harder to model if trying to include ever-changing and unpredictable policy choices about border, asylum, and visa policies (see figure 3). Simultaneously, most evidence points to climate mobility being primarily within countries, particularly rural-to-urban, so these models also cover a key part of the phenomenon. Some of these models, or 19 percent, model rural-urban flows specifically, and an additional 43 percent likely account for it when looking at the projection of internal migration. Thirteen models, or 35 percent, cover both internal and international (cross-border) migration.

Key Finding 4: More Than Half of Models Use Gravity or Agent-Based Modeling Approaches

Ten of the models reviewed are gravity models, which predict aggregate movement between places based on their size, wealth, and the distance between them (a proxy for “attractiveness”), with climate variables layered in (see figure 4). Notably, most of these gravity models were developed and refined by the same group of researchers, including Bryan Jones and colleagues at the Center for Integrated Earth System Information. These models include Groundswell I (2018), Groundswell II (2021), GCCM’s Africa Shifts (2023), and the C40 Cities Future Urban Landscapes (2024). Each model uses different inputs and assumptions, and recent iterations have made small tweaks for context or accuracy.

Another ten models are ABMs, of which three cover Bangladesh. Other models cover Burkina Faso, Kiribati, Maldives, Mali, Nepal, Senegal, and Tuvalu. ABMs can provide more granular, policy-relevant findings (see “Uses Cases” below), but they are assumption-heavy, context-specific, and require heavy data and technical lifts to create, limiting their transferability across regions.

Key Finding 5: Sea-Level Rise Is the Most Covered Climate-Related Hazard

Thirty-eight percent of all models incorporate sea-level rise as the primary or stand-alone hazard driving migration (see figure 5). Sea-level rise is a popular hazard to model because it is directional and cumulative rather than episodic, so it can be projected as a steadily rising surface, intersected with elevation and population data, and translated into the unambiguous outcome of uninhabitable land. Meanwhile, more than half of the models reviewed include sea-level rise alongside other hazards, such as flooding, temperature rise, and rainfall variability. Two models capture more unique impacts, such as coral bleaching and wildfires. But a host of other climate hazards and related impacts, such as glacial melt, ocean acidification, and agricultural pests, have not been modeled, likely because of lack of data, limited relevance, and less policy attention.

Key Finding 6: Most Models Focus on Long-Term Time Horizons (2050, 2100)

A majority of models focus on 2050- and 2100-time horizons for two principal reasons: First, scientists argue that the effects of climate change only become clear over longer time horizons. Second, the climate data the models rely on are produced on those same timescales. The standard emissions scenarios are designed to show how the climate diverges under different futures, and they barely separate from one another before about 2040, so a projection to 2030 captures mostly ordinary year-to-year variability rather than a climate signal. The models that do project the nearer term often work around this in one of two ways: by filling in the decades between the standard scenario dates or by focusing on a hazard whose near-term path is already well established, such as sea-level rise. A handful of models produce 2030 and 2040 estimates that fit policy cycles better. The Global Center for Climate Mobility’s Africa Shifts Model (Amakrane et al. 2023), Mediterranean Sea-Level Rise (SLR) Model (Reimann et al. 2023), the C40 Cities Model (2024), and the Climate Change: Migration and Economics (CliC:ME) Model (Burzynski et al. 2026) allow users to explore projections in ten-year increments (see figure 6).

Thinking Through Use Cases for Policymakers

Many of the models we assessed were not designed primarily with policymaking in mind, and some are better suited to certain types of policymakers than others. Policy stakeholders consulted across sectors referred to four primary use cases for climate mobility modeling: increasing political buy-in and advocacy around climate mobility policies, supporting long-term policy and strategic planning, guiding project and program design, and strengthening local and community planning. This section demystifies which models serve which use case, and why.

Use Case 1: Political Buy-In and Advocacy

Most stakeholders use modeling to generate a sense of urgency around climate and mobility and to make the case within their own organization for why the issue deserves attention and resources. This is especially true among governments and funders, where senior leaderships face competing demands and need clear evidence on why climate mobility should be a priority. For example, one department within the United Kingdom’s Foreign, Commonwealth, and Development Office explored a pilot climate mobility model to generate data on climate-related migration from key source countries to Europe and the United Kingdom to generate internal interest in the matter. The Climate Displaced Persons Act introduced by U.S. Senator Edward Markey cites the 2020 Ecological Threat Register’s projection of 2.1 billion people at risk of displacement to induce action.

Activists also have long used estimates of climate migration modeling to call for stronger climate action and migration policies. For example, ActionAid released a report using a refined version of Groundswell’s gravity modeling approach in South Asia to make the case that the region was “set to treble by 2050 due to climate inaction on global warming.”

Modeling plays an important role in raising awareness and advocacy. However, as argued above, modeling efforts are strengthened when their underlying figures, geographic scope, and scenarios travel alongside the headline claim. Doing so guards against both inaccuracy and the tendency for a striking number to displace the policy argument it was meant to support.

Use Case 2: Long-Term Policy and Strategic Planning

Many policy stakeholders engage regularly in long-term policy and strategic planning, and climate mobility models that project out to 2050 or 2100 can align well with those planning horizons. Bangladesh is a clear example of a country incorporating such modeling into its long-term planning. Its 2022 National Adaptation Plan references the future projections in the World Bank’s Groundswell report to highlight the unique risks and vulnerabilities of the country.

Other long-horizon planning processes run on similar timelines. In the Global North, examples include processes such as the U.S. State Department’s Quadrennial Diplomacy and Development Review, which includes long-term blueprints for diplomatic and development efforts abroad, and the U.S. National Intelligence Council Global Trends reports, which focus on fifteen-year future trends relevant to national security. In the Global South, some countries think through fifty-year development time horizons, including for the African Union (Agenda 2063) and in places such as Bangladesh (Vision 2050 and Delta Plan 2100), Rwanda (Vision 2050), and Ethiopia (Vision 2050). These plans are all possible candidates for incorporating global or regional models to flag long-range risks and identify hot spots worth planning around.

Where more complex, cross-sectoral planning is being conducted, CGE models may offer more value, since they capture how climate-driven migration interacts with labor markets, trade, and economic output, rather than treating migration as an isolated variable. How a planner uses a CGE model depends on what the plan is trying to achieve. In the Global North, CGEs can help anticipate demographic decline and identify where attracting migrant labor and skills will be necessary to sustain economic output. In the Global South, CGEs can help planners understand how their economies may need to be systematically reoriented—for instance, away from climate-exposed agriculture—as mobility patterns shift over decades.

Use Case 3: Project and Program Planning

Beyond long-term planning, climate mobility modeling can inform near-term decisions about how and where policymakers and practitioners should invest in climate mobility programs. Such programs range from interventions targeting hot spots of climate-driven out-migration to preparing communities where the modeling anticipates an increase in arrivals. The World Bank’s Groundswell model has been used in the design and approval processes of a few bank operations (for instance, as part of the justification for a flood infrastructure investment in Niger).

For many models, time frames may be a limiting factor. Most stakeholders work on projects and planning cycles that span one to five years. Models with long time frames may be less helpful in justifying and shaping immediate interventions when there are so many other pressing short- and medium-term needs and the models have so much uncertainty in their long-term estimates. In those cases, a handful of models with nearer-term projections can be helpful, such as the Caribbean Shifts Model (2025) and the Mediterranean SLR model, which make projections for mobility at the regional level available as early as 2030.

Prioritizing Place

Modeling can identify where interventions are most needed, particularly by identifying hot spots of in-migration and out-migration. In a context of scarce resources, national and international actors need to prioritize where they invest and thus need to know what places will see out-migration (and may need investments so people can stay if they wish) and where places will see in-migration (and may need investments to build out infrastructure and services for such growth).

Gravity and CGE models at national and regional scales, such as Groundswell I (Rigaud et al. 2018) and II (Clement et al. 2021), Africa Shifts (Amakrane et al. 2023), Great Caribbean Shifts (Rosengartner et al. 2025), and CliC:ME (Burzynski et al. 2026), can identify such hotspots. There are slight differences, with some models more granular than others, but gravity models generally can give a broad understanding of movement in the country or region. At an even more granular level, CGEs may prove more useful. One illustrated case is a comparison of the in- and out-migration hotspots provided by the Africa Shifts Model versus the CliC:ME Model for Ethiopia.

The GCCM’s Africa Shifts Model shows broad strokes of movement, where green areas are in-migration hotspots and red areas are out-migration hotspots—the darker the color, the higher the level of movement (see figure 7).

Addis Ababa is marked as a site of out-migration, with southern, peri-urban parts of the city experiencing in-migration (see figure 8). However, other nearby towns are obscured. The gravity model considers factors that influence place attractiveness, in this case, the impact of topography first on water access and agricultural productivity and then on population distribution.

The CliC:ME Model (2026) takes a similar color-coded approach, where blue means in-migration and red means out-migration (see figure 9). However, the model provides more detailed in- and out-migration projections at a lower administrative level.

While both models show similar results, they are not identical. The CliC:ME Model projects that Addis Ababa will see substantial in-migration (see figure 10). This is likely because Addis Ababa is such an important economic hub for the country.

Even with these insights, understanding the mechanisms behind this pattern requires pairing gravity modeling with qualitative research (for instance, to explain diverging quantitative model estimates in Addis Ababa). The Groundswell reports, for example, used six case studies to add contextual depth that the numbers alone cannot provide. In their Uganda deep dive, consultations allowed the World Bank to identify additional contextual issues in in-migration hot spots Mbala, surrounding parts of Kampala, and Ntungamo, such as high poverty rates, informal settlements, and weak infrastructure.

Investing for Impact

In addition, some climate mobility models estimate the impact of different interventions, including in-migration flows, and thus provide evidence for project design. For example, in their Mediterranean SLR Model, Lena Reimann and others explore how coastal adaptation policies, such as managed retreat, coastal wetland restoration, and coastline protection, are likely to influence both the quantity and spatial distribution of future migration patterns. This model found that while submergence due to sea-level rise could result in over 20 million internal migrations by the year 2100, highly engineered protective measures like dikes, sea walls, and barriers could bring that estimate down to as low as 2 million.

Other approaches cover a wider range of potential interventions. Nicolas Choquette-Levy and others assess how interventions like cash transfers, remittance banks, and index-based insurances affect the levels of migration and immobility experienced by an agricultural community in Nepal, including many families who lack the resources to move. By allowing for direct engagement with household-level decisionmaking, the ABM in this study offers insights—amid worsening environmental conditions—into the uptake of varying adaptation strategies such as migration and cash-cropping under different intervention scenarios. It finds, for example, that a combination of all three interventions could facilitate migration for close to a third of households for which it would otherwise be out of reach.

Ensuring Targeted Investments

During our stakeholder consultations, several participants stated that it is necessary to know both the number of people moving and the profiles of who is moving to ensure targeted investments. Most climate mobility models do not disaggregate to this level. ABMs are a notable exception, simulating individual- or household-level decisionmaking rather than aggregate flows—but usable ABMs currently exist for only a small subset of countries, which limits their near-term applicability (see figure 11).

For example, ABM work in Senegal has demonstrated the significantly increased resilience to both short- and medium-term climate shocks (drought and salt-water intrusion) among individuals with either vocational or university degrees. In combination with the finding that climate shocks may foster increased population movements to an interior crescent or safety corridor comprised by the departments of Podor, Sedhiou, and Kolda (that have historically been sending regions), these modeling efforts provide concrete targets for economic development investments. For instance, benefits could be seen in the trade and service sectors in the regions most likely to absorb these new workers, along with parallel local governance measures to secure adequate housing, land tenure, and access to social services.

Use Case 4: Local and Community Planning

Local and municipal planners can use climate mobility modeling to prepare infrastructure, housing, and service capacity. If a model predicts an influx of climate migrants, a city can plan housing stock, school enrollment, healthcare, and transit demand, all of which take years to adjust. For example, rapid urbanization across Africa, driven in part by significant rural-urban migration (including climate-related migration) has strained urban infrastructure and capacities. In response, Cities Alliances’ urban expansion planning approach helps cities to forecast urban population growth in the next thirty years and to build out urban peripheries (where migrants tend to settle) and connect them to the core city before migrant settlements grow unsustainably in poorly serviced areas. Such long-term planning, used by cities across both low- and high-income countries, could be better served with localized climate mobility modeling.

Understanding out-migration also matters, since it erodes the property and sales tax base a municipality depends on, so understanding that trajectory early lets local governments plan for revenue shortfalls.

Modeling can also inform land use decisions—for example, whether it still makes sense to permit development in a flood-prone or fire-adjacent zone, or whether managed retreat is the more viable long-term path. That question ties directly into cost-benefit tradeoffs between adaptation (seawalls, cooling infrastructure) and retreat, and modeling gives planners the data to make that case credibly.

One model, made by C40 Cities, provides a more in-depth look at ten cities in the Global South: Accra, Amman, Bogotá, Curitiba, Dhaka, Freetown, Karachi, Rio de Janeiro, Salvador, and São Paulo. A modification to the approach used in the Groundswell reports, the “INCLUDE” model is among the first to analyze internal climate migration at the local level. The results provide an in-depth profile for each city, which details not only the number of projected climate migrants (in ten-year time steps) but also a breakdown of their age, gender, the climate stressor most likely to have driven their movement, and, perhaps most importantly, a high-resolution mapping of the parts of the city where climate-affected populations are expected to move to and away from.

An Agenda for Making Climate Mobility Models More Usable

The section above demonstrates how policymakers can use climate mobility models, as well as the myriad ways existing models cannot answer policymakers’ questions with enough accuracy, granularity, or at all. The models are constrained in scope, with many (1) covering limited climate hazards and only a subset of types of movement such as migration but not forced displacement, or internal only, (2) using long, fifty-year time horizons unhelpful for program cycles, or (3) offering estimates of movement but not modeling the impact of different types of interventions.

Still, even though these models face a range of data and methodological limitations, which academic researchers continue to debate, they are proliferating and becoming more sophisticated. (For example, 62 percent have been published since 2020.) As the field of climate mobility modeling grows, it will have to reckon with a structural methodological challenge. Current models are split between two families: gravity, econometric, and computable general equilibrium models, which are geographically portable but behaviorally shallow, and agent-based models, which are behaviorally rich but geographically rigid. Closing that gap—and making models genuinely useful to the policymakers who would fund and use them—will require not just methodological advancement, but also a distinct research agenda and new ways of working, organized around seven key priorities.

Modeling the Effects of Policy Interventions

This is perhaps the most significant priority in the field: very few existing models are built to test counterfactuals or simulate how interventions (for example, early warning systems, livelihood support, or managed retreat) change migration outcomes. This reflects a range of data challenges, as well as, in some cases, a normative reluctance to focus on what prevents people from moving. But these are the questions policymakers are asking, and building policy levers explicitly into model structures would turn these tools from passive projections into genuine decision-support instruments. This would be a significant methodological lift, but one with mature analogues in public health and economic policy modeling, where intervention modeling is already standard practice.

Moving Toward a Modular, Fit-for-Purpose Ecosystem

The modeling field is likely better served by a suite of fit-for-purpose tools mapped to specific policy questions than by the search for a single “best” model. A practical next step would be for modelers, donors, and policymakers to build a shared taxonomy of policy questions and map future models onto it. Modelers have begun something along these lines with the Mobility and Migration Modeling Intercomparison Project, which uses coastal Bangladesh as a first case study. But more needs to be done, both to get existing models into the hands of policymakers and to make the next generation fit for purpose. Bilateral donors and philanthropies are well placed to fund that coordination, since no single research group can build it alone.

Reorienting Toward the Policy Cycle

Current models are often built around scientific timescales—decadal projections, long-run climate scenarios—that do not align with how governments actually plan and budget, typically in cycles of one to five years. There are some exceptions (see the “Key Findings” section). Generally, however, modelers need to build shorter-horizon variants where feasible or, when models do play out until 2100, estimate findings on a decade-by-decade basis until then. Simultaneously, shorter time frames allow both researchers and practitioners to evaluate model findings (for instance, seeing how estimates through 2030 play out in reality, without waiting until 2050 or 2100).

Getting the timing right will likely require direct partnerships with government planning offices, since budget and policy cycles vary considerably across national and subnational contexts. It may require diverting research attention away from long-term modeling toward efforts to develop and evaluate medium-term estimates. It may also require a different set-up of funding and research processes—for instance, donors funding researchers to continuously update their models each year (or every three to five years), instead of funding them to produce one-off models.

Expanding Geographic Coverage

Existing models are heavily concentrated on a narrow set of Global South contexts and the United States. In some cases, big climate-related hazards such as heat, drought, and wildfires—which are already upending different regional contexts, including in Europe and Australia—remain entirely unmodeled. In other cases, country-wide future projections do not meet the needs and expectations of organizations and policymakers working in specific metro regions, such as Detroit or Chicago in the United States. In addition, modeling of immigration to the Global North is also limited.

Methodologically, gravity and CGE approaches are geographically portable enough to extend to these cases; the harder task is adapting agent-based behavioral assumptions—built on informal labor markets and weak safety nets—to contexts with formal insurance, asylum systems, and different migration infrastructures. But covering more countries will require modelers, funders, and policy partners to invest in countries that may be lower priorities, have less data availability, or host fewer research partners—all of which are challenges that will take time and continued effort to overcome.

Improving Spatial and Demographic Granularity

Some policymakers, particularly local planners and national governments, need to know where people are moving on a more granular level (for example, neighborhood flows, not just aggregate flows). Ideally, their movement would be disaggregated by age, gender, income, and/or occupation to best orient planning.

However, because this is as much a data availability and quality problem as a modeling one, modelers could get more granular when more granular administrative or survey data exists. Where possible, modelers should prioritize subnational resolution and should advocate for, and partner with, data collection efforts capable of feeding finer-grained inputs into their models. This may mean more donor and government investment in data collection and more research efforts to triangulate administrative data to get more granular. This work should default to open-source data as much as possible, even if initially limited.

Instead of waiting for national governments to collect and share more granular data, modelers may also need to work more directly with local authorities to either generate data in a specific city (for example, via surveys) or to find creative, local solutions to access that data (for example, via housing data that might be held by city authorities). While this would lead to less generalizable findings and methodologies, if done in close partnership with local stakeholders, these types of modeling approaches could be particularly impactful.

Moving From “How Many” to “Who, Why, and When”

While some policymakers care about headline numbers, effective policymaking requires going beyond volume and knowing more about the profile of movers and the drivers behind migrants’ decisions. In addition, in order to target interventions in the most impactful and timely manner, some policymakers need to know not just the resulting numbers in 2030, but also the threshold or “trigger point” at which migration increases at a rate and scale above average.

Agent-based modeling approaches can answer many of these questions, but they are so locally specific and resource-intensive that they cannot be deployed everywhere. Researchers and practitioners should be more strategic in selecting where they invest in agent-based modeling: Evidence should be generated in places where the needs are greatest and where policymakers will use that data. And modelers may need to think through hybrid approaches that pair quantitative modeling with qualitative or survey-based methods, which are lighter-weight and more transferable than the current agent-based modeling method.

Integrating Emerging AI Methods

A layer of the field not addressed above is the growing use of machine learning. Humanitarian and academic actors have begun testing forecasting tools driven by artificial intelligence (AI). Such efforts include the Danish Refugee Council’s Foresight model approach, developed with IBM, which projects displacement one to three years into the future, and hybrid approaches that pair machine-learning conflict forecasts with agent-based displacement models. These efforts speak directly to the shorter-horizon planning gap described above. Evidence from the more mature field of AI-based weather and climate modeling, however, argues for caution rather than enthusiasm. Such models already outperform physics-based counterparts on many near-term forecasts, but they have so far failed to reproduce slower-moving climate dynamics that unfold over months and years—precisely the kind of variability that matters most for migration decisions. Machine learning tools are also often the least transparent instruments available, contrasting with the field’s need for outputs that policymakers can interpret and trust. Modelers exploring AI methods should treat them as approaches to test alongside, not automatically ahead of, the tools described above; and they should hold them to the same validation and interpretability standards proposed for the field as a whole.

Conclusion

The critique that has followed climate mobility modeling for three decades—that its numbers are too large, too confident, and too easily detached from their assumptions—has been productive. It has made the field more careful. But it has also set the terms of the conversation narrowly, treating the central problem as one of accuracy and prioritizing the fixing of methodologies over making modeling more usable. Evidenced by our interviews, accuracy is not what stands between these models and the decisions they might inform: Relevance is.

That distinction matters because the two problems have different solutions. A more accurate projection to 2050 does not help a municipal planner decide whether to permit development in a flood zone or a donor choose between livelihood support and early warning investment in the next funding round. What would help is a different set of outputs: shorter horizons; finer spatial resolution; disaggregation by age, income, and occupation; explicit representation of policy levers; and honest treatment of immobility as the more common outcome. And this points to a design, not accuracy, problem.

However, the task of bridging gaps does not belong to a single group. Modelers will need to not only innovate their methodologies but also listen more to policymakers’ needs—even when those needs are not easily answerable or raise difficult normative questions. Policymakers will need to work within their governments both to make their own data publicly available to feed into such models and to be clearer about what precise questions they need modelers to focus on. And instead of an ad-hoc, siloed effort, this will require researchers, policymakers, data providers, and donors to get much more collaborative—and funders to invest in such collaboration. The field does not need a single best model. It needs a portfolio of models, made public and accessible, with their limitations marked and policy use cases as their guiding light.

text:
GOTHENBURG, Sweden, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Minesto, leading ocean energy developer, has received the European Commission's STEP Seal (Strategic Technologies for Europe Platform) for its proposed Euro Dragon Farm project in Ireland. The recognition follows the project's recent selection by the European Commission to enter Grant Agreement Preparation (GAP) for funding of EUR 20.2 million under the EU Innovation Fund. It highlights the project's strategic relevance to Europe's ambitions for greater energy security, resilience and industrial competitiveness. In parallel, Minesto's CEO, Dr Martin Edlund, is speaking today at the European SET Plan Conference in Cork, Ireland.

The STEP Seal, also known as the Sovereignty Seal, is a European Commission quality label awarded to high-quality projects that contribute to the objectives of the EU's Strategic Technologies for Europe Platform (STEP). The Euro Dragon Farm received the STEP Seal following its evaluation under the EU Innovation Fund, where the project was selected for Grant Agreement Preparation.

The STEP Seal recognition underlines Euro Dragon Farm's alignment with Europe's efforts to strengthen its clean technology capabilities and industrial competitiveness. Beyond recognising the project's quality, the STEP Seal is designed to facilitate access to complementary public and private investment, creating further opportunities for projects advancing strategic technologies in Europe.

Minesto speaks at European SET Plan Conference in Ireland

Minesto's CEO, Dr Martin Edlund, is speaking today at the 20th Strategic Energy Technology Plan (SET Plan) Conference in Cork, Ireland, taking place on 4-5 November. The conference is co-organised by the European Commission, Ireland's Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment and the Irish EU Presidency.

The conference brings together European policymakers, industry leaders, investors and research stakeholders to discuss how Europe can accelerate the development and deployment of strategic energy technologies, strengthen industrial competitiveness and advance energy security.

Dr Martin Edlund will contribute to the session "Startups, scaleups and innovative companies in the clean energy technology domain", highlighting the role of innovative companies in bringing new clean energy technologies to market.

The typical first step would be to refer it to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
It will usher in a new kind of energy and climate politics.
From the moment he rode down the escalator 11 years ago, Donald Trump has defined himself by his climate change denial.
But doing so required everyone, liberals and progressives alike, to articulate more moderate views on energy and climate policy.
At least one former climate activist won on Tuesday by running against data centers and large-scale solar.
text:
Proponents of the bill view the election results as a clear endorsement of BAAJA. Energy bills were on the ballot, and “to reduce energy prices is to pass permitting reform,” Jason Grumet, the CEO of the American Clean Power Association, said during a call with reporters on Wednesday.

Jane Flegal, a senior fellow at the Searchlight Institute, argued on X that “most of the things” Democrats can do to address energy affordability at the federal level are in BAAJA, such as reforms to speed up the buildout of transmission lines, utility oversight, greater certainty for clean energy developers, and provisions to force data centers to cover their costs. “Dems shouldn’t wait on permitting. BAAJA is a good bill, and the filibuster and veto don’t go away in January,” she wrote. But the real reason not to wait, she added, is that if Democrats win the White House in 2028, they will need to “hit the ground running, especially on energy affordability,” and reform “takes years to implement.”

Joe Brazauskas, a partner at the government relations firm Bracewell, said during a post-election webinar on Wednesday that he’ll be watching for four indicators of how the permitting reform deal will fare in the coming days and weeks. First, will the senators who negotiated the deal come back with a major push for the bill?

So far, they don’t seem to be backing down from plans to put the package to a vote next Monday, November 9. “We don’t have more years to lose as clean energy projects sit on the sidelines, and there’s no guarantee Congress would ever find another compromise that would be able to pass the Senate,” Senator Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, one of the bill’s authors, told me in a statement. “Democrats ran and won on affordability, and this bill lowers costs for families and will allow us to start delivering on our election promises. It’s a bird in the hand. We’d be fools not to take it.”

Senator Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, the bill’s other Democrat author, provided similar comments to Politico. “We’ve been trying to pass permitting reform for the better part of a decade,” he said. “It doesn't necessarily get easier just because of who the chair is. This is the closest we have come to actually finding something that can get signed into law. I’m not going to wait.”

The second indicator is what Trump does next. Will he make any substantive wind farm approvals? Grumet said he doesn’t think the legislation will move forward unless a “significant number of those projects” being held up in the Department of Defense review process are released. With the Senate vote scheduled for Monday, the clock is ticking. Grumet was bullish that Trump would play ball, noting that “every interaction we’ve had with the administration affirms that they want to close this deal.”

There’s also the question of how hard the president will gun for the deal more generally. As I’ll explain, the bill could face steep hurdles with key Republicans in the House that may require the president’s cajoling to overcome. Several speakers in the Bracewell webinar suggested that Trump may want some legislative wins to cement his legacy. Whether that translates into a push in the lame duck, or a potential deal in the next Congress, remains to be seen.

The third indicator is whether and how the bill’s authors address the issues raised around tribal consultation and “project certainty” in an amendment before the vote. There are signs that these can be resolved. Before the election, Punchbowl News reported that the Coalition of Large Tribes, whose members control a large portion of tribal lands in the country, was negotiating to improve the bill with technical fixes rather than fighting it altogether. Several bill proponents also told me that fixes for project certainty were underway.

It’s still unclear, however, whether small technical fixes will be enough to rally more support for the bill in the House, or alternatively, if those changes turn out to be more substantive, whether they threaten the bill’s delicate bipartisan balance.

The last indicator is, will Democratic leadership support the bill? Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has not yet shared his views. “The Democrats’ performance was so overwhelming last night that the outside groups that talk to Democrats, the ENGOs, have to be emboldened,” Brazauskas said. “They have very strong views on the Clean Water Act provisions, the Endangered Species Act provisions, Judicial Review, and I really think that that will impact how that’s viewed by Democrats on the Hill.”

If the bill does pass the Senate next week, it faces an uncertain road in the House, and not just because of opponents like Huffman. Republican leadership will have to make a strategic choice about where to send it.

The typical first step would be to refer it to the House Energy and Commerce Committee. At least as of a few weeks ago, however, the committee chair, Representative Brett Guthrie of Kentucky, was looking for changes to the transmission section of the bill, which would have costly consequences for Southeast electric utilities, as it would support the construction of new interregional transmission lines that compete with their business models.

If House leadership wants to avoid Guthrie’s committee, they could send the bill to the House Rules Committee, which could tee it up for a simple majority vote. The Rules Committee is also controlled mostly by southern Republicans, however, who may have some of the same sympathies as Guthrie. This is where Trump’s commitment to getting the deal done would likely be crucial.

Another option is to move the bill through “suspension of the rules,” a procedural tactic that allows the House to consider legislation without a rule from the Rules Committee — although this would mean the bill would require a two-thirds majority to pass. It is typically reserved for bills with broad consensus, such as when Congress renames post offices.

One final potential pathway is to attach a Senate-passed version of the bill to must-pass legislation, such as a government funding package or the annual military authorization bill. Congress successfully enacted the Energy Act of 2020 by attaching it to a consolidated appropriations measure after Donald Trump lost the presidential election to Joe Biden. That bill was not as controversial as BAAJA, however, and so the approach may be too risky.

Hanging over all of this, and affecting how the numbers stack up for a vote, is another question the Democratic landslide has now raised. How many House Republicans will even show up for work in the lame duck?

But the newest result beggared belief: 75% of Americans now said they would oppose a data center in their town. Most would strongly oppose it. When was the last time, I thought, that 75% of Americans agreed about anything? Was this real?

Sure looks like it. As Michigan’s newest senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed said earlier this year: People really effing hate data centers. And they apparently really hate Donald Trump, too, and the Iran War, and higher gas prices.

On Tuesday night, Democrats … well, pick your synonym. They routed Republicans. Annihilated them. Crushed them, broke them, and heard the lamentations of their donors. Democrats captured at least 54 seats in the Senate and could take more than 260 seats in the House. The national House vote snapped more than 15 points in their favor, and key demographic groups whose preferences have defined the Trump era — such as Hispanics, young men, and white voters without a college degree — all swung in the double digits to Democrats.

For millennials like me, the wave elections par excellence have been 2006, when liberals took back Congress from a desperately unpopular George W. Bush, and 2010, when the Tea Party caroused against Barack Obama. This election was bigger than either, on par with the anti-Watergate tsunami of 1974 that shaped the Democratic Party for a generation and put a new class of professional-minded reformers at its helm. Unlike in 1974, though, the new Democratic majority will not rely on an old guard of state’s rights conservatives. The South turned indigo on Tuesday night, it’s true, but that was thanks to the normal politics of booming American cities and suburbs, not century-old polarization left over from the Civil War. This is a new kind of Democratic mega-majority.

It will usher in a new kind of energy and climate politics. From the moment he rode down the escalator 11 years ago, Donald Trump has defined himself by his climate change denial. His antipathy for decarbonization and clean energy reached new heights in his second term, as his administration waged a war on renewables and dismantled the government’s already-weak ability to regulate greenhouse gas pollution. At the same time, it embraced the artificial intelligence boom and gave some of the world’s wealthiest companies a blank check to pollute.

Now that is all over. Although Trump still has two years left in the White House, he will limp to 2029 without a pliant Congress, a supportive public, or an aura of invincibility. We should, to be sure, expect at least a few Cabinet resignations in the next few weeks, so the expiring GOP Senate can confirm their replacements; and federal agencies will still roll their regulatory agendas uphill in case the GOP wins the White House in 2028. Some Trump policies — like his nuclear plan — may even meet with Democratic approval. But the administration’s fossil fuel revolution is over. And everything that Trump has done on climate and energy since taking office, especially his family’s penetration of favored mining firms, will soon face scrutiny in the new year.

That will all be good for the fight against climate change. And yet it would be wrong to presume that this new era will look like the last one — or that these new congressional Democrats will be Green New Dealers or even ardent environmentalists. “We cannot change anything unless we accept it,” Jung wrote, and Democrats have finally overturned Trumpism in part by accepting its real force in American politics. I don’t mean their willingness to accept Trump’s conduct, to be clear: The No Kings rallies and the Minneapolis rebellion saw to that. But since Kamala Harris lost, Democrats have for the first time treated Trump as a normal Republican opponent — and their fight against him not as a “battle for the soul of the nation,” as President Biden liked to put it, but as a simple verdict on a powerful establishment politician.

That has meant learning from Trump, and from his energy and affordability politics in particular. Chief among those lessons: Voters really, really care about low prices; they especially really, really care about cheap energy; and they will reward politicians who share their concerns. Zohran Mamdani, Mikie Sherill, and Abigail Spanberger pioneered these appeals last year, playing down their respective climate goals and (in Sherill’s case) running on cheaper power bills. State and congressional Democrats in 2026 picked up that strategy and ran with it.

They had help. Inexplicably, Trump undercut his promises to start no new foreign wars and cut energy bills in half by launching a new Iran war that nearly doubled some energy prices. By one estimate, Americans have paid more than $100 billion in higher fuel costs since March. Trump’s compact with voters broke in that moment. Tuesday is the result.

Democrats know it. Look at Annie Andrews, for instance, the new Democratic senator from South Carolina (!). She wants to “suspend the gas tax, unleash American energy, and get gas prices down” — in other words, she seeks to cut taxes on fossil fuels. But Andrews also wants to restore the solar and wind tax credits and increase public transit spending. And she devotes an entire paragraph of her policy brochure to the need for bipartisan permitting reform.

What distinguishes Andrews isn’t her toughness on fossil fuels, but her opposition to data centers. She wants a two-year nationwide moratorium on the facilities, to end their tax breaks, and force them to stop passing on higher electricity costs to ratepayers. Almost every single Senate Democrat who won on Tuesday, in fact, promised to make data centers pay for their full cost of electricity service — it might be the caucus’s most unifying policy. (The bipartisan permitting bill, whose fate remains uncertain as of writing, would mandate it.)

Much like Andrews, this new class of congressional Democrats sought to embrace every kind of energy source except for coal. Senator-elect James Talarico, a Democrat of Texas — get used to saying that — promised voters that “we can add to our hundreds of thousands of oil, gas, wind, solar, and battery jobs by creating new jobs” in geothermal and hydrogen. Mary Peltola, who seems likely to clinch her Alaska Senate race, argued for oil and gas’s ongoing importance, too. Adam Hamilton of Kansas, Scott Colom of Mississippi, and Andrews of South Carolina all spoke of their “all of the above” energy policy. None of these candidates are climate deniers — they all want to restore the wind and solar tax credits, and many spoke of increasing climate resilience funding — but they all have vowed to grow the energy system, not revolutionize it. Even Abdul El-Sayed, who wrote a 2019 Guardian op-ed advocating for the Green New Deal, disavowed that policy and opposed a government EV mandate.

The new state-level Democrats will push the party even further in this direction. Had Talarico alone won in Texas, he might have been able to walk a careful line on fossil fuels, recognizing oil and gas as the status quo without seeking to expand their reach. But Gina Hinojosa will also be the state’s next governor, with a much more direct role in managing the Permian Basin. To keep her job, she will have to accept that Texans' livelihoods depend on oil and gas, in the same way that Mamdani has had to recognize the reality of Wall Street's centrality to the economy of New York City. Democrats will face tough trade-offs.

They also won’t be any more radical about the 10% of U.S. emissions that come from American agriculture. If the Democrat Scott Colom holds out and wins Mississippi’s senate seat, it will be in no small part thanks to a viral commercial chiding the Republican incumbent for telling voters to choose a cheaper protein than beef. “Pick another protein?” an everyman griller asked the camera. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

This is one reason why Tuesday’s victory might feel a smidge bittersweet for some climate defenders. Democrats have finally trounced Trumpism at the ballot box. Progressives like El-Sayed have shown they can win in battleground states, provided a favorable national environment, and moderates have stormed the heart of MAGA America.

But doing so required everyone, liberals and progressives alike, to articulate more moderate views on energy and climate policy. As recently as 2020, belief in the climate crisis unified the Biden coalition. Now, Democrats have tacitly accepted — as a price of winning big majorities — some cognitive dissonance between what they think the science says (that climate change is an urgent and worsening problem) and what domestic politics demands (that voters still care more about cheap energy).

In other words, more than just the Trump era ended on Tuesday. The old Obama dream finally died too. In the wake of the 2012 election, Democrats imagined a permanent progressive majority shorn of right-leaning white voters. That fantasy never materialized, and chasing it may have even led the party astray. Now they have built a new congressional coalition with energy moderates at its core.

Which is not to say that Democrats will give up on decarbonizing the economy. We can expect this new congressional class to expand clean energy, push for more transmission lines, and revive electric vehicle subsidies as a solution to high gas prices. Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, who won one of the night’s most convincing victories, repeatedly mentioned microplastics and “forever chemicals” in his speeches, linking the contamination of human bodies to the corruption of the body politic. The fight against conventional air and water pollution, I suspect, will come back big.

The next era of American climate politics, in other words, will look different from the last one. Fossil fuel companies have long been climate advocates’ primary foil. At the national level, data centers and Big Tech could eclipse them. At least one former climate activist won on Tuesday by running against data centers and large-scale solar. Artificial intelligence, after all, is the country’s fastest growing form of industrial energy use, and it creates far fewer jobs than a chip fab or steel mill. For these reasons, you can imagine a kind of reformed normie environmentalism with anti-AI characteristics taking root in the next administration. Perhaps it already has.

Decarbonizing the economy is steady and long-term work, “a slow boring of hard boards,” to quote the political thinker Max Weber, and the politicians who next turn the screws hardest may not sit on Capitol Hill. The historic size of Tuesday’s swell means Democrats won key state offices that they haven’t held in a generation — on public utility commissions, fossil fuel regulators, and in state legislatures. They will be eager to wield their powers. With its new Democratic trifecta, for instance, Pennsylvania could allow community solar, mandate battery storage, and restrict utility profits. Decades of low-hanging climate policy will soon be plucked.

Amid all of this excitement, Democrats should keep failure in mind — the president’s and their own. Since 2020, Democrats have tried to revolutionize the energy system, reindustrialize the country, and overhaul the economy without recognizing the existence of any trade-offs between those goals. They failed, and voters hated it. President Trump and Republicans tried to reinthrone fossil fuels, give birth to a “superior intelligence,” and otherwise bring back a gloomy spoof of the midcentury American economy — without accepting any trade-offs. They failed too, and as we learned last night, voters hated them even more than they hated Biden.

The United States really does need to get better at commercializing batteries and making electric vehicles; it really must cut pollution, lower energy prices, and significantly boost its electricity generation. Both parties have failed to make progress on those goals so far. Democrats have shown they can learn from Donald Trump’s mistakes. Now we’ll see if they can learn from their own, too.

Tesla shares fell over 3% on Wednesday while SpaceX shares fell 3.8%.

Before the election, several Congressional Democrats who will now be serving in the majority made it clear that their oversight powers across a number of domains would be turned on the Trump-supporting sometimes-trillionaire.

“We think the market fears Democrats will look to target Tesla, as Tesla CEO Elon Musk heavily campaigned for the Republican Party leading up to the election,” Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein wrote in a note to clients.

AI-related companies

But of course Elon Musk isn’t just a Trump-connected electric car and battery chief executive, he also runs an artificial intelligence model developer and “neocloud” (i.e. a builder and renter out of data centers for artificial intelligence) by the name of SpaceX (it also launches rockets).

Several other companies who rent out compute to AI developers saw their shares decline, including CoreWeave (down 10%) and Nebius (down over 6.5%), as Democrats who criticized data center developers won up and down the ballot, including at the state level in data-center-heavy states like Georgia, Texas, and Ohio.

The results imply “incrementally negative AI sentiment on greater expectations for data center restrictions,” Morgan Stanley equity strategists wrote in a note to clients.

“Any investors adding 10 or more GW of compute to SpaceX's SI business in 2027 may want to revise down. State pushback on terrestrial/atmospheric datacenters has a head of steam,” Morgan Stanley analyst Adam Jonas wrote in a note to clients.

Semiconductor companies Nvidia and Broadcom were also down around 3% and 2% respectively.

Firm power companies (including clean ones)

Of course those data centers are largely consumers of power, so as the data center industry got sick, the power industry caught a cold.

Companies that own fossil fuel and nuclear power plants were hit hard today. Shares of Vistra (which has a 44,000-megawatt power plant portfolio) were down almost 14%, Constellation (which owns and operates 21 nuclear reactors) was down 6% and Talen (which owns 14 power plants largely in the PJM region) fell 8.5%. GE Vernova, which has been riding the AI boom by selling gas turbines to power plant developers, was down over 9%.

“Laggards include anything that touches data centers,” Jefferies analyst Julien Dumoulin-Smith wrote in a note to clients. “Expect a difficult unwind day given the scale of the upset in the single biggest state for data center activity,” he wrote, referring to Texas.

And Fervo, the enhanced geothermal developer, really is being treated like a "normal" energy company: its shares were down 4.5%. X-Energy, the advanced nuclear developer, was also down almost 8.5%.

Utilities, especially one specific utility

The vertically integrated utility Southern Company was essentially on the ballot by way of its subsidiary Georgia Power in the Georgia Public Service Commission race and lost. Georgia Power represents about 60% of Southern’s earnings. “Southern Company remains the clearest commission-control risk after Democrats sweep Georgia’s two PSC seats,” Dumoulin Smith wrote.

Across the whole sector, newly elected governors and public utility commissioners could put pressure on the return on equity that utilities are allowed to earn on their investments.

“ROEs are one of the only things utility regulators have to reduce rates,” Rains told me.

Winners

Clean Energy

In the energy sector, the big winners were renewables. The S&P Global Clean Energy Transition Index was up over 3% today, while the Danish wind manufacturer Vestas was up almost 3%, while shares in Orsted, the Danish wind developer, were up around 5%. Domestic solar First Solar was up 5% while Sunrun, the solar installer, was up almost 1.5%.

“The blue wave improves the federal outlook for renewables, with Democratic leaders pledging to restore wind and solar tax credits if they regain congressional control,” Dumoulin-Smith wrote.

But the Democratic victory does not necessarily mean the end of the war on offshore wind, although it puts the industry’s defenders in a stronger position.

“While a positive development, we believe it is premature to call a renaissance in US offshore wind,” Morningstar analyst Tancrede Fulop wrote in a note to clients.

EV makers not named Tesla

Shares in Rivian were up almost 6%, while Lucid shares were up almost 12%, indicating bullishness for the larger EV sector as Democrats may be able to push for a return to subsidies for electric vehicles or harsher mileage standards while also putting pressure on Elon Musk personally.

The stock market as a whole

The market is up over 1.5%, likely thanks to oil prices dropping.

text:
A new car affordability crisis and punishing gas prices are driving an unprecedented number of used car buyers to consider going electric, and that increased demand without a corresponding increase in supply means these used EVs are flying off dealer lots.

Days on the lot. That’s dealer-speak for the average number of days a given vehicle typically sits in inventory before finding a buyer. That’s critically important to dealers, since the vehicles on their lots are commonly financed through something called floorplan credit, and every additional day a car spends on a dealer’s lot can mean another day of interest payments and another day closer to a curtailment. Days on the lot can be even more important to dealers when it comes to cars owned outright, as well, as the dealers can have significant cash tied up in vehicles they’ve purchased outright, and every day those cars sit is another day that money isn’t working for them elsewhere.

That’s what makes this month’s fastest-selling used EVs particularly interesting, because these used EVs aren’t just selling fast for electric vehicles – they’re selling fast, period.

Powered up, makin’ progress

Dealer news sources Automotive News and Cox Automotive report that the average new car spent 82 days on the lot in October, with a 75-day target being an industry-wide benchmark. At the same time, the Audi Q4 Sportback e-tron Quattro with its 258-mile EPA-estimated range is turning in just 29.8 days. (!)

Advertisement - scroll for more content

That Audi’s not alone. In a recently-released vehicle pricing study, iSeeCars reported that the Toyota BZ4x, Lexus RZ300e, Honda Prologue, and Borrás-family favorite Polestar 2 are all turning in an average of 35 days or less, with the BMW i4, iX, Kia EV6, and Chevrolet Equinox EV just a day or two behind.

“The results reveal a market where EVs are appreciating in average asking price much faster than other drivetrains, while also spending less time waiting for buyers,” said iSeeCars Executive Analyst Karl Brauer, who found that average transaction prices for EVs rose 9.8% last month as ICE-powered vehicles stayed steady, rising just 0.3%. “Hybrids are experiencing moderate improvements in price and selling speed, while gasoline-powered vehicles have seen their selling times increase,” he adds, “despite relatively stable prices.”

Used electric vehicles averaged a price of $32,533 in September 2026, up $2,896 from the $29,637 ATP recorded a year earlier.

text:
The company announced Thursday that it had raised $16.5 million in a Series A round that closed last month. The funding will help expand its electronic trading platform, which lets institutions buy and sell uranium while blockchain tracks ownership of the material held at a storage facility.

The round was led by Blockchain Capital, with participation from existing investors Portal Ventures and Christian Angermayer’s Apeiron Investment Group. The financing follows a $6.1 million seed round in 2025, backed by Framework Ventures. Uranium Digital declined to disclose its valuation following the latest funding round.

“The whole point of Uranium Digital is to build out the technical infrastructure to allow the trading [of] nuclear fuels, analogous to how the traditional financial world trades gold, oil, gas, etc.,” Uranium Digital CEO and cofounder Alex Dymala-Dolesky told Fortune.

There certainly appears to be growing demand for nuclear energy and the uranium that powers it. Last month, Amazon announced plans with reactor developer X-energy and electric utility company AEP to explore building 12 small modular reactors in Indiana to supply electricity to its data centers and the regional grid. Meta, meanwhile, struck a deal in January to help reactor developer Oklo build up to 1.2 gigawatts of nuclear capacity in Ohio, with initial power expected as early as 2030. And in August 2025, Google announced a similar partnership with Kairos Power and the Tennessee Valley Authority to bring a 50-megawatt nuclear plant online by 2030.

But those reactors will need uranium—a fuel that remains cumbersome to buy and sell because of the market’s antiquated trading system, according to Dymala-Dolesky.

An untapped market

Dymala-Dolesky came up with the idea for Uranium Digital while trading commodities at a New York hedge fund. With an economics degree and a stint at Canadian investment bank Canaccord, he had grown accustomed to buying and selling metals like copper and silver on a screen. He wanted to trade uranium the same way, but found no comparable option.

By 2024, he decided to quit his job to build the trading platform. He recruited Jack Rindner, a former Goldman Sachs senior analyst in corporate treasury, to be his cofounder, and the two launched Uranium Digital that same year. The company now has 11 employees across Canada, New York and Hong Kong.

Yuan Han Li, a partner at Blockchain Capital, was already an investor in uranium miners when he heard about Uranium Digital over coffee with a friend who worked at Portal Ventures, the startup’s lead pre-seed investor. She introduced him to Dymala-Dolesky.

When Li brought the company to his colleagues, their first reaction was surprise.

“Everyone was honestly pretty perplexed because people just didn’t realize how antiquated the uranium market really is,” he said.

As they dug deeper, they saw a business that could serve not just investors seeking exposure to uranium prices, but miners that wanted to lock in sale prices and utilities that needed to secure fuel.
