title: The US and the EU Bet on the Wrong Race in Zambia - German Marshall Fund
description:
From increasing domestic processing to extending bilateral critical mineral agreements, both are looking to de-risk.
The initial reflex in Washington and Brussels has been to read de-risking as a race against China for access.
Connecting Copper China, Zambia’s largest export market for refined copper, relies on mineral transport corridors.
While the EU signed a strategic partnership MoU with Zambia in 2023, its broader Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) targets 40% domestic processing by 2030.
President Hakainde Hichilema, re-elected in August after a first term that did little to ease the cost of living, campaigned on turning Zambia’s copper deposits into jobs and prosperity.
text:
Copper runs through everything the world's largest economies are racing to build over the coming decade, including electricity networks, electric vehicles, and data centers. The vulnerability of these inputs lies not in the mines but in the middle of the value chain. China absorbs around 60% of global unrefined copper and produces around 50% of its refined output, a share that is increasing. For the United States and the EU, this dependency risk has prompted protective measures. From increasing domestic processing to extending bilateral critical mineral agreements, both are looking to de-risk.

Zambia holds some of the world’s largest copper reserves, putting it at the center of the wider contest for access to African minerals to secure supply chains.

The initial reflex in Washington and Brussels has been to read de-risking as a race against China for access. Their strategies have therefore concentrated on the first link of the chain: extraction and the corridors that carry its output to the coast. Zambia shows why this misses the target. China’s leverage lies not in mining but in refining, the stage that turns concentrate into usable metal, and refining is precisely what Zambia lacks the capacity and power to expand. To reduce their dependence on Chinese refining, Western partners must recognize that their interests converge with Zambia’s. Lusaka wants to move beyond extraction and will favor partners that invest in refining and the stages beyond it. Those that fund only mines and railways risk financing supply chains that still run through China.

Connecting Copper

China, Zambia’s largest export market for refined copper, relies on mineral transport corridors. The main example is the TAZARA railway, which links landlocked Zambian mines to Tanzania’s Indian Ocean coast. China helped build the line in the 1970s after Western lenders refused to finance it. Chinese firms are now set to upgrade it for $1.4 billion, ensuring a steady flow of copper to Chinese refineries and manufacturing centers.

In reaction, Washington and Brussels placed their interests in the Lobito Corridor, a revived old colonial rail line linking the DRC to Angola, refurbished through a loan from the US government's development bank. A new 800km greenfield line to connect Zambia is planned, but unlikely to carry freight before 2030. Western leaders often brand the Lobito Corridor as a game-changing counterweight to China, but the facts on the ground tell a far less binary story of the corridor’s success in de-risking.

At the same time, the domestic policies of the United States and the EU focus on bringing mineral processing back within their borders or closer to home, which sidesteps the urgent need for deeper partnerships with African producers. While the EU signed a strategic partnership MoU with Zambia in 2023, its broader Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) targets 40% domestic processing by 2030. Most refined supply will thus come from non-European sources. Yet the Act suggests no public de-risking mechanism designed for refining in African countries. In the United States’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), clean energy incentives were scrapped, which ended the electric-vehicle tax credits that drove investment in the copper supply chain, weakening Washington’s own demand signal.

What Zambia Is Building

Zambia’s own priorities point to the stage the West is neglecting. President Hakainde Hichilema, re-elected in August after a first term that did little to ease the cost of living, campaigned on turning Zambia’s copper deposits into jobs and prosperity. Mining is central to the country’s economy, representing 72% of its total foreign export earnings and contributing 9% of GDP. Lusaka is therefore building policies to move beyond the raw-export model and capture more value from its resources at home. To keep processing in the country, it levies a 10% export duty on unrefined copper concentrate. However, in a sign of how thin refining capacity remains, the duty has been waived since August 2025 while domestic smelters undergo repairs.

Corridors fit into this strategy, but where most see a corridor as a route out for raw materials, Zambia sees the industrial base it can build along it. Lower transport costs ensure that mines with higher onsite processing demands are commercially competitive and connect regional initiatives. For example, Zambia and the DRC agreed to establish special economic zones for battery-precursor manufacturing along the Lobito railway, which could allow entry into a new section of the supply chain.

This logic is part of a continental wave of value-addition restrictions, including Zimbabwe’s pioneer raw mineral restrictions—which resulted in the country’s first domestic lithium sulphate exports this year. Washington and Brussels should recognize that this shift operates on a different layer from access. It decides where processing happens, not who reaches the mine. Zimbabwe’s lithium sulphate was produced domestically, but in a facility owned by China’s Huayou Cobalt. By aligning with domestic policy, Beijing kept its place in the chain, secured the partnership, and reinforced its dominance.

The Power in Processing

Rather than aligning with any single power, Lusaka is using intensifying great-power rivalry as leverage for its own growth. China holds a structural head start, built over decades of investment in Zambia’s mines, railways, and energy infrastructure, and through off-take agreements with non-Chinese mines. This is a strategy the EU and the United States cannot replicate due to time constraints and fundamentally different market models. They should instead differentiate their offer by backing the priorities of Zambia’s National Critical Minerals Strategy (NCMS) and the African Green Minerals Strategy (AGMS), which emphasize ownership, co-industrialization, and electrification.

Energy is the biggest operating cost in refining. Recent IEA findings state that it accounts for 44% percent of total production costs in Africa. While the NCMS sets out frameworks for Zambia to claim economic ownership of its resources, energy remains its main vulnerability. Recently, drought-induced load shedding forced domestic smelters to shut down, and industry estimates suggest that at least 2,000 megawatts of new generation are needed to meet the country’s output target. Zambia is thus looking for partners to end its energy deficits.

On top of energy partnerships, new partnerships should be built through market access clauses. To send clearer signals to private investors, both should extend friend-shoring through critical mineral agreements that define eligibility by stage of transformation rather than by mine of origin, so that African-processed materials, such as Zambian refined copper cathode or battery precursors from the planned special economic zones, count as eligible inputs. The US-Zambia minerals agreement now under negotiation is an immediate test. Granting this market access would connect Western de-risking with Zambia’s pursuit of autonomy and growth.

What Zambia Reveals

When Washington initially attempted to leverage a $1.5 billion health aid package to secure preferential access to critical minerals, Lusaka pushed back, insisting that humanitarian aid and mineral rights be decoupled. The ultimate signing of a standalone health deal with mineral negotiations moved to a separate economic track shows how critical minerals can be treated to capture economic growth. African producers are negotiating stage by stage, pricing each concession against their own industrial plans. Partners who invest in the stage a producer wants to reach next will gain supply security as a by-product. For Washington and Brussels, resource security and African value addition can meet not only at the mine, but further up the value chain.

title: Trump's veto could limit Democrats' energy policy changes | National | themountaineer.com
description: (The Center Square) - President Donald Trump’s energy dominance policies could face challenges after sweeping election victories by Democrats at both the state and national levels, energy market experts say.
text:
(The Center Square) - President Donald Trump’s energy dominance policies could face challenges after sweeping election victories by Democrats at both the state and national levels, energy market experts say.

When the new Congress is seated in January, incoming Democratic majorities are expected to push efforts to increase oversight of methane emissions, limit drilling on federal lands and in offshore areas, and tighten environmental permitting requirements on new plants and equipment.

Trump declared an energy emergency during his first hours in office in January 2025, invoking the National Emergencies Act to accelerate fossil fuel development. In a flurry of executive orders since then, the president has made U.S. energy dominance one of his primary economic objectives, framing it as a matter of national security.

Tom Pyle, president of the Washington-based American Energy Alliance , told The Center Square that attempts by newly elected Democratic majorities to roll back those executive actions will be neutralized by Trump’s veto pen.

"They can do Congressional Review Act resolutions on his rulemakings," Pyle said — referring to the fast-track legislative tool Congress can use to overturn federal rules adopted since the president took office. "They can pass them, but they’ll be vetoed."

Pyle noted that while a Democratic majority can leverage committee leadership positions to launch investigations and issue subpoenas, the president’s veto will still leave the Trump administration's core deregulatory agenda – and the sweeping legislative victories won through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed last year – largely intact.

“It’s one thing to make a bunch of campaign promises. It’s another thing to deliver on them," Pyle said. "Democrats will have a very difficult challenge if they intend to try to undo the very policies that President Trump has enacted that make it easier to produce energy, easier to move it around this country."

Pyle said election results at the state level are a reason to worry. “The story of the night is Texas — it really was a wipeout,” said Pyle. “Texas Democrats will need to tread very carefully because oil and gas is their bread and butter. It will be interesting to see how the Democrats in Texas treat the industry there,” said Pyle.

Ed Hirs, an energy fellow and energy economist at the University of Houston, said the Democrats' control of Congress will have little effect on U.S. energy production. He said it is global markets and prices — not Washington politics — that really drive American energy production.

America had energy dominance under President Biden, too, and had approached it during the Obama years, Hirs said. Now, with energy prices high because of geopolitical events, the nation’s oil and gas production is at a new record level, said Hirs.

“Trump has ensured the energy dominance of the United States, perhaps inadvertently, by undertaking this war against Iran,” Hirs told The Center Square. “We are now facing several years of having higher oil and LNG prices, which will benefit the United States, for sure.”

While gross national product will be higher, gasoline prices will be, too, said Hirs. “But prices are higher because of the war, not because of market conditions,” he said.

Hirs added that high global crude oil prices have begun to depress consumption in the United States. "U.S. consumption of crude and refined products dropped by more than 2% last year because of those higher prices,” said Hirs.

The Trump EPA is proud to approve this commonsense win for Maricopa County and businesses throughout the area,” said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin.
Through cooperative federalism, the Trump EPA worked with Maricopa County and Arizona to promote prosperity while fulfilling the agency’s core mission of protecting human health and the environment.
Background In October 2026, while in Maricopa County, Administrator Zeldin a second innovative air quality rule by Maricopa County, Rule 204, covering ERCs from nonroad engines.

text:
November 5, 2026

WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) took a historic step by approving a first-of-its-kind air quality rule that will enable the building and expansion of manufacturing, power plants, and other critical industries without increasing emissions in Maricopa County, Arizona. Known as “Rule 205,” Maricopa County’s Air Quality Department’s innovative air regulation will unlock a new source of emission reduction credits (ERCs) for businesses to offset emissions, as is required for the area under the Clean Air Act (CAA). By providing a new avenue for businesses to be able to build in the County, while still meeting federal air requirements, EPA is working in partnership with Maricopa County to bring new economic investment and good-paying jobs to the community. The final action proves once again that there does not have to be a binary choice between protecting the environment and growing the economy.

“When states, that know their economies and environment best, come up with a creative way to grow their economies while working within environmental requirements, EPA should work with them to get it across the finish line. The Trump EPA is proud to approve this commonsense win for Maricopa County and businesses throughout the area,” said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin. “EPA will continue to work with our regulatory partners to find ways to protect our environment while making sure regulations work under real world conditions.”

“Maricopa County has developed a practical, market-based tool that allows business to build and expand while keeping Clean Air Act protections in place,” said EPA Pacific Southwest Regional Administrator Mike Martucci. “EPA’s approval of Rule 205 reflects our commitment to working with local partners to support economic growth and protect health in Arizona.”

Portions of Maricopa County are currently designated as “Moderate” nonattainment for the 2015 Ozone National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS). As a result, major stationary sources, including power plants and manufacturing facilities, must obtain a preconstruction permit from the County and offset any increase in emissions, per the CAA, to build or expand in a nonattainment area. Today’s final action will allow mobile source owners and operators who permanently reduce nitrogen oxide or volatile organic compound emissions to trade those reductions as ERCs to stationary sources wishing to build or expand in the County’s nonattainment area. Historically, ERCs have only been generated and traded between stationary sources. However, EPA has found that this new plan meets statutory requirements under CAA section 173 and will enable the stationary sources to meet all CAA building requirements for an area in “Moderate” nonattainment for the 2015 Ozone NAAQS. EPA does not expect this rule to increase air emissions in the area.

The Trump EPA firmly believes its local and state regulatory partners are best positioned to understand the unique needs of their regions. Through this final action, Maricopa County and Arizona have worked within federal requirements to find a unique, market-based regulatory structure that meets the area’s economic and environmental needs. Through cooperative federalism, the Trump EPA worked with Maricopa County and Arizona to promote prosperity while fulfilling the agency’s core mission of protecting human health and the environment.

Read EPA’s final approval of Rule 205.

Background

In October 2026, while in Maricopa County, Administrator Zeldin a second innovative air quality rule by Maricopa County, Rule 204, covering ERCs from nonroad engines.

On March 23, 2026, EPA finalized a determination not to reclassify the Phoenix-Mesa area from “Moderate” to “Serious” nonattainment under the 2015 NAAQS. Consistent with CAA section 179B, EPA found that the Phoenix-Mesa area would have met federal ozone air quality standards by its August 3, 2024, deadline had it not been for emissions coming to the area from outside the United States.

Under the CAA, EPA established the 2015 Ozone NAAQS at 70 parts per billion.

name: Clean Energy
title: How Democrats used the midterms to turn affordability concerns into 'green populism'
description:
The election results may shake up negotiations in a controversial permitting reform bill that would clear the way for both clean energy and fossil fuel projects.
The incumbent Republican voted to phase out Biden-era clean energy tax credits, while Mendoza campaigned on investing in clean energy to save money for ratepayers.
Democrat Ed Markey, co-author of the Green New Deal, won his Senate race in Massachusetts.
Voters in Eugene, Oregon, passed a measure called the Eugene Clean Energy Fund that places a 2% fee on corporations like Amazon and Walmart and allocates those funds toward supporting renewable energy and clean energy jobs training.
It was based on the 2018 Portland Clean Energy Fund, which has invested $1.7bn in climate and clean energy in that Oregon city.
text:
Climate-forward Democrats swept into power Tuesday night as a blue tsunami flipped the Senate, House and several governors’ races. Voters were laser-focused on affordability, and experts said Democrats succeeded in linking cost-of-living concerns with rising energy prices, datacenters and, to some extent, the climate crisis. They may have even created a path for a “new climate politics”.

The results delivered a sharp rebuke of Donald Trump, who started a war with Iran that raised gas pump prices across the country and exposed the fragility of fossil fuels, all while the US oil industry earned $130bn in profits since the war began. Household energy costs soared, driven by various factors including constraints on renewables, climate disasters and a datacenter boom.

But how to articulate this before the election was a matter of debate among Democrats known for “climate forward” views: should they talk about the worsening climate crisis directly or keep messaging tight on affordability? Some senior figures including Gavin Newsom warned about “climate hushing”.

In the end, as one analysis on Wednesday put it, the results showed “candidates can win on green economic populism”.

Successful candidates “made connections between the cost of living crisis and the climate crisis, and how the same bad actors–such as utilities, oil companies, corporate landlords, and data center developers–are driving both”, said the analysis, by the thinktank Climate and Community Institute (CCI).

It found the candidates with the “strongest alignment with green economic populism won 39 of 56 (70 percent) of federal races for House and Senate in which they ran, including 6 of 7 in the Senate and 33 of 49 (67 percent) in the House”. The results show that “voters want leaders who will make life affordable and stand up for working people against elites, and climate is a critical part of that equation,” said Johanna Bozuwa, the CCI’s executive director.

While climate was not at the heart of this election, voters were focused on intersecting issues, said environmentalist and author Bill McKibben. “Energy prices played a significant role, and so did the war in Iran, and those are linked,” he said. “Those are both about the president’s strategy of oil dominance, which people are realizing is expensive folly … [The blue wave] was a rejection of this focus on oil as the way to power the future.”

Datacenters became a key focus of voters’ ire, he added: “There’s no question it was the biggest crossover issue to get Republicans, Democrats and independents going in the same direction.”

The debate about how to talk about the climate in elections will continue – but attention will shift to how Democrats use their success when the new Congress forms.

Holding power in the House and Senate will give Democrats the ability to launch investigations, and subpoena witnesses and documents. The representative Jared Huffman, the top Democrat on the House natural resources committee, has vowed to investigate big oil’s skyrocketing profits amid the war in Iran.

Climate-forward Democrats now have several avenues to push their agenda. Trump must compromise with Democrats to pass budgets, giving them the power to add climate provisions. Controlling the Senate means Democrats can prevent the appointments of anti-climate federal judges, cabinet officers and sub-cabinet positions.

The election results may shake up negotiations in a controversial permitting reform bill that would clear the way for both clean energy and fossil fuel projects. However, McKibben noted, as newly elected candidates won’t take their seats until January, the permitting bill could be pushed through at a 9 November Senate vote.

McKibben called on Democrats to use their leverage over the budget to restore funding to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and other agencies that have faced dire cuts to climate science. And, he said, big oil companies are pushing for legislation that would give them immunity from climate damages, and Democrats should “raise holy hell and do everything they can to stop it”.

Climate advocates elected to the House

A handful of climate advocates won House seats Tuesday night. In a tight race in Arizona’s sixth congressional district, Democrat JoAnna Mendoza declared victory against Republican congressman Juan Ciscomani. The incumbent Republican voted to phase out Biden-era clean energy tax credits, while Mendoza campaigned on investing in clean energy to save money for ratepayers. She also advocated for water security, including protecting groundwater and cleaning up Pfas in drinking water.

In another close race in the Central valley, Democrat Randy Villegas, a 31-year-old college professor, declared victory in California’s 22nd congressional district against Republican incumbent David Valadao. Villegas campaigned on an “all of the above” approach to energy, supporting oil and gas jobs while calling for more jobs in solar, geothermal and battery storage. The son of Mexican immigrants, Villegas supports stronger heat protections for farm workers as temperatures increase each year. When Trump entered office, he halted federal heat protections for outdoor workers.

Democrat Brad Lander, who has also pushed for heat protections for outdoor workers, won New York’s 10th congressional district, a reliably blue district. He opposed the controversial Northeast Supply Enhancement methane gas pipeline that governor Kathy Hochul revived under Trump.

Will Lawrence, a 36-year-old climate activist and co-founder of the youth-led environmental group the Sunrise Movement, declared victory in a purple congressional seat in Michigan after campaigning for state and federal moratoriums against hyperscale datacenters. However, he has recently expressed skepticism of large-scale clean energy projects, too. As Grist reported, his politics have shifted away from the Green New Deal, which advocated for a massive clean energy build-out, and toward a politics of community control over projects.

McKibben, who door-knocked for Lawrence all election, said it was “really remarkable” to see him come up through the climate movement and overcome $4m in Trump Pac-funded attack ads to win.

“Voters sent a clear message across the country: we are tired of politicians putting corporations over people,” Lawrence wrote in a statement. “We are going to stand up to the Trump administration that hands favors to polluters and Big Tech while rolling back climate protections. Voters are looking for leaders who will fight to protect our land, air, and water, and push clean energy that lowers bills and protects ratepayers. It’s the work I built my career on, and I’m ready to legislate on it in Congress.”

On Wednesday morning, Democrat Cait Conley was declared winner in the race for New York’s 17th district, a suburban battleground. Conley has called climate change a “national security crisis”, and has vowed to fight for federal investments in solar, wind and geothermal, and to pressure the Trump administration to rejoin the Paris climate agreement.

Senate seats swept by climate-forward Democrats

The blue wave brought climate advocates into Senate seats, too. In one of the fiercest battleground races in the country, Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan. El-Sayed supported the Green New Deal and has advocated moving toward 100% renewable energy. He expressed support for state and local datacenter moratoriums, and ran on a platform of affordability and taking money out of politics. He criticized his opponent for accepting past donations from big oil companies and DTE Energy, an unpopular investor-owned utility that has increased energy bills in Michigan.

In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown won his Senate race against Republican Jon Husted. Brown’s campaign focused on the expansion of datacenters across the state, which has the fourth-highest number of proposed and operational datacenters of any state. As Ohio’s lieutenant governor, Husted helped attract datacenters to the state with tax breaks. Brown ran ads calling Husted the “face of datacenters”, connecting his support for the industry to rising electric bills, which have gone up by 34% in Ohio since 2022. In a leaked memo in August, Republicans acknowledged: “More than any other thing in this race, datacenters are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”

James Talarico won Democrats their first Texas Senate seat in decades against Republican Ken Paxton. Once an outspoken climate advocate, Talarico has since moderated his position in the face of Republican attacks that claimed he was against the oil and gas industry. In 2022, Talarico said “fossil fuels are destroying the planet”, and in 2021, he introduced the Texas Climate Action act, which didn’t pass but would have established greenhouse gas reduction targets. Now he’s proposing an “all of the above” approach to energy that protects the fossil fuel industry while investing in renewables.

In North Carolina, Roy Cooper defeated former oil and gas lobbyist Michael Whatley to gain yet another Senate seat for the Democrats. When he was governor of the state, Cooper pushed for climate policies despite a Republican-controlled legislature that resisted his goals. This election cycle, Cooper tied Whatley to cost-of-living concerns by calling out his investments in Duke Energy, an investor-owned utility that had asked the North Carolina Utilities Commission to approve a rate hike before the election.

Democrat Ed Markey, co-author of the Green New Deal, won his Senate race in Massachusetts. The incumbent, who was favored to win, was one of the few national politicians to explicitly campaign on federal clean energy investments, green union job creation and climate accountability.

Meanwhile, the midterms were an expensive and unsuccessful excursion for Elon Musk, and for big oil and gas, as Emily Atkins of Heated reported, with the industry spending at least $182m to try to get Republicans elected.

Democrats swept a handful of governors’ races, giving them the chance to introduce climate policies at the state level. One of the fiercest climate advocates of the bunch, Deb Haaland, won the New Mexico governor’s race, becoming the country’s first female Native American governor. As interior secretary under Joe Biden, she integrated climate science and Indigenous knowledge into department policies and established a climate taskforce to accelerate renewable energy development on public lands. She was a supporter of the Green New Deal and opponent of the Keystone XL pipeline.

In a big upset, Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor’s race, replacing Republican Greg Abbott, the incumbent since 2015. After hundreds of people died in the 2021 polar vortex, Hinojosa advocated for a Texas climate plan that would reduce emissions and prevent climate disasters in the state, which has the highest carbon emissions in the country.

In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governor’s race, becoming the first Black woman governor in the country after campaigning on slowing down and reassessing datacenter expansion to ease utility bills. As mayor of Atlanta, she testified before Congress about the climate crisis and committed her city to achieving 100% clean energy by 2035.

Democrat Amy Acton won the Ohio governor’s race after a battle over datacenters and utility bills. Acton promised to place a conditional moratorium on datacenters, and to appoint Ohio public utilities commissioners who would focus on lowering consumer costs. In a purple state, she campaigned on an “all of the above” approach to energy, including nuclear, fossil fuels and solar, although she faces constraints to solar expansion due to the state’s restrictive law SB52.

Climate victories in utility races and ballot measures

Electricity bills were a major issue this election amid broader affordability concerns, and nine states held elections for state utility commissioners, who oversee energy bills and datacenters. Perhaps the most closely watched of these races was the Georgia public service commission, which flipped from Republican to Democratic control Tuesday night. Since 2022, the average Georgia power residential bill has gone up by $43 per month, or $516 per year, partly driven by datacenter growth.

Several climate-related ballot measures passed Tuesday night. Voters in Eugene, Oregon, passed a measure called the Eugene Clean Energy Fund that places a 2% fee on corporations like Amazon and Walmart and allocates those funds toward supporting renewable energy and clean energy jobs training. The measure is expected to generate at least $15m annually beginning no later than 2030. It was based on the 2018 Portland Clean Energy Fund, which has invested $1.7bn in climate and clean energy in that Oregon city.

In Michigan, a ballot measure supported by El-Sayed passed, prohibiting state-regulated electric and gas utilities like DTE Energy from making campaign contributions to candidates for office who oversee them. However, another ballot measure that aimed to replace investor-owned DTE with a public utility was narrowly defeated. The measure was part of a broader “public power” movement that aims to lower utility bills by replacing investor-owned utilities with public utilities.

text:
This article is part of a series about the 50th anniversary of the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act.

As more lithium-ion batteries and solar panels reach end of life each year, some recyclers are asking for new federal regulations to keep up with the proliferation of — or the possible dangers of — these emerging waste streams.

The U.S. EPA is considering updating the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act to establish distinct universal waste rules for solar panels and lithium-ion batteries. The goal is to offer more specific regulations for how to safely manage materials that are currently languishing in a regulatory grey area.

The EPA’s universal waste designation is meant to make collection and storage easier than what the process would be like under more strict hazardous waste rules. In general terms, handlers of universal wastes don’t need to meet the same regulatory and paperwork requirements as hazardous waste, such as providing a manifest or obtaining a certain permit. Universal wastes may also be stored for longer periods or at higher volumes.

Ubiquitous items like batteries, pesticides, lamps and mercury-containing equipment are managed as universal waste, and aerosol cans were most recently added in 2019.

Proponents say a specific universal waste designation for lithium-ion batteries and solar panels could make regulatory pathways more straightforward, which could in turn make recycling safer and help the industry collect more material, including critical minerals.

In 2023, EPA first announced it planned to introduce a draft rule encompassing both lithium batteries and solar panels, but that has not yet been published. The EPA’s unified agenda currently lists the estimated final rule date for August 2027.

EPA officials told participants at the Association of State and Territorial Solid Waste Management Officials’ annual meeting in Virginia last week that a draft rule was still in the works and might be published sometime in the spring for public comment.

“Our focus is getting the rulemaking out as fast as we can within our process,” said Kathy Lett, an EPA environmental protection specialist in the agency’s RCRA office, during the meeting.

Lithium-ion battery management rules versus reality

Relevant battery management regulations were made around 30 years ago, before lithium-ion batteries became common. The regulations were “mainly designed for lead-acid batteries,” said Eric Frederickson, vice president of operations at The Battery Network. “Those provisions are clearly not talking about lithium-ion batteries.”

Lithium-ion batteries can store high amounts of energy in a format that’s smaller and lighter than most other types. But these same qualities can make them dangerous to handle or store if not properly managed because of their risk of starting fires.

The EPA considers most end-of-life lithium-ion batteries to be hazardous waste, but unofficially allows these spent batteries to be managed under RCRA’s more general, streamlined universal waste rules.

However, EPA still expects those batteries to end up at a permitted hazardous waste recycler or permitted treatment, storage or disposal facility.

That position isn’t written into RCRA. Instead, it’s in a 12-page guidance memo written by EPA in 2023. In it, the agency says universal waste standards already cover batteries with lithium chemistries. It’s a document some recyclers and waste groups say is a stopgap measure in the absence of a specific RCRA regulation.

Robin Wiener, president of the Recycled Materials Association, said it’s common for EPA to issue memos, clarification letters and FAQ documents in response to questions from industries or associations.

She described this guidance as “relevant but nonbinding,” which is why the recycling industry typically seeks regulatory changes that have a more permanent effect. Such changes can also offer clearer guidance to states, she said.

So how are recyclers and collection programs currently handling end-of-life lithium-ion batteries?

“It’s a little bit all over the place,” said Kristyn Oldendorf, senior director of public policy at the Solid Waste Association of North America. SWANA, along with the National League of Cities and the U.S. Conference of Mayors, called for universal waste regulatory reform in a memo to the EPA in 2024. The National Waste & Recycling Association is also monitoring the EPA rulemaking process.

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Waste Dive free daily newsletter

Some of SWANA’s members include municipalities that host community collection events or manage a drop-off site. These municipalities typically aren’t responsible for transporting or recycling those batteries. But they often have questions about collection strategies, she said.

“I see a lot of different ways for how lithium-ion batteries are handled on site. Sometimes they’re manually taping the ends. Sometimes they have a specialized collection bucket. The labeling varies,” she said. “Everyone’s doing their best to safely handle the batteries, as far as storing them and how long they’re storing them. But it doesn’t seem like there’s really clear regulations on how to do that.”

Another grey area in current RCRA standards is how to manage the batteries once they’re collected.

Sometimes, damaged or broken batteries can still be handled as universal waste, but sometimes they must be managed as hazardous waste if there’s a “breach in an individual cell casing,” according to the EPA memo.

That puts the onus on recyclers and generators to assess batteries and pick whether they’ll send a load as universal waste or if they’ll follow the stricter hazardous waste regulations, Frederickson said.

Storage is also an ambiguous area of RCRA’s current universal waste regulations, according to members of ASTSWMO’s battery working group. That group supports the creation of lithium-ion-specific rules under RCRA’s universal waste rule.

Hazardous waste storage permitting under RCRA can be costly, so some recyclers and secondary handlers store spent batteries using universal waste handler provisions, which allow storage for one year.

Read More in Regulation

However, ASTSWMO believes these universal waste rules lack safety standards specific to lithium-ion batteries’ tendency to catch fire. There’s currently minimal regulatory safety oversight because universal waste rules aren’t written for that kind of fire danger, the group wrote in a July position paper, which was based on a survey of officials in 45 states.

“EPA should adopt universal waste regulations designed to minimize the threat of fires and the subsequent spread of fires at facilities that store lithium batteries,” the group wrote.

The group advocates for a few universal waste provisions that would require specific non-combustible storage containers and rules for how facilities are set up to handle fires. The group also proposes that handlers which accumulate lower quantities under the 11,000-pound threshold for universal waste should still notify regulators, allowing for inspectors to track whether their site may become a higher-risk location.

Oldendorf said the industry also hopes for rules that clarify responsibilities and add necessary safety features, but without also adding burdensome requirements for facilities that weren’t designed to store high volumes of batteries.

“A MRF is not designed to be accepting lithium-ion batteries, but they’re getting in there,” she said, and that means MRFs sometimes have to store batteries for a short period of time before they can be safely collected.

“We don’t want it to be so overly regulated that you now need to get a special permit and all the special equipment and everything when you don’t even want the batteries in the first place,” she said.

Clearer regulations for lithium-ion batteries under RCRA could also have the indirect benefit of reducing fire risk, Frederickson said.

Lithium-ion batteries are already responsible for numerous MRF and waste facility fires each year. A new universal waste rule wouldn’t eliminate that fire risk, Frederickson said, but it could help get batteries out of waste streams in the first place by offering clearer regulatory pathways.

Without specific end-of-life rules for lithium-ion batteries, regulators must take an ad-hoc approach to monitoring the transportation, storage and management of batteries on a state by state basis. Tailored federal rules could help establish a more level playing field for handlers and recyclers, ASTSWMO said.

This could also help encourage stronger collection networks that divert batteries away from MRFs while also spurring investment in recycling and other needed infrastructure, the organization said. ASTSWMO estimates only about 5% of lithium batteries in the U.S. are recycled.

“Without a clear regulatory framework, industry will not invest in this critical recycling infrastructure.”

Shedding light on solar panel recycling regulations

Meanwhile, solar panel recyclers are advocating for their own set of changes to RCRA. They say the existing law isn’t designed to handle the upcoming surge of solar panels approaching end of life.

The way solar panels are managed varies widely by whether they contain hazardous metals or not, as well as who’s considered the “generator” of the solar panel waste. Some types of solar panels can be managed using RCRA’s universal waste rules, but only if specific requirements are met.

Some proponents, including a coalition of power company groups and recycling organizatons like ASTSWMO and SWANA, want solar panels to be broadly managed under the universal waste category. They say the existing rules can be confusing and don’t match the reality of how solar panels are currently recycled.

Putting all solar panels under universal waste designation would also make collection and storage requirements more realistic and help support recyclers, they say.

EPA agreed to consider a possible universal waste standard for solar panels after a 2021 petition from a coalition of power and manufacturing groups called for regulations that better fit the needs of the industry.

Solar panels are generally considered hazardous waste under RCRA. If these end-of-life panels come from a commercial, industrial, or “utility-scale” source, they must be evaluated for toxic materials such as lead and cadmium. If those metals are present above a certain threshold, the panel is classified as hazardous waste and must be managed under RCRA Subtitle C. But if it passes the testing process, it can be considered non-hazardous solid waste.

Yet groups like ASTSWMO say the amount of hazardous materials could vary widely from panel to panel, even from the same model and manufacturer. That could mean testing every panel separately, a process some participants at the ASTSWMO annual meeting last week said was time-consuming and sometimes frustrating when a region has limited sources.

Designating solar panels as universal waste could remove or ease the requirement to test every batch prior to collection, thus speeding up the recycling process, proponents say.

Streamlined universal waste rules could also improve solar panel recycling systems in other ways, according to the petition from energy industry groups. It could allow solar panels to be stored for up to a year instead of the strict 90- to 180-day limits currently set by hazardous waste regulations, allowing recyclers to collect enough panels to coordinate bulk transports and make overall recycling volumes more economically viable.

Recyclers also hope better regulatory certainty will help spur more stable investments in the solar industry and reduce regulatory bottlenecks that can make it hard for existing recyclers to operate.

“A lack of an established recycling market for end-of-life solar panels means that a majority of these materials end up in municipal landfills,” SWANA and municipal groups wrote.

Power companies who sent the 2021 petition are also hoping more streamlined regulations could lower their costs.

States like California and Hawai’i already regulate solar panels as universal waste. Experts say this could provide some examples of how a federal universal waste category could look in practice. But these “patchwork” state rules also contribute to solar panels being regulated unevenly across the country, contributing to higher costs for some utilities and instability in the solar panel recycling industry, they said.

Looking ahead: critical minerals and federal bill influences

Proponents of RCRA updates for both batteries and solar panels say there’s a growing sense of urgency to modernize these rules.

Battery recyclers say fire incidents are growing more and more common. Solar panel recyclers say there’s a growing tide of solar panels expected to be retired soon, and regulatory uncertainty could drive more of these panels to landfills.

Some waste and recycling groups have urged EPA to work more quickly on a rule that the agency announced almost three years ago. State and local officials echoed that sense of urgency during ASTSWMO’s annual meeting last week.

Frustrations over the long wait for a draft rule have also prompted federal elected officials to step in.

Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, introduced the Battery Recycling for America’s Competitive Economy Act, which aims to compel the EPA to finalize rulemaking on lithium-ion batteries as a category of universal waste under RCRA within 18 months of the bill’s passage. It passed the House on Sept. 15.

Broader geopolitical factors could also influence the journey to update universal waste rules for lithium-ion batteries and solar panels due to the critical minerals these items contain.

The federal government in recent years has made it an economic and manufacturing priority to boost U.S. domestic supply chains for critical minerals used in electronics, batteries and magnets. That’s mainly because countries like China corner the market on certain minerals used to make those items.

That conversation has picked up speed recently due to tariffs and the war in Iran, which has strained supply chains for some industries. Those factors have also prompted lawmakers to introduce other legislation, including a bill to formalize a national critical minerals recovery strategy.

During a House hearing in July, Rep. Miller-Meeks said battery handlers and recyclers have “wrestled with a lack of clarity and confusion surrounding current regulations.” She argued that outdated RCRA rules “have made it harder for American recyclers to compete” with China in the critical minerals arena.

Clearer RCRA rules might help address efforts to divert more batteries for recycling and help boost recycling efforts, which could more efficiently feed the U.S. demand for critical minerals contained inside the batteries, Frederickson said. He described lithium-ions as an “incredibly rich secondary feedstock source” for critical materials.

Some generators are managing lithium-ion batteries as hazardous waste but not under universal waste rules, he said. The challenge with that pathway is that those batteries might end up being sent for hazardous waste incineration instead of being considered for recycling.

“At that point, the nickel, the cobalt, the manganese, the copper and the lithium are all removed from the critical material supply chain,” he said.

Solar panels are also considered to have a range of valuable materials including silver, tellurium and indium, “among other valuable materials,” according to the solar industry petition.

The EPA itself has drawn the connection between more straightforward recycling efforts and more robust critical minerals recycling, noting in its lithium-ion battery memo that safe recycling “conserves the critical minerals and other valuable materials that are used in batteries and is a more sustainable approach than disposal.”

Senior Visuals Editor Shaun Lucas and Managing Editor Cole Rosengren contributed to this story.

text:
PLANO, Texas -- The 2027 RAV4 remains Toyota's benchmark small SUV, offering a fully electrified lineup in a choice of HEV and PHEV powertrains, available FWD or AWD, and a broad range of grades tailored to different driving lifestyles. It continues the momentum of the sixth-generation model while adding two notable updates for the new model year: a revised suspension for the RAV4 Woodland grade, pushing ground clearance up to 9.1-inches, and the addition of a NACS port for all PHEV grades.

What's New

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 continues to deliver the breadth, efficiency, and capability that have made it a sales leader in the Toyota lineup, while adding thoughtful updates that enhance utility for the Woodland grade and charging convenience for PHEV customers. Updates for 2027 include:

Woodland receives new suspension components, including new springs, shocks, and jounce bumpers – giving it 9.1 inches of ground clearance

Woodland also receives redesigned all-weather floor and cargo mats

All PHEV grades now have a NACS port and DC fast charging (Level 3) capability

Charging port now located on left (driver's side) for all PHEV grades

Onboard AC charger (Level 1 and 2) is now 11-kW on all PHEV grades

All grades receive backup camera washer

AWD models – Receive Multi-Terrain Select with Rock & Dirt and Mud & Sand modes

Multi-Terrain Select replaces Trail mode

Snow mode now accessed via drive mode select switch alongside Normal, Eco, Sport, and Custom

Remote Connect trial increases from 1 year to 5 years for all grades

The 2027 RAV4 HEV models are expected to start arriving at Toyota dealerships across the United States later this year, with 2027 RAV4 PHEV models expected to start arriving in early 2027. Hybrid models have a starting Manufacturers Suggested Retail Price (MSRP) of $32,300 (LE FWD grade) and PHEV models have a starting MSRP of $42,100 (SE grade), excluding Delivery, Processing and Handling fee. Click here for the latest Toyota Pricing information.

Exterior

The 2027 RAV4 carries forward the all-new sixth-generation design with three distinct exterior themes: core, rugged, and sport. RAV4's exterior proportions emphasize SUV strength and utility, with a high ride height, large tires, upright rear cargo area, and the unique Toyota hammerhead front-end treatment. Sculpted body surfaces, chiseled fenders, and distinctive LED lighting help create a modern and confident appearance across the lineup.

Distinct styling cues differentiate between each grade.

The functional LE, XLE Premium, and Limited core grades feature a clean and refined look. Woodland models add rugged visual elements and outdoor-ready details.

The sporty SE and XSE grades bring darker exterior accents, more aggressive trim elements, and performance-inspired character. Available two-tone paint combinations and unique wheel treatments further distinguish the grades.

The RAV4 GR SPORT incorporates sport style with functional components, like a front lip and rear wing spoiler for balanced downforce; air ducts in the front grille and bumper to help channel air and reduce drag; offset wheels with performance tires for maximum grip; and drive battery placement that lowers its center of gravity and stabilizes the chassis. It also has one additional inch of overall width due to wider fender flares.

Interior

Inside, the 2027 RAV4 continues with a modern, functional cabin designed around comfort, flexibility, and technology. A clean center stack organizes major controls, while the center console maximizes usability with thoughtful storage and convenience features.

A 12.3-inch digital gauge cluster is standard across the lineup, providing a bright, customizable display with integrated multimedia information. Depending on grade, the cabin can also include Toyota's shift-by-wire system, SofTex®-trimmed heated and ventilated seats, wireless charging, and a JBL® Premium Audio system.

Cargo versatility remains a priority, with a rear seatback that folds flat on all grades to expand utility and an available hands-free power liftgate that helps ease access. Grade-specific materials, stitching, trim accents, and color treatments give each RAV4 trim their own personality.

Two Great Powertrain Choices – Hybrid or Plug-In Hybrid

The 2027 RAV4 remains a fully electrified lineup, with Toyota continuing to offer HEV and PHEV powertrains.

Hybrid models use Toyota's fifth-generation hybrid system with a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine and have 222 net combined horsepower on FWD models and 229 net combined horsepower on AWD models. The HEV lineup manufacturer-estimated fuel economy ratings are as follows:

PHEV models use Toyota's sixth-generation PHEV system with a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine that works in concert with electric motors and a high-capacity traction battery. PHEV models have electronic on-demand AWD, standard, and 321 total system horsepower.

An advantage of PHEV models is that they can give drivers the best of both worlds: pure electric driving for daily local trips and a gasoline engine backup for long road trips. For 2027, all RAV4 PHEV models will have a NACS charging port, helping to improve charging convenience and compatibility in North America.

The PHEV lineup city/highway/combined manufacturer-estimated fuel economy ratings and all-electric driving ranges are as follows:

Drivetrain and Handling

The 2027 RAV4 continues to ride on the Toyota New Global Architecture-K platform with chassis and suspension tuning intended to deliver a smooth, composed driving experience. To bolster handling, Toyota engineers focus on body rigidity, suspension components, braking control, and steering response for a RAV4 that is both easy and fun-to-drive. HEV-equipped models have a choice of either FWD or AWD, depending on grade. PHEV models continue to have standard AWD.

Toyota's AWD system is designed to enhance traction, stability, and cornering confidence by intelligently distributing driving force between the front and rear wheels as conditions change. It also has Multi-Terrain Select (MTS), an off-road driving system that automatically adjusts engine throttle, brake pressure, and traction control to match the specific surface on which you are driving.

The Woodland grade now benefits from a new suspension and increased ground clearance for added capability. GR SPORT continues as the most performance-focused grade, with GR-tuned suspension and steering, functional aerodynamics, and exclusive chassis tuning developed in partnership with TOYOTA GAZOO Racing.

Toyota Audio Multimedia System & Connected Technology

The system has six-speakers, standard, and supports wireless Apple CarPlay® and Android Auto™. A 12.9-inch touchscreen with JBL® Premium Audio system with 9-speakers, including subwoofer, and amplifier is standard on the Limited and available on the XSE grade.

Interior tech features include standard multiple USB-C ports, and available wireless Qi charging and 1500W AC outlet in the rear cargo area. In addition, the 2027 RAV4 includes a 12.3-inch digital gauge cluster with customizable settings, integrated multimedia information, speedometer, electric drive meters – like energy monitor and battery charge meter, drive mode indicators, charging information and more.

The 2027 RAV4 includes 5-year Connected Services trials for Safety Connect, Service Connect, and Remote Connect. It has a 30 day/Unlimited GB trial for Wi-Fi Connect. Additional services, such as Drive Connect*, are also available. Connected Services are 5G network dependent, visit Toyota Connected Services to learn more.

With an active Remote Connect trial or subscription, the XLE Premium, Woodland, XSE, and Limited grades are also Digital Key capable, which enables a smartphone to be used instead of a physical key and along with the Toyota app, owners can check charging status, start or stop charging, locate nearby charging stations and manage remote vehicle functions.

name: EPA
title: Can engineering solve the forever chemical problem? | Cornell Chronicle
description:
It’s what science can do to better understand the problem, and what engineering can do to solve it.
Faster solutions for a forever problem Industrial production of PFAS began to ramp up in the 1940s and continues today.
One of the best ways to solve the problem, Helbling said, is to limit the production and use of PFAS in the first place.
Helbling said the work illustrates how environmental engineering has become critical to helping tech industries grow responsibly.
Environmental engineering, however, offers the promise of better solutions.
text:
Among the technical inquiries spanning topics like cyclodextrin polymers and mass spectrometry that were stacked in Damian Helbling’s inbox was a question about four golden retrievers.

A local woman had contacted Helbling, a professor in Cornell’s School of Civil and Environmental Engineering and a leading researcher of trace organic chemicals in water, wanting to know if it was safe for her dogs to swim in a nearby pond.

“I also have a golden retriever that loves to swim and I absolutely sympathize with this question,” Helbling said, “but I hesitate to give a concrete answer when people ask me such specific questions about the safety of their water. As a researcher, I tend to look at the situation through a totally different lens.”

For Helbling, the question isn’t simply whether a pond is safe. It’s what science can do to better understand the problem, and what engineering can do to solve it.

Few contaminants illustrate that challenge better than PFAS, or per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, commonly known as “forever chemicals.” The family of synthetic chemicals includes thousands – and by some definitions, millions – of compounds used in products ranging from non-stick cookware and firefighting foams to medical devices and food packaging. Their defining characteristic is the incredibly strong bond between carbon and fluorine atoms, which makes them exceptionally durable but also remarkably difficult to break down in the environment.

That persistence has made PFAS a growing public health concern, with studies showing that exposure to some PFAS may be linked to a variety of harmful health effects. As policy makers reconsider drinking water standards and monitoring of industrial PFAS discharges, environmental engineers like Helbling are racing to better understand, detect and remove the chemicals from water supplies.

Faster solutions for a forever problem

Industrial production of PFAS began to ramp up in the 1940s and continues today. As a result, “forever chemicals” are found nearly everywhere – in water, air, soil and even in the blood of people and animals throughout the world, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

One of the best ways to solve the problem, Helbling said, is to limit the production and use of PFAS in the first place. He and his research group are helping advance that effort through “Faster Solutions for Forever Chemicals,” an IBM-led project funded by the National Science Foundation that is developing computational tools to help manufacturers identify PFAS in their supply chains and replace them with safer alternatives.

“Companies don’t necessarily know where or how they are using PFAS in the manufacturing processes,” Helbling said. “They just know that there is a product they can acquire from some supplier that helps them make their widget faster or better or more resilient. We are trying to help companies track down PFAS in their supply chains and discover new chemistries that can provide the same benefits while being less persistent in the environment and less toxic.”

That challenge is easier said than done. PFAS are widely used because they can resist heat, repel water and withstand harsh manufacturing conditions, among other properties. Replacing them requires understanding exactly what makes each PFAS useful for a particular application before designing a new molecule that delivers the same benefit.

Rather than synthesizing and testing thousands of potential replacements in the lab, the “Faster Solutions for Forever Chemicals” project is using IBM’s expertise in AI to screen candidate molecules and predict which candidates are most likely to deliver the desired performance and have the smallest impact on the environment.

The team also wants to avoid “regrettable substitutions” that replace one harmful chemical with another.

“That's why we’re using AI to answer questions like: Is this replacement molecule going to be persistent in the environment? Is it going to accumulate in organisms? Is it going to be a public health threat?” Helbling said. “Eliminating hazardous chemicals from manufacturing processes overnight isn’t realistic, but understanding where or how they are used and pursuing safer alternatives is essential.”

But what happens to the PFAS that still can’t be replaced?

Engineering molecular nano sponges

When safer alternatives aren’t yet possible, the problem changes. It’s no longer how to eliminate PFAS from manufacturing processes, it’s how to capture and destroy them before they enter the environment.

To do this, Helbling has spent the past decade designing specialized polymer materials that selectively capture PFAS from water. He describes them as molecular nano sponges.

“Imagine dropping a tiny sponge into a glass of contaminated water,” Helbling said. “Instead of soaking up the water itself, the sponge selectively attracts PFAS molecules. Remove the sponge, and the water is cleaner. That’s the idea that motivates this work.”

Behind that simple analogy lies sophisticated chemistry. The polymers contain molecular receptors engineered to recognize the unique features of fluorinated compounds. Because different industries use different kinds of PFAS, the materials must also be customizable.

Helbling compares the process to building a molecule with a set of Legos.

“We’ve learned how to remove certain functional groups from the polymers and put new ones on to tailor these materials for specific applications,” Helbling said. “We can look at a new PFAS and say, ‘I bet we need the Lego set to look like this for this situation.’”

The technology grew out of a long-running collaboration with polymer chemist Will Dichtel, formerly of Cornell and now at Northwestern University. Helbling and Dichtel are now commercializing the technology through a startup company and partnerships with other stakeholders.

Once concentrated inside the nano sponges, the chemicals can be destroyed using emerging chemical treatment methods. That approach is far more practical than trying to destroy PFAS dispersed throughout millions of gallons of water, Helbling said.

Of course, before PFAS can be removed they first have to be found. While most researchers focus on a relatively small number of well-studied compounds, many other PFAS have never been fully characterized – and in some cases, scientists don’t even know they exist.

The hunt for hidden PFAS

Every mystery starts with a clue.

For Helbling, the first clue to discovering a hidden PFAS often appears as an unexplained signal inside an acquisition from his high-resolution mass spectrometer. His lab uses the technology to analyze water samples without knowing beforehand which chemicals they contain. The resulting data becomes a molecular fingerprint of everything in the sample. From there, Helbling’s team uses computational tools to search for subtle patterns that point to previously unidentified PFAS.

“This is a really valuable technology, especially when you have new industries thinking about this problem and becoming more concerned about PFAS in their wastewater,” Helbling said. “We have helped industries quantify known PFAS in their wastewater emissions, and we have also helped them discover more exotic and unknown PFAS that are unique to their industry or even their company.”

The work has proven especially valuable for the semiconductor industry, where manufacturers often use proprietary fluorinated chemistries that aren’t included on standard monitoring lists. Through collaborations with the industry and Cornell’s NanoScale Science and Technology Facility, Helbling’s lab has characterized PFAS that are uniquely associated with semiconductor manufacturing processes such as photolithography and plasma etching. Their research was among the first to identify these compounds in semiconductor wastewater, and that work led Helbling to being selected as the 2023 recipient of the Sustainable Future Award from the Semiconductor Research Corporation.

While semiconductor manufacturing is not considered the primary source of PFAS contamination, the research is helping manufacturers identify opportunities to develop safer alternatives at a time when the United States is aggressively expanding domestic chip manufacturing.

Helbling said the work illustrates how environmental engineering has become critical to helping tech industries grow responsibly.

“The tech industry is aware of emerging concern and regulations on trace chemicals such as PFAS in their emissions,” Helbling said. “My industry partners tell me that they need environmental engineers to help them innovate in a responsible way. If a Cornell student wants to be in the tech industry but their passion is in the protection of fragile ecosystems or public health, environmental engineering is absolutely a way to do both.”

Following forever chemicals

If PFAS have a future, Helbling wants artificial intelligence to predict it.

AI has become one of his lab’s most powerful research tools, helping to forecast how forever chemicals will transform, travel and accumulate long before those processes unfold in the real world. By analyzing decades of scientific literature, machine learning models can predict how newly designed PFAS are likely to behave once they enter the environment.

“There are an uncountable number of PFAS that may exist in the environment, and many of them transform over time through natural environmental processes to end up as the relatively few PFAS that the Environmental Protection Agency is focused on regulating,” Helbling said. “We have developed tools to predict those transformations to forecast how the chemical composition of a contaminated site might evolve over years or decades.”

Another project uses AI to answer a different question: Whose PFAS are these anyway?

Supported by the U.S. Department of Defense, the research examines the chemical fingerprints left behind by different sources, including firefighting foams, landfills, wastewater treatment plants and industrial facilities. After training machine learning models on well-characterized samples, the models can predict where contamination originated.

“That information could help industries and regulators prioritize cleanup efforts and identify responsible sources,” Helbling said. “And these methods are transferable. They’re applicable to lots of environmental problems beyond PFAS.”

The lab is also using machine learning for the FLX PFAS Project, founded by Helbling and his students to collect and analyze water samples throughout New York’s Finger Lakes region. The results are then shared online with the public. As the project’s dataset grows, Helbling hopes researchers will soon be able to predict the likelihood that PFAS are present in any body of water in the Finger Lakes region.

Helbling knows people want certainty. They want to know whether the water is safe, whether their families are at risk and, sometimes, whether their dogs can go for a swim. Science can’t always provide simple answers to people. Environmental engineering, however, offers the promise of better solutions.

text:
(Reuters) – Big victories by Democrats in congressional races and beyond in midterm elections on Tuesday were a rebuke to President Donald Trump and will likely affect U.S. energy and environment policy in many ways.

Here are some of the issues that could be in play in the months ahead as Democrats take control of the Senate and House of Representatives in January.

PERMITTING BILL

U.S. lawmakers had been hoping to pass sweeping bipartisan legislation known as the permitting bill this year that would sharply reduce deadlines the government has to approve massive fossil and renewable energy projects. The Democratic wins could increase pressure from environmental groups, who say the bill has too many concessions for oil and gas, to push consideration of the bill into next year. TD Cowen cut its outlook for the bill’s success from about 40 percent to about 25 percent.

PRESSURE ON DATA CENTERS

Democrats seized on bipartisan opposition to the rapid buildout of AI data centers and voter anger at Big Tech companies. Across the country, 33 of 34 ballot initiatives aiming to restrict data center construction won the backing of voters. Some victorious Democrats supported pauses or rules on data center construction. There is now an increased likelihood of more oversight and scrutiny of AI risks, more protections for utility ratepayers, and stricter reporting requirements for energy consumption and pollution.

SOLAR, WIND SUBSIDIES

Some industry advocates see a possible path, either this year or in 2027, to extending or reviving tax credits for wind and solar projects that were eliminated or phased out under Trump’s 2025 tax and spending law. The effort could also include the extension of a clean energy manufacturing tax credit.

(Reporting by Valerie Volcovici and Nichola Groom; additional reporting by Jihoon Lee, Heejin Kim and Kyu-seok Shim in Seoul; writing by Timothy Gardner and Paul Simao)

text:
A flurry of recent major announcements show that utilities and companies including Google and Amazon are seeking to leverage nuclear uprates as part of a broader strategy to meet growing power supply needs.

Utilities have been using power uprates since the 1970s as a way to increase the power output of their nuclear plants, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission notes. Over the past 20 years, it has approved uprates that have given the nation’s electricity grid an additional six gigawatts, the equivalent of six large reactors.

“We’re aware the U.S. nuclear fleet is interested in requesting more uprates over the coming years that could mean another two gigawatts for the grid. We’re already looking at our past reviews to see how we can process these requests as efficiently as possible while maintaining safety,” it notes on its website.

On its website, NRC also provides details on Expected Applications for Power Uprates (by unit) and future Submittals of Applications (by unit).

DOE Initiative Aims to Increase Nuclear Power Output Through Uprates and Restarts

In March, the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Nuclear Energy detailed a new effort that will use existing nuclear energy infrastructure to put more power on the grid.

The Utility Power Reactor Incremental Scaling Effort (UPRISE) “strives to significantly expand the United States' nuclear energy capacity by increasing the power output of existing reactors, bringing dormant facilities back online, and completing stalled projects.”

UPRISE aims to make a significant contribution to the effort by targeting the most cost-effective and immediate methods to significantly increase nuclear energy capacity.

The initiative focuses on extending reactor lifespans through license renewals, boosting output via power uprates, restarting dormant facilities and optimizing operating plant efficiency with modern technologies including advanced fuel technologies.

The UPRISE initiative aims to achieve 2.5 GW of additional nuclear capacity by 2027 and 5 GW of total additional nuclear capacity by 2029.

Georgia Power and Google Agreement

In September of this year, Georgia Power and Google announced a new agreement under which Google will support uprates on Georgia Power’s owned portion of the nuclear units at Plants Vogtle and Hatch in Georgia that will allow the facilities to add approximately 96 megawatts of new capacity to the electric grid to serve Georgia Power customers. The agreement is subject to approval by the Georgia Public Service Commission (PSC).

Google’s subscription is expected to enable approximately $900 million in projected benefits to customers over the life of the units, Georgia Power said. The agreement is included in filings (Docket 44280, Docket 56002) made at the Georgia PSC. The filings also include a new Nuclear Uprate (NU-1) tariff structure as well as a request to approve a new extended power uprate (EPU) for Plant Hatch 1 & 2.

An EPU for Plant Vogtle 1 & 2 was previously approved by the Georgia PSC in the 2025 Integrated Resource Plan (IRP).

DOE Unveils Conditional Loan Commitment of Up to $4.2 Billion to Finance Uprates, Modernization

DOE's Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF) on Oct. 5 announced a conditional loan commitment of up to $4.2 billion to finance nuclear uprates and modernization across Vistra’s nuclear fleet in Pennsylvania and Ohio.

DOE said the projects will preserve nearly 4 gigawatts of reliable baseload power and add 433 megawatts (MW) of new nuclear capacity, helping meet growing electricity demand in Pennsylvania, Ohio, and across the PJM Interconnection region.

Vistra’s planned investments at Beaver Valley in Pennsylvania and Davis-Besse and Perry in Ohio will produce more electricity from existing nuclear plants without requiring new transmission corridors or equivalent new generation resources, while supporting the plants’ operation for an additional 20 years beyond their existing licenses, DOE noted.

EDF’s conditional loan commitment also includes an option to finance potential future uprates at Vistra’s Comanche Peak Nuclear Power Plant in Texas.

While this conditional commitment indicates DOE's intent to provide a loan, Vistra must satisfy certain technical, legal, environmental, and financial conditions before the Department enters into definitive financing documents and funds the loan, DOE said.

DOE Unveils Conditional Loan Commitment to Finance Uprates, Modernization at Constellation Energy Nuclear Plants

In late October, the DOE’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing announced a conditional loan commitment of up to $5 billion to finance nuclear uprates and modernization across Constellation Energy’s nuclear fleet in Illinois, Maryland, and Pennsylvania.

The modernization efforts will add nearly 1.1 gigawatts (GW) of electricity, "strengthening the grid and lowering costs for millions of Americans across the PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM) and Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) regions," DOE said.

Constellation’s planned investments at Braidwood, Byron, Clinton, Dresden, LaSalle, and Quad Cities in Illinois; Calvert Cliffs in Maryland; and Limerick in Pennsylvania "will produce more electricity from existing nuclear plants, maximizing America’s existing energy infrastructure while supporting growing demand for affordable, reliable, and secure power," DOE said.

EDF’s conditional loan commitment also includes an option to finance future uprate projects at additional Constellation facilities.

While this conditional commitment indicates DOE’s intent to provide a loan, Constellation must satisfy certain technical, legal, environmental, and financial conditions before the Department enters into definitive financing documents and funds the loan.

Google and Constellation Announce Agreement

Google and Constellation Energy on Oct. 6 announced a long-term strategic clean energy collaboration to bring 890 megawatts of new nuclear capacity onto the PJM Interconnection grid to meet growing demand and increase grid reliability.

The 20-year power purchase agreement will enable investments in new equipment and technology at 11 Constellation-owned nuclear units in Illinois, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey, increasing thermal and electrical efficiency to unlock additional reliable, firm power to serve the grid.

This capacity is entirely new, expanding total electricity generation available across the PJM footprint.

In addition to expanding nuclear generation, the companies entered into a 15-year energy supply agreement for an additional 2,700 MW in PJM's fleet. This financial structure ensures that Constellation's operating generation assets continue to deliver energy and capacity to the PJM market, the news release said.

The 890 MW of incremental capacity delivered through this collaboration equals the output of several Small Modular Reactors or a large new conventional reactor.

The initiative directly advances the goals of the federal government's UPRISE program, the news release noted.

Key elements of the comprehensive commercial agreement include:

• Direct supply expansion: Adding 890 MW of carbon-free capacity to the grid through targeted investments at multiple nuclear plants, with the first uprate expected to be delivered by 2028.

• Revenue certainty: Ensuring continued operations through a 2,700 MW, 15-year agreement that ensures existing assets remain economically viable without taking resources off of the grid.

• Demand flexibility integration: Incorporating operational load-shaping and demand-response capabilities to curtail non-critical power consumption during high-stress grid events.

• Economic and community investment: Sustaining high-skilled union maintenance, engineering, and operations employment across host communities in the Mid-Atlantic and Midwest. Across six nuclear sites in Illinois, Pennsylvania and New Jersey, the agreement helps sustain roughly 4,400 existing jobs, creates approximately 7,200 new construction jobs during the building period and represents more than $4.3 billion of new investment by Constellation.

Energy Northwest, BPA Unveil Plan to Boost Nuclear Plant’s Output

Public power entities are also pursuing nuclear uprates.

In 2025, the Bonneville Power Administration approved implementation of an Extended Power Uprate project that increases the output of Energy Northwest’s Columbia Generating Station, which is the Pacific Northwest’s third largest generating resource and only operating nuclear energy plant.

The EPU is an approximately $700 million project that will increase the station's electrical output by 162 megawatts by 2031.

Following 18 months of in-depth analysis, BPA's approval allowed the project to move into its next phase.

Energy Northwest and BPA will collaborate on planning and implementation. Once completed, the additional 162 megawatts of firm capacity could power approximately 125,000 homes, strengthening the Pacific Northwest's energy portfolio.

Columbia Generating Station, a 1,207-megawatt nuclear energy facility near Richland, Washington, is owned and operated by Energy Northwest.

The EPU will increase electrical output by upgrading and replacing equipment — including turbines, heat exchangers, and the generator — while maintaining high safety standards and improving reliability. Nuclear energy facilities have successfully implemented uprates since the 1970s to boost clean energy generation from existing plants.

The project will involve approximately 30 individual upgrades, primarily focused on increasing the size of pumps and motors. These enhancements coincide with biennial refueling outages, creating new job opportunities for skilled workers.

Additionally, 24 megawatts of energy-efficiency upgrades will be incorporated during the next three refueling outages in 2027, 2029 and 2031, bringing the total increase to 186 megawatts. This expanded capacity will be added to BPA's federal system power, serving consumer-owned utilities across six Northwest states.
