title: AI Data Centers Are Fueling a Nuclear Comeback
description:
It led to the closure of most of Germany’s nuclear plants, and nuclear power once again appeared to be in retreat.
As 2026 draws to a close, the question is whether this latest attempt to revive nuclear energy is gaining real traction.
According to Burt, the advantages of nuclear energy include operational reliability, zero emissions, and insulation from fuel price volatility.
IIR is tracking more than 100 nuclear energy projects across North America.
Google is working with NextEra Energy Resources to restart the Duane Arnold Energy Center, which was shuttered in 2020.
text:
There was supposed to be a nuclear renaissance in the early 2000s. Then the Fukushima disaster in Japan halted that momentum. It led to the closure of most of Germany’s nuclear plants, and nuclear power once again appeared to be in retreat.

Today, the urgent need for more electricity to support AI data centers is giving the sector fresh impetus. Data Center Knowledge covered the trend in February. As 2026 draws to a close, the question is whether this latest attempt to revive nuclear energy is gaining real traction.

“Investment is rising for new and existing nuclear assets amid a sector revival,” said Britt Burt, an analyst at research firm Industrial Info Resource (IIR).

After years of almost no new construction investment, the nuclear spark reignited in 2024. IIR estimates that spending on new projects will total about $20 billion in 2026 and rise to nearly $50 billion by 2029. That growth is being driven not only by surging data center construction, but also by broader increases in electricity demand, the expansion of domestic manufacturing, and the need to replace aging power fleets.

Between late 2026 and 2029, IIR expects $68.3 billion in new nuclear plant spending and around $30 billion more for the expansion, maintenance, or revamp of existing facilities. A large share of that spending is expected to land in Canada, with Ontario and Alberta accounting for roughly $40 billion combined. Texas is next with $15 billion, followed by Tennessee at $10 billion.

According to Burt, the advantages of nuclear energy include operational reliability, zero emissions, and insulation from fuel price volatility. It also creates opportunities for behind-the-meter power. The challenges, however, remain formidable: massive capital costs, public opposition, potential fuel bottlenecks for advanced reactors, and a nuclear workforce that has largely aged out.

IIR is tracking more than 100 nuclear energy projects across North America. Sixty-one involve small modular reactors (SMRs), and 11 involve installing new conventional nuclear reactors. Additional projects include life extensions, modernizations, relicensing, and uprates to existing plants, as well as several efforts to restart retired nuclear assets to supply data centers.

“This signals a genuine nuclear energy revival after decades of stagnation,” Burt said.

Federal Support and Hyperscaler Deals Build Momentum

The US Department of Energy recently offered Constellation Energy a loan of up to $5 billion to finance nuclear uprates and modernization at eight plants in Illinois, Maryland, and Pennsylvania. The work could add more than 1 GW to the grid. Earlier this year, the DOE also launched a program with funding support for 2.5 GW of additional nuclear capacity by 2027 and 5 GW by 2029.

Rather than waiting until the next decade for new nuclear assets to come online, the goal is to expand output from existing reactors, reopen dormant facilities, and extend the lives of older plants.

Meanwhile, hyperscalers are lending their financial muscle to a variety of nuclear projects. Amazon is working with American Electric Power and X-energy on a 1 GW SMR project in Indiana. Microsoft has a 20-year power purchase agreement with Constellation Energy for power from the refurbished Three Mile Island plant in Pennsylvania, now known as the Crane Clean Energy Center. Google is working with NextEra Energy Resources to restart the Duane Arnold Energy Center, which was shuttered in 2020.

SMRs, Restarts, and Fusion Expand Nuclear’s Role

Multiple types of nuclear initiatives are now underway. In addition to restarting or refurbishing older plants and developing new SMR designs, nuclear fusion is drawing greater attention.

Bellevue, Washington-based ExoFusion is among the companies focused on fusion design, simulation, and innovation. At the Data Center World Power conference in late September 2026, ExoFusion CEO Romi Mahajan outlined an energy stack built from multiple generation technologies. Rather than treating renewables, natural gas, and nuclear as competing alternatives, he argued that all of them will play a part in tomorrow’s energy mix and in providing reliable power for data centers and AI workloads. That view aligns with the approach many hyperscale developers are taking as they pursue every available avenue to secure the power they need.

Far from being purely theoretical, fusion is moving forward along the development timeline. Type One Energy, based in Knoxville, Tennessee, plans to start construction of a fusion power plant at the Tennessee Valley Authority’s Bull Run Energy Complex in Clinton, Tennessee, in 2027.

“The prototype’s purpose is to validate assumptions, advance open science, and [help] train a workforce rather than solve immediate data center power needs,” said Patrick Ellis, director of business development at Type One Energy.

Some of Type One Energy’s design elements are already operating at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and at Germany’s Wendelstein 7-X project.

Even so, it may still be years before fusion produces large-scale commercial plants.

Matthias Knolker, head technical solutions architect at General Atomics Magnetic Fusion Energy, said grid-connected commercial fusion demonstration plants and power purchase agreements may not emerge until the mid-2030s. GW-scale deployments, he said, may have to wait until the early 2040s.

While fusion research and development continues, SMRs and the rejuvenation of old nuclear plants are more likely to bear fruit on a timeline that matters to data center operators. The first operating SMRs may be only a couple of years away.

“US progress on SMRs is gaining momentum, but regulatory, financing, and workforce barriers remain,” Knolker said.

Cameron Hughes, an associate at law firm Orrick, said nuclear energy will need an all-of-the-above approach that advances traditional large reactors, SMRs, plant restarts, and power uprates. The market, she said, will decide which forms of nuclear energy prove most viable. On the regulatory front, she pointed to progress in reducing long delays, including long Nuclear Regulatory Commission review timelines.

“Recent reforms have cut key reviews to roughly 18 months,” Hughes said. “Additionally, modularization, factory fabrication, and supply chain improvements could compress deployment schedules once initial commercial projects are built.”

The Big Question: Can Nuclear Deliver Fast Enough?

Nuclear energy is clearly advancing on multiple fronts. It is drawing more funding, scientific support, and entrepreneurial interest than it has in decades. Whether that momentum will translate into enough timely capacity to serve the urgent power needs of AI data centers remains an open question.

“The nuclear renaissance is dependent on aligning many factors – science, engineering, capital, political will, and a skilled workforce,” Mahajan said.

text:
The Andersons Inc. today announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Harvestone Low Carbon Partners (HLCP), an industry leader in low-carbon ethanol that owns and operates three ethanol production facilities in North Dakota and Indiana from Energy Capital Partners, for $915 million. Approximately half of the purchase price is attributed to expected 45Z and 45Q tax credit cash flows, with the remainder to the underlying base ethanol operations and additional low-carbon opportunities. Upon closing, The Andersons' (the Company) combined ethanol production platform will have approximately 730 million gallons of annual capacity. The purchase price includes a normalized level of working capital. The transaction is subject to customary adjustments and closing conditions.

HLCP has a demonstrated track record of innovation in renewable fuels, including the development and commercialization of vertically integrated carbon capture and sequestration (CCS) capabilities. Its facilities are strategically positioned to serve low-carbon fuel markets, supported by established customer relationships. Its operating CCS infrastructure reduces the carbon intensity of ethanol production and enables the business to capture value through low-carbon fuel markets and applicable tax incentives, with additional benefits anticipated from projects under development.

"Our Renewables strategy is centered on expanding our low-carbon production platform through disciplined investments and capturing the growing value of renewable fuels," said Bill Krueger, president and CEO of The Andersons. "We have been evaluating ethanol plant acquisition opportunities for several years, and HLCP is exactly what we have been looking for. Its production economics, established low-carbon ethanol capabilities, and strategically advantaged locations complement our existing network and together represent a combination that is difficult to replicate. We believe this acquisition strengthens our Renewables business and creates a differentiated platform for profitable growth and attractive long-term returns for our shareholders. We look forward to welcoming the HLCP team to The Andersons."

title: A new bill could change how the US builds energy infrastructure | MIT Technology Review
description:
A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US.
The key question is whether this will cut greenhouse-gas emissions from the US energy sector or push them higher still.
Clean energy groups like the American Clean Power Association have largely come out in favor of the bill too, with the group’s analysis finding that it could unlock 350 gigawatts of new clean energy for the grid.
But any deal would ultimately need to win Trump’s signature, limiting what a future bill might be able to change.
In a world where permitting new projects is easier, we’ll see more clean energy, but we’ll see more natural gas, too.
text:
A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US.

With the dust barely settled on this week’s momentous midterms, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on November 9. It’s a plan that could finally start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved, as part of something called permitting reform. People on both sides of the political aisle have been pushing for this type of change for some years.

The key question is whether this will cut greenhouse-gas emissions from the US energy sector or push them higher still.

The federal permitting system is designed to protect the environment against industrial pollution from large projects like power plants, transmission lines, and natural-gas pipelines. Today, permitting is governed by a range of laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act. And if there’s one thing you might know about the current state of permitting in the US it’s that it’s slow and incredibly complicated.

So in its 417 pages, BAAJA attempts to tighten things up. The bill has provisions that narrow the sorts of projects that need to apply for federal permits and others that enact deadlines in hopes of speeding up a process that today can take years. (There are also specific provisions about transmission planning, mining, and the rest of the kitchen sink; this thing is dense.)

One thing to know about this bill is that it’s largely technology neutral: It opens the doors for the buildout of projects involving both fossil fuels and renewables. So there’s a weird mishmash of legislators and outside groups supporting it.

The bill’s four sponsors in the Senate are two Republicans and two Democrats. The White House has backed this permitting reform bill, with its Council of Economic Advisors finding that it would reduce review times and have economic benefits like boosting GDP.

Clean energy groups like the American Clean Power Association have largely come out in favor of the bill too, with the group’s analysis finding that it could unlock 350 gigawatts of new clean energy for the grid.

Some environmental groups, however, oppose the bill, or parts of it. An assessment from the Natural Resources Defense Council says the parts about transmission could have substantial benefits for the grid, but the narrowing of environmental reviews could be damaging for public and private lands.

Many in the climate world have long been calling for permitting reform, arguing that renewables stand to benefit more than fossil fuels. The thinking is that solar and wind power are some of the cheapest sources available today, so if we unlock the ability to build more energy, they are likely to win out economically.

A few early analyses have tried to quantify just what BAAJA would mean for emissions in the US. One, from the think tank Rhodium Group, found that in the best-case scenario, the bill would cut economy-wide emissions by 4%, reduce annual energy bills by $78 per household, and add 200 gigawatts of new clean energy by 2040. In the worst case, emissions would stay about the same.

Another report, from the nonprofit research group Resources for the Future, found that the bill could cut power-sector emissions 6% by 2041 and save more than $350 billion on system costs by midcentury.

But there are some concerns that this permitting bill’s real effect would be to open the floodgates for new natural-gas plants. As data centers have put more pressure on the grid, a wave of such plants have been announced.

“You get down to a trade-off between essentially growing the clean electricity industry on the one hand and then, as a compromise, growing the fossil-fuel industry on the other,” says Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

To quantify that trade-off, Kircher also modeled the potential emissions effects of the bill and found that if BAAJA had been in place in 2025, energy sector emissions would have been higher than the actual baseline. Health and mortality risks associated with air pollution would also have increased.

This bill is scheduled for a Senate vote on November 9, well before the next Congress takes control. It’s not clear what the dramatic victories for Democrats might mean for the legislation, which was expected to pass the Senate with largely Republican support if a few Democrats got on board. Democrats could decide to wait for next year, when they’ll have control of both chambers. But any deal would ultimately need to win Trump’s signature, limiting what a future bill might be able to change.

In a world where permitting new projects is easier, we’ll see more clean energy, but we’ll see more natural gas, too. And while prices could get lower, that could push demand for electricity higher, leading to more emissions overall.

Simplifying the permitting system and cutting red tape is a worthy goal. But when it comes to emissions, it still really matters what, exactly, you want to build.

title: OEMs, Dealers Balance Stock as Hybrid Demand Dominates Mexico
description:
While North American industry roadmaps once anticipated an accelerated transition directly into battery electric vehicles (BEVs), distribution data from Mexican showrooms indicates a multi-tiered adoption curve.
Plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) expanded 207% to 15,464 units, while fully electric models totaled 13,768 units.
The Charging Deficit and Consumer Preference Tracking Consumer feedback tracked across dealership networks mirrors findings from major institutional automotive surveys.
Routine maintenance on pure battery electric vehicles generates an estimated 30% to 40% less revenue than equivalent ICE or hybrid services due to fewer mechanical moving parts, fluids, and wear items.
Franchised dealers, who rely heavily on service bays for gross profit, are using this data to push OEMs for broader hybrid allocations.
text:
Automotive original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and national dealership networks in Mexico are overhaul­ing commercial inventory forecasting, deploying granular dealer management analytics, regional allocation models, and multi-powertrain showroom strategies to navigate an uneven consumer shift away from pure internal combustion toward electrification.

While North American industry roadmaps once anticipated an accelerated transition directly into battery electric vehicles (BEVs), distribution data from Mexican showrooms indicates a multi-tiered adoption curve. According to domestic market data compiled by the Mexican Association of Automotive Distributors (AMDA) and the Mexican Automotive Industry Association (AMIA), and reported byMexico Business News, electrified vehicle sales reached 95,037 units during the first half of 2026, up 44% year-over-year.

However, standard internal combustion engine (ICE) models continue to represent the vast majority of mainstream automotive retail, while standard hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) dominate low-emission deliveries, claiming 65,805 units during the first six months of the year. Plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) expanded 207% to 15,464 units, while fully electric models totaled 13,768 units. This pronounced disparity has prompted OEM corporate planning offices and independent dealer groups to replace generalized nationwide sales projections with localized monitoring protocols.

Real-Time DMS Integration and Regional Turn Rates

Dealership groups in Mexico’s top metropolitan hubs—principally Mexico City, Guadalajara, and Monterrey—are leveraging modernized Dealer Management Systems (DMS) integrated directly with OEM supply chain portals. These systems track showroom "days-of-supply" metrics broken down strictly by propulsion architecture: ICE, HEV, PHEV, and BEV.

Showroom data indicates that traditional ICE passenger sedans, light commercial vans, and pickup trucks maintain standard inventory turns, cycling off dealership lots within 25 to 35 days. By comparison, high-ticket battery electric SUVs without dedicated fast-charging ecosystems often experience inventory holding cycles exceeding 70 days. Dealerships bear financing costs on floorplanned vehicles, making slow-moving EV stock an immediate threat to operational margins.

To mitigate this financial risk, automakers are utilizing geographic allocation strategies. As highlighted by MBN, 55.7% of all low-emission vehicle sales are concentrated in just four states: Mexico City (21,766 units), the State of Mexico (12,736 units), Nuevo Leon (9,947 units), and Jalisco (8,513 units).

In response, OEMs are concentrating their HEV and PHEV shipments into central metropolitan dealerships where environmental incentives—such as exemption from the capital’s Hoy No Circula driving restrictions and verification tax waivers—create genuine consumer pull. Conversely, distributors across northern industrial hubs and agricultural centers in the Bajio receive heavier allocations of traditional gasoline and diesel utility vehicles, where highway range and heavy payload capacities keep combustion demand resilient.

The Charging Deficit and Consumer Preference Tracking

Consumer feedback tracked across dealership networks mirrors findings from major institutional automotive surveys. According to findings from the EY Mobility Consumer Index, approximately 60% of Mexican consumers still intend to purchase conventional ICE vehicles, while only 23% intend to acquire a pure BEV.

Electric vehicles require specialized diagnostics, high-voltage handling, and new maintenance protocols, yet many independent and dealer workshops continue to rely on tools and expertise designed for combustion engines.

Beyond charging deficits, dealership associations monitor service absorption rates closely. Routine maintenance on pure battery electric vehicles generates an estimated 30% to 40% less revenue than equivalent ICE or hybrid services due to fewer mechanical moving parts, fluids, and wear items. Franchised dealers, who rely heavily on service bays for gross profit, are using this data to push OEMs for broader hybrid allocations.

This consumer and dealer preference for bridge powertrains is reinforced by the J.D. Power Mexico APEAL Study, which reported that hybrid powertrains score the highest levels of customer satisfaction and emotional appeal in Mexico, providing improved fuel economy without requiring access to non-existent public fast-chargers.

OEM Manufacturing Realignments

Automotive manufacturers are adjusting production schedules in Mexican assembly plants to reflect retail demand realities. High-profile strategic shifts, such as Honda's decision to halt production of the Ramos Arizpe-built Prologue EV in favor of expanding its hybrid vehicle lineup across North America, illustrate how assembly lines are reorienting around multi-energy platforms.

At the same time, commercial fleet monitoring through associations like AMAVe (Mexican Association of Vehicle Leasing Companies) indicates that corporate fleet managers are adopting hybrids for urban corporate pools and last-mile logistics to meet ESG targets, while keeping medium- and heavy-duty logistics reliant on diesel ICE until megawatt charging corridors are established along federal freight arteries like Highway 57.

Commercial and Regulatory Outlook

Over the next 18 months, OEMs and distributors will closely track potential tariff changes and trade reviews tied to the USMCA. In particular, potential regulatory revisions by the Ministry of Economy regarding tariff exemptions on imported electric models from Asia will impact competitive showroom pricing against locally built ICE and hybrid vehicles.

For both automaker executive suites and dealership dealer principals, maintaining flexible manufacturing allocations and managing showroom days-of-supply through granular DMS telemetry will remain the primary defense against vehicle inventory stagnation in Mexico’s bifurcated automotive market.

text:
The vision for the stadium project includes new housing and jobs. EGLE awarded a $1 million Brownfield Redevelopment Grant to help bring that part of the project to life. The grant will pay for additional environmental assessments, removal of contaminated soil, barriers to prevent contact with any remaining contamination, and a vapor venting system for the new five-story, 245,515 square-foot building. It will also have 11,682 square feet of commercial space, which is expected to create 25 new jobs.

EGLE funding will not be used for costs directly connected to stadium use, specific stadium utilities, or dedicated infrastructure.

One of the goals of this project is to make the stadium and team part of the southwest Detroit community, particularly the Corktown and Mexicantown neighborhoods. That’s why the city of Detroit and the soccer club have agreed on a $2 million community benefits package that will include:

Funding for local non-profits

A revolving loan fund for small businesses

Art and murals that highlight the area’s history

Complimentary tickets for neighborhood groups

title: Robinson Carbon to invest $16.3M in Louisiana manufacturing facility
description:
The investment also will support the retention of 22 existing positions at Robinson Lumber Company, the fifth-generation family business behind Robinson Carbon.
The facility will convert wood manufacturing byproducts into biochar, a carbon-rich material used in agriculture, horticulture and environmental remediation.
Robinson Carbon is the carbon products division of Robinson Lumber Company, which was founded in New Orleans in 1893.
Since then, the products have changed many times over, but our passion for wood products hasn’t,” Robinson Carbon CEO Garner Robinson said in a statement.
To secure the investment, Louisiana offered Robinson Carbon an incentives package that includes a $550,000 performance-based grant for site and infrastructure improvements.
text:
Robinson Carbon plans to invest $16.3 million to establish a biochar manufacturing facility at England Airpark in Alexandria, creating 42 direct jobs and expanding the company’s operations into a new market for Louisiana’s timber industry.

Louisiana Economic Development announced the project, which is expected to generate an additional 60 indirect jobs, bringing the total potential employment impact to 102 jobs in Central Louisiana. The investment also will support the retention of 22 existing positions at Robinson Lumber Company, the fifth-generation family business behind Robinson Carbon.

Construction is scheduled to begin in November, with production expected to start in the second quarter of 2027. The company has begun hiring for its Alexandria operations.

The facility will convert wood manufacturing byproducts into biochar, a carbon-rich material used in agriculture, horticulture and environmental remediation. The project is expected to create a new market for wood residuals generated by Louisiana sawmills.

According to the company, the plant will operate two rotary drum pyrolysis reactors capable of processing approximately 100,000 metric tons of Southern yellow pine residuals annually into 16,500 metric tons of biochar.

The company plans to source raw materials from nearby mills and manufacture biochar to meet customer specifications for applications ranging from soil improvement to pollution remediation.

Robinson Carbon has relocated a pilot reactor from its manufacturing operation in New Albany, Indiana, to Alexandria, where it will be used to train employees before commercial production begins.

The company also expects the facility to generate approximately 40,000 carbon dioxide removal certificates annually once it receives certification under the Puro Standard. Each certificate represents one metric ton of carbon dioxide removed from the atmosphere.

Louisiana Economic Development Secretary Susan B. Bourgeois said the investment demonstrates how the state’s established industries can expand into emerging markets.

“Louisiana has long been a leader in turning our natural resources into products used around the world. For more than 130 years, the Robinson family has been part of that history, and we are grateful for their continued commitment to Louisiana,” Bourgeois said in a statement.

Robinson Carbon is the carbon products division of Robinson Lumber Company, which was founded in New Orleans in 1893. The business has grown from selling Louisiana longleaf pine into an international wood products manufacturing and distribution operation serving customers in more than 70 countries.

“My great-great-grandfather founded our company in New Orleans in 1893 selling Louisiana longleaf pine. Since then, the products have changed many times over, but our passion for wood products hasn’t,” Robinson Carbon CEO Garner Robinson said in a statement. “Biochar is an exciting opportunity to make something truly new out of wood, and we look forward to planting new roots in Central Louisiana.”

The Alexandria project represents the company’s expansion into industrial-scale biochar manufacturing, combining its existing wood products supply network with technology designed to convert timber byproducts into commercial materials.

To secure the investment, Louisiana offered Robinson Carbon an incentives package that includes a $550,000 performance-based grant for site and infrastructure improvements.

The company also is expected to participate in the state’s High Impact Jobs and Industrial Tax Exemption programs, which provide incentives for qualifying business investments and job creation.

England Economic and Industrial Development District Executive Director Ralph Hennessy said the project strengthens England Airpark’s role as a location for industrial development and advanced manufacturing.

Chris Masingill, president and CEO of Louisiana Central, said the investment will connect the region’s established timber industry with new manufacturing opportunities.

“By connecting our region’s longstanding timber and wood products industry with innovative manufacturing technologies, this project strengthens our industrial base, creates high-quality jobs, and opens new markets for Louisiana’s natural resources,” Masingill said in a statement.

text:
By Staff Writer

Arab Finance: Egypt is stepping up efforts to localize automobile manufacturing and related industries, with plans to expand electric vehicle production and increase local content in vehicles, Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly said during a meeting to review the government's automotive localization plan.

In the meeting attended by Minister of Industry Khaled Hashem and Assistant Minister of Industry for Strategic Affairs Mohamed Sami, Madbouly noted that industrial growth is a key government priority, with a particular focus on the automotive sector.

The government is also prioritizing electric vehicle manufacturing and its inputs as part of its strategy to promote the green transition, reduce reliance on conventional fuels, and lower the import bill, Madbouly added.

For his part, Hashem outlined a partnership involving an unnamed international company, Egyptian industrial group El Araby Group, and the Arab Organization for Industrialization (AOI) to manufacture seven types of metal automotive components locally, targeting an annual output of 8 million units.

Efforts to develop the industry's technical workforce also include cooperation between the Brazilian Association of the Tool Industry (ABINFER) and Egypt's Productivity and Vocational Training Department to establish a vocational school specializing in molds and dies.

In EV battery manufacturing, Hashem highlighted a partnership between an international company and Egyptian bus manufacturer Manufacturing Commercial Vehicles (MCV) to supply batteries for buses, alongside an agreement under development with another international company to provide batteries for vehicles manufactured locally. The ministry is also exploring cooperation with a global manufacturer and AOI to establish domestic production of electric motors.

Hashem said a major international company planned to begin producing three electric vehicle models in 2027, with annual production targeted at 100,000 vehicles by 2032 and 222,000 vehicles by 2032. Local content is expected to start at 10% and rise to 27% by 2032.

The minister also highlighted the start of local EV production by Chinese automaker Dongfeng in partnership with Egypt-based SN Automotive and state-owned El Nasr Automotive Manufacturing Company, using El Nasr's production lines.

Beyond vehicle assembly, the government is working to expand domestic manufacturing of automotive components, including metal parts, batteries, and electric motors.

Alongside these manufacturing initiatives, the government is working to localize laboratory testing for automotive components and upgrade the Engineering Industries Technology Center in 10th of Ramadan City to strengthen technical support for local suppliers.

Hashem also reviewed cooperation with international companies to establish EV charging stations and develop the infrastructure and operating framework needed to support their expansion.

The meeting further addressed progress under the Automotive Industry Development Program (AIDP), which aims to increase local manufacturing within the automotive sector.

The minister discussed incentives and facilities currently under consideration to encourage automakers to establish EV production operations in Egypt, in line with the government's plans to expand the use of clean-energy vehicles.

title: Turkey's solar boom shines ahead of a UN climate summit but coal and other fossil fuels loom large
authors: Mehmet Guzel And Suzan Fraser, Associated Press
description:
Still, advocates for robust action on climate change say Turkey's cleaner energy ambitions stand in sharp contrast to its continued reliance on coal.
Duygu Kutluay, a campaigner with the Beyond Fossil Fuels advocacy group, said Turkey has made plans for a major push in renewable energy.
Many experts have recently argued that a key mission — combating climate change by reducing greenhouse gas emissions — has been failing.
And the last two summits have ended with little agreement on how to reduce emissions, the final texts not even mentioning fossil fuels.

text:
KARAPINAR – Row after row of solar panels stretches across a vast landscape in the central Turkish province of Konya, turning sunlight into electricity — and helping Turkey, the host of the upcoming U.N. climate summit, spotlight its efforts to expand renewable energy.

Still, advocates for robust action on climate change say Turkey's cleaner energy ambitions stand in sharp contrast to its continued reliance on coal.

Campaigners also argue the country lacks concrete plans to transition away from fossil fuels such as oil, gas and coal, which when burned release greenhouse gases that heat the planet.

Turkey’s Energy Ministry says coal remained the country’s largest source of electricity last year, accounting for 33% of generation. But it stressed that the share of solar and wind in electricity generation stood at nearly 23%.

Turkey has one of Europe's largest solar farms

The town of Karapinar in Konya is home to the Kalyon Karapınar YEKA-1 Solar Power Plant, which boasts more than 3 million solar panels perched on a terrain equivalent to the size of 2,600 soccer fields.

Operational since 2023, it generates enough electricity each year to meet about 0.7% of the country’s power demand, according to plant director Burak Dogru.

“We prevent approximately 1.75 million metric tons of carbon emissions every year,” Dogru told The Associated Press — evidence, he says, of how Turkey has been directing its economy and energy sector toward cleaner energy sources.

Turkey’s total greenhouse gas emissions in 2024, the last year for which data is available, reached 584.5 million metric tons of CO2 equivalent, according to the Turkish Statistical Institute.

Duygu Kutluay, a campaigner with the Beyond Fossil Fuels advocacy group, said Turkey has made plans for a major push in renewable energy.

“But these plans contain neither a roadmap for a coal phase-out, nor any planning for a phase-out of other fossil fuels, including gas,” Kutluay cautioned, adding that this is "not compatible” with Turkey's pledge to reach net-zero emissions by 2053.

Turkey is also looking to nuclear power to reduce its energy dependence. The country’s first plant is under construction on the Mediterranean coast, with plans for additional reactors still under consideration.

Concerns and criticism rise ahead of the summit

Some 265 kilometers (165 miles) away from Konya, the Nov. 9-20 summit in the Mediterranean city of Antalya will bring together tens of thousands of delegates, world leaders, business and civil society representatives for discussions on implementing climate goals.

The summit — officially, the Conference of the Parties, or COP31 — comes against a backdrop of deepening concerns over energy security and the Iran war, which has led to a rise in gas and oil prices and sent countries scrambling to meet energy needs.

Many experts have recently argued that a key mission — combating climate change by reducing greenhouse gas emissions — has been failing.

The United States, the world’s richest nation and second-biggest carbon polluter after China, will again be absent from the summit, after U.S. President Donald Trump withdrew the U.S. from global climate negotiations.

And the last two summits have ended with little agreement on how to reduce emissions, the final texts not even mentioning fossil fuels.

Turkey’s environment and climate change minister, Murat Kurum, who will preside over the summit, has said he wants COP31 to focus on turning climate commitments into action rather than new targets.

To that aim, Turkey will push a “climate implementation bridge,” an initiative to help countries turn climate pledges into action by connecting them with financing, technology and other support.

“Today, the world is not merely waiting for new decisions," Kurum said while presenting summit priorities earlier this year. "What the world wants is to see past decisions put into practice.”

Turkey has cast itself as an environment steward

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has insisted his country is committed to environmental protection and combating climate change, and first lady Emine Erdogan has championed a “zero waste” campaign to encourage recycling and a more responsible use of resources.

COP31 will also prioritize electrification and reduction of waste and methane emissions, Kurum has said.

However, the Climate Action Tracker, which measures countries’ progress against goals of the 2015 Paris Agreement, has described Turkey’s climate targets and policies as “critically insufficient.”

The agreement set a target of limiting global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) compared to the early 1800s, directing countries to develop policies that would help meet that goal.

Meanwhile, human rights groups accuse Ankara of dismissing environmental concerns and frequently arresting activists.

Earlier this year, a court annulled an environmental impact assessment for a planned expansion of a coal-fired power plant at Afsin-Elbistan in southeastern Turkey. The ruling was hailed by environmentalists as a major victory.

But shortly afterward, plans emerged to expand another coal-fired power plant in Canakkale, in the country's northwest.

Like other Mediterranean nations, Turkey faces mounting risks from heat waves, drought, water scarcity, wildfires and flooding. Last month, rains described as the heaviest in more than 80 years caused severe floods in Istanbul, Turkey’s largest city, and left eight people dead.

Turkey was announced as the host of COP31 following a tug-of-war with Australia, which also wanted to host the summit. As a compromise, Australia has been leading consultations to help set the summit's agenda and will be in charge of summit discussions.

Climate advocates have slammed the summit for being awarded to coal-reliant Turkey; coal-exporter Australia has also come under criticism.

But U.N. Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell defended the choice, saying in February that a COP host country’s status on fossil fuels does not determine the success or failure of a summit.

With “Turkey and Australia leading this process, there is every opportunity to deliver a very strong outcome," he said.

___

Fraser reported from Ankara, Turkey. Associated Press journalists Serra Yedikardes in Trabzon, Turkey, and Ayse Wieting in Istanbul contributed to this report.

Play00:40

Clean energy under attack in the US, Yellow Door CEO says

US election results could put renewables back into focus, executive says

Rising hydrocarbon prices are also supporting the case for clean energy, Yellow Door Energy CEO says

Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress during the US midterm elections is expected to signal a policy shift favouring renewable energy.

"Clean energy has been under attack by the US administration over the last couple of years," said Yellow Door Energy's chief executive Jeremy Crane, expressing optimism ahead of Cop31 in Turkey.

The "One Big Beautiful Bill Act", signed by President Donald Trump in July, repealed more than $500 billion earmarked for clean energy investments, costing nearly 37,000 jobs in 2025.

The Iran war has disrupted global oil and gas supplies, accelerating demand for on-site solar energy generation as businesses seek energy independence and grid resilience.

Yellow Door Energy, with 500 megawatts of solar projects across the Middle East and Africa, is expanding in Saudi Arabia, Qatar and South Africa.

The US midterm election results has brought back hope for renewables after the Trump administration's "attacks" on clean energy, according to a sustainable energy executive.

Coupled with sky-high fuel prices, the adoption of renewable energy is likely to further increase, Jeremy Crane, chief executive of Emirati solar energy company Yellow Door Energy told The National.

“Clean energy has been under attack by the US administration over the last couple of years,” he said at the Abu Dhabi energy conference Adipec.

In July, the US President Donald Trump signed the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” that repealed over $500 billion slated for clean energy investments, just one of many pro-fossil-fuel actions during his second term. A report by E2 found that the US clean energy workforce lost almost 37,000 jobs in 2025.

With Democrats winning control of the House and the Senate during the midterms, a shift in policy is expected.

“We're optimistic. I'm hoping that as the currents change in the US, we might see a renewed tailwind for renewables, and I hope that Cop 31 will be a showcase for that,” Mr Crane said.

Sustainable energy will take centre stage at the United Nations' 31st Climate Conference (Cop 31), which runs from November 9-20 in Antalya, Turkey.

“I'll be watching the headlines, the agreements that are signed, and the rhetoric to hopefully see a renewed view that clean energy is a very important part of the future for our world and the Middle East,” Mr Crane added.

With the Iran war disrupting oil and gas supplies globally, Yellow Door Energy's services are becoming more relevant, he said.

“More and more businesses are looking to generate what they need, where they need it,” Mr Crane said.

“If you can generate power on your premise, not be subject to the need to import fuel, not be subject to potential threats to grids, that's a big advantage. Coupling solar with storage is a way to expand that and provide additional resiliency to whatever might come.”

Due to the war, the company has had construction delays as well as assets stuck in ports, which forced a rerouting of its logistics network. However, its energy facilities have not experienced any direct fallout.

“We have been enormously fortunate that because of our business model of distributing our assets, and having them where the consumption takes place, we've seen virtually no impact on all of our operating sites,” Mr Crane said.

“In terms of operating assets, we've seen little to no delay, and we expect that to continue regardless of what the future holds.”

Bright prospects

Yellow Door Energy, which currently has 500 megawatts of solar projects in the Middle East and Africa, expects continued growth in 2027.

“Saudi Arabia is a large and growing market for us,” Mr Crane said. “We've got our first projects under construction in Qatar for logistics company GWC, that's been a big portfolio growth.”

It is also boosting business in Abu Dhabi, working with companies like Aldar and PureHealth.

Outside the region, South Africa is a vital market, with up to three projects expected to hit financial close before the end of the year.

“We're blessed to be in a strong business financial position as the region goes through some volatility,” Mr Crane said.

Looking ahead, he is “very optimistic” about the role that the UAE will play in energy transition.

“The targets set here [in the UAE] for decarbonising the grid, for bringing in clean energy, are driven first and foremost by economics,” he said.

“We're now seeing the UAE also being a showcase for resilience and trying to bring the latest technologies, storage, demand management into the grid as a fantastic role model for the region and the world.”

HOCHUL SABOTAGES CLIMATE; SOCIALISTS RENEW FIGHT FOR PUBLICLY-OWNED RENEWABLE ENERGY

Elected officials and New Yorkers call to double down on the only viable solution to rising energy costs and the climate crisis: public power.

Media Contact: climate@socialists.nyc

NEW YORK, NY — Governor Hochul has continuously condemned New Yorkers to higher bills, toxic smog, rolling blackouts, and climate disasters by delaying and sabotaging New York’s climate action since the day she took office. Now public power is the only way to deliver an affordable, resilient, healthy future.

With or without the Climate Leadership & Community Protection Act, New York’s task hasn’t changed. We know continued reliance on fossil fuels — and fossil-fueled politicians like Kathy Hochul — is killing us. The only way to meet our climate goals is with a publicly-controlled energy system that takes our future out of fossil fuel corporations’ hands. With the governor’s climate sabotage and private clean energy development failing to deliver progress, aggressive public renewables buildout is the only viable way to cut pollution while stabilizing New York’s increasingly unstable energy system.

Thanks to New York’s democratic socialist legislators, we are taking critical steps forward for public power: today, we’ve secured $100 million for publicly-owned renewable energy projects in this budget. Now, along with all of New York’s democratic socialist State Senators and Assemblymembers, we will fight to ensure that New York State builds 15 gigawatts of publicly-owned renewable energy.

State Senator Kristen Gonzalez said, “The Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act was meant to phase out peaker plants like the one in my District. Almost six years after it passed, residents of Queens and Brooklyn are still breathing dirty air from polluting power plants and paying more than ever for utilities. We won’t settle for a broken future. Public renewables are the way forward, and I look forward to fighting for the full 15 gigawatts of public renewable energy we need to shut down these smokestacks once and for all.”

Assemblymember Claire Valdez said, “New York is the first state in the country to weaken its emissions targets, thanks to Governor Kathy Hochul. By killing the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act, Governor Hochul has chosen, once again, to enrich corporations and billionaires at the expense of any New Yorker that might hope for lower utility bills, cleaner air to breathe, or a planet to live on. But the fight against the climate and affordability crises isn’t over. Publicly-owned renewable energy can guarantee lower bills, good union jobs, and a sustainable future. Building 15 gigawatts must be our first step.”

Assemblymember Diana Moreno said, “Peaker plant pollution in my district is so notable that they call our neighborhood “Asthma Alley.” The Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act was meant to make it easier to transition off destructive fossil fuels and toward a healthier future. But instead, Governor Hochul is throwing our community under the bus to keep her fossil fuel donors rich. Weakening our climate laws won’t lower our bills. We need publicly-owned renewable energy to make our energy system affordable while cutting pollution. 15 gigawatts of public renewables is the way forward for New York.”

Assemblymember Emily Gallagher said, “We are in an existential moment. The scientific community is sounding the alarm on the livability of our planet while the federal government rolls back all environmental protections and investments in green technology. The oligarchs are building bunkers while they fund climate denialism and get rich off new oil and gas projects. For Governor Hochul to force through climate law rollbacks in the budget is a blatant and unconscionable handout to her fossil fuel donors. We have the technologies we need to shift the trajectory. Public renewable energy is cheaper and less volatile than oil and gas, and this budget funded it to the tune of $100 million — a victory that would not be possible without the ongoing sustained pressure of our movement. I will keep fighting until we build 15 GW of public renewable energy to protect New Yorkers’ health and safety, reduce energy costs, and create good union jobs”

Assemblymember Marcela Mitaynes said, “When Governor Kathy Hochul rolled back New York’s landmark climate legislation, she also rolled back Black and Latino New Yorkers’ dream of a healthier and more affordable future, withholding billions in investments from communities like Sunset Park and Red Hook that have long borne the burden of toxic pollution and fossil fuel infrastructure. The peaker plants operating in Sunset Park pollute not only our neighborhood, but also neighboring Red Hook across the harbor, contributing to the asthma and respiratory illnesses our families disproportionately face. Instead of lowering energy bills, creating union jobs, and shutting down the dirty facilities making our communities sick, the Governor is allowing corporate utilities to continue profiting off environmental injustice. Our communities deserve better, and New York must move forward with at least 15 gigawatts of public renewables to deliver cleaner air, lower costs, and the healthy future working-class New Yorkers were promised.”

Assemblymember Phara Souffrant Forrest said, “Governor Hochul is breaking her promises to New Yorkers by expanding dirty energy infrastructure. She’s opened the door to new fracked gas power plants in New York City, rolled out the red carpet for a new Trump pipeline, and is now rolling back our climate law to keep fossil fuels burning. Our communities are the ones who pay the price with our bills, with asthma attacks, and with deadly heatwaves. It’s time to take out the corruption and build an energy system that puts our communities first. That means building 15 gigawatts of public renewables that will actually lower our bills, cut pollution, and deliver a healthy future for our children.”

Assemblymember Sarahana Shrestha said, “New York has the tools to solve its energy crisis but Albany refuses to use them. The New York Power Authority can build 15 gigawatts of public renewables cheaper and faster than any private developer, yet renewable energy as a share of our grid has flatlined under Hochul’s watch. New Yorkers are done waiting. It’s time for Governor Hochul to stop pouring gas on the fire and build the public renewables New Yorkers need.”

The Build Public Renewables Act, developed by NYC-DSA and passed in 2023, empowers the state to build publicly-owned renewable energy sources to lower bills, create thousands of union jobs, and lower pollution. Building 15 gigawatts of public renewables — enough to power 12 million households — is estimated to raise $725 million in utility bill credits for low and middle income New Yorkers, create more than 20,000 union jobs, and ensure the timely shutdown of super-polluting peaker plans in New York City by 2030.

Renewable energy is the fastest and cheapest way to add more power to our grid, boost reliability, and cut pollution. Adding these energy sources will help avert blackouts and drive energy prices down. Yet the private sector has been unable to deliver at the scale needed, particularly amid the loss of IRA tax credit due to Trump administration cuts. NYC-DSA legislators understand the reality: the more public renewables we build, the more relief we can deliver.

text:
Market Value (2025): USD 98.6 Bn

What is the EV Battery Market forecast to be worth by 2036?

USD 115.6 billion in 2026 to USD 567.5 billion by 2036 at a 17.2% CAGR.

The valuation of the EV battery market was USD 98.6 billion in 2025, with packs for battery-electric passenger cars forming the base of revenue.

Revenue will grow from USD 115.6 billion in 2026 to USD 567.5 billion by 2036 as new cell plants come online in Europe, North America and Asia.

A 17.2% CAGR reflects higher electric vehicle output, wider model choice and steady gains in energy density per pack.

Year Basis Market Value (USD billion) 2025 Actual 98.6 2026 Estimate 115.6 2036 Forecast 567.5 CAGR 2026 to 2036 Forecast period 17.2%

Source: Fact.MR analysis. Updated Nov 5, 2026

What are the defining numbers behind EV Battery Market growth?

The 2026 to 2036 period will add USD 451.9 billion in new value, led by lithium-ion cells fitted to passenger cars in the 50-110 kWh range.

Demand Drivers in the Market

Electric car sales grew by 20% worldwide to exceed 20 million units in 2025, so one in four new cars sold was electric [1]. Each of these vehicles needs a traction battery, which ties battery revenue directly to vehicle output.

Public funding is targeting the battery supply chain. The European Commission’s Industrial Action Plan for the automotive sector, published in March 2025, earmarks EUR 1.8 billion for a secure supply chain of battery raw materials [2].

Traceability rules are lifting the value of each pack. Under the EU Batteries Regulation, electric vehicle batteries must carry a QR code linked to a digital battery passport from 18 February 2027 [3].

Truck and bus fleets are moving to electric drive, and these vehicles use packs several times bigger than a passenger car. Higher capacity per vehicle lifts revenue even where unit volumes stay modest.

Key Segments Analyzed

By Battery Type: Lithium-ion will hold 71.4% share in 2026, since its energy density and mature production lines suit nearly every electric vehicle platform.

By Vehicle Type: Passenger Cars will account for 58.3% of 2026 value, as private buyers and ride-hailing fleets switch to battery-electric models.

By Application: Electric Vehicles will capture 40.5% in 2026, given that fully electric drive needs the most battery capacity per vehicle.

By Battery Capacity: 50-110 kWh will represent 42.6% of 2026 revenue, because this band gives mainstream cars a usable range without excess pack weight.

Analyst Opinion at Fact.MR

Shambhu Nath Jha, Principal Consultant at Fact.MR, states, “Battery cost per kilowatt-hour will set the pace at which electric cars match combustion models on price. Cell makers that can switch between LFP and nickel-rich chemistries on the same line will win more automaker programs. Solid-state cells will enter premium models first, while lithium-ion packs will carry volume through 2036.”

Strategic Implications

Cell manufacturers should place new capacity near automaker assembly plants, cutting freight costs and meeting local content rules.

Automakers should qualify at least two cell chemistries per platform so that pack supply can follow shifts in mineral prices.

Material suppliers should secure long-term offtake for lithium, nickel and graphite, as cell plants lock in supply years before production starts.

Investors should weigh recycling and second-life capacity, since battery passport and recovery rules will turn spent packs into a tracked resource.

Growth will be widest in Germany at 19.8%, where a large car industry is converting its model ranges to battery-electric drive. Brazil follows at 18.1%, helped by a new vehicle program that ties tax treatment to efficiency and recyclability. The United States will grow at 16.3%, as a large vehicle base meets uneven buyer incentives. The United Kingdom will grow at 14.6% as gigafactory capacity arrives later than in continental Europe. Japan closes the range at 12.9%, since hybrids still take a large part of its new car sales and full-electric adoption starts from a low base.

How does the EV Battery Market break down by segment?

Lithium-ion will lead Battery Type at 71.4%; Passenger Cars will head Vehicle Type at 58.3%; Electric Vehicles will top Application at 40.5%; 50-110 kWh will hold Battery Capacity at 42.6% in 2026.

Which Battery Type leads?

Lithium-ion holds 71.4% of 2026 sales.

Battery Type Share (2026) Lithium-ion (Leading segment) 71.4% Other segments combined 28.6%* Total 100.0%

Source: Fact.MR analysis. Updated Nov 5, 2026

Automakers choose lithium-ion cells because they store more energy per kilogram than older chemistries and are built at global scale. Within this group, lithium iron phosphate cells are gaining share in entry models, as they cost less and resist overheating. Nickel-rich cells keep their place in long-range and performance cars. Cathode choice is a large part of cell cost, which is why demand for lithium-ion battery cathodes tracks the chemistry mix closely. Production is heavily concentrated, as China accounted for over 80% of battery cell output in 2025 [1]. Nickel-metal hydride packs remain in some hybrids, and lead-acid units serve low-speed vehicles. Interest in solid-state battery technology is rising, although volume production is still limited.

What supports Passenger Cars within Vehicle Type?

Passenger Cars take 58.3% of 2026 revenue.

Vehicle Type Share (2026) Passenger Cars (Leading segment) 58.3% Other segments combined 41.7%* Total 100.0%

Source: Fact.MR analysis. Updated Nov 5, 2026

Private car buyers now find electric models in almost every size class, from small hatchbacks to seven-seat SUVs. Each new model brings a dedicated pack design, and automakers often source the cells from two suppliers. Growth in the wider electric vehicle industry therefore feeds battery orders well before cars reach showrooms. Commercial vehicles are the next source of volume. Electric trucks reached 9% of truck sales worldwide in 2025 [1], and city operators keep adding units to the electric bus fleet. Two-wheelers use small packs but sell in high numbers across South and Southeast Asia, which makes the electric two-wheeler segment an important outlet for compact cells.

How does Application shape demand?

Electric Vehicles account for 40.5% of 2026 value.

Application Share (2026) Electric Vehicles (Leading segment) 40.5% Other segments combined 59.5%* Total 100.0%

Source: Fact.MR analysis. Updated Nov 5, 2026

Fully electric vehicles carry no combustion engine, so the battery supplies all propulsion energy. This design needs the most capacity per vehicle and the most demanding thermal control. Packs also rely on a battery management system to balance cells, track health and protect against overcharging. Hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles use smaller packs, yet they keep selling in volume. Hybrid, battery-electric and plug-in hybrid models took about 22% of United States light-duty sales in 2025, up from 20% in 2024 [4]. Battery requirements in these vehicles depend on how far each model can drive on electricity alone.

What leads the Battery Capacity segment?

50-110 kWh takes 42.6% of 2026 demand.

Battery Capacity Share (2026) 50-110 kWh (Leading segment) 42.6% Other segments combined 57.4%* Total 100.0%

Source: Fact.MR analysis. Updated Nov 5, 2026

Mainstream electric cars need enough stored energy for a full day of mixed driving, and packs in this band deliver it. Going bigger adds weight, cost and charging time. Many automakers offer two pack sizes within this range on the same model. Packs below 50 kWh serve city cars, plug-in hybrids and two-wheeler platforms. The 111-200 kWh and above 200 kWh bands belong mostly to vans, trucks and buses, where daily mileage justifies the extra capacity.

What is accelerating EV Battery Market adoption, and what is holding it back?

Rising electric vehicle sales, new cell plants and steady chemistry gains are driving demand. Restraints come from the capital needed for a gigafactory and from swings in lithium and nickel prices. What supports EV battery adoption in Germany?

19.8% CAGR, supported by automaker model conversions and new domestic cell plants.

German automakers are moving whole model ranges to battery-electric platforms, and suppliers are adding pack assembly near their plants. Just over 545,100 battery-electric cars were newly registered in Germany in 2025, equal to 19.1% of all new car registrations [5]. Battery-electric and plug-in hybrid cars together took 30.0% of new registrations, up from 20.3% in 2024 [5]. That jump in one year shows how quickly local pack demand is rising.

How is Brazil developing demand?

18.1% CAGR, helped by the MOVER program and fresh investment in electrified vehicle lines.

Brazil’s car industry is adding hybrid and electric models to local production lines. Decree No. 12,435 of 15 April 2025 regulates the Green Mobility and Innovation Program (MOVER) and sets energy efficiency and recyclability requirements for new vehicles sold or imported from 1 June 2025 [6]. Cradle-to-grave carbon footprint requirements will apply from 1 January 2027 under the same decree [6].

What is supporting United States adoption?

16.3% CAGR, backed by a large vehicle base and new domestic cell capacity.

The United States has a large light vehicle fleet and a growing network of cell plants in the Midwest and South. Battery-electric vehicles were 7.2% of model year 2024 vehicle production, and plug-in hybrids added 2.5%, according to the EPA [7]. Buyer demand weakened after tax credits expired in late 2025, which tempers near-term growth [4]. Hybrid sales keep rising, and that still adds demand for smaller packs.

How is the United Kingdom developing demand?

14.6% CAGR, reflecting a growing zero emission fleet and new gigafactory capacity.

The United Kingdom had 1,505,000 zero emission cars licensed at the end of June 2025, which was 38% more than a year earlier [8]. Local cell supply is also expanding. In May 2025, the government announced GBP 1 billion of financing for a new AESC gigafactory in Sunderland that can supply batteries for up to 100,000 electric vehicles a year [9]. The plant will create 1,000 jobs and raise national capacity six-fold [9].

12.9% CAGR, owing to national battery targets and solid-state research.

Japan has deep experience in cell chemistry and supplies batteries to automakers worldwide. Hybrids still take much of the home market, so full-electric demand grows from a lower base. In June 2026, METI revised its battery strategy as the Battery and Power Industry Strategy, which targets a domestic manufacturing base of 150 GWh a year between 2030 and the mid-2030s [10]. It also aims for full-scale commercialization of all-solid-state batteries around 2030 [10].

Chinese cell makers CATL, BYD and CALB compete on scale and LFP cost, and they now take that model abroad. CATL began trial operations in its new cell building in Debrecen, Hungary, in September 2026 [11].

The plant is designed for 100 GWh once complete [11]. LG Energy Solution has widened its offer with LFP pouch cells for Ampere, the EV unit of Renault Group, its first large-scale LFP supply contract for EVs [12]. text:
As the results rolled in and Democrats took control of Congress Tuesday night, U.S. Sen. Ron Wyden wrote a single word on social media that summed up the party’s newfound power: “Subpoenas.”

Wyden is one of at least six longtime Pacific Northwest lawmakers who could rise to powerful positions after Democrats regained control of the House and Senate in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Wyden, 77, is poised to become chair of the U.S. Senate Committee on Finance, which oversees policies on taxation, trade, tariffs, health care programs like Medicare and Medicaid, and more. In a statement Wednesday morning, he laid out his plans to crack down on what he called the unjustly rich and powerful, from corrupt bankers to insurance companies to pharmaceutical executives.

“I’m putting the special interests that have worked hand-in-hand with Trump to rip off American families for the last year and a half on notice,” said Wyden, who is in his fifth term in the upper chamber. He added that “when I am chair, they will be forced to answer to the Senate Finance Committee for their role in hurting the American people and enabling Trump’s corruption.”

Wyden isn’t alone. Democrats in Oregon and Washington — many of whom have been in Congress for decades — are in the direct line to chair positions on committees that control everything from federal spending to transportation to armed services.

It’s unclear precisely who will inherit which roles, and how the party plans to use the power voters granted in a stunning rebuke of the Trump administration. Most Democrats in this article did not return an inquiry from OPB on their plans for a new Congress.

The party may be hard-pressed to make significant legislative accomplishments, given President Trump’s veto power. Still, the shift from Tuesday’s election has many Democrats in the region well-positioned to block signature parts of the Trump administration’s agenda and launch high-profile investigations that could roil Congress.

For example, U.S. Sen. Jeff Merkley, who was reelected to a fourth term on Tuesday, is the ranking member of the U.S. Senate Committee on the Budget. As chair, he told OPB he would aim to slash wasteful defense spending and reverse Republican-backed tax breaks like those in the One Big Beautiful Bill, which he and other Democrats view as disproportionately benefitting the wealthy.

U.S. Rep. Adam Smith, a Washington Democrat who has served nearly three decades in Congress, is the ranking member of the House Armed Services Committee, which has the authority to investigate the military’s operations in places like Iran, Ukraine and Latin America.

A week before the election, he told Time that he supported impeachment proceedings against Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. “I think we have to try, even if it doesn’t succeed,” Smith told Time.

In a statement Wednesday, Smith said the committee would “conduct vigorous oversight” and “demand public transparency and accountability” from the Trump administration. Among many things, he said the committee would investigate wasteful defense spending, the deployment of the National Guard to American cities and the “the blatant and corrosive politicization of our Armed Forces and purging of the ranks based on loyalty and ideology are high on the list.”

“The list of potential oversight topics is long, but the illegal war against Iran is top of mind for me and the American people,” Smith said. “So too are sweetheart deals and favoritism to certain entities and individuals.”

U.S. Sen. Patty Murray, a Washington Democrat in her sixth term, is the vice chair of the U.S. Senate Committee on Appropriations, which helps control federal spending. On Tuesday, as Democrats took back Congress, she wrote on the social media platform X: “This former preschool teacher is going to teach President Trump a simple lesson: The power of the purse belongs to CONGRESS!”

“It’s NOT Trump’s money. Taxpayer dollars belong to the American PEOPLE,” Murray said.

In addition, U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, a Washington Democrat in her fifth term, is the ranking member of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation; U.S. Rep. Rick Larsen, of Washington, is the ranking member of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee; and U.S. Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, an Oregon Democrat who is the longest current tenured member of Oregon’s House delegation, is vying for the top job on the House Education and the Workforce Committee.

“I’m running to lead the Education and Labor Committee so we can save public education and meet this moment by lowering costs, rebuilding trust with working families, and holding the Trump administration accountable,” Bonamici said in a statement to X.

Democrats will now be jockeying for positions and deciding how much of their political capital to spend on local issues — from homelessness to the environment to transportation — versus pushing back against the president, said Paul Manson, a professor in the Portland State University Center for Public Service.

Having so many politicians in critical roles could influence some issues that are especially critical in the Pacific Northwest. Many are primed to gain such positions due to their long careers in elected office.

“We tend to return our incumbents here in the Northwest,” Manson said. “Seniority is sort of something we accrue a little bit more quickly than some of our other sister states.”

Such authority isn’t unprecedented in the region. Oregon Sen. Mark Hatfield, a moderate Republican first elected in 1966, was the chairman of the appropriations committee. Oregon Sen. Bob Packwood, who was elected to five terms before resigning in disgrace in 1995, was the chairman of the finance committee.

But Manson noted that many of these politicians were Republicans.

“Now we’re in this new era,” Manson said. “It is some new ground in that sense just because it’s on the other side of the aisle.”

—

Conservation and clean energy groups, represented by Earthjustice, agreed to settle their challenge to a proposed rate hike by Bonneville Power Administration (BPA). The settlement, once approved by the BPA administrator, will reduce the financial burden on BPA’s customers by close to $40 million.

BPA is the federal agency that sells Columbia Basin hydropower and operates much of the Northwest’s power grid.

Initially, BPA had proposed raising an additional $250 million through its rate hike, which could have resulted in an increase to customers’ bills of up to 6.3%. Instead, as a consequence of the proposed settlement, BPA would collect a total of $212 million. The settlement also increases the likelihood that that BPA will refund money to its customers in 2028.

In its stated justification for the rate increase, BPA blamed measures put in place by a federal court in Oregon found to be necessary to protect imperiled Columbia Basin salmon. The Idaho Conservation League, Sierra Club, and the NW Energy Coalition, represented by Earthjustice, intervened in BPA’s rate proceeding, arguing the agency was prematurely seeking the increase and exaggerating the cost of implementing the court order. The groups also observed BPA was ignoring other factors, such as weather, energy demand, and regional prices that influence both BPA’s expenses and revenues.

That happened before in 2018, when BPA claimed that it needed to immediately raise rates because of a similar court order and yet still managed to end the year with a $123 million surplus.

The groups also argued that the agency could, if it chose to do so, avoid a rate hike by absorbing any costs that may arise from the order. According to BPA’s own forecasts, its financial position is secure, and BPA appears capable of responding to additional costs without raising customer rates while blaming salmon for doing so.

“BPA is required to make decisions that are economically sound while also protecting endangered salmon and steelhead,” said Earthjustice Attorney Michael Mayer. “This settlement would reduce the impact on electricity customers, but at the same time, BPA still insists on raising rates. BPA’s overall approach here is faulty, and there are better alternatives.”

“BPA is fully capable of maintaining our grid and promoting cheaper, cleaner energy options without compromising on salmon protections. We intend to work with BPA to make sure that happens,” said Bill Arthur, chair of the Snake/Columbia River Salmon Campaign at the Sierra Club.

“Energy affordability is top of mind for everyone. We are pleased that this settlement should keep keep $40 million in people’s pockets. We know that BPA can do better and will keep pushing for solutions that protect both people and salmon in the Northwest,” said Ben Otto, policy director at the NW Energy Coalition.

“This settlement provides some relief to consumers at a time when people are struggling to pay their bills. We will keep fighting for consumers while making sure that salmon are not ignored,” said Brad Smith, conservation director at the Idaho Conservation League.

Background

None of the participants in the proceeding objected to the proposed settlement within the deadline to do so. The settlement must still be officially adopted by BPA, but the agency intends to finalize its decision no later than early December.

This rate proceeding follows other recent rate increases. BPA previously raised its rates by close to 9% when setting rates for fiscal years 2026 through 2028, and at the end of 2025, it imposed a $40 million surcharge on its customers, effectively raising rates by another 2%.

The court’s order at the center of this rate case came about after the clean energy, conservation, and fishing groups, represented by Earthjustice, returned to federal court in Oregon last fall in response to the Trump administration unilaterally terminating the historic Resilient Columbia Basin Agreement. Signed in 2023, the agreement was intended to pause the parties’ long-standing litigation for a decade while a set of federal commitments were implemented to restore salmon populations, honor Tribal treaty obligations, and build out the region’s clean energy resources.

The court ordered more water to be “spilled” over eight dams on the Lower Columbia and Lower Snake rivers to protect juvenile salmon migrating downstream. The order is a temporary emergency measure, needed because of the government’s repeated failure to adequately protect salmon. As noted by the court, the responsible agencies have a “disappointing history of government avoidance and manipulation instead of sincere efforts at solving the problem and genuinely remediating the harm.”

The last few months of conflict with Iran have exposed an uncomfortable truth: despite becoming the world’s largest oil producer, the United States remains remarkably vulnerable to the whims of the global oil market. Our reliance on imported oil has fallen, but our vulnerability to gasoline and diesel price shocks has not.

Higher domestic oil production helps, but it can only do so much. In a globally connected market, disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz or attacks on Russian refineries still send prices soaring. Domestic oil production will remain critical for decades, but the best protection against volatile oil prices is to reduce consumption — or, where possible, eliminate it altogether.

For the first time, we have an alternative.

Electric vehicles (EVs) offer a paradigm-shifting opportunity for U.S. energy security. They can free drivers from the gas pump and, as battery technology improves, offer an increasingly viable alternative for trucking fleets and heavy equipment.

Global consumers bought more than 20 million EVs in 2025. In China, nearly 55% of new car sales are electric. In the United States, it’s just 10%. China’s enormous EV fleet has helped cushion its economy from the latest oil shock. The same could increasingly be true here.

Seizing this energy security opportunity requires a recalibration of American energy policy around two essential priorities: abundant, affordable electricity and secure mineral supply chains.

EVs offer significant fuel savings over gasoline-powered cars. Cheaper electricity will only widen that advantage. Affordable power is hardly guaranteed. With electricity prices rising across much of the country, policymakers must prioritize adding generating capacity, modernizing the grid and removing barriers to energy development.

Texas offers an instructive example. The state has paired rapid electricity demand growth with an extraordinary buildout of new generation. Long synonymous with oil and gas, Texas now leads the nation in wind power and is second in solar generation.

Affordable, abundant electricity is a challenge we know how to solve. Building secure mineral supply chains is a taller order.

Minerals may not fuel EVs, but they are essential to building them. EVs rely on far more mineral inputs than conventional vehicles, including lithium and graphite for batteries and copper for wiring. Yet the United States remains dangerously dependent on imported minerals — especially from China, which has repeatedly used its mineral dominance as a source of geopolitical leverage.

Replacing U.S. dependence on volatile global oil markets with dependence on Chinese-controlled mineral supply chains would hardly be an energy security victory. Fortunately, the United States has vast mineral resources. The challenge is turning that neglected potential into productive capacity.

The push to expand domestic mining and mineral processing and forge partnerships with mineral-producing nations marks important progress, but it requires sustained follow-through. Bipartisan permitting legislation advancing in Congress could speed U.S. mineral production and rebuild the industrial capacity needed for the nation’s energy future.

For decades, Americans have endured one oil shock after another. We finally have an opportunity to break that cycle. Freedom from oil price shocks shouldn’t come at the cost of a new dependence on China. The path to lasting American energy security must run through abundant domestic energy and the minerals needed to power it.

John Adams is the president of Guardian Six Consulting. He wrote this for InsideSources.com .
