text:
What is the world on track for?

In today’s uncertain world, it is increasingly difficult to understand what the next few years, let alone the next few decades, will bring for global decarbonization. Assessing the likely pace and scale of continued progress in decarbonizing the global economy over the coming years is a challenge, but despite significant uncertainties, there are clear signals that renewable power and electric vehicles will continue to transform the global energy system. Renewables accounted for 86% of global power capacity additions in 2025, and one in four new cars sold worldwide was electric. These technologies offer increasingly competitive alternatives to fossil fuels. Displacing fossil fuels in other sectors like heavy industry, aviation, and shipping has proved more difficult, but emerging technologies that address some of these hard-to-abate sectors of the economy are increasingly ready for commercialization in a growing number of markets.

A baseline for assessing further action

Understanding what the world and nations are on track for today is a critical starting point for charting a path to where we need to go from here to avoid the worst impacts of climate change. To date, the global community has largely relied on models to project global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions pathways to assess the necessary ambition of global and national emissions pledges and illustrate how the economy would need to adjust to achieve those targets. Now, a much wider array of actors is trying to understand how the economy will transform as the global energy transition continues to unfold and how they can accelerate that progress even further.

To meet this need, the Rhodium Climate Outlook (RCO) provides a shared baseline of energy, emissions, and temperature projections for use by a wide range of global stakeholders to assess where we are and what additional progress is needed, including:

Probabilistic global and regional emissions and energy projections that capture uncertainty in economic and population growth, oil and gas prices, and clean energy technology costs.

Econometrically based policy projections based on real-world evidence of country-level policy drivers to construct a baseline projection of how policy is likely to evolve going forward, absent a major acceleration from current trajectories.

Emissions projections for all greenhouse gases, not just CO2.

Probabilistic temperature projections derived directly from our emissions projections but including climate system uncertainty as well.

The Rhodium Climate Outlook is produced using an integrated modeling platform that combines these critical features: Rhodium’s Global Energy Model (RHG-GEM). RHG-GEM captures uncertainty in economic and population growth, coal, oil, and natural gas prices, and clean energy technology costs under likely policy evolution (see the Technical Appendix for more detail).

The result is our RCO Baseline, which provides probabilistic GHG emissions and energy outcome ranges based on the most up-to-date outlook for key drivers through the end of the century. This RCO Baseline illustrates what the world is likely on track for, absent a major acceleration in the pace of climate policy ambition or accelerated innovation and investment in emerging technologies beyond their current trajectory. It is the starting point for assessing what additional action is needed to go above and beyond what the world is already on track to achieve, and specifically:

What regions and sectors of the economy are making the most progress in the clean energy, low-GHG transition, and what are the potential barriers to further progress;

Which regions and sectors are falling behind, and where is an acceleration of policy, investment, and deployment most needed;

Where expected cost reductions in mature clean technologies don’t go far enough to deploy at scale in regions with slow-to-evolve climate policy;

How the emergence of new technologies that are nearing maturity can further reduce emissions; and

Where additional technology innovation is most needed, and where new technologies would have the largest impact on future GHG emissions.

Key findings

In this year’s outlook, we find that clean electricity makes substantial progress, but slower change in other sectors limits the decline in global emissions. The following sections examine that contrast, including what growing electrification means for power demand and the evolving sectoral and geographic landscape of global emissions in the decades ahead. Key findings include:

Global emissions decline modestly despite a transitioning energy system, with mean warming expected to reach 9°C in 2100. Mean GHG emissions reach 47.4 gigatons of CO2e in 2050, a reduction of 10% from today’s levels, with a likely range (covering roughly two-thirds of modeled outcomes) of 42.0–52.7 gigatons CO2e. Global emissions progress begins to stall after mid-century, however, as rising industrial emissions offset some of the reductions from the power sector. The likely range of global temperature rise is 2.3–3.4°C by the end of the century.

The share of global emissions shifts away from China and OECD economies. Together, China and OECD economies account for 37% of global emissions in 2050 on average, a significant drop from their current share of 54%. Emissions growth in India, Africa, and other non-OECD countries in Asia offsets part of the reductions in these regions.

Cleaner power expands with rising electricity demand. Wind and solar generation grow to over seven times today’s levels by 2050 (from 5,500 TWh in 2025 to a mean of 39,300 TWh in 2050), while fossil generation is expected to fall by 23% on average.

Electric demand from buildings drives overall load growth in most of the world, while data centers drive rising US demand. Electricity’s share of end-use energy rises from 21% today to 28% by 2035 on average, falling short of the global target of 35% electrification by 2035, which was announced as part of the COP31 Action Agenda. Demand in buildings, including for cooling, contributes 60% of the expected increase by 2035. In the US, we project that data centers account for 62–77% of gross electricity demand growth from 2025 to 2030.

Industry continues to be the highest-emitting sector with little change, but declining steel emissions are a bright spot. Growth in chemicals, refining, and other industries offsets emission reductions in steel and other subsectors. Industry, currently the highest-emitting sector, remains the largest source of emissions in 2050, at 15.6 gigatons CO2e on average.

Emissions from the transport sector remain high, even while electric vehicles (EVs) gain market share. Electric light-duty vehicles reach 40% of new sales in 2030 on average (likely range 35–45%) and 71% in 2050 (62–80%). However, slow fleet turnover keeps emissions from cars and trucks high, while aviation and shipping emissions continue to rise.

Global emissions decline modestly despite a transitioning energy system

In our 2026 outlook, global greenhouse gas emissions are projected to decline only modestly by mid-century in the mean projection. From a peak of 52.8 gigatons CO2e in 2024, emissions are expected to fall to 47.4 gigatons in 2050, a reduction of 10% from 2024 levels (likely range of 42.0 to 52.7 gigatons, a 0.2-21% reduction) (Figure 1).

The decline begins to lose momentum after mid-century, however. Mean emissions reach about 46.2 gigatons CO2e in 2060 (13% below 2024 levels) before rising to 47.3 gigatons in 2100 (10% below 2024 levels). After 2060, power emissions continue to fall, but that improvement is outweighed by emissions growth from industry. The likely range widens to 37.4–57.0 gigatons by 2100 (29% below to 8% above 2024 levels), and the very likely range (90% probability) to 31.4–65.6 gigatons (41% below to 24% above 2024 levels). The broader late-century range underscores how much the long-term outcome depends on economic and technological developments that remain uncertain.

Emissions shift away from China and OECD economies

The small decline in global emissions masks a much larger change in the geographic distribution of those reductions. OECD economies accounted for 45% of global emissions in 2000, compared with China’s 12%. By 2024, their shares were almost equal, at 28% and 26%, respectively. China alone accounted for 61% of the net global increase from 2000 to 2024. But looking ahead, China’s emissions are expected to decline rapidly, with OECD economies’ emissions continuing their more moderate rate of decline through mid-century. As a result, the bulk of future emissions growth becomes concentrated in the rest of the world. Together, China and the OECD are projected to account for 37% of global emissions in 2050 on average, down from 54% in 2024 (Figure 3).

China and OECD countries are expected to cut emissions over the coming decades even as their electricity demand rises steeply. In our outlook, both China and the OECD generate substantially more electricity by 2050, but wind, solar, and other low-carbon sources replace a growing share of fossil-fuel generation. In China, that change reverses the emissions effect of decades of coal-led power expansion and delivers most of the reduction in China’s total emissions, from 13.9 gigatons CO2e in 2024 to a mean of 7.5 in 2050 (likely range 6.1–8.6 gigatons), a 46% reduction. In the OECD, where energy systems and vehicle markets are more mature, cleaner power is accompanied by lower direct emissions from transport and buildings. Existing clean-technology adoption and its continued development reduce the emissions associated with economic activity, bringing OECD-wide emissions from 14.7 gigatons in 2024 to a mean of 10.0 in 2050 (likely range 8.9–11.1 gigatons), a 32% reduction.

Global power sector emissions fall, while emissions from industry remain stubbornly high

Turning to the sector level, global emissions from all major sectors have either grown or fluctuated around a long-term average over the past three decades. In our outlook, emissions from some sectors peak and decline. However, we anticipate progress across sectors will be uneven. The industry and power sectors were the two largest sources of global emissions in 2024, at 15.7 and 15.0 gigatons, respectively. They follow very different paths in our outlook. Power benefits from established, increasingly competitive wind and solar technologies, together with storage and other low-carbon sources. Many industrial processes still rely on fuels and chemical reactions for which low-emission alternatives are less widely deployed (Figure 5).

By 2050, we find that power emissions are expected to fall by 6.1 gigatons, or 40% below 2024 levels, on average, dropping to 9.0 gigatons. Power’s share of global emissions falls from about 28% in 2024 to 19% in 2050, moving it from the second largest to third largest source. Direct emissions from buildings also decline by 14% from 2024 levels, from 3.7 to 3.2 gigatons, as improvements in equipment and a growing role for electricity reduce direct fuel use. Transport moves in the opposite direction, however, rising by 3%, from 8.4 to 8.6 gigatons in our mean projection, as cleaner vehicles do not fully offset growth in road travel, aviation, and shipping. These divergent sectoral outcomes leave a much smaller reduction in total emissions than the power transition alone would suggest.

This larger role for wind and solar is accompanied by substantial storage deployment, which shifts electricity to periods when renewable output is lower. Mean global four-hour battery capacity rises from 89 GW in 2023 to about 3,240 GW in 2050, with a likely range of 2,270–4,210 GW. China reaches about 1,710 GW, up from 36 GW; the OECD reaches 880 GW, up from 52 GW; and the rest of the world reaches 650 GW, up from 2 GW.

Global electrification on track to reach 28% of total energy by 2035

Clean power can reduce emissions beyond the electricity sector as vehicles, buildings, and industry replace direct fossil-fuel use with electricity. As COP31 President, Türkiye announced the “35 by 35” Global Electrification Pledge and Action Agenda calling for increasing electricity’s share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035.

Electricity supplied about 21% of reported global final energy in 2024. In our outlook, that share rises to 28% in 2035 on average, with a likely range of 27–29% absent additional action to drive current market trends and policy further than their current glide path. Closing that gap would require faster replacement of direct fuel use, alongside the expansion of clean power.

There is considerable regional variation in electrification shares, however (Figure 11). In our baseline, China and OECD countries in Europe reach the highest electrification shares by 2035, but their starting points shape the story. China is all but guaranteed to meet the goal, as its share rises from 28% to a likely range of 37–40%. OECD countries in Europe make a substantial gain, climbing 14 percentage points from 20% to 34%, with the likely range (33–36%) spanning the target. We see similar progress in other parts of non-OECD Asia, which rises from 20% to 29% in the coming decade. India alone is expected to rise from 18% to 26%. Other regions starting from a low base, like Africa, Russia, and the Middle East, see less progress in the coming decade, however. In the next section, we explore the sectoral trends driving the different regional outcomes we see here.

The story of rising electrification rates is complex. In addition to rising electrification of end uses that have conventionally relied on fossil fuels, the rise of overall electric demand—driven by rising incomes and expanded electricity access, soaring cooling demand, and the emergence of power-hungry data centers—is also shifting the landscape for overall electrification rates and changing the importance of electric power as a core driver of economic growth and prosperity worldwide. The next section examines these differences in absolute demand and where the additional electricity goes.

Rising power demand in buildings drives global electric load growth; data center boom primarily a US story

The expansion of data centers and artificial intelligence has brought renewed attention to soaring electricity demand, but the sources of growth differ considerably across regions. Rhodium Group’s Taking Stock 2026 outlook for the US projects that data centers account for 62–77% of gross US electricity demand growth from 2025 to 2030. Globally, the picture is different: rising electricity use in homes, businesses, and transport contributes much more.

In our baseline, we project global electricity demand to rise by 46% between 2024 and 2035 on average (likely range of 37–54%). Demand from buildings—including demand for appliances, cooling, and heating but excluding data centers—contributes about 7,600 TWh of additional demand by 2035, or 60% of the mean increase of roughly 12,650 TWh. Power demand in buildings is expected to grow rapidly as rising incomes allow more households to acquire air conditioners and appliances, while expanding commercial activity increases electricity use in businesses. Warmer conditions further raise cooling requirements, partly offset by reduced heating needs. Our outlook incorporates Climate Impact Lab research to capture these opposing effects. Climate change is a significant driver of rising demand, but the broader expansion of electricity use also reflects economic development, equipment ownership, and the services that households and businesses consume.

Industry starts from a very different position, using about 13,600 TWh in 2024, nearly half of reported electricity demand. Its 1.7% net increase from 2024 to 2035 combines growth in chemicals, steel, and electricity used to produce hydrogen with lower use in other industry and refining. The pattern also differs by region: India’s industrial electricity demand increases by about 410 TWh, while China’s falls by about 570 TWh from 2024. Taking Stock projects US industrial electricity demand, including agriculture, to rise by about 45 TWh from 2025 to 2035 in its mid scenario.

As we highlight in the following section, growing electrification of transport is expected to account for 2,700 TWh, or 21%, of the global increase in electricity demand from 2024 to 2035, driven largely by the replacement of gasoline- and diesel-powered vehicles with electric models. Data centers contribute another 1,450 TWh, or 11%, with their growth concentrated in a smaller set of markets. Agriculture accounts for about 740 TWh, or 6%, while industry contributes 230 TWh, or 2%.

Buildings lead demand growth in both China and India, but the region-specific drivers differ. China adds about 3,640 TWh by 2035, or 29% of the global increase, with buildings and transport together adding 3,510 TWh, reflecting wider use of electric equipment and faster vehicle electrification. Lower industrial electricity use offsets a portion of that growth in China, however. India’s increase is smaller in absolute terms, about 1,620 TWh, but represents a doubling of demand in the course of just a decade. Buildings contribute 840 TWh, alongside increases in industry and agriculture as energy needs expand. Data centers remain a smaller driver in both: 12% of China’s net increase and 3% of India’s.

The US has a different balance. In Taking Stock’s mid scenario, data centers add about 380 TWh from 2025 to 2035, or 81% of the net increase of about 465 TWh. Transport adds about 120 TWh and industry, including agriculture, adds about 45 TWh, while buildings, excluding data centers, use about 75 TWh less electricity. Data centers consequently dominate the US demand increase.

In OECD countries in Europe, buildings and transport account for about 1,960 TWh, or 82%, of the increase. Vehicle emissions standards drive electric vehicle adoption, and in buildings, rising demand for air conditioning adds cooling load (buildings overall add about 1,090 TWh, or 45% of the region’s net increase), while electric heating shifts demand away from heating fuels. Heat pumps require less energy per unit of heat than resistance heating, and warmer weather reduces heating needs, so these changes do not translate one-for-one into electricity growth. Together, buildings and transport nevertheless add far more demand than data centers.

Electric vehicle sales rise rapidly, but slow fleet turnover keeps transport emissions stubbornly high

Electric vehicles are already changing new-car markets. EVs made up one-quarter of global new-car sales in 2025, marking a rapid scale-up, bringing EV shares of the global passenger vehicle fleet to a record 5%. In our outlook, the electric share of global light-duty vehicle sales reaches 40% in 2030 on average (35–45% likely range) and 71% in 2050 (62–80% likely range). Electrification proceeds more slowly in heavy-duty vehicles: their electric sales share rises from 3% in 2023 to 24% in 2030 on average, and 42% in 2050 (22–60% likely range) (Figure 13).

That uptake makes transport a substantial new source of electricity demand even before it delivers large reductions in the sector’s total emissions. Mean transport electricity use rises from an estimated 558 TWh in 2024 to 1,822 TWh in 2030 and 8,648 TWh in 2050 (6,610–10,598 TWh likely range) (Figure 13).

These emission reductions are offset by rising emissions across other industrial subsectors, however. Other-industry emissions—including paper and pulp, food production, and non-ferrous metals—rise 18% by mid-century from 2.9 to 3.4 gigatons, chemicals from 1.4 to 1.5 gigatons, and emissions from refining are expected to double (rising from 0.7 to 1.4 gigatons) in the next 25 years on average. Despite a likely decline in emissions from oil and gas production and coal-mining methane (with a 6% drop on average), together they remain the largest industrial source of emissions and could even increase in some pathways.

We also find that the geographic distribution of industrial emissions changes over the coming decades. China’s industrial emissions fall considerably by mid-century, dropping 28% on average, from 5.4 gigatons in 2024 to 3.9 in 2050, driven by structural population changes and the underway transition to a developed economy. We see the inverse of this occurring across India, Africa, and the Middle East, which together see emissions rise 36% on average, from 3.6 gigatons in 2024 to 4.9 by mid-century. Those three regions account for 31% of industrial emissions in 2050, up from 23% in 2024; China’s share falls from 34% to 25% (Figure 16). Growth in these markets offsets much of the reduction in emissions from China. The choices made when adding new production capacity will increasingly determine whether industrial emissions decline in absolute terms, rather than simply moving their center of growth.

text:
After years as collateral damage in Donald Trump’s war on climate action, the Democrats’ sweeping triumph in the US midterm elections has emerged as a victory for the global renewable energy industry too.

Across the world’s financial centres the market value of renewable energy developers climbed as the election results confirmed the Republicans had lost control of the Senate and House of Representatives.

For the world’s largest offshore wind developer, Ørsted, the shift in power could spell a reprieve from the White House’s assaults on the Danish company’s multibillion-dollar offshore wind investments off the north-east US coast.

Ørsted’s market value jumped by almost 10% within hours of the Democratic victory, before closing nearly 5% higher. The share price of other European renewables companies active in the US also climbed. Portugal’s EDP Renewables and the French utility Engie rose by more than 3%. Shares in Germany’s RWE added about 1%.

The clean energy market rally marks a modest boost for Ørsted, which has lost more than 70% of its market value since Trump returned to the White House in 2025 and resumed his salvoes against the industry as it struggled against fast-rising interest rates and supply chain pressures.

The White House has levelled multiple stop-orders against Ørsted’s Revolution Wind project since the re-election of Trump, a vocal supporter of the fossil fuel industry, who has repeatedly opposed the development of “ugly, costly and inefficient” windfarms in the US and abroad.

The impact has been chilling for the burgeoning US renewables sector too. The US is home to renewable energy projects with a combined capacity of 388 gigawatts, or enough to power more than 83m American homes. The sector also directly employs more than 400,000 people across the country.

This fleet of wind, solar, hydro and geothermal power projects has made up about 30% of the electricity generated across the US this year – well below the 50% share across the EU and China’s 40%.

While there is no binding US-wide clean energy target, there are 24 states, plus the District of Columbia, with plans to achieve 100% clean electricity or net zero carbon emissions between 2035 and 2050.

But there has been growing disquiet over whether the forecast surge in electricity-hungry AI datacentres poses a threat to green targets by increasing the US reliance on gas power plants – and energy costs.

“This was unquestioningly an energy election,” said Brenda Shaffer, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Global Energy Center. Rising concerns over energy costs and the looming impact of datacentres on energy supplies had played a key role in Republican defeat, she said.

The Democrats’ decisive control of the US House of Representatives and its majority in the Senate may reduce the risk of further political interference and bring fresh confidence to the US renewable energy industry, according to market analysts.

The Democratic house would be able to block further repeals of solar and wind tax credits, said Claudio Galimberti, the chief economist at the consultancy Rystad Energy. Battery storage credits would also now have a stronger defender in budget negotiations, and the administration’s roughly $4bn in offshore wind lease buybacks would face greater scrutiny, he added.

While it was too early to call this a turning point for US offshore wind, said Tancrede Fulop, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar in the Netherlands, the election outcome might lower the risk of further regulatory disruption and provide a more stable backdrop for projects under development.

“For companies that have spent the past few years dealing with regulatory delays and shifting political priorities, a more supportive backdrop should provide some much-needed confidence around projects already under development,” he said.

This in turn may ease investor jitters around regulatory uncertainty and support confidence in future project returns, according to analysts at Barclays, which could make new US renewable energy projects cheaper to finance.

The future was even brighter for developers hoping to build new onshore renewable energy projects, including batteries, which are typically decided at state level, said Shaffer.

A string of Republican states have turned blue – including Texas, Maine, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa and North and South Carolina – potentially ushering in greater support for clean energy investments.

The “blue wave” had made it clear that “affordable, reliable power is a priority”, according to Jason Grumet, the chief executive of the American Clean Power Association (ACP). “And our industry is ready to deliver it.”

text:
When Michelle Martinez talks about climate change, she does not begin with temperatures, emissions, or models and projections.

She begins with people. For Martinez, the inaugural director of the Tishman Center for Social Justice and the Environment at the University of Michigan (U-M), climate change is already being experienced through the housing, economic, and political crises confronting communities today. And that makes climate justice inseparable from a more basic civic question: Who has the power to decide what happens to a community?

The Tishman Center, established in 2021 at U-M’s School for Environment and Sustainability, was created around a particular idea of what a university can do in that struggle. Made possible through gifts from The NorthLight Foundation and Dan and Sheryl Tishman, the center connects students with environmental justice organizations and community leaders, supports community-led research, and prepares students to work on the problems communities are already facing.

That model grew partly from what Martinez felt was missing during her years working in environmental justice in Detroit.

“What I really needed from the university was a constant and steady support, with actionable research that could result in policy change,” she said.

Communities' needs, however, rarely follow the timetable of academic research. Environmental justice organizations may be responding to air pollution permits, legislative calendars, or the proposed siting of major developments while researchers are still developing a study.

“Communities like mine often need a more engaged and rapid response,” Martinez said, “but also a kind of scholarship that relies on relationship building.”

That distinction is central to how Martinez describes the Center's approach. The goal is not only to bring university expertise into communities, but to change how students and researchers understand their role.

“When we start to see ourselves as researchers, or as students in higher education, as participants in civic society, we can really start to change our orientation towards the expert,” she said.

The Center’s Climate Justice Movement Catalysts Fellowship reflects this idea by placing students in community organizations and supporting them with mentorship, financial assistance, and professional development. The Center describes the fellowship as a way to build leadership while contributing research and capacity to environmental justice organizations.

For Alexandrah Walker, a Catalyst Fellow working with the College of Menominee Nation’s Sustainable Development Institute, that relationship begins with listening. After first visiting the institute in January, she continued building relationships with its staff through summer visits and online meetings. Her work included mentoring undergraduate interns, helping them develop work plans, discussing their goals and troubleshooting challenges as they progressed.

“Working in/for/with community really requires you to cast your ego aside and what you think you know, and instead listen and strive to build healthy reciprocal relationships centered on trust and respect while being cognizant of cultural boundaries and customs,” Walker said.

Her experience illustrates the Center’s philosophy in practice. The work is not only about bringing knowledge acquired in a university into a community. It also requires students to build relationships, understand local contexts, and support people in pursuing their own goals.

In one example Martinez discussed, students worked with a Sikh community whose approach to sustainability was rooted in its cultural traditions. Practices such as energy efficiency and composting became more meaningful when they were connected to the community's existing values.

“Nobody was against those things, but by embedding it into cultural tradition, it had a place. It had a home,” Martinez said.

She described another project in northern Michigan involving tribal knowledge, land governance and technology. The work brought together efforts to reclaim Anishinaabe fire management practices with LiDAR technology and elders' knowledge. The point was not to replace community knowledge with technical expertise, but to bring different forms of knowledge into the same conversation.

That same approach is increasingly relevant as new pressures emerge.

Martinez is now working with roughly a dozen environmental justice organizations around the Great Lakes to understand how communities are thinking about the rapid growth of data centers. Many of these communities already live with the legacy of fossil-fuel infrastructure. Data centers introduce another major demand for energy and land, raising questions about who benefits from development and what communities want in return.

In Minnesota, Martinez recalled, organizers who had previously mobilized around protecting immigrant communities became involved in a fight over a proposed data center. When the city asked what the community wanted, the answer was not necessarily another technological solution. They wanted housing for people experiencing homelessness.

“The sort of intersectional approach, what civil society needs amidst climate chaos and political crises, is far more robust and responsive,” Martinez said.

For Martinez, this is part of what a just transition requires: communities having enough power to articulate what they actually want their future to look like.

“We really are trying to change the priorities of how people vision the future,” she said.

The Center's investment in students also extends beyond their time at Michigan.

Martinez pointed to Dr. Malu Castro, now a postdoctoral fellow at U-M’s School for Environment and Sustainability, as one example. Castro works with Kyle Whyte on Indigenous land restoration efforts and teaches courses on Indigenous sustainability and Indigenous rights. His scholarship grew from work on an ʻāina, or land, back initiative on Molokaʻi in Hawaiʻi, examining the theoretical and practical questions surrounding financing and pricing in Indigenous land restoration.

Martinez added that students with the resources, relationships, and space to pursue community-rooted work can carry those relationships into their scholarship and professional lives. The university becomes less of a place where knowledge is produced about communities and more of a place where people develop the capacity to work with them.

(The Center Square) - President Donald Trump’s energy dominance policies could face challenges after sweeping election victories by Democrats at both the state and national levels, energy market experts say.

When the new Congress is seated in January, incoming Democratic majorities are expected to push efforts to increase oversight of methane emissions, limit drilling on federal lands and in offshore areas, and tighten environmental permitting requirements on new plants and equipment.

Trump declared an energy emergency during his first hours in office in January 2025, invoking the National Emergencies Act to accelerate fossil fuel development. In a flurry of executive orders since then, the president has made U.S. energy dominance one of his primary economic objectives, framing it as a matter of national security.

Tom Pyle, president of the Washington-based American Energy Alliance , told The Center Square that attempts by newly elected Democratic majorities to roll back those executive actions will be neutralized by Trump’s veto pen.

"They can do Congressional Review Act resolutions on his rulemakings," Pyle said — referring to the fast-track legislative tool Congress can use to overturn federal rules adopted since the president took office. "They can pass them, but they’ll be vetoed."

Pyle noted that while a Democratic majority can leverage committee leadership positions to launch investigations and issue subpoenas, the president’s veto will still leave the Trump administration's core deregulatory agenda – and the sweeping legislative victories won through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed last year – largely intact.

“It’s one thing to make a bunch of campaign promises. It’s another thing to deliver on them," Pyle said. "Democrats will have a very difficult challenge if they intend to try to undo the very policies that President Trump has enacted that make it easier to produce energy, easier to move it around this country."

Pyle said election results at the state level are a reason to worry. “The story of the night is Texas — it really was a wipeout,” said Pyle. “Texas Democrats will need to tread very carefully because oil and gas is their bread and butter. It will be interesting to see how the Democrats in Texas treat the industry there,” said Pyle.

Ed Hirs, an energy fellow and energy economist at the University of Houston, said the Democrats' control of Congress will have little effect on U.S. energy production. He said it is global markets and prices — not Washington politics — that really drive American energy production.

America had energy dominance under President Biden, too, and had approached it during the Obama years, Hirs said. Now, with energy prices high because of geopolitical events, the nation’s oil and gas production is at a new record level, said Hirs.

“Trump has ensured the energy dominance of the United States, perhaps inadvertently, by undertaking this war against Iran,” Hirs told The Center Square. “We are now facing several years of having higher oil and LNG prices, which will benefit the United States, for sure.”

While gross national product will be higher, gasoline prices will be, too, said Hirs. “But prices are higher because of the war, not because of market conditions,” he said.

Hirs added that high global crude oil prices have begun to depress consumption in the United States. "U.S. consumption of crude and refined products dropped by more than 2% last year because of those higher prices,” said Hirs.

title: Disentangling the economic opportunities of onshoring EV production in Brazil
description:
Despite the rapid growth of EV sales, Brazil’s EV manufacturing industry remains in its infancy, with only three automakers assembling completely knocked-down (CKD) and semi knocked-down (SKD) kits domestically.
It estimates the economic potential of gradually onshoring EV manufacturing, battery production, and charging infrastructure investments in Brazil, and compares these estimates with recent trends in the internal combustion engine vehicle (ICEV) industry.
To provide a comprehensive analysis of the EV value chain, this study uses multiregional input-output data to obtain a detailed picture of the economic potential of onshoring EV production.
We assess three scenarios to model a growing extent of onshoring: the CKD Assembly scenario, in which onshoring is limited to CKD assembly; the Onshoring No Battery scenario, in which EV production is localized with no domestic battery production; and the Full Onshoring scenario, representing onshoring of the entire EV production process, including battery production.
In this context, we find that the gradual onshoring of EV production can capture substantial VA, even without domestic battery production.
text:
Electric vehicles (EVs) are reshaping global automotive production. In 2025, one in four new cars sold worldwide were electric; in Brazil, battery electric vehicles comprised 7% of light-duty vehicle sales in the first half of 2026, more than double the market share observed in 2025. Electrification has disrupted traditional market dynamics, as many legacy automakers have struggled to keep pace with emergent EV-native manufacturers.

Despite the rapid growth of EV sales, Brazil’s EV manufacturing industry remains in its infancy, with only three automakers assembling completely knocked-down (CKD) and semi knocked-down (SKD) kits domestically. Moreover, the assembly of imported EVs alone adds limited domestic content to production. Brazilian policymakers are now faced with difficult questions and trade-offs concerning how much to protect the country’s flex fuel-dominant auto industry or, conversely, to build domestic EV manufacturing capacity. The first choice risks a sizable increase in EV imports in the coming years, as further reductions in EV purchase prices are expected to drive rising sales. The second choice is promising but not easy, and entails several fundamental policy questions: How can Brazil upgrade its industrial capacities in EV manufacturing? Which parts of the value chain are worth pursuing and incentivizing?

This report seeks to quantify the prospective economic benefits of producing EVs in Brazil. It estimates the economic potential of gradually onshoring EV manufacturing, battery production, and charging infrastructure investments in Brazil, and compares these estimates with recent trends in the internal combustion engine vehicle (ICEV) industry. The results focus on value added (VA)—which measures the portion of output value that is converted into national income in the form of gross domestic product—to understand which production steps hold greater economic potential and which industries stand to gain from onshoring EV production.

To provide a comprehensive analysis of the EV value chain, this study uses multiregional input-output data to obtain a detailed picture of the economic potential of onshoring EV production. We increment the input-output data with a synthetic industry for EV manufacturing and a new industry for battery production while also capturing the potential of charging infrastructure investments. We assess three scenarios to model a growing extent of onshoring: the CKD Assembly scenario, in which onshoring is limited to CKD assembly; the Onshoring No Battery scenario, in which EV production is localized with no domestic battery production; and the Full Onshoring scenario, representing onshoring of the entire EV production process, including battery production.

The results show that, independent of the EV transition, Brazil’s ICEV industry has experienced a decline in domestic content. The share of imported inputs used in domestic ICEV production increased from 10% in 2010 to 16% in 2022, while imported VA almost doubled in the same period, reaching 28%. This trend suggests a structural change in the country’s automotive industry in which higher VA parts and processes have been gradually offshored.

In this context, we find that the gradual onshoring of EV production can capture substantial VA, even without domestic battery production. In our scenario analysis, CKD assembly alone resulted in a significant loss of domestic income compared with current ICEV manufacturing in Brazil. For every $1 spent on EVs, only about one quarter was converted into domestic VA. Upgrading Brazil’s participation in the EV value chain to produce all core EV components resulted in an 83% projected increase in domestic VA under the Onshoring No Battery scenario when compared with the CKD Assembly scenario; this scenario also achieved a VA multiplier much closer to that of current ICEV production. Finally, the Full Onshoring scenario increased domestic VA by 56% in comparison to the Onshoring No Battery scenario and achieved a VA multiplier higher than that of the ICEV industry.

Figure ES1 illustrates the domestic VA generated in these three scenarios, plus a scenario with full onshoring that also accounts for the charging infrastructure investments that would be required to accommodate a moderate increase in EV adoption by 2030. Across all scenarios, substantial portions of domestic VA accrued to high-skill service industries such as legal, financial, and advertising services, as well as to wholesale and retail trade (including dealerships). In the Onshoring No Battery and Full Onshoring scenarios, manufacturing industries such as EV manufacturing, battery manufacturing, metals, and chemicals captured about half of domestic VA.

We also find that Brazil is well positioned to upgrade its role in the EV value chain through the provision of industrial incentives conditioned by measurable performance criteria and limited to a pre-determined duration. Based on the modern industrial policy literature, and considering the results of the study, this analysis supports the following policy recommendations:

Use existing incentives—made conditional on firm performance and with pre-established phaseout dates—to align the domestic content of Brazil’s EV production with its industrial capabilities in the near term. For example, the Brazilian government could stand firm on phasing out current SKD and, perhaps shortly after, CKD quotas by January 2027 (Moraes, 2026). This would avoid the risk associated with turning these quotas into a permanently extendable benefit, which could further delay the expansion of EV manufacturing operations beyond assembly.

Adjust current policies supporting EV adoption to establish feasible and increasing local content requirements. For instance, policymakers could include domestic content requirements for light-duty vehicles as a qualifying criterion for Brazil’s new selective tax on polluting vehicles, in addition to vehicle emissions (Lei Complementar nº 214, 2025). This would help encourage consumers to purchase EVs with higher domestic content compared with imports.

Create favorable conditions for battery cell manufacturing in the long term by incentivizing upstream and downstream nodes of the battery value chain. Among other measures, Brazil could extend eligibility for incentivized bond issuance (debêntures de infraestrutura and debêntures incentivadas) further downstream. The current framework already covers some battery-grade materials such as lithium carbonate and nickel sulfate (Portaria Normativa MME nº 120, 2025), but policymakers could extend the framework to more active materials such as iron phosphate and lithium iron phosphate as well as battery pack and cell assembly. On the demand side, maintaining a stable and predictable schedule of battery energy storage system capacity auctions could help attract battery-related investments alongside EV demand (Rocha, 2026).

text:
Democrats won both chambers, but the White House still holds the veto pen. We ran the override math, checked how past split governments got deals done, and lined up the energy fights that matter for prices: tax credits, permitting and LNG.

By Energy News Beat | Nov. 4, 2026 | Results as of mid-morning Central

If you filled up this morning, you paid an average of $4.124 for a gallon of regular, according to AAA. A year ago it was $3.053. Diesel is $6.275, up from $3.694. Voters noticed, and on Tuesday they handed Democrats both chambers of Congress. So the question at the kitchen table is a fair one: does a Democratic Congress make that number go down, go up, or do nothing at all? Here is what we can verify this morning, and what we cannot.

What was actually called

The Associated Press projects Democrats will control both the House and the Senate. Ballotpedia and Politico report Democrats flipped seven Senate seats, in Kansas, Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina, while holding Georgia and Michigan; The Guardian shows them gaining more than two dozen House districts.

The counts are still moving. As of about 9 a.m. Eastern, The Guardian had the Senate at 54 Democrats, counting two independents, to 44 Republicans, with 33 of 35 races called. Ballotpedia, as of 1:30 a.m. Eastern, had the same Senate split and a House majority of at least 231 to 141; the Guardian later had the House at 228 to 139 with 367 seats called. Many House seats remain uncalled, so the final House margin is not known.

Two Senate races are open. In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom led Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by 43 votes, 462,821 to 462,778, with about 44,000 ballots left, per WDAM. In Alaska, AFP had Democrat Mary Peltola ahead of Sen. Dan Sullivan 48.2 to 47.9 percent with 74 percent counted, but the lead has changed hands overnight in other outlets’ counts. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, and a result may take weeks.

The veto math

Here is the number that matters most. Under Article I, Section 7 of the Constitution, Congress overrides a veto only with two-thirds of those present and voting in each chamber. With every seat filled and every member voting, that is 67 senators and 290 House members.

Democrats have 54 Senate seats now and 56 at most. They would need at least 11 Republicans, and 13 at the current count, to override. In the House, with at least 231 seats, they would need about 59 Republicans. President Trump knows it. He told CBS News “I think they’re gonna want to work with me. Otherwise I’d just veto everything and they’re not gonna want that.”

History backs him up on the odds. Per the Senate’s veto table, Trump issued 10 regular vetoes in his first term and Congress overrode one. In this term he has vetoed two bills, and neither was overridden. President Obama was overridden once in 12 vetoes and President Biden never in 13.

Gridlock or deals? What 2011 and 2019 tell us

Divided government has not meant zero laws. In 2011, with a Republican House, a Democratic Senate and President Obama, the debt-ceiling standoff ended in the Budget Control Act, which passed the House 269 to 161 and the Senate 74 to 26 and was signed Aug. 2, 2011.

The closest match to today is 2019 and 2020: a Democratic House, a Republican Senate and President Trump. On Dec. 18, 2019, the House impeached him. The next day, the same House passed the USMCA trade deal 385 to 41, and it became law in January 2020. That August, Trump signed the Great American Outdoors Act, which cleared the Senate 73 to 25 and the House 310 to 107.

The biggest energy law of that era rode on a spending bill. The December 2020 omnibus, which passed the Senate 92 to 6, carried the Energy Act of 2020 as Division Z, plus an HFC phasedown and carbon-capture provisions, and tax extenders including the wind production credit through 2021 and the 45Q carbon-capture credit through 2025. Days later, Congress overrode Trump’s veto of the defense bill, 322 to 87 in the House (roll call 253) and 81 to 13 in the Senate. That is what it takes: a must-pass bill with big Republican support.

The lesson for energy is that deals happen when they ride on must-pass bills and draw large bipartisan margins. Stand-alone partisan bills mostly die at the veto.

The IRA credits: what is already gone

The 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Public Law 119-21, rewrote the Inflation Reduction Act. Per the IRS, the new and used EV credits ended for vehicles bought after Sept. 30, 2025. The home efficiency and rooftop solar credits ended for work after Dec. 31, 2025. For wind and solar farms, IRS Notice 2025-42 says the main credits end for projects placed in service after Dec. 31, 2027, unless construction began by July 4, 2026.

That July 2026 date has passed, so the wind and solar cliff is already set unless Congress changes the law and Trump signs it. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer has vowed to restore clean energy credits, Axios reports, but Axios also calls some IRA restoration ideas “largely symbolic” for now. One analyst told DW, “It’s not going to be anything at the scale of the IRA.” The likelier openings are narrower: home efficiency, the manufacturing credit that largely survived, and advanced nuclear.

Permitting: the deal that could move first

The one energy bill with real momentum is permitting reform. The House passed the SPEED Act 221 to 196 in December 2025; it sits in a Senate committee. In the Senate, a bipartisan package negotiated with the White House, the American Affordability and Jobs Act, could see votes as early as Nov. 9, ENR reports. It would shorten environmental reviews and the window for lawsuits, and require data-center developers to pay the power costs of running their facilities. The two bills would still have to be reconciled.

That makes the lame-duck session, before new members are sworn in, the window to watch. Axios reports that some House progressives think they can get a better deal next year, while backers see almost no chance of a more liberal bill Trump would sign. Unions, the American Petroleum Institute and contractor groups back the bill; some environmental groups and Rep. Rashida Tlaib, who called it a “gift to big oil and big tech,” oppose it.

What Sen. Armstrong told ENB

Sen. Alan Armstrong, R-Okla., joined the ENB podcast on Wednesday (ENB interview). The former Williams Companies CEO was appointed to the U.S. Senate by Gov. Kevin Stitt and sworn in March 24; his term ends Jan. 3, 2027, and he did not run in November (Senate bio, AP). He said that when the Senate returns Nov. 9, “the first vote on the floor will be a cloture vote for the permitting reform bill, which is an incredibly powerful bill if we can get it across the floor.” That matches ENR’s reporting. The House is harder: “getting it through the House here by the end of the year and by the time the new Congress comes in is going to be a real challenge.”

Asked about other Republican priorities before January, he said “there is not going to be any time for anything new coming into the process.” Members can still file bills in a lame duck. Stu’s reading is that floor time, not filing, is the limit, so the permitting bill already before the Senate is the realistic shot at lower energy costs this year.

To lawmakers: the thin-majority lesson

Armstrong said constituents keep asking why Republicans did not just pass their agenda: “You control the House and the Senate.” His answer: “We don’t control the Senate with 53 votes.” Under the 60-vote rule, he said, “You have to be very clear about what your priorities are in a situation where you have 53 votes and need 60.”

He described what happened instead. Ahead of the midterms, “we as a caucus chose to put NIL, the NIL bill ahead of permitting reform as a priority on the floor because it was a popular issue,” and floor time went to votes taken “just to say you voted on it.” Meanwhile gas peaked at $4.50 and, per Grist and Axios, voters were angry about prices. ENB cannot prove one caused the other, but Stu reads it as the core lesson: a thin majority that spends its floor time on message votes gives voters nothing to show at the pump.

The new majority faces the same math. In a Senate of 54 to 56 Democrats, Armstrong expects a handful of Republicans able to side with Democrats to hold outsized sway: “There’s going to be four to six people who will have a lot of power.” His advice, from running a company: the “most important thing you can do is agree on what the top priorities are and keep everybody aligned on those.”

LNG export approvals

LNG export approvals sit with the Department of Energy under the Natural Gas Act, not with Congress. As of Sept. 30, DOE had issued 45 long-term authorizations to export to any allowed country, totaling 55.9 billion cubic feet a day. U.S. export capacity is more than 20 Bcf a day, and over 38 Bcf a day is operating or under construction. A Democratic Congress can hold hearings and use spending bills, but it cannot reverse those approvals without a law Trump would sign or Congress could pass over his veto.

What it means for your prices

Gasoline follows crude oil, refining and taxes far more than any bill Congress passes. EIA weekly data show regular averaged about $2.94 in late February 2026, then jumped to $3.96 by late March and peaked at $4.50 the week of May 11. Grist and Axios both tie voter anger to those prices, and Grist also points to the war with Iran. As of Nov. 4, the AAA

Power bills are rising almost everywhere. In August, U.S. residential electricity averaged 18.16 cents a kilowatt-hour, up from 17.57 a year earlier, per EIA. In the states where Democrats flipped Senate seats, Maine rose from 28.14 to 32.11 cents, Ohio from 17.55 to 19.38 and Iowa from 15.48 to 17.06. California, at 29.75 cents, was still among the highest in the nation, but it was down from 30.92.

How consumers and investors are reading it

For households, the near-term watch list is data-center cost rules, any affordability package from the House, and whether a spending deal restores bill-help or efficiency money. Axios reports Democrats plan an affordability agenda with energy as a key pillar, but no detailed energy plan has been released.

For investors, the bigger risk is not new law but new uncertainty. Wind and solar developers face a 2027 placed-in-service deadline that only a signed law can move. LNG and pipeline developers face more oversight hearings, but DOE approvals stand. One commentary, citing MIT research, argues permitting, not tax credits, is the binding limit on how fast new power can be built (The Rebuild). Industry groups told Congress in October that permitting reform can “help improve energy affordability” (ENR).

Caveats and criticism

Control of Congress is an AP projection, and seat counts will change as votes are counted. Two Senate seats are uncalled. None of the new members takes office until January. Party-line comparisons of state prices show correlation, not cause: fuel mix, weather, wildfire liability and grid rules all matter. Critics on the left say the permitting bill weakens environmental review; critics on the right say any return of the IRA credits will raise federal spending and bills. Neither side has bill text from the new majority yet.

title: Trump's veto could limit Democrats' energy policy changes | National | thecentersquare.com
description: (The Center Square) - President Donald Trump’s energy dominance policies could face challenges after sweeping election victories by Democrats at both the state and national levels, energy market experts say.
text:
President Donald Trump at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., March 4, 2025. Official White House Photo via Flickr / United States Government Work

(The Center Square) - President Donald Trump’s energy dominance policies could face challenges after sweeping election victories by Democrats at both the state and national levels, energy market experts say.

When the new Congress is seated in January, incoming Democratic majorities are expected to push efforts to increase oversight of methane emissions, limit drilling on federal lands and in offshore areas, and tighten environmental permitting requirements on new plants and equipment.

Trump declared an energy emergency during his first hours in office in January 2025, invoking the National Emergencies Act to accelerate fossil fuel development. In a flurry of executive orders since then, the president has made U.S. energy dominance one of his primary economic objectives, framing it as a matter of national security.

Tom Pyle, president of the Washington-based American Energy Alliance , told The Center Square that attempts by newly elected Democratic majorities to roll back those executive actions will be neutralized by Trump’s veto pen.

"They can do Congressional Review Act resolutions on his rulemakings," Pyle said — referring to the fast-track legislative tool Congress can use to overturn federal rules adopted since the president took office. "They can pass them, but they’ll be vetoed."

Pyle noted that while a Democratic majority can leverage committee leadership positions to launch investigations and issue subpoenas, the president’s veto will still leave the Trump administration's core deregulatory agenda – and the sweeping legislative victories won through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed last year – largely intact.

“It’s one thing to make a bunch of campaign promises. It’s another thing to deliver on them," Pyle said. "Democrats will have a very difficult challenge if they intend to try to undo the very policies that President Trump has enacted that make it easier to produce energy, easier to move it around this country."

Pyle said election results at the state level are a reason to worry. “The story of the night is Texas — it really was a wipeout,” said Pyle. “Texas Democrats will need to tread very carefully because oil and gas is their bread and butter. It will be interesting to see how the Democrats in Texas treat the industry there,” said Pyle.

Ed Hirs, an energy fellow and energy economist at the University of Houston, said the Democrats' control of Congress will have little effect on U.S. energy production. He said it is global markets and prices — not Washington politics — that really drive American energy production.

America had energy dominance under President Biden, too, and had approached it during the Obama years, Hirs said. Now, with energy prices high because of geopolitical events, the nation’s oil and gas production is at a new record level, said Hirs.

“Trump has ensured the energy dominance of the United States, perhaps inadvertently, by undertaking this war against Iran,” Hirs told The Center Square. “We are now facing several years of having higher oil and LNG prices, which will benefit the United States, for sure.”

While gross national product will be higher, gasoline prices will be, too, said Hirs. “But prices are higher because of the war, not because of market conditions,” he said.

Hirs added that high global crude oil prices have begun to depress consumption in the United States. "U.S. consumption of crude and refined products dropped by more than 2% last year because of those higher prices,” said Hirs.

Updated on Nov. 4, 2026 at 8:26 p.m. CT

Republican State Rep. Brandun Schweizer has conceded the State House 104th District race to his Democratic challenger Mary Catherine Roberson. In a Facebook post, he congratulated his opponent and said that his office is available for a smooth transition.

“We will do everything we can to ensure that constituent services continue as seamlessly as possible,” Schweizer wrote. “Because at the end of the day, this position has never been about any one person or political party. It’s about the people we have the privilege of serving.

“I will be praying for you, for wisdom in the decisions you make, for strength during the difficult days, and for success in doing what is best for the families and communities of East Central Illinois. When you succeed in serving our district, our communities succeed, and that is something we should all want.”

As of November 4, 2026, the Associated Press reported Roberson leading Schweizer with 51.3% of the vote and 15,211 votes to his 14,266 across the district.

Roberson is a lifelong resident of Danville. She currently serves as an aide to U.S. Rep. Robin Kelly of Illinois’ 2nd congressional district. The mother of three also worked with the Champaign County Community Coalition to develop the Community Gun Violence Reduction Blueprint.

In a September 2026 interview with IPM News, Roberson said the loss of jobs is the most pressing challenge in the district. She proposed trainee programs for developing industries as a possible solution.

“I think partnering with Parkland and Danville Area Community College and ensuring that we’re on the front end of clean energy jobs, so that when they come we have the workforce to support them,” said Roberson.

Updated on Nov. 4, 2026 at 1:08 a.m. CT

With the polls closed, results across East Central Illinois are coming in for this year’s midterm election.

Since mail-in votes may still be counted if they are postmarked and arrive up to two weeks after Election Day, some races may remain too close to call Tuesday night.

Voters in the area went to the polls for several races, including the Champaign County Clerk, County Sheriff, Illinois’ 13th congressional district and a competitive race for District 104 in the State House. Several school and local school and municipal proposals were also on the ballot.

East Central Illinois unofficial election results

Vote tallies are listed below according to the Champaign County Clerk’s office and the Illinois State Board of Elections. These numbers will be updated as additional ballots are counted.

Champaign County Clerk (4-year term)

Aaron Ammons (D-incumbent): 35,415

Alan Anderson (R): 30,670

Champaign County Sheriff (4-year term)

Dustin D. Heuerman (D-incumbent): 47,306

Gregory A. Worrell (R): 20,542

Unofficial results show Democratic incumbent Dustin Heuerman has defeated Republican challenger Gregory Worrell.

In his third term as sheriff, Heuerman said he will focus on reducing gun violence — and ensuring law enforcement responds appropriately to people having mental health crises.

“My goal is to make sure that Champaign County is as safe as possible, and, you know, we’re serving the Champaign County residents to our best ability,” he said.

The sheriff has been in office since 2018 and was reelected in 2022.

Yes: 21,395

No: 10,780

Mahomet-Seymour school bond referendum

Shall the Board of Education of Mahomet-Seymour Community Unit School District Number 3, Champaign and Piatt Counties, Illinois, build and equip a new Junior High School Building, improve the site thereof, and issue bonds of said School District to the amount of $84,000,000 for the purpose of paying the costs thereof?

Yes: 4,931

No: 2,266

Rantoul ballot questions

Shall the Village of Rantoul abandon the method of electing trustees from districts so that trustees shall be hereafter elected on a village wide basis?

Yes: 1,576

No: 1,260

Shall the Village of Rantoul allow cannabis businesses to locate and operate within the village?

Yes: 1,612

No: 1,236

Voters in Rantoul appear to have approved a referendum to elect village trustees to at-large seats instead of by district.

The decision would reverse a 2018 referendum that divided the village into six districts.

“All of the six trustees would be elected at-large, which means that everyone in the village that is registered to vote would be able to vote for [the] trustees,” said Rantoul Mayor Sam Hall.

Rantoul voters also supported passage of an advisory referendum to overturn the village’s current ban on cannabis dispensaries.

Hall said the referendum would still need approval from the village board.

“It could mean revenue that we don’t have if we, you know, go down that road. So that’s always good to think about is additional revenue, but for now we got to clear a few hurdles.”

Rantoul trustees first voted in 2019 to prohibit cannabis-related companies from operating within the village borders.

Illinois Pension Code advisory referenda

Shall the State of Illinois repeal amendments to the Illinois Pension Code that penalize American businesses for boycotting the State of Israel?

Champaign Township:

Yes: 3,416

No: 2,114

Cunningham Township:

Yes: 7,922

No: 3,282

Voters in Cunningham and Champaign Townships approved advisory referendum questions supporting the repeal of an Illinois law that prohibits the state’s pension fund from investing in companies that boycott Israel.

The referendum is non-binding – so the results do not change state law.

But supporters of the repeal, like Urbana resident Bryan Maxwell, say they hope it sends a message to lawmakers.

“We’re just trying to signal to lawmakers that a majority of Americans don’t support constitutional rights being undermined by a foreign government,” he said. “They don’t approve of being weaponized against Illinois workers.”

Six other townships across the state — in Oak Park, Normal, DuPage, Medina, Kickapoo and Peoria — also voted in favor of similar referendum questions.

text:
MARY LOUISE KELLY, HOST:

Today is a day for all of the superlatives. Unbelievable, unprecedented, stunning - just a few of the words being used to describe Democratic victories across the country in midterm elections.

AILSA CHANG, HOST:

And just to recap, Democrats won majorities in both houses of Congress, picking up at least seven seats in the Senate. Two races in Mississippi and Alaska are still too close to call. Democrats also took control of the House, flipping more than two dozen seats, with races yet to be called.

KELLY: They also picked up five governorships. They captured control of at least nine state legislative houses. So how did they do it? And what might Democratic control of Congress look like? Those are a couple of the questions I'm going to put now to NPR White House correspondent Emily Feng, congressional reporter Eric McDaniel and senior political editor and correspondent Domenico Montanaro. We got a whole team here. Domenico, I'm going to throw you the question that I had waking up this morning. Did the Democrats win or did the Republicans lose?

DOMENICO MONTANARO, BYLINE: Yeah, it's not really an either-or. Clearly, the overriding factor, though, was Donald Trump. I mean, his unpopularity, the war in Iran, rising prices, the growing gap between the uber-rich and the middle class. I mean, some $12 billion spent on this election while other people are struggling to buy gas. All of that together created a huge backlash, maybe call it a Trump-lash. Democrats, though, also did recruit very good candidates. You don't win in places like Iowa, Texas, Kansas as Democrats without candidates who can make the most of the moment and be good fits for their states. They showed real level of authenticity. That will give them a big opportunity to show what Democrats did wasn't just a big midterm asterisk.

KELLY: And one more to you, Domenico, because we've been talking a lot, you and I, about polling these last few weeks. Were the polls going to work? Could we trust them? In the end, they did all right.

MONTANARO: In the end, they did do OK. You know, they pointed in the right direction. If anything, they underestimated Democratic support. But we don't know how many people decided late, you know, after when the polls had been conducted before the election. And things usually do break in one direction in midterms. It happened in 2006. It happened again in this election. Polls predicted Democrats plus 8 on the generic congressional ballot. It wound up being bigger, closer to plus 13, which is massive and no one would have believed it beforehand. Even with the underestimation, all the signs were there for a pretty big wave with what the polls were showing, but people were rightfully cautious given the polling errors we've seen over the past decade that had underestimated Republican support.

KELLY: Yeah.

MONTANARO: It's just very difficult in this age, when there's been such a major political realignment, to poll.

KELLY: Eric McDaniel, you cover Congress.

ERIC MCDANIEL, BYLINE: Indeed, I do.

KELLY: Lucky you. Here's my question to you. What happens immediately? Because Republicans still control the House and the Senate for the next couple months. Does anything change between now and January?

MCDANIEL: Well, I mean, it only gets harder for Republicans, right? They've got a narrow majority right now in the House, a small majority in the Senate. But good luck to them getting every one of those folks who lost back into Washington to pass legislation on a party-line basis. There's not a lot of incentive...

KELLY: Yeah.

MCDANIEL: ...To come back to town. And that's important stuff. That's government funding. That's more money for the Iran war. They also have to figure out what their leadership looks like next. Our friend Barbara Sprunt is reporting that current Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, Republican of Louisiana, he won't seek reelection as the top House Republican. That sets up a battle between at least two folks, Jim Jordan of Ohio and Steve Scalise of Louisiana. Jim Jordan's pugnacious. He's a brawler. He could be dispositionally well suited to counter Democrats' investigation-heavy agenda. Scalise is sort of a party man. He's a committed Trump ally, but generally seen as less pugnacious than Jordan.

But - and this is speculation on my part - I think there's probably an appetite for someone willing to take a more Trump-skeptical stance as a party leader - right? - given the mollywhopping voters just delivered the party because of the president.

KELLY: Yeah. And then agenda? I mean, how do we expect Democrats are going to use their newfound majorities come January?

MCDANIEL: They'll act on the things they campaigned on. That's cost of living. That's perceived political corruption. They talk about cost of living from healthcare to housing. But with Trump still in the White House, I don't expect that those bills will absolutely become law. In perceived public corruption, expect bills on lawmaker stock trading and then investigations into investigations into investigations - every part of Trump's life from his administration's agenda and the extent of his relationship with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The likely incoming House oversight chair, Robert Garcia, Democrat of California, posted on Twitter last night, simply, lawyer up.

KELLY: Lawyer up. Sounds ominous. Emily Feng, hop in here. What's the mood at the White House like today?

EMILY FENG, BYLINE: Yeah, so I am at the White House today. It's quiet, but it's also surreal, and that's because the president has had one public event so far today, and it was not about the election. It was to talk about his East Wing ballroom construction project. He had hundreds of construction workers who were building it come in. And at this event, he spent most of his time talking about the quality of the marble that he was using and his new helipad and really not about the election. However, last night, a White House official told NPR that the mood watching these results come in was, quote, "defiant at the White House." And then today, Trump's Truth Social media account shared a picture of a red hat with the word veto written on it because Trump has said he is going to veto most bills brought to him by a Democratic Congress.

More broadly, the sense I get is the mood in the Republican Party is one of confusion and of soul searching. As my colleagues have just pointed out, these midterms were a big rebuke of Trump himself. He has been quick to point out he was not literally on the ballot, but voters rejected his policies, you know, his economic policies and tariffs, the war in Iran. And even his own vice president today, JD Vance, broke with Trump and wrote on X that he thinks one of the primary reasons behind Republican losses was the war in Iran. So today, when Trump was celebrating, you know, the last steel ceiling beam that was being put in place in the ballroom project, reporters asked him if he regretted, perhaps, the Iran war costing the GOP the House and the Senate, and he said this.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: Probably it's true, but at the same time, if I had it to do again, I'd have to do it again because long-term, it's the only answer. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon.

KELLY: Interesting. So, I mean, Emily, is there any sign, any indication that President Trump might be willing to change course with the war in Iran?

FENG: He seemed to soften his stance a little today. He said today he could end the war, quote, "anytime" he wanted. He said last night on Fox & Friends that he would still strike Iran, though, if Iran, quote, "does not behave." But also that the two countries could have a diplomatic ending to this, that they could sign something to end the war. He has warned that any new major strikes would happen after the midterms, but he's already said he will not use nuclear weapons. He told Politico last night he does not need to use nuclear weapons against Iran.

KELLY: Eric, back to you. One of the outgrowths of the war in Iran has, of course, been high diesel prices, high gas prices. Affordability, affordability, affordability, which was a huge factor in the election, we're told.

MCDANIEL: Such a huge factor.

KELLY: Yeah. I mean, can congressional Democrats do much about that? Can they bring prices down when they aren't going to control the White House for at least two years?

MCDANIEL: I mean, let's see, right? Democrats can send bills to the president's desk, but they can't make him sign. That said, they can make a real stink about the fact that they've made changes they say would be positive for the American people and that the president is, say, standing in their way. That kind of public pressure could matter. The president wants to be liked. He's signaled some openness to dealmaking. And there's leverage, like government funding, getting rid of the filibuster, confirming the president's picks to various posts, that could help grease the wheels of dealmaking. But it's not going to be easy for Democrats, but I don't want to pretend like movement is impossible either.

KELLY: Do Democrats feel like they have a mandate? Did voters give them a mandate?

MCDANIEL: I mean, I don't know that there is such a thing as a mandate in today's political environment, right? This was about the president - 38% approval rating, 70% of the public peeved about the war in Iran. Gas prices up 40% year over year. Democrats had the right message about how to address it, but their favorability rating as a party is still minus 14. Chuck Schumer's among the most disliked men in America. Domenico can talk about this more, but last night saw huge swings across demographics, groups that had swung to President Trump in 2024. And so now Democrats have to do the hard work convincing those folks to stay in their corner. This isn't a captured electorate, by any means.

KELLY: Yeah, this is the problem, Domenico - right? - with you win an election, and you inherit the problems and they become yours. What risks come with these wins for Democrats?

MONTANARO: Yeah, I mean, right now, Democrats are the dog that caught the car. So can they drive, right? I mean, they can do a lot of things here. They can block judges and cabinet members. They can stop Trump's legislative agenda, whatever that winds up being, if he would have wanted to do anything. But they really have to be careful on how they message this and not to overpromise and underdeliver. I mean, that's something voters have become all too familiar with from politicians in Washington.

The reality is it's unlikely Democrats are going to have a real good-faith negotiating partner in Republicans in trying to get big things done. And it's looking like Donald Trump is not wanting to be a Bill Clinton, Newt Gingrich-style triangulator. So, you know, look to the states. Democrats flipped a bunch of state legislatures and will have trifectas in state governance in some key places. So while Washington maybe will be mired in inertia, it's the states that will be the incubators for policy, and we'll see how those policies are received by voters, particularly in purple and red states.

KELLY: All right. That's one thing to keep an eye on. Let me do a quick lightning round and just run through what else we should be watching for as we try to make sense of what just happened. Eric?

MCDANIEL: I'll let my colleagues take the serious stuff. I've got a fun one. Nonvoting members. There are more than a million Americans, like many of us who live in this city, who lack voting representation in Congress. But there's a fresh-faced class of new nonvoting members from the Virgin Islands, Guam and, yes, Washington, D.C., going to the Hill to advocate for civil rights for those they represent.

KELLY: Excellent. Domenico?

MONTANARO: I mean, 2028 starts now. January and February, we're going to see announcements probably for the presidency - presidential candidacies. And Trump and this Trump-lash, how is that going to reshape the Republican field? I guarantee you there's going to be more people running now than they - than who would have before.

KELLY: Trump-lash. We shall watch for it. Emily, you get the last word.

FENG: Two things from me. Given that the economy and gas prices are concerns for voters, the easiest way to address that would be to end the war with Iran. So will there be serious diplomatic negotiations again with Iran? And a second thing - in about two weeks, Trump heads to China. He's going to meet with the Chinese leader again, maybe even Russia's Vladimir Putin. So I'm curious, now that he's more constrained at home, will he try to make some kind of grand foreign policy bargain abroad with these heads of state?

KELLY: That's NPR's Emily Feng, Eric McDaniel and Domenico Montanaro. Thanks to all three of you. Please go get some sleep now (laughter).

MONTANARO: Great to be here.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.
