name: Congress
title: Can the Blue Wave Help Keep the Amazon Green?
description:
Prior diplomatic backing for environmental and human rights defenders evaporated.
Investigations could focus on the most nefarious components of the Donroe Doctrine, like the human rights impact of the Shield of the Americas initiative.
We will build on existing relationships with Congressional champions for human rights and climate justice, striking up new collaborations with the incoming activist members.
After years of environmental rollbacks and human rights abuses, this moment offers something we have been short on – hope.
Hope for environmental justice, for human rights, and for the future of the Amazon and her peoples.
text:
Democrats have won control of the U.S. House and Senate in the November 3 midterms. The good news is that when the new Congress takes office in January, lawmakers will have more power to scrutinize U.S. policies that affect the Amazon and shape the spending bills that fund them.

What should Congress do with that power and where can it start? Among other opportunities, it can press to block U.S. funding for aerial fumigation in Colombia, investigate the human rights impacts of U.S. security operations, and work directly with Indigenous leaders and legislators from Amazonian countries.

Trump 2.0 has been catastrophic for the Amazon rainforest and her peoples. The so-called Donroe Doctrine is advancing an authoritarian project of hemispheric domination to catalyze natural resource extraction to the benefit of the U.S., particularly oil and critical minerals. The U.S.-led Shield of the Americas initiative, launched earlier this year, exemplifies a military approach to dealing with transnational organized crime, to the detriment of addressing the social and economic roots of illicit economies now gripping the Amazon. Elon Musk’s DOGE ignominiously fed USAID into a veritable woodchipper, eliminating any positive support the U.S. was providing toward local initiatives for alternative development and environmental protection. Prior diplomatic backing for environmental and human rights defenders evaporated. Trump and Rubio intervened in national elections to help elect authoritarians, most notably in Colombia.

Trump’s anti-rights and anti-climate policies couldn’t come at a worse time for the Amazon. The biome is reaching an ecological tipping point, potentially shifting from a greenhouse gas sink to a net emitter. Governments continue to expand the extractive frontier deeper and deeper into the rainforest, increasingly piercing into the most remote areas. The manifold threat to communities and environment posed by illegal gold mining, coca cultivation, and illegal logging has erupted in recent years. And defenders on the front line – many of them women community leaders – are under pressure from death threats and violent attempts on their lives.

Some Congressional Representatives and Senators have spoken out against Trump policies in Latin America and the Amazonian region over the last two years: twenty members signed a resolution led by Rep. Delia Ramirez in opposition to the Donroe Doctrine and in favor of a new Good Neighbor Policy. Many members publicly denounced the naked election interference in both the Colombian and Brazilian elections. Just last week, 18 other members of Congress joined Rep. Mark Pocan to send a letter to Secretary of State Rubio, opposing any U.S. support for Colombia’s effort to reinitiate the failed strategy of aerial fumigation to eradicate coca cultivation in the rainforest.

With Congressional Democrats in the minority, however, the political impact of their efforts has been limited. Last night changed all that.

The votes from the U.S. midterm elections are still being counted, but the overall results are clear: Democrats will have a significant majority in both the U.S. House of Representatives and, extraordinarily, in the Senate. The majority is especially crucial in the House, where Democrats will not only have the Speakership, but control of committees, giving them the power to convene hearings, launch oversight investigations, and initiate international delegations. They can also pass legislation, including the appropriations bill that determined funding for the U.S. federal government.

We’re seeing not only a greater quantity, but also a greater quality of Democrat. Dozens of incoming Congresspeople are progressive in orientation and activist in nature. A larger portion of the caucus are publicly committed to rights, justice, and diversity. The Senate reflects that shift too, with Peggy Flanagan elected as the first Native American woman to serve in the chamber. They are critical of the corporate agenda that has heavily influenced the Democratic party for decades.

A number are very interested in building international ties with their counterparts – incoming Members like Darlializa Avila Chevalier (NY), Chris Rabb (PA), and Adam Hamawy (NJ) attended the Panamerican Congress in Uruguay this past August. The number of Spanish and Portuguese speaking Congresspeople will increase precipitously.

Many people worked hard for this outcome, and we should celebrate. That said, we also need to temper our expectations for the coming years. Trump will still be an imperial president, who has been laying the groundwork to attempt to ignore Congress. He still controls the federal bureaucracy, which can continue to do immense damage. It will be incumbent on the new Congress to find creative ways of blocking and minimizing that damage, while also presenting an alternative vision to help Democrats win the presidency in 2028.

In this hopeful but challenging context, what should the 120th Congress do to accompany Amazonian peoples as they defend their territory? Working closely with Amazonian partners – including Indigenous legislators – Amazon Watch will coordinate with Congressional champions and allies to carry out the following actions and policies.

Leverage the power of the purse strings: Congress should restrict funding for harmful U.S. policies in the Amazon, like military operations and support for aerial fumigation. Anticipating a Democratic presidency, they should maintain support for U.S. foreign assistance in the appropriations process. Additionally, they should expand U.S. financial support for important multilateral institutions like the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights and the UN Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues, among many others.

Use their megaphone: Given the tremendous risk that local environmental and land defenders face – and their crucial role in protecting the Amazon – ally Congresspeople should regularly express political and diplomatic support for them. To maximize press coverage, they should speak out via English, Spanish, and Portuguese channels. On the issue of supporting defenders, they should join the Leaders Network for Environmental Activists and Defenders (LEAD Initiative).

Bang the gavel: Now that Democrats will run committees and subcommittees, they should incorporate Amazon themes and community leaders into the work of proposing and hosting hearings, launching oversight investigations and coordinating Congressional Delegations. Investigations could focus on the most nefarious components of the Donroe Doctrine, like the human rights impact of the Shield of the Americas initiative.

Build peer partnerships: Devise long-term bilateral relationships with like-minded legislators from Amazonian countries like Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru. Also, find ways to participate in and support the work of outstanding international collaboratives of legislators like the Parliamentarians for a Fossil Free Future. Work with those peers to promote the Santa Marta Process for a just transition away from fossil fuels and efforts at the United Nations to devise a new protocol against crimes that affect the environment.

Amazon Watch will work with Amazonian partners and allies to ensure that the future of the rainforest and her peoples are squarely on the agenda of the new U.S. Congress. We will build on existing relationships with Congressional champions for human rights and climate justice, striking up new collaborations with the incoming activist members. We will also identify strategic opportunities for action by grassroots friends of the Amazon, to make your voice heard.

After years of environmental rollbacks and human rights abuses, this moment offers something we have been short on – hope. Hope for environmental justice, for human rights, and for the future of the Amazon and her peoples. We will not let it pass. We will keep pushing for a future where rights are respected and the planet is protected.

Celebration broke out at Oakshire Public House on election night as early results showed Eugene voters backing Measure 20-388, which would establish the Eugene Clean Energy Fund.

Initial results showed more than 57% of voters supporting the measure.

It would charge roughly 70 large businesses in Eugene a 2% fee to help fund city climate and energy projects, including renewable energy programs, clean-energy job training, green infrastructure and future innovation.

“We are as a community taking steps to make the billion-dollar corporations that profit off of us contribute back to building those community benefits, and we’ve come together and made it happen,” said Alexi Miller, a newly elected at-large member of the Eugene Water & Electric Board.

The fee, which would be implemented in January of 2029, would apply to businesses with more than $1 billion in national gross profits and more than $500,000 in gross profits in Eugene.

The first funds from the fee must begin being allocated by 2030, but it could start in 2029.

"We actually looked really closely to make sure that none of our local big businesses would meet that threshold. So think about Nancy's, Yogi Tea, or Jerry's Hardware; none of those companies came even close to meeting the threshold," Deputy Director of the Sierra Club’s Clean Heat Campaign Dylan Plummer said.

A community commission will oversee the fund and allow for public input on what projects to prioritize with some funds dedicated to existing projects like EWEB's energy efficiency upgrades.

"EWEB already has extremely generous incentives for solar and for heat pumps and energy efficiency programs for homeowners. The fund allows for some of the money to go directly into these existing programs to help expand them. So that's one of the first things we want to see is that EWEB's programs become even more generous and be able to be adopted by more folks including homeowners and renters," Plummer said.

The final vote to approve projects belongs to the city council.

Job creation is also a big element of the fund.

"One of the things that I think hasn't been talked about enough is that this is going to be a huge jobs program that will create good paying union jobs in Eugene and help build clean energy infrastructure," Plummer said.

Plummer says that includes heat pump installers, solar installers, people to build renewable energy and transportation projects, and electrical and construction workers.

Opponents say they're concerned about the long term financial impact on the community as those businesses take on the new fee.

"The idea is there; it's wonderful, and I think the money will probably be spent as planned. It will be good for the community, " Eugene Resident Matt Bailey said. "But in the long term, these organizations have to make decisions. And it's going to come down to whether or not to do business here, whether or not to keep employees full time, whether to cut hours, whether to raise their prices here in Eugene."

The commission to oversee the fund will include one city council member, one EWEB representative, a representative from the Human Rights Commission, one Sustainability Commission representative, as well as five city appointed community members.

Some businesses, including health care providers and grocery stores, would be exempt from the fee.

The fund has a built in auditing process with an outside audit happening every four years.

text:
As Donald Trump nears the end of his first two years in his second term, his administration is aggressively targeting the Environmental Protection Agency to roll back climate and environmental regulations. The EPA was established under Republican President Richard Nixon in response to widespread public outrage about the state of the environment in the 1960s and early ’70s.

Under Trump-appointed EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, his staff has been slashed, programs cut and grants already announced rescinded. Many former staffers have joined the Environmental Protection Network or EPN, which now counts 800 volunteers who are experts in their fields, along with 30 paid staff.

Between The Lines’ Melinda Tuhus spoke with Marc Boom, who served as a senior advisor in the Office of Policy at the EPA and is now senior director for public affairs with the Environmental Protection Network. Here he talks about what needs to happen to restore the EPA no matter which party controls Congress after the election and the most important issues Congress needs to address in the lame duck period.

MARK BOOM: The current majority has actually helped advance the deregulatory agenda of the Trump administration. Congress overturned pollution protections, passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which took funding for pollution monitoring and enforcement technology away. It also postponed the methane pollution charge. It has kind of supported what’s been going on, although the administration has certainly gone farther than what Congress has done. And I’d say at the same time, it hasn’t really provided the sustained scrutiny that we need into what these impacts could be, especially the health impacts of these changes. If you just look at the voting record of who supported and who opposed, the Democrats have laid out that they’re not supportive of that agenda. The committee ranking members have sent a lot of oversight requests for information and have laid out some of their thoughts on getting answers to these big questions. And so far we haven’t seen EPA responding to those in the way that would actually provide the information people need to understand what’s been happening.

I think whoever controls Congress should be asking hard questions of this administration about what is the impact of their actions to understand how they got there? Who was part of the process? How did this get decided? Was it based on the science? Did you look at the health impacts? Anyone should be asking those things, but it is certainly clear right now that the Democrats are already lining up to ask those harder questions.

MELINDA TUHUS: So what do you think are some of the biggest issues that an EPA that really was about environmental protection would address if the opportunity arises?

MARK BOOM: What we’ve seen over the last nearly two years has been rolling back protections on pollution and either weakening them or delaying them or waiving them entirely. An agency that was focused on health and environmental protection would have a completely different approach and they would be looking for ways to increase the protection for communities. If you had a different approach at EPA, that’s what it would look like. I’m not expecting that any change in Congress, if it happens, would actually affect the administration’s approach, but it could certainly create more of a record of what’s happening and they could use their oversight powers to say who is doing what and how did you come to these conclusions? I think there’s been some recent articles that highlight the need for this. The New York Times just had a piece about how pollution waivers for ethylene oxide, which is a cancer-causing air pollutant, how those waivers happened, how career staff were pushed to the side, how scientific findings were ignored, and how industry had a seat at the table in deciding—I mean, one, they only had to send in an email to get the waiver, but then they also had a seat at the table for the actual rollback.

Those are questions that Congress should be understanding. There was also a story from the national desk, which is run by the Sinclair Network on PFAS protections and how EPA has been sitting on a lot of scientific studies and surveys and other things that would actually allow it to go after PFAS at the source and prevent it from getting into our waters, but they’ve been sitting on it and they haven’t been moving it forward. And the loss of science at the agency and the sidelining of science is really an undercurrent for all of these actions. The traditional scientific review process that looks at what is the risk of these chemicals, that has been completely sidelined.

MELINDA TUHUS: Like you said, the administration’s still the administration, but if they don’t have both houses of Congress in their pocket, what might happen?

MARK BOOM: One place where congressional attention is really needed is on data centers. Almost all communities are dealing with some type of data center development. While our leaders are looking at things like electricity bills, they should also be looking at the health costs. So EPN actually has a report called the Hidden Health Costs of AI Data Centers. It looks at the pollution costs to this and found that they’re quite substantial and that all of the actions that this federal government has been taking are going to make that pollution worse.

description:
Texas voters on Tuesday elected a Democrat to the Railroad Commission, the regulator of the state’s oil and gas industry, for the first time since 1990.

text:
Texas voters on Tuesday elected a Democrat to the Railroad Commission, the regulator of the state’s oil and gas industry, for the first time since 1990. They also elected a Democratic governor who promised to halt new data center construction. Democrats running against data centers took the governorships of Georgia and Ohio and won control of Georgia’s utility regulator. Voters cast those ballots with gasoline at its highest Election Day price on record.

State Rep. Jon Rosenthal, a former oilfield engineer who calls himself a “drill baby, drill Democrat,” defeated Republican Bo French for a seat on the three-member commission, which oversees oil and gas production, pipeline safety and natural gas rates. Republicans, who have held every seat since 1994, keep a 2-1 majority. Rosenthal ran on lower energy costs, plugging abandoned wells, closer oversight of natural gas infrastructure and managing data center power demand. He has proposed a first-of-its-kind fee on oil and gas wastewater injected underground.

Gina Hinojosa defeated Gov. Greg Abbott on promises to impose a moratorium on new data centers, tighten rules on their water and power use and end their tax breaks. Texas holds more than 25% of the data center capacity planned in the United States by 2030. As of August, 474 GW of projects were seeking connection to the ERCOT grid, more than five times its all-time peak demand. Elon Musk, the top donor of the midterms with a reported $446 million spent on Republicans, posted on X on Wednesday that data centers in space were “looking pretty appealing right now.”

Keisha Lance Bottoms won the Georgia governorship after campaigning for a statewide data center moratorium. Amy Acton beat Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio on a conditional moratorium that would make data centers cover their own utility costs. In Georgia, Democrats Peter Hubbard and Sheila Edwards won seats that give the party a 3-2 majority on the Public Service Commission, which sets Georgia Power’s rates. Those rates rose more than 18% over three years, with the increases tied to the Vogtle nuclear expansion.

Regular gasoline averaged $4.15 a gallon on Election Day, according to AAA, against $3.80 in 2022, and diesel averaged $6.29. The Iran war has pushed the average gasoline price in Trump’s second term above the Biden-era average, and the diesel crunch is set to last well into 2027. Trump told Fox News on Tuesday night that “part of it was Iran” when explaining Republican losses.

text:
The government plans to announce a package of measures to strengthen the competitiveness of the electric vehicle industry this month.

Business groups have urged the government to extend domestic production tax credits to electric vehicles and expand support for auto parts makers transitioning to EV-focused supply chains.

The Ministry of Economy and Finance held the first meeting of its "corporate vitality task force" at Korea Development Bank on Thursday, chaired by First Vice Minister Kwon Dae-young. Attendees included representatives from six major business federations — among them the Korea Chamber of Commerce and Industry, the Federation of Korean Industries and the Korea Enterprises Federation — as well as the Korea Automobile Manufacturers Association, public and private research institutions, and state-run bank research units. The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources and the Financial Services Commission also participated.

Participants said policy support for corporate technology innovation and investment must keep pace as the global auto industry restructures around electric vehicles and autonomous driving. They called for domestic production tax credits to be extended to EVs as a way to encourage local manufacturing of finished vehicles, and pressed for expanded transition support to help parts suppliers adapt to a supply chain increasingly centered on electric vehicles.

"Swift adaptation and technological innovation by our companies are more important than ever," First Vice Minister Kwon said. "We will listen carefully to a wide range of views and actively incorporate them into the electric vehicle industry competitiveness plan to be announced in November."

The meeting also took up "K-shaped polarization" — diverging growth trajectories across companies, industries and regions. Participants agreed that active policy responses are needed, warning that productivity gaps could widen further as businesses undergo AI transformation. Kwon said the government must build an industrial ecosystem in which large enterprises, small and medium-sized enterprises, advanced industries, traditional industries, the Greater Seoul area and regional economies all grow together, adding that the gains from growth must translate into local industries and jobs.

The TF serves as the working-level group under a public-private consultative body on corporate innovation support launched in March under the deputy prime minister's chairmanship. The Ministry of Economy and Finance plans to use the TF to identify on-the-ground obstacles to corporate investment and innovation, and to discuss government support measures covering taxation, finance and regulation.

text:
Hyundai Motor's stock price is strong on the prospect that the eco-friendly car support policy will be strengthened again. It is interpreted as reflecting expectations that the Trump administration's tough fossil fuel-oriented policy will be put on hold as the Democratic Party controls both the Senate and the House of Representatives in the U.S. midterm elections.

As of 10:09 a.m. on the 5th, Hyundai Motor's stock price was trading at 295,500 won, up 4.23% from the previous day. At 9:13 that day, it rose to 308,000 won, recovering to the 300,000 won mark during the day for the first time in five trading days since the 29th of last month.

Hyundai Motor's stock price has risen for the first time in a long time due to the overwhelming dominance of the Democratic Party in the U.S. midterm elections. In other words, expectations have spread that the reduction of electric vehicle support and auto tariff policies, which have been a burden on Hyundai Motor's stock price, could change.

Recently, Hyundai Motor's stock price has been weak due to the Trump administration's policy direction and tariff burden. Since the end of September last year, the Trump administration has ended the tax credit for electric vehicle purchases, which had reached up to $7,500 for new cars. Expectations for growth of related industries have also weakened as they put more weight on fostering the fossil fuel industry than on expanding the supply of electric vehicles. As a result, Hyundai Motor's stock price plunged 29.6% over the past two months from September to October.

On the other hand, the Democratic Party of the United States is relatively favorable to expanding the supply of electric vehicles and supporting new and renewable energy. As a result, expectations are growing that discussions on restoring eco-friendly car support measures will resume, and observers say that Hyundai Motor, which expanded its production facilities in the U.S., could benefit from policy changes.

The prospect of easing the tariff burden also stimulated investor sentiment. Hyundai Motor and Kia have been under pressure for profitability due to U.S. tariffs on Korean cars. Analysts say that the Democratic Party could take the lead in Congress and check the Trump administration's tariff policy.

Strong sales in the U.S. market are also positive. Hyundai Motor's U.S. sales in October rose 5% from the same month last year to 73,452 units, the highest ever in October. Sales of hybrid vehicles increased 20% and Ioniq 5 increased 21%.

However, uncertainty still remains until the policy to support eco-friendly cars is actually restored. A new Congress, controlled by the Democratic Party, will be launched in January next year and President Trump's veto will be maintained. Additional legislation and political negotiations are needed to change the existing tariff and electric vehicle purchase tax credit system.

text:
For two years, the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump and Republicans in the U.S. Congress have exerted almost absolute control of U.S. environmental policy, reorienting government support away from climate action, clean energy and stricter pollution controls to further embrace fossil fuels and deregulation.

That’s about to change in a big way. After securing decisive majorities in both the House and Senate in a historic blue wave Tuesday, Democrats will have new leverage. Former officials and policy experts expect them to use it to step up scrutiny of the Trump administration’s record on energy and the environment. The shakeup could also complicate, or sink, a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.

With both chambers flipped, Democrats next session will set the agenda for hearings and will wield investigative powers, able to issue subpoenas for officials and industry to testify or produce documents for review. Their victory allows for a level of oversight that’s simply not possible for the minority party.

Appropriations could be a focus, given that the Trump White House has repeatedly frozen and withheld funds appropriated by Congress, such as for National Science Foundation and Environmental Protection Agency grants.

“I would expect Congress to reassert its oversight of the budget and start looking at what they’re going to do to enforce that,” said Josh Freed, senior vice president for the climate and energy program at the liberal think tank Third Way.

Democrats are planning investigations into Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and his team, including over the bungled Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool upgrades and officials’ dealings with oil and gas companies, Politico has reported. EPA chief Lee Zeldin may also face scrutiny, especially since Rep. Zoe Lofgren, a California Democrat and ranking member of the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, recently accused him of failing “to produce a single responsive document, communication or record” after myriad requests.

Another possible target of investigators: businesses that made deals with or got regulatory reprieves from the administration.

“Democrats with gavels and subpoena authority in one or both chambers are going to put significant countervailing pressure on industry,” said Zealan Hoover, who was a senior EPA advisor during the Biden administration.

He anticipates congressional reviews of companies that cut deals to trade offshore wind leases for fossil fuel infrastructure and got out of Clean Air Act requirements.

As election returns rolled in on Tuesday night, Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts, a Democrat on the Committee on Environment and Public Works, posted on X, “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing.”

Clinching the Senate as well as the House means Democrats will have more resources to dedicate to investigations. They’ll also have more power to block Trump nominees for senior agency and judicial jobs going forward.

The midterms also have the potential to impact policy before the next session of Congress — through the fate of the controversial permitting reform bill, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. A handful of Republicans and Democrats in the Senate announced in late September that they’d secured a deal to speed up the approvals of pipelines, power lines and other infrastructure projects. But since then, a number of Democrats, environmentalists and other stakeholders have raised concerns with the proposal.

Going into the elections, senators were planning to introduce an amendment to the bill in the coming days, followed by a procedural vote and final vote within weeks; the House likely wouldn’t vote until after Thanksgiving.

But it’s an open question whether there’s sufficient Democratic support to pass the deal now. There’s a possibility that the party decides to punt discussions down the road to when they also control the White House, some policy experts have warned, noting that Trump has already threatened to veto any legislation coming out of a Democrat-controlled Congress. If they drop the issue now, there’s a strong chance that an alternative doesn’t pass until there’s a Democratic president.

“There were some pretty significant structural problems with the first version that came out,” said Rep. Sean Casten, a Democrat from Illinois, on a Wednesday press call. “But I think it’s premature until we see the manager’s amendment” — the forthcoming proposed changes — “to know whether that bill is something that can get through the Senate, much less the House,” he added.

Looking to the next session, Casten said that he’s among a group of House Democrats that’s already been tapped by New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to be elected speaker, to come up with “what are going to be the top 10 bills that we roll out at the start,” including one on energy affordability. For legislation to pass, he said, there will need to be some Republican buy-in because “we don’t have veto-proof majorities in the House or Senate, in spite of all the wins we had last night.”

Outside of Congress, the midterm results could lead to more climate action at the state and local levels, said former Washington Gov. Jay Inslee, a Democrat, in the same briefing. There will soon be about 30 states with Democratic governors, he noted, and new trifectas will give the party control of both the executive and the legislature in several more states.

text:
Food markets are essential components of urban food systems around the world. For local communities, these vibrant and often bustling spaces are key access points for fresh and affordable produce. However, as market stalls empty throughout the day, waste bins fill up with bruised fruit, vegetable trimmings, spoiled food, and expired goods — all usually mixed with other trash. This organic waste represents a significant opportunity for energy and nutrient recovery for local communities, while also reducing methane emissions.

A market’s waste is typically hauled to a dumpsite or landfill, where the organic material decomposes in low-oxygen conditions and produces methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Unless captured, that methane escapes into the atmosphere and contributes to near-term warming — methane traps over 80 times more heat than CO2 over a 20-year time frame. Poorly managed organic waste can also stink, attract pests, and threaten to overwhelm disposal facilities quickly nearing capacity — all while missing the opportunity to recover nutrients and energy.

Exhibit 1: The status quo: Straight to the landfill

A circular alternative

Adopting a more circular approach to waste management could seize the opportunity for nutrient and energy recovery, starting from where waste is generated. Organic waste from food markets can be directed toward two well-established treatment options: composting, to improve soil quality, or anaerobic digestion, for energy production. The site-specific technology choice depends on the amount and type of waste, land, and funding available, as well as operator capacity and demand for the end products generated.

Exhibit 2: Closing the loop: Recovering nutrients and energy from market waste

Composting: Returning nutrients to the soil

Composting is the process in which microorganisms break down organic material in the presence of oxygen. Over time, the organic material (often called ‘feedstock’ in this context) becomes a soil-like product called compost. When mixed into topsoil (for example, in a vegetable garden), finished compost replenishes soil with the nutrients, helps improve soil structure and water retention, and supports plant growth.

Composting operations can vary in scale. In this context, a smaller operation might serve one market or a few nearby markets, while a larger facility might aggregate organic waste across a city for processing. Composting is often considered a simpler technology than anaerobic digestion, due to its cheaper equipment and lower technical demand. However, facility operators must still actively manage the feedstock mix, moisture, temperature, and odors and ensure that the end product is of sufficiently high quality to improve crop production or generate revenue as a product sold by the facility.

Anaerobic digestion: Converting waste into renewable energy

Like composting, anaerobic digestion also relies on microorganisms to break down organic material, however, this process takes place in a sealed tank without oxygen. The two main outputs are biogas and digestate. Biogas, which is mostly methane and CO2, can be used directly for heat or cooking, burned in a generator to produce electricity, or further upgraded into renewable natural gas. The end use depends on the project’s scale, the quality and consistency of the gas, and nearby energy demand. The material remaining after digestion is digestate; when properly processed, digestate can be used as a fertilizer or soil additive, returning nutrients to the soil.

Anaerobic digestion is generally more complex and expensive than composting. Sustained operation requires a steady supply of high-quality feedstock, trained operators, reliable equipment and maintenance, and ongoing demand for the end products (e.g. sale to others, or use by the operator itself). Where these conditions are in place, a digester can turn organic waste into useful energy and soil products.

An untapped opportunity to close the loop across fresh produce markets

Market waste represents an especially important opportunity for resource recovery in lower-income countries, where food and yard waste make up more than half of municipal solid waste. Markets also provide a relatively concentrated and steady organic waste flow, which can make collection more efficient than collecting small quantities from individual households. Organic waste treatment can also create jobs in collection, material handling, facility operations, and end product distribution, while helping cities reduce their reliance on disposal facilities, improve local air quality, and mitigate methane emissions.

Of course, there are many ways for markets to divert organic waste from landfills and implement these solutions. For example, a market that generates too little feedstock, or lacks sufficient space for composting or biodigester equipment, may be better served by joining with nearby markets and communities to aggregate their organic waste at a shared processing facility. Each city and market should tailor its approach to local waste volumes, available space, infrastructure, and operational needs.

Supporting organic waste treatment expansion through project preparation

While treatment of market waste through composting and anaerobic digestion provides multiple benefits, municipalities often face significant barriers to scaling these projects, including unreliable feedstock quality, weak policy and regulatory frameworks, limited technical capacity in the local workforce, and difficulty recovering project costs (either through cost savings or revenue generation). RMI is helping address these challenges through our continued engagement in Nigeria and the Philippines, identifying and evaluating projects that are technically and financially viable.

By assessing feedstock quantity and quality, technical and economic feasibility, project risks, and engaging key stakeholders, RMI supports communities and project developers in preparing their projects for financing. We are also developing a replicable cost recovery framework to improve the economic viability and long-term sustainability of similar projects, a critical precondition for scaling pilot projects and achieving larger-scale deployment. Together, these efforts aim to expand organic waste treatment and strengthen its long-term sustainability in the Global South.

The supplemental proposal is not a final rule, and it does not replace the November 2025 proposal.

text:
By STAFF REPORTS

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers released a significant new step in the long-running effort to redefine “waters of the United States,” or WOTUS, heading into the Labor Day weekend. Once the Oct. 9 deadline hit, the agencies received 88,835 public comments.

On Sept. 4, just as most people were getting started on their extended Labor Day weekend, the agencies announced a Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that adds new regulatory alternatives to the WOTUS rule they originally proposed in November 2025.

The WOTUS rule defines which waters and wetlands are subject to federal jurisdiction under the Clean Water Act, including the Section 404 dredge-and-fill permitting program. Public comments can be read on the Regulations.gov website.

The supplemental proposal is not a final rule, and it does not replace the November 2025 proposal. Instead, EPA and the Corps are expanding the range of options they may consider before adopting a final WOTUS definition.

The agencies proposed the initial rule on Nov. 20, 2025, as part of their effort to implement the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2023 decision in Sackett v. EPA. A 45-day public comment period closed Jan. 5, generating more than 220,000 comments. EPA and the Corps say the new supplemental proposal responds to issues raised during that process and provides another opportunity for targeted public input.

The new document focuses primarily on two of the most important jurisdictional questions in the rule: what qualifies as a “relatively permanent” water, and what constitutes the “continuous surface connection” necessary for federal jurisdiction over certain wetlands.

The November proposal contemplated using a “wet season” standard in both areas. The supplemental proposal now puts a substantially different option on the table: generally limiting “relatively permanent” waters to perennial waters, meaning waters that stand or flow continuously throughout the year under ordinary conditions, subject to limited exceptions for droughts, dry spells and similar temporary interruptions.

For wetlands, the agencies are also seeking comments on an alternative that would require perennial surface water in the wetland to be continuously connected with another jurisdictional waterbody so that it is difficult to determine where the waterbody ends and the wetland begins.

These are additional alternatives, not decisions EPA and the Corps have already made. The agencies specifically state that they will consider the supplemental options alongside those contained in the November 2025 proposal and will not prejudge the contents of the final rule.

The document released Sept. 4 was a pre-publication version. It was updated and officially appeared in the Federal Register on Sept. 9, which set off a new 30-day public comment period focused on the supplemental alternatives. The EPA and Army Corps must now review and consider those comments alongside the comments already received on the original proposal as they develop a final WOTUS rule.

The development is particularly relevant in Florida, where the distinction between federal WOTUS jurisdiction and the state’s broader Environmental Resource Permitting (ERP) program directly affects wetland permitting and the interaction between ERP and Clean Water Act Section 404 requirements.

text:
EUGENE, Ore. - Eugene's Clean Energy Fund appears headed for approval as Measure 20-388 leads with 57% voter support in initial election results.

The measure requires large retailers to pay an annual 2% fee to finance a clean energy fund. A large retailer is defined as one with sales in Eugene, gross profits exceeding $1 billion nationally and $500,000 in Eugene.

"This is critical money that our city needs to support those who are impacted first and worst by the extreme weather events that we've seen over the last couple of years," said Iboa, co-chief petitioner for the Eugene Clean Energy Fund. "I'm so excited to get started on making sure that this thing really does what it says it's going to do."

In Oakridge, voters overwhelmingly rejected Measure 20-387, a five-year ambulance service operations tax. The measure would have replaced a $17 monthly fee by imposing a tax.

Western Lane County voters approved Measure 20-389, renewing a five-year option levy for emergency medical and ambulance services. The levy serves about 20,000 residents.

Douglas County voters are easily passing Measure 10-216 with 63% approval. The $16 million bond measure will improve schools, safety and capacity in the Glide School District and receive a matching $6 million grant.

In Coos County, voters are supporting Measure 6-231, a lodging tax that would add another 2.5%, bringing the total hotel tax to 12%. However, North Bend's Measure 6-232 is failing. The five-year local option tax for pool operations and maintenance would have added $168 annually to the owner of a $300,000 home.

Linn County voters are rejecting Measure 22-216, the Lebanon five-year local option levy for jail operations, with 80% voting against it. The measure would have cost the owner of a $300,000 home $318, raising about $1.7 million annually.

Measure 2-160, which includes both Linn and Benton County voters, is passing comfortably in both counties. The measure renews the current five-year local option tax for Corvallis School operations and will fund and maintain current service levels and operations across the district.

In Benton County, Measure 2-157, the North Albany Rural Fire Protection District levy, is passing by a lopsided margin. The measure will cost the owner of a $300,000 home $210 annually.

text:
Over the past decade, Texas has attracted Japanese investment by building a more competitive business environment and improving connectivity across the North American market. In the last few years, that relationship has witnessed growth focused more on advanced technology.

While automotive manufacturing remains central, new partnerships have arisen in advanced materials, semiconductors, life sciences, energy infrastructure, electric vehicle batteries and space technology.

For Japanese companies, the state represents more than a gateway to the United States. It has become a place where long-term investment and industrial innovation thrive simultaneously because Texas has created new investment opportunities and built infrastructure to ensure smooth supply chains within the United States and the rest of North America.

Playing the long game

Toyota’s decision to consolidate its spread-out operations into a single campus in the Lone Star State was part of the car giant’s long-term strategy to strengthen its business in the entire region, including Canada and Mexico.

From its base in Plano, the automaker now connects manufacturing, sales, research and mobility activities across the continent more efficiently, in terms of both time and cost.

“Texas reflects the scale and diversity of the North American market and provides a strong foundation for long-term growth. By bringing our headquarters’ functions together in Texas, we can operate as one North America-led organization and make faster, market-driven decisions,” said Toyota Motor North America President and CEO Tetsuo Ogawa.

Since entering the United States nearly 70 years ago, Toyota has invested more than $50 billion directly in the country and will increase that figure to beyond $60 billion over the coming years through a diversified approach toward electrification (hybrid, plug-in hybrid, battery electric and fuel cell technologies), meeting changing customer needs while strengthening domestic manufacturing.

No minor players

Amid an increasingly competitive climate to attract investment, both domestic and local, Cedar Park, like several other fast-growing cities across central Texas, has developed a specialized, innovative ecosystem to differentiate itself from those of its larger neighbors.

According to Arthur Jackson, Cedar Park’s chief economic development officer, the city has focused on Japanese companies, which he believes will benefit significantly from the city’s expanding innovation economy.

“We are building on our successful partnerships, like that with TDK, Nissin Ion and Rigaku Technologies, while strengthening our life sciences, aerospace and advanced manufacturing sectors. Our goal is to create an environment where innovative companies can grow alongside one another and find the talent they need to succeed,” Jackson said.

Meanwhile, Seguin adopted a similar strategy while keeping to its deeply rooted manufacturing heritage. Located between Austin and San Antonio, the city has become home to automotive suppliers, metalworking operations and semiconductor-related manufacturers.

“Our priority is to help existing manufacturers transition into advanced manufacturing while attracting suppliers and strategic partners that strengthen the entire ecosystem. Japanese companies value relationships built on proven success, and Seguin offers both the infrastructure and commitment to support long-term investment,” said Seguin’s Director of Economic Development Alora M. Wachholz.

To complement its strategy, the government of Seguin wants to enhance the skills of the city’s workforce through a new Texas State Technical College campus, while investing in new infrastructure and developing new sites for future projects.

Merging energy and technology

In Houston, Japan and Texas have strengthened a long-running partnership through major investments in energy and emerging technologies.

For Mitsubishi Corp., Texas has served as a strategic platform for long-term growth, as seen in its investment in natural gas producer Aethon, which is now rebranded as Adamas Energy.

“Our investment shows Mitsubishi’s long-term commitment to Texas. Its abundant energy resources, business-friendly environment and highly skilled workforce make it an ideal base for expanding energy, infrastructure and next-generation industries,” said Shuji Kobayashi, president and CEO of Mitsubishi International Corp.’s office in Houston.

Beyond energy, Mitsubishi is also investing in Texas-based Starlab Space, which is developing a commercial successor to the International Space Station and expanding its presence in the growing space economy.

Onward and upward

The next phase of the Japan-Texas partnership has gone beyond its usual sectors, such as traditional manufacturing, and extended into advanced manufacturing, clean energy and artificial intelligence.

For Japanese companies seeking long-term growth in North America, Texas offers more than competitive operating conditions. The state provides well-built infrastructure, seamless connectivity, an experienced public sector, a committed private sector and accommodating local communities.

In return, Japanese investment brings an innovative spirit, high-value jobs and steadfast loyalty to its chosen partners.

title: What Michigan election results mean for data centers, DTE, clean energy - Planet Detroit
description:
Rogers initially expressed support for streamlining data center development before saying in August that he supports a statewide, one-year data center moratorium.
Nessel intervened in the regulatory filings for DTE’s contracts for the Oracle and OpenAI data center in Saline Township and Google data center in Van Buren Township, and filed appeals after contracts were approved for both facilities.
In 2023, a Democratically controlled Michigan legislature passed the Clean Energy and Jobs Act, which looks to achieve 100% clean energy generation by 2040.
This citizen-led ballot initiative would have created a municipal energy utility board that could have eventually replaced DTE Energy in the city.
Opponents said the effort would have been extremely expensive and set back Ann Arbor’s efforts to deliver clean energy and other city services.
text:
Democrats scored major victories in Tuesday’s midterm election, taking control of the U.S. House and Senate, including Senate wins in Republican strongholds like South Carolina and Texas.

In Michigan, the party maintained control of the governor’s office and state Senate, while also taking the Michigan House majority — a trifecta that could enable Democrats to protect the state’s clean energy law and advance other environmental protections.

The Michiganders for Money Out of Politics ballot initiative to ban political contributions by utilities and major government contractors passed with 81% of the vote, according to the Secretary of State. The state’s constitutional convention ballot measure, which environmental advocates warned could endanger environmental safeguards, failed with 74% of voters opposed, state data shows.

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s victory over Republican Mike Rogers, a former Congressman, for Michigan’s open U.S. Senate seat was among the most closely watched contests in the country. It may prove consequential to efforts to federally regulate data centers.

El-Sayed released “terms of engagement” for data centers in January that he said will protect other utility ratepayers from data center costs, ensure community engagement and community benefits, protect energy reliability, safeguard water resources, and require projects to comply with clean energy laws.

Data centers face intense opposition in many Michigan communities, and many candidates called for moratoriums and guardrails to prevent impacts to the environment or utility ratepayers.

Rogers initially expressed support for streamlining data center development before saying in August that he supports a statewide, one-year data center moratorium.

El-Sayed voiced his support for Medicare for All throughout the campaign.

He criticized DTE Energy’s political spending, which he said helped the company gain fast-tracked approval for its Oracle and OpenAI data center contracts in Saline Township.

El-Sayed said during the Senate primary that he was the only candidate in the race who received no donations from corporate political action committees, including those funded by DTE.

Savit says he will continue Nessel’s ratepayer work

Utility accountability emerged as an issue in the Michigan attorney general contest. The winner of the race, Washtenaw County Prosecutor Eli Savit, said he would continue outgoing Attorney General Dana Nessel’s work of intervening on behalf of ratepayers in cases before the Michigan Public Service Commission.

During her eight-year tenure, Nessel intervened in many gas and electric rate cases, calling on regulators to sharply reduce rate hikes requested by DTE, Consumers Energy, and other investor-owned utilities. Nessel intervened in the regulatory filings for DTE’s contracts for the Oracle and OpenAI data center in Saline Township and Google data center in Van Buren Township, and filed appeals after contracts were approved for both facilities.

Savit told Planet Detroit in September that utility rates “should be geared toward ensuring reliability and should be no more than is necessary to do that.”

He also challenged utilities’ returns on equity, or the profit passed on to shareholders, and the inclusion of expenses like travel and lobbying in rate cases.

Savit’s opponent, Eaton County Prosecutor Doug Lloyd, a Republican, expressed concern about ratepayer affordability in an April interview with the WDIV-TV program “Flashpoint.” He emphasized the attorney general’s law enforcement responsibilities in media appearances, telling WDIV that “one main focus of government should be public safety.”

Democratic sweep may safeguard clean energy legislation

Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson’s victory over U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township) in the governor’s race, and Democratic control of the Michigan Legislature, could pave the way for further action on climate and energy prices, environmental advocates say.

Courtney Brady, with the environmental group Evergreen Action, said in a statement that voters chose leaders who will bring down energy costs, with clean energy as part of the solution.

“Michigan has an opportunity to protect families from rising data center costs, hold utilities accountable, and accelerate the deployment of affordable clean energy,” Brady said.

In 2023, a Democratically controlled Michigan legislature passed the Clean Energy and Jobs Act, which looks to achieve 100% clean energy generation by 2040.

In March, Republicans introduced legislation entitled “Project Lighthouse” that would repeal the state’s clean energy mandates. State Rep. Pauline Wendzel, R-Watervliet, called the requirements “arbitrary” and said they benefit investor-owned utilities at ratepayers’ expense.

Analysis by 5 Lakes Energy and Evergreen Action said that Project Lighthouse would increase residential utility bills in the long term. Ben Poulson, state government affairs director at the Michigan League of Conservation Voters, told Planet Detroit in June that the legislation would repeal programs used to lower energy waste and hold utilities accountable.

Utility money initiative wins; public power comes up short

Proposal 2, the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics ballot initiative, to bar political spending by utilities and contractors doing significant business with state, succeeded Tuesday after receiving support from Democrats running for statewide office and over 80 organizations.

Christy McGillivray, co-chair of the MMOP steering committee, said in August that anger over DTE and Consumers‘ proposed rate hikes could drive support for the ballot initiative.

“Michiganders are fed up with this pay-to-play system and overwhelmingly agree that our government should work for people, not powerful corporations,” she said.

The Mackinac Center for Public Policy conservative think tank filed a federal lawsuit Tuesday against Benson and Nessel alleging that Proposal 2 violates free speech protections, The Detroit News reported.

Representatives for utilities and Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan challenged the ballot initiative, saying it would silence their employees who look to engage in the political process.

Another challenge to DTE Energy fell short Tuesday. Ann Arbor’s Proposition E lost 52% to 48%. This citizen-led ballot initiative would have created a municipal energy utility board that could have eventually replaced DTE Energy in the city.

Backers of the Ann Arbor for Public Power ballot initiative argued it was the best way to improve energy affordability and reliability in the city, and accelerate the transition to renewable energy.

Opponents said the effort would have been extremely expensive and set back Ann Arbor’s efforts to deliver clean energy and other city services.

One potential solution already has bipartisan backing: permitting reform.
Timmons drew a parallel to Sen. Whitehouse’s leadership on permitting reform, praising his efforts to expand energy infrastructure and create opportunities for American manufacturers.
He also pointed to the NAM’s “America on Hold” report, which found that permitting delays cost manufacturers nearly $8 billion annually.
The Laborers’ International Union of North America also called for permitting reform in an op-ed in The Hill.

text:
Democrats swept control of the House and Senate in Tuesday’s elections, intensifying the focus in Washington on addressing the economic pressures facing Americans. One potential solution already has bipartisan backing: permitting reform.

The big picture: Voters sent a clear message Tuesday: They are frustrated with the persistently high cost of living (The Wall Street Journal, subscription). For manufacturers and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, permitting reform offers a bipartisan path to meet soaring demand for energy, unlock new energy supplies and bring down costs for families and businesses all while supercharging manufacturing in America.

A bipartisan push: Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) today acknowledged the ongoing negotiations, saying, “We have a bipartisan group working on permitting, permitting reform and hopefully they’ll come up with a good deal on that.”

But the election has also raised questions about whether lawmakers will advance the existing agreement during the lame-duck session or revisit negotiations in the new Congress.

Building momentum: Just ahead of the election, NAM President and CEO Jay Timmons and Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), ranking member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and key architect of the permitting reform legislation introduced in the Senate, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, convened a permitting reform roundtable that followed a facility tour at manufacturer Cooley Group in Pawtucket, Rhode Island.

The NAM-hosted event brought together leaders from manufacturing, organized labor and the business community to build support for the bipartisan agreement, negotiated by Sens. Whitehouse, Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Martin Heinrich (D-NM) and Mike Lee (R-UT).

Participants included Cooley Group President and CEO and NAM Executive Committee member Dan Dwight; Partnership for Rhode Island Executive Director Liz Catucci; Rhode Island Manufacturers Association President and CEO Melissa Travis; Greater Providence Chamber of Commerce President Laurie White; Laborers’ International Union of North America General Secretary-Treasurer Mike Sabitoni; and Rhode Island AFL-CIO President Pat Crowley.

Policy, not politics: Timmons emphasized that the agreement reflects shared priorities that transcend party lines: lower costs, more jobs, greater investment and responsible environmental stewardship.

“This bill is not about politics; it’s about the success of manufacturers here in the United States,” Timmons said, praising the four Senate negotiators for putting country over party.

“It’s a good thing when we have a stronger economy with more jobs and lower costs and a cleaner environment, all at the same time,” said Sen. Whitehouse. “So that’s what our intention is to deliver here. And I appreciate the terrific work that was done in the Senate to pull this together. … This was a good example of solid bipartisan work. It took a ton of time and a ton of effort.”

A historic connection: Timmons highlighted a personal connection between Sen. Whitehouse and the NAM that dates back more than 130 years. Thomas Dolan, the NAM’s first president in 1895 and Sen. Whitehouse’s great-great-grandfather-in-law, was a woolen manufacturer who later entered the energy business, helping develop the nation’s emerging electrical grid.

Timmons drew a parallel to Sen. Whitehouse’s leadership on permitting reform, praising his efforts to expand energy infrastructure and create opportunities for American manufacturers.

Calling Cooley Group an “American success story,” Timmons praised the century-old manufacturer and its 300 employees for driving innovation and creating jobs in Rhode Island.

“We want to make sure companies like Cooley have every tool that they need to make the next 100 years even more competitive than the last,” Timmons said. He also pointed to the NAM’s “America on Hold” report, which found that permitting delays cost manufacturers nearly $8 billion annually.

Sen. Whitehouse’s warning: During the roundtable, Sen. Whitehouse pushed back on the idea that Democrats should wait until the new Congress to negotiate a different deal if they made significant electoral gains.

“I vehemently disagree with that strategy,” Sen. Whitehouse said, arguing that delaying action could jeopardize an agreement that has a path to passage in both chambers and a presidential signature.

“Don’t sacrifice now for later,” he urged, emphasizing the importance of securing the benefits of the current agreement rather than restarting negotiations.

“This [isn’t] over, but I think we’re in a good place, assuming that the administration does what it has said it will do with respect to making its regulatory posture for clean energy fair,” he concluded.

Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-NM), a lead negotiator who is poised to chair the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee next year, echoed that urgency. “It doesn’t necessarily get easier just because of who the chair is,” Sen. Heinrich told Punchbowl News today. “This is the closest we have come to actually finding something that can get signed into law, and I’m not going to wait.”

Cooley Group says: Dwight emphasized why permitting reform matters so much to companies like his.

“Permitting is an important protection that does not need to come at the expense of growth,” he said. “Companies like Cooley Group will be able to continue our investments to decrease our environmental footprint without compromising business growth.”

“As manufacturers, we know what happens when reviews are duplicative and unpredictable. Investments are delayed, costs rise and opportunities to expand good jobs [disappear],” Dwight said. “Faster, more predictable permitting would bring infrastructure projects online sooner and unlock business growth for manufacturers of every size.”

Business and labor agree: The roundtable also highlighted the costs that permitting uncertainty imposes on employers and workers alike.

Dwight explained that faster permitting could help manufacturers expand domestic sourcing and reduce dependence on foreign suppliers.

Sabitoni stressed that “when business and labor and then government get on the same page, that’s usually when good things happen,” underscoring the importance of collaboration to advance the legislation, while Crowley emphasized the need to build new energy infrastructure to create jobs and achieve environmental goals.

Catucci pointed to the importance of regulatory certainty in attracting businesses and investment to Rhode Island, noting that delays cost money and jobs.

Travis praised Sen. Whitehouse’s “tenacity and determination” in building bipartisan support for legislation critical to Rhode Island’s nearly 1,800 manufacturers employing approximately 75,000 people.

More labor groups join the push: On Tuesday, four more unions joined the three unions who already endorsed the bipartisan legislation: Iron Workers, Sheet Metal Workers, Boilermakers and Teamsters joined Engineers, Laborers and Plumbers in a letter first reported by Politico. The NAM highlighted labor’s support on X.

The Laborers’ International Union of North America also called for permitting reform in an op-ed in The Hill.

In the news: The NAM’s roundtable was scooped by Punchbowl News in its Friday Midday newsletter as well as by reporter Josh Seigel on X. Punchbowl also covered it in its Monday AM newsletter, which Siegel amplified on X. In addition, the event was covered by Providence Business First (subscription), whose reporter, Mary Serreze, attended the event. Sen. Whitehouse highlighted the roundtable on X, amplified by Timmons, as well as in a press release.

A united message: Timmons and Sen. Whitehouse also joined forces in a video highlighting the bipartisan push for permitting reform and the importance of getting a deal across the finish line.

The bottom line: As Congress returns to Washington following the election, the coalition is focused on converting the support into legislative action—and addressing one of the cost drivers holding back American investment, job creation and economic growth.

text:
Data centres were on the ballot in the US midterm elections, with Democratic candidates who pledged to halt development claiming victory on Tuesday night.

The states of Texas, Georgia, and Ohio, which have become magnets for firms wanting to build out data centres to power artificial intelligence, voted for Democratic candidates who have vowed to crack down on the technology.

More than half of Americans are more fearful than excited about AI, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center poll.

They are also concerned about data centres, which use massive amounts of energy, make a lot of noise and cause pollution, and require a lot of land. At least 45 data centre projects were disrupted in the second half of 2026 due to local opposition, according to Data Center Watch, a research project run by the company 10a Labs.

US President Donald Trump has championed the build-out of data centres and in September, called a pushback against them and AI safety concerns “all a hoax,” adding that “data centres are great, and they make people wealthy, and they make states wealthy”.

More than 50% of respondents said AI and data centres were a “crucial or a major factor” in their decision to vote in the midterm elections, according to an NBC exit poll.

"Data centres weren’t the reason most people voted, but they gave the affordability argument a local, visible target and clearly drove votes," said Heather West, geotechnology practice head at consultancy firm Eurasia Group.

"Voters oppose data centres in their own communities by wide margins, and that opposition crosses party lines, as we see in data centre ballot measures," she told Euronews Next.

What does the vote mean for data centres now?

Texas has lured in the tech giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Oracle, Microsoft, Google, Meta, and Amazon with tax breaks and promises of land and energy.

Republican governor Greg Abbott tried to make the state an AI “epicentre” in September, but he later shifted course and paused permits for new data centres pending an audit.

The U-turn followed his Democratic opponent Gina Hinojosa pledged to temporarily halt all new data centre construction until there were legal safeguards.

"Multiple states - most importantly Texas, Ohio, and Georgia - now have governors who are vocally sceptical of data centres, and those states host nearly half of the US AI data centre buildout," said West.

But she said despite Hinojosa's pledge to maintain a moratorium, her power to go beyond Abbott’s temporary, grid-driven pause is "limited".

This will add "friction," as "it doesn’t stop the buildout," West said.

"Projects already permitted or under construction will largely proceed. The friction hits the next wave: local fights, slower permitting, and pressure to make data centers pay for their own power.

"That changes where companies build and what it costs them, but we don’t expect them to turn away from these projects.”

Elon Musk, who pumped $474 million (€420 million) into the Republicans for the midterms and has been building his "Colossus" - a massive cluster of AI-native data centres and supercomputers in Memphis - wrote on X “data centres in space looking pretty appealing right now,” following Tuesday’s election result.

In Ohio, voters fiercely rejected data centres, with 15 municipalities passing bans or implementing other restrictions.

Meta has planned to spend $1 billion (€890m) to construct a data centre in Ohio, and Amazon Web Services has also planned to spend $2 billion (€1.78bn) in the state.

title: Voters Demanded Change – on the Environment, and Democracy - Earthjustice
description:
On Tuesday, Americans voted for a change in direction – including on the environment.
Data centers were one major issue on the ballot.
With rising power demand for data centers and rising energy costs, this election was also about the future of energy.
These were the opposite of sleepy races: Voters are understanding the connection between data centers, utility rates, and regulatory bodies.
The oil and gas industry presented voters with a false choice between prosperity and policies aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions.
text:
On Tuesday, Americans voted for a change in direction – including on the environment.

Data centers were one major issue on the ballot. On Tuesday, data center bans or restrictions passed in at least 38 jurisdictions and counting across the country. In the states where the buildout is happening fastest, including Georgia, Ohio, and Texas, governors’ races turned on voter recognition of the need for stronger guardrails and robust community protections.

With rising power demand for data centers and rising energy costs, this election was also about the future of energy. Voters angry about growing energy bills focused attention on races for seats on the Georgia Public Service Commission, the body that regulates utilities in that state. Similar dynamics were seen in races for two seats on the Arizona Corporation Commission, another utility regulator, and one seat on the Texas Railroad Commission, which regulates the oil and gas industry.

These are small agencies with tremendous power. With these seats, there is an opportunity to usher in clean energy for people who are struggling with soaring energy costs. These were the opposite of sleepy races: Voters are understanding the connection between data centers, utility rates, and regulatory bodies.

And, in the midst of a rush to drill more oil and gas and entrench our fossil fuel dependence, voters rejected a ballot measure to establish a constitutional “right to gas” in Colorado, a major oil-and-gas-producing state. The oil and gas industry presented voters with a false choice between prosperity and policies aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Voters know better.

Among the most important debates in the country is how to build the infrastructure we need faster without running over people and wrecking the things we can’t afford to lose. For example, clean water and clean air. This “abundance” debate has its origins in the California housing crisis, and it has come to stand for the proposition that deregulation is the answer to our country’s problems. As data centers show what speed without guardrails looks like, the debate came full circle in California, with voters rejecting Prop 45, a sloppy effort to kill environmental review in the permitting process for even the most consequential projects.

This election is a thrilling reminder and a profound challenge: We can move forward together in this country if we are willing to throw in together, believe in our ambition for real change, and act on it.

Over the last two years, too many people have underestimated American voters and their ability to care about all the things that matter at once. This election was about the cost of living and an economy that must work infinitely better for everyone. It was also about our health, our health care, and the health of the communities where we live and work. It was about justice and the rights that Americans are not going to give up, no matter how much money is spent and how much power is abused to create division and drive despair.

People across this country did the real work to organize and vote. A whole bunch of courageous, good people stepped up to lead this work. The hope that millions of Americans felt on election night is a call to the most ambitious action. Let’s get to work!
