text:
The Democratic Party won a commanding victory in Tuesday’s midterm elections. As of Wednesday morning, the party had secured control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, as well as several state governments. The party’s strong performance, driven in part by voters’ anger over inflation and the war in Iran, reached into traditional Republican strongholds like Ohio and South Carolina. The sweep will have profound consequences for climate action in the United States, even with President Donald Trump still in the White House.

Flipping control of Congress will allow the Democrats to hinder Trump’s numerous attempts to roll back federal climate policy. In the first two years of Trump’s term, party leaders could do little more than write strongly worded statements to administration officials. They were powerless to stop the suspension of clean energy funding, the elimination of climate rules for power plants and motor vehicles, and the hollowing-out of agencies like the U.S. Forest Service and the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

Now, the party will have a lot more leverage. Democratic senators and members of Congress can issue subpoenas to force administration officials to testify before Congress, and could even impeach Trump administration figures over funding clawbacks and staff reductions that Democrats have called unlawful. Democrats will also have control over must-pass funding bills, and Trump will have to negotiate with them in order to avoid a government shutdown. This could lead to the restoration of some funding for energy and climate resilience programs that Republicans have been trying to whittle down. With majorities in the Senate and the House, the party could even seek to reimpose some of the clean energy tax credits that Republicans rescinded last year.

Turnover at the state level, where officials are still counting votes, may be even more significant. Democrats gained full control of the state government in Wisconsin, Arizona, and Pennsylvania, according to election analysts, ending in some cases decades of Republican or divided government. This could allow the passage of meaningful climate policy in much of the country for the first time. In Pennsylvania, for instance, state house Democrats have said they intend to pass bills making it easier to build community solar, warehouse solar, and battery energy storage, as well as preventing local governments from banning renewables. In Georgia, Democrats flipped both the governor’s mansion and control of the public service commission, which regulates electric utilities.

While Trump’s approval ratings are underwater on almost every major issue, energy prices were among the most salient issues in many races. The gasoline price hike caused by Trump’s invasion of Iran was perhaps the most consequential, but voters in many places were also concerned about their heating bills (Maine) and homeowner’s insurance premiums (Florida). In state races in Texas and Ohio, and in bellwether House districts like one in central Pennsylvania, skepticism over the AI boom may also have driven voters to oust incumbents who supported data centers.

Here are some of the most consequential outcomes for climate change and the environment. We’ll continue to update this post as more results and analysis come in.

House Democrats could make the Trump administration spend money on the climate

Upon taking office, the Trump administration attempted to withhold billions of dollars in climate money, much of it from the landmark Inflation Reduction Act signed into law by Joe Biden in 2022. These freezes threw a number of major climate projects into limbo — the Department of Energy halted experimental projects for hydrogen production in Pennsylvania and decarbonized cement in California, while the Environmental Protection Agency froze a $7 billion community solar program.

Those days may soon be over. Chellie Pingree, the lead Democrat who oversees funding for the Environmental Protection Agency and Interior Department on the powerful House Appropriations Committee, says that she has prepared a long list of investigations and subpoenas for Trump administration officials, including EPA chief Lee Zeldin. She also intends to use the power of the purse to force the administration to spend climate money. Funding bills could include provisions that would deny agencies core operational funds or restrict travel money for leading officials unless they doled out solar and energy funding as Congress previously instructed them to.

“We can put a lot more teeth into the next appropriations bill,” she said. “We can say, ‘OK, fine, if you’re not going to spend the money, we have the power to withhold other funding.’”

— Jake Bittle

Texas elects Democratic senator for the first time in nearly 40 years

Texas joined other Southern states in flipping blue for the first time in decades. Senator-elect James Talarico, a Democrat, supports an all-of-the-above energy strategy, which includes protecting oil and gas jobs while also growing renewable energy. This moderate approach proved important in a state that provides over 40 percent of the nation’s oil and gas.

As a state representative, Talarico authored and introduced the Texas Climate Action Act in 2021. While the bill did not advance, it aimed to establish targets for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and set energy efficiency standards, with an emphasis on local resiliency.

Talarico beat out Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general, who is widely considered friendly to the oil and gas industry. He’s been embroiled in scandal for years and was impeached in 2023 by the Texas House. Paxton’s track record likely helped Democrats obtain this victory.

— Celeste Guajardo

Two climate hawks survive Republican redistricting

Kaptur is the longest-serving woman in the House. She has been a leading opponent of the Department of Energy’s efforts to redirect Inflation Reduction Act money away from clean energy and toward fossil fuels. She has alleged that these redirections violate federal law, and would likely lead investigations into the Energy Department’s actions in a Democratic-controlled Congress. The Ohio state Legislature redrew her district to encompass more conservative areas along Lake Erie, but she held on to her seat comfortably.

— Jake Bittle and Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

Democrats flip control of Georgia utility commission for first time in decades

Democrats secured both Public Service Commission seats on the Georgia ballot, giving the party majority control of the powerful utility regulation board for the first time in 30 years.

Democrat Peter Hubbard successfully defended his District 3 seat against a challenge from former commissioner Fitz Johnson, while Democrat Shelia Edwards defeated Republican Josh Tolbert to take the District 5 seat.

The commission regulates utilities, including the behemoth Georgia Power, meaning commissioners have final say over how the state’s largest utility makes energy and how much customers pay for it. The board has drawn increased scrutiny in recent years because of a series of rate hikes and the scramble to produce enough energy for the massive spike in demand that Georgia Power predicts will result from the data center boom. The utility’s plans to meet that demand rely heavily on fossil fuels.

Georgia is one of 10 states where utility regulators are elected rather than appointed.

— Emily Jones

A flip in an area devastated by Helene

In western North Carolina, where Hurricane Helene caused billions of dollars of damage two years ago, Democrat Jamie Ager defeated Republican Jennifer Balkcom for an open seat in the House of Representatives. Ager, a longtime farmer, made the area’s slow hurricane recovery a centerpiece of his campaign. He criticized Representative Chuck Edwards, who dropped out of the race after a sexual harassment scandal, for doing too little to deliver aid for Asheville and its surrounding counties. Grist reported last month that at least some voters blamed Republicans for the slow recovery. In a rally held on the eve of the election, President Trump promised to deliver more hurricane aid money, but only if North Carolina elected Republicans. The district around Asheville did not take the bait — not only did Ager win the state’s 11th House District, but Democrat Roy Cooper, the state’s former governor, easily won a Senate race, flipping a seat that had been held by Republicans.

— Jake Bittle

An ex-Sunrise activist wins in Michigan

William Lawrence, a co-founder of the climate activism group Sunrise Movement, appears to have prevailed in a razor’s-edge House of Representatives race in central Michigan. Lawrence, a 36-year-old progressive, ousted freshman Republican Tom Barrett in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, a bellwether area encompassing Lansing and its suburbs. He made opposition to data centers a focal point of his campaign, calling for a national moratorium on data center development. He also aligned himself with activists and residents who have opposed large-scale renewable energy projects in the Lansing area. In an interview with Grist last month, Lawrence said that many utility-scale solar projects don’t benefit the communities around them. The Associated Press has not yet called the race, but Lawrence’s campaign told Grist that Barrett has conceded.

— Jake Bittle

Democrats win after attacking Republicans on data centers

In one of the night’s biggest upsets, Texas state Representative Gina Hinojosa ousted incumbent Governor Greg Abbott after campaigning on a data center moratorium and accusing Abbott of selling out to the tech industry.

And at least three legislative seats flipped blue after Democrats aggressively criticized Republican incumbents for being too friendly to data centers. Democrat Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Jon Husted in Ohio’s special Senate election after state Democrats put up billboards stating: “See that data center? Jon Husted did that.” Likewise, Democrat Paige Cognetti beat Republican Rob Bresnahan in Pennsylvania’s 8th Congressional District after she ran television ads associating Bresnahan with data centers and comparing tech companies to polluting mining corporations. (Bresnahan has owned stock in data center companies.) And in South Carolina’s Senate race, voters pushed Annie Andrews to a surprise win over incumbent Darline Graham after Andrews highlighted that a new pro-data center super PAC spent $1.5 million dollars on ads for her opponent, whom she nicknamed “Data Center Darline.”

Both Husted and Bresnahan had previously welcomed data centers to their regions, but later attempted unsuccessfully to pass regulations constraining them once the facilities became a hot-button issue. Data centers are massively unpopular with voters across the political spectrum, polls have shown. The facilities have become a growing source of demand for electricity from fossil fuels.

— Austin Corona, Sachi Kitajima Mulkey, and Jake Bittle

Data centers upend municipal politics

Further down the ballot, it’s hard to find a place where data centers didn’t lose. In addition to the marquee congressional and governor’s races where voter sentiment about the AI boom may have helped oust Republican incumbents, dozens of towns and cities passed pauses or bans on data center development, according to The Washington Post. In many cases, these restrictions passed by enormous margins — in Sunbury, Ohio, where Amazon proposed a $2 billion project, voters rejected the facilities by an almost 60-point margin.

The AI issue also upended local elections, and perhaps the best example is in Pine Island, Minnesota. Google has proposed building a large new data center there, one that would be powered exclusively by clean energy and would include big subsidies for electric ratepayers. But voter outrage over the project caused a previous mayor to resign and led a first-time politician to mount a campaign against the interim replacement. That challenger, Mark Lang, won with well over 60 percent of the vote.

— Jake Bittle

A FEMA defender sails to victory in Florida

Representative Jared Moskowitz, a Democrat, easily hung onto his seat in Congress, surviving a challenge from Scott Singer, a Trump-backed Republican, in Florida’s redrawn 25th congressional district. His third-term victory defies the right-wing effort to make his district significantly redder with new boundaries, and keeps one of America’s most vocal FEMA reformers in Congress.

Moskowitz, once appointed Florida’s emergency management director by Governor Ron DeSantis, championed bipartisan legislation to pull FEMA out of the Department of Homeland Security and make it an independent, cabinet-level agency — just as the Trump administration seeks to cut its funding and shift more responsibility onto states. He has also introduced bills that would let states voluntarily administer federal disaster housing and public assistance, and proposed a reinsurance backstop that would help cover catastrophic losses after disasters like hurricanes.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

Michigan gets utility money out of politics

Voters in Michigan passed a measure to limit corporate spending in elections, and in a nationwide first, successfully went after the state’s electric and gas utilities. Supporters of Proposal 2 leveraged ratepayers’ growing dissatisfaction with utilities around power bills, unreliable service, and data centers. The measure is one of the most ambitious attempts in the country to limit corporate influence in politics, which it will do by preventing utility-funded political action groups and utility executives from contributing to state political campaigns. Groups that oppose the measure have contended that Prop 2 will stifle corporations’ speech protections under the 2010 Citizens United decision. And while experts are fairly confident the measure will face legal challenges and won’t get all utility money out of politics, Prop 2 advocates maintain it’s a step toward accountability.

— Vivian La

A governor who at least acknowledges climate change in Florida

Republican Byron Donalds has defeated Democrat David Jolly for occupancy of Florida’s governor’s mansion. Donalds, who currently represents Florida’s 19th Congressional District, will be the state’s first Black governor. He doesn’t believe humans play any role in global warming, but he’s more willing to discuss the issue than the current governor, Ron DeSantis, who signed the state’s infamous “don’t say climate change” law.

That matters in a state especially battered by sea level rise, coastal erosion, and storms. The skyrocketing costs of home insurance were a central issue in this race, and Donalds promised to bring them down by increasing competition in the state’s private market. In 2025, Donalds notably co-introduced bipartisan legislation with Democrat Jared Moskowitz to reform federal disaster aid by making FEMA an independent Cabinet-level agency. In the weeks before voters went to the polls, he also pledged investment in restoring coastal habitats. Donalds seems likely to carry on DeSantis’ other environmental policies, such as supporting data center development and attacking wind and solar projects.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

A MAGA loyalist who says no to drilling in Florida

Republican Senator Ashley Moody defeated the progressive Democrat Angie Nixon to retain her seat, which Florida Governor Ron DeSantis appointed her to last year. Moody’s brief stint in Washington hints at what’s to come: She introduced a resolution to overturn Biden-era efficiency standards and supported the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which ended federal tax credits for clean energy installations like rooftop solar and batteries. Previously, as Florida’s attorney general, she joined a lawsuit challenging emissions reduction targets on highways.

But in Florida, a state grappling with coastal erosion and rising sea levels, some environmental protections are popular across party lines: Last year, even as Trump pushed to open offshore drilling in other states, Moody introduced the American Shores Protection Act to ban the practice off Florida’s coast through 2032.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

This story has been updated with analysis of additional races and trends.

text:
Local governments, schools, nonprofits and other tax-exempt entities received almost $2.5 billion in federal incentives for eligible energy projects in the first two years after the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) was passed. That’s according to new Internal Revenue Service (IRS) data recently released by Senate Finance Committee Democrats that highlights the impact of the IRA’s direct pay provision. Direct pay allows public and nonprofit entities without tax liability to access certain clean energy tax credits as a direct cash reimbursement.

Direct pay and clean energy projects

About a dozen clean energy credits are eligible for direct pay, including key buildings-related tax incentives such as the Section 48E investment tax credit, which can be used for on-site solar or storage; the Section 48(a) credit for geothermal heat pumps; and the Section 30C credit for electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure. The new IRS data shows that more than 1,000 entities per year claimed direct pay, and communities increased their uptake by 50% between 2023 and 2024 as awareness grew.

These clean energy projects not only deliver cost savings to local communities but also bring other benefits such as improved performance, resilience, health and safety, economic growth, and more. The Senate Finance Committee report highlights some of those success stories:

Hart County Schools in Kentucky received almost $800,000 from direct pay to install geothermal heat pumps, thermal storage and solar. The project will cut energy usage by 52% and save the district $6.7 million over 20 years.

Greene County Community School District in Iowa is leveraging direct pay for its on-site solar project, which is anticipated to deliver up to $400,000 in annual energy savings.

St. Patrick's Episcopal Church in Georgia received $30,000 in direct payment for a 90-panel rooftop solar array, helping the church save thousands of dollars on their electric utility bills.

Phased-out credits

While direct pay remains in place as a highly impactful tool for public and nonprofit entities, unfortunately some of the clean energy credits eligible for direct pay were phased out under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) enacted last year. OBBBA established a Dec. 31, 2027, sunset for solar under Section 48E, with a four-year safe harbor for projects that started construction before July 4 of this year. Section 30C was also terminated, with EV charging projects required to be placed into service by June 30 of this year to claim the credit. Meanwhile, storage technologies remain eligible for the Section 48E investment tax credit but now must demonstrate compliance with complex prohibited foreign entity requirements to qualify.

On the positive side, the Section 48(a) credit for geothermal heat pumps remains in place through 2034, with no prohibited foreign entity requirements. That presents a significant opportunity for nonprofit and public buildings to evaluate and plan geothermal investments while leveraging direct pay for the coming years.

What USGBC is doing

Looking ahead to next Congress, USGBC will continue to advocate for rebuilding and expanding energy efficiency and clean energy tax credits available for direct pay to accelerate the impact that this tool has already had in just a few short years. In fact, USGBC is working on a proposal for a new federal tax credit for energy efficiency improvements in existing commercial buildings, including nonprofit and public buildings. The Building Energy Affordability and Resilience tax credit would provide up to a 30% credit for projects that demonstrate energy usage intensity improvements through retrofit measures. With direct pay, the proposed incentive would help schools, hospitals, municipal buildings, and other nonprofit or public buildings make whole-building energy efficiency improvements.

There is significant opportunity to invest more in our country’s public and nonprofit buildings to address acute deferred maintenance backlogs and to transform these facilities into energy-efficient, sustainable, resilient assets for their communities, and direct pay has an important role to play in enabling that investment.

To engage with us on advocacy for direct pay incentives, consider signing up for the USGBC Advocacy Working Group.

text:
Voters in Eugene, Oregon, have approved a ballot measure to create a Clean Energy Fund.

The measure imposes a 2% tax on the profits of large retailers with significant sales in the city.

Funds will be used for projects like energy efficiency upgrades, community solar, and job training.

Eugene Clean Energy Fund backers celebrated Nov. 3 as early returns showed the ballot measure was all but certain to pass. Derided by local business interests as a tax that would drive up prices on consumer goods, the measure seeks to collect 2% of local profits from billion-dollar companies that make at least $500,000 selling products in Eugene.

The fund is modeled on legislation that went into effect in Portland in 2018 that has collected more than $1 billion and paid for numerous projects. Portland's fee has been used to pay for efficiency upgrades at thousands of homes, to distribute 20,000 free air conditioning units, widen sidewalks, plant trees, install community solar and train thousands of people to work in renewable energy.

Advocates for Eugene's fund estimate it could collect $15 million a year to pay for similar projects. As of Tuesday night, the measure was passing 58% yes to 42% no.

Dozens of Clean Energy Fund supporters gathered outside Oakshire Public House in Eugene's Whiteaker neighborhood to watch initial results and celebrate the measure's success.

Joel Iboa, chief petitioner for the Clean Energy Fund, told the Register-Guard the measure has been a long time coming.

"It took a lot. It took a lot of conversation, a lot of coalition building, it took a tremendous amount of fundraising, trust building with a variety of organizations in Eugene, Lane County and statewide," Iboa said.

Starting in 2029, the city would collect 2% of these retailers' Eugene profits minus profit from basic groceries, medicines, garbage, recycling and health care services. The measure creates a new Clean Energy Fund Committee, primarily made of people with clean energy experience, to advise the mayor and City Council on how to spend the money.

Once the measure officially passes, the next step is implementation. Iboa said stakeholders must form a governance board and make sure promises to voters are kept.

"Now, it is making sure what's promised in the Clean Energy Fund comes to fruition, whether that be weatherization, clean energy projects or apprenticeship programs," Iboa said. "The sky is the limit. We've seen what the Portland clean energy fund has been able to do these last couple of years and I'm excited to see what we do here."

Jennifer Davis, executive director of Beyond Toxics and an advocate for the Clean Energy Fund, said the measure will help many in the community get energy efficiency upgrades, lower electricity bills and assist low-income community members who disproportionately feel the impact of climate change to become more resilient.

"This is huge for our community, so thank you so much," Davis said.

title: Gas turbines and batteries are cashing in as AI data centers can't wait for the grid
description:
“As people need AI, large AI data centers will move forward one way or another,” said Shen Wang, an Omdia analyst.
Data center developer and operator Aligned Data Centers illustrates the scale of the buildout.
Analyst firm Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $3 trillion in ongoing AI data center projects worldwide, with roughly two-thirds in North America.
Now, with gas turbines in short supply, some data centers are going further and using gas engines as their primary source of power.
BTM gas turbines, reciprocating engines, and batteries offer different advantages, but all can help developers reduce their dependence on lengthy utility interconnection timelines.
text:
The behind-the-meter (BTM) trend is gaining momentum as data centers deal with the shortage of available grid power in many areas and lengthening interconnection queues.

Research firm Omdia projects data centers could deploy 35 GW of BTM power by 2030. Most developers would prefer to buy electricity from utilities or independent power producers (IPPs). But with billions of dollars in AI infrastructure at stake, they don’t have the patience to wait.

“As people need AI, large AI data centers will move forward one way or another,” said Shen Wang, an Omdia analyst.

Data center developer and operator Aligned Data Centers illustrates the scale of the buildout. The company reports nearly 100 facilities under construction, plus about 50 active operating sites.

“There is huge growth in data center expansion now compared to 10 years ago,” CEO Phill Lawson-Shanks said.

Analyst firm Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $3 trillion in ongoing AI data center projects worldwide, with roughly two-thirds in North America. Not all those projects are assured significant grid capacity on their proposed completion timelines. As a result, many developers are opting for a combination of battery energy storage systems (BESS) and an onsite power plant to fuel their AI ambitions.

BESS boom

Investment in battery energy storage systems (BESS) is booming. Omdia forecasts BESS could exceed $50 billion a year by 2030, compared with nearly $10 billion in 2026.

BESS is finding a home across several fronts. Those data centers opting for wind or solar energy are harnessing BESS to store energy to compensate for intermittency. Adding BESS to solar means data center can run on solar during the day and use batteries at night.

Others are ordering BESS to replace backup generators and to act as a buffer against grid instability or large load swings from AI applications. Oracle, for example, is incorporating BESS into its AI infrastructure to help manage sudden changes in electricity demand.

“Traditional grids and power plants can’t cope with the massive power swings produced from AI data centers that can happen several times a second,” said Ram Nagappan, vice president of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure’s AI infrastructure. “BESS can act as a buffer to dampen these power swings, which is emerging as a new requirement for AI data centers.”

Batteries are also being paired with natural gas generation. Frontier Infrastructure is purchasing 16 Baker Hughes NovaLT gas turbines for U.S. data center projects, with BESS and synchronous condensers planned to help manage rapid demand changes.

Turbine demand

AI-driven electricity demand has strained an already tight gas turbine supply chain.

With large-frame turbine delivery slots increasingly booked years in advance, developers are turning to smaller turbines and mobile generation packages to accelerate deployment.

The Oracle/OpenAI Stargate site in Abilene, Texas, illustrates the approach. Its power strategy includes GE Vernova LM2500XPRESS mobile turbines, Solar Turbines Titan 350 units, and Dynamis Power Solutions DT35 packages. This site could eventually span 4 million square feet across eight buildings and consume as much as 1.2 GW of energy.

Dynamis’ 35-MW DT35 package uses an LM2500+G4 gas turbine in a two-trailer configuration.

Dynamis has placed a couple of big orders with Baker Hughes, intended mainly for data center sites. The first agreement started with 10 LM9000 turbines for Dynamis’ planned 70-MW DT70 package, along with 15 additional LM2500, LM6000, and LM9000 units, providing about 1.3 GW of mobile generation capacity.

A subsequent agreement added 76 NovaLT16 turbines, paired with gearboxes and Brush generators, for Dynamis’ DT17 platform.

“The market is demanding utility-grade power solutions that deliver lower emissions without the complexity and expense of water, which is what our Dynamis DT17 platform was engineered to provide,” Dynamis Power Solutions CEO Matt Crawford said.

Synchronous condensers

Gas turbine plants are often paired with synchronous condenser capability, allowing them to switch between generating power and providing grid stability services. Existing plants can add this capability by installing a clutch, such as those made by SSS Clutch of New Castle, Delaware, between the gas turbine and the generator. New data center projects are following suit, specifying clutches for grid stability in the natural gas turbine plants they’re building alongside their facilities.

“By specifying the addition of synchronous self-shifting (SSS) clutches along with generators, the data center may be able to obtain double duty for its investment by providing stability services to the power grid,” SSS Clutch Company CEO Morgan Hendry said. “We are also seeing hybrid arrangements that combine a synchronous condenser with BESS.”

Henry noted the technology is also being incorporated into some European data center power systems alongside uninterruptible power supply (UPS) equipment.

Piller Energy Systems’ UniBlock technology is one example of a system designed to provide power conditioning and continuity during electrical disturbances.

“Besides providing backup generation when utility power is lost, the generator can filter out utility disturbances and protect against incidents that can cause outages or affect power quality,” Hendry said. “If only UPS batteries are used for this function repeatedly, it reduces their life expectancy.”

Gas engine growth

Gas engines have been steadily replacing diesel engines as backup generators at data centers for years, and that trend shows no sign of slowing. Now, with gas turbines in short supply, some data centers are going further and using gas engines as their primary source of power.

Caterpillar, for example, has received a 2-GW equipment order for American Intelligence & Power’s Monarch Compute Campus in West Virginia, with the potential to expand to 6 GW.

The project includes plans for more than 100 Caterpillar G3516 Fast Response natural gas generator sets, each rated at 1.5 MW, to operate in parallel. BESS will help handle rapid load swings, while gas engines will use selective catalytic reduction (SCR) technology to meet emission targets.

Wärtsilä is also supplying dozens of 10-MW 50sg natural gas engines for a nearly 300-MW data center project in Ohio.

“Data center developers are facing increasing time-to-power challenges due to grid connection delays,” said Risto Paldanius, vice president of Americas at Wärtsilä Energy. “Quick access to power combined with high reliability, fuel efficiency, and exceptional heat resilience makes natural gas engines the ideal power supply for data centers.”

Time to power

For now, data center developers are prioritizing the fastest available path to energizing their facilities.

BTM gas turbines, reciprocating engines, and batteries offer different advantages, but all can help developers reduce their dependence on lengthy utility interconnection timelines.

Some on-site power plants could eventually be transferred to local utilities or sold to independent power producers (IPPs) as grid infrastructure catches up.

“Time to power wins,” Applied Digital Chief Operating Officer Laura Laltrello said. “The AI race favors builders who can energize fast — compute demand isn’t going to slow down.”

title: Permitting reform is likely move for Democratic controlled US Congress | Wood Mackenzie
description:
But permitting reform has a path that other Democratic priorities do not.
Permitting reform would also remove regulatory delays for short laterals, pipeline interconnections, and compressor upgrades that are necessary for behind-the-meter (BTM) power.
"The wind industry's best bet for permitting reform is to be included in a national bill across multiple technologies and to have Congress monitor implementation," said Warrier.
States step up as federal policy outlook remains uncertain Should federal energy policy stall under divided government, state-level energy policies and market rules will take on even more importance.
"While we see the potential and likelihood for advancing permitting reform, there is a wider concern over how policy is created, managed, and implemented in the US," said Brown.
text:
With Democrats capturing the House of Representatives and Senate in the US mid-term elections, permitting reform could be a top agenda for advancing power growth and reducing energy costs in the US, according to Wood Mackenzie analysis. The elections came amid rising energy costs driven by the conflict in Iran, which drove peak diesel and jet fuel prices in the US roughly 2.5 times higher than pre-war forecasts. Prices should ease as the conflict subsides, though the hardest-hit products will still be 30% above pre-war forecasts in 2027.

Congress has three policy levers to address energy affordability, each with very different odds:

Permitting reform: Bipartisan interest makes it, in Wood Mackenzie’s view, the likeliest route to faster gas, transmission and wind approvals. Nuclear, CCUS, and upstream get an incremental boost.

Subsidies for renewable energy: Democrats have proposed several expansions, but a presidential veto makes new credits unlikely.

Large-load cost rules: Federal mandates face legal and political resistance, so states will set cost allocation policy for data centers.

A Democratic Congress does not guarantee legislative success under a Republican White House. President Trump retains veto authority, and executive agencies can dilute the impact of any legislation that does pass. But permitting reform has a path that other Democratic priorities do not. The midterm results point to a sentiment shift in the US. The cost of energy has emerged as a check on the president's agenda, creating common ground for both parties on affordability.

With rapid development in data centers and power infrastructure, the US will see load growth lifted 3% from 2026 to 2035, driving wholesale power prices up 46% in Wood Mackenzie’s base case over the same time period and making affordability a likely key driver for permitting goals.

"While we see the likelihood for permitting reform, how policy is legislated and implemented remains a risk to the US economy," said David Brown, Director, global integrated energy research for Wood Mackenzie. "Entrenched partisanship could fuel policy stagnation and regulatory confusion."

Most likely option — Permitting reform

Supported by key Senate architects and a coalition of clean energy developers, oil and gas producers, mining operators and trade unions, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) could speed up infrastructure approvals.

Key initiatives include:

Mandates that environmental impact analyses under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) are fully completed within two years

Prevents federal agencies from revoking permits

Limits litigation to a 150-day window after project environmental approvals are issued

Mandates a 9-month timeline for evaluating water quality dredge and fill permits required for new gas pipelines

Permitting reform matters most for front-of-the-meter gas-fired power, which is typically located away from gas supply basins and requires new pipelines to support Wood Mackenzie's forecast of 166 GW of net new natural gas-fired capacity from 2026 to 2035. Permitting reform would also remove regulatory delays for short laterals, pipeline interconnections, and compressor upgrades that are necessary for behind-the-meter (BTM) power. Wood Mackenzie reports BTM gas demand is approaching 6 billion cubic feet per day (bcfd), about 6% of US domestic gas demand excluding LNG and piped supply.

"Without reform, midstream bottlenecks are likely to return, stifling upstream investment and pushing regional gas and power prices higher, most acutely in the power-hungry Northeast," said Siddhant Warrier, research analyst, North American power for Wood Mackenzie. "Prolonged pipeline delays would also slow data center development, a high priority for both parties."

High-voltage transmission speeds up — but who pays is in question

With congestion costs exceeding $10 billion a year and high-voltage completions in the 2020s running at under half the 2010s rate, the need for faster grid buildout is urgent. BAAJA addresses the permitting side of that challenge, mandating one-year NEPA assessments, protecting against permit revocation, and limiting post-approval litigation to a 150-day window. The next legislative frontier will be inter-zonal cost allocation: who pays for a line that crosses multiple utility territories and benefits multiple states.

Wind: new legislation will help clear the permitting backlog

The Restoring Renewable Energy Parity Act would require the Defense Department to sign mitigation agreements for pending wind, solar and transmission projects and overturn executive actions targeting renewables. But wind carries added risk: the President has targeted it directly, and the federal government controls offshore leasing.

"The wind industry's best bet for permitting reform is to be included in a national bill across multiple technologies and to have Congress monitor implementation," said Warrier.

States step up as federal policy outlook remains uncertain

Should federal energy policy stall under divided government, state-level energy policies and market rules will take on even more importance. States hold broad statutory authority over retail electricity, utility regulation, and siting, cementing their independence from federal gridlock.

The midterm gubernatorial results highlight this dynamic. In Texas, the election of Gina Hinojosa as Governor marks a significant shift in data center policy. The incoming regulatory environment could increase execution risk for developers with longer permitting and community approval timelines if Hinojosa's platform becomes law in the January 2027 legislative session.

Texas will remain a leading market for data center investment given its renewable resources, natural gas infrastructure and regulatory autonomy from FERC, but the new Governor will push for new constraints on speed to power in the Lone Star State.

Supply chain: executive order adds new uncertainty

An August executive order restricting bulk-power equipment from 24 countries, including China, adds a further layer of complexity. Implementation rules due in late December will clarify exposure for grid-connected data centers. New restrictive policies under the order could exacerbate existing supply chain deficits, 18% for power transformers and 14% for substation transformers.

Can a sentiment shift solve big problems in the US?

"While we see the potential and likelihood for advancing permitting reform, there is a wider concern over how policy is created, managed, and implemented in the US," said Brown.

Brown noted that economic headwinds could create divergence, with Congress focusing on affordability issues and the Executive branch pursuing foreign policy agendas that create policy confusion and stagnation. Veto power from the White House could derail significant advancements as well.

"The US has had moments of bipartisanship when it needed them most. Twenty years ago, Democrats took Congress amid an unpopular US-led war in the Middle East, resulting in deep partisan gridlock," Brown continued. "But the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 raised Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards, set lighting and appliance efficiency standards and expanded renewable fuels with bipartisan support. A similar effort is needed now to build affordable energy at home and for the US to keep global leadership in AI."

text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

SPRINGFIELD — The Illinois Environmental Protection Agency has launched a Clean Trucks Program intended to help the state’s fleet operators move from diesel to zero-emission vehicles, with the goals of lowering fuel costs and building a cleaner freight system.

The program, part of the agency’s broader Driving a Cleaner Illinois initiative, begins with two efforts: a $3 million Clean Fleet and Freight Concierge Service and $935,220 in grant funding to help operators replace older diesel trucks.

“The Clean Trucks Program will provide individualized support to fleets that may be interested in transitioning from diesel to electric but aren’t sure where to start,” Illinois EPA Director James Jennings said in a statement. He said the agency wants every fleet operator, regardless of size, to have access to credible information and technical assistance.

The concierge service is funded through the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s Climate Pollution Reduction Grant Program. Illinois EPA received the federal funding in 2024 to support the deployment of zero-emission commercial vehicles and charging infrastructure. The agency is now seeking qualified firms to run the service, which will help small and medium-sized fleets explore electric vehicles and the charging equipment they require.

The service will cover the northern and southern regions of Illinois, defined as the areas served primarily by the PJM and MISO electric grids. PJM and MISO are regional grid operators that manage the flow of electricity across multiple states.

The grant money comes from the federal Diesel Emissions Reduction Act program, which lets participating states fund grant, rebate, and loan programs aimed at cutting diesel emissions. A Notice of Funding Opportunity posted on the Driving a Cleaner Illinois webpage says the funds can cover up to 45% of the cost of replacing eligible diesel-powered Class 5-8 trucks with new battery-electric models. Those classes generally include medium- and heavy-duty trucks, starting at about 16,000 pounds in gross vehicle weight.

The agency said the funds will help fleets reduce local air pollution and shield their operations from volatile diesel prices. It described the two efforts as the start of a push to pair hands-on, fleet-specific guidance with financial incentives that address the upfront costs of electrification.

Fleet operators and others seeking more information can visit the Driving a Cleaner Illinois and Climate Pollution Reduction Grant webpages or contact the Driving a Cleaner Illinois team.

Illinois EPA was created in 1970 under the Illinois Environmental Protection Act. The agency says it is the longest-standing state environmental protection agency in the country.

text:
November 4, 2026

This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.

Democrats on Tuesday won control of both houses of Congress and a decisive mandate to put a check on Donald Trump’s tumultuous presidency, a victory propelled by voter anger over high prices, corruption and the unchecked spread of data centers.

Some of the same concerns helped to lift Democrats to victories in statehouses, where they gained a majority of the country’s governorships for the first time in more than a decade.

Voters in Ohio, South Carolina and Texas—states Trump won by double digits two years ago—put Democrats over the top in the U.S. Senate. And the Democratic wave surmounted a seawall of money: the unprecedented spending the GOP’s tech industry allies poured into the races in recent weeks to protect the status quo and their freedom from regulation.

Activists believe the result sets the stage for renewed environmental and climate policy, even though candidates seldom mentioned those issues by name in their campaigns. They argue that any action Congress takes on voters’ top issues—soaring energy prices, undue industry influence and the surge of artificial intelligence infrastructure—will curb the upward trajectory of U.S. fossil fuel consumption that Trump has encouraged.

“Voters rejected the Trump administration’s failing energy policies, which have pushed electricity bills higher,” said David Kieve, president of EDF Action, the political arm of the nonprofit Environmental Defense Fund, which invested $18 million in the midterms. “Families know that blocking clean energy raises rates. Paying companies to abandon wind projects, canceling grants meant to lower rural utility bills, and using emergency orders to keep coal plants running when cleaner, cheaper options are available all moved us in the wrong direction.”

A Broad Reaction to Republican Policies

A president’s party typically loses seats in Congress in midterm elections, and in the face of that history, Trump urged voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot.” The results indicated that voters listened. Trump’s sagging approval became a millstone Republicans were forced to carry, as opponents attacked them for their complicity in an unpopular war that had caused U.S. energy prices to soar. (The decision to unilaterally join Israel in airstrikes against Iran on Feb. 28 resulted in “incalculable political damage for Trump’s party,” political pundit Charlie Cook wrote on the eve of the election.)

In unfortunate timing for Republicans, the U.S. oil industry last week reported its profits—$130 billion over the past six months, or triple the earnings of one year ago, all due to the war-related run-up in prices. On the campaign trail, Trump tried to frame the oil industry’s boon as a blessing for Americans.

“They’re making hundreds of billions of dollars—our country is—on oil,” Trump said at an Oct. 26 rally in Georgia. Trump said his advisers warned him not to mention that “because people are paying a little bit higher,” but he said he didn’t care how his words would be portrayed. “I don’t give a damn,” he said. “We’re making a freaking fortune!”

But Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) seemed to better capture the mood of his state’s voters in his last days of campaigning for reelection: “Under failed president Donald J. Trump, it costs more than ever in American history to fill up your truck, stock your fridge, visit the doctor or power your home.” Ossoff coasted to re-election as expected, and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Republican Rick Jackson to win the Georgia governor’s race.

Opposition to data centers helped Democrats in many races, such as in Ohio, where Democrat Sherrod Brown staged a political comeback and defeated Republican Sen. Jon Husted. Brown dubbed his opponent “the face of data centers,” and sought to tie Husted to tax breaks and other policies that have attracted the giant computing centers to Ohio.

Trump’s foes—including environmental groups—blanketed the airwaves in swing states and districts with ads tying the pain of high gasoline and electricity prices to cozy Republican relationships with oil and utility companies, tech giants and the insurance industry. “Voters are not simply frustrated, they’re angry at monopoly utility companies, Big Tech, and Big Oil, who are making record profits while families struggle,” said Sara Schreiber, senior vice president of LCV Victory Fund. The super PAC of the League of Conservation Voters became one of the leading outside issues groups supporting Democrats on both state and federal ballots, with a $110 million investment in the midterms.

Cabinet members like Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin and U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins fanned out into states like Iowa where Republicans were in deep trouble. They touted Trump deregulatory policies and offered aid to farmers. But pre-election polling showed key Trump administration messages on environmental protection fell flat. More than 70 percent of likely voters in Iowa, Ohio and Texas felt rollback of environmental regulations would have either no impact on making their lives more affordable or would make things more expensive, according to early October polling by The Cook Political Report, New River Strategies and GS Strategy Group.

And the polling showed voters were more worried about the inflationary impact of Republican energy policies than Democratic climate policies. About 60 percent blamed “Republicans’ support for the war with Iran, trade wars, and billions in giveaways for data centers” for high energy prices; only about 40 percent said they were more concerned about “Democrats’ radical environmental policies like the Green New Deal.”

James Talarico overcame a fusillade of tech industry money to become the first Democrat that Texas will send to the U.S. Senate in 33 years. The world’s richest man, Elon Musk, alone contributed an unprecedented $445 million to super PACs, much of it to bolster Talarico’s scandal-plagued Republican opponent, Attorney General Ken Paxton. Talarico made Musk’s effort to buy the seat an issue in the campaign, which resonated in a state that has been convulsed over the spread of Big Tech facilities.

Across the country, 56 percent of voters said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their picks for Congress, according to polling by The Wall Street Journal. Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, seeing the tidal wave of opposition grow, imposed a temporary moratorium on new facilities in Texas. But his moves were not enough to win him re-election. State Rep. Gina Hinojosa will become the first Democratic governor of Texas since Ann Richards left office in 1995.

After pulling off her surprise victory in the South Carolina Senate race, Democrat Annie Andrews spoke of the moment as a rebellion against the status quo. “You have shown the nation that in this era of partisan divides, of vitriol and name calling, in a politics dominated by billionaires and special interest groups and insiders in Washington, D.C., that we will not bow down, that we will not back down, and we will chart our own course,” she told her supporters.

As Washington enters a period of divided government, governors and state legislatures will have an opportunity to lead on climate and energy policy in ways that the federal government won’t or can’t.

Democrats retained governors’ offices in Arizona, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, flipped control from Republicans in Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas, and were on track to add other wins in closely watched races.

“Because of your hard work, Ohio has chosen unity and decency over division and hate,” said Ohio Governor-elect Amy Acton, a former director of the state public health agency.

Democrats also won the two open seats on the Georgia Public Service Commission, a utility regulator, giving the party a 3-2 edge. The panel had been controlled by Republicans for decades and the new majority has an opportunity to address consumer concerns about rising utility bills.

Oversight Ahead

A key win for climate came early in the night with the re-election of Rep. Kathy Castor (D-Fla.), despite Florida Republicans’ failed efforts at redistricting to favor the GOP. Castor, who represents storm-prone Tampa, served as chair of the House Select Committee on the Climate Crisis during Trump’s first term and has been leader of a project to develop a legislative agenda on the economy and environment for the new Congress. The so-called Thriving Economies Project unveiled a menu of 800 policy recommendations in September designed to win bipartisan support, many of them tapping into the concerns that animated voters in the midterms. (One example: Creating a Strategic Energy Affordability Reserve, drawing from windfall oil and gas profits.)

title: AEP, Google Advance $4 Billion Fuel-Cell Project to Power Cheyenne Data Centers
description:
One of the principal advantages of fuel cells for AI data center development is modularity.
Fuel cells also present an opportunity for closer integration with emerging high-voltage DC data center architectures.
Cheyenne's Larger Power Development The AEP project is one component of a much broader energy development effort taking shape around Google's planned data center expansion near Cheyenne.
Black Hills says the agreements are designed to protect existing retail customers against cost shifting associated with Google's planned data center.
The agreements reflect a broader industry shift toward assigning more of the financial responsibility for dedicated data center infrastructure to the customers creating the demand.
text:
A Power Commitment That Began Two Years Earlier

Although Google's participation was publicly identified in October 2026, the procurement strategy underlying the Cheyenne project dates to November 2024, when Bloom Energy announced an agreement with AEP covering up to 1 gigawatt of solid oxide fuel-cell equipment. As Data Center Frontier reported at the time, the agreement included an initial commitment to purchase 100 MW, with options for an additional 900 MW. The arrangement was intended to help AEP serve large commercial and industrial customers facing growing electricity requirements without waiting for the completion of conventional grid infrastructure upgrades.

The relationship advanced in January 2026, when AEP disclosed in a regulatory filing that an unregulated subsidiary had committed approximately $2.65 billion to purchase a substantial portion of the fuel-cell capacity covered by its earlier option. The company also reported a 20-year agreement to sell the planned facility's entire electricity output to an unidentified investment-grade customer, now confirmed as Google. The equipment purchase formed part of the project's development history, rather than representing a separate $2.65 billion investment in addition to the $4 billion project announced in October.

The scale of the investment is significant, but so is the transaction structure. Rather than requiring Google to own and operate the generation equipment directly, the arrangement places development and ownership responsibilities with an established energy company while providing the hyperscaler long-term access to the facility's electricity output. For AEP, it also represents an opportunity to deploy capital in support of large-load customers beyond its traditional regulated utility territory.

At approximately $4 billion for 702 MW, the project represents roughly $5.7 million per megawatt of planned generating capacity. That figure offers a measure of the investment's capital intensity, although it is not directly comparable with the construction cost of a conventional gas-fired power plant without accounting for differences in project scope, fuel infrastructure, electrical integration and operating characteristics.

The price Google will ultimately pay for electricity has not been publicly disclosed. Neither party has released the PPA's pricing structure, including any energy charges, capacity payments or other detailed commercial terms.

Why Fuel Cells Are Attracting Hyperscale Investment

Solid oxide fuel cells are an established technology, but their deployment at the scale proposed for Cheyenne represents a significant evolution in how data centers obtain electricity. Depending on their configuration, the systems can operate on natural gas, biogas or hydrogen. Unlike conventional combustion-based generators, they convert fuel into electricity through an electrochemical process. When operating on natural gas, the fuel is reformed into a hydrogen-rich mixture that reacts with oxygen ions passing through a solid ceramic electrolyte, producing electricity, heat, water vapor and carbon dioxide. The process avoids conventional combustion but does not eliminate carbon emissions when natural gas is the primary fuel.

One of the principal advantages of fuel cells for AI data center development is modularity. Standardized generating assemblies can be combined into larger installations, allowing capacity to be added incrementally rather than requiring construction of a single large generating unit. This flexibility offers a potential scheduling and investment advantage, enabling developers to coordinate additional generating capacity with successive phases of data hall construction, electrical commissioning and computing equipment deployment. As DCF's reporting on emerging behind-the-meter power strategies has documented, modular generation is becoming an increasingly important consideration in the development of large AI campuses.

Multiple independent fuel-cell modules can also reduce dependence on any single generating unit, potentially allowing individual modules to be serviced or replaced without shutting down the entire installation. That distributed architecture offers operational flexibility, although its contribution to overall reliability depends on how the generating equipment is integrated with the facility's electrical infrastructure.

Modularity alone does not guarantee the availability required by hyperscale operations. Fuel-cell installations must still be engineered as part of a complete power delivery system incorporating appropriate electrical redundancy, energy storage, backup capacity, protection and control systems. The ability to accommodate changing AI workloads, maintain stable power quality and manage equipment failures remains essential regardless of the generation technology.

Fuel cells also present an opportunity for closer integration with emerging high-voltage DC data center architectures. In September 2026, Bloom promoted an 800-volt DC-native power architecture designed to reduce conversion equipment, electrical losses and infrastructure costs. Because its solid oxide fuel cells generate direct-current electricity, Bloom contends that the technology could simplify the power delivery chain for next-generation AI systems. That approach aligns with the broader industry transition toward 800V DC distribution for high-density AI infrastructure.

AEP and Google have not disclosed whether the Wyoming installation will employ a DC-native distribution architecture or rely on conventional power conversion and interconnection equipment. The distinction will be important in determining how closely the fuel-cell installation can be integrated with the data center's electrical infrastructure and whether the potential efficiency and equipment savings of direct-current generation can be realized.

Carbon Capture Is Part of the Plan, Not Yet an Operating Result

AEP says the Cheyenne project is being designed to incorporate carbon-capture technology, with the objective of delivering near-zero-emissions electricity from a natural gas-fueled installation. Whether that objective can be achieved will depend on the design, performance and integration of a capture system that has not yet been publicly detailed.

According to Bloom Energy, its solid oxide fuel-cell technology produces a relatively concentrated carbon dioxide stream, potentially simplifying capture compared with conventional gas-fired generating equipment, where carbon dioxide is diluted in much larger volumes of combustion exhaust. The manufacturer maintains that this characteristic could reduce some of the equipment requirements, energy consumption and costs associated with carbon capture.

In February 2025, Bloom announced a partnership with Chart Industries to advance carbon-capture technology for its fuel-cell systems. The arrangement combines Bloom's electrochemical generation technology with Chart's gas-processing capabilities, with the aim of preparing captured carbon dioxide for industrial use or permanent geological storage. The companies presented the partnership as a potential pathway to lower-carbon, continuously available power for energy-intensive customers, including data centers.

The technical advantages remain distinct from demonstrated environmental performance at the Cheyenne site. AEP has not publicly disclosed a guaranteed capture rate, identified the carbon-capture equipment supplier for the facility, or detailed the transportation, utilization or permanent storage arrangements for the captured carbon dioxide. Those elements will be necessary to determine whether the project can meet its stated emissions objective, and what additional infrastructure and operating costs will be required.

The distinction is particularly relevant to Google's broader energy strategy. In its June 2026 environmental report, the company acknowledged that its AI infrastructure expansion is proceeding faster than electricity grids are decarbonizing, complicating efforts to achieve its climate objectives. Natural gas-powered fuel cells equipped with effective carbon capture could help address part of that challenge. Their ultimate environmental value, however, will depend not only on carbon-capture performance but also on upstream methane emissions, the energy required to operate the capture system and whether the captured carbon dioxide is permanently stored or eventually released.

Cheyenne's Larger Power Development

The AEP project is one component of a much broader energy development effort taking shape around Google's planned data center expansion near Cheyenne.

Eight days before AEP's announcement, Black Hills Corp. disclosed definitive agreements with Google covering an arrangement that combines grid-connected electricity, new natural gas generation and privately contracted power resources. Effective September 30, 2026, the agreements provide for a resource portfolio totaling approximately 2.7 GW, including reserve margins, to support the planned campus.

Under the arrangement, Black Hills will provide up to 590 MW of grid-connected energy service while managing approximately 2.1 GW of Wyoming-based, third-party contracted resources through a privately managed microgrid. The company plans to invest $1.8 billion between 2027 and 2029 to construct 564 MW of natural gas generation at its existing Cheyenne Prairie Generating Station site. The remaining 26 MW of grid-connected service will come through a combination of market purchases and retail utility service. Initial electricity service is expected in late 2027, with demand projected to ramp toward its peak in 2030.

An important question is how AEP's planned 702 MW fuel-cell installation fits within that larger resource portfolio. Neither AEP nor Black Hills has publicly confirmed whether the fuel-cell capacity is included in the approximately 2.1 GW of third-party generation Black Hills is contracted to manage. Consequently, the AEP announcement and Black Hills' resource figures should not be treated as additive measures of generating capacity.

Another major participant is Tallgrass, which is advancing the Cheyenne Power Hub in southeast Wyoming. In May 2026, Tallgrass and Mitsubishi Power Americas identified two M501JAC gas turbines for the project's initial phase, representing approximately 1,150 MW of planned generation. Tallgrass has described the power hub as an investment exceeding $7 billion, with natural gas supplied through its Rockies Express Pipeline system. The project is intended to provide dedicated power to a large-scale data center within the Switchgrass Industrial Park, although the precise relationship between its planned capacity and the broader Black Hills resource portfolio has not been fully established in public disclosures.

The destination for much of this infrastructure is Google's Project Tembo, previously known as Project Jade, a proposed data center campus in the Switchgrass Industrial Park south of Cheyenne. Laramie County planning records identify a development encompassing approximately 716 acres, with a revised plan calling for four major data center buildings totaling about 3.08 million square feet, along with supporting office, logistics and network facilities.

The project has undergone a significant change in development structure. Crusoe, which had been associated with the earlier Project Jade proposal, withdrew from the development in 2026. Subsequent county filings identify Google, operating through its subsidiary Jupiter Star Holdings LLC, as the party responsible for the revised campus proposal. The changes reduced the planned development from five principal data center buildings to four, while retaining the broader ambition of a major hyperscale installation supported by dedicated power infrastructure.

Beyond the generation technologies themselves, the Cheyenne agreements illustrate how utilities and independent power developers are adapting their business models to serve hyperscale customers.

AEP's established utility operations span 11 states, encompassing substantial transmission, distribution and generating assets serving regulated customers. Wyoming lies outside that traditional service territory. Through Cheyenne Fuel Cell LLC, AEP is instead participating as a generation developer and majority owner under a long-term commercial agreement with a specific hyperscale customer. The arrangement enables AEP to pursue large-load opportunities beyond its established regulated footprint without relying exclusively on conventional rate-regulated utility investment.

Black Hills represents a related but different model. Under its agreements with Google, the company will own new generation through an unregulated affiliate, provide grid-connected electricity service and receive fees for coordinating third-party generation and other resources through the private microgrid. The company will therefore combine traditional utility service with dedicated generation investment and contracted energy management responsibilities.

Black Hills says the agreements are designed to protect existing retail customers against cost shifting associated with Google's planned data center. Those protections include provisions addressing full recovery of generation investment, early termination, customer credit support and changes in project costs. Google has also provided $399 million in refundable advances for procurement of long-lead equipment, which Black Hills expects to reimburse by June 30, 2027.

The agreements reflect a broader industry shift toward assigning more of the financial responsibility for dedicated data center infrastructure to the customers creating the demand. As Data Center Frontier has reported in its examination of evolving state policies, regulators are increasingly requiring large-load customers to demonstrate credible power commitments and assume responsibility for infrastructure costs that might otherwise fall on existing utility ratepayers.

The consequences of a delayed, reduced or canceled data center development become considerably more complicated when utilities and their partners have already purchased turbines, secured transformers or begun constructing generation facilities specifically to support the project. Long-term contracts, financial guarantees and customer funding commitments do not eliminate those risks, nor do they establish that cost-shifting protections will work as intended under every circumstance. They do, however, provide a framework for allocating financial exposure among the developer, power providers and other customers.

These arrangements also raise operational and regulatory questions about how privately contracted generation interacts with the wider electricity system. As DCF's analysis of behind-the-meter power regulation has explored, dedicated generation does not necessarily eliminate dependence on transmission infrastructure, grid support or other utility services. The practical division of responsibilities among generation owners, utilities and data center operators remains central to determining both reliability and cost.

The Challenge of Delivering 702 MW by 2028

AEP's announced schedule provides just over two years from the October 2026 announcement to bring the full 702 MW fuel-cell installation into operation. Modular construction may offer advantages over conventional large-scale generating projects, but the schedule will still require substantial coordination across equipment manufacturing, site development, fuel supply and electrical infrastructure.

The installation will need natural gas supply arrangements, electrical interconnection and distribution infrastructure, construction logistics, protection and control systems, regulatory approvals and long-term operating support. Each must be developed in coordination with the generating equipment itself, and delays in one area could affect the availability of the overall system.

AEP has not disclosed the project's exact physical footprint, the number and configuration of fuel-cell modules or a detailed phased commissioning schedule. Nor has it provided public details on how the fuel-cell installation will operate alongside the other electricity resources being developed to support Google's Cheyenne expansion. The extent to which the facility will rely on conventional AC infrastructure or employ elements of Bloom's proposed DC-native architecture also remains unclear.

The timing of power availability will need to align with successive stages of data hall construction, commissioning of electrical and cooling systems, and installation of computing hardware. That coordination is particularly important for AI infrastructure, where power demand can increase sharply as large concentrations of accelerators and supporting equipment are brought online.

The challenge extends beyond the initial commissioning schedule. Once operational, the generation portfolio will need to support demanding availability requirements while accommodating equipment maintenance, variations in computing load and the operating characteristics of multiple power sources. The resulting system must deliver not simply enough generating capacity on paper, but dependable electricity under real operating conditions.

The Cheyenne buildout will test more than the ability to deploy hundreds of megawatts of fuel cells on an accelerated schedule. It will test whether multiple generation technologies, financing structures and operating arrangements can be coordinated into a reliable power system for hyperscale computing.

For AEP, Google and their partners, the central challenge is no longer simply securing generating capacity. It is turning a portfolio of ambitious power commitments into an operating infrastructure system.

title: Opinion: Congress should help deliver Iowa wind energy - The Gazette

description: Iowa has already demonstrated what is possible when wind resources are developed at scale. But new generating capacity cannot deliver its full value if transmission constraints prevent electricity from reaching
text:
Instead of investigating or punishing employees who don’t st…





The sun sets behind wind turbines Feb. 24, 2021, in the countryside east of Victor, Iowa.

Congress has an opportunity to make America’s energy system more affordable, reliable and efficient while reducing emissions. It should seize it.

It’s an opportunity Congress should not miss. Affordable, reliable electricity is the foundation of a strong economy, helping businesses, manufacturers and families manage household costs.

The bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, introduced in the Senate in September, offers a practical path forward. The bipartisan bill would reform federal permitting to help get energy and infrastructure projects built more efficiently. It aims to provide clearer timelines and greater certainty while maintaining important environmental safeguards.

Iowa has a particular stake in getting this right.

In 2024, wind generated about 44.3 million megawatt-hours of electricity in Iowa — nearly 63% of the state’s total electricity generation. That is an extraordinary resource, placing Iowa among the nation’s leaders in wind-powered electricity. But producing electricity is only half the equation. Transmission lines are needed to deliver that power where homes, farms, manufacturers and businesses need it.

Iowa generates more electricity than it consumes and sends substantial amounts to neighboring states. Yet getting electricity from where it is produced to where it is needed requires a modern, well-connected grid. Regional transmission investments can help reduce congestion, improve reliability and allow utilities to draw on available electricity across state lines when demand rises or generation changes.

That is why permitting reform matters to Iowa. When necessary infrastructure is delayed, affordable electricity can be harder to deliver. Consumers and businesses can miss out on potential savings, and the grid can become less efficient. A more predictable permitting process can help move important projects forward while preserving environmental review and public input.

U.S. electricity demand is rising as businesses expand, manufacturing grows and data centers require more power. Iowa’s agricultural producers, food processors, manufacturers and other employers need infrastructure capable of meeting that demand reliably and affordably. The bill also requires data centers to pay for the grid upgrades they require, helping protect electricity customers from shouldering those costs.

Iowa has already demonstrated what is possible when wind resources are developed at scale. But new generating capacity cannot deliver its full value if transmission constraints prevent electricity from reaching customers. Improving permitting and transmission processes can help bring more power onto the grid.

Reform should not mean abandoning environmental protections or ignoring affected communities. It should mean clearer timelines, fewer procedural delays, and a process that gives developers and communities greater certainty. Responsible development, public input and environmental safeguards can go hand in hand.

Iowa has abundant energy resources, a strong agricultural and manufacturing economy, and the potential to contribute even more to the nation’s energy supply. Realizing that potential requires infrastructure capable of delivering electricity efficiently and a permitting system that allows essential projects to move forward responsibly. Sens. Chuck Grassley and Joni Ernst have an opportunity to support a bipartisan approach.

Iowa has the energy. Congress should help clear the path to delivering it.

Susan Atkinson is a writer on energy and climate issues with Citizens Climate Lobby.
