text:
by Kari Lydersen

This story was originally published by Canary Media.

Can a utility commit to building massive gas plants and still achieve zero carbon emissions?

DTE Electric in southeast Michigan says yes, and it outlines how in a 20-year plan currently being considered by regulators. The key, the utility says, will be carbon capture and sequestration — collecting carbon dioxide emissions from two proposed gas-fired power plants and storing them underground.

Michigan state law says power generation must be carbon-free by 2040. The gas plants would go online in 2031 and 2032, and carbon capture equipment would be added by 2035, according to the long-range integrated resource plan that DTE filed with the state public service commission in September.

The problem, as critics see it, is that carbon capture and sequestration has not been successfully deployed by electric utilities in the U.S. thus far.

Even if the technology becomes economically viable, public opposition to the technology is likely to remain strong, as evidenced by the response to the Michigan Legislature’s efforts to adopt a carbon sequestration law. Public outcry has also erupted in neighboring states over plans for carbon dioxide pipelines and injection wells.

In other words, DTE proposes to invest billions of customers’ dollars in gas plants that are dependent on a nascent and uncertain solution to comply with state law on emissions that would harm the climate and public health.

Utilities across the country are grappling with the same predicament of needing to meet steep increases in energy demand driven by data centers while also transitioning to clean energy.

DTE’s plan calls for closing the half-century-old, 3-gigawatt Monroe coal plant and building 15 GW of renewables — mostly solar — and 4.5 gigawatts of energy storage. The utility also proposes two new gas-fired plants totaling 2.1 GW in the Detroit area, one of them in the same county as the coal plant. That’s more than double the amount of gas-fired generation DTE proposed to add in the long-range plan it filed four years ago. At that time, it said 946 megawatts of gas-fired generation with carbon capture could fill the gap left by the coal plant closure.

While DTE has framed the gas plants as simply replacing the retiring coal plant, clean energy advocates believe that the expanded plan is meant to accommodate upcoming data centers. DTE has signed contracts with Oracle and Google for a combined 2.4 gigawatts’ worth of power, and its proposal cites ​“2.4 GW of new customer load” as among the changes since the 2022 plan was filed.

“Just looking at the numbers, it’s hard not to draw that direct link,” said Helen Li, senior attorney with the nonprofit law firm Earthjustice, which represented environmentalists in regulatory proceedings over the planned Google data center.

“DTE is trying to lock in billions of dollars of new gas plants now on the promise that later they will seek to spend billions more to try to bring those plants into compliance with Michigan laws. Both of those issues should be fully evaluated now before DTE is allowed to start spending ratepayer money locking in new fossil generation.”

Over the coming year, state regulators will study and decide whether to approve DTE’s proposal. A DTE spokesperson declined to comment and referred Canary Media to the company’s website.

Costs and doubts

Michigan first passed a clean energy law in 2008, and a 2023 update laid out what types of energy can be used to meet the requirement that the state’s utilities generate 80% of their power from clean sources by 2035 and 100% by 2040. Sixty percent of generation must come from renewables by 2035. The law says gas plants can comply for the nonrenewable but ​“clean” portion of generation if they capture at least 90% of emissions from their smokestacks.

Whether that will happen is highly debatable.

The financial and industry analytics firm S&P Global notes in a report that carbon capture and sequestration ​“is a mature and scalable technology for decarbonizing hard-to-abate sectors. However, despite over 50 years of operations, CCS remains at early stages of deployment.”

The report cites cost, financial risk, market uncertainty, and the complexity of constructing and monitoring the infrastructure as reasons that the technology is used in only a small number of sites worldwide. Most of those are related to enhanced oil recovery, in which the carbon dioxide is used to push oil out of waning reservoirs, providing an additional revenue stream.

The one commercial power plant in the U.S. to use carbon capture — the Petra Nova project at a Texas coal plant — has had a rocky history, including a three-year shutdown and missed targets. The Environmental Protection Agency last year reported that ​“it is extremely unlikely that the extensive infrastructure for CCS can be deployed” by the 2032 compliance date set under the Biden rule,” as E&E News noted.

Carbon capture equipment on power plants is expensive in part because it takes a considerable amount of electricity to operate, and that electricity must be clean if the goal is zero emissions.

DTE estimates it will take $6.4 billion to build the two new gas plants. The cost of carbon capture and sequestration is hard to predict, so the plants’ price tag could balloon higher.

“It’s incredibly expensive,” said Charlotte Jameson, chief policy officer of the Michigan Environmental Council, which has intervened in the regulatory process for DTE’s long-range plan.

“When we’re talking about carbon capture and sequestration, we’re not just talking about the actual capture technology on the smokestack, which is expensive in and of itself, but also building out infrastructure to pipe the carbon dioxide to a place where it can be sequestered. I think it would be really easy at this juncture to undervalue what it would cost. That’s a huge, risky bet for ratepayers and Michigan as a whole.”

In recent months, regulators have been hashing out how much data centers will pay to help build the generation they need. While these proceedings are separate from DTE’s long-range plan, advocates see them as related — and worry that residents will wind up shouldering too much financial burden.

On October 30, the Michigan attorney general requested that the public service commission reexamine DTE’s contract with Google to power its planned data center, citing the risk that ratepayers will be charged unfairly.

Clean energy implications

While some advocates would prefer not to see new data centers at all, they argue that if the facilities must be built, their need for electricity could be met without increasing emissions or relying on carbon capture.

“We are looking to ensure that DTE is maximizing the full suite of clean technologies — renewables, storage, demand response, transmission, et cetera,” Earthjustice’s Li said, ​“rather than defaulting to more fossil generation, for meeting the needs of its ratepayers and serving AI new data center load.”

Nationwide, experts and regulators have indeed called on data centers to be flexible with the amount of power they use at a given time, so utilities don’t have to build extra capacity to meet periods of peak demand.

The Michigan Environmental Council’s Jameson is worried that the state’s clean energy law won’t force DTE to ensure that the gas plants capture their emissions. The law allows for multiple extensions to the deadlines for reasons including grid reliability, feasibility of installing renewables, and other factors.

“Those off-ramps are written pretty broadly,” Jameson said, noting that they were adopted before the data center boom. ​“So if data center load makes it too difficult to meet renewable energy standards, there is a lot of risk we just blow through our renewable energy standards and clean energy targets and those become effectively meaningless.”

Mark Templeton, director of the Abrams Environmental Law Clinic at the University of Chicago, has represented community groups in other proceedings involving DTE. He noted that the utility’s 2022 long-range plan ​“was critically important in establishing the schedule for closing significant coal-fired power generation.”

“This is equally important in terms of figuring out what the replacement is,” he said. ​“Locking in continued use of gas is better than coal, but that’s not saying much.”

text:
A virtual unknown has unseated one of the most powerful Republicans in Indiana elected office.

Democrat Lauren Cole, a clinical trial coordinator, defeated House Speaker Todd Huston 52% to 48%.

"This victory belongs to every person who believed in this campaign and helped make it possible," Cole said on social media. "To the voters of District 37: thank you for trusting me to represent you. This campaign was always about putting people first, and that's exactly what I intend to do."

House District 37 covers parts of Hamilton County. It's among the more than a dozen seats to flip for Democrats so far, shattering the GOP's 14-year supermajority in the House.

Cole ran on a platform of access to affordable healthcare, strengthening public school funding and investing in workers.

Huston, of Fishers, was first elected to the chamber in 2012. He has served as speaker since 2020.

His stunning defeat comes even though caucus leaders usually represent comfortably drawn districts.

"This was an incredibly challenging midterm election and ultimately the national headwinds were too difficult to overcome in a number of our races," Huston said in a written statement. "We're so proud of our team and all our candidates who stepped up to serve and spent countless hours in their communities, listening to voters and talking about the issues that matter to Hoosiers."

He said he was disappointed by the results but was proud of the progress "we've made in Indiana to grow our economy, bring good-paying jobs to our state, lower taxes and create thriving communities where people want to live, work, start a business and raise their family. It's been the honor of my life serving Hoosiers in Hamilton County and across our great state. I'm grateful for the opportunity and all that we've accomplished together."

text:
By Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - The outcome of the US Senat…

WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Big victories by Democrats in congressional races and beyond in midterm elections on Tuesday were a rebuke to President Donald Trump and will likely affect US energy and environment policy in many ways.

Here are some of the issues that could be in play in the months ahead as Democrats take control of the Senate and House of Representatives in January.

IRAN WAR

Unified Democrats in Congress could take several actions to slow down the US war with Iran, which has led to soaring prices for diesel and gasoline. Those measures could include attaching conditions on spending to encourage the US to reach a deal to keep open the Strait of Hormuz waterway between Iran and Oman and holding back confirmations of officials.

"With both chambers now capable of passing resolutions, holding back war funding and delaying confirmations, the administration faces a shorter political runway and greater institutional pressure to find a Hormuz deal," said Claudio Galimberti, chief economist at Rystad Energy, a research group.

PERMITTING BILL

US lawmakers had been hoping to pass sweeping bipartisan legislation known as the permitting bill this year that would sharply reduce deadlines the government has to approve massive fossil and renewable energy projects. The Democratic wins could increase pressure from environmental groups, who say the bill has too many concessions for oil and gas, to push consideration of the bill into next year. TD Cowen cut its outlook for the bill's success from about 40% to about 25%.

POTENTIAL CONGRESSIONAL PROBES

Democratic lawmakers, who will now head congressional committees, could launch probes of Trump administration policies and issues, ranging from the US oil deals with Venezuela to a diesel deal with Russia. Democrats could also probe whether oil and gas companies were rewarded with tax breaks, subsidies and rollbacks of environmental regulations after then-candidate Donald âTrump asked them for $1 billion in donations during the 2024 presidential campaign.

Democratic and Republican senators last month called on Trump to reverse course on the diesel issue, saying the administration failed to consult with Congress. The Trump administration could refuse or delay responses to subpoenas, but investigations could slow the administration's energy policy.

TRADE PARTNERS COULD PUSH BACK ON ALASKA LNG, NUCLEAR

The Democratic sweep could embolden Japan and South Korea to delay committing hundreds of billions of dollars in US investments. Projects the Trump administration has said it will support include the proposed Alaska LNG project, worth up to $54.4 billion, to transport natural gas from the northern part of the state to domestic and Asian customers. The administration also has backed nuclear power projects.

"Democrats seem to perceive that the investment commitments were forced on allies," said Heo Yoon, an economics professor at Sogang University in Seoul.

Last month Seoul confirmed that it would invest $22.3 billion in a Texas gas project to power AI data âcenters and $120 billion to build eight nuclear reactors in the US. But those agreements are not binding.

PRESSURE ON DATA CENTERS

Democrats seized on bipartisan opposition to the rapid buildout of AI data centers and voter anger at Big Tech companies. Across the country, 33 of 34 ballot initiatives aiming to restrict data center construction won the backing of voters. Some victorious Democrats supported pauses or rules on data center construction. There is now an increased likelihood of more oversight and scrutiny of AI risks, more protections for utility ratepayers, and stricter reporting requirements for energy consumption and pollution.

SOLAR, WIND SUBSIDIES

Some industry advocates see a possible path, either this year or in 2027, to extending or reviving tax credits for wind and solar projects that were eliminated or phased out under Trump's 2025 tax and spending law. The effort could also include the extension of a clean energy manufacturing tax credit.

GEORGIA REGULATOR

In Georgia, Democrats won a majority on the five-member Public Service Commission for the first time in 31 years. That development is expected to lead to changes for the regulator overseeing utilities at a time when data center investment has been pouring into Georgia. The commission will be responsible for determining how much new generation, transmission and grid infrastructure is needed and who pays for it. The Democrats campaigned to lower rising electricity bills and tighten oversight of utility investment plans.

TEXAS OIL, GAS REGULATOR GETS FIRST DEMOCRAT SINCE 1990

Democrat Jon Rosenthal, an oil and gas engineer, won the open seat on the three-member Texas Railroad Commission, which regulates the state's oil and gas industry. He is the first Democrat to hold a seat on the commission since 1990. Though the commission will still have a Republican majority, Rosenthal is expected to influence the regulator's response to issues facing Texas, such as data center permitting, grid reliability and reining in the disposal of toxic oil and gas wastewater.

(Reporting by Valerie Volcovici and Nichola Groom; Additional reporting by Jihoon Lee, Heejin Kim and Kyu-seok Shim in Seoul; Writing by Timothy Gardner and Paul Simao)

text:
University of Wyoming researchers have secured federal funding to analyze the possibility of turning retiring coal-fired power plant sites in Wyoming into small modular nuclear facilities, similar to what’s happening with TerraPower’s Natrium power plant under construction near Kemmerer.

Professor Haibo Zhai, UW’s Roy and Caryl Cline Distinguished Chair in Engineering, will evaluate the technical feasibility, economic viability, workforce implications and community considerations associated with converting retiring coal-fired power plant sites into power-generating nuclear reactors in the state. The two-year study has a total budget of $645,000, with $513,000 of that funded by a U.S. Economic Development Administration program aimed at helping coal communities.

“A recent study by the U.S. Department of Energy indicates that 30 percent of U.S. coal-fired power plants are projected to retire by 2035. Repowering retiring coal power plants with small modular reactors can leverage existing facilities, infrastructure and local coal workforce to provide significant benefits, including reduced up-front investment and construction time, preservation of jobs and tax revenue for coal communities, and increased grid reliability,” Zhai says. “Many coal jobs, such as electricians, mechanics and engineers, can be transferable to nuclear operations after additional training, preserving the workforce in local communities. And advanced nuclear energy can create new, high-salary jobs, as nuclear plants need more workers with specialized technical or engineering degrees, including bachelor’s, master’s and doctoral degrees.”

Wyoming has numerous coal-fired power plants in operation, some of which are envisioned for eventual retirement -- such as Pacificorp’s Naughton plant at Kemmerer -- or to transition to natural gas or other power sources. Meanwhile, the demand for electricity is growing nationally and in the state, driven by artificial intelligence and associated data centers.

“The expansion of data centers in Wyoming is raising challenges for electric power systems, including rapid growth for electricity demand, power grid congestion and reliability during extreme weather, and resource competition,” Zhai says. “Small modular reactors are an option for data centers because they are flexible and provide emissions-free, reliable power at stable prices. We will assess the fuel supply and cost for electricity generation by repowered plants dedicated for data centers and determine whether and what repowered plants are suitable as an affordable, reliable power source for data centers in different locations.”

The study will look at a number of critical issues, including site infrastructure, physical site characteristics, water availability, permitting, technical feasibility and economic viability.

Coal and nuclear plants have important similarities, such as large site footprints, steam cycles, cooling systems and power grid connections, Zhai says. But there are differences. The researchers will explore reusing the sites, office buildings, electric devices, transformer stations and power grid connections, as well as deployment of nuclear reactors through direct or indirect integration with some existing facilities of coal-fired plants.

Zhai notes that the success of a coal-to-nuclear transition also will rely on local communities’ receptiveness and on the collaboration with various stakeholders, including electric power utilities, local regulators, the Wyoming Business Council, the Wyoming Energy Authority, the Wyoming Department of Workforce Services, UW and the state’s community colleges. Based on the identified site and plant candidates most suitable for coal-to-nuclear conversions and workforce requirements, the researchers will estimate the amount of private investment on repowered plants and the net number of permanent jobs that could be created.

The experience in Kemmerer shows that an advanced nuclear power plant may create up to 11,600 construction jobs and roughly 250 permanent jobs.

“Based on what our research finds, we will identify the local communities with sites and retiring power plants suitable for coal-to-nuclear conversions and then develop community-specific engagement plans to gauge public perception, understanding and value regarding a coal-to-nuclear transition,” Zhai says. “The engagement plans will narrow communications to the identified communities and local stakeholders to solicit their interests, priorities, concerns and opinions.”

In addition to Zhai’s faculty position in UW’s Department of Civil and Architectural Engineering and Construction Management, he is a Wyoming Excellence Chair and an adjunct professor in UW’s School of Energy Resources and School of Computing. Other team members include Ph.D. students Chengcheng Lyu and Md Sharmon Hossain Arnob; postdoctoral researchers Asad Ullah and Ayush Singh; and research programmer Karen Kietzke.

“Repowering retiring coal-fired power plants with small modular reactors has the potential to preserve the physical and human capital of the electric power sector while strengthening power grid stability,” Zhai says. “The coal-to-nuclear conversion leverages existing civil infrastructure or facilities and reduces the cost and complexity of building new nuclear power plants.”

text:
WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) – Big victories by Democrats in congressional races and beyond in midterm elections on Tuesday were a rebuke to President Donald Trump and will likely affect US energy and environment policy in many ways.

Here are some of the issues that could be in play in the months ahead as Democrats take control of the Senate and House of Representatives in January.

IRAN WAR

Unified Democrats in Congress could take several actions ​to slow down the US war with Iran, which has led to soaring prices for diesel and gasoline. Those measures could include attaching conditions on ‌spending to encourage the US to reach a deal to keep open the Strait of Hormuz waterway between Iran and Oman and holding back confirmations of officials.

“With both chambers now capable of passing resolutions, holding back war funding and delaying confirmations, the administration faces a shorter political runway and greater institutional pressure to find a Hormuz deal,” said Claudio Galimberti, chief economist at Rystad Energy, a research group.

PERMITTING BILL

US lawmakers had been hoping to pass sweeping bipartisan legislation known as the permitting bill this year that would sharply reduce deadlines the government has to approve massive fossil and renewable energy projects. ‌The Democratic ​wins could increase pressure from environmental groups, who say the bill has too many concessions for oil and ⁠gas, to push consideration of the bill into next ⁠year. TD Cowen cut its outlook for the bill’s success from about 40% to about 25%.

POTENTIAL CONGRESSIONAL PROBES

Democratic lawmakers, who will now head congressional committees, could launch probes of Trump administration policies and issues, ranging from the US oil deals with Venezuela to a diesel deal with Russia. Democrats could also probe whether oil and gas companies were rewarded with tax breaks, subsidies and rollbacks of environmental regulations after then-candidate Donald Trump asked them for $1 billion in donations during the ​2024 presidential campaign.

Democratic and Republican senators last month called on Trump to reverse course on the diesel issue, saying the administration failed to consult with Congress. The Trump administration could refuse or delay responses to subpoenas, but investigations could slow the administration’s energy policy.

TRADE PARTNERS COULD PUSH BACK ON ALASKA LNG, NUCLEAR

The Democratic sweep could embolden ⁠Japan and South Korea to delay committing hundreds of billions of dollars in US investments. Projects ⁠the Trump administration has said it will support include the proposed Alaska LNG project, worth up to $54.4 billion, to transport natural gas ​from the northern part of the state to domestic and Asian customers. The administration also has backed nuclear power projects.

“Democrats seem to perceive that the investment commitments were forced ​on allies,” said Heo Yoon, an economics professor at Sogang University in Seoul.

Last month Seoul confirmed that it would invest $22.3 billion in ‌a Texas gas project to power AI data centers and $120 billion to build eight nuclear reactors in the US. But those agreements are not binding.

PRESSURE ON DATA CENTERS

Democrats seized on bipartisan opposition to the rapid buildout of AI data centers and voter anger at Big Tech companies. Across the country, 33 of 34 ballot initiatives aiming to restrict data center construction won the backing of voters. Some victorious Democrats supported pauses or rules on data center construction. There is now an increased likelihood of more oversight and scrutiny of ⁠AI risks, more protections for utility ratepayers, and stricter reporting requirements for energy consumption and pollution.

SOLAR, WIND SUBSIDIES

Some industry advocates see a possible path, either this year or in 2027, to extending or reviving tax credits for wind and solar projects that were eliminated or phased out under Trump’s 2025 tax and spending law. The effort could ⁠also include the extension of a clean energy manufacturing tax ‌credit.

GEORGIA REGULATOR

In Georgia, Democrats won a majority on the five-member Public Service Commission for the first time in 31 years. ⁠That development is expected to lead to changes for the regulator overseeing utilities at a time when data center investment ​has been pouring ‌into Georgia. The commission will be responsible for determining how much new generation, transmission and grid infrastructure is needed ​and who pays for ⁠it. The Democrats campaigned to lower rising electricity bills and tighten oversight of utility investment plans.

TEXAS OIL, GAS REGULATOR GETS FIRST DEMOCRAT SINCE 1990

Democrat Jon Rosenthal, an oil and gas engineer, won the open seat on the three-member Texas Railroad Commission, which regulates the state’s oil and gas industry. He is the first Democrat to hold a seat on the commission since 1990. Though the commission will still have a Republican majority, Rosenthal is expected to influence the regulator’s response to issues facing Texas, such as data center permitting, grid reliability and reining in the disposal of toxic oil and gas wastewater.

(Reporting by Valerie Volcovici and Nichola Groom; Additional reporting by Jihoon Lee, Heejin Kim and Kyu-seok Shim in Seoul; ​Writing by Timothy Gardner and Paul Simao)

text:
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright visited the Palisades Nuclear Power Plant in Covert Township, Michigan, on October 29, 2026 — a milestone moment for what would be the first-ever recommissioning of a shuttered American nuclear facility.

Wright was joined by U.S. Representative Bill Huizenga, USDA Under Secretary Glen Smith, DOE’s Gregory Beard, and Holtec President and CEO Dr. Kris Singh for a tour of the plant and a gathering with Palisades employees, skilled trades workers, and community leaders. The visit formally recognized the progress made by the plant’s workforce and the government partnerships driving this unprecedented restart effort.

Secretary Wright tours Palisades alongside federal and state officials

Wright’s October 29 visit pulled together a delegation that reflected the project’s unusual mix of federal, state, and private players. U.S. Representative Bill Huizenga covered the region’s congressional interests, while USDA Under Secretary for Rural Development Glen Smith attended alongside Gregory A. Beard, who runs the DOE’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing. Holtec President and CEO Dr. Kris Singh rounded out the group for the plant tour.

It served as a formal acknowledgment of the workforce’s efforts and of the layered federal-state-local partnerships that have made this project possible.

After walking the facility, the delegation addressed a large gathering inside — Palisades employees, skilled trades workers, and local government and community leaders whose daily work has kept this restart on track.

The visit wasn’t purely symbolic. It served as a formal acknowledgment of the workforce’s efforts and of the layered federal-state-local partnerships that have made this project possible. For a plant that once looked headed for permanent closure, that kind of visible federal attention carries real weight.

Federal loan, state funding, and private investment underpin the restart

Few nuclear projects anywhere have been stitched together from this many funding sources at once. The Palisades restart draws on a U.S. Department of Energy loan, direct funding from the State of Michigan, and significant capital from Holtec itself — an arrangement unusual even by the standards of large energy infrastructure projects.

Beyond the financing, there’s revenue certainty from the demand side. Wolverine Power Cooperative and Hoosier Energy both signed long-term power purchase agreements with Palisades, locking in future electricity buyers before the restart was complete. The project describes those deals as instrumental in making the finances work.

Early utility buy-in matters in nuclear development because power purchase agreements reduce the revenue risk that otherwise makes lenders nervous about long-horizon projects. Here, they appear to have helped unlock the broader financing stack.

The result is a funding model that doesn’t fit neatly into any standard category — part public loan, part state grant, part private equity, part contracted revenue. Whether that structure becomes a template for future nuclear projects remains an open question.

Restart will restore 805 megawatts of baseload power and preserve local jobs

When Palisades comes back online, it’s expected to return approximately 805 megawatts of electricity to the grid. Baseload generation — power that runs continuously, regardless of weather or time of day — is exactly what this represents, and that distinction matters more now than it did a decade ago.

As renewable capacity grows across the Midwest, grid operators increasingly value sources that can fill in when the wind isn’t blowing and the sun isn’t shining. Palisades’ return would add a meaningful block of always-on capacity to a region managing rising electricity demand.

The local employment picture is equally significant. The project preserves hundreds of high-quality jobs in Southwest Michigan — skilled trades and plant operations positions that pay well and tend to anchor communities. For Covert Township and the surrounding area, the difference between a decommissioned plant and an operating one is measured in livelihoods.

The plant isn’t back online yet, though. Its return to service depends on completing fuel loading, passing required testing, clearing inspections, and meeting all operational readiness standards — steps that take time and can’t be skipped.

What still has to happen before Palisades can restart

The NRC’s role here is central and closely watched. Palisades won’t resume operations until it satisfies all applicable U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission requirements and relevant industry standards. That’s not a formality — it’s the condition that determines whether the plant runs at all.

Outstanding work includes completing fuel loading, conducting mandatory testing, and passing inspections. These aren’t administrative checkboxes; they’re the technical verification steps confirming a plant is safe to operate. Given that Palisades shut down in 2022 and entered the early stages of decommissioning, regulators are navigating genuinely new territory. No specific restart date has been publicly announced. The project team has described the work as a progression, moving through each phase as it’s completed.

What the Palisades restart means for U.S. nuclear energy

Palisades is widely considered the first U.S. nuclear plant to attempt a restart after entering decommissioning — which makes it a test case, not just for this facility, but for the broader question of whether shuttered American nuclear plants can be brought back into service at all.

Wright’s visit, the multi-agency delegation, and the public recognition of the workforce all point to how seriously the federal government is treating the outcome. DOE financing, state partnership, utility agreements, and private investment working in combination reflect a deliberate effort to make this succeed — and to document what it takes if others want to follow.

text:
Business

Democrats win PSC majority, which could affect Georgia Power bills

Peter Hubbard and Shelia Edwards defeat GOP challengers as voter backlash from rising power bills carries over in midterms.

2 hours ago

Last year, consumer anger over rising energy bills helped a pair of Democrats win seats on the powerful five-member board that regulates Georgia Power.

On Tuesday night, amid a national blue wave, Democrats claimed the majority on the Georgia Public Service Commission for the first time in more than 20 years.

The victories tee up likely battles over future power bills, whether Georgia Power will adopt cleaner energy sources and whether more nuclear power could one day come into play.

Voters reelected Democratic incumbent Peter Hubbard to a six-year term. Hubbard won an unusual one-year term last November after beating Republican incumbent Fitz Johnson, who tried unsuccessfully Tuesday to regain his seat.

Voters on Tuesday also elected Democrat Shelia Edwards to the panel, which regulates the rates and profits of Georgia Power and Atlanta Gas Light. Edwards bested Republican Josh Tolbert, whose candidacy was supported by more than $3 million from proindustry groups in efforts to keep GOP control of the commission.

“The voters have spoken, and I am ready to go to work on their behalf,” Edwards said.

Along with Commissioner Alicia Johnson, those wins give Democrats three seats on the panel.

“We appreciate the work of the members of the Georgia PSC, including past and current commissioners, in building the electric grid we all depend on and we congratulate Commissioner Hubbard on his reelection and Commissioner Edwards on her election to the PSC. We look forward to working with them both,” Georgia Power spokesperson Meredith Stone said.

‘Didn’t flip … by accident’

The PSC is a wonky, quasi-judicial agency that has operated largely out of the public eye until last year when Georgians, frustrated over their rising power bills, voted out two Republican incumbents.

National attention on rising utility bills and data centers have thrust this year’s races into the spotlight. Outside groups have poured an unprecedented amount of money into both races, with the total amount exceeding $5 million.

Observers said the 2025 races werereferendums on power bills after the then-GOP controlled commission had approved six rate increases in three years, raising rates on the average household by a combined $43 a month. Supporters have said that momentum has continued into this year’s race even after Georgia Power took steps to freeze basic rates and then lower bills over the summer.

Power bills and the influx of data centers coming to Georgia have continued to draw the ire of voters. What’s more, climate groups, which raised more than $2 million for Hubbard, Edwards and other Democratic candidates, pushed the message that planet-warming fossil fuels from power plants and gas pipelines are driving up utility bills.

“Georgians didn’t flip this Commission by accident. This has been years in the making. In communities across Georgia, people have organized around high power bills and demanded more accountability from the people and corporations making decisions about their energy future,” said Brionté McCorkle, executive director of Georgia Conservation Voters Action Fund. “Tonight, voters changed who has the power to make those decisions. Now the test is what happens next.”

Georgians have taken the frustration — and sometimes anger — over rising power bills into the commission hearing room. During public comment periods, some of the speakers have condemned PSC members, with some removed from meetings.

Advocates, activists and others have accused the commission of not being transparent in their decision making. That criticism has largely centered on Georgia Power’s contracts with data centers, the PSC’s approval of Georgia Power’s natural gas-heavy expansion and contentions from critics the panel has not done enough to protect customers against rising power bills.

“This (election) shows just how much people care about data centers and rising power bills,” said Codi Norred, executive director of Georgia Interfaith Power & Light.

A shake-up to a comfortable relationship

A change of party control at the PSC is going to shake up what has been a longstanding comfortable relationship between the commission, Georgia Power and Atlanta Gas Light, and the companies’ lobbyists.

The PSC is not scheduled to review Georgia Power’s rates and profits again until 2028, and even then, the utility has committed to slicing $15 off what monthly bills would otherwise be without that agreement.

But regulators still face several issues in the coming years that could influence how much Georgia Power customers pay each month.

The electric company is in the middle of an unprecedented expansion of its power grid, mostly to serve data centers and is scheduled to file its next long-term energy plans in 2028.

During the primary races, PSC candidates on both sides of the aisle questioned the validity of Georgia Power’s projections on how much it needed to build out its power grid for data centers, arguing that much of the company’s plans were based on speculation.

Although a previous commission signed off on Georgia Power’s expansion last year, it is likely that the new regulators will revisit the utility’s plans.

Georgia Power’s corporate parent, Southern Co., released a plan in 2020 to have net-zero carbon emissions across its entire footprint by 2050. The electric company continues to lean heavily on planet-warming fossil fuels, however, reversing course on plans to shutter nearly all of its coal-fired power plants by the end of the decade and building more gas plants as part of its expansion.

The utility has leaned on building traditional power plants, arguing they are the most secure for keeping the power grid up and running. Solar energy, particularly combined with battery storage, has become a more affordable alternative in recent years without producing planet-warming emissions.

Meanwhile, the United Nations recently issued stark warnings that the world is set to cross a dangerous planet-warming threshold of 1.5 degrees Celsius unless countries take immediate steps to curb emissions from power plants, the transportation sector and other sources.

The PSC does not regulate Southern, but Hubbard said he plans to hold the company to its word through its Georgia utility.

“I look forward to helping fulfill Southern Company’s goal of net zero emissions by 2050,” said Hubbard.

Public documents show that Georgia Power may be positioning itself to build more nuclear power in the future. The electric company became the first — and only — utility in the nation to build two new reactors from scratch in roughly 30 years.

The reactors, which generate emission-free electricity, were roughly seven years behind schedule, and their original forecast budget of $14 billion grew to more than $30 billion by the time they were finished.

The utility has been spending more money to explore potential sites for nuclear plants, documents show, setting up the company for extreme scrutiny from regulators because of their cost.

Company officials have stressed that it does not want to build another reactor for now, but observers have said they wouldn’t be surprised if the utility entertains that option in its next Integrated Resource Plan.

text:
The German carmaker BMW has issued its second profit warning in a year, blaming the costs of a restructuring programme including significant job losses in the face of continuing competition from China.

The company is the latest to issue a profit downgrade in the German car sector, after Mercedes-Benz last week cut its profit outlook. Western automakers have struggled to keep pace with lower-cost Chinese rivals, which has led to reduced sales in China and a rise in Chinese exports to Europe.

BMW signalled a potential for losses after slashing its profit margin to between -0.5% and 0.5% this year and blamed fourth-quarter costs tied to the restructuring that includes 8,000 job cuts in its home market. At the beginning of the year, BMW had considered a margin of 4-6% would be possible.

It reported an 11% drop in third-quarter pre-tax earnings on Wednesday to €2.1bn (£1.75bn). Sales in China fell 22% in the first nine months of the year, which BMW said was in line with a broader downturn ⁠in that market.

The chief executive, Milan Nedeljković, said: “Current developments in our industry call for decisiveness and swift implementation. We will therefore specifically intensify and accelerate structural measures.”

China “remains a key focus”, Nedeljković added, with the group’s Neue Klasse ​revival of its model offering beginning in ​China this month with the launch of the iX3.

BMW follows Volkswagen in making painful restructuring costs caused by the rapidly changing market. Because of the rapid launch of its new generation of electric vehicles, the company is writing off parts of its previous vehicle and technology generations and pricing in the costs of the redundancy programme.

The operating ‌margin in BMW’s core ‌automotive business narrowed to 3.4%, beating analysts’ forecast of 3.1% but declining from 5.2% a year earlier. Excluding restructuring charges, the margin would be above 2%, within its previous forecast range, the company said.

text:
Ford Motor Company (F +4.26%) investors finally have a little less red ink to stare at in the company's electric vehicle (EV) business. Whether that means an EV turnaround is taking shape is another question entirely, and there's a little evidence we'll get to later that could emphasize the turnaround is still down the road.

During the third quarter, Ford's Model e division narrowed its EBIT loss from $1.41 billion to $1.058 billion, a noticeable improvement of roughly 25%. And in raw figures, it's $352 million less in losses, which investors certainly won't complain about.

But before anyone starts polishing the turnaround trophy, there's a catch. Revenue declined even faster, falling 31% to approximately $1.2 billion. The smaller loss is real, but treating it as proof Ford has cracked EV profitability could be fool's gold. Let's dig in and look more closely at Ford's Q3 results.

Look more closely

Ford attributed its progress to cost reductions and efforts to align its first-generation EV business with demand while investing in future products -- more on the latter, in a moment. For investors, it's pretty simple in that selling more vehicles isn't much of an accomplishment if the effort leaves shareholders with an even bigger financial headache.

In fact, Model e's EBIT margin deteriorated from negative 79.1% to negative 86.5% year over year. In other words, Ford's total Model e losses shrank, but those losses consumed a larger percentage of revenue. The takeaway is that investors shouldn't conflate a smaller total loss with a healthier operating margin or a stronger business segment.

The bigger test is coming

For long-term investors, the more important development may be Ford's Fathom midsize electric pickup and the Universal EV platform underpinning it. Ford plans to launch Fathom in the fourth quarter of 2027. The company has announced a starting MSRP of $28,350 for the standard-range version, excluding taxes and fees. The platform also brings a redesigned manufacturing process, including large castings and three vehicle sections assembled separately before joining together. Ford intends that simpler approach to improve cost and quality.

For Ford to compete with EV rivals such as Tesla and Rivian Automotive as it drives toward profitability, an attractive sticker price is only part of the equation. Ford needs to attract EV customers at costs that leave room for profit, which hasn't always been a strength of Detroit automakers producing lower-priced vehicles. It's also partly why Ford has focused more on full-size trucks and SUVs and less on sedans, with the exception of the traditional Mustang, over the past decade.

Another note to remember is that Ford isn't only competing with pure EVs; it arguably has an edge over more traditional rivals such as General Motors when it comes to hybrids. Ford's CEO, Jim Farley, has previously noted that not only are many of its hybrids already profitable, they can even be more profitable than their gasoline-powered counterparts. With the conflict in the Middle East contributing to higher gas prices, more consumers have looked toward hybrids before full EVs.

Management expects higher expenses in 2027 and sees the next significant profitability improvement likely in the first half of 2028 as the Universal EV platform, and other developments such as Ford Energy, ramp up. Model e breakeven, however, remains a more distant 2029 target. That makes Fathom's launch a milestone and potential production breakthrough, rather than an instant financial boost.

text:
California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra will take the reins during a delicate time for California.

He faces the prospect of deeper federal healthcare cuts, skyrocketing wildfire costs and a persistent cost-of-living crisis. But many of the specifics of his policies are still unknown after he ran a quiet race as a Democrat in a safe blue state, promoting few programs and avoiding making commitments.

Here’s what to know about what Becerra will tackle and how he’ll govern.

He’s open to new taxes

Becerra opposed the billionaire tax ballot proposition, saying he does not think taxing assets is a stable way to provide state revenues. And while he’s said he believes the wealthy should pay their “fair share” in taxes, he hasn’t explicitly endorsed any new income taxes.

But he has signaled that he supports the idea of taxing corporations whose workers are paid so little they qualify for public benefits, or potentially ending tax credits to those companies. The state Department of Finance is studying what that kind of tax would look like and is expected to deliver recommendations to lawmakers next year.

He has also said he’s considering a controversial proposal for the state to tax drivers based on their miles driven as a way to pay for road and highway repairs. The state collects that funding through gas taxes, but that source is expected to decline by $31 billion over the next decade as more drivers adopt electric vehicles.

“I take no pleasure in telling people taxes are for a purpose,” he told reporters last week. “I believe that users should pay for (roads).”

Big decisions on climate and energy

Becerra has emphasized the need to keep energy affordable while California continues its clean energy transition.

One program he’s pushing would give low-income households two hours of free electricity each day during daytime hours when solar energy is abundant and usage is low. The program, which he’s calling “power hour,” would be limited to utility customers who already qualify for assistance programs.

He’s said he wants to “continue the path toward clean energy, but while we’re on that path we have to make sure we stabilize the prices,” including by drilling more oil in-state and will decide whether to keep California’s 2030 deadline to ban the sale of new gas cars on the state of electric vehicle charging infrastructure.

He’ll also face pressure from investor-owned utilities that have been pushing lawmakers and outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom to reduce how much they must pay to insurance companies and fire victims when their equipment sparks destructive wildfires.

If Newsom doesn’t resolve the issue in the next two months, Becerra will have to deal with it when he takes office; so far he’s declined to take a position, calling the debate a “food fight” between insurers and utilities.

Healthcare for undocumented immigrants

As a first-term congressmember from Los Angeles in 1993, Becerra caused a splash on Capitol Hill by arguing with an elder Democratic statesman over a plan to single out legal immigrants for social safety net cuts — he opposed it. He’s said he will seek to reverse restrictions to Medi-Cal that forced tens of thousands of immigrants who are in California illegally off the program.

Immigration has remained a key issue throughout his career. As governor, he’s promised to enforce new state laws that aim to curb immigration agents’ use of force and activities on state property.

Newsom had expanded immigrant health coverage gradually to all income-qualifying adults but he began rolling back some coverage last year amid a budget deficit and unexpectedly high healthcare costs.

“My values and my fiscal beliefs tell me that anyone who works hard in California should have access to the healthcare they need for themselves and for their family and they should be able to afford it, and that includes undocumented,” Becerra told KQED.

Continuing Newsom’s death penalty moratorium

Newsom placed a moratorium on the death penalty in 2019 when he took office, citing his moral opposition to executions, and during his terms he began to dismantle the state’s death row at San Quentin. Prisoners sentenced to death have since been moved to other prisons.

California has not executed any inmate since 2006. Newsom is considering whether to commute the death sentences of more than 560 prisoners to life sentences without parole but even if he doesn’t, don’t expect Becerra to resume executions.

As attorney general, Becerra defended death sentences and said he supported them in principle, but said during the campaign that he would continue California’s moratorium over concerns about racial bias and wrongful convictions.

He calls himself a ‘pragmatic progressive’

In a party undergoing a yearslong identity crisis over how far left to push its policies, Becerra chooses incremental change over progressive moonshots.

In his more than two decades in Congress, he had the ear of both progressive advocates and established Democratic leadership and was a close ally of former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, though the pair had a testy moment in 2009 when Becerra wanted her to push harder for a public option in the Affordable Care Act.

This year, he backed away from his longtime support for single-payer healthcare, saying it’s a longshot for California with the Trump administration unlikely to give the state permission to launch.

Even before that, he said he valued experience over grand promises like Medicare for All. As President Joe Biden’s health secretary, for example, he said he focused on expanding coverage.

“When I was helping Hillary Clinton in 2016, my daughters wanted to vote for Bernie Sanders,” he said in an interview. “And I kept saying to them, I get it, I understand. I want Medicare for All … But we got to get (things) done, and I want someone who’s actually been in the thick of things.”

text:
Future producer participation in USDA’s Rural Energy for America Program (REAP) could be limited under new rules announced on Oct. 1.

Those rules now require farmstead renewable energy projects to be completed and operational for 12 months before farmers can apply for cost-share funds — at a reduced level.

According to Michigan Farm Bureau (MFB) Conservation and Regulatory Relations Specialist Tess Van Gorder, the organization has “significant concerns about the requirement,” which places significant risk on farmers pursuing any REAP project.

In written comments to USDA on the revised REAP rules, Van Gorder said MFB fully supports efforts to update program details, especially with the emphasis on reducing red tape, promoting fiscal responsibility, and safeguarding prime agricultural farmland.

“However, we have concerns that some of the new requirements may shift significant financial risk to farmers and negatively impact the usefulness of the program,” said Van Gorder, adding farmers may see projects as too risky to invest in actual construction without knowing if they will receive a REAP grant.

“Furthermore, it is highly unlikely they would be able to get traditional financing to cover upfront costs because there is no guarantee they would receive a grant to pay back those costs,” Van Gorder added.

Under previous REAP rules, Van Gorder said proposed projects were submitted, reviewed, revised and approved prior to money being spent by farmers, providing certainty that they would meet all program requirements.

“If a project is completed and operational prior to a farmer ever applying, there is a significant amount of risk put on program participants that may end up with a project that is functioning, but did not fully meet USDA requirements,” she noted.

Those requirements could include environmental review documentation, compliance with requirements for threatened and endangered species, and compliance with requirements regarding cultural resources.

Although USDA’s regulatory impact analysis concluded the revisions would help support farmers, Van Gorder predicted it will do just the opposite by increasing uncertainty about which costs the grant can cover and whether a completed project meets grant eligibility requirements.

“Michigan Farm Bureau urges USDA to allow farmers to apply for and receive grant approval before beginning work on a project,” Van Gorder said.

“Approval before construction, with reimbursement contingent on project timelines or at project completion, would help protect taxpayer dollars while providing farmers with the certainty needed to invest in projects that support their operations.”

A significant shift in REAP cost-sharing requirements could also limit farmer participation, according to Van Gorder, noting the new REAP rules requires producers to cover 75% of project costs, up from the previous 50% cost-share limit.

“In the current farm economy, the increased producer contribution requirement combined with the elevated costs of project components may put otherwise viable projects out of reach,” said Van Gorder, who urged USDA to consider a lower required producer cost share contribution.

While commending efforts to preserve farmland by prohibiting installation of projects on farmland, Van Gorder said MFB suggested modifications are needed that would allow farmers to utilize adjacent farmland that isn’t ideally suited for crop production.

“Alternative options for ensuring protection of farmland could include the exclusion of ‘prime farmland’ from ground mounted solar or special considerations for specialty crop acres,” Van Gorder said. “Farmers know their land best and should be able to make decisions best suited to their operations.”

MFB is also seeking clarity and flexibility on provisions capping the size of projects based solely on energy use over the previous 12-month period, noting the provision doesn’t account for extreme weather conditions and/or planned farm expansions.

Likewise, Van Gorder said MFB has concerns over the “simple payback” methodology to determine REAP grant eligibility, noting there can be wide swings in energy demand in any given year driven by weather and crop conditions, suggesting it could be an average of three years or more to account for those variations.

title: EV Credits, Emissions Rules and Tariffs: Where Each One Is Written and Who Can Change It - Yahoo
description:
The IRS says the new clean vehicle credit and the previously owned clean vehicle credit are available only for vehicles acquired on or before Sept. 30, 2025.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) announced its final fuel economy rule on Sept. 28, 2026.
Tariffs Come From a Proclamation, and the Rates Differ by Country Vehicle tariffs rest on Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.
And the new Congress convenes in January, when any bill or resolution on credits, fuel economy penalties or tariffs could be introduced.
Which of the three, the credits, the emissions and fuel economy rules, or the tariffs, do you expect to affect your next vehicle purchase first?
text:
News organizations projected Democratic majorities in the House and the Senate after the November 3 midterm elections, and the new Congress is due to convene in January. What that means for auto policy after the midterms depends on where each rule is written, because federal vehicle rules come from three different places: statutes, agency rulemakings and presidential proclamations.

This article covers where the EV tax credits, the emissions and fuel economy standards, and the vehicle tariffs sit today, and which of them a new Congress could reach by passing a law. It does not forecast what lawmakers will do.

EV Credits Are Written Into Law, With an End Date

The federal clean vehicle credits are set by statute, and the statute now carries a cutoff. The IRS says the new clean vehicle credit and the previously owned clean vehicle credit are available only for vehicles acquired on or before Sept. 30, 2025. The qualified commercial clean vehicle credit is also unavailable for vehicles acquired after that date. The change came through Public Law 119-21, signed July 4, 2025. Auto Wire covered the moment the credit ended.

One exception remains. The IRS treats a vehicle as acquired if the buyer entered a binding written contract and made a payment on or before Sept. 30, 2025, even when the car was delivered later. Because the dates sit in the tax code and not in an agency rule, any new federal credit would need new legislation. Some states run their own programs, which Auto Wire has covered in its guide to state EV rebates.

Emissions and Fuel Economy Sit With Two Agencies and a $0 Penalty

The EPA signed a final rule on Feb. 12, 2026 that rescinds its 2009 greenhouse gas endangerment finding and repeals all of its greenhouse gas standards for light-, medium- and heavy-duty vehicles and engines. The rule was published in the Federal Register on Feb. 18 and took effect April 20, 2026. The notice says petitions for review go to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) announced its final fuel economy rule on Sept. 28, 2026. The rule covers model years 2022 through 2031 and takes effect Nov. 30, 2026. NHTSA projects a combined fleet average of about 34.9 mpg in model year 2031, made up of 40.2 mpg for passenger cars and 26.4 mpg for light trucks. The Department of Transportation says the rule also ends the credit trading program starting in model year 2028.

Two details are easy to miss. First, the civil penalty for missing a fuel economy standard is zero. Public Law 119-21 set it at $0, and NHTSA's analysis assumes no penalties, so the targets exist without a fine attached to them. Second, NHTSA says a provision of federal law, 49 U.S.C. 32902, keeps it from considering electric vehicles when it sets the standards. The projected averages are built on gasoline, diesel and non-plug-in hybrid vehicles only, and automakers can still earn credit for EVs under a Department of Energy formula.

Congress has two routes to these rules. It can change the underlying statutes, as Public Law 119-21 did with the penalty. It can also use the Congressional Review Act, which lets Congress disapprove an agency rule through a joint resolution that goes to the president like any other bill. On June 12, 2025, the president signed three such resolutions disapproving EPA decisions that had granted California waivers, and the White House statement said the EPA cannot approve future waivers that are "substantially the same."

Tariffs Come From a Proclamation, and the Rates Differ by Country

Vehicle tariffs rest on Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962. A March 26, 2025 proclamation set a 25 percent tariff on listed automobiles entered on or after April 3, 2025, with parts following by May 3. It says the tariffs stay in place "unless such actions are expressly reduced, modified, or terminated."

The U.S. Trade Representative's July 1, 2026 report to Congress lists the current rates. Vehicles from the European Union, Japan and South Korea face a 15 percent all-in baseline, and the United Kingdom has a 10 percent rate on a quota of 100,000 vehicles. Vehicles that qualify under USMCA are tariffed only on their non-U.S. content, and U.S.-assembled vehicles can claim an offset of 3.75 percent of MSRP through April 30, 2030.

The report also notes that Commerce had not published a process for applying the tariff to only the non-U.S. content of USMCA-qualifying parts, so those parts remain exempt for now. Automakers have been reporting the cost. Audi's quarterly report attributed a 27 percent first-quarter drop in North American deliveries primarily to U.S. tariffs and the end of U.S. electric-car subsidies, and Volkswagen's investor presentation put its tariff burden at 2.1 billion euros through September.

What Will Show Whether Anything Changes

Four things are scheduled or on the record. The NHTSA rule takes effect Nov. 30, 2026. Challenges to the EPA rule are directed to the D.C. Circuit. Commerce could publish the USMCA parts process. And the new Congress convenes in January, when any bill or resolution on credits, fuel economy penalties or tariffs could be introduced.

Which of the three, the credits, the emissions and fuel economy rules, or the tariffs, do you expect to affect your next vehicle purchase first?

text:
Texas has elected Democrat James Talarico to the Senate for the first time in 38 years, Keisha Lange has become the first Black woman to serve as governor, Abdul al-Sayer is the first Muslim senator and Deb Haaland is the first Native American woman to become governor. Both the House and the Senate are once again firmly in Democratic hands. A blue wave has swept across the Republican party and the MAGA right, leaving no one standing.

The most significant message came on X from former US president Barack Obama, who commented on the Democrats’ midterm election victory: “Tonight, the American people sent a clear message — they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face”. His words sounded like a warning – not merely the beginning of the end for Donald Trump (“If my name was on the ballot, we would have won big!” was the president’s first reaction) and Trumpism, but for the entire global populist movement, from Milei to Meloni. “While this administration has another two years in office, our job now is to roll up our sleeves, make changes wherever we have the power to do so, prevent further damage, and lay the groundwork for the future”, Obama added.

The results are overwhelming. At the time of writing, projections indicated the Democrats had elected 54 senators, well over half the seats, while in the House of Representatives, 255 of 435 members had been elected. The evening began with a string of major victories: Senator Ossoff secured re-election in Georgia, Ray Cooper wrested North Carolina from the Grand Old Party and Chris Pappas held on to the Democratic seat in New Hampshire, becoming the first openly gay man to win a Senate seat. Then came the sensational result in South Carolina.

But the night’s defining moment came from Texas, where James Talarico soundly defeated his opponent, polling 1.1 million more votes than conservative Ken Paxton, and definitively placing the Christian Democrat (some have even labelled him a ‘Catholic communist’ due to his left-wing views, openly inspired by the Gospel) in the running as a future candidate for the White House. By this point, Trump had realised that the political shift to the left was inevitable and conceded that he would “accept the election results”. He nevertheless vowed to fight back with presidential vetoes, thereby also missing his last chance to act in a presidential manner and declare his willingness to work with the new Congress.

There is considerable apprehension in Washington. From today, the Democratic Party will wield significantly more power. Democratic senators and members of Congress can issue subpoenas compelling administration officials to testify before Congress. They could also launch impeachment proceedings against Trump administration members over funding cuts and staffing reductions, particularly in environment-related sectors. Democrats will also have control over budget spending. This could even lead to the reinstatement of some funding for energy and climate resilience programmes that the Republicans have sought to cut.

Even moderately pro-environment senators such as James Talarico – who, to win in Texas, had to back an all-source energy strategy aimed at safeguarding jobs in the oil and gas sector whilst promoting the development of renewable energy – are in favour of new emissions legislation. As a state representative, Talarico drafted and introduced the Texas Climate Action Act in 2021. Although the bill failed to progress, it sought to set greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets and establish energy efficiency standards, with a particular emphasis on local resilience.

Many of the newly elected members of Congress, meanwhile, oppose the invasion of mega data centres. At least three legislative seats have gone to Democrats after they fiercely criticised incumbent Republican senators for their overly favourable stance towards data centres. Democrat Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Senator Jon Husted in the Ohio Senate special election, after state Democrats put up billboards bearing the message: “See that data center? Jon Husted did that”. Democrat Paige Cognetti defeated Republican Congressman Rob Bresnahan in Pennsylvania’s 8th Congressional District after running television adverts linking him to data centres and comparing technology companies to polluting mining corporations. It later emerged that Bresnahan owned shares in companies operating in the data centre sector. And in the South Carolina Senate race, voters handed Annie Andrews a surprise victory over Senator Darline Graham after she highlighted the fact that a new data centre-friendly super PAC had spent 1.5 million dollars on advertising in support of her opponent, whom she had nicknamed “Data Center Darline”.

description:

Deliver a fairer deal for consumers Consumers should have confidence that the energy system is working in their interests.
The Bill formally recognises the role local communities play in the clean energy transition.
How does the Bill deliver these objectives?
For further information on individual measures, see Energy Independence Bill: factsheets.
text:
Summary

Energy is an everyday essential. Yet for too long families and businesses have paid the price for an energy system that is not working in their interests.

When global fossil fuel prices spike, bills rise. When homes are poorly insulated, people pay more than they should to keep warm. And when markets do not work fairly, consumers can be left without the protections they deserve.

The Energy Independence Bill is about fixing that.

The Bill introduces a package of reforms to build an energy system that works for consumers: delivering a fairer deal for households and businesses, helping people cut their energy use through warmer homes, making sure communities benefit from local energy projects, and securing more homegrown clean power so Britain is less exposed to volatile global fossil fuel markets.

Together, these measures will help put more money in people’s pockets, strengthen energy security and support good jobs and investment across the country.

What are the government’s objectives in legislating?

Deliver a fairer deal for consumers

Consumers should have confidence that the energy system is working in their interests.

The Bill strengthens the role of Ofgem as a consumer champion, equipping the regulator with tougher powers to protect households and businesses, crack down on unfair practices and keep pace with a rapidly changing energy market.

It also gives government greater flexibility to support vulnerable households when needed and locks in measures that reduce costs on bills.

Upgrade homes and empower communities

The best way to cut energy bills is to upgrade, electrify and insulate homes to ensure they are more energy efficient.

The Bill enables delivery of the Warm Homes Plan, helping millions of people live in warmer homes that are cheaper to heat, meaning they are less vulnerable to rising energy costs.

The Bill formally recognises the role local communities play in the clean energy transition. It ensures communities hosting new onshore wind and ground-mounted solar projects benefit directly through the provision of community benefit funds that can be used flexibly according to local needs. It also raises the ambition of our plans to give local people opportunities to take a shared ownership stake in projects near them, by expanding the projects that could be in scope and enabling communities to buy a larger share.

Together, these measures help more communities participate in and benefit from the clean energy transition - putting wealth, power and ownership back in the hands of working people.

Deliver homegrown clean energy we control

The only way to protect people from future fossil fuel price shocks is to generate more of our own clean power here in Britain.

The Bill removes barriers to building the clean power infrastructure we need, from new energy generation to vital grid upgrades, helping build a more secure, resilient and efficient energy system.

By accelerating the transition to homegrown energy, the Bill will help break Britain’s dependence on global fossil fuel markets and provide greater long-term stability for consumers.

How does the Bill deliver these objectives?

The estimated net social benefit from this primary legislation is £3.2 billion. Secondary legislation needed to fully implement the Bill’s measures is expected to unlock a further £19.3 billion of net social benefits, taking the total estimated net present social value to £22.6 billion.

For further information on individual measures, see Energy Independence Bill: factsheets.

Deliver a fairer deal for consumers

The Bill will:

cut energy bills for families by placing the exchequer funding of 75% of the domestic costs of the Renewables Obligation on an enduring legal basis, removing around £90 a year of costs on average from household bills as part of the £150 reduction announced at the 2025 Autumn Budget

strengthen Ofgem’s duties, remit and enforcement powers so it can act faster against wrongdoing and secure stronger redress when households and businesses are let down, transforming the regulator into a consumer champion

bring energy brokers and price comparison services under Ofgem regulation, with powers to set consistent standards, order compensation, impose fines and ban rogue operators. This could save businesses more than £100 million a year in costly mis-selling and hidden commissions

expand government’s ability to design and deliver targeted support with energy costs for low-income and vulnerable households when required

enable the removal of charges on electricity exported to the grid and enable cheaper electricity at times of excess generation, giving households greater control over their energy costs

Upgrade homes and empower communities

title: What's next for US energy policy after the midterm elections? | MIT Technology Review
description:
I’ve been locked in to my various screens since results from midterm elections started to roll in last night.
But even if the federal government isn’t likely to pass laws that overhaul energy and climate policy, the midterm results could be a big deal for energy, especially at the state and local level.
Among the broadest effects of these election results, though, will be for the data center industry.
Nearly every single one of these measures looks set to come down against data center development, as of the morning of November 4.
During her campaign, Hinojosa called for a law to completely pause data center development; if passed, it could have major implications for both the state’s grid and the data center industry more broadly.
text:
I’ve been locked in to my various screens since results from midterm elections started to roll in last night. And it didn’t take long to see the beginning of the blue wave: Democrats took control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate, a dramatic swing from Donald Trump’s victory two years ago.

While the results are striking, we probably won’t be seeing some of the big climate and energy policy shifts that have come in recent years as Congress and the presidency have changed hands. Instead, we’re entering a period of divided government, with a Congress that will likely do battle with Trump’s White House over the next two years. But even if the federal government isn’t likely to pass laws that overhaul energy and climate policy, the midterm results could be a big deal for energy, especially at the state and local level.

Let’s step back for just a moment to put these results in context. Readers might remember huge laws affecting climate and energy that were passed in just the last four years. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act included massive support for clean energy, including tax credits and government grants and loans.Then the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act essentially slashed much of the support and financial incentives in the IRA from two years before.

What those two laws had in common was a period when the government was entirely united, with the Senate, House of Representatives, and presidency all controlled by the same party—the Democrats in the first case and the Republicans in the second

Now Democrats have captured a majority in both the Senate and the House. But Donald Trump is still in the White House. And crucially, neither chamber is anywhere close to a two-thirds Democratic majority. That’s the ratio that would be needed to override a presidential veto.

So even if Congress puts together new legislation to boost climate measures and clean energy, Trump will need to sign it—and that dramatically narrows the scope of what might happen legislatively between now and the next election.

There could be some bipartisan compromises. One interesting bit of legislation to watch immediately after the election is what happens with permitting reform. In late September, a bipartisan group of senators put forward a bill that would overhaul how new energy projects are reviewed and approved in the US. The law aims to cut red tape and speed up the permitting process.

The Senate is set to vote on that package, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, on November 9, before the new Congress takes control in January. The White House has supported the bill, and it could pass the Senate if just a handful of Democrats join the Republican majority. But now, we might see Democrats wait until next year to try to renegotiate a deal, though anything would still need to pass muster with Trump.

Among the broadest effects of these election results, though, will be for the data center industry. According to tracking from Ballotpedia, there were 41 local ballot questions related to data centers. And overwhelmingly, voters chose to restrict their development. Nearly every single one of these measures looks set to come down against data center development, as of the morning of November 4.

And AI critics fared well in their races, too. Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the governor’s seat in Texas, ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. During her campaign, Hinojosa called for a law to completely pause data center development; if passed, it could have major implications for both the state’s grid and the data center industry more broadly.

We might not see dramatic new climate- or energy-related federal legislation between now and the next major US election. But many voters signaled, and quite loudly, that they wanted a change. We’ll see how much will shift in the next two years, and where that leaves us.

This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here.
