text:
INDIANAPOLIS – The Indiana Department of Environmental Management (IDEM) has announced a significant red tape reduction effort with the rescinding of more than a quarter of the agency’s Non-Rule Policies.

IDEM has also identified hundreds of federal policies that should be considered for elimination. These actions are part of an agency-wide focus to increase transparency, strengthen accountability, and ensure agency guidance remains aligned with statutory authority.

A non-rule policy document (NPD) is an agency-drafted interpretation of an environmental statute or rule. While NPDs are not intended to have the force of law, they can influence agency decision-making and guide regulated entities. Under legislation recently enacted by the Indiana General Assembly, IDEM’s NPDs must be reviewed and re-adopted every five years.

“Business and communities benefit when standards are clear and free from bureaucratic burdens,” said Gov. Mike Braun. “By cutting unnecessary red tape, Indiana can better focus on achieving meaningful environmental outcomes.”

In October, IDEM announced plans to rescind 26 of its 103 non-rule policies that were identified as outdated, unnecessary, or overly burdensome. IDEM also transmitted a letter to U.S. EPA Deputy Administrator David Fotouhi outlining opportunities to enact swift and common-sense regulatory reforms by withdrawing potentially hundreds of similar federal quasi-regulatory guidance documents. In September, Fotouhi visited Indiana to announce the approval of Indiana’s Coal Combustion Residuals permitting program alongside Governor Braun.

Across the IDEM offices of Air, Land and Water Quality, eliminating the 26 non‑rule policies will remove approximately 176 pages of outdated guidance.

Among the NPDs identified:

— Water-006: Wetlands Deed Restriction – Identified as obsolete, duplicative, and conflicting with regulations.

— Air-017: Submission of Annual Non-Methane Organic Compound Reports for Municipal Solid Waste Landfills – Originally issued in 1998, rules have been repealed by subsequent rulemaking.

— Air-035: Permitting Ethanol Production Facilities – Originally issued in 2011, has since been suspended by rulemaking.

— Waste-0058: Use of Chipped Tires in Sewage Systems – Originally issued in 2005, has been suspended by subsequent rulemaking.

“While non-rule policies can serve useful purposes, without oversight they can evolve into shadow regulations,” said IDEM Commissioner Clint Woods. “Routine review is essential to keeping our regulatory framework clear, consistent, and aligned with statutory authority. This is one of the most significant single-day reductions in unnecessary red tape in Indiana’s history. ”

This review is part of IDEM’s broader effort to modernize its regulatory framework and aligns with recent executive orders from Governor Braun. Executive Order 25‑17, Promoting Freedom and Opportunity for Hoosiers by Reducing Regulation and Controlling Regulatory Costs, requires state agencies to reduce their regulatory requirements by 25 percent by 2029.

Consistent with its review of state policies, IDEM submitted recommendations to U.S. EPA identifying more than 500 federal guidance documents and agency actions that warrant review, consolidation, update, or elimination. EPA policies, most of which are cataloged in the recently relaunched Guidance Portal, are far more extensive than the state’s with tens of thousands of guidance documents.

These “shadow regulations often do not go through a robust process… for public notice and comment, administrative procedures, scientific and information quality, or interagency review,” Commissioner Woods said in the letter to Deputy Administrator Fotouhi.

“U.S. EPA must act swiftly to ensure all documents contained within the Guidance Portal are current and align with U.S. EPA’s operational practices and formally rescind those that are outdated or have been subsequently superseded by other documents,” Commissioner Woods continued. “State agencies, like IDEM, rely on EPA guidance to implement federal programs efficiently and consistently.”

“I applaud IDEM for undertaking this meaningful work to ensure its non-rule policy documents are aligned with statutory requirements and provide clarity to the regulated community,” said Dr. John Graham, Chair of the Indiana Environmental Rules Board, former Dean of the Indiana University School of Public and Environmental Affairs (2008-2019), and former Administrator of the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (2001-2006). “Federal quasi-regulatory activities can cost states like Indiana thousands of jobs and impose millions in extra compliance costs for manufacturers and everyday consumers without going through a rigorous process subject to judicial, economic, or interagency review.”

Over the next several weeks, IDEM will remove the identified non-rule policies from the “Effective” page of its website and will add them to the “No Longer Effective” page with a watermark stating they are “Rescinded.” IDEM will also notify the Legislative Services Agency of the relevant updates.

text:
November 4, 2026 By Carol Britton Meyer

The Town of Hingham recently received $3.7 million under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), which provides billions of dollars in federal tax credits to encourage communities such as Hingham to invest in energy-efficient projects and promote clean energy technology.

In Hingham’s case, the new Foster School was eligible for a tax credit because it was built with a geothermal well-based heat pump system. Following completion of the project, Sustainability Coordinator Patricia Burke successfully applied for the credit, which is provided under the Internal Revenue Code.

The Select Board recently agreed to apply the $3.7 million to the Capital Project Cost and Debt Service Stabilization Fund (CPCDSS), which was established at the 2022 Special Town Meeting.

At that meeting, voters approved the new public safety facility and Foster School projects, along with the allocation of $7 million in unassigned fund balance to the new stabilization fund. The fund was created to pay capital costs and/or offset a portion of the debt service on bonds issued to build the public safety facility and/or the new Foster School.

Since then, funds have been appropriated annually from the CPCDSS through Town Meeting votes to help offset the debt service on the bonds for the two projects, thereby mitigating tax increases, Select Board member Julie Strehle explained in response to a follow-up email from the Hingham Anchor.

“Since the completion of these projects, funds set aside for these purposes have been appropriated annually from the CPCDSS fund by a town meeting vote, which has mitigated tax increases to pay debt service on the bonds for these two projects,” she explained.

During the Select Board discussion about the tax credit, Strehle compared it to receiving a rebate on an energy-efficient appliance.

“It’s like a rebate on the purchase of an energy-efficient appliance, which you can use to pay down your credit card bill on that appliance purchase,” she said.

Strehle proposed that the Select Board submit an article for next spring’s Annual Town Meeting to transfer the $3.7 million into the CPCDSS fund. This would allow the town to continue using the stabilization fund to offset debt and reduce the tax impact of the projects.

The money is currently in the town’s unassigned fund balance, Town Administrator Tom Mayo said.

“It makes sense to apply these funds to the Foster School project and have taxpayers get as much of a benefit as possible to lower the tax impact,” Select Board Chair Liz Klein said.

Select Board member William Ramsey agreed, noting that “more information [is] to come regarding what the impacts will be.”

text:
The repudiation of the Republican agenda on display in the US midterms is already having ripple effects throughout the world market. When it comes to green energy — which has suffered under the Trump White House’s supply-chain restrictions, subsidy repeals, and de-facto prohibition on federal climate-change research — the impact of the November election results was immediate euphoria, a sign that the industry expects a revival under the upcoming Democratic machine.

Renewable energy stocks soared across Asia and Europe on Wednesday as investors scrambled to get in on what they assume will be a return to a favorable regulatory regime in the US, which will have massive consequences for the world market.

Shares for the Danish wind-farm developer Orsted, for example, had shot up by around six percent at the time of writing. As OilPrice.com observes, Orsted is the world’s biggest developer of offshore wind projects — a flashing green sign from global energy investors.

In South Korea, stocks associated with solar power and battery production pulled ahead on the election news, even as AI chip stocks crumbled. For example, Hanwha Solutions Corp, a major player in both the global- and US-solar trade, was up over 18.5 percent on the day, at least temporarily stopping a months-long tumble.

Back in the US, stocks for the largest solar panel manufacturer in the Western hemisphere First Solar exploded, shooting up 8.1 in premarket trading and rising 9.5 percent as of midday Wednesday (and that’s despite some weak sales guidance and the inherent regulatory uncertainty that comes with US midterms.)

NextEra Energy, the world’s largest electrical utility holding company by market cap was also in the green, up about 3.8 percent on the day.

The big caveat here will be around Donald Trump’s tariffs on renewable energy supply chains. Though Chinese manufacturing has unleashed cheap photovoltaics on the global market at a simply unprecedented scale, the US market remains largely insulated by crushing import duties imposed by the Republican party.

Whether that tariff regime holds will be one of the key indicators to watch as Democrats take control of the US legislature in January — but for now, investors are clearly feeling the buzz.

Commenting on the publication of the Energy Independence Bill today, RenewableUK’s CEO Tara Singh said:

“The Bill is a welcome recommitment to clean power. It rightly highlights the benefits that onshore wind brings to local communities. The onshore wind industry already supports 15,000 jobs and invests £75 million a year in community benefit funds schemes throughout the UK. These help to pay for priorities that people choose for themselves, such as local electricity discount schemes, or funding for community buildings, skills and training and tackling fuel poverty.

We’re keen to engage with Ministers on measures such as reforming capital allowances to reduce the cost of investment in wind energy, ways to accelerate the planning system, and the design of the new Energy Wealth Fund which will invest in renewable and low-carbon energy infrastructure across the UK. text:
With Democrats capturing the House of Representatives and Senate in the U.S. mid-term elections, permitting reform could be a top agenda for advancing power growth and reducing energy costs in the U.S., said a report from Wood Mackenzie.

Rising energy costs driven by conflict in the Middle East have elevated power affordability to a central bipartisan concern. With data center buildouts and electrification pushing U.S. electricity demand up 3% annually from 2026 to 2035, Wood Mackenzie projects wholesale power prices will rise 46% over the period, making grid access for clean energy a primary legislative priority.

While a Republican White House creates a high threshold for expanding renewable energy tax credits, federal permitting reform stands out as the single policy track with cross-party momentum, said the report.

Wood Mackenzie points to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) as the primary vehicle to accelerate utility-scale solar, battery energy storage systems (BESS), and high-voltage transmission lines. Key initiatives in the draft legislation include:

Completing National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) environmental impact reviews within a strict two-year deadline

Prohibiting federal agencies from retroactively revoking issued construction and operating permits

Restricting post-approval legal challenges to a 150-day window following an environmental record of decision

Mandating a firm nine-month review timeline for Clean Water Act Section 404 dredge-and-fill permits required for linear grid infrastructure

For solar and storage asset owners, streamlined permitting is vital for connecting large-scale generation and deploying co-located solar-plus-storage to bypass constrained transmission corridors.

Grid bottlenecks remain an acute obstacle to renewable deployment, with annual transmission congestion costs exceeding $10 billion and high-voltage line completions in the 2020s running at less than half the pace of the prior decade. BAAJA targets linear infrastructure by establishing one-year NEPA assessments and the 150-day litigation cap for high-voltage transmission assets, accelerating the delivery of remote utility-scale solar and storage generation to urban demand centers.

“The wind industry’s best bet for permitting reform is to be included in a national bill across multiple technologies and to have Congress monitor implementation,” said Siddhant Warrier, research analyst for North American power at Wood Mackenzie.

Equipment supply chain constraints present an additional bottleneck for solar and storage facilities. An August executive order restricting bulk-power equipment from 24 nations, including China, is set to impact hardware availability ahead of final guidelines in December. Current market deficits stand at 18% for power transformers and 14% for substation transformers.

Despite potential executive friction, Wood Mackenzie notes historical precedent where divided government yielded landmark energy legislation, citing the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 as a model for bipartisan compromise during tight power markets.

“While we see the likelihood for permitting reform, how policy is legislated and implemented remains a risk to the U.S. economy,” said David Brown, director of global integrated energy research for Wood Mackenzie. “Entrenched partisanship could fuel policy stagnation and regulatory confusion.”

text:
For Ford Motor Company(NYSE: F) investors, the exciting part of selling a truck used to be, well, selling the truck for the juicy margins that it hauled. Then the customer drove away, and everyone hoped they would return when it was time for another one.

Ford increasingly wants the relationship to last beyond those purchases, and it could help change the narrative about operating in a low-margin industry by boosting the high-margin services Ford is hoping to grow. Software subscriptions and connected services give the automaker more ways to earn money after the initial sale, and as mentioned, these often come with much higher software-industry-like margins.

Its latest results suggest that opportunity is becoming more than something management puts on an earnings presentation. Rival General Motors(NYSE: GM) offers an encouraging example of what it could become.

The sale isn't the finish line

Ford reported more than 1.7 million active paid software subscriptions through September, increasing more than 40% year over year. Meanwhile, its U.S. Q3 vehicle sales declined 6.6%, emphasizing the growth opportunity beyond the sale. The figures measure different activities, but the contrast is useful in showing that software growth doesn't have to move in lockstep with new U.S. vehicle sales.

Ford also reported record quarterly software-services revenue, with BlueCruise and connectivity leading that business's revenue growth, although it didn't disclose specific revenue numbers. However, that still matters because Ford can sell useful services throughout a vehicle's ownership period. It doesn't need to manufacture another lucrative F-150 every time it wants to sell another month of service subscription. GM, on the other hand, did disclose more specific numbers to consider.

GM shows the money!

GM's OnStar business generated more than $800 million in recognized revenue during Q3, increasing 15% year over year. Within that business, Super Cruise revenue grew approximately 60%, with management targeting roughly $400 million for the full year. That's real revenue, rather than another shiny technology that executives promise will eventually make money.

There's more revenue waiting in the wings. GM ended Q3 with $6.8 billion in deferred revenue from OnStar services, including Super Cruise, up roughly 40% year over year. That represents revenue it hasn't earned yet because it still needs to deliver the services. For example, when a vehicle purchase includes several years of the service, GM allocates part of the sale to those services and recognizes that revenue over time. It gives investors better visibility into future revenue, although the costs of providing those services still have to come out.

Ford's subscription count isn't directly comparable with GM's broader OnStar base. But the investment opportunity is similarly focused on earning more from vehicles already in customers' driveways. This opportunity has the potential to grow alongside the adoption of electric vehicles (EVs), which are typically far more advanced in software, technology, and over-the-air update capabilities.

What it all means

Nobody needs another subscription just because they already own an expensive truck. We all have a seemingly ever-increasing number of subscriptions. These services have to earn their keep through convenience, useful features, or helping businesses keep vehicles working. Ford hasn't disclosed a stand-alone software profit margin in these results, either. Developing and maintaining those services costs money.

Still, growing paid subscriptions at Ford and rising digital revenue at GM give investors something concrete to watch. It also helps Ford and GM slowly change the narrative that the automotive industry is forever a low-margin business, but these services will have to substantially grow over the next decade to expand not only their contribution to the automakers' top and bottom lines, but to expand into a larger piece of overall fleets on the road. It will take years to increase the penetration of these services.

Look for continued growth, customers renewingafter introductory periods, and evidence that the additional revenue supports stronger profits and hopefully higher overall margins. The truck sale still matters, but what happens after the customer takes the keys should matter more and more going forward.

National battery storage capacity reached nearly 58 gigawatt-hours in 2025, the largest year of new capacity on record, and the market is expected to install an additional 500GWh of storage between 2026 and 2031, a 250% increase over the previous five-year period, according to the American Clean Power Association.

Although battery investment has accelerated across utility-scale, large industrial and data center applications, commercial buildings remain “largely untapped,” creating opportunity, GridPoint said.

“Despite this momentum, market adoption of BESS is still in its early stages,” ULI and ULSE say in their report, released Oct. 27. “Many property owners remain uncertain about where to start, which technologies fit their building type, and how local utility conditions affect financial returns. Community resistance in some jurisdictions, driven by fire safety concerns over large battery installations, has led to development slowdowns in select markets.”

Even with these impediments, factors including grid stress, corporate decarbonization mandates and the growing premium for energy-secure assets suggest that on-site storage will be an increasingly standard component of real estate underwriting and development strategy in the years ahead, the report says.

“GridPoint was founded on the belief that commercial buildings could play a much more active role in the energy system,” GridPoint co-founder and CEO Adrian De Luca said in a statement. “Over two decades later, the need for that is becoming much more urgent. We have the customers, the performance data, the building controls and the field infrastructure already in place to integrate storage as the next layer to transform our installed base into a much larger distributed energy resource.”

GridPoint says adding battery storage to its platform allows operators to lower energy costs and add grid revenue. BESS reduces peak demand and charges by shifting when a facility draws power from the grid, while stored energy and flexible capacity can also be used to earn payments through utility and capacity programs so commercial facilities capture value when the power system needs capacity, the company says.

Demand charges — utility fees based on a building’s peak electricity consumption — often represent 30% to 50% of a commercial electricity bill, according to research from the National Laboratory of the Rockies. The analysis estimates there are roughly 5 million commercial customers in the U.S. who can subscribe to retail electricity tariffs that have demand charges in excess of $15 per kilowatt, or over a quarter of the 18 million commercial customers nationwide.

ULI and ULSE say that these charges are a particularly powerful driver of market adoption as they allow operators to shave peaks by discharging cheap stored energy during high-demand windows. Federal incentives are also still favorable for BESS, especially when considering energy community and domestic content incentives, while 13 states have also established procurement mandates aimed at boosting behind-the-meter storage.

What changed and why Hydro-Quebec delayed the plan

Hydro-Quebec has extended its C$200 billion investment timeline by six years to 2041. The company says demand is rising more slowly than expected versus its 2023 action plan, which aimed to add generation and bolster transmission by 2035 to address an energy shortfall, support an electric vehicle buildout, and meet US export commitments.

That US footprint got bigger this year with two new lines carrying Quebec power south: the Blackstone Inc. backed Champlain Hudson Power Express into New York City and Avangrid Inc.'s New England Clean Energy Connect. But with some EV battery manufacturing projects scrapped and EV adoption taking longer, "The increase in demand is more gradual than expected," spokesperson Cendrix Bouchard said.

Supply, demand and the numbers you should know

In a 15-year supply blueprint released Tuesday, Hydro-Quebec projects capacity requirements will hit 52,000 megawatts by 2041 - a 30% rise - with transportation electrification responsible for more than half of the increase. Hydro-Quebec expects it could be a net buyer of electricity through 2041 and, even if reservoirs refill by 2028, assumes imports could exceed exports until then as demand growth outpaces supply.

Installed capacity is around 45,000 MW today. The utility targets nearly 11,800 MW of additional contribution to capacity balance by 2041, a metric that reflects how much dependable capacity is available when intermittent sources are not producing. Example: Hydro-Quebec aims to install 11,000 MW of wind to yield an effective 2,300 MW contribution.

Because reservoirs are low, the utility is already buying power on outside markets, among them US spot markets. Most new capacity will come from wind and hydro, and TC Energy Corp.'s natural gas plant in Becancour will be upgraded after having been largely idle since 2006, when it was commissioned.

Big contracts, disputes and what it could mean for your portfolio

In August, Hydro-Quebec entered a new 50-year supply agreement worth near C$50 billion with Newfoundland and Labrador. The strategy includes upgrades to lift Churchill Falls Labrador Corp.'s output and the construction of a run-of-river plant at Gull Island on the Churchill River, where Hydro-Quebec would serve as the lead builder.

Legal friction is rising around cross-border sales. The company said, "The dispute arises from disagreements related to certain delivery interruptions that occurred during the exceptional winter conditions of January and February 2026," and cited force majeure. The three distributors have also sued, asserting their right to hold back the payments.

The bottom line: a longer build timeline, softer near-term demand, hydrology risk and active export contracts point to a utility balancing imports with growth projects. For investors with exposure to transmission developers, wind suppliers, or counterparties to Hydro-Quebec contracts, execution on capacity additions and the legal outcomes around New England deliveries will be key swing factors for revenue visibility.

text:
Washington, DC; November 4, 2026: A group representing Kentucky coal producers is intervening in a lawsuit over the Environmental Protection Agency’s repeal of its 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards for Fossil Fuel-Fired Electric Generating Units. The Kentucky Coal Association (KCA) argues that the court should affirm the repeal because the EPA exceeded its statutory authority and unconstitutionally exercised legislative power by issuing the emissions rule.

“Agency guidelines should not reshape the American energy economy without clear authorization from Congress,” said Matt Gilliam, an attorney at Pacific Legal Foundation. “The EPA had no authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuel-fired power plants in the first place. Its 2024 rule wrongly limited energy producers’ ability to make productive use of our natural resources, threatening Americans’ access to affordable, reliable energy. We urge the court to affirm the rule’s repeal.”

The EPA repealed its 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards on September 17, 2026, stating that the emissions rule was unachievable and imposed unreasonable costs on energy producers. Shortly afterward, the American Lung Association challenged the repeal and asked the court to require the agency to reinstate the emissions rule.

Represented at no cost by Pacific Legal Foundation, KCA filed a motion to intervene in the case in support of the EPA’s repeal. The court granted the motion on November 3. KCA argues that the agency lacked congressional authority to impose such sweeping restrictions on energy producers, making the emissions rule an unconstitutional exercise of legislative power.

title: Opening Remarks at the Third China–Africa Energy Cooperation Project Promotion ... - PeaceAu.org
description:
Thank you for your commitment to promoting the Africa Agenda in China!
The theme of this conference, “Building a China–Africa Green Energy Partnership,” is closely aligned with the energy vision of the African Union’s Agenda 2063.
First, China–Africa energy cooperation has aligned with the AU’s continental agenda.
The China–AU Energy Partnership has provided a platform for policy dialogue and technical exchanges.
May the tree of China–Africa friendship remain evergreen.
text:
Your Excellency Liu Yang, Vice Governor of Hunan Provincial People's Government

Honorable Liu Deshun, Chief Engineer of the National Energy Administration

Your Excellency Mrs. Nardos Bekele-Thomas, the Chief Executive Officer of AUDA-NEPAD

Honorable Yi Yuechun, President of China Renewable Energy Engineering Institute (CREEI)

Distinguished guests,Ladies and Gentlemen.

Good morning.

It is a distinct honor to be with you in Yueyang, a city of significant historical and cultural heritage. As one of the co-organizers of this conference, the African Union Permanent Mission to China extends a warm welcome to our African brothers and sisters who have travelled great distances, and to all guests attending the Third China–Africa Energy Cooperation Project Promotion Conference. Today, Chinese and African friends have gathered here across vast distances, bearing witness to the long and enduring friendship between China and Africa.

I wish to acknowledge the presence of Her Excellency Dr. Nardos Thomas Bekele-Thomas, the CEO of AUDA-NEPAD, the Ambassadors of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Côte d’Ivoire, the Kingdom of Lesotho, Chargé d' Affaires of Libya, and Zambia, as well as a number of African diplomats based in Beijing. Thank you for your commitment to promoting the Africa Agenda in China!

Let me from the outset on behalf of H.E. Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Chairperson of the AU Commission commend H.E. President Xi Jinping for his strong and clear leadership that continues to deepen China-Africa relations. As we meet here today, China under the able leadership of President Xi is celebrating its two miracles of rapid economic growth and long-term social stability.

The theme of this conference, “Building a China–Africa Green Energy Partnership,” is closely aligned with the energy vision of the African Union’s Agenda 2063. Agenda 2063 establishes integration and infrastructure connectivity as central pillars of Africa’s transformation and explicitly envisions regional and continental power pools as key instruments for integrated, resilient and sustainable energy development. Africa has substantial renewable energy resources, including solar, wind and hydropower. Turning these resource advantages into development momentum is, first and foremost, a process of implementing Africa’s own plans. The AU has adopted the African Green Hydrogen Strategy, the African Energy Efficiency Strategy and Action Plan, and the African Energy Transition Strategy and Action Plan, providing a continental framework for a just, inclusive and equitable energy transition. The AU is ready to work with China to promote the application and diffusion of clean energy technologies and equipment in Africa, so that green energy cooperation serves Africa’s industrialization, energy security and self-reliant development.

In this connection, I would like to offer three observations in light of the AU’s continental frameworks.

First, China–Africa energy cooperation has aligned with the AU’s continental agenda. Agenda 2063 identifies the Programme for Infrastructure Development in Africa (PIDA) as the core implementation framework for the infrastructure sector. The second Priority Action Plan of PIDA emphasises cross-border transmission, hydropower and regional power interconnection. These projects are gradually producing results: the Kenya–Tanzania interconnection has been commissioned, linking the Eastern Africa Power Pool and the Southern African Power Pool and providing an early demonstration of the African Single Electricity Market (AfSEM) and the Continental Power System Masterplan (CMP); a hydropower project jointly developed by Zambia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has entered the implementation stage; and pre-feasibility studies for cross-border corridors such as Burundi–Tanzania and Angola–the DRC have been completed. Clean energy projects implemented by Chinese enterprises in Africa are creating synergies within this continental planning framework and aligning with Africa’s own agenda. The China–AU Energy Partnership has provided a platform for policy dialogue and technical exchanges. The AU appreciates this and looks forward to further aligning cooperation with the project pipelines of PIDA and CMP.

Second, we should connect this promotion platform to Africa’s priority project pipeline. The solar, wind, hydropower and grid projects promoted at this conference are consistent with the direction of AfSEM and CMP, which the AU is advancing. AfSEM aims to establish a unified electricity market across the continent, while CMP provides a roadmap for connecting Africa’s major power pools and expanding the continent’s installed capacity over time. The AU’s priority is to move beyond planning documents and turn cross-border interconnection and clean generation projects into bankable and deliverable projects. Africa has abundant renewable energy resources, and China has vast experience in clean energy technologies and engineering construction. The complementarity between the two sides is clearly reflected in these specific corridors and projects. The AU hopes that all participants will fully utilize this platform to conduct in-depth matching around the priority project pipeline already identified by the continent, and to incorporate cooperation outcomes into the implementation process of PIDA and CMP, so as to benefit the African people more widely.

Third, we should deepen the green energy partnership on the basis of Africa’s own frameworks. Africa’s energy transition must be just, inclusive and development-oriented. The AU has made clear that energy cooperation should serve universal access, industrialization and long-term energy security, rather than the expansion of installed capacity alone. The AU is ready to work with China to strengthen cooperation in expanding renewable energy development, cross-border energy infrastructure connectivity, green technology innovation, capacity building and personnel training, and investment and financing support. We should focus on supporting the implementation of the PIDA energy project pipeline and CMP priority interconnection corridors, and on supporting Africa in building local capacity in manufacturing, maintenance and operations.

At the same time, the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) provides a market for local production of energy technologies and components in Africa. Green energy cooperation should be linked to Africa’s industrialization process, so that new electricity generation contributes to local value creation to the maximum extent feasible.

Distinguished guests, dear friends! Seventy years ago, China and Africa embarked on a historic course of friendly exchanges; seventy years later, Africa is at a critical stage in moving the energy goals of Agenda 2063 from blueprint to implementation.

I would like to conclude by reaffirming the AU’s readiness to partner with China to promote more deliverable, sustainable and African-owned outcomes in China–Africa green energy cooperation, through its various instruments, most notably PIDA, AfSEM and CMP, as implementation tools. Needless to say, doing so would contribute to building the all-weather China–Africa community with a shared future for the new era through energy cooperation in the spirit of mutual respect, equality and mutual benefit.

I wish all our esteemed participants fruitful deliberations and good health.

May the tree of China–Africa friendship remain evergreen.

Long live the Sino-African partnership.

Xie Xie

text:
Texas — with its cowboy hats, slow-smoked barbecue, and de-regulatory stance — was supposed to be the California antidote for tech bros fed up with Silicon Valley's Democratic politics.

Well, Texas just got a lot bluer.

On Tuesday, voters handed Democrats control of the House and Senate. In Texas, they selected James Talarico for the Senate and Gina Hinojosa for the governor's mansion, despite massive Republican spending backed by Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.

Now, the tech-world frustration is starting to trickle out.

"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk wrote on X.

Jason Calacanis, a tech investor and co-host of the "All-In Podcast," had a similar reaction.

"I never expected Texas to turn blue," he wrote on X. "Ugh, I moved here to get away from the left lunacy!"

Chamath Palihapitiya, another "All-In" co-host, was more dire during a Tuesday-night livestream.

"There's only one thing that sinks the US economy," he said. "That's the AI trade. And the only way to sink the AI trade is to sink the data centers. And the only way to sink the data centers is to sink the power. And all the power that matters right now is in West Texas."

Alex Cohen, the Texas-based CEO and cofounder of AI healthcare company Hello Patient, had a blunter response on X: "RIP AI it was fun while it lasted."

The Lone Star State had not elected a statewide Democratic candidate since Ann Richards won the governor's race in 1990. Talarico is the first Democrat to win a Texas Senate election since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988.

Not everyone in tech is angry at the results. LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman, a prominent donor for Democrats, called the midterm elections, including the Texas results, "an overwhelming wave against Trump and his cronies," in a post on X.

As of publication, several outspoken Texas-based tech figures — including David Sacks, Travis Kalanick, and Blockchain co-CEO Lane Kasselman — had not posted about the results.

Arkansas Department of Energy and Environment (“E&E”) Secretary Shane Khoury sent an October 30th letter to United States Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) Region 6 addressing the federal agency’s September 30, 2026 “120-day Letter” on Intended Area Designations for the 2024 Primary Annual PM2.5 NAAQS. See Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OAR-2024-0078.

The E&E letter provides Arkansas’ views on designation of Air Quality Control Regions (“AQCRs”) in the state as either attainment/unclassifiable or nonattainment for the 2024 primary annual fine particulate matter (“PM2.5”) National Ambient Air Quality Standard (“NAAQS”).

Sections 108 and 109 of the Clean Air Act require that EPA identify air pollutants utilizing certain criteria and set NAAQS for each. Particulates are one of the six air pollutants currently designated as criteria air pollutants and are therefore subject to NAAQS. Section 109 requires that EPA promulgate primary NAAQS for the pollutants identified under Section 108.

Section 109(d)(1) of the Clean Air Act mandates a periodic review of each NAAQS. Depending on the results of the review, EPA must determine whether the existing air quality criteria and NAAQS should be revised.

EPA had modified under the Biden Administration the PM2.5 to a more restrictive 9.0 µg/m3. The previous PM2.5 standard was 12.0 µg/m3. However, under the Trump Administration EPA has argued that that the revised PM2.5 NAAQS was an unlawful tightening. The federal agency unsuccessfully requested that a federal appellate court vacate the rule before an area designation deadline of February 7, 2026.

EPA subsequently notified all 50 states, the District of Columbia, 5 territories, and 67 Tribes of its intended approach for area designations under the Biden-era 2024 revised NAAQS for PM2.5. Further, EPA provided an opportunity for states, territories, and Tribes to submit additional information within 30 days along with a Notice of Availability in the Federal Register to receive feedback.

EPA stated that the opportunities for further input represented a step toward complying with the court order issued by the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California requiring designations for AQCRs by February 6, 2027.

In response to the September 30th EPA Region 6 letter, E&E states that it agrees with the federal agency’s intention to designate most areas in the State attainment/unclassifiable. Further, E&E states that for each Arkansas area that Enclosure 1 identifies as possibly not meeting the standard, it explains why EPA should designate that area as unclassifiable. Those areas include:

Pulaski County, in the Little Rock-North Little Rock-Conway, AR Core Based Statistical Area (“CBSA”).

Garland County, in the Hot Springs, AR CBSA.

Union County, in the El Dorado, AR CBSA.

Little River and Miller Counties, the Arkansas portion of the Texarkana, TX-AR CBSA.

By way of summary, Arkansas states and further amplifies on the following arguments:

The information available to EPA supports an unclassifiable designation.

The court-ordered schedule has left the necessary analyses incomplete.

Fire-influenced data have not been reviewed.

Contribution to the Texarkana, Texas monitor has not been analyzed.

The Arkansas Department of Energy and Environment – Division of Environmental Quality will submit exceptional events demonstrations.

MNRE's latest notification recognises 7,117 MW of N-type TOPCon solar cell manufacturing capacity at Avaada Electro's Butibori facility in Maharashtra

Advanced G12 TOPCon technology with manufacturer-declared cell efficiency reaching up to 26.8% reinforces India's growing capabilities in solar manufacturing.

MUMBAI, India, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Avaada Electro Limited, the solar manufacturing arm of Avaada Group, has achieved a significant milestone in India's clean energy manufacturing journey, with 7,117 MW (7.117 GW) of N-type TOPCon solar cell manufacturing capacity enlisted under the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy's (MNRE) 13th revision of the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) List-II, dated 28 October 2026.

The enlistment marks an important step in Avaada Electro's journey towards building a globally competitive solar manufacturing enterprise and strengthening India's domestic solar technology ecosystem.

At a time when the world is seeking more diversified and resilient clean energy supply chains, India's ability to manufacture advanced solar cells at scale is becoming increasingly important. Avaada Electro's Butibori facility in Maharashtra represents a significant contribution to this national ambition.

Advanced Technology: Making Every Watt Count

A key highlight of the latest ALMM enlistment is Avaada Electro's G12 N-type TOPCon solar cell technology, with manufacturer-declared maximum cell efficiency reaching up to 26.8% and the highest listed average cell efficiency of 25.89%.

The company's G12 full-cell model has a declared maximum power output of 11.81 watts per cell.

These technical parameters reflect the potential of advanced TOPCon technology to generate more electrical power from a given silicon cell area, supporting the development of higher-power solar modules.

As solar technology advances, improving conversion efficiency remains an important pathway towards better utilisation of materials, manufacturing resources and installation infrastructure.

For Avaada Electro, the focus is not simply on achieving higher technical specifications, but on translating technological progress into consistent product quality, dependable performance and competitive manufacturing economics.

Manufacturing at Scale: Strengthening India's Solar Supply Chain

With 7.117 GW of annual enlisted nameplate capacity, Avaada Electro's Butibori manufacturing facility actual production and saleable output will depend on operating utilisation, manufacturing yields and product mix.

The scale of this manufacturing platform strengthens Avaada Electro's ability to serve India's expanding solar industry, including module manufacturers, renewable energy developers and engineering, procurement and construction companies.

It also contributes to the development of domestic manufacturing capabilities at a time when India is working to strengthen supply-chain resilience, promote industrial self-reliance and reduce dependence on imported solar components.

Beyond Capacity: Building a Culture of Manufacturing Excellence

Avaada Electro believes that manufacturing leadership cannot be measured by installed capacity alone.

Long-term competitiveness requires continuous improvement in cell efficiency, production yields, product reliability, manufacturing productivity and cost per watt.

The company is building its manufacturing approach around three fundamental principles:

First Time Right: Building quality into every stage of production.

Every Time Right: Delivering consistent quality through disciplined processes.

Everything Right: Integrating product performance, operational excellence, responsible manufacturing and customer satisfaction.

Through its continued investment in advanced TOPCon technology and manufacturing capabilities, Avaada Electro aims to build a dependable domestic supply platform capable of competing on quality, technology and cost.

Chairman's Statement

Commenting on the milestone, Vineet Mittal, Chairman and Whole-time Director, Avaada Electro Limited, said, "India's clean energy future cannot depend only on how much solar power we install. It must also depend on how much technology we develop, how much we manufacture ourselves, and how effectively we compete with the world.

Our 7.1 GW TOPCon solar cell manufacturing enlistment is an important milestone in that journey.

But manufacturing leadership is not about building the biggest factory. It is about making better products, improving efficiency every day, maintaining uncompromising quality and earning the trust of customers through consistent performance.

At Avaada, we believe that every improvement in technology must ultimately create value for our customers, for the environment and for our country. Our ambition is simple to Make in India. Compete with the world. Make every watt count. This milestone is not the destination. It is another step towards demonstrating that India can build advanced clean energy technology at scale and with globally competitive standards."

Supporting India's Energy Security and Manufacturing Ambitions

India's energy transition presents an opportunity that extends far beyond renewable power generation. It offers the country a pathway to develop advanced industrial capabilities, create skilled employment, strengthen domestic supply chains and become an important participant in global clean energy manufacturing.

Avaada Electro aims to contribute to this transformation by combining manufacturing scale, technological development, disciplined operations and long-term customer relationships.

As the solar industry evolves, the companies that succeed will be those capable of delivering not only more manufacturing capacity, but also greater productivity, consistent quality and better value from every watt.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C.—Growth Energy, the nation’s largest biofuel trade association, called on the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to quickly finalize its proposed reallocation rule that accounts for lost gallons from recent small refinery exemptions (SREs) under the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS).

At a hearing today, Growth Energy General Counsel Joe Kakesh expressed the organization’s support for EPA’s proposal, noting that reallocation should be a normal part of EPA’s administration of the RFS. “Just as it has the authority—and obligation—to incorporate projected SREs into renewable volume obligations (RVOs), EPA also has the authority and obligation to reallocate excess 2025 SRE RINs to other RVOs, here for 2026 and 2027,” he said in testimony. “In doing so, EPA meets Congress’ statutory mandate that EPA ‘ensure’ that renewable volume obligations are met. In fact, EPA should fully account for excess SRE RINs every year, not just for 2025.”

“EPA is right to account for every lost SRE gallon,” said Growth Energy CEO Emily Skor. “Especially in a time of record profits, refiners shouldn’t be able to simply cast off their RVO blending obligations onto the American biofuels industry,” she added, pointing to recent earnings reports from oil refineries that received SREs in August.

The Wall Street Journal recently reported that refiners are “printing money.”

“Despite recent announcements of near-record profits, refiners are asking for even more handouts, urging EPA to walk away from President Trump’s commitment to fully account for lost biofuel gallons and make producers and farmers whole,” added Skor. “At a time when farms are facing a sixth consecutive year of negative returns, and consumers are pleading for relief at the pump, we shouldn’t be looking for new ways to line refiners’ pockets. EPA must adhere to President Trump’s vision by limiting the impact of SREs and driving down costs by increasing the use of homegrown biofuels.”

Financing the transition without deepening debt The gap between LDCs' energy needs and available finance remains substantial.
Since 2010, LDCs' debt service burden has nearly quadrupled, rising at a faster rate than in other developing country groups.
The Just Transition Mechanism should help countries overcome barriers to accessing appropriate finance, including by strengthening coordination with existing climate finance institutions and development partners.
COP31 can take forward these principles when deliberating the development and eventual delivery of the mechanism.
text:
At COP31, governments have an opportunity to turn their commitment to equitable just transitions into practical support for countries facing some of the greatest barriers to implementation. The test at COP31 is whether the foundations for a mechanism can be secured that supports the transitions LDCs need, rather than one built primarily around the experiences and priorities of wealthier economies.

An effective just transition also depends on stronger global climate action. LDCs are already losing development gains to intensifying climate impacts, and the risks to their economies and livelihoods will grow as warming continues. Stronger emissions reductions this decade are essential to limiting the height and duration of overshoot and putting the world on a path back to well below 1.5°C by 2100.

Established at COP28, the UAE Just Transition Work Programme (JTWP) aims to advance equitable and inclusive transition pathways that support sustainable development and poverty eradication, in line with the goals of the Paris Agreement. Building on these discussions, governments at COP30 in Belém agreed to develop a Just Transition Mechanism to strengthen international cooperation, technical assistance, capacity-building and knowledge-sharing with its detailed functions and governance arrangements still to be determined.

Different starting points for a just transition

Just transition discussions have largely been shaped by the experiences of industrialised economies, where the challenge is to phase out fossil fuels, decarbonise established industries and support affected workers and communities.

For most LDCs, the challenge is different. Limited energy access, low levels of industrialisation and inadequate infrastructure mean that countries must expand essential services and economic opportunities while avoiding carbon-intensive development. High debt burdens, limited public finances and increasingly severe climate impacts make this task even harder.

Energy deficits remain substantial. In 2024, electricity access stood at 60.4% in LDCs, compared with 90.3% across low- and middle-income countries. Recent data shows that 17 of the 20 countries with the largest electricity access deficits were LDCs.

Their energy systems also differ significantly from those of industrialised economies. Traditional biomass remains a major source of household energy in many LDCs, particularly for cooking and heating, reflecting limited access to modern, clean energy alternatives.

For LDCs, a just transition must therefore support the expansion of affordable, reliable and clean energy alongside economic development, poverty reduction and climate resilience.

An opportunity to build cleaner energy systems

LDCs have the unique opportunity to leapfrog energy systems to renewable technologies, avoiding the carbon-intensive pathways that industrialised economies are now tasked to replace. But realising this potential requires substantial investment. Despite significant renewable energy potential, LDCs continue to lag behind other vulnerable country groups. In 2024, installed renewable electricity-generating capacity stood at just 43 watts per person in LDCs, compared with 114 watts in landlocked developing countries and 125 watts in Small Island Developing States.

This gap reflects the scale of investment required to meet growing energy demand while pursuing low-emission development. Without timely access to finance, technology and technical expertise, LDCs risk missing opportunities to build cleaner energy systems and becoming locked into infrastructure that may prove costly to replace in the future.

Financing the transition without deepening debt

The gap between LDCs' energy needs and available finance remains substantial. Despite facing some of the world's highest levels of energy poverty, LDCs received just 15% of international public financial flows for clean energy to developing countries in 2024 — USD 3.7 billion. This represented an 11% decline from 2023. Around two-thirds of these flows were provided through debt-based instruments.

This reliance on loans is particularly problematic for countries already facing severe debt pressures. Since 2010, LDCs' debt service burden has nearly quadrupled, rising at a faster rate than in other developing country groups. In 2024, LDCs spent 22.3% of government revenue on servicing debt, reducing the resources available for essential services, energy infrastructure and climate action.

For countries with limited fiscal space, debt-financed transitions risk creating further economic vulnerabilities. Governments face difficult trade-offs between meeting immediate development needs and making the long-term investments required for low-carbon, climate-resilient economies.

Increasing access to finance is therefore only part of the challenge. The terms of that finance also matter. Grant-based and highly concessional finance, alongside measures that create fiscal space, will be essential if LDCs are to invest in clean energy and climate resilience without deepening debt vulnerabilities.

The Just Transition Mechanism should help countries overcome barriers to accessing appropriate finance, including by strengthening coordination with existing climate finance institutions and development partners.

Protecting livelihoods and creating decent jobs

For many LDCs, a major employment challenge is the vulnerability of existing livelihoods to climate change, alongside the need to create millions of new jobs.

Agriculture remains the largest source of employment across LDCs, leaving substantial portions of the workforce exposed to rising temperatures, droughts and other climate impacts. Informal employment is also widespread, with many workers lacking access to social protections.

Climate impacts are already threatening agricultural productivity and rural livelihoods, adding to the challenge of economic diversification and employment creation.

At the same time, LDC labour markets are expected to receive 13.2 million new entrants annually until 2050. Creating decent employment opportunities at this scale will require investment in skills, productive capacity, emerging industries and economic diversification.

The green transition offers opportunities to create employment in renewable energy, infrastructure and other emerging sectors. But these opportunities will not necessarily reach vulnerable workers without deliberate policies to support skills development, access to decent work and social protection.

An LDC-responsive just transition must therefore extend beyond the energy sector, supporting climate-resilient livelihoods, economic diversification and opportunities for informal workers. It must also recognise that climate adaptation and resilience are central to protecting jobs and livelihoods, particularly in sectors already experiencing the impacts of climate change.

An LDC-responsive Just Transition Mechanism

The COP30 decision already recognises several of these challenges, including energy poverty, limited institutional capacity, high debt burdens and the need for grant-based and highly concessional finance. COP31 can take forward these principles when deliberating the development and eventual delivery of the mechanism.

For LDCs, a responsive mechanism is one that can expand clean energy access, create decent jobs, strengthen climate resilience and improve access to finance without worsening debt pressures. Its effectiveness will depend on whether it can address these interconnected challenges in ways that reflect LDCs' own development priorities., including through:

Supporting country-driven transition pathways

Improving access to appropriate finance

Delivering practical technical assistance and capacity-building

Ensuring inclusive governance and participation

Together, these priorities would help ensure that the mechanism addresses the interconnected challenges facing LDCs, complementing existing support arrangements.

As governments prepare to operationalise the Just Transition Mechanism (JTM) at COP31 in Antalya, they have an opportunity to ensure it responds to these different starting points and recognise the distinct development priorities, financial constraints and climate vulnerabilities of the 44 LDCs as they pursue their low-carbon, climate-resilient economies.

text:
Korean companies are recalculating the costs and benefits of their U.S. operations after Democrats swept the midterm elections and took control of both chambers of Congress. Chipmakers including Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and SK hynix (000660.KS) are visibly on edge over the prospect of tighter rules on artificial intelligence data centers, while solar companies such as Hanwha (000880.KS) and OCI Holdings (010060.KS) see an opening in expanded renewable energy support. Battery makers stand to gain if the U.S. electric vehicle market rebounds in earnest, following a recovery already under way in energy storage systems.

Expectations and concerns are running in parallel among chipmakers, business sources said on the 4th. The immediate worry is a push to tighten rules on data center construction, citing AI safety along with power and environmental issues. With Democrats projected to sweep Senate and gubernatorial races in Texas, Ohio and Georgia — all hubs for AI data centers — concern has grown that permits could be delayed. Slower groundbreaking on new data centers would inevitably weigh on demand for server DRAM and high-bandwidth memory.

On the other hand, the prospect that Democrats can check the Donald Trump administration's attempts to scale back CHIPS Act subsidies is a positive for Samsung Electronics and SK hynix. The Trump administration has pushed to renegotiate subsidies finalized under the Joe Biden administration, a move some Democratic lawmakers have criticized as a misstep. Samsung Electronics is set to receive $4.745 billion in subsidies tied to its investment in the Taylor, Texas, plant.

Some analysts say data center rules will not translate directly into reduced investment. "Data centers have a large impact on local tax revenue and regional economies, so it will be difficult for state governments to ban construction outright," said Kwon Hee-jin, an analyst at KB Securities. "Rules are more likely to be adjusted toward shifting electricity costs onto data center operators or allowing construction on the condition that they secure their own power." In that case, Big Tech firms would have to build substations, transmission networks and generation facilities themselves, which could actually increase total infrastructure spending. That would open a new source of demand for Korean power equipment makers.

Automakers expect little relief on tariffs. The 15% tariff imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act falls under executive authority and is likely to remain in place regardless of which party controls Congress. "Congressional oversight of how the administration carries out policy may strengthen, but a sharp change in tariff measures is hard to expect," said Cho Sung-dae, head of the trade research division at the Korea International Trade Association. With Washington maintaining its focus on protecting domestic industry and securing supply chains, auto tariffs and pressure to expand U.S. production will persist even under a different Congress, he said. Still, a Democratic-controlled Congress could renew momentum behind policies to expand EV adoption, prompting Hyundai Motor (005380.KS) and Kia (000270.KS) to sharpen their electrification capabilities.

For shipbuilders, the key variable is how far the U.S. will allow its naval vessels to be built overseas. The National Defense Authorization Act passed by the House includes a provision barring funds from being allocated for the construction of combat ships at foreign shipyards, while the Senate Armed Services Committee version would permit some non-combat vessels to be built abroad.

Shinhan Securities (008670.KS) said that if the stance against building naval vessels overseas hardens, expectations for newbuilding orders through MASGA — the Korea-U.S. shipbuilding cooperation project, short for Make American Shipbuilding Great Again — would diminish, narrowing opportunities to maintenance, repair and overhaul work, block supply and local shipyards. Still, the prevailing view is that the broader framework of cooperation will hold, given that rebuilding U.S. shipbuilding is a bipartisan goal and MASGA investment is being driven by the administration.

The renewable energy industry is more upbeat. With Democrats campaigning on restoring clean energy tax credits under the Inflation Reduction Act, companies with large production bases in the U.S., such as Hanwha Solutions (009830.KS), are being cited as beneficiaries. Solar in particular is expected to benefit, as the push to exclude Chinese supply chains is seen continuing regardless of the election outcome, leaving Korean firms positioned to pick up share.

Korean companies are watching the shift in congressional power so closely because their U.S. operations now account for a far larger share of their business. A survey of overseas affiliates at 28 large business groups by corporate data provider CEO Score found that U.S. affiliates numbered 1,308 at the end of June this year, up 232.0% from 394 a decade earlier. The U.S. share of all overseas affiliates also jumped to 26.5% from 13.0%.

U.S. affiliates of Samsung, SK, Hyundai Motor, LG and Hanwha rose sharply over the same period, to 888 from 240. Hanwha, which expanded its solar and energy storage units, posted the largest increase, to 374 from 63, followed by SK, to 243 from 40, and Hyundai Motor, to 112 from 55.

text:
Today, Clean Fuels VP of Federal Affairs Kurt Kovarik, Regulatory Affairs Director Kate Shenk, and Governing Board Chair Kent Engelbrecht each testified at EPA’s virtual public hearing on the Proposed Reallocation of Additional 2025 Small Refinery Exemptions.

In April, EPA’s final rule on 2026-2027 Renewable Fuel Standards included an estimate that 2025 small refinery exemptions would total 990 million RINs. In August, EPA granted 2025 exemptions totaling 1.76 billion RINs. In October, EPA proposed to add supplemental volumes to the 2026-2027 Renewable Fuel Standards to reallocate 100% of the difference between its April estimate and August final action. Clean Fuels supports EPA’s proposal to reallocate 100% of the difference and split the supplemental volume between 2026 and 2027 obligations.

Kurt Kovarik stated, “We strongly support EPA’s proposal to reallocate the gallons equally to 2026 and 2027 volume obligations. We ask the agency to finalize this supplemental rule as soon as possible – certainly by the end of the year – to ensure that the robust volumes for 2026 and 2027 are not eroded by small refinery exemptions, past or future.”

“Any delays in finalizing this rule will have real market impacts similar to what we saw when the SREs were granted in August,” Shenk added. “Timely action before the end of the year will be crucial to address diesel supplies and prices. Biodiesel and renewable diesel producers will respond to this rule and the stability of the RFS program the same way we ramped up production when the Set 2 Rule was finalized in April.”

Kovarik concluded, “The clean fuels industry is delivering on the goals for the RFS – making investments in rural America, creating new jobs, and massively increasing America’s energy supply. U.S. companies throughout the biodiesel, renewable diesel, and SAF supply chain have announced new investments in capacity since earlier this year, based on the robust RFS volumes.”

text:
A Strategic Agenda for the Next Majority

By Public Citizen

Public Citizen Congressional Oversight Roadmap for 120th Congress

Executive Summary

Public Citizen is a national nonprofit consumer advocacy organization that uses research, litigation, lobbying, and public education to challenge corporate power and promote government accountability. We work at the federal, state, and local levels to advance equitable access to health care, protect consumers, strengthen democracy, defend workers’ rights, promote climate justice, increase transparency, and support financial reform.

This document is intended to help inform a strong congressional oversight agenda for the next majority following the 2026 election. We craft this understanding that, while one or both chambers may flip, the need to use the next Congress’s oversight tools to show that they can work for regular people remains essential. We must use these tools to expose corruption and corporate favoritism within this administration, building a public record that lays the groundwork for the policy reforms that will improve daily life.

This document outlines investigative priorities centered on accountability, transparency, affordability, and the protection of everyday Americans from abuses of power, corporate misconduct, and harmful public policy decisions. Recent actions by the Trump administration and aligned interests have raised serious concerns about corruption, weakened consumer protections, attacks on democratic safeguards, rising costs for families, and erosion of independent government institutions.

The recommendations are organized across major issue areas, including corruption and abuse of power, economic pressures facing families, health care affordability, financial and consumer protection, democratic accountability, climate and energy, artificial intelligence, and corporate concentration. They include proposals for hearings, investigations, subpoenas, reports, and legislative reforms designed to uncover misconduct, build a public record that can catch attention, and advance durable policy solutions. Key priorities include examining conflicts of interest involving presidential financial ventures, misuse of taxpayer resources, politicized contracting, executive branch ethics loopholes, attacks on voting access, misuse of confidential taxpayer data, weakened consumer and financial protections, harmful health care rollbacks, anti-competitive corporate practices, and unchecked deployment of emerging technologies. The report also identifies opportunities to modernize ethics laws, strengthen public participation in rulemaking, reinforce scientific integrity, and restore trust in institutions relied upon by millions of Americans.

We intend this oversight agenda to be coupled with clear, early, and bold policy prescriptions, implemented through legislation, to demonstrate our commitment to unrigging our system, fighting corruption, and creating a progressive economic system that delivers for working families. We also hope it begins to lay the groundwork for the passage of this legislation in any future governing moment and creates a record of clear enforcement actions that an incoming administration can take. This document is offered as a roadmap for a proactive oversight agenda that constituents will understand as a “fight” mentality and celebrate—centered on working families, democratic accountability, and the principle that no administration, corporation, or politically connected actor is above the law.

Table of Contents

Section I: Cost of Living, Affordability, and Corporate Greed

Section II: Health, Safety, and Public Protection

Section III: Democracy, Transparency, and Rule of Law

Section IV: Big Tech, AI, and the New Corporate Threats

Section V: Climate, Energy, and Environmental Accountability

Section VI: Corruption, Abuse of Power, and Government for Sale

Section I: Cost of Living, Affordability, and Corporate Greed

Families are paying more for food, health care, housing, utilities, and daily necessities while many corporations report strong profits and receive favorable treatment. Oversight should examine where and how policy choices shifted costs onto working Americans while rewarding wealthy interests.

1.1 Big Ugly Law: Subsidize the Rich While Stealing from Working Americans

Oversight Type: Investigations and Hearings

Problem: Congressional Republicans enacted the “Big Beautiful Bill” (OBBBA), delivering substantial tax cuts to corporations and high-income households while cutting core safety-net programs, including SNAP and Medicaid. These cuts are forcing states, providers, and food banks to absorb increased demand with fewer resources. Major corporate beneficiaries collectively worth more than $2 trillion received roughly $30 billion in tax benefits while cutting more than 45,000 jobs. Despite promises that these tax cuts would spur hiring, raise wages, and expand domestic investment, early evidence suggests many corporations are directing the financial gains toward executive compensation, shareholder distributions, and stock buybacks rather than investments that benefit workers or consumers.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold hearings and open an investigation with state administrators, food bank leaders, health care providers, impacted individuals, labor representatives, economists, and executives from major corporate beneficiaries of OBBBA’s tax provisions to examine: (1) the real-world impacts of SNAP and Medicaid cuts on working families and state budgets; (2) how corporations used the financial gains from OBBBA, including decisions related to layoffs, wages, hiring, domestic investment, executive compensation, stock buybacks, and shareholder distributions; and (3) whether the economic promises used to justify OBBBA—including job creation, wage growth, and business investment—have materialized. Subpoena executive compensation records, investor presentations, workforce data, stock buyback disclosures, shareholder distribution data, and internal corporate communications discussing the anticipated use of OBBBA tax benefits. Issue a report comparing corporate promises with actual outcomes.

Why It Matters: OBBBA represents a deliberate transfer of public resources from working families to corporations and wealthy households. Americans deserve to know whether those tax benefits produced the promised economic gains—or instead enriched executives and shareholders while families lost access to food assistance, health care, and economic security. If corporations receiving billions in tax benefits are cutting jobs, increasing executive pay, expanding stock buybacks, and rewarding shareholders instead of investing in workers, Congress has an obligation to expose that broken promise and ask a fundamental question: Who is this economy really working for?

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Ways and Means; Senate Finance

1.2 Trump’s Pharma Pact: Secret Deals, Higher Prices, Same Old Scam Oversight Type: Investigations and Hearings

Problem: The White House announced secretive deals with more than a dozen drug companies to supposedly lower drug prices, but the administration and drug companies refuse to make these deals transparent. The public doesn’t know what pricing conditions are being required of companies in deals, which drugs are affected, or which health programs will have access to lower prices. We do not know how the secret-deal prices compare with prices already available through health programs like Medicaid. Patients can’t afford to take this administration at its word.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold investigative hearings highlighting how drug companies entering deals with the White House continue to price gouge American patients. Investigations and subpoenas could seek details of these deals from the administration and expose them to the public. Reports could also highlight ongoing pricing abuses by companies party to secret deals and benefits granted by the administration to companies uncovered in an investigation.

Why It Matters: Four in 10 U.S. adults ration treatment because of cost. The administration is claiming to provide relief through secret deals with drug companies. People deserve to know what their elected officials are doing to lower drug prices for them, or if they’re all talk and protecting drug companies’ ability to price gouge.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Energy and Commerce; Senate Finance

1.3 Trump’s Merger Machine: Favors for Friends, Costs for You Oversight Type: Investigations and Hearings

Problem: The Trump administration has waived through a series of mergers or ended antitrust enforcement to benefit favored companies: Paramount-Skydance, Paramount-Warner Bros. (expected), Ticketmaster, Hewlett-Packard-Juniper, a host of Big Tech acquisitions. These mergers are concentrating economic and political power, driving up prices, and constricting consumer choices.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold hearings that require testimony from Ticketmaster CEO Michael Rapino, Hewlett-Packard Enterprise CEO Antonio Neri, Paramount Global leadership, Warner Bros. Discovery CEO David Zaslav, and executives from other corporations that benefited from weakened or abandoned antitrust enforcement. As a case likely to remain unsettled through 2026 and into 2027, the proposed Paramount-Warner Bros. transaction should serve as a central case study, with testimony from Hollywood workers, writers, actors, independent creators, and consumer advocates regarding the effects of media consolidation on jobs, wages, local journalism, creative independence, and consumer choice. Subpoena testimony from current and former DOJ Antitrust Division officials, including personnel forced out or sidelined after refusing to rubber-stamp administration-favored mergers, as well as antitrust scholars and former enforcement officials who can explain how political interference distorted merger review and enforcement decisions.

Why It Matters: Media mergers are delivering media properties to Trump-affiliated companies, slanting news coverage and cultural outputs. Mergers are raising prices and costing jobs. Larger companies are gaining dangerous influence over the political process and using it to drive their agendas—including ever more concentration.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Judiciary; Senate Judiciary

1.4 The New Robber Barons: Corporate Welfare for Billionaires, Stagnant Wages for You

Oversight Type: Investigations and Hearings

Problem: The U.S. is experiencing historically extreme levels of wealth concentration driven not simply by market forces, but by deliberate policy choices that disproportionately benefited large corporations, dominant investors, and top executives. The Trump tax cuts and related corporate policies accelerated this trend by delivering substantial benefits to highly profitable corporations while weakening labor protections, undermining worker bargaining power, and reducing public investment. Billionaires including Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg, and Stephen Schwarzman now wield extraordinary economic and political influence, with some individuals possessing more wealth than tens of millions of Americans combined. Many corporations receiving major tax advantages subsequently reported record profits, increased executive compensation and shareholder payouts, expanded stock buybacks, and continued aggressive lobbying campaigns while workers faced rising costs, stagnant wages, layoffs, and growing economic insecurity. Private equity firms, major technology companies, fossil fuel corporations, and dominant retailers have further consolidated economic and political power, raising concerns that public policy increasingly serves concentrated wealth rather than working families.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold hearings examining the mechanisms driving extreme wealth concentration and the role federal policy has played in accelerating it, including corporate tax breaks, stock buybacks, executive compensation practices, weakened labor protections, consolidation, and industry lobbying campaigns. Require testimony from ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy, Blackstone CEO Stephen Schwarzman, labor economists, tax policy experts, union representatives, and workers affected by layoffs, wage stagnation, rising costs, or reductions in benefits. Examine whether corporations that benefited substantially from Trump-era tax policies used those gains to increase executive compensation, shareholder payouts, and stock buybacks while continuing aggressive lobbying efforts against labor, tax, consumer protection, and antitrust reform. Subpoena lobbying disclosures, executive compensation records, stock buyback data, tax filings, investor communications, and internal corporate documents discussing the anticipated use of tax savings and political advocacy strategies.

Why It Matters: The growth of the K-shaped economy is threatening American democracy and forcing tens of millions of Americans to scrape by on survival even as the new robber barons accumulate unimaginable wealth. This oversight effort can both recognize that people are struggling and begin to explain why.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Ways and Means; Senate Finance; House Education and Workforce; Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions

1.5 Corporate Shrinkflation, Price Gouging and the Rip-Off of Everyday Americans

Oversight Type: Investigations and Hearings

Problem: Large corporations across food, consumer goods, travel, ticketing, banking, and delivery sectors have increased profits by charging more while giving consumers less through greedflation, junk fees, and opaque pricing practices. Many companies used inflation and supply chain disruptions as cover to raise prices beyond underlying costs, even while reporting strong earnings and expanded margins.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold hearings and open investigations into whether dominant firms such as Amazon used inflationary conditions to engage in price gouging, fee extraction, or deceptive pricing. Subpoena internal pricing strategies, investor presentations, margin analyses, and communications discussing the use of inflation narratives to justify increases. Require testimony from major food manufacturers, airlines, ticketing companies, banks, hotel chains, and consumer advocates. Issue a report recommending stronger fee transparency, anti-price-gouging enforcement, and competition reforms.

Why It Matters: Families can absorb only so many hidden charges, smaller products, and unjustified price hikes before household budgets break. When corporations exploit crises to raise profits, Americans pay more for groceries, travel, banking, and daily necessities while executives and shareholders benefit. This is a direct affordability issue and a test of whether markets serve the public or merely extract from it.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Energy and Commerce; Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation; House Financial Services; Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs

1.6 Medicare Advantage: Deny and Delay Care, Stick Seniors with the Bill Oversight Type: Investigations, Hearings, and Report

Problem: Medicare Advantage companies continue to profit by delaying and denying care. Medicare Advantage has never fulfilled its initial promise of providing care at a lower price than traditional Medicare. Instead, it has forced seniors to navigate narrow networks, jump through hoops to access needed care, and driven up premiums for traditional Medicare enrollees. Vertical and horizontal integration have led to concerning consolidation in the health care system, increasing prices and limiting access.
