Committee/Jurisdiction: House Oversight and Government Reform; Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs; House Judiciary; Senate Judiciary

6.4 Pardons for Sale: How Trump’s Pay-to-Play System Erased Penalties and Hurt Victims

Oversight Type: Investigations and Hearings

Problem: President Trump abused the pardon power: He pardoned the January 6 insurrectionists. Outside the January 6 pardons, more than one-third of his pardons in the first year were granted to people convicted of fraud or fraud-adjacent charges. His pardons have led to the cancellation of $1.5 billion in fines and restitution, including more than $1 billion owed to victims. Pardons have been granted to those who have contributed to Trump-affiliated election committees or who have hired Trump-affiliated lobbyists. And Trump has suggested he will grant broad pardons to those serving in the current administration.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold hearings and require testimony from recipients of controversial pardons, along with those witnesses who are fraud victims, investors, consumers, law enforcement officers, and others harmed by the underlying crimes whose restitution, accountability, or legal remedies were diminished by pardon decisions.

Why It Matters: This would be an embarrassing hearing for any member defending people who attacked the Capitol or committed fraud against consumers and investors. text:
WASHINGTON (November 4, 2026) — The United States held its midterm elections on November 3, with voters deciding control of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate, alongside gubernatorial, state legislative and local races across the country. The results will shape the political landscape for energy and climate policy at the federal, state and local levels.

Following is a statement from David Widawsky, Director of World Resources Institute United States:

“The message from voters is clear: Americans want greater economic security, relief from rising costs and an energy system that works for them. This election put a bright spotlight on how this country’s outdated energy system and dependence on fossil fuels leave families and businesses exposed to unaffordable price shocks.

“American consumers are bearing the burden of rising electricity prices as rapid data center growth stretches the capacity of the aging US grid, while government actions have hindered the deployment of clean and affordable energy. From farmers in the Midwest to truckers at the pump to families struggling with household bills, Americans are feeling the strain.

“The new Congress has an opportunity to deliver on issues that cut across party lines like sky-high energy costs, data centers, promising energy technology innovations like geothermal and industrial batteries, and building a modern, resilient grid. These are practical solutions that can put money back in Americans’ pockets, strengthen the economy and lay the groundwork for more ambitious action.

“Some of the biggest opportunities for progress may come at the state and city level. New governors, state legislatures and mayors have the power to move quickly on solutions that address the needs of their constituents: strengthening local economies, creating jobs and lowering bills. From ensuring data centers provide real benefits to communities to expanding clean energy, modernizing the grid, enabling affordable and accessible housing, and improving public transit, state and local leaders can walk-the-talk that climate action delivers real benefits for people.”

text:
European Parliament lawmakers on Wednesday backed a relaxation of the EU's 2035 car emissions target from 100% to 87.5%, as pressure mounts on Brussels to give the struggling automotive industry more flexibility in its transition to electric vehicles.

MEPs on the Parliament's environment committee voted to ease emissions requirements for new cars and vans, allowing manufacturers more leeway to meet their climate obligations.

The move goes further than the European Commission's proposal, which would have lowered the 2035 target from a 100% reduction in emissions to a 90% cut.

Under the parliamentary compromise, manufacturers using climate-friendly steel would receive an additional 7.5% credit, while the target for vans would fall from 90% to 80%.

The vote marks a significant shift in EU climate policy and the balance of power in Parliament, where a broad political consensus once supported progressively tighter CO2 emissions standards.

With soaring energy costs threatening Europe's industrial competitiveness, lawmakers are increasingly focused on protecting the automotive industry. EU car production remains roughly 19% to 20% below pre-pandemic levels in 2019, according to the think tank Bruegel.

Related

Seven EU countries pressure European Commission to rethink 2035 diesel and petrol car ban

EU carmakers to comply with 90% emissions reduction by 2035 as full combustion engine ban scrapped

The compromise was negotiated by the centre-right European People's Party (EPP), the centre-left Socialists and Democrats (S&D) and the centrist Renew Europe group, reflecting the EPP's longstanding demands for greater flexibility for carmakers facing fierce competition from China, sluggish electric vehicle sales and rising production costs.

The three groups had already reached a compromise, with a similar version approved by Parliament's transport and industry committees on October 22.

Italian MEP Massimiliano Salini, the EPP's lead negotiator on the legislation, hailed the vote as a victory for his group's campaign to relax the restrictions on combustion engines.

"The EPP Group managed to bring Europe's political centre together behind a clear objective: backing our car industry, protecting European jobs and giving manufacturers the freedom to develop the best technologies," Salini said.

The EPP, which previously helped sustain EU climate legislation alongside the Socialists, Liberals and Greens, has increasingly challenged the pace and design of the green transition, at times joining forces with the far right.

The Greens have warned that the move threatens the cross-party consensus that underpinned Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's Green Deal.

Breaking with the past

The vote marks a shift away from the EU's original plan to effectively end sales of new combustion engine cars from 2035, despite backing from several EU countries and electric lobby groups.

The Green Deal was a flagship achievement of the 2019–2024 European Parliament, when the Greens held 18 more seats than they do today.

The original 2035 zero-emission target for new cars and vans was ultimately adopted in 2023, despite resistance from parts of the centre-right. The Greens were among its strongest defenders, seeing it as essential to give manufacturers a clear investment signal and accelerate the shift to electric vehicles.

Related

What went wrong for the EU election-losing Greens and Liberals?

However, the current reversal is also a reflection of the political pressure that has built up since then, with several critics arguing the EU lacks adequate charging infrastructure for the uptake of EVs.

Faced with mounting demands from carmakers and national governments, particularly Germany and Italy, the Commission rolled back its original proposal in December 2025, proposing instead to weaken the 2035 target from a 100% to a 90% reduction in tailpipe emissions.

The remaining 10% could be compensated through credits linked to EU-made low-carbon steel and sustainable fuels. This would allow plug-in hybrids and even diesel- and petrol-powered vehicles to remain on the market beyond 2035 — a significant concession to the argument that the green transition must not come at the expense of industrial competitiveness.

EPP push tech flexibility

The EPP argues that carmakers need more technological leeway to remain competitive and protect jobs. The compromise with the S&D and Renew suggests that concerns about industrial competitiveness are increasingly cutting across traditional political divisions in the Parliament.

Overall, the political agreement forged on Wednesday reflects growing unease among EU governments and lawmakers about the speed and cost of the automotive transition.

Germany and France, home to two of Europe's largest automotive industries, have been among those calling for greater flexibility, carving out their own Franco-German car deal, in which climate-friendly steel plays a much smaller role.

Veteran German MEP Peter Liese, the EPP's climate policy spokesperson, hailed the political will from the different groups.

"We want climate neutrality, but with the rules we have now agreed on, we are also ensuring technology neutrality. I am personally convinced that the future belongs to electric cars. But electric vehicles with range extenders and plug-in hybrids with a long electric range will also have a role to play in 2035 and beyond," Liese said.

Related

Exclusive: EU Commissioner Hoekstra defends scrapping 2035 ban on combustion engines

France and Spain back 2035 diesel and petrol car ban, letter reveals

Green lawmakers have criticised the proposed changes, warning that weakening the 2035 requirements could slow the transition to electric mobility and undermine investment certainty for manufacturers that have already committed to electrification.

German Green MEP Michael Bloss described the vote as a "bad deal" for the European car industry, saying the political back-and-forth is more harmful than the high production costs in Europe.

"While sales of electric cars are skyrocketing, the majority of the European Parliament is sending a signal of uncertainty. The fact that Social Democrats and Conservatives are helping to jeopardise investment security and industrial jobs is a contradiction that could hardly be more glaring," Bloss told Euronews.

"Europe has the factories and skilled workers to build top-of-the-line cars for the electric age, but it needs clear political support for this direction."

The deal must still secure the backing of Parliament's full plenary and survive negotiations with EU member states before becoming law.

text:
India has set ambitious clean energy and climate targets, including achieving 500 GW of non-fossil fuel-based electricity capacity by 2030 and attaining net-zero emissions by 2070. Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO) serves as one of the key policy instruments to accelerate renewable energy adoption by mandating obligated entities to procure a specified percentage of their electricity from renewable energy sources.

With the evolving regulatory landscape—including the introduction of Renewable Consumption Obligation (RCO), Energy Storage Obligation (ESO), the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), and increasing emphasis on distributed renewable energy- obligated entities are required to remain updated on changing compliance requirements, reporting mechanisms and upcoming technologies. Strengthening institutional understanding of these developments is essential to ensure effective implementation, regulatory compliance, and achievement of Uttar Pradesh’s renewable energy goals.

To support this objective, Uttar Pradesh New and Renewable Energy Development Agency (UPNEDA), in collaboration with the Centre for Science and Environment (CSE), is organizing another one day capacity building workshop in Ghaziabad, covering stakeholders in Western Uttar Pradesh. The workshop will provide participants from the region with an overview of the evolving renewable energy policy landscape, demonstrate the Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO) Portal, and explain compliance procedures. It will also showcase successful renewable energy interventions from obligated entities, facilitate peer learning from other states RPO compliance experiences, and create a platform for panel discussions among regulators, brokers, vendors, technical experts, and obligated entities to address implementation challenges and explore emerging opportunities in renewable energy procurement, storage, and carbon markets.

Join our free webinar The Post-Election Playbook: Opportunities to Advance Clean Economy Policy on Thursday, November 12 at 4PM ET. Ceres experts will deep dive into the election results and what they mean for the private sector. This webinar is free and open to the press. Register here.

BOSTON — The U.S. election results show decisive support for clean, affordable energy, as voters elected leaders nationwide committed to lowering energy costs and meeting rising demand with clean solutions.

Ceres urges the incoming Congress to refocus federal policy on reducing costs for businesses and consumers by modernizing the power grid, doubling down on clean manufacturing, and deploying affordable, homegrown wind, solar, batteries, and efficiency solutions. New state policymakers also have opportunities to strengthen successful clean energy policies to build modern, more affordable, and more reliable energy systems.

“Energy was a top issue this election season, and voters delivered a clear mandate for Congress to bring electricity prices down by deploying clean, affordable power.” said Ceres CEO and President Mindy Lubber. “They can begin this year by passing the Senate’s bipartisan permitting deal, which includes strong provisions to ease transmission development and ensure permit certainty for urgently needed clean energy projects. But lawmakers must also work together to develop the next generation of clean energy and pollution reduction policies, which will insulate American businesses and consumers from volatile prices and geopolitical conflict. The future of the American economy depends on it.”

Ceres and its Policy Network, along with other corporate and investor leaders from across the economy, will engage leaders on Capitol Hill to fine tune the next round of clean energy and grid modernization policies to bring down energy prices and to ensure they are enacted at the next available opportunity. Our federal priorities for the end of 2026 and the new Congress starting next year include:

Passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act before the end of 2026. Enacting this strong bipartisan deal this year would allow lawmakers to use 2027 and 2028 to ensure robust implementation and work on the next round of policies to bring down prices by deploying affordable, homegrown clean energy. Ceres and our Policy Network will continue to support this effort and advocate on Capitol Hill through the end of the year, and we will work with policymakers to address some of the concerns raised across the environmental community.

Restoring targeted clean energy incentives to address high prices and rising electricity demand from data centers. The new majority in Congress has an opportunity to take lessons from the past few years to shape new, long-term solutions that ensure America has durable clean energy and climate policy that reduces costs for years to come.

Expanding home efficiency programs and distributed energy resources. Lawmakers should look to data centers to pay for home energy upgrades for consumers and programs to modernize the grid and deploy smart appliances and rooftop solar.

Addressing the growing bipartisan call to protect the freedom to invest. Lawmakers should bring legislation to the floor of both chambers addressing both state laws that limit investor voices and the SEC’s continued rollback of shareholder rights. Ceres and our Freedom to Invest initiative will continue to educate state and federal lawmakers on the importance of both issues.

Building a more resilient economy. Lawmakers must use this opportunity to reduce climate pollution and secure supply chains for the future by accelerating both manufacturing and deployment of cost-saving clean solutions.

Ceres and major businesses will also encourage new governors and state legislators to continue strong efforts around the country to deploy clean energy and address rising prices.

“In the states, the work to tackle energy affordability has already begun. Now, it’s time to double down,” said Lubber. “States like Virginia, Illinois, Arizona, and California have strong proposals on the table to tackle energy affordability right now, and Ceres will be working across the country to educate a new slate of governors and state legislators on why these policies matter and how they should be implemented. The business perspective is uniquely valuable in the states at this decisive moment. This election is an opportunity to work together to build a cleaner, more resilient economy.”

In 2026, more than two dozen major companies working with Ceres called on state policymakers around the country to tackle rising energy prices by optimizing the power grid, accelerating clean power deployment, and expanding energy efficiency programs. Ceres led business advocacy efforts to educate governors and state legislators on many of these priorities. They are laid out in more detail in Powering Affordability: A Business-Backed Playbook for a Modern Clean Energy System.

Working together with businesses and investors, the election results present an opportunity to educate a new slate of state policymakers on these priorities — and on the benefits of strong state clean energy policies already in place.

description:

The 50% Drop in Democrats Who Would Consider a Tesla The sharpest single figure comes from reporting that cites Edwards.
S&P Global Mobility: Where Former Tesla Owners Went Preference surveys tell you what people say.
Competitive Comparison: How Each Camp Wins Former Tesla Buyers Each rival group offers former Tesla owners something different, and the strategies are worth comparing even without hard sales figures.

text:
Democrats turning away from Tesla is now one of the clearest brand-and-politics stories in the car market. As Mezha.net reported on November 4, 2026, some Democratic supporters have grown less favorable toward the company after Elon Musk aligned himself politically with Donald Trump. The report also asks the question buyers care about most: if not a Tesla, then what?

The answer is messy. No single model has emerged as the Democratic default, and the available data does not say every Democratic owner is leaving for political reasons. What the numbers do show is a spread of destinations, led by German luxury badges and a Japanese giant, plus a handful of American and Korean EVs and hybrids. Our earlier look at Tesla’s European rebound covered a different market, but it shows how fast brand fortunes can swing.

This analysis sticks to what named sources have confirmed. That means a Strategic Vision ranking from February 2025, S&P Global Mobility switching data from September 2025, and a short list of alternative models that reporting has tied to former Tesla shoppers. Where the evidence runs out, we say so. The goal is to separate the signal from the noise in a topic that attracts plenty of both, and to file it under hardware because a car is, in the end, the largest piece of consumer hardware most people buy.

·

Google · Preferred Sources

Don't miss new tech stories on Google

Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions.

Add Now

Democrats Turning Away From Tesla: What the Reporting Says

The core claim is narrow and well supported. Mezha.net says some Democratic supporters have become less favorable toward Tesla since Musk aligned with Trump. The word “some” matters. Nobody has shown that Democrats as a bloc have dumped the brand, and no source we reviewed confirms that claim.

Two lines of evidence carry the story. The first is preference data, meaning how Democrats rank and rate vehicles. The second is behavior data, meaning where people who already owned a Tesla went next. They come from different firms, cover different periods, and answer different questions, so treating them as one number would be a mistake.

Preference data comes from Strategic Vision, a research firm whose president, Alexander Edwards, has become the go-to voice on how politics colors car shopping. Behavior data comes from S&P Global Mobility, which tracks what owners buy when they leave a brand. Between them, they give a fair picture of attitude and action. Neither proves motive.

The Confirmed Data Points at a Glance

Before going further, it helps to lay out exactly what is on solid ground. The table below lists every specific figure and date we can attribute to a named source, and nothing beyond it.

Six rows, three distinct sources, and a clear gap: none of them states what share of Tesla’s overall customer base is Democratic or how many owners have actually left. That absence shapes everything that follows.

Strategic Vision’s MLV Index and the Mercedes-Benz EQB

The headline number in this story is 604. That is the score the Mercedes-Benz EQB earned on Strategic Vision’s Most Loved Vehicle (MLV) Index in a report released February 14, 2025, placing it first among vehicle owners who identify as Democrats. The index measures owner affection rather than sales volume, so a high score says people who already drive the car love it, not that many people bought it.

That distinction is easy to lose. A small-volume vehicle can top an affection index because its owners self-selected, paid attention to the purchase, and tend to be enthusiasts. The EQB’s win tells us Democratic owners of that SUV rate it very highly. It does not tell us Democrats are queuing at Mercedes dealers in place of Tesla stores.

Still, the ranking carries symbolic weight. For years, Tesla was the default prestige EV for progressive buyers. Seeing a Mercedes-Benz model, a conventional luxury brand with an established dealer network, land at the top of a Democratic owner index suggests the aspirational slot is no longer Tesla’s alone.

The 50% Drop in Democrats Who Would Consider a Tesla

The sharpest single figure comes from reporting that cites Edwards. According to that reporting, the proportion of Democrats who said they would “definitely consider” buying a Tesla fell by 50% after Musk publicly endorsed Trump. Half of a once-reliable consideration set vanished in one survey measure.

Consideration is the top of the sales funnel, and it is the part automakers fight hardest to protect. A buyer who never considers your car never test drives it, never configures it, never gets a financing quote. Cutting that stage in half does not halve sales, because plenty of owners keep buying for non-political reasons. It does shrink the pool of shoppers Tesla can convert.

We are deliberately not attaching a calendar date to that drop beyond “after the endorsement.” The year attached to this figure in the material we reviewed does not line up with the endorsement timeline most readers remember, and we would rather flag the ambiguity than repeat a date we cannot reconcile. What matters for analysis is the size of the swing and its direction.

Edwards described the pattern in a way that cuts against a popular assumption. Per Grist’s reporting, Republicans grew as a share of Tesla buyers not because more Republicans flocked to the brand, but because Democrats pulled away from it. In his words, the shift happened “not because more Republicans flocked to the brand, but because Democrats pulled away from it.” The Republican share rose on arithmetic, not on a conservative buying wave.

S&P Global Mobility: Where Former Tesla Owners Went

Preference surveys tell you what people say. Registration data tells you what they did. S&P Global Mobility’s September 2025 report falls in the second camp, and it names two clear winners among owners who left Tesla for another brand: Toyota and Mercedes-Benz.

Toyota and Mercedes-Benz Lead the Pack

The pairing is striking because the two brands sit at opposite ends of the market. Toyota sells on reliability, hybrids, and low drama. Mercedes-Benz sells on luxury, status, and an expanding electric lineup. Tesla owners, in other words, did not all flee in one direction. Some traded down in complexity and cost, others traded across to another premium badge.

That split is consistent with the Strategic Vision finding. Mercedes-Benz shows up at the top of the Democratic owner affection ranking and at the top of the switching chart. When two independent datasets point to the same brand, the signal deserves attention, even if neither one can say why.

BMW Among the Leaders in Shared Body Styles

S&P Global Mobility also noted that, among body styles Tesla itself offers, BMW ranked among the leading brands receiving former Tesla owners. The qualifier is important. Tesla sells a narrow range of shapes, so the comparison pool is limited to sedans and crossover-style vehicles where a like-for-like switch is possible. BMW’s strength there makes sense given its long history in compact luxury sedans and SUVs.

Readers tracking how German makers are adapting their driver-assistance and city-driving features can see one example in our piece on BMW’s city assistant rollout, which shows the brand investing in driver-assistance features, an area Tesla has long marketed hard.

The Cars Democrats and Ex-Tesla Buyers Are Choosing

Beyond the Mercedes-Benz EQB and the brand-level switching data, reporting has named four specific models that some former Tesla buyers picked instead. The list mixes pure EVs with a hybrid, which tells its own story. The table summarizes them alongside the EQB, with the type of powertrain and the source of the mention.

A word of caution on reading this table. These are examples that appeared in coverage, not a ranking by volume. No source we reviewed says any single alternative can be called “the” car Democrats are choosing overall. The Santa Fe Hybrid’s presence is a good reminder: a family that wanted a practical crossover may have decided a hybrid fit better than anything in Tesla’s lineup.

Yahoo Finance ran a piece with the headline “Musk turned Democrats off Teslas at a critical time. Here’s what they bought instead”, which frames the same question from the shopper’s side. Its framing matches what the data suggests: the answer is plural.

Leaving Tesla Does Not Mean Leaving Electric Vehicles

The most useful takeaway for the broader EV industry is that reduced Democratic interest in Tesla did not necessarily mean abandoning electric vehicles. Reported alternatives included other EVs and hybrids, which means the electrification trend survives even as one brand loses a slice of its most loyal political audience.

For automakers, that is the good news. A Democrat who walks away from Tesla but buys a Cadillac LYRIQ or a Hyundai IONIQ 6 is still an EV customer. A Democrat who picks a Santa Fe Hybrid is at least a step toward lower emissions. Only the brand, not the technology, has lost ground in those cases.

The money question sits right behind it. Buyers who stay with EVs often weigh incentives heavily, and those incentives vary by state. Our rundown of state EV rebates after the federal credits shows how much local policy can tilt a purchase, which can matter more than brand sentiment once a shopper reaches the price sheet.

Politico added to the picture on October 26, 2026, with a story headlined that Democrats face a big question on electric vehicles, as the political appeal of EV tax credits fades inside the party. Brand fatigue and policy fatigue are separate trends, but they land on the same buyers.

Historical Context: From Prius-Style Virtue to Political Badge

To understand why the reversal stings, it helps to remember how strongly Democrats once embraced the brand. Edwards told Grist that Tesla finally gave Democratic buyers a Prius-like image of being thoughtful, paired with the excitement of a real luxury sports car. That mix of virtue and fun was rare, and it made the cars an easy fit for progressive households.

Prominent Democrats said as much in public. In a 2022 Mercury News story, former Delaware Sen. Tom Carper described swapping a high-mileage Chrysler Town & Country minivan for a Tesla Model Y and saving on gasoline, and said, “It’s just so much fun to drive.” In the same piece, Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly talked about his Model S and said, “This car is a lot of fun to drive. It’s also generally good for the environment, right? Zero emissions.”

Those comments predate the political break, and they show what Tesla had going for it: performance and environmental credentials in one package. The environmental halo still exists today, but the political one has flipped for a share of the audience. The product did not change as quickly as the badge’s meaning did.

NPR covered the early stage of that turn in March 2025 under the headline “Tesla is losing liberal fans. Can Republican buyers fill the gap?” The question in that headline is still open. Edwards’s point about arithmetic suggests Republican buyers gained share mostly because Democrats subtracted themselves, not because conservatives surged in.

The leadership side of the Tesla story has kept moving too. Our report on Musk’s merger pay vote shows the CEO remains a central, polarizing figure in how investors and customers see the company.

What Is Still Unconfirmed

Good reporting on this topic means holding the line on what we do not know. Three claims remain unconfirmed, and they are exactly the ones headlines tend to assume.

The third row deserves attention. Practical issues like vehicle size, body style, service access, charging convenience, and model availability could explain many switches without any politics at all. A family that needs a bigger vehicle than a Model Y, or a driver who found service appointments slow, might leave for reasons unrelated to Musk. The available reporting presents these as possible explanations, not confirmed individual motivations, and we treat them the same way.

That leaves an honest ambiguity. Politics clearly dented consideration among Democrats, as the 50% figure shows. But the exact weight of politics versus practicality in any single sale is unknowable from these datasets.

Market Impact for Tesla and Its Rivals

The market impact reads differently depending on where you sit. For Tesla, a shrinking pool of Democratic shoppers means leaning harder on other segments, and the NPR question about Republican buyers is exactly that bet. For German luxury makers, the data is a gift: Mercedes-Benz tops both the affection ranking and the switching chart, and BMW rides along in shared body styles.

For Toyota, the S&P Global Mobility result is a quiet endorsement of its strategy. It never chased pure-EV leadership, yet it still ranks as a top landing spot for people leaving the EV pioneer. That supports the view that a meaningful group of buyers wants an electrified, low-hassle vehicle more than a technology statement.

For General Motors and Hyundai, the Cadillac LYRIQ and the IONIQ 6 appearing in the reporting is a validation of their EV bets. Edwards said, according to reporting citing him, that people can be “just as fond of their Hyundai, GM, Rivian, or BMW.” Rivian’s mention is a useful marker too, since it signals that startups beyond Tesla can earn the same kind of owner loyalty.

Used-car shoppers may feel the ripple effects as well. If more owners trade out of Teslas, the used market sees more supply, and certified programs from rivals become part of the conversation. Our coverage of Hyundai’s certified used program and its battery checks shows how a rival is already courting that crowd.

Competitive Comparison: How Each Camp Wins Former Tesla Buyers

Each rival group offers former Tesla owners something different, and the strategies are worth comparing even without hard sales figures.

German luxury (Mercedes-Benz, BMW): status and a familiar dealer network. Mercedes-Benz leads on owner affection and switching, BMW leads among shared body styles.

Toyota: reliability and hybrid options for people who want less friction. It ranked as a top beneficiary in S&P Global Mobility’s data.

Hyundai: two entries, the IONIQ 6 for pure EV shoppers and the Santa Fe Hybrid for those who want a bridge technology.

General Motors (Cadillac): the LYRIQ gives domestic-brand loyalists a premium EV.

Rivian: mentioned by Edwards as a brand whose owners can be as fond of their vehicles as any Tesla driver.

The pattern suggests that no single rival has locked in the defecting audience. That is bad news for any brand hoping for an easy conquest and good news for shoppers, who now have more credible options than they did when Tesla owned the segment.

Outside the US, the competitive picture is shifting too. Our report on China’s EV share forecast from Sinopec shows how quickly rivals elsewhere are scaling, a reminder that Tesla’s competition is global even when the political story is American.

Five Predictions for the Next 12 Months

The following are our own analytical expectations, not confirmed facts. We offer them to help readers frame what to watch, and none of them rests on a number we cannot source.

More brand-by-party surveys will appear. The Strategic Vision and S&P Global Mobility releases set a template, and other research firms tend to follow once a metric gets headlines.

Mercedes-Benz and BMW will lean into the story. Marketing that stresses EV credentials without politics is the safest play for brands that benefit from Tesla’s problem.

Hybrids will keep taking part of the defecting audience. The Santa Fe Hybrid and Toyota’s presence suggest a segment that wants electrification without charging anxiety.

Tesla will court new buyer groups. Losing Democratic consideration pushes the company toward other demographics, and pricing or features aimed at them will follow.

Political framing of EV purchases will keep getting more complex. With Democrats cooling on both a brand and, per Politico, on federal tax credits, the old rule that EVs are a progressive purchase looks shakier every quarter.

The one thing we would not predict is a quick reversal. Opinion shifts tied to a public figure’s politics tend to stick until something larger changes the picture.

What Shoppers Should Weigh Before Switching

For readers deciding what to do with this information, the data offers a few practical anchors. First, separate feelings about a company from the hardware you will live with every day. A car is a multi-year commitment, and the daily experience (range, charging access, seat comfort, service wait times) usually matters more after the first month than the badge.

Second, price in incentives and resale. State rebates, local utility programs, and used-market demand can swing total cost by thousands of dollars, and those variables change faster than brand reputation. Our guide on whether an old car or a new EV is greener is a useful companion when the decision is about environmental impact, not only status.

Third, match the body style to your life. Reporting notes that vehicle size, body style, and model availability may explain some switches. If you need cargo space or a third row, a Tesla lineup built around a few shapes may simply not fit, and no political story is needed to explain the move. You can find more consumer-hardware coverage in our hardware section.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are Democrats turning away from Tesla?

Mezha.net reports that some Democratic supporters have become less favorable toward Tesla after Elon Musk aligned politically with Donald Trump. Reporting citing Strategic Vision’s Alexander Edwards says the share of Democrats who would “definitely consider” a Tesla fell by 50% after Musk’s endorsement. Practical factors may explain individual switches, but those are not confirmed motives.

Which car do Democrats love most?

A Strategic Vision report released February 14, 2025, ranked the Mercedes-Benz EQB highest among vehicle owners who identify as Democrats, with 604 points on the Most Loved Vehicle (MLV) Index. That is an owner-affection ranking, not a sales ranking.

Which brands gained most from Tesla owners switching?

S&P Global Mobility reported in September 2025 that Toyota and Mercedes-Benz were the largest beneficiaries. Among body styles Tesla also offers, BMW ranked among the leading brands receiving former Tesla owners.

Which specific models have former Tesla buyers chosen?

Reported alternatives include the Cadillac LYRIQ, Hyundai IONIQ 6, Hyundai Santa Fe Hybrid, and Mercedes-Benz EQE SUV. These are examples from coverage, and no single model has been confirmed as the overall Democratic choice.

Are Democrats giving up on electric vehicles?

No. Reduced interest in Tesla did not necessarily mean abandoning EVs. Reported alternatives included other electric vehicles and hybrids.

Is every Democratic Tesla owner leaving over politics?

That claim is unconfirmed. The evidence points to some Democratic supporters becoming less favorable, and practical factors such as size, body style, service, charging, or availability may drive some switches. Reporting presents those as possible explanations only.

Did Republicans buy more Teslas as a result?

Alexander Edwards told Grist that Republicans grew as a share of Tesla buyers “not because more Republicans flocked to the brand, but because Democrats pulled away from it.” The shift came from Democratic subtraction, not a surge of new conservative buyers.

description:
The bill includes several key Democratic priorities for building out clean energy projects, including making it easier to construct and upgrade transmission infrastructure, forcing data center developers to pay for the energy and transmission infrastructure needed for their operations, and providing permitting certainty for all energy projects.
Peters said he believes that the legislation would improve affordability across the United States, aid the development of clean energy, and increase grid reliability.
Revisiting clean energy and electric vehicle tax credits Another top priority for Democrats in the next Congress will be reintroducing federal tax credits for clean energy resources and electric vehicles that the GOP scrapped last year.
Democrats implemented massive spending on clean energy with the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022, which was the most significant climate-related bill in U.S. history in terms of spending on clean energy.
Supporting new technologies Democratic energy policy isn’t just about propping up wind and solar projects or accelerating the phase out of fossil fuels.
text:
The No. 1 issue: permitting reform

Democrats have been broadly supportive of passing legislation to streamline the federal permitting process, making it easier to build power lines, highways, and other essential infrastructure.

Many within the party view it as essential to connecting wind and solar to the grid.

But Democrats have been hesitant to back bipartisan legislation because they worry that the Trump administration would not fairly implement changes to the permitting system and would continue to block renewable energy projects.

Two key Senate Democrats struck a deal with Republicans in late September to introduce the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA.

The bill includes several key Democratic priorities for building out clean energy projects, including making it easier to construct and upgrade transmission infrastructure, forcing data center developers to pay for the energy and transmission infrastructure needed for their operations, and providing permitting certainty for all energy projects.

“I personally hope that we pass the Senate package in the lame duck,” Rep. Scott Peters (D-CA), who sits on the Energy and Commerce Committee and acts as the Climate Task Force chair of the New Democrat Coalition, told the Washington Examiner.

Peters said he believes that the legislation would improve affordability across the United States, aid the development of clean energy, and increase grid reliability.

“I think it will resolve a lot of the issues that have been dogging us for a long time around energy,” he said.

The bill is set to be put to its first vote in the Senate Nov. 9. If it passes, the House would then consider it.

Not all House Democrats are in favor of moving on the bill immediately after the election and would like to pick up the issue in the next Congress, criticizing changes to environmental laws such as the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, and National Environmental Policy Act.

Rep. Jared Huffman (D-CA), the ranking member of the Natural Resources Committee, has repeatedly called for Democrats to wait on permitting negotiations.

“It will be a priority,” Huffman told the Washington Examiner in October. “But it will be thoughtful and responsible permitting reform that includes the grid improvements and clean energy buildout, but also protects our natural environment in appropriate ways and doesn’t throw tribes and front-line communities under the bus.”

Many policy experts have said that permitting reform is crucial to the success of other energy measures.

Xan Fishman, executive vice president for energy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, described permitting reform as the “great enabler.”

“Any other kind of good energy policy that you might want to pass — whether it’s pure energy focused or whether it’s, you know, looking at the environmental outcomes of energy — Any of those really do require … permitting to have happened first,” he said.

Revisiting clean energy and electric vehicle tax credits

Another top priority for Democrats in the next Congress will be reintroducing federal tax credits for clean energy resources and electric vehicles that the GOP scrapped last year.

Democrats implemented massive spending on clean energy with the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022, which was the most significant climate-related bill in U.S. history in terms of spending on clean energy. The IRA expanded and established a broad set of tax credits for renewable energy resources, energy efficiency technologies, and carbon capture and storage projects, as well as electric vehicles.

Republicans cut many of these subsidies just three years later through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The bill, signed into law last summer, ended incentives for wind and solar projects by the end of 2027. It also eliminated a $7,500 credit for consumers purchasing electric vehicles.

Huffman told the Washington Examiner that he’d “love to see” those subsidies revisited, particularly those for electric vehicles. But he said that passing any bill reintroducing those subsidies would be an uphill battle.

“I’m interested in doing whatever I can, but I also know who’s in the White House for the next two years. …I’m pretty clear-eyed about that,” Huffman said.

Fishman is skeptical that reinstating the credits will gain much traction, given how politicized the subsidies had become.

“Obviously a tax credit has an affordability hook,” he said. “So, I do think some will push for that, but I don’t know — I don’t know that it’ll find consensus.”

Some Democrats, however, have indicated that there is more support for clean energy tax credits across the aisle than one might expect.

Rep. Mike Levin (D-CA) pointed out that last year, nearly two dozen Republicans signed a letter supporting keeping the subsidies in place, even though they ultimately voted in favor of cutting them.

“I think there is bipartisan support for restoring the credits, particularly once Donald Trump’s power over the Republican Party diminishes,” he said, later adding that even if some Republicans in Congress won’t admit their support publicly, “they certainly talk about it privately.”

Oversight of the Trump administration

Even before the midterm elections, Republicans were bracing for Democratic-led investigations into the Trump administration if the majority flipped in either chamber.

In September, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) said the caucus was preparing a sweeping oversight agenda, focusing on possible corruption within the administration, particularly as the fossil fuel industry has benefited heavily from Trump’s second presidency.

Huffman told the Washington Examiner that an “enormous amount of oversight and investigation work” has to be done under a Democratic majority, saying “there’s no avoiding it.”

“Some of the most controversial corruption schemes have taken place within the jurisdiction of this committee,” he said, referring to the Natural Resources Committee.

Huffman, in particular, has already begun investigating, requesting records from corporate sponsors of the Freedom 250 celebrations this year regarding donations, access to federal officials, and other benefits.

Investigations led by a majority into an opposing party in power have become a norm for nearly every election cycle. In 2023, House Republicans also launched an extensive oversight campaign targeting the Biden administration after they flipped the lower chamber.

Levin warned that this pendulum of policy reversals every two to four years “creates real havoc” for project developers, regardless of the industry.

“Government policies become a wild card that impede investment and development,” Levin said.

Supporting new technologies

Democratic energy policy isn’t just about propping up wind and solar projects or accelerating the phase out of fossil fuels. For many members, it is crucial to also look toward supporting the development of advanced energy technologies that lack the capital to be commercially viable alternatives for businesses today.

This includes next-generation nuclear power, nuclear waste recycling, geothermal, fusion, and even battery storage.

Peters told the Washington Examiner that there is a “governmental responsibility” to boost these developing technologies, whether through research, federal funding, or subsidies.

“The places where innovation is just beginning, government help is appropriate,” he said. “But for a lot of these technologies that are already out there, I think in particular renewables, just making the process less cumbersome is going to have an immediate effect.”

Levin also expressed interest in pursuing policies that would boost technologies such as geothermal energy, hydropower, and nuclear power.

“Anything we can do to push the envelope, reduce emissions, and deliver better ways for people to generate electricity and move goods around, move people around, build buildings, grow food, and lead the world — I’m all for it,” he said.

Working across the aisle

While investigating and reversing actions taken by Republicans over the last two years might help Democrats achieve some of their goals, Levin said the focus should be on advancing policies that can get 60 votes in the Senate.

“Getting there is easier said than done, though,” he said.

Peters shares that same sentiment, telling the Washington Examiner that unless one party has 60 senators, everything has to be bipartisan.

“If you’re just gonna be talking to Democrats, you’re just gonna be giving speeches,” he said. “You’re not gonna be getting anything done. And so I’m very committed, you know, as part of doing my job, to find Republicans and Democrats who are willing to work on solutions.”

That doesn’t mean voters should expect Democrats to only pursue bipartisan legislation at every turn.

Policy experts still expect the party to put forward legislation meant to curb climate change.

Fishman suggested these might appear more as “messaging bills,” that Democrats would not expect Trump to sign or that wouldn’t get 60 votes in the Senate.

“My suspicion is that rather than being explicitly climate-focused bills, that they’re more likely to be in the affordability space, but not inconsistent with a desire for reduced emissions,” Fishman said.

West Virginia Starts With Polluted Water West Virginia University starts from a different feedstock.

text:
Last month, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) named the University of Kentucky and West Virginia University among 16 schools sharing $16 million in workforce prizes, a fresh bet on the two states that have spent a decade showing rare earths can be pulled from coal and polluted mine water. The research has cleared the lab, and the harder test now belongs to buyers, who need a qualified product that arrives the same way every month at a cost that holds.

Funding and a working pilot show that the chemistry can be done. Only a signed purchase agreement shows that someone will pay for the output, and most coal-based rare earth efforts in Appalachia have not reached that point.

Kentucky's Pilot Results Came Early

The University of Kentucky's work has a long record. By the end of a second project phase, its pilot plant produced mixed rare earth oxide concentrates of up to 98% purity, the National Energy Technology Laboratory (NETL) reported in February 2021. A mixed concentrate is an intermediate product, though, and a magnet maker needs individual elements separated to its own specifications, with known impurities and the same composition from one batch to the next.

The university's next step started with a $5 million federal award announced Jan. 3, 2025. The project targets rare earths and graphite from a type of coal that naturally carries high concentrations of both, naming dysprosium, neodymium and praseodymium among its elements. A pilot plant is meant to test processes that could cut the cost of producing rare earth oxides by 20%, while the step that turns purified oxides into metal is still at bench scale.

Pilot data will feed the design of a commercial plant producing 1 to 3 metric tons of purified rare earth oxides a day, the university said. Project lead Rick Honaker, a professor of mining engineering, described the separation step as "an innovative process called microbubble-assisted solvent extraction." The University of Alabama and Virginia Tech are partners.

West Virginia Starts With Polluted Water

West Virginia University starts from a different feedstock. Its A34 facility at Mount Storm, opened in 2022 with the state Department of Environmental Protection, recovers rare earths from acid mine drainage, the metal-laden water that seeps from old coal workings. The university calls it the first integrated pilot-scale facility of its kind in the country.

"For a decade, we've been proving we can extract rare earths from acid mine drainage at coal sites," Vice Provost Mark Gavin said when the university launched a Rare Earth Elements Initiative in May. Its current federal project, Rare Earth Metal Production from Acid Mine Drainage, carries $5 million in federal money and $1.3 million in cost share and runs from October 2024 through September 2027, with a goal of producing salable rare earth metals.

Commercialization sits with Mission Critical Materials, a startup formed in December 2025 to license the university's process. In January it signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding naming REalloys, a company building separation, metal and magnet operations, as its preferred downstream and offtake partner. The startup said it has produced concentrates above 95% rare earth oxide and expects to supply "several hundred tonnes" of heavy rare earths to REalloys over the coming years, and the two companies said they would negotiate a definitive multi-year offtake agreement during 2026.

Mark Jensen, chairman and chief executive of Indiana-based American Resources, said his company began pulling metals out of mine water in 2015 to offset environmental costs at its Appalachian coal operations. It concentrated them "from parts per billion to 2% to 8%, and then realized we could do nothing with it," he said. Conventional solvent extraction would have used more chemicals than the metals were then worth, which pushed the company to develop its own refining process.

The water-treatment angle can help the economics where treatment is already required. Whether mineral sales offset that cost depends on recovery expenses, product value and who carries the treatment obligation, and mine cleanup obligations can shift after approval, as Montana's Butte site has shown.

Federal Money Arrives in Stages

Washington is funding several stages at once. On July 1, the Energy Department selected five coal-based projects for about $75 million under its Mines and Metals Capacity Expansion program, including Peabody Energy, American Resources and CONSOL Innovations' Pennsylvania pilot. "American industrial facilities have the potential to produce valuable critical materials from coal and coal byproducts," said Audrey Robertson, the department's assistant secretary.

The department also stated that "selection for award negotiations is not a commitment by DOE to issue an award or provide funding." Jensen, whose company is one of the five, said in September that "the money hasn't technically been unlocked yet."

His description of the feedstock shows where the cost sits. American Resources says it holds more than 20,000 acres in the region, where rare earths sit in coal refuse piles and in the clay above and below the seams, already mined and lying at the surface. Jensen called the material "very low concentrate" and said the work now is figuring out "how do you concentrate that material economically and safely." He said coal refuse is not yet the company's primary feed but could become "a true domestic source" within a couple of years, because the material has already been mined.

Federal workforce money is moving in parallel. The PROSPECT program that funded the Kentucky and West Virginia prizes opened an implementation round on Oct. 30 that closes Nov. 25, and the department estimates the country will need about 6,000 new mining engineers over the next decade.

Cost Curves Decide Which Waste Streams Win

Some producers already plan for a market without price supports. "Price floors will go away. They will not be in existence forever," Jensen said. "You have to be able to compete globally on cost curves."

Coal is not the only waste stream courting rare earth and critical mineral buyers. Researchers are also testing ways to turn arsenic-laden mine waste into high-purity metal, and the competition for qualification slots at magnet and alloy makers will favor producers that can show sustained operating data first.

For Kentucky and West Virginia, the next proof points are concrete. A definitive offtake agreement between Mission Critical Materials and REalloys would be the first binding commercial contract tied to the West Virginia process, and Kentucky's pilot results will show whether the promised 20% cost cut survives scale. Until then, buyers can request samples for testing, but they still cannot count these sources as production volume.

text:
Key Takeaways

Stocks have historically rallied after midterm elections.

A divided Congress could create new investment opportunities.

Here are three plays to take advantage and three areas to avoid.

By Sean Brodrick

Reviewed by: Jim Nelson

2026 midterm election results continue to roll in this morning here in the U.S.

While several key local races have yet to be called, Democrats appear set to take control of both the House and the Senate.

Stock futures dipped on the news last night. But the major U.S. indices opened higher.

Wall Street’s reactions fit what history shows …

A divided government has rarely been a problem for the economy.

After all, a divided government can force negotiations over federal budgets and spending priorities. In other words, the market is betting that deficits and debt will grow more slowly.

You can see this view reflected in rising gold prices this morning. Gold is also climbing because the U.S. dollar is weaker — which is the bigger story for your savings.

Gridlock can slow the spending, but it won’t fix the debt. That’s why we’re asking you to add your name to the Declaration of Dollar Independence. Learn more here.

We could see more wild swings in the market before the election results are fully digested.

I think the smart thing to do now is to get cash together and make your shopping lists of what you want to buy before …

The Midterm Boom!

Since 1950, the S&P 500 racked up gains after the midterms from November through April. That’s 19 times in a row!

Why? Once an election is over, investors can start pricing in the political reality rather than endlessly speculating about what MIGHT happen.

And circling back to political gridlock, that isn’t necessarily bad news for stocks. It can make major policy changes more difficult.

Trump’s Veto Threat

Before you wonder or worry too much about what Democrats plan to do in office …

(Though you can see what I believe are the top 15 items here) …

Remember that — as long as President Trump is in the White House — the odds of the Dems passing any new laws are near zero.

Why? Veto power!

Under Article I, Section 7 of the U.S. Constitution, the president possesses veto power over any bill passed by Congress.

Overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds supermajority in both the House (290 votes) and the Senate (67 votes) — margins neither party has commanded in decades.

Even if the results point to a so-called “blue-nami,” Democrats likely would not come close to reaching those numbers in any standard majority scenario.

In fact, late last night, President Trump told CBS News:

“I have total veto power and I'm sure we'll be able to work things out … I think they're gonna want to work with me. Otherwise, I'd just veto everything, and they're not gonna want that."

However, America voted because it wanted to see change.

Here’s Where You Could See Changes Fairly Quickly

Four areas to watch …

Appropriations. Legally, the president cannot spend a single dollar that Congress does not appropriate. Trump might decide to spend money anyway.

The Supreme Court ruled in 2024 that President Trump has absolute immunity for “core” Constitutional powers, and presumptive immunity for other acts. So, if that happens, expect fireworks.

Tariffs. A Democratic Congress may try to seize back control over tariffs from Trump.

A study from the Tax Foundation shows Trump’s tariffs cost consumers roughly $820–$1,000 on average per household.

Getting rid of Trump’s tariffs would help consumers and be a win for Democrats.

President Trump would likely veto any bill to eliminate his tariffs. But there might be enough Republicans with an eye on 2028 to override his veto.

Investigations. Democrats can hold hearings with sworn witnesses and organize all sorts of investigations into corruption, including corporate corruption. They’ll be able to stage impeachment hearings again, and those could extend beyond the president.

Judges & Appointees. Dems could also refuse to seat any new Trump judges or appointed officials. This won’t affect America’s finances, so I’ll leave that battle to others.

So, that’s the big picture. As an investor, you should be thinking about “What should I be buying … and what should I be selling?”

I have three ideas for you to buy, and three to sell.

Three Groups to Buy

#1. Healthcare Providers & Medicaid/ACA Beneficiaries. Democrats hold a firm block against more Medicaid funding cuts and can protect hospital reimbursement rates.

Companies including HCA Healthcare (HCA) and Tenet Healthcare (THC) benefit directly from insured patient volume and government reimbursement.

You can also play this through the Healthcare SPDR (XLV).

#2. Green(er) Energy. Republicans slashed green energy tax credits that were in Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act.

Since more than 70% of utility-scale clean energy, battery gigafactories and solar component plants are located in Republican-held congressional districts, Dems might find enough support to override a presidential veto if they move to reinstate those subsidies.

The iShares Global Clean Energy ETF (ICLN) and the Invesco Solar ETF (TAN) could get a boost if reinstating that funding becomes a Democratic priority.

#3. Consumer Staples. Democrats will try to do something to help low-income families.

In previous budget standoffs, Democrats routinely asked for protections for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), expansions to the Child Tax Credit and support for working-class purchasing power.

Walmart (WMT) and Target (TGT) stand to benefit. You can also play this using the Consumer Staples SPDR (XLP).

3 Groups That Are at Risk

Nothing is certain, but it’s likely that those companies that benefited handsomely from President Trump will also face scrutiny and funding cuts.

We have some time — the new Congress won’t be seated until next year, and it will take months for any investigations to get going.

Still, there are areas of concern …

#1. Private Prisons. Private prison operators, including CoreCivic (CXW) and The GEO Group (GEO),may face serious funding restrictions. They could also face probes into their cost-per-bed profits and lobbying relationships.

Keep in mind that private prisons function under longer-term contracts, and long-term contracts won’t go away.

But a Democratic Congress could slash or stop funding for detention facilities and beds used by Homeland Security.

#2. Companies Connected to the Trump Sons. Don Jr. and Eric are on the boards of — or advisers to — at least five public companies and uncounted private firms.

Several landed big, fat government contracts once the Trump boys got on board. It’s likely there will be investigations into those contract awards.

If you own a company with a Trump on the board, you might have even bought it for that reason. I’m not saying you should rush to sell; I’m saying that you should be aware of what might be coming.

#3. Meta Platforms & SpaceX. Meta (META) is fundamentally a sound and growing company. But the headlines don’t always focus on the financials.

The company faces allegations of child safety and exploitation; illicit drug sales on Facebook and Instagram; algorithms designed to be addictive; deceptive privacy practices; antitrust activities and more.

Don’t be surprised if Metaends up in Congress’ sights when Dems get the power to hold hearings.

Meanwhile, there are allegations that Elon Musk throttled Starlink’s satellite internet service to limit Ukrainian military operations. That might weigh on Musk’s SpaceX (SPCX).

Ready, Aim, Firearms

When President Obama was elected, gun sales surged.

President Biden — same thing.

Even though the presidential election is two years away, don’t be surprised if guns and ammo sales enjoy an immediate uptick.

That’s good news for companies like Smith & Wesson Brands (SWBI). It’s one of America's oldest and best-known firearms manufacturers, producing pistols, revolvers and rifles.

It sports a dividend yield near 4%, too! Shares gained some 2.5% in today’s pre-market trading. And at just around $13 a share, it’s an inexpensive way to protect yourself during the next few months.

Bottom line: Now that we know what to expect, the real work begins. Not just in Congress, but right here in our own portfolios.

The best news to come out of the 2026 midterms is this:

Investors can be the real winners of this election — history is on our side. And this shopping list is designed to help continue that tradition.

All the best,

Sean

title: US midterms and climate: Could Trump loss be a win for energy bills, renewables and emissions?
description:
The sweeping win will curb President Trump’s power and male it less likely he will be re-elected at the next elections.
What about the impact on energy bills in Europe?
Will energy bills in Europe get cheaper?
So while a drop in energy bills is unlikely in the short-term, the outlook is certainly brighter than it was yesterday.
The Trump administration has weakened and dismantled many important climate measures, from the landmark 2009 climate ‘endangerment finding’ underpinning federal emissions rules to tax incentives for clean energy.
text:
The Democrats have won a historic victory in the US midterm elections, taking control of both the House and the Senate. The sweeping win will curb President Trump’s power and male it less likely he will be re-elected at the next elections.

Democrats won in states that have voted Republican for decades – and where Trump won by double digits just two years ago. The results lay bare Americans voters' deep frustrations over high prices, the Iran war and climate policy.

“While climate was rarely on the ballot by name, Trump’s anti-climate policies shaped the outcome. Energy security, affordability, quality jobs and resilient communities now form a single, coherent agenda, and yesterday’s vote rejected the policies that have made each of them worse,” says Lisa Sachs, Associate Professor at Columbia Climate School.

Trump has been terrible news for climate action in the US, kneecapping previous administrations' progress in cutting the carbon emissions of the world’s second biggest polluter, behind China.

Under Trump’s command, the US government is “actively obstructing the clean energy transition while simultaneously incentivising the production and consumption of fossil fuels,” according to Climate Action Tracker.

Can a Democrat-controlled Congress rollback Trump’s anti-climate policies? Could they end the energy crisis precipitated by the Iran war? What about the impact on energy bills in Europe? Euronews Earth spoke to climate experts to get their analysis.

Will energy bills in Europe get cheaper?

Energy bills across Europe have risen steeply since Trump attacked Iran, leading to unrest and deaths across the Middle East and a huge bill for US taxpayers. In terms of energy, damaged oil and gas infrastructure and the closure of the Hormuz Strait have limited oil and gas supplies, leading to price hikes worldwide.

Trump has already acknowledged that the Iran war played a role in his party’s defeat, telling Fox News, “I think a part of it was Iran, but at the same time, people understood the importance of what I’ve done with Iran.”

To end the Iran war, the newly elected Democrat senators would need to get two-thirds of both chambers of Congress to support a withdrawal. This would mean some Republicans also needing to be onboard. But even without this, starting today, they can curb a lot of action through tighter restrictions on the military budget, as well as demanding investigations into the war.

So while a drop in energy bills is unlikely in the short-term, the outlook is certainly brighter than it was yesterday.

Could US emissions drop under the Democrats?

As the world’s second biggest emitter of greenhouse gases, the US is one of the countries most responsible for global warming. Since we all share the same climate, we need every country to be moving fast to replace fossil fuels with clean energy sources like wind and solar.

Trump’s “drill, baby, drill” policies have seen the US double down on emissions-heavy fossil fuels while moving away from cleaner energy sources like wind and solar.

Democrats could provide more support for renewables and electrification, while at the same time scrutinising new oil and gas drilling projects, methane emissions and fossil-fuel subsidies. They could also push for stronger environmental standards and enforcement.

Can the Democrats reverse Trump’s anti-climate policies?

The Trump administration has weakened and dismantled many important climate measures, from the landmark 2009 climate ‘endangerment finding’ underpinning federal emissions rules to tax incentives for clean energy.

While the Democrats won’t necessarily be able to overturn past rulings, they have gained important new powers to curb the damage.

They can launch investigations into potential corruption and conflicts of interest, examine cuts to environmental agency staff and funding, and scrutinise plans for oil and gas expansion.

They will also have more power to oppose future attacks on climate policy. Having greater influence over future budgets and spending legislation could allow them to add environmental provisions to major bills.

The Senate’s ability to confirm future cabinet and federal judge appointments could have a big impact too, since the latter sit for a lifetime, meaning they retain power far beyond the presidential term.

President Trump still has the power to veto any legislation passed by Congress, however, which can only be overridden with the support of two-thirds of both chambers.

States that have turned from red to blue could see renewed political momentum behind climate and environment policies, for example support for clean energy projects.

Could the Democrats prioritise clean energy over data centres?

Data centres are increasingly drawing opposition across the US by “increasing emissions, driving up household power bills and competing with communities for water, often where it is already scarce,” says Sachs of Columbia Climate School.

Big tech-owned centres often get to skip the queue and get connected to the grid quicker than renewable energy sources, like wind and solar farms, raising concerns about how limited electricity infrastructure is being allocated.

Growing frustration over the cost of electricity, the influence of tech billionaires like Elon Musk, and the environmental footprint of data centres may have angered voters enough into voting against the Republican party.

While Trump has cancelled many clean energy projects and funding, there is hope that newly elected Democrats could start to turn the tide and lead their states back toward renewables.
