title: Google Announces Digital Infrastructure Expansion, Local Jobs, Water Replenishment, and ...
description:
The latest investment builds on Google’s more than 15-year presence in Malaysia and expands on the company's digital infrastructure investment announced in 2024.
In addition, Google’s computing capacity in Selangor will support its upcoming Google Cloud region in Malaysia for enterprise customers.
Ruth Porat, President and Chief Investment Officer, Alphabet and Google, said: “Google is committed to growing our presence responsibly, delivering lasting value for Malaysia’s economy and people.
Guided by the Malaysia MADANI framework and the Malaysia Digital 2030 Action Plan, our goal is to cultivate an ecosystem that strengthens Malaysia's technological capabilities, protects public resources, and empowers our people.
About Google Google’s mission is to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible and useful.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia, Nov. 4, 2026 — Google today unveiled its plan for responsible digital infrastructure development in Malaysia, including an investment of US$15 billion over the next two years (2027 to 2028). Announced in the presence of YAB Dato' Seri Anwar bin Ibrahim, Prime Minister of Malaysia, Google’s integrated plan delivers energy-efficient data center campuses in industrial zones and new collaborations to upskill approximately 800,000 Malaysians by 2031, bolster local water security, and add more than 1 gigawatt (GW) of clean energy capacity to Malaysia’s National Grid.

The latest investment builds on Google’s more than 15-year presence in Malaysia and expands on the company's digital infrastructure investment announced in 2024. Since opening its first local office in 2011, Google has helped shape and grow the nation’s digital ecosystem through successive skilling initiatives1 and products2 tailored to local needs. Today, Malaysia is one of Southeast Asia’s most dynamic digital economies, driven by 99% internet penetration and rapid AI adoption across government agencies, businesses, and consumers.

To support Malaysia’s next phase of growth and meet rising local demand, Google’s in-country infrastructure will provide the world-class computing capacity needed to run homegrown, next-generation digital and AI applications. It will also power Google services—such as Search, Maps, and Chrome—used daily by millions of people and organizations across Malaysia and the Asia-Pacific region. This footprint includes Google’s first data center campus in Elmina Business Park, Selangor—which is now operational—and new, planned campuses in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan.

In addition, Google’s computing capacity in Selangor will support its upcoming Google Cloud region in Malaysia for enterprise customers. Google Cloud’s full-stack capabilities enable organizations like AEON360, AirAsia, Bank Muamalat Malaysia Berhad, Gamuda, Hong Leong Bank, Maxis, the Selangor Technical Skills Development Centre, the Ministry of Digital, and the Ministry of Higher Education to accelerate their delivery of secure, high-performance, low-latency services and to develop and scale advanced, custom AI solutions.

Ruth Porat, President and Chief Investment Officer, Alphabet and Google, said: “Google is committed to growing our presence responsibly, delivering lasting value for Malaysia’s economy and people. This investment aligns with Malaysia’s development priorities—providing the foundational computing capacity to deliver the upside of innovation across the country while adding local power and water resources as our operations scale. At the community level, Google is proud to partner with local suppliers to expand their expertise and to equip workers, students, and entrepreneurs with in-demand skills, enabling Malaysians to capture the new opportunities unlocked by this computing capacity.”

YB Gobind Singh Deo, Minister of Digital, said: “Google’s comprehensive blueprint sets a high standard for sustainable, high-impact digital infrastructure development in Malaysia. Guided by the Malaysia MADANI framework and the Malaysia Digital 2030 Action Plan, our goal is to cultivate an ecosystem that strengthens Malaysia's technological capabilities, protects public resources, and empowers our people. Through its commitment to clean energy and water resilience, alongside deep partnerships with Malaysian institutions and enterprises, Google is helping to anchor a high-value digital economy where local businesses, workers, and communities directly benefit from the transformative potential of AI and digital innovation.”

Fueling economic growth and long-term job creation

Google is working with a domestic supply chain of more than 80 Malaysian entities to develop and operate its infrastructure in the country, spanning construction and civil engineering; network infrastructure; power and cooling system components; and services like logistics, legal, catering, and waste management. This collaboration will continue over the data centers’ multi-decade operational lifecycle, enabling these suppliers to build on their proven strengths and move up the value chain—both locally and globally—creating skilled jobs and driving sustained growth in their respective sectors.

The construction phase of Google’s new campuses (2027 to 2028) is expected to contribute an annual average of US$1.1 billion to Malaysia’s GDP and support more than 37,000 local jobs per year, generating US$378 million in average annual labor income. Approximately 6,000 of these jobs are estimated to be in construction.

Once operational, the facilities are projected to sustain more than 9,000 local jobs per year, with wages averaging 45% above the national median. This includes long-term, on-site specialist roles—such as data center technicians, mechanical engineers, electrical engineers, logistics operations managers, and physical security managers—as well as contractor roles with local suppliers and workers at the shops, restaurants, and amenities patronized by these employees and their families.

Google has already established a full local on-site team for its operations at Elmina Business Park and is actively recruiting local technical and facilities management talent for its other planned campuses.

Workforce development to help Malaysians capture new opportunities

Beyond direct hiring, Google is expanding Malaysia’s broader talent pipeline so local communities can benefit from the growth driven by its infrastructure. Today, the company announced four new programs aimed at upskilling 800,000 Malaysians over the next five years (2027 to 2031), focusing on educators and youth, microentrepreneurs, civil servants, and vocational jobseekers, starting with communities in the states that host its campuses:

Experience AI Malaysia: A collaboration with the Ministry of Education, Penang Science Cluster, and the Raspberry Pi Foundation to help advance AI literacy in classrooms nationwide by certifying educators to teach students aged 11 to 14 each year. With a curriculum focused on hands-on learning, the program will equip students with critical thinking skills to direct AI in active problem-solving and evaluate its outputs.

Jelajah AI MSME: A collaboration with Pepper Labs to help grassroots businesses develop practical digital assets, such as searchable online business profiles and digital storefronts, to reach customers beyond their neighborhoods. Backed by Pepper Labs’ experience delivering digital and AI skills training at Pusat Sebaran Maklumat Nasional (NADI) centers, the program will run hands-on clinics for a pilot cohort of microentrepreneurs across Selangor and Negeri Sembilan, before scaling to serve participants annually nationwide.

Anjakan Kemahiran AI Demi Rakyat (AKAD Rakyat): A collaboration with Arus Academy to equip council officers and constituency members with AI literacy skills and productivity tools annually, targeting 19 local government councils (Pihak Berkuasa Tempatan) in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan. The program will also appoint dedicated AI champions within these councils to modernize workflows, helping frontline staff automate routine paperwork and deliver more responsive public services.

Data Center Institutes (DCIs): Google plans to establish DCIs in selected polytechnics in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan. Starting in 2027, this initiative aims to train and place local Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) jobseekers for data center deployment and operations roles. It will deliver a 10-week curriculum led by industry experts—featuring practical training with a physical data center simulator provided by Google—to prepare candidates for on-site roles at hyperscale facilities.

The new programs complement Google’s existing efforts to invest directly in communities in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan. These include Future Skills 4 All with UNICEF Malaysia, CelcomDigi, the Malaysia Digital Economy Corporation, and Arus Academy, which offers coding lessons to students, paving the way for higher education in technology disciplines, and Pathway to Prosperity with the United Nations Institute for Training and Research and the Selangor Human Resource Development Centre to equip early- and mid-career professionals in Selangor with skills in data center operations.

Earlier this week, Google also announced new education and training initiatives with SOLS Foundation to establish Solar and Energy Labs in local public schools and equip youth from lower-income backgrounds and Indigenous communities to enter skilled trades in clean energy.

Google’s approach to responsible water stewardship

At each data center location, Google uses a data-driven water risk framework to assess watershed health and only considers water cooling if local resources are healthy and resilient. In Selangor and Negeri Sembilan, Google’s water risk assessments, conducted with industry-leading environmental scientists, hydrologists, and water sustainability experts, concluded that local watershed supplies were not at high risk of scarcity or depletion, informing its decision to use water cooling at its campuses.

To help sustain long-term water resilience, Google has been working with the Global Environment Centre (GEC) and the Petaling Jaya City Council to deploy nature-based solutions for Taman Aman Lake—such as floating constructed wetland cells that help with algae bloom reduction—to improve its water quality to intended targets while enhancing biodiversity and delivering community benefits.

In addition to this initial project and its development of an off-river storage reservoir and water treatment plant in Negeri Sembilan, Google today announced two new water replenishment projects:

Sungai Buloh and Sungai Selangor river basin stewardship: Google and GEC are expanding their collaboration to deploy nature-based solutions and community-led initiatives, including constructed wetlands, riverbank bioengineering, and pollution monitoring in these two watersheds, which support domestic and economic needs for millions of residents in Kuala Lumpur and Selangor. Since the rivers face sediment runoff and pollution from urban activities, the proposed upstream interventions will help improve raw water quality, enhance riverine ecosystems, and reduce filtration and treatment burdens on downstream treatment plants to bolster water security.

School-based water resilience centers: Google is collaborating with CLEAN International, Water Watch Penang, and Gravity Water to install 20,000-liter storage tanks, rainwater harvesting systems, and self-closing faucets at four schools in Selangor. This lowers the schools’ operating costs by replacing municipal water with harvested rainwater for non-potable needs and curbing unintended water loss. During unscheduled municipal supply disruptions, each school can provide at least two weeks of emergency water capacity for up to 2,000 community members.

The water replenished through these projects is quantified using the Volumetric Water Benefit Accounting methodology and audited by independent third-party hydrologists. To help communities understand how Google uses and manages water responsibly, the company discloses its operational data centers’ annual water consumption by location in its Environmental Report.

Water is a key component of data center operations. Because the servers and chips that power the digital world generate heat, facilities often use water cooling to lower their energy demand. Water cooling can reduce a data center’s energy use by approximately 10% compared to air cooling.

Adding clean energy capacity and safeguarding electricity affordability

Google today announced plans to bring more than 1 GW of new clean energy capacity to Malaysia’s National Grid. This aims to increase the country’s power supply and accelerate its clean energy transition alongside the growth of the digital economy, on top of Google’s ongoing partnerships with consortiums led by Shizen Energy-Solarvest and TotalEnergies to support grid resilience and decarbonization.

Anchored by its collaboration with Tenaga Nasional Berhad, Google plans to enable the development of new clean energy generation facilities under Malaysia’s Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme. To account for the intermittency of energy sources like solar, the collaboration will also explore pioneering round-the-clock clean energy projects in Malaysia.

Google will also pay for 100% of the power its data center campuses use and the direct infrastructure costs required to connect them to the grid, while complying with all applicable local regulations.

In 2027, Google plans to invest in new community-based initiatives in Malaysia that further strengthen grid resilience and safeguard energy affordability, including programs that bring down electricity bills for households in the states hosting its infrastructure. This builds on Google’s household electrification work with SOLS Foundation, which has installed solar systems for off-grid Orang Asli homes in Kampung Sungai Relang and Kampung Air Kuning, and will expand to Kampung Sejantung next year.

On top of adding clean energy capacity and protecting affordability, Google designs its facilities to minimize the electricity they require in the first place. The company outfits all its data centers with custom-designed networking equipment, coolant distribution units, power distribution systems, and chips for both general-purpose computing and AI workloads. This enables Google to operate its campuses at a highly efficient Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) of 1.12 to 1.14 in warmer tropical climates like Malaysia’s—performing significantly better than the industry average of 1.54—with quarterly PUE figures disclosed for each site once it is fully operational.

About Google

Google’s mission is to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible and useful. Through products and platforms like Search, Maps, Gmail, Android, Google Play, Google Cloud, Chrome, and YouTube, Google plays a meaningful role in the daily lives of billions of people and has become one of the most widely known companies in the world. Google is a subsidiary of Alphabet Inc.

title: Here's What the Historic Blue Wave Means for Trump's Climate Rollbacks - Gizmodo
authors: Grist staff, Grist, George Dvorsky, Matthew Phelan, Ellyn Lapointe, Grist staff
description:
Flipping control of Congress will allow the Democrats to hinder Trump’s numerous attempts to roll back federal climate policy.
Democrats could gain control of the state government in purple states, ending in some cases decades of Republican or divided government.
In places like Texas and Ohio, skepticism over the AI boom may also have driven voters to oust incumbents who supported data centers.
— Jake Bittle Democrats win after attacking Republicans on data centers At least three legislative seats flipped blue after Democrats aggressively criticized Republican incumbents for being too friendly to data centers.
Supporters of Proposal 2 leveraged ratepayers’ growing dissatisfaction with utilities around power bills, unreliable service, and data centers.
text:
The Democratic Party has gained control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, as well as several state governments. The party’s strong performance, driven in part by voters’ anger over inflation and the war in Iran, reached into traditional Republican strongholds like Ohio and South Carolina. The sweep will have profound consequences for climate action in the United States, even with President Donald Trump still in the White House.

Flipping control of Congress will allow the Democrats to hinder Trump’s numerous attempts to roll back federal climate policy. In the first two years of Trump’s term, party leaders could do little more than write strongly worded statements to administration officials. They were powerless to stop the suspension of clean energy funding, the elimination of climate rules for power plants and motor vehicles, and the hollowing-out of agencies like the U.S. Forest Service and the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

The party now has a lot more leverage. Democratic senators and members of Congress can issue subpoenas to force administration officials to testify before Congress and could impeach Trump administration figures over funding clawbacks and staff reductions that Democrats have called unlawful. Democrats will also have control over must-pass funding bills, and Trump would have to negotiate with them in order to avoid a government shutdown. This could even lead to the restoration of some funding for energy and climate resilience programs that Republicans have been trying to whittle down.

Turnover at the state level, where officials are still counting votes, may be even more significant. Democrats could gain control of the state government in purple states, ending in some cases decades of Republican or divided government. This could allow them to pass meaningful climate policy for the first time—in Pennsylvania, for instance, state house Democrats have said they intend to pass bills making it easier to build community solar, warehouse solar, and battery energy storage, as well as preventing local governments from banning renewables. In Georgia, Democrats flipped both the governor’s mansion and control of the public service commission, which regulates electric utilities.

While Trump’s approval ratings are underwater on almost every major issue, energy prices were among the most salient issues in many races. The gasoline price hike caused by Trump’s invasion of Iran was perhaps the most consequential, but voters in many places were also concerned about their heating bills (Maine) and homeowner’s insurance premiums (Florida). In places like Texas and Ohio, skepticism over the AI boom may also have driven voters to oust incumbents who supported data centers.

Here are some of the most consequential outcomes for climate change and the environment. We’ll continue to update this post as more results and analysis come in.

Texas elects Democratic senator for the first time in nearly 40 years

Texas joined other Southern states in flipping blue for the first time in decades. Senator-elect James Talarico, a Democrat, supports an all-of-the-above energy strategy, which includes protecting oil and gas jobs while also growing renewable energy. This moderate approach proved important in a state that provides over 40 percent of the nation’s oil and gas.

As a state representative, Talarico authored and introduced the Texas Climate Action Act in 2021. While the bill did not advance, it aimed to establish targets for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and set energy efficiency standards, with an emphasis on local resiliency.

Talarico beat out Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general, who is widely considered friendly to the oil and gas industry. He’s been embroiled in scandal for years and was impeached in 2023 by the Texas House. Paxton’s track record likely helped Democrats obtain this victory.

— Celeste Guajardo

A climate hawk survives Republican redlining

Her district was redrawn to eliminate her, but voters in Florida’s 14th congressional district reelected Democratic Representative Kathy Castor anyway.

Castor — referred to as a “climate hawk” by E&E News — has spent much of her long career in Congress raising the alarm about climate change. Between 2019 and 2022 she chaired the House Select Committee on the Climate Crisis and has otherwise made reducing carbon pollution and preparing communities for climate impacts central to her legislative agenda. In March, she backed the Energy Bills Relief Act, which proposed restoring energy upgrade tax credits and connecting more clean energy to the grid. She has also strongly opposed data centers in the Tampa area that she serves, warning that the facilities could drive up her constituents’ utility costs while straining local water supplies.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

Democrats flip control of Georgia utility commission for first time in decades

Democrats secured both Public Service Commission seats on the Georgia ballot, giving the party majority control of the powerful utility regulation board for the first time in 30 years.

Democrat Peter Hubbard successfully defended his District 3 seat against a challenge from former commissioner Fitz Johnson, while Democrat Shelia Edwards defeated Republican Josh Tolbert to take the District 5 seat.

The commission regulates utilities, including the behemoth Georgia Power, meaning commissioners have final say over how the state’s largest utility makes energy and how much customers pay for it. The board has drawn increased scrutiny in recent years because of a series of rate hikes and the scramble to produce enough energy for the massive spike in demand that Georgia Power predicts will result from the data center boom. The utility’s plans to meet that demand rely heavily on fossil fuels.

Georgia is one of 10 states where utility regulators are elected rather than appointed.

— Emily Jones

A flip in an area devastated by Helene

In western North Carolina, where Hurricane Helene caused billions of dollars of damage two years ago, Democrat Jamie Ager defeated Republican Jennifer Balkcom for an open seat in the House of Representatives. Ager, a longtime farmer, made the area’s slow hurricane recovery a centerpiece of his campaign. He criticized Representative Chuck Edwards, who dropped out of the race after a sexual harassment scandal, for doing too little to deliver aid for Asheville and its surrounding counties. Grist reported last month that at least some voters blamed Republicans for the slow recovery. In a rally held on the eve of the election, President Trump promised to deliver more hurricane aid money, but only if North Carolina elected Republicans. The district around Asheville did not take the bait—not only did Ager win the state’s 11th House district, but Democrat Roy Cooper, the state’s former governor, easily won a Senate race, flipping a seat that had been held by Republicans.

— Jake Bittle

Democrats win after attacking Republicans on data centers

At least three legislative seats flipped blue after Democrats aggressively criticized Republican incumbents for being too friendly to data centers. Democrat Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Senator Jon Husted in Ohio’s special Senate election after state Democrats put up billboards stating: “See that data center? Jon Husted did that.” Likewise, Democrat Paige Cognetti beat Republican Representative Rob Bresnahan in Pennsylvania’s 8th congressional district after she ran television ads associating Bresnahan with data centers and comparing tech companies to polluting mining corporations. Bresnahan has been revealed to have owned stock in data center companies. And in South Carolina’s Senate race, voters pushed Annie Andrews to a surprise win over Senator Darline Graham after she highlighted that a new pro-data center super PAC spent $1.5 million on ads for her opponent, whom she nicknamed “Data Center Darline.”

Both Husted and Bresnahan had previously welcomed data centers to their regions but later attempted unsuccessfully to pass regulations constraining them once the facilities became a hot-button issue. Data centers are massively unpopular with voters across the political spectrum, polls have shown. The facilities have become a growing source of demand for electricity from fossil fuels.

— Austin Corona and Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

A FEMA defender sails to victory in Florida

Representative Jared Moskowitz, a Democrat, easily hung onto his seat in Congress, surviving a challenge from Scott Singer, a Trump-backed Republican, in Florida’s redrawn 25th congressional district. His third-term victory defies the right-wing effort to make his district significantly redder with new boundaries and keeps one of America’s most vocal FEMA reformers in Congress.

Moskowitz, once appointed Florida’s emergency management director by Governor Ron DeSantis, championed bipartisan legislation to pull FEMA out of the Department of Homeland Security and make it an independent, cabinet-level agency—just as the Trump administration seeks to cut its funding and shift more responsibility onto states. He has also introduced bills that would let states voluntarily administer federal disaster housing and public assistance and proposed a reinsurance backstop that would help cover catastrophic losses after disasters like hurricanes.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

Michigan gets utility money out of politics

Voters in Michigan passed a measure to limit corporate spending in elections, and in a nationwide first, successfully went after the state’s electric and gas utilities. Supporters of Proposal 2 leveraged ratepayers’ growing dissatisfaction with utilities around power bills, unreliable service, and data centers. The measure is one of the most ambitious attempts in the country to limit corporate influence in politics, which it will do by preventing utility-funded political action groups and utility executives from contributing to state political campaigns. Groups that oppose the measure have contended that Prop 2 will stifle corporations’ speech protections under the 2010 Citizens United case. And while experts are fairly confident the measure will face legal challenges and won’t get all utility money out of politics, Prop 2 advocates maintain it’s a step toward accountability.

— Vivian La

A governor who at least acknowledges climate change in Florida

Republican Byron Donalds has defeated Democrat David Jolly for occupancy of Florida’s governor’s mansion. Donalds, who currently represents Florida’s 19th congressional district, will be the state’s first Black governor. He doesn’t believe humans play any role in global warming, but he’s more willing to discuss the issue than the current governor, Ron DeSantis, who signed the state’s infamous “don’t say climate change” law.

That matters in a state especially battered by sea level rise, coastal erosion, and storms. The skyrocketing costs of home insurance were a central issue in this race, and Donalds promised to bring them down by increasing competition in the state’s private market. In 2025, Donalds notably co-introduced bipartisan legislation with Democrat Jared Moskowitz to reform federal disaster aid by making FEMA an independent cabinet-level agency. In the weeks before voters went to the polls, he also pledged investment in restoring coastal habitats. Donalds seems likely to carry on DeSantis’ other environmental policies, such as supporting data center development and attacking wind and solar projects.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

A MAGA loyalist who says no to drilling in Florida

Republican Senator Ashley Moody defeated the progressive Democrat Angie Nixon to retain her seat, which Governor DeSantis appointed her to last year. Moody’s brief stint in Washington hints at what’s to come: She introduced a resolution to overturn Biden-era efficiency standards and supported the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which ended federal tax credits for clean energy installations, like rooftop solar and batteries. Previously, as Florida’s attorney general, she joined a lawsuit challenging emissions reduction targets on highways.

But in Florida, a state grappling with coastal erosion and rising sea levels, some environmental protections are popular across party lines: Last year, even as Trump pushed to open offshore drilling in other states, Moody introduced the American Shores Protection Act to ban the practice off Florida’s coast through 2032.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

title: Stellantis to switch 'many' European nameplates to LFP batteries - Automotive Logistics
description:

Stellantis' existing LFP investment Read more: Stellantis and CATL break ground on LFP gigafactory in Spain Stellantis’ 50:50 joint venture with battery maker CATL – Contemporary Star Energy – has broken ground on a 50 GWh lithium phosphate battery (LFP) gigafactory in Zaragoza, Spain, next to Stellantis’ assembly plant there.

Stellantis' LFP battery plant in Zaragoza could play a significant role in supporting this scale-up when it begins production.
text:
Speaking during the company's Q3 2026 results call, Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa revealed that from 2027, the battery chemistry in "many" of Stellantis' European nameplates will be switched from nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) cells to lithium iron phosphate (LFP) ones.

Filosa did not specify which nameplates would be affected by the switch, nor did he quantify the expected savings. He described the change as one of two "very important competitive moves" planned for 2027 and said it would deliver "substantial" savings in battery costs.

Competition, demand and cost pressures

Stellantis' announcement cannot be separated from the context in which it was made. The decision comes as the company faces pressure from Chinese competition, a challenging pricing environment, growing battery electric vehicle (BEV) demand and continued profitability concerns in Europe.

Read more: UK and EU automotive leaders urge policymakers to "level the playing field" with Chinese OEMs

Chinese OEMs' market share of new vehicle sales in Europe has grown rapidly in recent years, prompting UK and EU policy debates to ensure fair competition.

Speaking during the Q3 results call, Filosa described the European market as "challenging", citing ongoing competition from Chinese automakers and difficult pricing conditions. Despite this, he said Stellantis continued to grow in the region, supported by strong demand for models based on its Smart Car platform and surging demand for BEVs, particularly in France, Germany and the UK.

In Q3 this year, Stellantis' EU30 passenger BEV sales increased 65% year-on-year, or 93% when including Leapmotor, while BEV light commercial BEV sales rose 46%.

However, higher BEV sales have also presented a profitability challenge for Stellantis. The company's adjusted operating loss in the Enlarged Europe region reached €311 million ($348m) in Q3 2026, a deterioration of €468m ($524m) compared with the same period last year.

Joao Laranjo, Stellantis' chief financial officer, said that despite higher volumes and continued industrial cost savings, regional profitability had been affected by an unfavourable sales mix, reflecting higher BEV sales alongside persistent pricing pressure.

Filosa also pointed to the pace of electrification in Europe, which he said was accelerating in response to higher oil prices and regulation. He argued that further regulatory changes were needed to create a level playing field for automakers, specifically calling for greater flexibility around CO₂ emissions requirements for passenger cars and light commercial vehicles, alongside the proposed 'Made in Europe' framework. He also identified the rise in raw material and memory chip costs as industry-wide pressures, saying manufacturers would need to address these through pricing and cost containment measures.

Against this backdrop, the planned switch from NMC to LFP cells in several Stellantis nameplates forms part of the company's wider effort to improve the cost competitiveness of its European line-up as BEV demand grows.

Stellantis' existing LFP investment

Read more: Stellantis and CATL break ground on LFP gigafactory in Spain

Stellantis’ 50:50 joint venture with battery maker CATL – Contemporary Star Energy – has broken ground on a 50 GWh lithium phosphate battery (LFP) gigafactory in Zaragoza, Spain, next to Stellantis’ assembly plant there.

In December 2024, Stellantis entered into a joint venture with Chinese battery manufacturer CATL to construct and operate a €4.1 billion ($4.3bn) large-scale LFP battery plant at Stellantis' existing site in Zaragoza, Spain.

The two partners broke ground at the site in November 2025. The plant was initially expected to be operational by the end of 2026, although Spanish news agency EFE reported earlier this year that the site is likely to begin production in 2027.

As well as localising its battery supply chain, the investment in the plant and in the diversification of its BEV battery chemistry was designed to enable Stellantis to bring more competitive, affordable BEVs to the European market.

The decision is in line with the company's 'Dare Forward 2030' strategy, which aims to make electric mobility more accessible and affordable while accelerating its transition towards an all-electric vehicle portfolio.

“Stellantis is committed to a decarbonised future, embracing all available advanced battery technologies to bring competitive electric vehicle products to our customers,” said Stellantis chairman John Elkann at the time of the announcement. "This important joint venture with our partner CATL will bring innovative battery production to a manufacturing site that is already a leader in clean and renewable energy, helping drive a 360-degree sustainable approach."

A spokesperson for Contemporary Star Energy – Stellantis and CATL's joint venture – described the LFP cells that will be produced in Zaragoza as complementary to the NMC batteries produced by Automotive Cells Company (ACC) – the joint venture between Stellantis – TotalEnergies and Mercedes-Benz, at its gigafactory in Douvrin, France.

Stellantis also invested €40m ($44.8m) in its first Battery Technology Center, at its Mirafiori complex in Turin, Italy. Opened in 2023, the 8,000 sq. m facility enhances the company's capabilities to design, develop and test battery packs, modules, high-voltage cells and software. It was described by Stellantis as the largest of its kind in Italy and amongst the largest in Europe.

The centre's cell testing facilities are intended to screen innovative battery chemistries, supporting Stellantis' wider dual-chemistry strategy. The company said this approach was designed to serve different customer requirements while improving cost competitiveness.

What does Stellantis' dual-chemistry approach mean for its supply chain?

Although Filosa has suggested "many" nameplates will make the switch to LFP, it is worth noting that not all nameplates will be affected. Stellantis will continue to pursue its dual-chemistry strategy, at least for now, albeit with a greater focus on LFP cells.

One potential benefit of this approach is reduced exposure to individual raw materials and their associated supply risks. NMC and LFP batteries use different combinations of materials, meaning that a greater use of LFP can reduce Stellantis' reliance on certain materials required for nickel-based chemistries.

Cobalt, for example, is used in NMC batteries but not in LFP cells. According to the International Energy Agency's Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026, cobalt prices in 2025 and early 2026 rose by around 130%, largely due to export restrictions imposed by the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

This is one example of how changes in raw material availability and prices can affect battery costs. Maintaining access to both chemistries could give the company greater flexibility in managing its battery sourcing and exposure to individual materials.

Using LFP batteries in more nameplates will, of course, mean Stellantis must ensure that its suppliers can provide sufficient quantities of the materials and components required, while its logistics providers must be able to accommodate the resulting changes in sourcing and material flows. Scaling up LFP supply efficiently will be important to avoiding bottlenecks and ensuring that the cost benefits of the switch can be fully realised.

Stellantis' LFP battery plant in Zaragoza could play a significant role in supporting this scale-up when it begins production. With planned annual capacity of up to 50GWh, the plant is set to supply LFP batteries for electric vehicles in the B, B SUV and C segments, as well as potentially for a light commercial vehicle (LCV). However, with Stellantis yet to confirm the specific nameplates affected by the planned chemistry change, the full extent of the plant's role in the transition remains to be seen.

title: What does a blue Texas sweep mean for Tesla, SpaceX & Elon Musk? | Electrek
authors: Jameson Dow, Fred Lambert, Micah Toll, Peter Johnson, Michelle Lewis
description:
After a historic election defeat in one of the most expensive elections in US election history, the state of Texas has turned blue.
Even the less high-profile races for court seats were swept by Democrats – three seats on the 15th Court of Appeals and four seats on the Texas Supreme Court.
Republicans rolled out the red carpet for Musk in Texas In 2021, Musk announced that Tesla would move its headquarters to Texas, after Musk got in a spat with California government because he didn’t want to follow COVID restrictions for worker safety.
Perhaps more notably for Musk personally, Texas has promised to allow Musk to get away with more financial shenanigans than states with more established business regulations might.
On a Texas state level, probably not all that much.
text:
After a historic election defeat in one of the most expensive elections in US election history, the state of Texas has turned blue. Along with this come potential implications for Elon Musk and his companies.

The US midterm election was yesterday, and ended up in a stunning result, with Democrats taking control of both houses of Congress by wide margins, and flipping seats that had been considered safe around the nation.

Perhaps most notably, many of these seats were in Texas – a republican stronghold which saw a clean sweep, with the Democrats winning every statewide contest. Republicans maintained some state legislative power and won the State Senate, but as of this writing Democrats are currently ahead in the count for the State House.

Despite huge spending, Democrats won almost everything

The highest profile contest was for Texas Senate, where James Talarico won by a 55-43 margin. This race set the record for the most expensive Senate race in the nation’s history, with over half a billion dollars spent on this one seat alone.

Advertisement - scroll for more content

About half of the total money spent on the race came courtesy of republican PACs, a method by which companies and the ultra-wealthy can launder money into bribes to buy elections. And most of the PAC money in the race came from one man, Elon Musk, who spent $212 million to support the enormously unpopular and scandal-ridden outgoing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton

That’s nearly half of the $474 million dollars that Musk put into this election cycle, suggesting that he saw this race of particular importance. And yet, his candidate lost miserably.

But the rout did not stop with Paxton. Paxton’s old job as AG is now going to be filled by Democrat Nathan Johnson. And Greg Abbott, the outgoing Governor, was defeated by Gina Hinojosa. Even the less high-profile races for court seats were swept by Democrats – three seats on the 15th Court of Appeals and four seats on the Texas Supreme Court.

And those results, even beyond the big-spending Senate race, could all matter quite a lot to Elon Musk.

Republicans rolled out the red carpet for Musk in Texas

In 2021, Musk announced that Tesla would move its headquarters to Texas, after Musk got in a spat with California government because he didn’t want to follow COVID restrictions for worker safety.

But the move wasn’t only about COVID restrictions – it was also about Musk’s vision of having more control over the business environment. And, by making allies with Ken Paxton and Greg Abbott, he has had quite a bit of control in Texas.

The two have rolled out the red carpet for Musk, giving him carte blanche in his adopted state.

Autonomous vehicle regulations have been changed, allowing driverless Robotaxis to operate where other states with more advanced regulations and transparency requirements would not. And many other laws benefitting Tesla and SpaceX have been passed. Paxton even sued Sam Altman, Musk’s chief AI rival, just weeks ago.

Perhaps more notably for Musk personally, Texas has promised to allow Musk to get away with more financial shenanigans than states with more established business regulations might.

With Tesla both headquartered and incorporated in Texas, it can now use special “business courts” instituted by Abbott at Musk’s own urging. If cases from these courts are appealed, they go to the 15th Court of Appeals, a court created by Abbott and filled with 3 hand-picked judges, intended to reduce the chance that a Democratic district court (say, one in Austin, whereTesla is headquartered) gets final say on any issue.

Several specific seats overseeing Musk went blue

But, the 15th Court of Appeals just had elections last night – and its three seats were flipped to Democratic control.

The 15th Court of Appeals also, just last week, stopped an inquiry into thousands of pages of emails between Abbott and Musk. The emails had been released, but are heavily redacted, with Abbott referring to the redacted portions as having “intimate” information in them.

And who made that request for inquiry into the emails? Gina Hinojosa, a name you might recognize, as she is the next Governor of Texas, as of last night.

As of yet, those emails have not all been released, so we don’t actually know exactly how much influence Musk was able to exercise over the state’s outgoing Governor. But given the changes we know about, the money Musk spent in Texas, and the thousands of pages of emails that have been redacted, it seems likely that there is something more to be found in them.

What does this mean for Musk’s companies?

So what does this all mean for Tesla, our main area of coverage here at Electrek?

On a Texas state level, probably not all that much. There’s no reason that Democrats in the state would interfere with Tesla’s production of electric vehicles – in fact, they’d probably encourage it more than republicans do. Talarico has stated that he supports Tesla – it is a large employer in the state, after all.

And certainly, the national wins by Democrats could be a boon for EVs, given how hostile republicans have been to them (and Musk has been the single largest supporter of that hostility towards EVs).

The same likely goes for SpaceX – perhaps a blue Texas will be more restrictive of the company’s improper usage of protected habitats, or building of data centers, or whatever the hell is going on on twitter. But the core businesses of space launches and Starlink don’t seem likely to go anywhere.

What does it mean for Musk himself?

For Elon Musk, though, things could be different. Given his “intimate” relationship with Abbott, the extreme amounts of money he spent on Paxton, and the highly personal nature of his truly ridiculous attacks against Talarico, it seems unlikely that he will have a similar level of allyship with Texas government actors as he did in prior years.

And given his high levels of spending on a party that is outright hostile electric vehicles, it seems clear that his personal fortunes are far more important to him than the well-being of his companies.

This is all important to note, because Musk has been working towards a scheme to merge SpaceX and Tesla, a deal which would likely be a detriment to both companies and all of their shareholders. Musk wants the deal so he can exercise more control over, and extract more personal wealth from, the combined entity.

But that scheme could rely on a favorable legal environment in Texas courts, an environment that just got less favorable.

And, given Musk’s penchant for childish lashings-out anytime he deems people insufficiently obsequious to his imagined greatness, could we see another situation where Musk encounters the tiniest amount of pushback from state government and then picks up his toys and leaves, as he already did in both California and Delaware? Time will have to tell. Keep your popcorn buckets primed and ready.

text:
Gina Hinojosa has defeated Gov. Greg Abbott in the Texas governor's race, a stunning outcome that ends three decades of Republican control in Texas and makes her the first Latina to ever lead the state.

"Here's what Texas said today, loud and clear: Your government belongs to you," said Hinojosa in her victory speech. "As your governor, I will never forget it."

At 10:17 p.m., the Associated Press called the race in Hinojosa’s favor. She was leading with about 57% of the reported vote to Abbott's 41%.

“It has been the joy of my life to have the opportunity to be the governor of the great state of Texas,” Abbott said during his concession speech. "There are still votes to be counted, but mathematically, we are not going to be able to win this election."

The victory denied Abbott a fourth term and elevated an Austin state representative who built her campaign around public education, household costs and criticism of the state's Republican leadership.

David Crockett, a political science professor at Trinity University, said before the election that a Hinojosa victory "would be perceived as an earthquake" because of Republicans' decades-long dominance in statewide elections.

But he cautioned that a single election wouldn't necessarily signal a lasting partisan shift. Democrats would need to demonstrate they could govern effectively and defend their gains in future elections.

"Can you get reelected or is this a one-off?" Crockett said, describing the challenge a Democratic governor could face.

The challenge of governing

Hinojosa's victory gives Democrats control of the governor's office for the first time since Ann Richards left office in 1995. But how much of her agenda she can accomplish will depend on the makeup of the Texas Legislature.

As governor, Hinojosa will have the power to sign or veto legislation and appoint leaders of state agencies. But major changes to public school funding, property taxes and the state's voucher program would require legislative approval.

Crockett said before the election that a Democratic governor could use vetoes to block legislation and appointments to influence how state policies are carried out. Passing her own agenda, however, would require finding common ground with lawmakers.

"Getting any meaningful legislation through is going to require them to find something they can agree on and that's not going to be easy," he said.

He pointed to public school funding as a possible area for compromise, although Hinojosa's opposition to vouchers could create friction with Republican lawmakers who support the program.

A campaign centered on education and affordability

Abbott, first elected in 2014, will leave office in January after a 12-year governorship marked by conservative policies on immigration, abortion, education and border security.

Education was a central dividing line between the candidates.

Hinojosa, a former Austin school board president, opposes private-school vouchers and state takeovers of local school districts. She has pledged to replace Education Commissioner Mike Morath with an educator, increase public school funding and overhaul the state's testing and accountability system.

Abbott championed the private-school voucher program created in 2025, arguing it gives parents more choices in their children's education. The program allows families to use public funds for private education expenses, with $1 billion allocated for the 2026-27 budget period.

Abbott also signed an $8.5 billion public-school funding package in 2025, including $4.2 billion for teacher and staff raises, along with funding for special education, early learning and school safety.

Both candidates also focused on lowering household costs, particularly property taxes.

Abbott proposed eliminating school district property taxes for homeowners through a constitutional amendment and tightening limits on property appraisal increases. Eliminating those taxes would require replacing a major source of public school funding.

Hinojosa proposed cutting corporate subsidies to help fund property tax relief, along with one-time $1,500 payments to Texas households from the state's Rainy Day Fund.

A victory with national implications

Hinojosa's victory comes as Democrats made gains in other major Texas races, including the U.S. Senate contest, where James Talarico defeated Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton.

Both Crockett and Nancy Sims, a political science lecturer at the University of Houston, said before the election that the national political environment could influence the governor's race, even with President Donald Trump absent from the ballot.

"If Democrats win in Texas in 2026, it will be because of anger at the federal government and at Donald Trump," Sims told The Texas Newsroom last week.

Sims said Democrats who won would need to address voters' concerns about the economy and public education. Crockett added that sustaining those victories would require demonstrating that Democrats could govern effectively.

Hinojosa will take office in January as the first Democratic governor of Texas in more than three decades. Her next challenge will be turning a historic electoral victory into a governing agenda — and determining how much of the change she promised voters can make it through the Texas Capitol.

text:
The transition to efficient, clean energy systems depends not only on raising ambition through multilateral processes, but also on building agile alliances and coalitions to address shared implementation challenges and fast track delivery – be it at bilateral, regional or sectoral level.

Middle powers matter in a new global order

Powering Across Divides: Clean energy cooperation in a fragmented world provides a political economy analysis of how the global clean power transition is being shaped in an increasingly fragmented and multipolar geopolitical context. Through an assessment of clean energy transition across 16 strategic economies, the report identifies common patterns in how national priorities, geopolitical dynamics and barriers to implementation are influencing progress.

Moving beyond national-level analysis, the report explores pathways for countries to turn shared strategic interests and complementary strengths into practical cooperation and reduced dependence on fossil fuels. Our analysis explores key areas to turn strategic alignment into delivery: identifying opportunities for new alliances and coalitions to accelerate the transition while strengthening energy security, economic resilience and prosperity.

Common energy transition dynamics across diverse economies

This report takes a diverse group of 16 economies as its starting point. It examines these countries, where they are in their transition journey, and what opportunities present themselves for international collaboration.

The first ten countries – Australia, Germany, Indonesia, Japan, Nigeria, Poland, South Africa, South Korea, Türkiye and the United Kingdom – are a cross-section of middle powers that are strategically important.

Six further countries – Brazil, China, Ethiopia, India, Mexico and the Philippines – are incorporated through shorter strategic spotlight analyses to reflect their particular systemic, diplomatic or regional relevance to the wider transition.

Bringing fresh impetus to international cooperation

Countries working together on clean power can strengthen energy security, reduce exposure to global supply shocks, support industrial competitiveness and build more resilient economies.

Partnerships can also allow countries to use their different strengths more effectively: bringing together broader renewable energy potential, demand, finance and technology. Connecting these complementary assets can create a cooperation dividend in which countries can achieve more, faster and at lower cost than they could by acting alone.

This means building a broader ecosystem of practical collaboration alongside the multilateral processes that set global ambition. Cross-country partnerships and coalitions can focus on the implementation challenges that are holding back the transition, from working on resilient supply chains and stronger grids to mobilising finance, developing technologies and integrating regional power systems.

Our analysis identifies four priorities for the next phase of the transition, for the international community as a whole and for countries acting jointly in smaller, more flexible groupings.

Recommendations

Place the pursuit of clean energy security at the centre of international diplomacy.

Support complementary pathways away from fossil fuels and towards electrification.

Mobilise finance and investment through practical delivery partnerships.

Use clean energy trade partnerships and regional infrastructure to diversify supply chains and accelerate investment.

BARCELONA, Spain, Nov. 04, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Wallbox N.V. (NYSE:WBX), a leading provider of electric vehicle (“EV”) charging and energy management solutions worldwide, today announced its financial results for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026 and provided a business update.
Third Quarter 2026 Highlights and Business Update:
Generated revenue of €24.2 million in the quarter.
Gross Margin landed at 36.5%, impacted by product mix.
Adjusted EBITDA was €(5.3) million, landing within guidance, improving 24% year-over-year and 32% compared to last quarter.
Continued improvement in operational efficiency resulted in a 34% year-over-year reduction in labor costs and operating expenses.
Launched the new generation of Pulsar Max across European markets, featuring ISO 15118-ready hardware, built-in RFID, and Ethernet connectivity for enhanced charging performance.
Secured €4 million of additional funding after the quarter through a convertible loan from existing shareholders.
Executive CommentaryEnric Asunción, CEO of Wallbox, said, “In the third quarter of 2026, order intake remained solid and our order backlog continued to grow, reaching €16.9 million at the end of September. However, this is not yet reflected in our revenue, as supply chain constraints continue to limit our ability to convert orders into deliveries on schedule. We are working closely with our suppliers and expect to resolve these constraints during the next quarters. At the same time, strong cost control allowed us to deliver adjusted EBITDA within our guidance.”
Mr. Asunción added, “With a robust backlog and customer demand, we are well positioned to grow once supply constraints ease. Our financing efforts are focused on securing sufficient working capital to support this growth with the €4 million of existing shareholders as the first example. At the same time, we are converting orders into deliveries in a disciplined way, which we believe will drive more efficient operations and continued progress toward profitability.”

title: Democrats Win Control of Congress Amid Energy Cost Concerns | KuCoin
description:
Voter opposition to data centers could delay construction of electricity-intensive AI infrastructure.
Democrats attacked Republican opponents over farmers' energy expenses in Iowa, Kansas and Ohio.
Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat, criticized Republican Greg Abbott for previously supporting data centers in a state where developers plan large projects.
Opposition to data centers also featured in Ohio, where Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Senator Jon Husted.
Husted and Bresnahan both drew criticism for supporting data centers.
text:
Democrats captured both chambers of Congress through Senate victories in Republican-leaning states and House victories across the country. Democrats also won several governorships previously held by Republicans. Expensive gasoline, record diesel prices and higher electricity bills contributed to voter dissatisfaction with President Trump and Republicans. Voter opposition to data centers could delay construction of electricity-intensive AI infrastructure.

Democrats attacked Republican opponents over farmers' energy expenses in Iowa, Kansas and Ohio. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat, criticized Republican Greg Abbott for previously supporting data centers in a state where developers plan large projects. Opposition to data centers also featured in Ohio, where Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Senator Jon Husted. In Pennsylvania, Paige Cognetti defeated Republican Representative Rob Bresnahan. Husted and Bresnahan both drew criticism for supporting data centers.

Democrats have not yet presented a detailed energy agenda. Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer linked Republicans to electricity costs in Schumer's initial remarks after election results arrived. Likely Speaker-in-waiting Hakeem Jeffries has pledged to advance an affordability agenda quickly, with energy among the central priorities. Jeffries assigned Representatives Nikki Budzinski, a Democrat from Illinois, and Mike Levin, a Democrat from California, to lead the "Gas and Utilities Affordability Working Group". The working group developed proposals that have not been made public.

The House Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition, which has more than 100 members, supported hundreds of proposals this year that could provide additional ideas. Some proposals, including assistance for advanced nuclear power, could attract support from both parties. However, other proposals, including reinstating some Inflation Reduction Act tax credits, would be mostly symbolic.

Schumer has outlined Senate priorities covering electricity grid development, affordability, consumer protections and clean energy. Schumer has promised to reinstate clean energy tax credits. Schumer has also pledged "systematic protection for consumers from rising prices." Other proposals include additional support for energy efficiency and clearer utility bills.

Democrats did not emphasize climate change in the party's midterm campaign messaging. Progressives could seek to restore an agenda explicitly centered on climate. Democrats are not expected to revive the select committee on climate change that Republicans dissolved after taking the House in 2022. No decision about restoring the committee has been announced. Democrats' reduced emphasis on climate messaging gives reason to doubt the committee's return, despite continuing global warming.

The election results could immediately influence negotiations over a bipartisan permitting agreement during the lame-duck session. Some House progressives argue that Democrats could secure a permitting agreement closer to progressive preferences next year. However, supporters of the current bill see virtually no political opportunity for a more liberal bill that Trump would sign or that could even pass the Senate.

The permitting dispute has divided the Democratic coalition. Multiple unions and the clean energy industry support the bill. However, many environmentalists remain undecided or oppose the bill outright. The dispute also reflects wider disagreements between the "abundance movement" and progressives seeking tougher restrictions on fossil fuels. Those disagreements could shape legislative priorities and presidential contenders' policy agendas beyond the lame-duck negotiations as competition for 2028 intensifies.

Democrats are preparing energy-related oversight covering Trump's diesel agreement with Moscow, offshore wind policies and other issues.

description:

text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

Oahu is a unique place. It’s the home of one of the largest clean tech incubators in the world, Elemental Impact, for a reason. Exorbitantly high electricity rates combined with ample natural resources make it an incredible laboratory to bring clean tech solutions to market. Rapid investment for WWII created a grid that was dependent on foreign oil. Path dependency (the idea that “what you know” becomes what you continue to do) hampered innovation and resulted in the creation of infrastructure (multiple power plants across multiple islands) that still, today, burns diesel fuel as large generators, to produce electricity for the island. Throw in a dependence on imported fuels that must come at least 3,000 miles to arrive, being the strategic hub for the entire Pacific theater of the U.S. military, one of the wildest weather years and hurricane seasons the island chain has ever seen AND the state’s economic dependency on tourism dollars, high cost of living, and low wages, and and wow – you’ve got yourself a puzzle and a half to solve in order to get the place to a sustainable future.

Analyst Mike Barnard loves a challenge, so he set forth to put together a roadmap to help Oahu get to 100% clean energy, which helps recirculate money in the state, lower costs, create jobs and foster economic resiliency.

Recently I gave a talk at Hawaii Tech Week in which I summarized this report, added in my own experience running an energy efficiency service that has now greened more than 20,000 homes and is saving Hawaii residents over $10 million a year on their utility bills, and then compiled the new and coming technologies that can help the island get off fossil fuels.

Mike’s report did something very important. The state’s own reporting and strategy looks at the big picture, a very difficult mountain to climb. Mike looked at that mountain and removed some of the false summits and unachievable viewpoints, resulting in a much more achievable and strategic pathway. What he did was eliminate the things we simply cannot fix right now – long distance flights, maritime bunkering, and military fuels – and tackled the problem of Oahu’s actual energy consumption for its residents. The result was that it was achievable, and there are technologies right now today that can be deployed in what he refers to as a “no regret stack” first and foremost.

I combined that with my approach, which was to showcase the economic resilience it creates. Case in point, an LED bulb saves so much money on Oahu that it pays for itself in 18 days. Every day after that, it is like change plinking in a piggy bank for the person who put it in. That builds economic resiliency for those who need it most. From LEDs to e-bikes to heat pump water heaters to balcony solar – it all adds up – fast payback periods, and financial independence.

Mike comes back to the things we simply can’t fix right now and argues that the tech will come – but for the duration of the 2020s and into the 2030s, we should be installing parking lot solar canopies, agrivoltaics, heat pump water heaters, and more.

Enjoy the video.

title: The Section 48D Gravy Train Should End - by Jack Salmon
description:
Of the CHIPS funds that I could match to publicly announced projects, two-thirds went to projects announced before the law was signed.
That tax credit, created in 2022, known as Section 48D, extends to construction that begins by the end of 2026.
The investment figure covers projects announced since 2020, but Section 48D was signed into law in 2022.
Another point worth making is that the semiconductor industry was thriving before the signing of the CHIPS Act and continues to thrive today.
The computer and electronic products sector, which includes semiconductor manufacturing, saw substantial input-price pressure consistent with margin compression.
text:
Congress is preparing to extend a semiconductor tax credit that is subsidizing investments companies had already decided to make. Of the CHIPS funds that I could match to publicly announced projects, two-thirds went to projects announced before the law was signed. Yet policymakers and industry lobbyists are presenting the program as a triumph and asking Congress to extend it through 2031 and expand it to additional activities.

2022 was a big year for corporate welfare as hundreds of billions of dollars in taxpayer funded subsidies were handed out through both the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) and the CHIPS and Science Act. The latter included $39 billion in subsidies for domestic chip manufacturing along with 25% (raised to 35% with the OBBBA) investment tax credits for costs of manufacturing equipment.

That tax credit, created in 2022, known as Section 48D, extends to construction that begins by the end of 2026. As we would expect, policymakers in congress have been calling for that Section 48D construction deadline to be extended through 2031, and it is possible that they will attempt to squeeze this into a tax extenders package in the coming weeks.

This would involve transferring another $40-50bn in taxpayers’ dollars to large semiconductor companies over the next 5 years. And as the Milton Friedman quote goes, there is nothing as permanent as a temporary government program. $50bn quickly becomes $100bn+ as corporate welfare is continuingly extended.

Another point worth making here, is that by artificially raising the returns to semiconductor investments, the credit encourages resources, including investment funds, labor, and construction capacity, to flow toward politically favored projects and away from potentially more productive uses elsewhere in the economy.

Along with policymakers, corporate lobbying groups are out in force calling, not just for extension of the credit, but also for expanding the credit to other activities. A coalition of business groups wrote a letter to congressional leadership earlier this year, in which they noted:

“To date, the tax credit has catalyzed over $640 billion in investments throughout the supply chain across 140 projects in 30 states—more than tripling U.S. semiconductor manufacturing capacity.”

The catalyzation of $640 billion in investment is based on announced investments, not money already spent. This is an important distinction because a GAO report found that only about 15 percent of companies receiving CHIPS subsidies had submitted milestone completion reports for their projects. Milestones relate to construction of facilities, installation and qualification of equipment, and meeting minimum production levels.

More importantly, the $640 billion figure is not a measure of investment eligible for Section 48D. It is a grand total of announced investment across the semiconductor supply chain, including chip design, R&D, and materials production, which the letter’s own footnote admits are excluded from the credit. They are, therefore, dishonestly using ineligible investments to claim that the credit succeeded, while simultaneously asking Congress to expand the credit to cover those same activities.

Not only did the $640 billion estimate ignore the counterfactual, but also the timing of the investment announcements. The investment figure covers projects announced since 2020, but Section 48D was signed into law in 2022. Meanwhile the industry describes a projected tripling of US capacity, but its own forecast shows America’s share of global capacity rising only four percentage points, from 10 percent to 14 percent.

Another point worth making is that the semiconductor industry was thriving before the signing of the CHIPS Act and continues to thrive today. This is not a sector in desperate need of taxpayer subsidies. For example, leading chip manufacturer, TSMC, is making record profits, with over $22 billion in profit last quarter, up 73% from last year.

The SIA’s own report makes it difficult to portray semiconductors as a struggling industry in need of rescue. US-headquartered firms generated $425 billion in sales last year, captured 53.4 percent of global semiconductor revenue, spent $76.8 billion on R&D, and announced more than $770 billion in new investment. The report supplies no counterfactual showing that taxpayers are needed to make these investments happen.

A corporate subsidy like 48D should be judged by what it changes, not by what follows it. This is the test of additionality. Did the subsidies buy investment that otherwise wouldn’t have happened, or were they transfers to large corporations being rewarded for investments that were coming regardless of the availability of subsidies?

In an attempt to answer this question, I matched each CHIPS grant to the Semiconductor Industry Association’s tracker of announced projects and dated each project’s first public announcement. Of the roughly $34 billion in grants I could match, $22 billion, or 65%, went to projects first announced before the law was signed. So did seven of the ten largest grants.

About $9 billion went to projects announced before the bill was even introduced in June 2020, led by TSMC’s Arizona fab, unveiled that May.

On a related note, real value added in US semiconductor and electronic-component manufacturing remained almost exactly where the pre-2022 trend predicted it would be, at about $138 billion in 2025 versus a trend value of roughly $139 billion (chained 2017 dollars).

Putting these together, it looks like the Section 48D subsidies were largely a windfall.

Defenders will say firms moved early because they saw subsidies coming. That’s possible, but it is their claim to prove. The evidence can’t tell anticipation apart from a shortage-driven investment cycle that was already under way. Before Congress extends the tax credit or funds another round of grants, the burden of proof should sit with those who want to spend more, not with taxpayers.

If policymakers are serious about supporting a robust and thriving domestic semiconductor industry, one of the ways to do that is by applying neutral cost-recovery rules available to all industries, not through politically allocated subsidies for favored companies.

OBBBA moved substantially in this direction, making full expensing permanent for equipment and domestic R&D while temporarily extending it to certain manufacturing structures. But it stopped short of genuinely neutral cost recovery. If policymakers are serious about supporting a robust domestic semiconductor industry, they should finish the job by applying neutral cost-recovery rules available to all industries.

Another way policymakers could increase output and production in the semiconductor sector would be to stop imposing taxes on the inputs for the very fabrication plants that they’re subsidizing. Fabs depend on more than 100 chemicals and materials, and the United States lacks capacity to scale production for roughly 60% of those inputs. Tariffs on chemicals, materials, equipment components, and construction inputs raise U.S. production and R&D costs.

The Federal Reserve Board’s recent manufacturing survey found that tariff-exposed subsectors experience faster growth in input prices. The computer and electronic products sector, which includes semiconductor manufacturing, saw substantial input-price pressure consistent with margin compression.

Similarly, in a survey of 156 semiconductor executives, 63% identified tariffs as a high concern for the next three years, while respondents reported that tariffs raise production costs and force changes in manufacturing strategy.

The United States still depends heavily on imported equipment, chemicals, materials, and components, so tariff relief would reduce costs across the entire supply chain without selecting particular companies or projects for federal subsidies.

That is the better way to support a semiconductor industry that is already globally competitive: remove economy-wide barriers to investment and production rather than continue sending targeted checks to politically favored firms. Congress should let Section 48D expire and allow the industry to compete on the strength of its underlying fundamentals.

Dedicated US sales office to open in the first quarter of 2027

US demand to be served from ASTA’s growing global production network

Oed (Austria), 4 November 2026 – ASTA Energy Solutions AG (“ASTA”), a leading manufacturer of copper winding and conductor components, has signed a long-term agreement (LTA) with Virginia Transformer Corporation, one of the leading North American manufacturers of power transformers, running through the end of 2029. It is ASTA’s first long-term agreement for the US market.

Virginia Transformer has been a customer of ASTA for many years – so far on the basis of individual orders. The new agreement follows the proven structure of ASTA’s existing LTAs: in a market where high demand meets limited production capacity, the customer secures long-term supply volumes. In return, ASTA gains planning certainty for the ongoing expansion of its plants.

The US market is an important growth market for ASTA: grid expansion, rising electricity demand and the addition of new generation capacity are driving demand for power transformers there. ASTA currently generates a single-digit percentage of its consolidated revenue in the US.

As announced, ASTA decided in the fourth quarter of 2026 on its next steps in the US market: as a first step, the company will open its own sales office in the United States in the first quarter of 2027 and significantly step up its market development on the ground. US customers will continue to be supplied from the global production network, whose capacity is currently being expanded at all sites as planned.

In the medium to long term, establishing its own manufacturing presence in the United States through an acquisition remains a strategic option. The company continues to actively monitor the market for such opportunities. Any such investment would have to meet ASTA’s quality standards and offer a return appropriate to the location. The current priority is the ramp-up of the existing plants.

Karl Schäcke, CEO of ASTA Energy Solutions AG: “Our first long-term agreement in the United States, with a partner that has trusted us for many years, is a strong signal. It affirms our approach: we grow together with our customers, as partners and with a sense of proportion. We do not rule out manufacturing in the United States in the future – but it has to match our standards for quality and returns. With our own sales office, we are now moving closer to our US customers and will supply them from our proven production network.”

About ASTA Energy Solutions AG

ASTA Energy Solutions AG is a leading global manufacturer of high-precision copper solutions for power generation, power transmission and e-mobility. With a corporate history spanning more than 210 years and around 1,600 employees at six sites on three continents, ASTA combines unique technological expertise with a global production network. Its long-standing customers include leading companies of the global energy transition such as Siemens Energy, GE Vernova, Hitachi and Andritz. Following its successful IPO in January 2026, ASTA was admitted to the SDAX of the Frankfurt Stock Exchange within a very short time and has since met the stringent transparency and reporting requirements of the Prime Standard.

text:
The VGF scheme will promote three types of technologies

30 GWh through Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS)

60 GWh through Pumped Storage Projects (PSP)

2 GWh through emerging storage technologies

The scheme includes a 'Domestic Content Requirement' (DCR) of 40% for battery storage systems, emphasising the use of locally manufactured components to boost domestic production.

“The scheme marks a significant step towards strengthening India's power sector infrastructure, facilitating large-scale integration of renewable energy and ensuring reliable, affordable and round-the-clock power supply. It will also provide an impetus to domestic manufacturing of battery energy storage systems, reduce import dependence and enhance the country's long-term energy security,” an official release stated.

The scheme would ensure the storage of surplus electricity generated from solar and wind energy sources. The stored electricity could be utilised during the peak summer season or when renewable energy generation declines. This will help ensure the availability of electricity 24x7.

The scheme would help develop 60 GWh of Hydro Pumped Storage Plant (PSP) capacity, 30 GWh of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) capacity and 2 GWh of capacity through alternative energy storage technologies, with a total estimated investment of Rs 97,600 crore.

The VGF support will help speed up the deployment of large-scale energy storage infrastructure in the country.

The allocation of energy storage capacity will be carried out through a tariff-based competitive bidding process. Public and private sector power distribution companies will be eligible for Viability Gap Funding (VGF) support for Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) and Hydro Pumped Storage Projects (PSP). Projects based on other energy storage technologies will be implemented by both public and private sector entities.

The scheme also aims to strengthen India's domestic energy storage manufacturing ecosystem by providing demand-side financial support and reducing reliance on imported components. As part of this push towards ‘Aatmanirbhar Bharat’, BESS projects will be required to meet a minimum Domestic Content Requirement (DCR) of 40%. The move is expected to boost domestic manufacturing, create new opportunities for Indian industry and complement existing government incentives for battery manufacturing.

In a post on X, PM Narendra Modi raised India’s dependence on other countries for critical minerals. He wrote, “Do you feel India should depend on other countries for processing the critical minerals that power our future? I certainly don’t! Lithium, nickel, cobalt…these are essential for EVs, batteries, electronics and defence. Yet, we remain heavily dependent on imports of refined materials. To address this, the Cabinet has approved a scheme to change this. Key highlights: New critical mineral processing plants. Capital subsidy to boost investment. Greater domestic value addition. Stronger supply chains. The principle is clear...India must have capabilities to build technologies of the future!”
