Parking lots occupy huge areas in shopping centers, offices, hospitals, airports and industrial facilities. Adding solar canopies above these spaces can turn otherwise unused overhead areas into electricity-generating infrastructure while providing shade for parked vehicles. Important Details: Dual-Purpose Space: Solar canopies generate electricity without requiring a separate ground-mounted solar farm. Vehicle Shade: Covered parking can reduce direct sunlight on vehicles and improve comfort when people return to their cars. Building Electricity: Generated power can help supply nearby offices, shops, warehouses and other facilities. EV Charging: Canopies can provide a convenient location for electric-vehicle charging stations. Reduced Land Competition: Using existing parking areas may limit the need to convert additional land for solar installations. Stormwater and Design: Well-designed canopies can incorporate drainage, lighting and other site improvements. Upfront Costs: Steel structures, foundations, electrical connections and construction over active parking areas can make projects more expensive than ground-mounted solar. Solar parking canopies are particularly attractive where daytime electricity demand is high and large parking areas already exist. Their value depends on sunlight, structural design, electricity prices and the site's energy needs. Imagine every major shopping center, airport and office parking lot generating electricity above the cars. How much unused urban space could we put to work? Source: Solar parking canopy project examples and the original installation referenced in the supplied Facebook post. #SolarEnergy #SolarCanopies #EVCharging #SustainableInfrastructure #DidYouKnow

Europe's renewable energy expansion is creating an unusual challenge: sometimes the electricity grid has more power available than the market can absorb. During these periods, wholesale electricity prices can turn negative, highlighting the need for better energy storage, flexible demand and stronger grid connections. Important Details: 1,223 Reported Hours: The headline cites 1,223 negative-price hours across Europe in the first quarter of 2026, compared with 119 hours in Q1 2022. More Renewable Generation: Expanding solar and wind capacity can create periods of abundant electricity production. Supply and Demand: Negative prices can occur when electricity supply exceeds demand and some generators cannot easily reduce output. Storage Gap: Batteries and other storage technologies can absorb surplus electricity and release it when demand rises. Grid Constraints: Limited transmission capacity can prevent excess electricity in one region from reaching customers elsewhere. Flexible Consumption: Industrial processes, EV charging and other controllable loads can help use electricity when it is plentiful. A Manageable Challenge: Negative prices can signal a need for better coordination between generation, storage, transmission and demand. The reported figures need to be checked against the original market data, including which European markets were included. Negative prices do not necessarily mean that every consumer receives free electricity, and they do not prove that solar alone caused the price drops. The paradox is fascinating: clean electricity can become so abundant at certain times that the market struggles to value every unit. Would you support more investment in large-scale batteries to make better use of surplus renewable power? Source: PV Magazine, May 2026. Verify the reported 1,223 and 119 hours and the geographic scope against the original data. #RenewableEnergy #SolarPower #EnergyStorage #Europe #DidYouKnow

Important Details: Balcony Solar: Compact solar panels can be installed on suitable balconies, terraces or other permitted spaces. Plug-In Systems: Certain designs connect to a household electrical circuit through approved equipment, subject to local electrical and safety rules. Apartment Access: These systems could offer an option for renters and residents who cannot install rooftop solar. Potential Bill Savings: Solar generation may offset some daytime electricity use, depending on system size and household consumption. Smaller Installations: Balcony systems generally produce much less electricity than full rooftop installations. Safety Standards: Proper mounting, wind resistance, electrical protection and compliance with utility requirements are essential. Policy Matters: Legislation alone does not guarantee immediate installation; implementation rules, building restrictions and technical standards may still apply. The key question is whether California's proposed or enacted rules make these systems legally and practically accessible. The exact legislative status should be checked against the original bill and official state guidance before assuming residents can already plug panels into their homes. Would you install a small balcony solar system if it could reduce your electricity bill? Source: Original California legislative or policy announcement linked in the supplied Facebook post; verify the bill's current status and implementation requirements. #BalconySolar #California #SolarPower #CleanEnergy #DidYouKnow

What if farmland could grow crops and generate electricity without sacrificing space for agricultural machinery? Elevated agrivoltaic systems are designed to place solar panels high enough above the ground for tractors and other farm equipment to operate underneath. Important Details: Dual-Purpose Land: Agrivoltaics combines solar electricity production with agricultural activity on the same land. Elevated Panels: Higher mounting structures can preserve access for tractors, harvesters and other farm machinery. Crop Protection: Partial shade may reduce heat stress for certain crops during hot weather. Water Benefits: Depending on the design, panel shade can reduce evaporation and help conserve soil moisture. Additional Farm Income: Electricity generation can create another potential revenue stream for farmers. Crop Selection Matters: Some crops benefit from partial shade, while others require more direct sunlight for optimal yields. Engineering Trade-Offs: Taller structures can increase installation costs and require careful consideration of wind loads, maintenance and machinery clearance. Italy's climate and agricultural landscape make the concept particularly interesting, but the benefits depend on the crop, panel spacing, local weather and project economics. The goal is not to replace farming with solar panels. It is to design systems where food production and renewable energy can coexist. Would you support elevated solar panels on agricultural land if farmers could continue cultivating their crops underneath? Source: Original Italian agrivoltaic project documentation linked in the supplied Facebook post. #Agrivoltaics #Italy #SolarEnergy #SustainableAgriculture #DidYouKnow

Spain's rapid growth in solar and wind power is changing how electricity is priced. During periods when renewable generation is abundant and demand is relatively low, wholesale electricity prices can fall below zero — meaning some generators effectively pay to keep supplying electricity to the market. Important Details: Negative Prices: These occur when wholesale market prices fall below zero, often because supply exceeds demand and some generators have incentives to continue producing. Solar's Influence: Strong midday solar generation can contribute to periods of abundant electricity supply. 347 Reported Hours: The headline cites 347 negative-price hours in Spain during the first quarter of 2026; the exact figure should be checked against market data. Why Prices Turn Negative: Grid constraints, inflexible generation, limited storage and insufficient demand can all contribute. Batteries Can Help: Storage systems can absorb excess electricity and release it when demand or prices rise. Flexible Demand Matters: Electric vehicles, industrial processes and other controllable loads can use more electricity when it is abundant. Consumers May Not Benefit Directly: Negative wholesale prices do not automatically mean household electricity customers are paid to consume power. The headline's claim of zero negative-price hours before 2023 needs clarification about the market, time interval and pricing measure being compared. The important point is that rising renewable generation can create both cheaper electricity and new challenges for grid flexibility. Would you support larger battery-storage projects to make better use of surplus solar power? Source: PV Magazine / Montel, May 2026. Adjustable Shade: Strategic shading may protect sensitive crops from excessive heat and intense sunlight. Crop-Specific Results: Some plants benefit from partial shade, while others need more direct sunlight to achieve good yields. Research Matters: Panel movement, crop selection, machinery access and installation costs all influence whether a system is practical. The key is finding the right balance: enough sunlight for healthy crops while producing meaningful amounts of electricity. The exact Dutch project and its results should be verified before drawing conclusions about its performance. Would you want to see solar panels integrated into more working farms? Industry voices say government-level support is needed for domestically made electric vehicles exposed to competitive risks from China.
text:
The export competitiveness of China's electric vehicles appears to have overtaken Korea's in the past two years. Analysts also said that if China continues to step up its push in the global market at the current pace, 2.2 trillion won—about 15% of Korea's electric vehicle export value—will be eroded in 2030.

On the 4th, according to "Korea's electric vehicle exports and competitiveness status and implications," analyzed by The Federation of Korean Industries using United Nations trade statistics (UN Comtrade), Korea's revealed comparative advantage (RCA) in electric vehicles fell from 2.92 in 2023 to 2.00 in 2024 and 1.48 in 2025.

RCA is an indicator that compares the share of a specific item in a country's total exports with that of total world exports. If a given country's RCA is greater than 1, it means the country has a comparative export advantage for that item in the global market. Korea still holds an edge in the electric vehicle institutional sector, but the figure has been cut in half in two years.

In 2019, the electric vehicle RCA for Korea and China was 3.02 and 0.19, respectively, a 16-fold gap. China's electric vehicle RCA then rose to 1.13 in 2022, 1.28 in 2023, and as high as 1.49 last year, overtaking Korea (1.48) in six years.

These shifts are also visible in global electric vehicle export figures. The export value share of Korea-made electric vehicles fell from 8.9% in 2019 to 8.1% in 2023, 6.2% in 2024, and 4.6% last year. While the global market is expanding rapidly, Korea's comparative advantage and export share in electric vehicles are falling at the same time.

Industry voices say government-level support is needed for domestically made electric vehicles exposed to competitive risks from China. Lee Sang-ho, head of the economic division at FKI, said, "China's electric vehicle industry, backed by strong support from its government, is rapidly securing the future auto market," and noted, "We need to consider policy support measures such as domestic production tax credits to expand the production base for domestic electric vehicles."

Electric vehicle finished cars were excluded from the domestic production tax credit targets the government released in Aug. However, as concerns mount over falling market share for domestic brands and weakening price competitiveness, lawmakers from both parties have introduced amendments to the Act on Restriction on Special Cases Concerning Taxation in succession, and the issue is under discussion in the National Assembly. Measures under review include granting a tax credit of up to 4 million won per domestically produced electric vehicle, or applying a regional preference coefficient for production outside the capital area.

text:
As the United Nation’s climate conference, COP31, begins next month, the world is gathering under sobering circumstances: The latest UNEP Emissions Gap report underscores the growing risk of warming past 1.5°C, and the widening gap between our current actions and where we need to be.

At the same time, shocks to energy markets, food systems, supply chains, and public finances have reinforced a false narrative that climate action should take a backseat to economic development and energy security.

Against this backdrop of economic turmoil and dire science, what should we expect from COP31?

Once again, this COP is being billed as an “implementation COP”. Every COP since Paris has been described in some way as an “implementation COP.” After so many uses, it begs the question: what is an implementation COP?

Perhaps a better way to label a COP is by how well it addresses the challenges that surround our daily lives. This doesn’t mean these questions will get resolved over two weeks in Türkiye—that is unrealistic. It’s not about new decisions or announcements, and that is not what the world wants or needs at the moment.

Instead, grappling with these challenges means honest conversations that grow our collective understanding of the obstacles ahead. It means mobilizing the stakeholders needed to tackle them, and building momentum behind solutions that can be implemented long after delegates return home. It’s about supercharging action on existing initiatives and commitments to ensure they’re delivered.

The questions we face at COP31 are heavy, indeed: At a moment when short-term pressures are competing with long-term climate goals for political attention, how can we demonstrate that climate action is not separate from economic resilience, energy security, affordability, and public well-being, but essential to all of them? Can we scale proven climate solutions quickly enough to deliver tangible benefits for people who face pressures on their wallets and livelihoods?

My colleagues at Environmental Defense Fund are showing up to face these questions head-on. Here’s what we’re bringing to Antalya:

Delivering near-term results through methane and superpollutants

At a moment when energy security concerns are reshaping climate policy and fuel prices remain volatile, one of the biggest energy opportunities is being wasted in plain sight: methane. Cutting methane remains one of the fastest ways to slow warming while delivering benefits people can feel today through cleaner air, improved health, and stronger energy security. Meaningful progress at COP31 would mean moving from pledges to implementation: countries showing concrete policies, projects, financing, and measurable emissions reductions, not just announcing new targets.

Methane action is one of the clearest opportunities to advance the COP30 Presidency’s roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels (TAFF). Success on methane requires many of the same ingredients we will need for the broader energy transition: strong data systems, effective regulation, access to investment, transparency, and international cooperation. Methane reduction is not separate from our broader energy transition. It is an early building block for delivering it, and an opportunity to demonstrate to the world that we can translate ambition into action.

The technologies needed to detect and reduce methane emissions are ready to be used now—but we still face obstacles to mobilizing these solutions into action at the speed and scale we need. Our work at EDF is focused on eliminating those hurdles: making transparent data available to accelerate accountability; helping governments design policy and regulations to reinforce energy security, affordability, and economic development; and unlocking the finance needed to drive methane action, particularly in emerging and developing economies. At COP31, EDF’s scientific, policy and market expertise to advance methane action and transition finance across oil and gas, agriculture and waste.

Building collaboration around multifaceted challenges

COP31 also offers an opportunity to continue working together on increasingly interconnected challenges. Energy security, food security, affordability, and climate change are becoming harder to separate. Rising fuel prices affect fertilizer costs, which in turn affect food production and prices.

Rather than tackling these challenges individually, a successful COP can help stakeholders identify solutions that make fuel and fertilizer systems simultaneously more secure, affordable, resilient, and lower-emitting. Our EDF team is bringing expertise across energy, agriculture, transportation, and industrial systems to Antalya, aiming to contribute practical insights and convene conversations on emerging solutions such as low-emissions ammonia and hydrogen-based e-fuels. We can no longer solve just one piece of the puzzle in silos; we need stakeholders across multiple sectors and initiatives working together to identify and adopt the solutions that deliver and endure.

Rethinking climate finance to unlock the needed resources

Finance remains one of our biggest barriers to implementation. The challenge is not simply mobilizing more capital, but improving the quality and accessibility of finance. This includes lowering the cost of capital, strengthening local financial ecosystems, and scaling tools such as high-integrity carbon markets and Article 6 cooperation as part of a broader capital stack. It also means ensuring that finance reaches the communities most affected by climate change and the transition itself, including Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities (IPLCs). Strengthening benefit-sharing approaches and improving access to finance for underserved regions can help ensure that climate investments deliver both emissions reductions and tangible development outcomes.

EDF brings decades of experience helping shape carbon market policy and transition finance approaches. By advancing market integrity, supporting innovative financing models, and identifying pathways to attract investment into emerging economies, EDF can help contribute practical solutions to a challenge that remains central to global climate progress. For example, financing structures that support methane capture technologies can be repaid through revenues from recovered gas sales, while additional income streams from high-integrity carbon credits can further improve project economics. These approaches help de-risk investment, attract private capital, and demonstrate how targeted methane abatement can deliver both near-term climate benefits and measurable financial returns.

Global Stocktake 2: a moment for reflection and recalibration

Finally, COP31 marks the start of the next Global Stocktake cycle. GST 2 provides an opportunity to assess where implementation is succeeding, where progress is falling short, and what needs to happen next.

EDF’s ability to connect science, policy, economics, and on-the-ground implementation positions it to help inform these discussions. By bringing evidence and lessons from work across methane, energy systems, and climate finance, EDF can help ensure the Global Stocktake serves not only as a measure of progress, but as a guide for accelerating action in the years ahead.

The greatest outcome of COP31 will not be found in the headlines, nor even in the closing text. It will be whether we leave with a clearer pathway to deliver solutions that reduce emissions, strengthen economies, and improve lives.

At a time when immediate challenges are competing for attention alongside long-term climate goals, the real task is not choosing between them. It is demonstrating that climate action can help address both.

text:
The United States is set for a divided government for the first time since Donald Trump’s return to the White House last year. Voters across the country overwhelmingly cast ballots for Democrats, handily securing the party’s control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. The victory came hours before polls closed in the nation’s westernmost reaches as Democrats flipped seats held by the GOP for decades in states such as Georgia, South Carolina, and Texas.

It was a seismic national shift to the left, spurred in no small part by voters’ opposition to infrastructure supporting artificial intelligence and anger over rising gas and electricity prices, particularly since Trump launched a war on Iran.

In an election widely seen as a referendum on Trump, Democrats trained their fire on the administration’s energy policies. Those include its moves to eliminate landmark climate regulations, its oversight of the U.S. buildout of data centers, its legally dubious deals to kill offshore wind farms, and repeals or redirections of funding for decarbonization.

Much of what the next Congress focuses on when it comes to energy policy hinges on what happens with the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, the permitting reform bill that has dominated Washington dealmaking discussions since the Senate unveiled the legislation at the end of September.

But key provisions in two of the most significant energy laws enacted in the past six decades — the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of 2021, better known as the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, and the Energy Act of 2020 — have either expired or are set to lapse next year. Reauthorizing the bipartisan measures in both laws will offer a new, Democrat-led Congress the chance to push legislative priorities such as bringing back key subsidies for renewables in a bid to rebalance the country’s energy future following Trump’s AI-fueled gas bonanza. Candidates who flipped districts that previously voted for Trump also vowed to crack down on data centers, which strongly suggests that the party will back legislation to curb the artificial intelligence buildout.

What Democrats want to do

Among the top policies Democrats plan to champion next year on clean energy is the restoration of the investment and production tax credits for wind and solar, which Republicans axed in their signature budget bill last summer.

“There’s broad recognition and an active effort by Democrats to reinstate many things done away with in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” Evan Chapman, a former Democratic staffer on the Hill who now serves as the senior director of policy at the think tank Clean Tomorrow, told me.

Bringing back the electric vehicle tax credit? Not so much. The provision in the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act gave a far larger write-off for cars made with batteries manufactured with domestically-produced minerals, giving a much-needed boost to U.S. miners. Yet the policy proved difficult to defend against populist anger over its benefits tilting largely toward wealthy drivers who bought electric vehicles as a second or third car.

The EV tax credit was another OBBBA casualty. Without that market signal, it seemed unlikely that all the decades-long mining and minerals projects proposed in the U.S. would find investors, illustrating what my colleague Matthew Zeitlin last year called the “paradox of Trump’s critical mineral crusade.”

But a battery boom is underway nevertheless, as large, standalone lithium-ion packs increasingly patch onto the grid to balance out supply over time, particularly in markets that generate a lot more solar and wind during the day than anyone can use.

“Batteries generally are an area of more and more confluence every day between Democrats and Republicans,” a source with direct knowledge of Democrats’ thinking who spoke on condition of anonymity to speak bluntly told me. “It’s unclear what anyone wants to do. Republicans don’t want to do more EV tax credits, but it could be a battery production tax credit that’s technology neutral.”

Asked whether such a policy could win GOP support, James Dozier, the chief executive of the Republican climate group Citizens for Responsible Energy Solutions, told me that anything that would boost domestic mineralsrepresented an area of broad agreement between the two parties. The Trump administration has strongly supported domestic mining and mineral processing as China retaliated against the president’s trade war by cutting off supplies of metals needed for weapons and batteries.

“Battery technology should be invested in,” he said.

Other bipartisan priorities with a high likelihood of legislative success include federal funding for or regulatory changes to make it easier to deploy geothermal energy, fusion, and nuclear fission.

Another top issue is the expansion of the Department of Health and Human Service’s Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program. Known as LIHEAP, the roughly $4 billion program provides funding to poor Americans struggling to pay utility bills in the winter. The program, administered through states, also funds home renovations to better insulate drafty houses and lower bills, offering a key tool to make good on Democrats’ promises to help rein in soaring utility costs. While Trump has proposed eliminating the program’s funding almost entirely, Congress ultimately added $20 million to LIHEAP’s budget in the last cycle.

The Democratic caucus is poised to include far-left hardliners such as New York’s Darializa Avila Chevalier, whose energy proposals range from a nationwide ban on data centers to calling on the federal government to take ownership stakes in more wind and solar projects. But the larger the Democratic majority, the less power the ideologues on the fringes can wield, Josh Freed, who heads the energy and climate program at the centrist Third Way think tank, told me.

“If Democrats get anywhere close to 230 seats, there’s going to be both a much bigger bloc of New Democrats and moderate Blue Dogs than there is in this Congress,” Freed said. “You’re going to see an agenda much more oriented around delivery and affordability than anything that’s more ideologically rooted.”

For example, he said, progressives may push for a national moratorium on data centers or a freeze on utility rates. “Those are things that won’t pass, but that you might see a handful of members who have a lot of leverage in a very narrow House try to move forward, along with Medicare for All and other issues that are dealing with energy,” Freed said. “But the more seats Democrats have, the more seats you’ll have that represent rural, energy-producing, and blue-collar constituencies. It’s going to be a much more all-of-the-above focus.”

What Democrats want to watch

The potential to pass bipartisan policies through a divided government over the next two years doesn’t mean it’s all kumbaya on the energy and climate front. Newly-enthroned Democratic committee chairs in the House are expected to hold hearings and open probes into a variety of actions by the Trump administration.

Few cuts at the Department of Energy stung quite as painfully as the Trump administration’s decision to terminate the Industrial Demonstrations Program, a $6.3 billion initiative designed to help commercialize emerging technologies to clean up heavy industry. The program funded 29 projects in its initial round, but former officials told me last year that just three looked likely to survive the Trump administration’s cuts. Meanwhile, the Chinese government expanded its own version of the program to more than 100 projects. Expect Democrats to start asking questions.

The billions of dollars in deals the Trump administration has promised to companies that surrender their federal leases for offshore wind projects are already facing legal challenges as states such as New York and California advance lawsuits. These policies are also poised for congressional oversight.

Likewise, the Energy Department’s effort to redirect federal spending earmarked to support decarbonization is ripe for a probe by Democrats. Specifically, lawmakers are expected to query the agency’s use of a $500 million grant to steelmaker Cleveland-Cliffs to support the relining of a coal-fired blast furnace at its Ohio mill rather than the construction of cleaner iron-making equipment at the plant.

One more area set to draw scrutiny is Trump’s move to bring previously independent agencies — the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission — under direct White House control.

“There’s going to be a lot more demand that these independent agencies regain their independence,” Paul Dickman, a former nuclear regulator who served in the George W. Bush and Obama administrations, told me. “Be that FERC, be that the NRC.”

In a statement late Tuesday night, the Sierra Club said its members had “organized, phonebanked, and knocked doors for these candidates up and down the ballot,” and now expected Democrats to “take ambitious action for the climate and our democracy.” The latter, the group made clear, meant going after the White House.

“They must hold the Trump administration accountable for its corruption and unlawful attempts to sacrifice the health and safety of our communities,” Sierra Club Executive Director Loren Blackford said, “and invest in a clean energy future for all of us.”

After Democrats secured control over his chamber, Senator Ron Wyden, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Committee on Finance, issued a one-word post on X: “Subpoenas.”

text:
Dara Kerr

in Commerce City, Colorado

As the first results rolled in, showing Democrat Manny Rutinel as the projected winner for the hotly contested toss-up congressional seat in central Colorado, the crowd whooped, hollered and started chanting, “Manny, Manny, Manny”.

The Commerce City event space was decorated with American and Colorado flags and the DJ spun classic rock hits: Joan Jett, Pink Floyd and Queen. Las Dos Americas served up taquitos, flautas and beans and rice.

Throughout his campaign, Rutinel has told his personal story of being raised by a single Latina mother. He worked at McDonald’s as a teen and went on to serve in the US Army Corps of Engineers and get a law degree from Yale. He became a state representative when he was 29 and was serving his second term when he announced he was running for Congress.

Rutinel is set to unseat Gabe Evans, a conservative Republican who has ran a campaign focused on fighting crime and “defending American values”, including the second amendment and freedom of expression.

Share

Updated at 22.28 EST

Rachel Leingang

in Des Moines, Iowa

As the polls closed in Iowa at 8pm local time, Iowa’s Democratic party chair, Rita Hart, took the stage at a watch party for the Democratic candidates to commend volunteers and campaign staff for all their work, saying all that was left was to wait on the results.

The Democrats here at the state historical society of Iowa, right by the state capitol in Des Moines, are feeling “nauseously optimistic”, Hart said. Hart knows just how close elections can be here: in 2020, she lost a congressional race in the state’s second district by just six votes. “A six-vote loss is a loss you never forget,” she said.

Iowa voters have been inundated with ads – so much so, Iowa Democrat Micki Henderson said, that her 12-year-old son got a campaign ad pop-up on his school-issued iPad. She’s found other Iowans open to hearing about candidates outside their typical party this year.

“When you’re talking about local things, like water, there’s much more middle ground,” Henderson said.

Alison Meagher, a 22-year-old who has been knocking doors for third congressional district Democratic nominee Sarah Trone Garriott each weekend for the last couple months, said she is feeling both fear and excitement while awaiting the results.

“I will say, selfishly, it is a little nice to be recognized again and be in the news,” Meagher said. “It’s been a little while since we’ve been purple. It’s exciting, it’s a rush.”

As she’s knocked doors, people have been willing to hear about Trone Garriott and other Democratic candidates, often saying they’ll do some more research when they can.

“I think it helps that we all shop at the same gas stations and all shop at the same supermarkets,” she said. “I’m coming to you as a peer.”

text:
The Democratic Party appeared set to win a commanding victory in Tuesday’s midterm elections. As of 11 p.m. Eastern on Tuesday night, the party was on track to gain control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, as well as several state governments. The party’s strong performance, driven in part by voters’ anger over inflation and the war in Iran, reached into traditional Republican strongholds like Ohio and South Carolina. A sweep would have profound consequences for climate action in the United States, even with President Donald Trump still in the White House.

Flipping control of Congress would allow the Democrats to hinder Trump’s numerous attempts to roll back federal climate policy. In the first two years of Trump’s term, party leaders could do little more than write strongly worded statements to administration officials. They were powerless to stop the suspension of clean energy funding, the elimination of climate rules for power plants and motor vehicles, and the hollowing-out of agencies like the U.S. Forest Service and the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

If Tuesday’s results hold, the party will have a lot more leverage. Democratic senators and members of Congress can issue subpoenas to force administration officials to testify before Congress, and could impeach Trump administration figures over funding clawbacks and staff reductions that Democrats have called unlawful. Democrats would also have control over must-pass funding bills, and Trump would have to negotiate with them in order to avoid a government shutdown. This could even lead to the restoration of some funding for energy and climate resilience programs that Republicans have been trying to whittle down.

Turnover at the state level, where officials are still counting votes, may be even more significant. Democrats could gain control of the state government in purple states, ending in some cases decades of Republican or divided government. This could allow them to pass meaningful climate policy for the first time — in Pennsylvania, for instance, state house Democrats have said they intend to pass bills making it easier to build community solar, warehouse solar, and battery energy storage, as well as preventing local governments from banning renewables. In Georgia, Democrats flipped both the governor’s mansion and control of the public service commission, which regulates electric utilities.

While Trump’s approval ratings are underwater on almost every major issue, energy prices were among the most salient issues in many races. The gasoline price hike caused by Trump’s invasion of Iran was perhaps the most consequential, but voters in many places were also concerned about their heating bills (Maine) and homeowner’s insurance premiums (Florida). In places like Texas and Ohio, skepticism over the AI boom may also have driven voters to oust incumbents who supported data centers.

Here are some of the most consequential outcomes for climate change and the environment. We’ll continue to update this post as more results and analysis come in.

Texas elects Democratic senator for the first time in nearly 40 years

Texas joined other Southern states in flipping blue for the first time in decades. Senator-elect James Talarico, a Democrat, supports an all-of-the-above energy strategy, which includes protecting oil and gas jobs while also growing renewable energy. This moderate approach proved important in a state that provides over 40 percent of the nation’s oil and gas.

As a state representative, Talarico authored and introduced the Texas Climate Action Act in 2021. While the bill did not advance, it aimed to establish targets for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and set energy efficiency standards, with an emphasis on local resiliency.

Talarico beat out Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general, who is widely considered friendly to the oil and gas industry. He’s been embroiled in scandal for years and was impeached in 2023 by the Texas House. Paxton’s track record likely helped Democrats obtain this victory.

— Celeste Guajardo

A climate hawk survives Republican redlining

Her district was redrawn to eliminate her, but voters in Florida’s 14th congressional district reelected Democratic Representative Kathy Castor anyway.

Castor — referred to as a “climate hawk” by E&E News — has spent much of her long career in Congress raising the alarm about climate change. Between 2019 and 2022 she chaired the House Select Committee on the Climate Crisis, and has otherwise made reducing carbon pollution and preparing communities for climate impacts central to her legislative agenda. In March, she backed the Energy Bills Relief Act, which proposed restoring energy upgrade tax credits and connecting more clean energy to the grid. She has also strongly opposed data centers in the Tampa area that she serves, warning that the facilities could drive up her constituents’ utility costs while straining local water supplies.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

Democrats flip control of Georgia utility commission for first time in decades

Democrats secured both Public Service Commission seats on the Georgia ballot, giving the party majority control of the powerful utility regulation board for the first time in 30 years.

Democrat Peter Hubbard successfully defended his District 3 seat against a challenge from former commissioner Fitz Johnson, while Democrat Shelia Edwards defeated Republican Josh Tolbert to take the District 5 seat.

The commission regulates utilities, including the behemoth Georgia Power, meaning commissioners have final say over how the state’s largest utility makes energy and how much customers pay for it. The board has drawn increased scrutiny in recent years because of a series of rate hikes and the scramble to produce enough energy for the massive spike in demand that Georgia Power predicts will result from the data center boom. The utility’s plans to meet that demand rely heavily on fossil fuels.

Georgia is one of 10 states where utility regulators are elected rather than appointed.

— Emily Jones

A flip in an area devastated by Helene

In western North Carolina, where Hurricane Helene caused billions of dollars of damage two years ago, Democrat Jamie Ager defeated Republican Jennifer Balkcom for an open seat in the House of Representatives. Ager, a longtime farmer, made the area’s slow hurricane recovery a centerpiece of his campaign. He criticized Representative Chuck Edwards, who dropped out of the race after a sexual harassment scandal, for doing too little to deliver aid for Asheville and its surrounding counties. Grist reported last month that at least some voters blamed Republicans for the slow recovery. In a rally held on the eve of the election, President Trump promised to deliver more hurricane aid money, but only if North Carolina elected Republicans. The district around Asheville did not take the bait — not only did Ager win the state’s 11th House district, but Democrat Roy Cooper, the state’s former governor, easily won a Senate race, flipping a seat that had been held by Republicans.

— Jake Bittle

Democrats win after attacking Republicans on data centers

At least three legislative seats flipped blue after Democrats aggressively criticized Republican incumbents for being too friendly to data centers. Democrat Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Senator Jon Husted in Ohio’s special Senate election after state Democrats put up billboards stating: “See that data center? Jon Husted did that.” Likewise, Democrat Paige Cognetti beat Republican Representative Rob Bresnahan in Pennsylvania’s 8th congressional district after she ran television ads associating Bresnahan with data centers and comparing tech companies to polluting mining corporations. Bresnahan has been revealed to have owned stock in data center companies. And in South Carolina’s Senate race, voters pushed Annie Andrews to a surprise win over Senator Darline Graham after she highlighted that a new pro-data center super PAC spent $1.5 million dollars on ads for her opponent, whom she nicknamed “Data Center Darline.”

Both Husted and Bresnahan had previously welcomed data centers to their regions, but later attempted unsuccessfully to pass regulations constraining them once the facilities became a hot-button issue. Data centers are massively unpopular with voters across the political spectrum, polls have shown. The facilities have become a growing source of demand for electricity from fossil fuels.

— Austin Corona and Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

A FEMA defender sails to victory in Florida

Representative Jared Moskowitz, a Democrat, easily hung onto his seat in Congress, surviving a challenge from Scott Singer, a Trump-backed Republican, in Florida’s redrawn 25th congressional district. His third-term victory defies the right-wing effort to make his district significantly redder with new boundaries, and keeps one of America’s most vocal FEMA reformers in Congress.

Moskowitz, once appointed Florida’s emergency management director by Governor Ron DeSantis, championed bipartisan legislation to pull FEMA out of the Department of Homeland Security and make it an independent, cabinet-level agency — just as the Trump administration seeks to cut its funding and shift more responsibility onto states. He has also introduced bills that would let states voluntarily administer federal disaster housing and public assistance, and proposed a reinsurance backstop that would help cover catastrophic losses after disasters like hurricanes.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

Michigan gets utility money out of politics

Voters in Michigan passed a measure to limit corporate spending in elections, and in a nationwide first, successfully went after the state’s electric and gas utilities. Supporters of Proposal 2 leveraged ratepayers’ growing dissatisfaction with utilities around power bills, unreliable service, and data centers. The measure is one of the most ambitious attempts in the country to limit corporate influence in politics, which it will do by preventing utility-funded political action groups and utility executives from contributing to state political campaigns. Groups that oppose the measure have contended that Prop 2 will stifle corporations’ speech protections under the 2010 Citizens United case. And while experts are fairly confident the measure will face legal challenges and won’t get all utility money out of politics, Prop 2 advocates maintain it’s a step toward accountability.

— Vivian La

A governor who at least acknowledges climate change in Florida

Republican Byron Donalds has defeated Democrat David Jolly for occupancy of Florida’s governor’s mansion. Donalds, who currently represents Florida’s 19th congressional district, will be the state’s first Black governor. He doesn’t believe humans play any role in global warming, but he’s more willing to discuss the issue than the current governor, Ron DeSantis, who signed the state’s infamous “don’t say climate change” law.

That matters in a state especially battered by sea level rise, coastal erosion, and storms. The skyrocketing costs of home insurance were a central issue in this race, and Donalds promised to bring them down by increasing competition in the state’s private market. In 2025, Donalds notably co-introduced bipartisan legislation with Democrat Jared Moskowitz to reform federal disaster aid by making FEMA an independent cabinet-level agency. In the weeks before voters went to the polls, he also pledged investment in restoring coastal habitats. Donalds seems likely to carry on DeSantis’ other environmental policies, such as supporting data center development and attacking wind and solar projects.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

A MAGA loyalist who says no to drilling in Florida

Republican Senator Ashley Moody defeated the progressive Democrat Angie Nixon to retain her seat, which Governor DeSantis appointed her to last year. Moody’s brief stint in Washington hints at what’s to come: She introduced a resolution to overturn Biden-era efficiency standards and supported the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which ended federal tax credits for clean energy installations, like rooftop solar and batteries. Previously, as Florida’s attorney general, she joined a lawsuit challenging emissions reduction targets on highways.

But in Florida, a state grappling with coastal erosion and rising sea levels, some environmental protections are popular across party lines: Last year, even as Trump pushed to open offshore drilling in other states, Moody introduced the American Shores Protection Act to ban the practice off Florida’s coast through 2032.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

description:

Instead, Korean companies must demonstrate how their operations contribute to U.S. manufacturing, employment and domestic sourcing to strengthen their position in negotiations with Washington.
Both parties, however, share an interest in rebuilding U.S. manufacturing capacity in industries considered critical to national and economic security.
This means Korean companies should not expect the Democratic takeover of Congress to bring an immediate improvement in trade conditions.
At the same time, Korean companies must avoid weakening their domestic industrial foundations through excessive overseas expansion.
text:
Hyundai Motor Group's massive investment in the United States is unlikely to shield the automaker from Washington's shifting trade policies, even after Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday's (local time) midterm elections, a trade expert said Wednesday.

The Democratic takeover of the House of Representatives and Senate is expected to strengthen congressional scrutiny of U.S. President Donald Trump's trade agenda, but is unlikely to fundamentally reverse Washington's push to revive domestic manufacturing, according to Shin Won-kyu, head of the global economic research team at the Federation of Korean Industries (FKI).

The automaker remains particularly vulnerable to changes in U.S. tariff and trade policies because of its growing investment in local factories and supply chains, which could limit its flexibility in responding to future policy shifts, the expert said.

"The biggest risk is weakened bargaining power after the investment is made," Shin said in a written interview with The Korea Times. "Plants cannot easily be moved once built, while tariff rates or calculation methods can change with a single proclamation."

Hyundai Motor Group is considered one of the hardest-hit corporations by the U.S. Donald Trump administration's tariffs, which have been in effect since April last year. Its heavy reliance on exports to the U.S. has left it particularly exposed to the impact of auto tariffs.

Identifying the tariff-sparked trade uncertainty as a long-term risk, Hyundai Motor Group has pledged to commit $26 billion (35 trillion won) for investment in the U.S. between 2025 and 2028, with a focus on expanding localized production there.

The carmaker is building an extensive U.S. manufacturing network, spanning steel production and finished vehicles. Its planned Louisiana steel mill, scheduled to begin operations in 2029, is part of the group's effort to establish a more localized supply chain.

Such investments, however, do not necessarily guarantee favorable trade treatment, Shin said. Instead, Korean companies must demonstrate how their operations contribute to U.S. manufacturing, employment and domestic sourcing to strengthen their position in negotiations with Washington.

"Hyundai Motor Group should quantify its contribution to U.S. sourcing and jobs, and make the case to both parties that it is part of American manufacturing," he said.

The Democratic Party's victories in both chambers are expected to give lawmakers greater room to scrutinize the Trump administration's trade policies. However, Shin said the change in congressional control would not necessarily translate into a significant easing of trade pressure on Korean manufacturers.

While Republicans have relied more heavily on tariffs to encourage domestic production, Democrats have generally favored subsidies and stricter labor and origin requirements. Both parties, however, share an interest in rebuilding U.S. manufacturing capacity in industries considered critical to national and economic security.

"The two parties differ in their tools, but there is a bipartisan consensus on reviving U.S. manufacturing, centered on economic security industries," Shin said.

This means Korean companies should not expect the Democratic takeover of Congress to bring an immediate improvement in trade conditions. Although stronger congressional oversight could constrain some aspects of the administration's trade agenda, major changes to existing tariff measures would remain difficult, particularly given Trump's executive authority over trade policy.

For Korean automakers and steelmakers, the distinction between tariff levels and the way tariffs are administered will be particularly important.

The 15 percent tariffs on Korean automobiles and 50 percent duties on steel remain significant burdens. Shin said changes in congressional control would be more likely to affect how such measures are implemented than to bring substantial near-term reductions.

A Democratic-controlled House could exercise stronger oversight of trade policy, potentially improving predictability for businesses, but that would not necessarily translate into lower costs, as Korean companies could face tighter requirements on product origins, labor standards and exports to China, even if tariff policies become less volatile, he said.

"Companies should prepare for an environment where tariffs swing less, but the rules become more demanding," Shin said.

He pointed to stricter origin requirements and export controls on advanced artificial intelligence chips as areas where bipartisan agreement could sustain regulatory pressure on foreign manufacturers.

For Korean steelmakers, Shin recommended emphasizing their role in addressing global overcapacity driven by China, while differentiating their products through high-grade automotive steel and stronger origin-tracking systems.

More broadly, he said Korea should use sectors in which Washington also depends on Korean expertise, including shipbuilding, power equipment and batteries, to rebalance bilateral economic relations.

Rather than relying solely on tariff negotiations, Seoul should push for a framework based on reciprocal investment and industrial cooperation, he said.

At the same time, Korean companies must avoid weakening their domestic industrial foundations through excessive overseas expansion.

Shin advocated what he called a "just-in-value" approach, under which research and development, core materials and high-value components remain in Korea, while production facilities requiring direct access to the U.S. market are established locally.

He also stressed the need for Washington to facilitate the implementation of existing investment commitments by addressing practical obstacles, including visas for skilled Korean workers and delays in permits.

"The Korea-U.S. alliance should be emphasized as a relationship of trust that goes beyond short-term political interests," he said.

title: The Senate permitting bill holds promise but needs amendments | Utility Dive
description:
In the Senate permitting reform bill (SB 5653), the true permitting reforms hold a welcome potential to get needed infrastructure built faster.
The Senate bill contains no geographic limits on FERC’s permitting power.
Read More in Transmission & Distribution My third amendment concerns one of the most onerous and frankly insulting provisions in the Senate bill.
The Senate bill allows FERC to start its backstop proceeding simultaneously with the state proceeding.
Over the past decade, transmission has been one of the fastest-growing drivers of power bill increases.
text:
Mark Christie is a former chairman of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and former chairman of the Virginia State Corporation Commission, and is the director of the William & Mary Law School Center for Energy Law and Policy.

Every true compromise in a polarized legislature contains candy for each side, but also requires each side to swallow some hairballs. In the Senate permitting reform bill (SB 5653), the true permitting reforms hold a welcome potential to get needed infrastructure built faster. The transmission provisions, however — which are not permitting reforms at all — contain some provisions that are indigestible if you care about rising consumer costs and respect for historic state authority over utilities.

The bill’s best transmission provisions seek to ensure that large-load customers pay the full costs they impose on the grid. The worst transmission provisions, however, can be fixed with the amendments described below. Before considering these amendments, it is important to understand that the Federal Power Act for nearly a century has recognized a clear and logical division between state and federal authority over the power grid: The states have authority over the siting and permitting of all physical assets within their borders, including generation and transmission. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has authority over the rates for interstate transmission services and wholesale power sales.

The current Senate bill blows up this century-old balance of authority by giving FERC the sweeping power to order a transmission line built in any state, without regard to the state’s own decision on the project or the opposition of the state’s residents who will be directly affected. Congress has enacted so-called “backstop siting authority” before, most recently in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act in 2021, but Congress strictly limited the geographic reach of FERC’s backstop authority to narrow geographic corridors established by the U.S. Department of Energy and only after DOE made a finding that the national interest required the establishment of each corridor.

The Senate bill contains no geographic limits on FERC’s permitting power. It expands FERC’s authority to override the states to every square inch of the country, a breathtaking expansion of federal power at the expense of a core state function: the permitting and construction of utility assets within their own borders, projects that could have huge impacts on the lives of their residents.

Fortunately, targeted amendments can minimize the most negative consequences of the bill’s overreaching provisions. Here are three recommended amendments:

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Utility Dive free daily newsletter

The bill allows FERC to order the construction of transmission lines based on a nebulous “public interest” standard. Such a standard is a blank check for FERC to approve trillions of dollars’ worth of transmission lines for whatever reason a presidential administration finds is in the “public interest,” as long as FERC adds general findings of some reliability improvements or consumer benefits, which can be claimed for every transmission line ever proposed. In the short term, FERC could use the bill’s grant of new authority to order transmission lines built to serve hyperscale data center development, a Trump administration priority. A future FERC could find that the public interest requires trillions of dollars of new transmission to meet “Net Zero” climate goals.

So my first recommended amendment is to remove the “public interest” and other general criteria, and instead require that FERC must find that the proposed line is the optimal solution to meet a proven reliability need at just and reasonable rates, compared to alternative solutions.

My second amendment addresses the critical role of states in cost allocation. FERC Order 1920 guaranteed to states in a multi-state region the right to reach an agreement on cost allocation for regional transmission projects and have that agreement submitted to FERC. The Senate bill should add an explicit guarantee that for regional transmission projects the states in each region have the right to agree on cost allocation and FERC shall presume such state agreement is just and reasonable.

Read More in Transmission & Distribution

My third amendment concerns one of the most onerous and frankly insulting provisions in the Senate bill. When we at FERC implemented the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act’s backstop siting authority, we gave each affected state one full year to conduct its permitting proceeding before FERC would start its own backstop proceeding. That allowed the state to develop a factual record and issue a decision within a reasonable period of one year.

The Senate bill allows FERC to start its backstop proceeding simultaneously with the state proceeding. That effectively renders the state proceeding meaningless, and states will perceive it exactly that way. Why should a state spend its time and limited resources on its proceeding when FERC is already doing its own? Any evidentiary record developed in the state proceeding may not even be available to FERC before it overrides the state. This provision in the Senate bill is nakedly punitive and overreaching and should be amended to give the states one full year to act before FERC can begin its own backstop proceeding.

Even if you don’t care about respecting state authority, you should care about the bill’s impact on consumers already struggling to pay their power bills. Over the past decade, transmission has been one of the fastest-growing drivers of power bill increases. The Senate bill as drafted could result in literally trillions of dollars of new transmission being ordered by FERC to serve whatever policy goals a president wants. These costs will flow right into consumers’ monthly bills.

text:
Regulatory uncertainty about US EPA 2027 heavy-duty standards spills into Canada

Canada’s Minister of the Environment issued an Interim Order that aligns certain provisions of Canadian emission regulations for light-, medium-, and heavy-duty engines and vehicles with those by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

In particular, the Interim Order aligns Canadian requirements for model year 2027 and later heavy-duty engines with the US EPA 2027 rule, as originally published in the US Federal Register in January 2023 [5724]. However, in July 2026, the EPA proposed several changes to the 2027 regulation that have not yet been finalized and could not be harmonized with by Canada. This creates regulatory uncertainty regarding the importation of heavy-duty trucks and buses into Canada after January 1st, 2027.

The general approach to setting vehicle emission standards in Canada has been to harmonize them with US EPA federal standards. An important aspect of this harmonization is the recognition of emission certificates issued by the US EPA. Most vehicles and engines are sold in Canada under the principle of concurrent sales, meaning that if a vehicle or an engine of a given model year is sold concurrently in Canada and the United States, the US EPA emission certificate is recognized as a proof of emission compliance and the vehicle or engine does not require a Canadian emission approval.

The current Canadian regulations require that heavy-duty engines imported to Canada comply with the EPA 2027 emission standards. The problem is that very few engines, if any, sold in the United States during the first several months of 2027 will comply with the EPA 2027 standards.

The EPA amendments proposed in July relax certain provisions of the 2027 regulation, such as the regulatory emission warranty and useful life periods, and the driver inducement rules for vehicles with SCR systems. To provide more regulatory lead time for manufacturers, the proposal introduces non-conformance penalties (NCP) that allow manufacturers to temporarily continue sales of non-compliant engines past the regulatory compliance dates.

According to trade media estimates, the price increase for an EPA 2027-compliant engine is expected to be between US$10,000 and $16,000 per truck, while the non-compliance penalties will likely be in the $7,000-$8,000 range. If non-compliant engines can indeed be sold in the United States at a price advantage, they are likely to be available for most of 2027 and beyond. Among engine manufacturers, only Daimler announced the availability of the EPA 2027-compliant Detroit Gen 6 DD13 and DD15 engines from January 2027 (with the DD16 to follow in January 2028).

It may still take several months before the EPA finalizes their 2027 amendments. In the meantime, several questions arise for Canada regarding the rules of importation of non-compliant heavy-duty engines and vehicles that are to be sold in the United States upon the payment of an NCP. At this time, less than two months before the January 2027 deadline, Canadian fleets have no way of knowing if they can order 2027 vehicles and, if so, what would be the vehicle price.

The Interim Order is valid for one year or until the relevant regulations are amended.

Among other provisions, the Interim Order suspends the application of GHG emission standards for heavy-duty trailers and introduces a number of modifications to the Canadian regulations to maintain alignment with the current US EPA emission standards for light-duty vehicles and with the EPA vehicle classifications.

description:
CATL has unveiled a dual-electric range extension battery designed to make electric heavy-duty trucks more practical and economical.
The main battery is a standardized, chassis-mounted swappable pack from QIJI Energy, CATL’s battery-swapping network for heavy trucks.
A range-extension power system behind the cab provides backup power and is equipped with a 77 kWh battery capable of 3C charging.
The backup battery increases the main battery’s depth of discharge from about 70% to over 95%, so the main battery can be returned at less than 5% state of charge.
“The combination of the dual-electric range extension battery and QIJI battery swapping offers the best solution for electrifying heavy-duty trucks,” said Jesse Yang, CEO of QIJI Energy.
text:
CATL has unveiled a dual-electric range extension battery designed to make electric heavy-duty trucks more practical and economical. Agreements for 13,000 units were signed at the unveiling.

The main battery is a standardized, chassis-mounted swappable pack from QIJI Energy, CATL’s battery-swapping network for heavy trucks. A range-extension power system behind the cab provides backup power and is equipped with a 77 kWh battery capable of 3C charging. The system uses a “1+X” architecture: the main battery stays compatible with the QIJI swapping network, and the range-extension battery can be customized for energy density, cold-climate operation or power. The two batteries can be developed and upgraded independently.

CATL says drivers of conventional battery-swapping trucks often return for a swap with unused capacity because they are reluctant to discharge the battery deeply. The backup battery increases the main battery’s depth of discharge from about 70% to over 95%, so the main battery can be returned at less than 5% state of charge. At that point, CATL’s switching technology transfers power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds.

The range-extension battery is independently owned and stays with the vehicle throughout its service life. The main battery can be leased according to seasonal freight demand. Seasonal leasing is designed to help fleets reduce rental costs during quieter periods.

QIJI has introduced 260# (432 kWh) and 300# (513 kWh) standardized swapping blocks alongside its existing 75# block, to accommodate a wider range of truck models and operating conditions. A swap takes five minutes, and QIJI says its first-time success rate is 99.99%.

Under QIJI’s battery-as-a-service (BaaS) model, customers pay for the net energy charged instead of the energy discharged, so they retain the value of energy recovered through regenerative braking. QIJI says this billing model reduces battery rental costs per kWh by up to 20% for users on basic plans.

“The combination of the dual-electric range extension battery and QIJI battery swapping offers the best solution for electrifying heavy-duty trucks,” said Jesse Yang, CEO of QIJI Energy.

title: Government Belatedly Scrambles to Revive EVs as Chinese-Made Rivals Surge
description:
As Chinese-made electric vehicles mount an increasingly strong challenge in the domestic market, the government has decided to support finished-vehicle production.
At the time, Deputy Prime Minister Koo Yun-cheol identified batteries and high-performance cathode materials as the core sources of competitiveness for electric vehicles.
◆Urgent need to strengthen price competitiveness against Chinese automakers... A deepening sense of crisis= The need for production tax credits has become increasingly apparent as the influence of Chinese automakers grows.
Domestic automakers now face the dual challenges of expanding sales while maintaining domestic production and strengthening price competitiveness.
◆Tax credits alone have limits... Future-vehicle technology and parts competitiveness must be supported= Even if domestic production tax credits are introduced, competitiveness will not recover immediately.
text:
As Chinese-made electric vehicles mount an increasingly strong challenge in the domestic market, the government has decided to support finished-vehicle production. The tax reform plan announced in August excluded finished electric vehicles from the domestic production tax credit, but the policy direction has shifted amid growing concerns over the declining market share of domestic vehicles and their weakening price competitiveness. After meeting with Euisun Chung, Executive Chair of Hyundai Motor Group, to discuss support measures for the auto industry, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and Economy Lee Hyung-il has also decided to take an active part in legislative discussions on related tax credits. Parliamentary discussions are gaining momentum as lawmakers from both the ruling and opposition parties introduce related bills and build consensus.

◆Support for batteries and materials, but not finished vehicles... A changing market landscape= In its tax reform plan announced in August, the government selected six sectors for domestic production tax credits: solar power, wind power, secondary batteries, semiconductors, key materials, and artificial intelligence (AI) robot components. The aim was to focus support on sectors with a weak domestic production base or strategic importance to economic security, but finished electric vehicles were not included. At the time, Deputy Prime Minister Koo Yun-cheol identified batteries and high-performance cathode materials as the core sources of competitiveness for electric vehicles. The government also considered that finished-vehicle manufacturers already had production facilities and sales networks, that incentives such as purchase subsidies were already in place, and that direct support could trigger trade friction.

However, industry and academic circles had called for support for finished-vehicle production even before the tax reform plan was announced. In April, the Korea Automobile & Mobility Association (KAMA), together with the Korea Auto Industries Cooperative Association and the Korean Metal Workers' Union, issued a joint labor-management proposal calling for the introduction of a tax incentive to promote domestic production of electric vehicles. In May, Oh Moon-sung, president of the Korea Tax Policy Association, also proposed at a tax policy seminar that output-based tax credits be introduced for nationally strategic sectors, including electric and hydrogen vehicles. Nevertheless, finished vehicles were ultimately left out of the August tax reform plan.

◆Urgent need to strengthen price competitiveness against Chinese automakers... A deepening sense of crisis= The need for production tax credits has become increasingly apparent as the influence of Chinese automakers grows. Domestic automakers now face the dual challenges of expanding sales while maintaining domestic production and strengthening price competitiveness. An official from the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy said, "Price competitiveness is also why domestic production tax credits are regarded by the industry as the most effective measure." The idea is that using the tax credit to lower vehicle prices could narrow the price gap with Chinese-made vehicles.

Lawmakers from both the ruling and opposition parties have introduced amendments to the Restriction of Special Taxation Act that would include electric vehicles among the eligible products. Measures under discussion include tax credits of up to 4 million won per domestically produced electric vehicle, and a proposal has also been made to apply a preferential coefficient for production outside the Seoul metropolitan area. An official from the Ministry of Finance and Economy said, "Deputy Prime Minister Lee has stated since his confirmation hearing that he would consider various support measures, including production tax credits for electric vehicles." The official added, "The specific details of the related bills will be determined during the National Assembly's review of the tax code amendments, and the government will actively participate in the discussions."

◆Tax credits alone have limits... Future-vehicle technology and parts competitiveness must be supported= Even if domestic production tax credits are introduced, competitiveness will not recover immediately. If support amounts only to tax benefits for existing production volumes, its impact could be limited. The credits should therefore be designed to be linked to new investment, increased production, domestic parts sourcing, and employment retention. To ensure that support for finished-vehicle manufacturers benefits parts suppliers and local economies, the government should support the transition of internal-combustion-engine parts suppliers to new businesses and retrain their workers, while also strengthening domestic supply chains for key components. An official from the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy said, "The share of internal-combustion-engine vehicles is declining further, and the market is being reshaped around future vehicles such as autonomous and electric vehicles." The official added, "Whether Korea secures a leading position in the future-vehicle market will determine the competitiveness of the Korean auto industry." The official continued, "Hyundai Motor will also invest, and the government is seeking to provide as much support as possible for research and development (R&D) investment."

title: Waaree Solar Americas doubles Texas module production capacity to 3.2 GW
description:
Waaree Solar Americas Inc. (WSA), the U.S. manufacturing arm of India’s Waaree Energies Limited, has initiated commercial operations on two new solar module lines at its facility in Brookshire, Texas.
The Brookshire expansion is central to the group’s “Make in U.S. for U.S.” domestic supply strategy.
Alongside an ongoing upgrade at its Arizona module plant, which is expanding from 1 GW to 1.6 GW, Waaree is targeting an aggregate U.S. manufacturing capacity of 4.8 GW during FY27.
Alongside its U.S. manufacturing investments, the company is executing a dual-track strategy to scale backward integration in India.

text:
Waaree Solar Americas Inc. (WSA), the U.S. manufacturing arm of India’s Waaree Energies Limited, has initiated commercial operations on two new solar module lines at its facility in Brookshire, Texas.

Each new line adds 800 MW of annual capacity, effectively doubling the Texas plant’s total output from 1.6 GW to 3.2 GW. Commercial production officially started on October 29, 2026, following board expansion approval granted in April 2025.

The Brookshire expansion is central to the group’s “Make in U.S. for U.S.” domestic supply strategy. Alongside an ongoing upgrade at its Arizona module plant, which is expanding from 1 GW to 1.6 GW, Waaree is targeting an aggregate U.S. manufacturing capacity of 4.8 GW during FY27.

Revenue from Waaree’s U.S. manufacturing operations increased to $154.8 million in Q2 FY27, up from $87.1 million in the corresponding prior-year period. U.S. domestic supply contracts now represent 43.8% of Waaree’s total consolidated order book of $7.05 billion, growing from 36% in Q1 FY27. Across all global markets, Waaree’s cumulative module backlog stands above 25 GW.

“Shifting trade policy has strengthened the case for local manufacturing, and that is exactly where we have invested,” said Sunil Rathi, Director at Waaree Group. “With Brookshire now at 3.2 GW and Arizona expanding, we are serving American customers from American factories, and our U.S. order book continues to grow every quarter.”

For Q2 FY27, Waaree Energies reported a 23.9% year-on-year increase in consolidated revenue from operations, reaching $895 million.

Alongside its U.S. manufacturing investments, the company is executing a dual-track strategy to scale backward integration in India. Waaree plans to increase domestic cell production capacity from 5.4 GW to 15.4 GW in FY27, while laying the groundwork for a 10 GW ingot and wafer manufacturing plant targeted for FY28 operational readiness.

According to data from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA), the broader U.S. solar and storage manufacturing sector has achieved substantial growth, reaching an operational U.S. module manufacturing capacity of 75.3 GWdc and an operational battery cell manufacturing capacity of 62.4 GWh. SEIA reports that the industry has attracted $41.9 billion in cumulative announced investments and supports a potential total of 74,626 jobs across the domestic supply chain.

title: If The US Military Gets Solar Power, Why Can't We? - CleanTechnica
description:
In the topsy-turvy world of today’s federal energy policy, solar power is a bad thing.
Various members of the President’s cabinet have advised that solar is “unreliable,” and that solar power plants routinely experience “catastrophic failure” with every sunset.
At 700 kW, the new array is peanuts compared to the megawatt scale common among modern solar power plants.
Circling back around to military applications, it’s not surprising to see solar power resurfacing as a resilient energy resource over at the Defense Department, regardless of last year’s sharp U-turn in federal energy policy.
Resiliency was front and center in the early 2000’s, when the Defense Department began pushing the envelope on solar power while the civilian market was still spinning its wheels.
text:
